natural number $k$, the kind of the gate, and a list $r$ of natural numbers, its references.

Such a pair is read as a gate by the shared (kind, references) decoding of flat circuit gates.

articles.title: The Circuit Value Problem
articles.statement:
The Circuit Value Problem is the decision problem that accepts
a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of such triples,
to a triple $(n, C, a)$ of a natural number $n$, a list $C$ of encoded gates and a list $a$ of
booleans such that the flat Boolean circuit on $n$ inputs obtained by decoding the gates of $C$
is well formed, $a$ has length $n$, and the evaluation of $C$ on $a$ is a nonempty list whose
last entry is true. It rejects every bitstring that does not decode.

articles.title: The Circuit Value Problem is P-complete
articles.statement:
The Circuit Value Problem is in P, and every
decision problem in P is log-space many-one reducible to the Circuit Value Problem.

## Sources

- R. E. Ladner, "The circuit value problem is log space complete for P", SIGACT News 7 (1975), 18-20; S. A. Cook, "A hierarchy for nondeterministic time complexity", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 7 (1973), 343-353.

articles.title: Well-formed encoded circuits
articles.statement:
A list $C$ of encoded gates, each a (kind, references)
pair, is well formed as a circuit on $n$ inputs when the flat Boolean circuit on $n$ inputs
obtained by decoding each pair of $C$ is well formed: every decoded gate references only strictly
earlier gates.

articles.title: Directed $s$-$t$ connectivity
articles.statement:
The decision problem of directed $s$-$t$ connectivity
accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when decoding $x$ with the canonical bitstring encoding of
tuples $(n, E, s, t)$, where $n$, $s$ and $t$ are natural numbers and $E$ is a list of pairs of
natural numbers, succeeds and gives a tuple such that $s < n$, $t < n$, and there are pairwise
distinct natural numbers $v_0, \dots, v_k$, all less than $n$, with $v_0 = s$, $v_k = t$ and
$(v_j, v_{j+1}) \in E$ for every $j < k$. Bitstrings that do not decode are rejected.

articles.title: ST-connectivity is NL-complete
articles.statement:
Directed $s$-$t$ connectivity is in NL, and every
decision problem in NL is log-space many-one reducible to directed $s$-$t$ connectivity.

## Sources

- S. A. Cook, "A hierarchy for nondeterministic time complexity" (1973) and the standard NL-completeness of directed reachability; see S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Chapter 4, and C. H. Papadimitriou, Computational Complexity, 1994, Theorem 7.3.

articles.title: Winning positions in Geography
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers, read as
directed edges, let $v$ be a natural number (the current vertex) and let $V$ be a list of natural
numbers (the visited vertices). For a natural number $k$ (the fuel), the predicate
$\mathrm{GeoWins}(k, E, v, V)$ is defined by recursion on $k$: $\mathrm{GeoWins}(0, E, v, V)$ is
false, and $\mathrm{GeoWins}(k + 1, E, v, V)$ holds exactly when there is a natural number $w$
with $(v, w) \in E$ and $w \notin V$ such that $\mathrm{GeoWins}(k, E, w, V')$ is false, where
$V'$ is the list $V$ with $w$ added at the front.

Read as a game, the player to move wins when they can move the token along an edge of $E$ to a
vertex not in $V$ from which the opponent does not win; a player with no such move, or with no
fuel left, loses.

articles.title: Geography as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The Geography decision problem accepts a bitstring $x$
exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of triples $(n, E, s)$ of a
natural number, a list of pairs of natural numbers and a natural number, to a triple with
$s < n$, with both entries of every pair in $E$ less than $n$, and with
$\mathrm{GeoWins}(n + 1, E, s, [s])$, where $[s]$ is the list whose only entry is $s$.
Bitstrings that do not decode are rejected.

A play never revisits one of the $n$ vertices, so the fuel $n + 1$ never runs out: the condition
says that the player who moves first wins Geography on the directed graph with vertices
$0, \ldots, n - 1$ and edge list $E$, with the token starting on $s$ and $s$ marked visited.

articles.title: Geography is PSPACE-complete
articles.statement:
The Geography decision problem belongs to PSPACE, and every
decision problem in PSPACE has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- T. J. Schaefer, "On the complexity of some two- person perfect-information games", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 16 (1978), 185-225.

articles.title: Quantifier alternations after a given quantifier
articles.statement:
For a quantifier $p$ and a quantifier
prefix $(q_1, v_1), \dots, (q_n, v_n)$, the number of indices $1 \le i \le n$ with
$q_i \ne q_{i-1}$, where $q_0 = p$.

articles.title: Number of quantifier blocks
articles.statement:
The number of maximal blocks of consecutive equal quantifiers
in a quantifier prefix $(q_1, v_1), \dots, (q_n, v_n)$: it is $0$ if $n = 0$, and otherwise $1$
plus the number of indices $2 \le i \le n$ with $q_i \ne q_{i-1}$.

articles.title: Truth of a quantified Boolean formula with circuit matrix
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a quantifier prefix,
a list of pairs $(q, v)$ of a quantifier $q$, $\exists$ (true) or $\forall$ (false), and a
variable $v \in \mathbb{N}$; let $\varphi$ be a matrix circuit and $\alpha$ an assignment of a
truth value to every natural number. Truth of $(P, \varphi)$ under $\alpha$ is defined by
recursion on $P$. If $P$ is empty, it means that $\varphi$ is nonempty and the value of its last
gate under $\alpha$ is true. If $P$ starts with $(q, v)$ followed by the prefix $P'$, it means that
$(P', \varphi)$ is true under $\alpha[v \mapsto \mathrm{true}]$ or under
$\alpha[v \mapsto \mathrm{false}]$ when $q$ is $\exists$, and under both when $q$ is $\forall$,
where $\alpha[v \mapsto b]$ agrees with $\alpha$ except that it sends $v$ to $b$.

articles.title: Evaluation of a QBF matrix circuit
articles.statement:
Given a matrix circuit $C = (g_0, \dots, g_{m-1})$, a
list of gates, and an assignment $\alpha$ of a truth value to every natural number, the list
$(s_0, \dots, s_{m-1})$ of the values of the gates of $C$, where $s_i$ is the value of the gate
$g_i$ given the values $(s_0, \dots, s_{i-1})$ of the earlier gates and the assignment $\alpha$.

articles.title: Variables of a QBF matrix circuit
articles.statement:
For a matrix circuit $C$, a list of gates, the list of
the variables $v$ of the gates of $C$ of the form $(0, [v])$, in the order of the gates of $C$ and
with repetitions.

articles.title: Well-formed QBF matrix circuits
articles.statement:
A matrix circuit $C = (g_0, \dots, g_{m-1})$, a list of
gates, is well formed when for every $j < m$ whose gate $g_j = (t, r)$ has kind $t \in \{2, 3, 4\}$
(negation, conjunction or disjunction), every reference $a$ in $r$ satisfies $a < j$.

articles.title: Evaluation of a QBF matrix gate
articles.statement:
Given a list $s$ of truth values (the values of the earlier
gates) and an assignment $\alpha$ of a truth value to every natural number, the value of a gate
$(t, r)$ is computed as follows, where $s_a$ is the $a$-th entry of $s$ if $a$ is less than the
length of $s$ and false otherwise: if $t = 0$ and $r = [v]$, it is $\alpha(v)$; if $t = 1$ and
$r = [b]$, it is true exactly when $b = 1$; if $t = 2$ and $r = [a]$, it is the negation of $s_a$;
if $t = 3$, it is true exactly when $s_a$ is true for every $a$ in $r$; if $t = 4$, it is true
exactly when $s_a$ is true for some $a$ in $r$; for every other gate it is false.

articles.title: Gates of a quantified Boolean formula matrix
articles.statement:
A gate of a matrix circuit is a pair $(t, r)$
of a natural number $t$, its kind, and a list $r$ of natural numbers, its references. The kinds
are read as follows: kind $0$ with $r = [v]$ is the variable $v$, kind $1$ with $r = [b]$ is the
constant true if $b = 1$ and false otherwise, kind $2$ is a negation, kind $3$ a conjunction and
kind $4$ a disjunction, where for kinds $2$, $3$ and $4$ the references are indices of gates.

A circuit matrix is thus an unrestricted Boolean formula with sharing, not a formula in
conjunctive normal form.

articles.title: $\mathrm{QSAT}_k$ is $\Sigma_k^p$-complete, uniformly in $k$
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$k \ge 1$, the decision problem $\mathrm{QSAT}_k$ lies in $\Sigma_k^p$, and every decision problem
$L$ in $\Sigma_k^p$ reduces to $\mathrm{QSAT}_k$ by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- L. J. Stockmeyer, "The polynomial-time hierarchy", Theoretical Computer Science 3 (1977), 1-22; A. R. Meyer, "A polynomial hierarchy" (see also S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Chapter 5).

articles.title: The decision problem $\mathrm{QSAT}_k$
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, $\mathrm{QSAT}_k$ accepts
a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the standard bitstring encoding, to a pair
$(P, \varphi)$ of a quantifier prefix $P = (q_1, v_1), \dots, (q_n, v_n)$, where each $q_i$ is
$\exists$ (true) or $\forall$ (false) and each $v_i$ is a natural number, and a matrix circuit
$\varphi$, such that: $P$ is nonempty and $q_1$ is $\exists$; $(v_1, \dots, v_n)$ is a
permutation of $(0, \dots, n - 1)$; every variable of $\varphi$ is less than $n$; $\varphi$ is
well formed; $P$ has exactly $k$ quantifier blocks; and $(P, \varphi)$ is true under the
assignment that sends every variable to false. A bitstring that does not decode is rejected.

articles.title: Concatenation of bitstring languages
articles.statement:
For sets $S$ and $T$ of bitstrings, their
concatenation is the set of all bitstrings $uv$ with $u \in S$ and $v \in T$.

articles.title: Evaluation of postfix regular expressions with squaring
articles.statement:
A list of natural-number tokens
is evaluated from left to right on a given stack of languages of bitstrings. Token $0$ pushes the
empty language, token $1$ pushes the language containing only the empty bitstring, and tokens $2$
and $3$ push the languages containing only the one-letter bitstring false, respectively true.
Token $4$ pops the top language $S$ and the language $T$ below it and pushes the concatenation
$TS$; token $5$ pops $S$ and $T$ in the same way and pushes $T \cup S$; token $6$ pops $S$ and
pushes its Kleene star; token $7$ pops $S$ and pushes its square $SS$. When the tokens run out,
the evaluation returns the language on the stack if the stack holds exactly one language. It
fails if the stack holds any other number of languages at the end, if a token is larger than
$7$, or if an operator token finds too few languages on the stack.

articles.title: Regular expressions with squaring: universality is EXPSPACE-complete
articles.statement:
The universality
problem for postfix regular expressions with squaring belongs to $\mathsf{EXPSPACE}$, and every
decision problem in $\mathsf{EXPSPACE}$ reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.
Here the universality problem accepts a bitstring exactly when it decodes to a list of
natural-number tokens whose postfix evaluation, started on the empty stack, returns the set of
all bitstrings.

## Sources

- A. R. Meyer and L. J. Stockmeyer, "The equivalence problem for regular expressions with squaring requires exponential space", Proceedings of the Thirteenth Annual Symposium on Switching and Automata Theory (1972), 125-129. (The exponential-time word problem in Stockmeyer- Meyer (STOC 1973) is membership, not universality.)

articles.title: Universality of postfix regular expressions with squaring
articles.statement:
This is the decision problem
that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of
lists of natural numbers, to a token list whose evaluation as a postfix regular expression with
squaring, started on the empty stack, succeeds and returns the set of all bitstrings. A bitstring
that does not decode to a list of natural numbers is rejected.

articles.title: Kleene star of a bitstring language
articles.statement:
For a set $S$ of bitstrings, its Kleene star is the
set of all concatenations $u_1 u_2 \cdots u_k$, for $k \ge 0$, of bitstrings
$u_1, \dots, u_k \in S$; the empty concatenation ($k = 0$) is the empty bitstring.

articles.title: The model checking, satisfiability and validity problems of the linear modal μ-calculus are PSPACE-complete
articles.statement:
**The model checking, satisfiability and validity problems of the linear modal
μ-calculus are PSPACE-complete**, like for linear temporal logic. Source:
M. Y. Vardi, "A temporal fixpoint calculus", POPL 1988, 250-259; cf. A. P. Sistla
and E. M. Clarke, "The complexity of propositional linear temporal logics",
JACM 32 (1985), 733-749.

articles.title: Linear μ-calculus model checking as a decision problem
articles.statement:
Model checking of the linear μ-calculus as a decision problem over bitstrings:
the input decodes to `(n, edges, worldVals, start, tokens)`, where `worldVals`
lists, per world, the atoms true at that world; the answer is whether the
decoded formula is closed, the structure is well-formed and total (every world
has a successor world, so the path quantification is not vacuous at deadlocks),
and every path from `start` satisfies the formula.

articles.title: Linear μ-calculus model checking on a finite Kripke structure
articles.statement:
Model checking a linear μ-calculus formula against a finite Kripke structure:
every infinite path `π` from `start` following `edges` satisfies `φ` at
position `0`, where the path turns the structure's valuation `worldVal` into a
word valuation.

articles.title: Linear μ-calculus satisfiability as a decision problem
articles.statement:
Satisfiability of the linear μ-calculus as a decision problem over bitstrings:
the input decodes to a formula token list, which decodes to a formula; the answer
is whether that formula is closed and satisfiable.

articles.title: Satisfiability of a closed linear μ-calculus formula
articles.statement:
A closed linear μ-calculus formula is satisfiable: some word and position
satisfy it under the empty environment.

articles.title: Linear μ-calculus validity as a decision problem
articles.statement: Validity of the linear μ-calculus as a decision problem over bitstrings.

articles.title: Validity of a closed linear μ-calculus formula
articles.statement:
A closed linear μ-calculus formula is valid: every word and position satisfy
it under the empty environment.

articles.title: Modal μ-calculus satisfiability as a decision problem
articles.statement:
Satisfiability of the modal μ-calculus as a decision problem over bitstrings:
the input decodes to a formula token list, which decodes to a formula; the answer
is whether that formula is closed and satisfiable.

articles.title: Satisfiability of a modal μ-calculus formula is EXPTIME-complete
articles.statement:
Sources:
D. Kozen, "Results on the propositional μ-calculus", Theoretical Computer Science 27
(1983), 333-354; E. A. Emerson and C. S. Jutla, "Tree automata, μ-calculus and
determinacy", FOCS 1991, 368-377.

articles.title: Satisfiability of a closed modal μ-calculus formula
articles.statement:
A closed μ-calculus formula is satisfiable: some Kripke model has a world
satisfying it under the empty environment.

articles.title: Lowest $n$ bits of a number, least significant first
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $i$ and $n$,
this is the list of booleans $(b_0, \dots, b_{n-1})$ of length $n$ in which $b_k$ is true exactly
when $\lfloor i / 2^k \rfloor$ is odd: the $n$ lowest binary digits of $i$, least significant bit
first.

articles.title: Value of a list of bits, least significant first
articles.statement:
A list of booleans
$(b_0, \dots, b_{m-1})$ represents the natural number $\sum_{k < m} [b_k]\, 2^k$, where $[b_k]$
is $1$ if $b_k$ is true and $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Gate values of an encoded circuit
articles.statement:
Let $C = (g_0, \dots, g_{m-1})$ be a list of gates,
each encoded as a (kind, references) pair, let $\alpha$ be a list of booleans and let $n$ be a
natural number. The gate values of $C$ on $\alpha$ are the values $(v_0, \dots, v_{m-1})$ of the
flat Boolean circuit on $n + 2$ inputs obtained by decoding every $g_j$, when input $i$ is given
entry $i$ of $\alpha$, read as false when $i$ is at least the length of $\alpha$.

articles.title: Outputs of an encoded circuit
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a list of $m$ gates encoded as
(kind, references) pairs, let $\alpha$ be a list of booleans and let $k$ and $n$ be natural
numbers. The last $k$ outputs of $C$ on $\alpha$ are the last $k$ of the gate values
$(v_0, \dots, v_{m-1})$ of $C$ on $\alpha$ as a circuit on $n + 2$ inputs, that is
$(v_{m-k}, \dots, v_{m-1})$; when $k > m$ they are all $m$ gate values.

articles.title: Encoded gates
articles.statement:
An encoded gate is a pair $(k, r)$ of a natural number $k$, the kind of
the gate, and a list $r$ of natural numbers, its references. This is the (kind, references)
encoding of the gates of a flat Boolean circuit.

articles.title: Valid gates of a succinct 3SAT descriptor
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a list of gates encoded as
(kind, references) pairs and let $n$ and $j$ be natural numbers. Gate $j$ of $C$ is valid when
$C$ has more than $j$ entries and its entry $j$ (counting from $0$) is one of: $(0, [i])$ with
$i < n + 2$ (an input gate); $(1, [b])$ with $b \le 1$ (a constant gate); $(2, [a])$ with
$a < j$ (a negation gate); or $(3, r)$ or $(4, r)$ where every entry $a$ of $r$ satisfies
$a < j$ (a conjunction or disjunction gate). Every other entry is invalid.

articles.title: Well-formed succinct 3SAT descriptors
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a list of gates encoded as
(kind, references) pairs and let $n$ be a natural number. The descriptor $C$ is well-formed for
$n$ when $C$ has at least $n + 1$ gates, every gate of $C$ is valid for $n$, and the flat Boolean
circuit on $n + 2$ inputs obtained by decoding every gate of $C$ is well-formed.

articles.title: Satisfied clauses of a succinctly described formula
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a list of gates encoded
as (kind, references) pairs, let $n$ and $i$ be natural numbers, and let $\sigma$ assign a
boolean to every natural number. Clause $i$ of the formula described by $C$ for $n$ is satisfied
by $\sigma$ when, for some $j < 3$, literal $j$ of clause $i$ of that formula is a pair $(v, s)$
with $\sigma(v) = s$.

articles.title: Literals of a succinctly described formula
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a list of gates encoded as
(kind, references) pairs and let $n$, $i$ and $j$ be natural numbers. Give $C$, as a circuit on
$n + 2$ inputs, the input consisting of the $n$ lowest bits of $i$ followed by the $2$ lowest
bits of $j$, each least significant bit first, and let $(o_0, \dots, o_{p-1})$ be its last
$n + 1$ outputs. Literal $j$ of clause $i$ is the pair $(v, s)$ with
$v = \sum_{k < \min(n, p)} [o_k]\, 2^k$, where $[o_k]$ is $1$ if $o_k$ is true and $0$
otherwise, and polarity $s = o_n$, read as false when $p \le n$.

articles.title: Succinct 3SAT
articles.statement:
Succinct 3SAT is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$
exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a pair $(n, C)$ of a natural
number $n$ and a list $C$ of gates encoded as (kind, references) pairs such that $C$ is a
well-formed descriptor for $n$ and some assignment $\sigma$ of booleans to the natural numbers
satisfies clause $c$ of the formula described by $C$ for every $c < 2^n$. Bitstrings that do not
decode are rejected.

articles.title: Succinct 3SAT is NEXP-complete
articles.statement:
The succinct 3SAT decision problem lies in NEXP, and every
decision problem in NEXP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- C. H. Papadimitriou, Computational Complexity, Addison-Wesley, 1994, Theorem 20.3 (succinct 3SAT is NEXP-complete); C. H. Papadimitriou and M. Yannakakis, "A note on succinct representations of graphs", Information and Control 71 (1986), 181-185.

articles.title: Fixed-length binary expansion (Succinct Circuit Value)
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $i$ and $n$,
this is the list of $n$ booleans $(b_0, \dots, b_{n-1})$, least significant bit first, where
$b_k$ is true exactly when $\lfloor i / 2^k \rfloor$ is odd. For $i < 2^n$ it is the $n$-bit
binary expansion of $i$; in general it is the $n$-bit expansion of $i \bmod 2^n$.

articles.title: Number with a given binary expansion (Succinct Circuit Value)
articles.statement:
A list of booleans
$(b_0, \dots, b_{m-1})$, read least significant bit first, denotes the natural number
$\sum_{k < m} [b_k] \, 2^k$, where $[b_k]$ is $1$ if $b_k$ is true and $0$ otherwise; the empty
list denotes $0$.

articles.title: Gate values of an encoded circuit (Succinct Circuit Value)
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a list of encoded
gates, $a$ a list of booleans and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Decode each gate of $C$ into a gate of a
flat Boolean circuit on $n$ inputs, and assign to input $j < n$ the entry $a_j$ of $a$, read as
false when $j$ is at least the length of $a$. The result is the list of the values of all gates
of the decoded circuit under this assignment, in order.

articles.title: Outputs of an encoded circuit (Succinct Circuit Value)
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a list of encoded
gates, $a$ a list of booleans and $k, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Decode each gate of $C$ into a gate of a
flat Boolean circuit on $n$ inputs and evaluate the decoded circuit with input $j < n$ set to the
entry $a_j$ of $a$, read as false when $j$ is at least the length of $a$. The outputs of $C$ on
$a$ are the last $k$ of the resulting gate values, or all of them if $C$ has fewer than $k$
gates.

articles.title: Encoded gates (Succinct Circuit Value)
articles.statement:
An encoded gate is a pair $(k, r)$ of a natural
number $k$, the kind of the gate, and a list $r$ of natural numbers, its references.

These pairs are the shared (kind, references) encoding of gates of flat Boolean circuits.

articles.title: Well-formed description circuits (Succinct Circuit Value)
articles.statement:
A list $C$ of encoded gates
is a well-formed description circuit on $n$ inputs when $C$ has at least $2n + 3$ gates and the
flat Boolean circuit on $n$ inputs obtained by decoding each gate of $C$ is well-formed, that
is, every gate references only strictly earlier gates.

The length bound guarantees that the $2n + 3$ outputs read as a gate description exist; without
it, missing outputs would silently read as false.

articles.title: Gate description in a succinct circuit (Succinct Circuit Value)
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a list of
encoded gates and let $n, i \in \mathbb{N}$. Decode each gate of $C$ into a gate of a flat
Boolean circuit on $n$ inputs and evaluate it with input $j < n$ set to bit $j$ of $i$, least
significant bit first, that is, true exactly when $\lfloor i / 2^j \rfloor$ is odd. The
description of gate $i$ of the circuit succinctly described by $C$ is the list of the last
$2n + 3$ resulting gate values, or of all of them if $C$ has fewer than $2n + 3$ gates.

articles.title: Evaluation of a succinct circuit (Succinct Circuit Value)
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a list of encoded
gates, $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $x$ a list of booleans. The gate values of the circuit with $2^n$
gates succinctly described by $C$ on input $x$ form the list $(v_0, \dots, v_{2^n - 1})$, where
each $v_i$ is the value of gate $i$ given $x$ and the values $(v_0, \dots, v_{i-1})$ of the
earlier gates.

articles.title: Decoded gate description (Succinct Circuit Value)
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a list of encoded gates,
let $n, i \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $d$ be the description of gate $i$ of the circuit succinctly
described by $C$: decode each gate of $C$ into a gate of a flat Boolean circuit on $n$ inputs,
evaluate the decoded circuit with input $j < n$ set to bit $j$ of $i$ (true exactly when
$\lfloor i / 2^j \rfloor$ is odd), and take the last $2n + 3$ gate values, or all of them if $C$
has fewer than $2n + 3$ gates. Read a list of booleans $(b_0, \dots, b_{m-1})$ as the number
$\sum_{k < m} [b_k] \, 2^k$, where $[b_k]$ is $1$ if $b_k$ is true and $0$ otherwise, so the
empty list reads as $0$. The information of gate $i$ is the triple $(t, p_1, p_2)$, where the
gate type $t$ is the number read from the first three entries of $d$, the first predecessor $p_1$
is the number read from the next $n$ entries, and the second predecessor $p_2$ is the number read
from all remaining entries; when $d$ is too short, each part uses only the entries that exist.

articles.title: Value of a gate of a succinct circuit (Succinct Circuit Value)
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a list of
encoded gates, let $n, i \in \mathbb{N}$, let $x$ be a list of booleans (the input) and let $v$
be a list of booleans (the values of earlier gates), where an entry outside $x$ or $v$ reads as
false. Let $(t, p_1, p_2)$ be the decoded description of gate $i$ of the circuit succinctly
described by $C$. If $i < n$, gate $i$ is an input gate and its value is $x_i$. Otherwise its
value is $v_{p_1} \land v_{p_2}$ if $t = 1$, $v_{p_1} \lor v_{p_2}$ if $t = 2$, $\lnot v_{p_1}$
if $t = 3$, true if $t = 4$, and false for every other $t$, including $t = 0$ and $t = 5$.

articles.title: Well-formed succinct circuit descriptions
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a list of encoded gates, read as a
flat Boolean circuit on $n$ inputs that describes a circuit $D$ with $2^n$ gates. For each gate
$i$ of $D$, let $t_i$, $p_i$ and $q_i$ be its gate type, first predecessor and second
predecessor, as decoded from the outputs of $C$ on the $n$-bit binary expansion of $i$. The
description is well formed when, for every $i < 2^n$: if $i < n$, then $t_i = 0$ (gate $i$ is an
input gate); and if $i \ge n$, then either $t_i = 4$ or $t_i = 5$ (a constant gate), or
$p_i < i$ and $q_i < i$.

articles.title: Succinct Circuit Value
articles.statement:
The decision problem Succinct Circuit Value accepts a bitstring
exactly when it decodes to a triple $(n, C, x)$ of a natural number $n$, a list $C$ of encoded
gates and a bitstring $x$ such that: $x$ has length $n$; $C$ has at least $2n + 3$ gates and,
read as a flat Boolean circuit on $n$ inputs, is well formed; the circuit $D$ with $2^n$ gates
succinctly described by $C$, whose gate $i$ is described by the outputs of $C$ on the $n$-bit
binary expansion of $i$, is well formed; and the last gate of $D$ outputs true when the first
$n$ gates of $D$ are fed the bits of $x$.

articles.title: Succinct Circuit Value is EXP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem Succinct Circuit Value
belongs to the class EXP, and every decision problem in EXP reduces to Succinct Circuit Value
by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- C. H. Papadimitriou, Computational Complexity, Addison-Wesley, 1994, Theorem 20.2 (succinct versions of P-complete problems are EXP-complete); S. A. Cook, "A hierarchy for nondeterministic time complexity", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 7 (1973), 343-353; R. E. Ladner, "The circuit value problem is log space complete for P", SIGACT News 7 (1975), 18-20.

articles.title: Evaluation of a quantified CNF formula
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula, let
$a : \mathbb{N} \to \{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ be an assignment, and let $Q$ be a
quantifier prefix, a list of pairs $(e, v)$ of a flag $e$ (true for $\exists$, false for
$\forall$) and a variable $v \in \mathbb{N}$. Write $a[v \mapsto b]$ for the assignment that
agrees with $a$ except that it sends $v$ to $b$. With the empty prefix, the formula holds under
$a$ when $a$ satisfies $\varphi$. With a prefix whose first entry is $(e, v)$ and whose remaining
entries form $Q'$, it holds under $a$ when, if $e$ is true, the formula with prefix $Q'$ holds
under $a[v \mapsto \mathrm{true}]$ or under $a[v \mapsto \mathrm{false}]$, and, if $e$ is false,
the formula with prefix $Q'$ holds under both $a[v \mapsto \mathrm{true}]$ and
$a[v \mapsto \mathrm{false}]$.

articles.title: TQBF as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The TQBF decision problem accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when
$x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a pair $(Q, \varphi)$, where $Q$ is a
quantifier prefix, a list of $m$ pairs $(e_1, v_1), \dots, (e_m, v_m)$ of a flag $e_i$ (true for
$\exists$, false for $\forall$) and a variable $v_i \in \mathbb{N}$, and $\varphi$ is a CNF
formula, such that $v_1, \dots, v_m$ are $0, 1, \dots, m - 1$ in some order, every variable
occurring in $\varphi$ is less than $m$, and the quantified formula with prefix $Q$ and matrix
$\varphi$ holds under the assignment that sends every variable to false.

articles.title: TQBF is PSPACE-complete
articles.statement:
The TQBF decision problem, of true quantified Boolean formulas
with a CNF matrix, lies in the class PSPACE of decision problems, and every decision problem in
PSPACE has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- L. J. Stockmeyer and A. R. Meyer, "Word problems requiring exponential time", Proceedings of the Fifth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 1973), 1-9; C. H. Papadimitriou, Computational Complexity, 1994, Theorem 7.4.

articles.title: UNSAT is coNP-complete
articles.statement:
The UNSAT decision problem lies in coNP, and every decision
problem in coNP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- S. A. Cook, "The complexity of theorem-proving procedures", Proceedings of the Third Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 1971), 151-158; L. A. Levin, "Universal search problems", Problems of Information Transmission 9 (1973), 265-266.

articles.title: UNSAT as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The UNSAT decision problem accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly
when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a pair $(n, \varphi)$ of a natural
number $n$ and a CNF formula $\varphi$ such that every variable occurring in $\varphi$ is less
than $n$ and, for every assignment $a$ of booleans to the variables $0, \dots, n - 1$, the
assignment that agrees with $a$ below $n$ and sends every variable $v \ge n$ to false does not
satisfy $\varphi$.

articles.title: Blum classes via an explicit threshold
articles.statement:
Let $\Phi$ be a Blum measure, $t$ a function from
$\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$ and $f$ a partial function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$. Then $f$
lies in the Blum class of $t$ with respect to $\Phi$ if and only if there are a program $c$ that
computes $f$ and a threshold $N$ such that for every input $n \ge N$ the cost $\Phi_c(n)$ is
defined and at most $t(n)$.

## Sources

- Blum, "A machine-independent theory of the complexity of recursive functions", *Journal of the ACM* 14 (1967), 322–336, Definition 2.

articles.title: Blum complexity class
articles.statement:
Given a Blum measure $\Phi$ and a function $t$ from $\mathbb{N}$ to
$\mathbb{N}$, the Blum class of $t$ consists of the partial functions $f$ from $\mathbb{N}$ to
$\mathbb{N}$ that are computed by some program $c$ whose cost $\Phi_c(n)$ is defined and at most
$t(n)$ for all but finitely many inputs $n$.

The bound is not required at every input: Blum's classes are defined up to finite exceptions,
and the finite exceptions are essential to the gap and union theorems (a program may be slow on
finitely many inputs without leaving the class).

## Sources

- Blum, "A machine-independent theory of the complexity of recursive functions", *Journal of the ACM* 14 (1967), 322–336, Definition 2.

articles.title: Blum complexity measure
articles.statement:
A Blum measure $\Phi$ assigns to every program $c$ and input
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ a partially defined cost $\Phi_c(n) \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfying Blum's two axioms:
$\Phi_c(n)$ is defined exactly when program $c$ halts on input $n$, and the relation
$\Phi_c(n) = m$ between $c$, $n$ and $m$ is decidable.

## Sources

- Blum, "A machine-independent theory of the complexity of recursive functions", *Journal of the ACM* 14 (1967), 322–336, Definition 1.

articles.title: Blum classes are monotone in the bound
articles.statement:
If `t` is eventually
dominated by `t'`, every function in the `t`-class is in the `t'`-class.

## Sources

- Blum, "A machine-independent theory of the complexity of recursive functions", *Journal of the ACM* 14 (1967), 322–336, Definition 2.

articles.title: Uniform constants for the exponential time-from-space bound
articles.statement: One pair of constants works for every input of the fixed machine.

articles.title: Polynomial-space decider runs in exponential time
articles.statement:
The same finite polynomial-space decider has an exponential time bound.
All constants precede every input. Halting comes from `Decides`, not space.

articles.title: First halting time is below the configuration-core bound
articles.statement: The first halting time is smaller than the canonical bound on reachable cores.

articles.title: NEXP is contained in EXPSPACE
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in NEXP, the class of
nondeterministic exponential time, also belongs to EXPSPACE, the class of deterministic
exponential space.

## Sources

- S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009 (NEXP ⊆ EXPSPACE by exhaustive simulation).

articles.title: NL is contained in P
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in NL, the class of nondeterministic
logarithmic space, also belongs to P, the class of decision problems computable in deterministic
polynomial time.

## Sources

- S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Theorem 4.14 (NL ⊆ P); C. H. Papadimitriou, Computational Complexity, 1994.

articles.title: NP is contained in PSPACE
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in NP also belongs to PSPACE, the class
of decision problems decidable in polynomial space.

## Sources

- S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, Cambridge University Press, 2009, Theorem 4.14 (NP ⊆ PSPACE); C. H. Papadimitriou, Computational Complexity, Addison-Wesley, 1994, Theorem 7.2.

articles.title: PSPACE is contained in EXP
articles.statement:
Every canonical polynomial-space language is in exponential time,
using its original finite multi-tape decider.

## Sources

- S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, Cambridge University Press, 2009, Chapter 4 (Space complexity).

articles.title: Halting space-bounded runs obey the core-count time bound
articles.statement: A halting, space-bounded run has an actual step bound.

articles.title: Exponential time bound from a space bound and halting
articles.statement: Exponential time from a visited-cell space bound and a halting run.

articles.title: Immerman-Szelepcsenyi theorem: NL = coNL
articles.statement:
The complexity class NL is closed under
complementation: a decision problem $L$ belongs to NL if and only if its complement, the decision
problem that is true exactly on the bitstrings where $L$ is false, belongs to NL.

## Sources

- N. Immerman, "Nondeterministic space is closed under complementation", SIAM Journal on Computing 17 (1988), 935-938; R. Szelepcsenyi, "The method of forced enumeration for nondeterministic automata", Acta Informatica 26 (1988), 279-284.

articles.title: Karp-Lipton theorem: NP in P/poly collapses PH
articles.statement:
If every decision problem in NP belongs to
P/poly (polynomial time with polynomial advice), then the polynomial hierarchy PH equals its
second level $\Sigma_2^p$.

## Sources

- R. M. Karp and R. J. Lipton, "Some connections between nonuniform and uniform complexity classes", Proceedings of the Twelfth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 1980), 302-309.

articles.title: Ladner's theorem: NP-intermediate languages exist
articles.statement:
If P $\ne$ NP, then there is a decision
problem $L$ in NP that is not in P and to which not every decision problem in NP reduces by a
polynomial-time many-one reduction; that is, $L$ is in NP but is neither in P nor NP-complete.

## Sources

- R. E. Ladner, "On the structure of polynomial time reducibility", Journal of the ACM 22 (1975), 155-171.

articles.title: Mahaney's theorem: sparse NP-complete sets imply P = NP
articles.statement:
If some decision problem is both
sparse and NP-complete, then the complexity classes $\mathsf{P}$ and $\mathsf{NP}$ are equal.

## Sources

- S. R. Mahaney, "Sparse complete sets for NP: solution of a conjecture of Berman and Hartmanis", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 25 (1982), 130-143.

articles.title: NP-complete decision problems
articles.statement:
A decision problem $L$ is NP-complete when $L$ is in NP
and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to $L$.

articles.title: Sparse decision problems
articles.statement:
A decision problem $L$ is sparse when there is a polynomial $p$
with natural-number coefficients such that, for every natural number $n$, the set of bitstrings
of length at most $n$ accepted by $L$ is finite and has at most $p(n)$ elements.

articles.title: Parameterized Clique
articles.statement:
The parameterized $k$-Clique problem answers a bitstring $x$ and
a parameter $k \in \mathbb{N}$ as follows. If $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring
encoding, to a pair $(n, E)$ of a natural number $n$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers,
the answer is true exactly when there is a list of $k$ distinct natural numbers, each less than
$n$, such that for any two distinct entries $u$ and $v$ of the list, $(u, v) \in E$ or
$(v, u) \in E$. If $x$ decodes to no such pair, the answer is false.

That is, on a well-formed input the answer says whether the graph on the vertices
$0, \dots, n - 1$ whose edges are the pairs in $E$, with direction ignored, has a clique of
size $k$.

articles.title: Fixed-parameter tractable problems
articles.statement:
A parameterized problem $P$ is fixed-parameter
tractable when there is a function $D$, from pairs $(x, k)$ of a bitstring $x$ and a natural
number $k$ to booleans, that is computable in FPT time and satisfies $P(x, k) = D(x, k)$ for
every bitstring $x$ and every $k \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: FPT-reductions
articles.statement:
A parameterized problem $P$ FPT-reduces to a parameterized problem $Q$
when there are a map $R$, sending each pair $(x, k)$ of a bitstring $x$ and a natural number
$k$ to such a pair $R(x, k) = (x', k')$, that is computable in FPT time, and a computable
function $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, such that for every bitstring $x$ and every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$, $k' \le g(k)$ and $P(x, k)$ is true if and only if $Q(x', k')$ is true.

articles.title: FPT time
articles.statement:
Let $\beta$ be a type with a canonical bitstring encoding. A function $R$
from pairs $(x, k)$ of a bitstring $x$ and a natural number $k$ to $\beta$ is computable in FPT
time when there are a computable function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a
polynomial-time computable function $A$ from pairs of bitstrings to $\beta$ such that
$R(x, k) = A(x, 1^{f(k)})$ for every bitstring $x$ and every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, where
$1^{f(k)}$ is the list of $f(k)$ booleans all equal to true.

Padding the input with $f(k)$ entries in this way is equivalent to a running time of
$F(k) \cdot p(n)$ for a computable $F$ and a polynomial $p$, where $n$ is the length of $x$;
the padding function must be computable, since otherwise every predicate on the parameter would
be fixed-parameter tractable.

articles.title: Parameterized problems
articles.statement:
A parameterized problem is a function that assigns a boolean
answer to every pair of a bitstring (a finite list of booleans) $x$ and a natural-number
parameter $k$.

articles.title: Parameterized complexity: FPT and W(1)-completeness of Clique
articles.statement:
Write $W[t]$ for the
$t$-th level of the W-hierarchy. The parameterized $k$-Clique problem lies in $W[1]$, and every
parameterized problem in $W[1]$ has an FPT-reduction to it. Every fixed-parameter tractable
parameterized problem lies in $W[1]$. For every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, $W[t] \subseteq W[t + 1]$.

## Sources

- R. G. Downey and M. R. Fellows, Parameterized Complexity, Springer, 1999 (W[1]-completeness of Clique); J. Flum and M. Grohe, Parameterized Complexity Theory, Springer, 2006.

articles.title: Depths of the gates of an encoded circuit
articles.statement:
For a list
$C = (g_0, \dots, g_{m-1})$ of gates encoded as (kind, references) pairs, the list of depths is
$(d_0, \dots, d_{m-1})$, where $d_j$ is computed from $d_0, \dots, d_{j-1}$ as follows. Write
$g_j = (c, r)$. If $c = 0$ or $c = 1$ (an input or constant gate), then $d_j = 0$; otherwise
$d_j$ is one plus the maximum of $d_a$ over the entries $a$ of $r$, where $d_a$ is read as $0$
for $a \ge j$ and the maximum over no entries is $0$.

articles.title: Gate values of an encoded circuit
articles.statement:
Let $C = (g_0, \dots, g_{m-1})$ be a list of gates
encoded as (kind, references) pairs and let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ be a list of booleans.
The gate values of $C$ under $a$ are the values $(v_0, \dots, v_{m-1})$ of the flat Boolean
circuit on $n$ inputs obtained by decoding each $g_j$ to a gate on $n$ inputs, evaluated at the
assignment that gives input $i$ the value $a_i$.

Decoding turns an input gate with index $i \ge n$ into the constant false, so such inputs read
as false.

articles.title: Wefts of the gates of an encoded circuit
articles.statement:
For a list
$C = (g_0, \dots, g_{m-1})$ of gates encoded as (kind, references) pairs, the list of wefts is
$(w_0, \dots, w_{m-1})$, where $w_j$ is computed from $w_0, \dots, w_{j-1}$ as follows. Write
$g_j = (c, r)$. The weft $w_j$ is $1$ if $c = 3$ or $c = 4$ (an AND or OR gate) and $r$ has
more than $2$ entries, and $0$ otherwise, plus, when $c = 2$, $c = 3$ or $c = 4$, the maximum of
$w_a$ over the entries $a$ of $r$, where $w_a$ is read as $0$ for $a \ge j$ and the maximum
over no entries is $0$.

articles.title: Depth of one encoded gate
articles.statement:
Let $d = (d_0, d_1, \dots)$ be a list of natural numbers
(the depths of earlier gates), where $d_a$ is read as $0$ when $a$ is out of range, and let
$(c, r)$ be a gate encoded as a (kind, references) pair. Its depth is $0$ if $c = 0$ or $c = 1$
(an input or constant gate), and otherwise one plus the maximum of $d_a$ over the entries $a$ of
$r$, the maximum over no entries being $0$.

articles.title: Predecessors of an encoded gate
articles.statement:
The predecessor list of an encoded gate $(k, r)$ is $r$
when $k$ is $2$, $3$ or $4$ (a NOT, AND or OR gate), and the empty list for every other kind.

Variable (kind $0$) and constant (kind $1$) payloads are a variable index and a constant value,
not predecessor gates; folding over them would attribute unrelated gates' weft or depth (for
example, an input gate $(0, [0])$ inheriting gate $0$'s depth).

articles.title: Weft of an encoded gate
articles.statement:
Given a list $w$ of wefts of earlier gates, where $w_a$ reads as
$0$ when $a$ is not a position of $w$, the weft of an encoded gate $(k, r)$ is $1$ if it is a
large AND or OR gate ($k \in \{3, 4\}$ and $r$ has more than $2$ entries) and $0$ otherwise,
plus the maximum of $w_a$ over the entries $a$ of its predecessor list (the maximum over an
empty list is $0$). In particular, input and constant gates have weft $0$.

articles.title: Encoded gates for weighted circuit satisfiability
articles.statement:
An encoded gate is a pair $(k, r)$ of a
natural number $k$, its kind, and a list $r$ of natural numbers, its references.

Gates are read as in the shared (kind, references) encoding of flat Boolean circuits on $n$
inputs: $(0, [i])$ is the input variable $x_i$ when $i < n$, $(1, [b])$ is the constant that is
true exactly when $b = 1$, $(2, [a])$ is the negation of gate $a$, and $(3, r)$ and $(4, r)$ are
the AND and the OR of the gates listed in $r$; every other pair, including $(0, [i])$ with
$i \ge n$ and $(2, r)$ with $r$ not of length one, evaluates to false.

articles.title: Well-formed encoded circuits
articles.statement:
A list $C = (g_0, \dots, g_{m-1})$ of encoded gates is
well-formed when every NOT, AND or OR gate references only strictly earlier gates: for every
$j < m$ such that $g_j = (k, r)$ has kind $k \in \{2, 3, 4\}$, every entry $a$ of $r$ satisfies
$a < j$.

articles.title: Weighted circuit satisfiability with bounded weft and depth
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $t$ and
$d$, weighted circuit satisfiability is the parameterized problem that, on a bitstring $x$ and a
parameter $k$, answers true exactly when $x$ decodes to a pair $(n, C)$ of a natural number $n$
and a list $C$ of encoded gates such that: every NOT, AND or OR gate of $C$ references only
strictly earlier gates; every gate of $C$ has weft at most $t$ and depth at most $d$; and there
is an assignment of $n$ Boolean values to the inputs, exactly $k$ of them true, under which $C$
has a last gate and that gate evaluates to true.

articles.title: The level $\mathrm{W}(t)$ of the W-hierarchy
articles.statement:
For a natural number $t$, $\mathrm{W}[t]$ is
the set of parameterized problems $P$ for which there is a natural number $d$ such that $P$
FPT-reduces to weighted circuit satisfiability for circuits of weft at most $t$ and depth at
most $d$.

articles.title: If P = NP then the polynomial hierarchy collapses to P
articles.statement:
If the complexity classes P and NP
are equal, then the polynomial hierarchy PH, the union of the classes $\Sigma_k^p$ over all
natural numbers $k$, is equal to P.

## Sources

- S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009 (PH collapses to P if P = NP); L. J. Stockmeyer, "The polynomial-time hierarchy", Theoretical Computer Science 3 (1977), 1-22.

articles.title: The polynomial hierarchy is contained in PSPACE
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in the polynomial
hierarchy PH belongs to PSPACE.

## Sources

- L. J. Stockmeyer, "The polynomial-time hierarchy", Theoretical Computer Science 3 (1977), 1-22; S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Theorem 5.4.

articles.title: Declared polynomial time for timed functions on bitstrings
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a timed function
that maps each list $x$ of Booleans to an output list $f(x)$ of Booleans together with a declared
time $t_f(x) \in \mathbb{N}$. Then $f$ computes in declared polynomial time when there is a
polynomial $p$ with natural-number coefficients such that, for every list $x$ of Booleans, both
$t_f(x)$ and the length of $f(x)$ are at most $p(|x|)$, where $|x|$ is the length of $x$.

Declared times are trusted annotations, not checked against any machine model, so this does not
make $f$ polynomial-time computable: for an arbitrary decision problem $L$, the function returning
the one-element list $[L(x)]$ with declared time $0$ satisfies it. The output-length bound is what
lets declared bounds compose.

articles.title: From declared-time to polynomial-time many-one reductions
articles.statement:
Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be decision
problems and let $f$ be a declared-time many-one reduction from $L_1$ to $L_2$. If the function
sending $x$ to the output of $f$ on $x$ is polynomial-time computable by a Turing machine for the
canonical bitstring encodings, then $L_1$ reduces to $L_2$ by a polynomial-time many-one
reduction.

The polynomial-time hypothesis must be proved separately for $f$; it does not follow from the
declared-time bound.

articles.title: A declared-time reduction followed by a decider for the target decides the source
articles.statement:
Let
$L_1$ and $L_2$ be decision problems, let $f$ be a declared-time many-one reduction from $L_1$ to
$L_2$, and let $g$ be a timed function from lists of Booleans to Booleans whose output on every
list $y$ is $L_2(y)$. Then for every list $x$ of Booleans, the timed function that runs $f$ on $x$
and then $g$ on its output returns $L_1(x)$.

Together with the preservation of declared polynomial time under such compositions, this is the
declared-time form of closure under reductions; no membership in the class P is claimed.

articles.title: Declared polynomial time is preserved under precomposition with a reduction
articles.statement:
Let $L_1$ and
$L_2$ be decision problems, let $f$ be a declared-time many-one reduction from $L_1$ to $L_2$, and
let $g$ be a timed function from lists of Booleans to Booleans that decides in declared polynomial
time. Then the timed function that on input $x$ returns $g(f(x))$, with declared time the declared
time of $f$ on $x$ plus that of $g$ on $f(x)$, decides in declared polynomial time.

If $p_f$ bounds the declared time and output length of $f$ and $p_g$ bounds the declared time of
$g$, then $p_f + p_g \circ p_f$ bounds the declared time of the composite.

articles.title: Declared polynomial time for timed deciders
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a timed function that maps each
list $x$ of Booleans to a Boolean $f(x)$ together with a declared time $t_f(x) \in \mathbb{N}$.
Then $f$ decides in declared polynomial time when there is a polynomial $p$ with natural-number
coefficients such that $t_f(x) \le p(|x|)$ for every list $x$ of Booleans, where $|x|$ is the
length of $x$.

This constrains only the trusted time annotation: it implies neither that $f$ is computable in
any machine model nor that $f$ is related to any particular decision problem.

articles.title: Declared-time many-one reduction is reflexive
articles.statement:
For every decision problem $L$, the timed
identity function, which returns its input with declared time $0$, is a declared-time many-one
reduction from $L$ to $L$.

articles.title: Declared-time many-one reductions compose
articles.statement:
Let $L_1$, $L_2$ and $L_3$ be decision problems.
If $f_1$ is a declared-time many-one reduction from $L_1$ to $L_2$ and $f_2$ is a declared-time
many-one reduction from $L_2$ to $L_3$, then the timed function that on input $x$ returns
$f_2(f_1(x))$, with declared time the declared time of $f_1$ on $x$ plus that of $f_2$ on
$f_1(x)$, is a declared-time many-one reduction from $L_1$ to $L_3$.

If $p_1$ and $p_2$ bound the declared times and output lengths of $f_1$ and $f_2$, then
$p_1 + p_2 \circ p_1$ bounds those of the composite.

articles.title: Declared-time many-one reduction by a timed function
articles.statement:
Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be decision
problems and let $f$ be a timed function that maps each list $x$ of Booleans to a list $f(x)$ of
Booleans together with a declared time. Then $f$ is a declared-time many-one reduction from $L_1$
to $L_2$ when $f$ computes in declared polynomial time and $L_1(x) = L_2(f(x))$ for every list $x$
of Booleans.

Because declared times are trusted annotations, this is not a polynomial-time many-one reduction
in the Turing-machine sense: nothing is established about the computability of $f$.

articles.title: Every decision problem has a timed decider in declared polynomial time
articles.statement:
For every decision
problem $L$ there is a timed function $f$ from lists of Booleans to Booleans that decides in
declared polynomial time and whose output $f(x)$ equals $L(x)$ for every list $x$ of Booleans.

The witness returns $L(x)$ with declared time $0$, treating the evaluation of $L$ as free. This is
why no complexity classes are defined by quantifying over timed functions.

articles.title: A timed verifier with polynomial-time output function puts its language in NP
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be
a decision problem, $p$ a polynomial with natural-number coefficients, and $V$ a timed function
from pairs of lists of Booleans to Booleans that verifies $L$ with witness bound $p$. If the
function sending $(x, w)$ to the output of $V$ on $(x, w)$ is polynomial-time computable by a
Turing machine for the canonical bitstring encodings, then $L$ is in NP.

The polynomial-time hypothesis must be proved separately for $V$; it does not follow from any
bound on the declared time of $V$.

articles.title: A timed decider with polynomial-time output function gives membership in P
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be
a decision problem and let $f$ assign to each bit string $x$ a timed computation, that is, a
Boolean return value together with a declared time in $\mathbb{N}$, whose return value equals
$L(x)$ for every $x$. If the function sending $x$ to the return value of $f(x)$ is
polynomial-time computable, then $L$ belongs to the class P.

The polynomial-time hypothesis must be proved for the specific decider: it does not follow from a
polynomial bound on the declared times, which are trusted annotations, since every decision
problem has a decider of declared time zero.

articles.title: A decider with polynomial declared time gives a verifier with polynomial declared time
articles.statement:
If a timed decider $f$ on bit strings has declared time bounded by a polynomial in the input
length, then the verifier that sends an input $x$ and a witness $w$ to $f(x)$, ignoring $w$, has
declared time bounded by a polynomial in $|x| + |w|$.

articles.title: Verifiers with polynomial declared time
articles.statement:
A timed verifier $V$, which assigns to each pair
of bit strings $(x, w)$ (an input and a witness) a timed computation returning a Boolean, runs in
declared polynomial time when there is a polynomial $q$ with natural coefficients such that the
declared time of $V(x, w)$ is at most $q(|x| + |w|)$ for all $x$ and $w$.

As for deciders, this constrains only the declared time, which is a trusted annotation, and
establishes no computability in any machine model.

articles.title: Pulling a verifier back along a declared reduction
articles.statement:
Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be decision
problems, let $f$ be a declared polynomial-time many-one reduction from $L_1$ to $L_2$, and let
$V$ be a verifier with polynomial declared time that verifies $L_2$ with witness bound $p$. Let
$V'$ be the verifier that on input $x$ and witness $w$ first runs $f$ on $x$, obtaining $y$, then
runs $V$ on $(y, w)$ and accepts when $V$ accepts and $|w| \le p(|y|)$; its declared time is the
declared time of $f(x)$ plus that of $V(y, w)$. Then $V'$ has polynomial declared time, and there
is a polynomial $p'$ with natural coefficients such that $V'$ verifies $L_1$ with witness bound
$p'$.

The proof takes $p' = p \circ r$ and the time bound $r(n) + q(r(n) + n)$ with $n = |x| + |w|$,
where $r$ bounds the declared time and output length of $f$ and $q$ bounds the declared time of
$V$.

articles.title: A decider is a verifier with witness bound zero
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a decision problem and let $f$
be a timed decider whose return value on every bit string $x$ equals $L(x)$. Then the verifier
that sends an input $x$ and a witness $w$ to $f(x)$, ignoring $w$, verifies $L$ with the zero
polynomial as witness bound, so only the empty witness is allowed.

Together with the fact that this verifier has polynomial declared time whenever $f$ does, this is
the declared-time form of $\mathrm{P} \subseteq \mathrm{NP}$ for named algorithms.

articles.title: Verifying a decision problem with a witness bound
articles.statement:
A timed verifier $V$, which assigns to
each pair of bit strings $(x, w)$ (an input and a witness) a timed computation returning a
Boolean, verifies a decision problem $L$ with witness bound $p$, a polynomial with natural
coefficients, when for every bit string $x$, $L(x)$ holds if and only if there is a witness $w$
with $|w| \le p(|x|)$ such that $V(x, w)$ returns true.

This is the verifier half of the definition of NP, phrased for a named timed verifier.

articles.title: The answer machine runs in one step
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a finite multi-stack machine with finite
stack alphabets, whose input alphabet is identified with the bits by $e$ and whose output alphabet
by $e_1$. For every non-blank cell $x$ of the single-tape emulation alphabet of $M$, the answer
machine of $M$, started on the one-cell tape $x$, halts within at most one step on the one-cell
tape holding the input-bit cell of the answer of $x$ (the bit telling whether $x$ holds
$e_1^{-1}(\mathrm{true})$ on the output stack).

articles.title: The reversal component
articles.statement:
The component machine with two stacks, the input stack $X$ and
the output stack $O$, both over the alphabet $\mathrm{Bool}$; the three labels mv, drop and done;
the program that moves the bits of $X$ onto $O$ (reversing them), pops $O$ once and halts; and
the stack list $[X, O]$.

articles.title: Reversing and dropping the first bit is polynomial-time
articles.statement:
A finite multi-stack Turing
machine whose input and output alphabets are both identified with the bits, together with a
polynomial $p$ with natural-number coefficients, such that for every bit list $x$, given bit by
bit as its own encoding, the machine outputs the reversal of $x$ with its first entry removed
(that is, $x$ without its last bit, in reverse order) within $p(|x|)$ steps.

articles.title: The decider within time
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a finite multi-stack machine with finite stack
alphabets, whose input alphabet is identified with the bits by $e$ and whose output alphabet by
$e_1$, and let $C$ be the emulation constant of $M$. Let $w$ be a bit list, $b$ a bit and $t$ a
natural number. Suppose $M$, started with its input stack holding the bits of $w$ in reverse order
followed by $\mathrm{true}$ (read through $e^{-1}$), is after exactly $t$ steps in the halting
configuration whose output stack holds just $e_1^{-1}(b)$, whose other stacks are empty and whose
internal state is the initial one. Then the single-tape decider of $M$, started on the tape of
input-bit cells of $w$, halts on the one-cell tape holding the input-bit cell of $b$ within
$C t (|w| + 1 + C t + 1) + 4$ steps.

articles.title: Stacks of the reversal component
articles.statement:
The two stack indices of the reversal component: the
input stack $X$ and the output stack $O$.

articles.title: Labels of the reversal component
articles.statement:
The three labels of the reversal component: mv (move
the input onto the output), drop (drop one symbol) and done.

articles.title: Problems in P are decided in polynomial time by single-tape machines
articles.statement:
Every decision
problem in the class $\mathrm{P}$ (defined with multi-stack machines) belongs to the class of
decision problems decided in polynomial time by single-tape machines.

The proof reverses the input, restricts the multi-stack machine to finite alphabets and emulates
it on a single tape within quadratic overhead.

articles.title: Program of the reversal component
articles.statement:
The multi-stack program over the stacks $X$ and $O$,
both with alphabet $\mathrm{Bool}$, with a Boolean internal state: at label mv it moves the bits
of $X$ one at a time onto $O$ (reversing them) and then goes to drop; at drop it pops $O$ once
and goes to done; at done it halts.

articles.title: Running the reversal component
articles.statement:
For every bit list $x$, the program of the reversal
component, started at label mv with internal state false, with the bits of $x$ on the input stack
$X$ and every other stack empty, reaches label done within at most $|x| + 2$ steps, with some
internal state and some stacks whose output stack $O$ holds the reversal of $x$ with its first
entry removed.

articles.title: Polynomial time on single-tape machines
articles.statement:
The class of decision problems $L$ for which
there are a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ with a designated default element, an injective map $\iota$
from the bits to $\Sigma$, a single-tape Turing machine $M$ over $\Sigma$ and a polynomial $p$
with natural-number coefficients such that, for every bit list $w$, the machine $M$ started on the
word $\iota(w)$ (the bits of $w$ mapped by $\iota$) halts on the one-cell tape $\iota(L(w))$
within $p(|w|)$ steps.

articles.title: Sums of polynomially bounded functions are polynomially bounded
articles.statement: A pointwise sum of polynomially bounded functions is polynomially bounded.

articles.title: Compositions of polynomially bounded functions are polynomially bounded
articles.statement: A composition of polynomially bounded functions is polynomially bounded.

articles.title: Constant functions are polynomially bounded
articles.statement: Every constant natural-valued function is polynomially bounded.

articles.title: The identity function is polynomially bounded
articles.statement: The identity function on natural numbers is polynomially bounded.

articles.title: The normalized polynomial bound is polynomially bounded and monotone
articles.statement: The normalized bound is itself polynomially bounded and monotone in its input.

articles.title: Products of polynomially bounded functions are polynomially bounded
articles.statement: A pointwise product of polynomially bounded functions is polynomially bounded.

articles.title: Polynomial bounds with equal coefficient and exponent
articles.statement: Polynomial growth is equivalent to a global bound whose coefficient equals its exponent.

articles.title: Powers of polynomially bounded functions are polynomially bounded
articles.statement: A fixed pointwise power of a polynomially bounded function is polynomially bounded.

articles.title: Emulation constant
articles.statement:
For a bundled multi-stack machine $M$, the emulation constant is
$C = 3(2B + 1) + P$, where $B = \sum_l |M(l)|$ is the total structural size of the statements
$M(l)$ over all labels $l$ (so each statement has size at most $B$), and $P$ is the push bound
of $M$, the total number of push instructions in its statements, which bounds the number of
pushes in one step.

articles.title: Running one statement on the emulator
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack machine and $N$ a
statement over the same stack alphabets, labels and internal states, and write $|N|$ for the
structural size of $N$. Let $H \in \mathbb{N}$, let $v$ be an internal state, let $S$ be a
family of stacks $S_k$, each of height at most $H$, and let $L$ be tape contents whose $k$-th
track lists $S_k$ from bottom to top, for every $k$. Running the translation of $N$ in the
$\mathrm{TM1}$ emulator of $M$ from state $v$, with the head at the bottom marker of $L$, gives
a configuration that reaches, in some number $m \le |N| (2 (H + |N|) + 2)$ of emulator steps,
a configuration representing the result of running $N$ from state $v$ on the stacks $S$: it
has the corresponding label and the same internal state, and its head is at the bottom marker
of a tape whose $k$-th track lists the $k$-th resulting stack from bottom to top.

articles.title: One multi-stack step costs at most $1 + B(2(H + B) + 2)$ emulator steps
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a
multi-stack machine in which the statement of every label has size at most $B$, and consider its
emulation by a single-tape machine with an internal store that keeps the stacks side by side on
its tape. Let $c$ be a configuration of $M$ in which every stack has height at most $H$, and let
$c_1$ be a configuration of the emulator that represents $c$. If $M$ moves from $c$ to $c'$ in one
step, then there is a configuration $c_1'$ of the emulator that represents $c'$ and that the
emulator reaches from $c_1$ in at most $1 + B(2(H + B) + 2)$ steps.

The size of a statement is its structural size as a term. This is a counted form of the
correctness of the emulation.

articles.title: Single-tape emulation of halting multi-stack runs
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a bundled multi-stack
machine with emulation constant $C$, and $L$ an input for its input stack. If $M$, started on
$L$, reaches after $t$ steps a configuration $c$ from which it does not step, then the
single-tape emulation of $M$, started on the encoding of $L$, reaches in some number
$n \le C t (|L| + C t + 1)$ of steps a configuration from which it does not step. That
configuration is the single-tape form of a configuration of the $\mathrm{TM1}$ emulator of $M$
that represents $c$: it has the corresponding label and the same internal state, and its head
is at the bottom marker of a tape whose $k$-th track lists the $k$-th stack of $c$ from bottom
to top.

articles.title: Quadratic overhead of the single-tape emulation
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a bundled multi-stack
machine with emulation constant $C$, and $L$ an input for its input stack. If $M$, started on
$L$, reaches a configuration $c$ after $t$ steps, then the single-tape emulation of $M$,
started on the encoding of $L$, reaches in some number $n \le C t (|L| + C t + 1)$ of steps the
single-tape form of a configuration of the $\mathrm{TM1}$ emulator of $M$ that represents $c$:
it has the corresponding label and the same internal state, and its head is at the bottom
marker of a tape whose $k$-th track lists the $k$-th stack of $c$ from bottom to top.

articles.title: The emulator walks right to the top of a stack
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack machine, $k$ a
stack, $L$ tape contents whose $k$-th track lists a stack $S$ from bottom to top, and
$n \le |S|$. In the $\mathrm{TM1}$ emulator of $M$, the configuration in the state that walks to
stack $k$ (for a given stack action and continuation), with internal state $v$ and head at the
bottom marker of $L$, reaches in exactly $n$ steps the same configuration with the head moved
$n$ cells to the right.

articles.title: The emulator walks back to the bottom
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack machine and $L$ tape
contents. For every $n$, in the $\mathrm{TM1}$ emulator of $M$, the configuration in the return
state (for a given continuation), with internal state $v$ and head $n$ cells to the right of the
bottom marker of $L$, reaches in exactly $n$ steps the same configuration with the head at the
bottom marker.

articles.title: Each step of the $\mathrm{TM1}$ emulator is at most three single-tape steps
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be
a multi-stack machine with a default label and a default internal state. If the
$\mathrm{TM1}$ emulator of $M$ goes from $c$ to $c'$ in exactly $m$ steps, then the
single-tape emulation of $M$ goes from the single-tape form of $c$ to the single-tape form of
$c'$ in at most $3m$ steps.

articles.title: The emulation halts where the multi-stack machine halts
articles.statement:
A halted configuration is
related only to configurations of the single-tape emulation that do not step.

articles.title: Savitch's theorem: NPSPACE = PSPACE
articles.statement:
The complexity class NPSPACE of decision problems
decided in polynomial space by nondeterministic multi-tape Turing machines equals the class
PSPACE of decision problems decided in polynomial space by deterministic multi-tape Turing
machines.

## Sources

- W. J. Savitch, "Relationships between nondeterministic and deterministic tape complexities", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 4 (1970), 177-192.

articles.title: Decoding inverts bitstring encoding
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a canonical bitstring
encoding. For every $a \in \alpha$, decoding the bitstring encoding of $a$ succeeds and returns
$a$.

articles.title: Decoding function of a bitstring encoding
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ with a canonical bitstring
encoding, bitstring decoding is the decoding function of that encoding: it sends each finite list
of booleans either to an element of $\alpha$ or to failure.

articles.title: Encoding function of a bitstring encoding
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ with a canonical bitstring
encoding, the bitstring encoding of $a \in \alpha$ is the finite list of booleans that this
encoding assigns to $a$.

articles.title: Bitstring encodings
articles.statement:
A canonical bitstring encoding of a type $\alpha$ consists of an
encoding map from $\alpha$ to finite lists of booleans and a partial decoding map from finite
lists of booleans to $\alpha$, such that decoding the encoding of any $a \in \alpha$ succeeds
and returns $a$.

## Sources

- a class version of Mathlib's `Computability.Encoding` specialized to the alphabet `Bool`, inlined from FormalConjectures (absent from Mathlib).

articles.title: The class coNP
articles.statement:
**The class coNP.** coNP is the set of decision problems $L$ whose complement, the decision
problem that accepts exactly the bitstrings that $L$ rejects, belongs to NP.

## Sources

- inlined from FormalConjectures (absent from Mathlib).

articles.title: Complexity classes
articles.statement:
A complexity class is a set of decision problems.

## Sources

- inlined from FormalConjectures (absent from Mathlib).

articles.title: Decision problems
articles.statement:
A decision problem is a function from finite lists of booleans
(bitstrings) to booleans.

## Sources

- inlined from FormalConjectures (absent from Mathlib).

articles.title: Self-delimiting form of a bitstring
articles.statement:
The self-delimiting form of a bitstring
$(b_1, \dots, b_n)$ is $(\mathrm{true}, b_1, \dots, \mathrm{true}, b_n, \mathrm{false})$: each
bit is preceded by $\mathrm{true}$ and the block is terminated by $\mathrm{false}$. In
particular the empty bitstring becomes $(\mathrm{false})$.

articles.title: Polynomial-time computability under given encodings
articles.statement:
Let $e_\alpha$ encode $\alpha$ as
words over an alphabet $\Gamma_\alpha$ and $e_\beta$ encode $\beta$ as words over $\Gamma_\beta$. A
function $f : \alpha \to \beta$ is polynomial-time computable with respect to $e_\alpha$ and
$e_\beta$ when there are a multi-stack Turing machine with finitely many stacks, function labels
and internal states and a finite input stack alphabet, identifications of its input and output
stack alphabets with $\Gamma_\alpha$ and $\Gamma_\beta$, and a polynomial $p$ with natural-number
coefficients, such that for every $a \in \alpha$ the machine, started at its main function in its
initial state with $e_\alpha(a)$ on its input stack and every other stack empty, halts within
$p(n)$ steps, where $n$ is the length of $e_\alpha(a)$, with $e_\beta(f(a))$ on its output stack,
every other stack empty and its internal state equal to its initial state.

## Sources

- inlined from FormalConjectures (absent from Mathlib).

articles.title: Polynomial-time computable functions
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be types with canonical
bitstring encodings. A function $f : \alpha \to \beta$ is polynomial-time computable when it is
polynomial-time computable with respect to the canonical bitstring encodings of $\alpha$ and
$\beta$.

## Sources

- inlined from FormalConjectures (absent from Mathlib).

articles.title: The complexity class NP
articles.statement:
NP is the set of decision problems $L$ (functions from lists of
booleans to booleans) for which there exist a polynomial $p$ with natural-number coefficients and
a polynomial-time computable function $R$ from pairs of lists of booleans to booleans such that,
for every list of booleans $x$, $L(x)$ is true if and only if there is a list of booleans $w$
whose length is at most $p$ evaluated at the length of $x$ and for which $R(x, w)$ is true.

Polynomial time is measured with respect to the canonical bitstring encodings.

articles.title: The complexity class P
articles.statement:
P is the set of decision problems (functions from lists of
booleans to booleans) that are computable in polynomial time by a deterministic multi-stack
Turing machine, with respect to the canonical bitstring encodings of inputs and outputs.

articles.title: Bounded parsing of self-delimiting blocks
articles.statement:
Given a bound $n$ and a list of booleans $s$,
the parse returns the empty list of payloads if $s$ is empty. If $s$ is nonempty and $n = 0$ it
fails. If $s$ is nonempty and $n = m + 1$, it parses one self-delimiting block from the front of
$s$, then parses the remaining list with bound $m$, and returns the first payload followed by the
payloads of the rest. It fails if either step fails. So the parse succeeds exactly when $s$ is
the concatenation of at most $n$ self-delimiting blocks, and it returns their payloads in order.

articles.title: Parsing a list of booleans into self-delimiting blocks
articles.statement:
Given a list of booleans $s$, this
repeatedly parses one self-delimiting block from the front of $s$ until $s$ is used up, allowing
at most as many blocks as the length of $s$, and returns the list of payloads in order. It fails
if some block fails to parse. The bound never binds, since every block uses at least one bit.
So the parse succeeds exactly when $s$ is a concatenation of self-delimiting blocks.

articles.title: Parsing one self-delimiting block
articles.statement:
Write booleans as bits, with true as $1$ and false as
$0$. Reading a list of bits from the front, a $0$ ends the block, and a $1$ followed by a bit $b$
contributes $b$ to the payload. The result is the payload together with the rest of the list
after the terminating $0$. Parsing fails if the list runs out before a terminating $0$ is read.

articles.title: Resource-bounded active step
articles.statement: An active step with a resource bound on its source.

articles.title: A halted state reaches its output with any time budget
articles.statement: A halted state reaches its output with any remaining time budget.

articles.title: Iterates of a halted state are constant
articles.statement: Every iterate of an already halted state is that state.

articles.title: Terminal iterates are stable
articles.statement: A terminal iterate remains unchanged at every later iteration count.

articles.title: Output reachability gives stable outputs and bounded iterates
articles.statement: Reachability gives stable outputs after the budget and bounds every iterate.

articles.title: Monotonicity of bounded runs in time and resources
articles.statement: Increasing time and resource bounds preserves initialized runs.

articles.title: Monotonicity of output reachability in the bounds
articles.statement: Increasing either bound preserves reachability.

articles.title: One iteration step with absorbing halted states
articles.statement: One iteration, preserving a state once its output is available.

articles.title: The output of a successful run persists
articles.statement: The output of a successful initialized run is present at every later time.

articles.title: Prepending a bounded step to a successful computation
articles.statement: Prepend an active bounded step to a successful computation.

articles.title: Output reachability via bounded iterates after halting
articles.statement: Finite visited-state bounds are equivalent to all-iterate bounds after halting.

articles.title: Characterization of output reachability by iterates
articles.statement: Exact source characterization, including bounds on all natural-number iterates.

articles.title: Output reachability from the iteration condition
articles.statement: The source iteration condition constructs a canonical bounded path.

articles.title: Output reachability within time and resource bounds
articles.statement: Reach an output in at most `T` active steps, with every state bounded by `S`.

articles.title: Canonical finite path to an output bounds all iterates
articles.statement: A canonical finite path ending in an output has the source's all-iterate bounds.

articles.title: Input-initialized iteration with absorbing halting
articles.statement: Iteration initialized by an input, with absorbing halting.

articles.title: Characterization of bounded runs by initialized iteration
articles.statement: The source `Runs` interface, stated using initialized iteration.

articles.title: Bounded run from an input's initial state
articles.statement: Reach an output starting from an input's initial state.

articles.title: Uniqueness of run outputs
articles.statement: Initialized runs have unique outputs.

articles.title: Uniqueness of reached outputs
articles.statement: Output values reached from the same state are unique, regardless of bounds.

articles.title: Decidability within time and space bounds, unfolded
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language of Boolean
strings and let $t$ and $s$ assign a natural number to every Boolean string. Then $L$ is decidable
within time $t$ and space $s$ in CSLib's sense, with the identity encoding of inputs, if and only
if there are a number $k$, a finite type of states and a deterministic Turing machine with $k$
work tapes over the Boolean alphabet that decides $L$ and, on every input $w$, runs in time $t(w)$
(every computation path of at least $t(w)$ steps ends in a halted configuration) and in space
$s(w)$ (every computation path visits at most $s(w)$ work-tape cells, summed over the work
tapes).

articles.title: A multi-tape machine deciding a language
articles.statement:
A deterministic multi-tape Turing machine over
the Boolean alphabet decides a language $L$ of Boolean strings when, on every input $w$, it
eventually halts with output the one-bit string $[\mathrm{true}]$ if $w \in L$ and
$[\mathrm{false}]$ if $w \notin L$.

articles.title: Deterministic space classes are monotone up to affine changes of the bound
articles.statement:
Let
$s_1, s_2 : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfy
$s_1(n) \le a \, s_2(n) + b$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then
$\mathrm{DSPACE}(s_1) \subseteq \mathrm{DSPACE}(s_2)$.

articles.title: Deterministic space classes on multi-tape machines
articles.statement:
For $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$,
$\mathrm{DSPACE}(s)$ is the set of languages $L$ of Boolean strings for which there are constants
$c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb{N}$, a function $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a deterministic
multi-tape Turing machine with Boolean tape alphabet and finitely many states such that, on every
input $w$ of length $n$, the machine halts with the one-bit output $[\mathrm{true}]$ if $w \in L$
and $[\mathrm{false}]$ otherwise, runs in time $t(n)$ (every computation path of at least $t(n)$
steps ends in a halted configuration) and runs in space $c_1 s(n) + c_2$ (every computation path
visits at most $c_1 s(n) + c_2$ work-tape cells, summed over the work tapes).

articles.title: Deterministic time classes are monotone up to affine changes of the bound
articles.statement:
Let
$t_1, t_2 : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $a, b \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfy
$t_1(n) \le a \, t_2(n) + b$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then
$\mathrm{DTIME}(t_1) \subseteq \mathrm{DTIME}(t_2)$.

articles.title: Time classes are contained in space classes
articles.statement:
For every $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$,
$\mathrm{DTIME}(t) \subseteq \mathrm{DSPACE}(t)$.

articles.title: Deterministic time classes on multi-tape machines
articles.statement:
For $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$,
$\mathrm{DTIME}(t)$ is the set of languages $L$ of Boolean strings for which there are constants
$c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb{N}$, a function $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a deterministic
multi-tape Turing machine with Boolean tape alphabet and finitely many states such that, on every
input $w$ of length $n$, the machine halts with the one-bit output $[\mathrm{true}]$ if $w \in L$
and $[\mathrm{false}]$ otherwise, runs in time $c_1 t(n) + c_2$ (every computation path of at
least $c_1 t(n) + c_2$ steps ends in a halted configuration) and runs in space $s(n)$ (every
computation path visits at most $s(n)$ work-tape cells, summed over the work tapes).

articles.title: P is contained in PSPACE
articles.statement:
On the deterministic multi-tape model,
$\mathrm{P} \subseteq \mathrm{PSPACE}$.

articles.title: Polynomial time on multi-tape machines
articles.statement:
$\mathrm{P}$ is the set of languages of Boolean
strings that lie in $\mathrm{DTIME}(n \mapsto n^d)$ for some $d \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Polynomial space on multi-tape machines
articles.statement:
