machine $M$, every $t \in \mathbb{N}$ and every cell $i \in \mathbb{Z}$, if cell $i$ holds the
symbol $1$ after $M$ runs for $t$ steps from the initial blank-tape configuration, then
$-t \le i \le t$.

articles.title: Head movement
articles.statement: A head movement is one of exactly two directions: left or right.

articles.title: A consistency-search machine blocks decidability at its size
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a formal theory
and $M$ a Busy Beaver machine with $n$ working states. Suppose that $M$ halts if and only if $T$
proves the false sentence, that $M$ halts whenever $T$ proves the halting sentence of $M$, that
$T$ is consistent, and that $T$ does not prove the non-halting sentence of $M$. Then $T$ does not
decide halting for all machines with $n$ working states.

The last hypothesis is the Gödel second-incompleteness content when $T$ is ZFC.

articles.title: A one-state machine that stays in its state on a blank never halts
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Busy Beaver
machine with a single working state $0$. If the transition of $M$ from state $0$ on reading the
blank symbol $0$ has next state $0$, then $M$ does not halt.

Such a machine marches in one direction forever: at every step the head is on a previously
unvisited blank cell.

articles.title: Non-halting sentence of a machine
articles.statement:
For a Busy Beaver machine $M$, the non-halting
sentence of $M$ is the sentence code with tag $1$ whose payload is the code of $M$; it stands
for "$M$ does not halt on the blank tape".

articles.title: At most $t$ ones after $t$ steps
articles.statement:
For every Busy Beaver machine $M$ and every
$t \in \mathbb{N}$, the number of ones of $M$ after $t$ steps is at most $t$.

articles.title: The number of ones grows by at most one per step
articles.statement:
For every Busy Beaver machine $M$
and every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the number of ones of $M$ after $t + 1$ steps is at most the
number of ones of $M$ after $t$ steps plus $1$.

articles.title: Number of ones after $t$ steps
articles.statement:
For a Busy Beaver machine $M$ and $t \in \mathbb{N}$,
the number of ones of $M$ after $t$ steps is the number of cells $i \in \mathbb{Z}$ with
$-t \le i \le t$ that hold the symbol $1$ in the configuration of $M$ after $t$ steps, started
on the blank tape.

Every one on the tape after $t$ steps lies in this window, since the head moves at most one
cell per step.

articles.title: Configuration after $t$ steps
articles.statement:
For a Busy Beaver machine $M$ and $t \in \mathbb{N}$,
the configuration of $M$ after $t$ steps is the result of applying the one-step map of $M$
$t$ times to the initial configuration on the blank tape.

articles.title: Score of a machine
articles.statement:
For a Busy Beaver machine $M$: if $M$ halts on the blank tape,
with halting time $T$, its score is the number of ones of $M$ after $T$ steps; if $M$ does not
halt, its score is $0$.

articles.title: Sentence codes
articles.statement:
The sentence code with tag $a$ and payload $p$ is the natural number
$4p + a$. The tags in use are $0$ (the coded machine halts), $1$ (the coded machine does not
halt), $2$ (the false sentence), and $3$ with payload the pairing code of $n$ and $B$ (every
halting $n$-state machine halts within $B$ steps).

Sentences are natural numbers rather than propositions, so provability does not collapse under
propositional extensionality.

articles.title: Head displacement
articles.statement:
The displacement of a head movement is $-1$ for a move to the left
and $1$ for a move to the right.

articles.title: Decidability through five states and the first undecidable size
articles.statement:
If a formal theory
$T$ decides halting for $n$-state machines for every $n \le 5$, and fails to decide halting for
$n$-state machines for some $n$, then the first undecidable size of $T$ is at least $6$.

This is the shape of the catalogue lower bound from the determination of the five-state Busy
Beaver value.

articles.title: Soundness for halting sentences
articles.statement:
A formal theory $T$ is sound for halting sentences
when, for every $n$ and every Busy Beaver machine $M$ with $n$ states, if $T$ proves the
halting sentence of $M$ then $M$ halts on the blank tape, and if $T$ proves the non-halting
sentence of $M$ then $M$ does not halt on the blank tape.

articles.title: One step of a Busy Beaver machine
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a machine with $n$ working states and let
$c$ be a configuration with head position $h$. If $c$ is halted, the step leaves $c$ unchanged.
Otherwise let $q$ be the current state, let $a$ be the symbol in cell $h$, and let
$M(q, a) = (b, d, q')$. The step writes $b$ in cell $h$, leaving every other cell unchanged, moves
the head to $h - 1$ if $d$ is left and to $h + 1$ if $d$ is right, and passes to the state $q'$,
which may be the halt state.

articles.title: Runtime of a Busy Beaver machine
articles.statement:
For a machine $M$ with $n$ working states, the runtime
of $M$ is its halting time on the blank tape if $M$ halts, and $0$ if $M$ does not halt. This is
the quantity whose maximum over all $n$-state machines is the shift function $S(n)$.

articles.title: Cells far from the origin stay blank
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a machine with $n$ working states,
started in cell $0$ on the blank tape. For every $t \in \mathbb{N}$ and every cell
$i \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $|i| > t$, the symbol in cell $i$ after $t$ steps is $0$.

articles.title: Proof-checker presentation of a ZFC-like theory
articles.statement:
A ZFC-like presentation consists of a
formal theory $T$, given by a provability predicate on sentence codes in $\mathbb{N}$, together
with a Boolean proof checker $\mathrm{check}(p, s)$ on pairs of natural numbers, such that the
following hold. A sentence code $s$ is provable in $T$ if and only if $\mathrm{check}(p, s)$ is true
for some $p \in \mathbb{N}$. $T$ is sound for halting: for every machine $M$, if $T$ proves the
halting sentence of $M$ then $M$ halts on the blank tape, and if $T$ proves the non-halting
sentence of $M$ then $M$ does not halt. For every machine $M$, if $M$ has halted within $t$ steps
for some $t$, then $T$ proves the halting sentence of $M$. Write $S(n)$ for the Busy Beaver shift
function, the largest halting time of a halting machine with $n$ working states, and call the
bound sentence for $n$ and $B$ the sentence code saying that every halting machine with $n$
working states halts within $B$ steps. For every $n \le 5$, $T$ proves the bound sentence for $n$
and $S(n)$. Whenever $T$ proves the bound sentence for $n$ and $B$, every halting machine with $n$
working states halts within $B$ steps. Whenever $T$ proves the bound sentence for $n$ and $B$ and a
machine $M$ with $n$ working states has not halted within $B$ steps, $T$ proves the non-halting
sentence of $M$.

No concrete syntax or proof checker for ZFC is given, and no presentation of ZFC is constructed;
the intended instance is ZFC with its standard proof checker. The state counts for
consistency-search machines in the literature depend on specific checker implementations and are
not asserted for arbitrary presentations.

articles.title: Recursively enumerable predicates are closed under conjunction
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type
with a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$. If $p$ and $q$ are recursively enumerable
predicates on $\alpha$, then the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \land q(a)$ is recursively enumerable.

The proof runs one semi-decision procedure, then the other.

articles.title: Decidable predicates are closed under conjunction
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on a
type $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If $p$ and $q$ are both decidable by
multi-stack machines, then so is the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \wedge q(a)$.

articles.title: Recognizable predicates are closed under conjunction
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates
on a type $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If $p$ and $q$ are both recognizable
by multi-stack machines, then so is the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \wedge q(a)$.

articles.title: Computable predicates are closed under conjunction
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a
primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$. If $p$ and $q$ are computable predicates on
$\alpha$, then the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \land q(a)$ is computable.

articles.title: Language of a Boolean test
articles.statement:
For a Boolean-valued function $f$ on words over an
alphabet $\sigma$, the language of $f$ is the set of words $u$ over $\sigma$ with
$f(u) = \mathrm{true}$.

articles.title: Searching a computable list with a computable test is computable
articles.statement:
Let $\gamma$ and
$\beta$ be types with primitive recursive encodings into $\mathbb{N}$, let $l$ be a computable
function sending each $x \in \gamma$ to a finite list $l(x)$ of elements of $\beta$, and let $g$
be a computable Boolean-valued function of $x \in \gamma$ and $b \in \beta$. Then the
Boolean-valued function that sends $x$ to true exactly when $g(x, b)$ is true for some $b$ in
$l(x)$ is computable.

The proof scans the indices of $l(x)$ by primitive recursion.

articles.title: Decidable languages have computable membership tests
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an
alphabet $\sigma$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If membership in $L$ is decidable by a
multi-stack machine, then there is a computable function $f$ from words over $\sigma$ to
Booleans such that $L$ is the language of $f$, that is, the set of words $u$ with
$f(u) = \mathrm{true}$.

articles.title: Bounded existential quantification preserves recursive enumerability
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and
$\beta$ be types with primitive recursive encodings into $\mathbb{N}$, let $R$ be a relation
between $\alpha$ and $\beta$ that is recursively enumerable as a predicate on pairs $(a, b)$, and
let $c$ be a primitive recursive function sending each $a \in \alpha$ to a finite list $c(a)$ of
elements of $\beta$. Then the predicate $a \mapsto \exists b \in c(a),\ R(a, b)$ is recursively
enumerable.

The proof is by dovetailing: it searches for a step bound $k$ at which the simulation of the
semi-decision procedure for $R$ halts on $(a, b)$ for some $b$ in $c(a)$.

articles.title: Selection for r.e. relations
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be types with primitive recursive
encodings into $\mathbb{N}$, and let $R$ be a relation between $\alpha$ and $\beta$ that is
recursively enumerable as a predicate on pairs $(a, b)$. Then there is a partial recursive
function $g$ from $\alpha$ to $\beta$ such that, for every $a \in \alpha$, if $g(a)$ is defined
then its value $b$ satisfies $R(a, b)$, and $g(a)$ is defined whenever some $b \in \beta$
satisfies $R(a, b)$.

The proof searches over pairs of a candidate $b$ and a step bound by dovetailing with the
step-bounded simulation of the semi-decision procedure for $R$.

articles.title: Existential projection preserves recursive enumerability
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be
types with primitive recursive encodings into $\mathbb{N}$, and let $R$ be a relation between
$\alpha$ and $\beta$ that is recursively enumerable as a predicate on pairs $(a, b)$. Then the
predicate $a \mapsto \exists b \in \beta,\ R(a, b)$ is recursively enumerable.

The predicate is the domain of the partial recursive function that selects a witness of $R$.

articles.title: Extending a list of pieces by a letter
articles.statement:
Given a letter $a$ and a list
$\pi = [u_1, \dots, u_k]$ of words, the extensions of $\pi$ by $a$ are listed as follows: first
$[[a], u_1, \dots, u_k]$, which starts a new piece $[a]$, and then, only when $k \ge 1$, also
$[a u_1, u_2, \dots, u_k]$, which puts the letter $a$ in front of the first piece.

articles.title: Bounded universal quantification preserves recursive enumerability
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and
$\beta$ be types with primitive recursive encodings into $\mathbb{N}$, let $R$ be a relation
between $\alpha$ and $\beta$ that is recursively enumerable as a predicate on pairs $(a, b)$, and
let $c$ be a primitive recursive function sending each $a \in \alpha$ to a finite list $c(a)$ of
elements of $\beta$. Then the predicate $a \mapsto \forall b \in c(a),\ R(a, b)$ is recursively
enumerable.

The proof searches for one step bound $k$ at which the simulation of the semi-decision procedure
for $R$ halts on $(a, b)$ for every $b$ in $c(a)$; the step-bounded simulation is monotone in $k$.

articles.title: Decidable languages are closed under Kleene star
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an
alphabet $\sigma$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If membership in $L$ is decidable by a
multi-stack machine, then so is membership in the Kleene star $L^*$, the set of all
concatenations $u_1 \cdots u_k$ with $k \ge 0$ and $u_1, \dots, u_k \in L$.

articles.title: Recognizable languages are closed under Kleene star
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an
alphabet $\sigma$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If membership in $L$ is recognizable by
a multi-stack machine, then so is membership in the Kleene star $L^*$, the set of all
concatenations $u_1 \cdots u_k$ with $k \ge 0$ and $u_1, \dots, u_k \in L$.

articles.title: Recognizable languages are closed under alphabet maps
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ and $\tau$ be
alphabets with primitive recursive encodings, let $f : \sigma \to \tau$ be primitive recursive,
and let $L$ be a language over $\sigma$. If membership in $L$ is recognizable by a multi-stack
machine, then so is membership in the image language
$f(L) = \{f(a_1) \cdots f(a_n) : a_1 \cdots a_n \in L\}$, obtained by applying $f$ letter by
letter to the words of $L$.

The recognizer searches for a preimage word by unbounded dovetailing. Every map between finite
alphabets is primitive recursive.

articles.title: Membership in a concatenation of languages
articles.statement:
For languages $L_1$ and $L_2$ over an
alphabet $\sigma$ and a word $w$ over $\sigma$, $w$ lies in the concatenation $L_1 L_2$ if and
only if there are words $u$ and $v$ with $w = uv$, $u \in L_1$ and $v \in L_2$.

articles.title: Recognizable languages are closed under concatenation
articles.statement:
Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be
languages over an alphabet $\sigma$ with a primitive recursive encoding. If membership in $L_1$
and membership in $L_2$ are recognizable by multi-stack machines, then so is membership in the
concatenation $L_1 L_2$, the set of words $uv$ with $u \in L_1$ and $v \in L_2$.

articles.title: Decidable languages are closed under concatenation
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be an alphabet with a
primitive recursive encoding. If $L_1$ and $L_2$ are languages over $\sigma$ whose membership
predicates are decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine, then the membership predicate of their
concatenation $L_1 L_2 = \{uv : u \in L_1, v \in L_2\}$ is also decidable by a multi-stack
Turing machine.

articles.title: Decidability by multi-stack machines is closed under complement
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then
so is its complement $\neg p$.

articles.title: Recursively enumerable predicates are closed under disjunction
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type
with a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$. If $p$ and $q$ are recursively enumerable
predicates on $\alpha$, then the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \lor q(a)$ is recursively enumerable.

The proof runs both semi-decision procedures in parallel.

articles.title: Decidable predicates are closed under disjunction
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a
primitive recursive encoding. If $p$ and $q$ are predicates on $\alpha$ that are decidable by a
multi-stack Turing machine, then so is the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \lor q(a)$.

articles.title: Recognizable predicates are closed under disjunction
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a
primitive recursive encoding. If $p$ and $q$ are predicates on $\alpha$ that are recognizable by
a multi-stack Turing machine, then so is the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \lor q(a)$.

articles.title: Computable predicates are closed under disjunction
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a
primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$. If $p$ and $q$ are computable predicates on
$\alpha$, then the predicate $a \mapsto p(a) \lor q(a)$ is computable.

articles.title: Partitions of a word into nonempty factors
articles.statement:
For a word $w$ over $\sigma$, this is the
list of all ways to write $w$ as a concatenation $w = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_k$ of nonempty words
$u_1, \dots, u_k$, each recorded as the list $[u_1, \dots, u_k]$. The empty word has exactly one
such partition, the empty list.

articles.title: Bounded split test
articles.statement:
Given Boolean tests $f$ and $g$ on words over $\sigma$, a word $w$ and
a natural number $n$, the split test is the Boolean value that is true exactly when there is some
$i < n$ such that $f$ is true on the prefix of $w$ of length $\min(i, |w|)$ and $g$ is true on
the remaining suffix of $w$.

articles.title: Splits of a word
articles.statement:
For a word $w$ over $\sigma$ of length $n$, this is the list of the
$n + 1$ pairs $(u, v)$ of words with $uv = w$, ordered by the length of $u$: for each
$i = 0, 1, \dots, n$ it contains the prefix of $w$ of length $i$ paired with the remaining
suffix.

articles.title: Decidable predicates are co-recognizable by multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then
$p$ is co-recognizable by a multi-stack machine, that is, its complement $\neg p$ is recognizable
by a multi-stack machine.

articles.title: Multi-stack co-recognizable predicates are exactly the co-r.e. predicates
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be
a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is co-recognizable by a multi-stack machine if
and only if its complement $\neg p$ is recursively enumerable, that is, the partial function on
$\alpha$ that is defined, with a trivial value, exactly where $\neg p$ holds is partial
recursive.

articles.title: Co-recognizability by multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an
encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A
predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is co-recognizable by a multi-stack machine when its complement
$\neg p$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine.

articles.title: Multi-stack decidable predicates are exactly the computable predicates
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine if and
only if it is computable, that is, $p$ is decidable and its Boolean characteristic function
$\alpha \to \mathrm{Bool}$ is computable.

articles.title: Post's theorem for multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an
encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A
predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine if and only if it is both
recognizable and co-recognizable by a multi-stack machine.

articles.title: Decidability by multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an
encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A
predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine when there is a function
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ computed by a multi-stack Turing machine, with input and output
numbers written in binary, such that for every $a \in \alpha$, $f(\mathrm{encode}(a)) = 1$ if and
only if $p(a)$.

articles.title: Decidable predicates are recognizable by multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then
$p$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine.

articles.title: Multi-stack recognizable predicates are exactly the r.e. predicates
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine if and
only if it is recursively enumerable, that is, the partial function on $\alpha$ that is defined,
with a trivial value, exactly where $p$ holds is partial recursive.

articles.title: Recognizability by multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an
encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A
predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine when there are a multi-stack
Turing machine $M$ and an identification of its input alphabet with the Booleans such that for
every $a \in \alpha$, $p(a)$ holds if and only if $M$ halts when started on the binary word of
$\mathrm{encode}(a)$.

articles.title: Codes with empty domain
articles.statement:
The set $E$ consists of the codes $c$ of partial recursive
functions on $\mathbb{N}$ that are defined on no input: for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the
function computed by $c$ is undefined at $n$.

articles.title: Equivalent codes
articles.statement:
The set $EQ$ consists of the pairs $(c_1, c_2)$ of codes of partial
recursive functions on $\mathbb{N}$ that recognize the same language, that is, whose computed
functions have the same domain: for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the function computed by $c_1$ is
defined at $n$ if and only if the function computed by $c_2$ is.

articles.title: A code defined nowhere
articles.statement:
There is a code $e$ of a partial recursive function on
$\mathbb{N}$ whose computed function is the empty partial function, undefined at every input.

articles.title: Halting-on-zero code
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function on $\mathbb{N}$, the
code $h(c)$ is the composition $k_0 \circ c \circ k_0$, where $k_0$ is the code of the constant
function $0$: whatever its input, $h(c)$ runs $c$ on $0$ and, if this halts, outputs $0$.

articles.title: Emptiness reduces to equivalence
articles.statement:
The set $E$ of codes of partial recursive functions
defined on no input is many-one reducible to the set $EQ$ of pairs of codes with the same
domain: there is a computable map $f$ from codes to pairs of codes such that, for every code $c$,
$c \in E$ if and only if $f(c) \in EQ$.

One can take $f(c) = (c, e)$ for a code $e$ defined nowhere.

articles.title: Halting on zero reduces to equivalence
articles.statement:
The set of codes $c$ of partial recursive
functions on $\mathbb{N}$ that halt on input $0$ (are defined at $0$) is many-one reducible to
the set $EQ$ of pairs of codes with the same domain: there is a computable map $f$ from codes to
pairs of codes such that, for every code $c$, $c$ halts on $0$ if and only if $f(c) \in EQ$.

One can take $f(c) = (h(c), k_0)$, where $h(c)$ runs $c$ on $0$ and then outputs $0$ whatever
its input, and $k_0$ is the code of the constant function $0$.

articles.title: Equivalence is not co-recognizable
articles.statement:
The set $EQ$ of pairs of codes of partial recursive
functions on $\mathbb{N}$ with the same domain is not co-recognizable by multi-stack machines:
no multi-stack machine, started on the binary encoding of a pair of codes, halts exactly when
the pair is not in $EQ$.

The complement of halting on $0$ would reduce to the complement of equivalence.

articles.title: Emptiness is undecidable
articles.statement:
The set $E$ of codes of partial recursive functions on
$\mathbb{N}$ that are defined on no input is not decidable by multi-stack machines.

By Rice's theorem: the identity function is defined, the empty function is not.

articles.title: Emptiness is not recognizable
articles.statement:
The set $E$ of codes of partial recursive functions on
$\mathbb{N}$ that are defined on no input is not recognizable by multi-stack machines: no
multi-stack machine, started on the binary encoding of a code, halts exactly when the code is
in $E$.

Since $E$ is co-recognizable, it would otherwise be decidable, by Post's theorem.

articles.title: Equivalence is not recognizable
articles.statement:
The set $EQ$ of pairs of codes of partial recursive
functions on $\mathbb{N}$ with the same domain is not recognizable by multi-stack machines: no
multi-stack machine, started on the binary encoding of a pair of codes, halts exactly when the
pair is in $EQ$.

articles.title: Emptiness is co-recognizable
articles.statement:
The set of codes of partial recursive functions
$\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that are defined on no input is co-recognizable by multi-stack
machines: some multi-stack machine halts on the binary encoding of a code $c$ exactly when the
function coded by $c$ is defined on at least one input.

articles.title: Nonemptiness is recognizable
articles.statement:
The set of codes of partial recursive functions
$\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that are defined on at least one input is recognizable by
multi-stack machines: some multi-stack machine halts on the binary encoding of a code $c$ exactly
when the function coded by $c$ is defined on some input.

The machine searches for an input $n$ and a step bound $k$ such that the evaluation of $c$ on $n$
halts within $k$ steps.

articles.title: Enumerating a predicate
articles.statement:
For a type $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, a
function $e$ assigning to each natural number $n$ either an element $e(n)$ of $\alpha$ or nothing
enumerates a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ when, for every $a \in \alpha$, $p(a)$ holds if and only if
$e(n) = a$ for some natural number $n$.

articles.title: Recognizable languages are enumerable
articles.statement:
For every type $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive
encoding and every predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ that is recognizable by a multi-stack machine, there
is a computable function $e$, assigning to each natural number either an element of $\alpha$ or
nothing, that enumerates $p$.

articles.title: Recognizable languages are exactly the enumerable ones
articles.statement:
For every type $\alpha$ with a
primitive recursive encoding, a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine
if and only if some computable function $e$, assigning to each natural number either an element
of $\alpha$ or nothing, enumerates $p$. This is Sipser, Theorem 3.21: a language is
Turing-recognizable if and only if some enumerator enumerates it.

articles.title: Enumerable languages are recognizable
articles.statement:
For every type $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive
encoding, every predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and every computable function $e$, assigning to each
natural number either an element of $\alpha$ or nothing, that enumerates $p$, the predicate $p$ is
recognizable by a multi-stack machine.

articles.title: Parametrized s-m-n theorem
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a primitive recursive encoding into
the natural numbers, and for each $a \in \alpha$ let $F_a$ be a partial function from
$\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$, such that $(a, x) \mapsto F_a(x)$ is partial recursive. Then there
is a computable map $g$ from $\alpha$ to codes of partial recursive functions such that for all
$a \in \alpha$ and $x \in \mathbb{N}$, the partial function with code $g(a)$ agrees with $F_a$ at
$x$: both are undefined, or both are defined with the same value.

articles.title: Codes with finite domain
articles.statement:
A code $c$ of a partial recursive function $\varphi_c$ on
$\mathbb{N}$ is finite when the domain of $\varphi_c$, the set of inputs on which $c$ halts, is
finite. The set of finite codes is denoted $\mathrm{FIN}$.

articles.title: Domain of the halts-within function
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function, let
$h_c$ be the partial function on $\mathbb{N}$ that on input $j$ outputs $0$ if $c$ halts on input
$0$ within $j$ steps (the step-bounded evaluation of $c$ on input $0$ with bound $j$ returns a
value) and is undefined otherwise. Then for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $h_c$ is defined at $k$ if
and only if $c$ halts on input $0$ within $k$ steps.

articles.title: Halts-within function
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function, $h_c$ is the
partial function on $\mathbb{N}$ that on input $k$ outputs $0$ if $c$ halts on input $0$ within
$k$ steps (the step-bounded evaluation of $c$ on input $0$ with bound $k$ returns a value) and
is undefined otherwise.

articles.title: Halting reduces to finiteness
articles.statement:
The set of codes of partial recursive functions that halt
on input $0$ is many-one reducible to the set of finite codes: there is a computable function $f$
from codes to codes such that, for every code $c$, $c$ halts on input $0$ if and only if the
partial function of $f(c)$ has finite domain.

articles.title: Non-halting reduces to finiteness
articles.statement:
The set of codes of partial recursive functions that do
not halt on input $0$ is many-one reducible to the set of finite codes: there is a computable
function $f$ from codes to codes such that, for every code $c$, $c$ does not halt on input $0$ if
and only if the partial function of $f(c)$ has finite domain.

articles.title: Finiteness is not co-recognizable
articles.statement:
The set of codes of partial recursive functions with
finite domain is not co-recognizable by multi-stack Turing machines: no finite multi-stack machine
whose input alphabet is identified with $\{0, 1\}$ halts on the binary encoding of the number of
a code $c$ exactly when the partial function of $c$ has infinite domain.

articles.title: Finiteness is undecidable
articles.statement:
The set of codes of partial recursive functions with finite
domain is not decidable by multi-stack Turing machines: there is no total function
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ computed by a finite multi-stack machine on binary encodings such
that, for every code $c$ with number $n_c$, $f(n_c) = 1$ if and only if the partial function of
$c$ has finite domain.

articles.title: Finiteness is not recognizable
articles.statement:
The set of codes of partial recursive functions with
finite domain is not recognizable by multi-stack Turing machines: no finite multi-stack machine
whose input alphabet is identified with $\{0, 1\}$ halts on the binary encoding of the number of
a code $c$ exactly when the partial function of $c$ has finite domain.

articles.title: Domain of the until-halts function
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function, let
$u_c$ be the partial function on $\mathbb{N}$ that on input $j$ is undefined if $c$ halts on input
$0$ within $j$ steps (the step-bounded evaluation of $c$ on input $0$ with bound $j$ returns a
value) and outputs $0$ otherwise. Then for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $u_c$ is defined at $k$ if
and only if $c$ does not halt on input $0$ within $k$ steps.

articles.title: Acceptance by a code
articles.statement:
A partial recursive code $c$ accepts a natural number $n$ when $c$
halts on input $n$ with output $0$. Acceptance is a predicate on pairs $(c, n)$; it is the analogue
of Sipser's $A_{\mathrm{TM}}$, where a machine may halt without accepting.

articles.title: A single code for the regularity reduction function
articles.statement:
For a pair $q = (c, n)$ of a partial
recursive code and a natural number, let $g_q$ be the partial function on $\mathbb{N}$ that on
input $x$ halts with output $0$ if $x$ is a perfect square, and otherwise runs $c$ on $n$ and,
if that halts, outputs $0$ (and is undefined if it does not). Write $\ulcorner q \urcorner$ for
the standard encoding of $q$ as a natural number, and $\langle a, b \rangle$ for the standard
pairing of natural numbers $a$ and $b$. There is a partial recursive code $U$ such that for every
such pair $q$ and every $x \in \mathbb{N}$, the value of $U$ at
$\langle \ulcorner q \urcorner, x \rangle$ equals $g_q(x)$ as a partial value: one is defined
exactly when the other is, and then they agree.

articles.title: A code that halts only on zero
articles.statement:
There is a partial recursive code $z$ that on input $0$
halts with output $0$ and on every input $x \ne 0$ does not halt.

articles.title: Some multi-stack machine has an undecidable halting set
articles.statement:
There is a multi-stack machine
$M$, with a bijection between its input alphabet and the Booleans, such that no multi-stack
machine decides, for $n \in \mathbb{N}$, whether $M$ halts when started on the binary
representation of $n$ (written in $M$'s input alphabet through the bijection).

The halting set of a code interpreter on input $0$ is r.e., hence the halting set of a
multi-stack machine, and deciding it would decide the halting problem.

articles.title: Halting of a code on an input
articles.statement:
A partial recursive code $c$ halts on a natural number $n$
when its evaluation at $n$ is defined. Halting is a predicate on pairs $(c, n)$; it is the analogue
of Sipser's $\mathrm{HALT}_{\mathrm{TM}}$.

articles.title: Acceptance reduces to halting
articles.statement:
Say a partial recursive code $c$ accepts a natural number
$n$ when $c$ halts on input $n$ with output $0$. Acceptance many-one reduces to halting: there is
a computable map $f$ from pairs $(c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number to such
pairs, such that for every pair $(c, n)$, the code $c$ accepts $n$ if and only if, writing
$f(c, n) = (c', n')$, the code $c'$ halts on $n'$.

The reduction runs the code, then loops unless the output is $0$.

articles.title: Halting reduces to acceptance
articles.statement:
Say a partial recursive code $c$ accepts a natural number
$n$ when $c$ halts on input $n$ with output $0$. Halting many-one reduces to acceptance: there is
a computable map $f$ from pairs $(c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number to such
pairs, such that for every pair $(c, n)$, the code $c$ halts on $n$ if and only if, writing
$f(c, n) = (c', n')$, the code $c'$ accepts $n'$.

The reduction runs the code, then outputs $0$.

articles.title: Halting reduces to regularity of halting sets
articles.statement:
There is a computable map $f$ from pairs
$(c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number to partial recursive codes such that for
every pair $(c, n)$, the code $c$ halts on $n$ if and only if the halting set of $f(c, n)$ (the set
of inputs on which it halts), read as a unary language, is regular. That is, halting many-one
reduces to regularity of halting sets.

The construction follows Sipser's proof of Theorem 5.3: $f(c, n)$ halts on every perfect square,
and on every input if $c$ halts on $n$.

articles.title: Mapping reductions are computed by multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on
primitive recursively encodable types $\alpha$ and $\beta$, and write $\langle x \rangle \in
\mathbb{N}$ for the code of $x$. Then $p$ is many-one reducible to $q$ if and only if there is a
function $f : \alpha \to \beta$ with $p(a) \iff q(f(a))$ for all $a \in \alpha$, together with a
function $F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that a multi-stack machine computes on binary
representations and that satisfies $F(\langle a \rangle) = \langle f(a) \rangle$ for all
$a \in \alpha$.

articles.title: The unary squares are not regular
articles.statement:
The unary language of the perfect squares, the set of
words over a one-letter alphabet whose length is $m^2$ for some $m \in \mathbb{N}$, is not regular.

The proof uses the pumping lemma: if a DFA with $N$ states accepted this language, pumping the word
of length $N^2$ by a block of length between $1$ and $N$ would give a length strictly between $N^2$
and $(N + 1)^2$.

articles.title: The halting problem is not co-recognizable by multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
For every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, the set of partial recursive codes whose program halts on input $n$ is not
co-recognizable by a multi-stack machine: no multi-stack machine halts on exactly the codes
whose program does not halt on input $n$.

articles.title: Acceptance is undecidable
articles.statement:
No multi-stack Turing machine decides, for pairs $(c, n)$ of a
partial recursive code and a natural number, whether $c$ accepts $n$, that is, halts on $n$ with
output $0$.

This is Sipser's Theorem 4.11, with partial recursive codes in place of Turing machines.

articles.title: The halting problem is undecidable by multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
no multi-stack machine decides whether a partial recursive code halts on input $n$.

articles.title: Halting is undecidable
articles.statement:
No multi-stack Turing machine decides, for pairs $(c, n)$ of a
partial recursive code and a natural number, whether $c$ halts on $n$.

articles.title: Rice's theorem for languages
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a set of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, and suppose
there are partial recursive codes $c_1$ and $c_2$ such that the domain of $c_1$ (the set of
inputs on which it halts) belongs to $P$ and the domain of $c_2$ does not. Then the property of a
partial recursive code $c$ that the domain of $c$ belongs to $P$ is not decidable by a
multi-stack Turing machine.

articles.title: Rice's theorem for partial recursive codes
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a set of partial functions
$\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$, and suppose there are partial recursive functions
$f \in C$ and $g \notin C$. Then the property of a partial recursive code $c$ that the partial
function computed by $c$ belongs to $C$ is not decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine.

articles.title: Regularity of halting sets is undecidable
articles.statement:
For a partial recursive code $c$, let
$\operatorname{dom}(c) \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be the set of inputs on which $c$ halts. The
property of $c$ that the unary language $\{w \in \{\ast\}^* : |w| \in \operatorname{dom}(c)\}$
is regular is not decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine.

articles.title: Codes with a regular halting set
articles.statement:
A partial recursive code $c$ has a regular halting set
when the unary language of its domain (the set of inputs on which $c$ halts), that is, the
language of the words over a one-letter alphabet whose length lies in the domain of $c$, is
regular.

This is a domain analogue of Sipser's $\mathrm{REGULAR}_{\mathrm{TM}}$, which asks about the
accepted words instead.

articles.title: Partial function of the halting-to-regularity reduction
articles.statement:
For a partial recursive code
$c$ and natural numbers $n$ and $x$, the value at $((c, n), x)$ is $0$ if $x$ is a perfect
square; otherwise it is defined exactly when $c$ halts on input $n$, and then it is $0$.

articles.title: Rice's theorem for multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a set of partial functions
$\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. If a multi-stack machine decides, for each partial recursive code,
whether the function the code computes lies in $C$, then for all partial recursive functions
$f$ and $g$, $f \in C$ implies $g \in C$.

articles.title: Decidability transfers along mapping reductions
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on
primitive recursively encodable types $\alpha$ and $\beta$. If $p$ is many-one reducible to $q$
and $q$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then $p$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine.

articles.title: The halting problem is recognizable by multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
For every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, the set of partial recursive codes whose program halts on input $n$ is
recognizable by a multi-stack machine.

articles.title: Recognizability transfers along mapping reductions
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on
primitive recursively encodable types $\alpha$ and $\beta$. If $p$ is many-one reducible to $q$
and $q$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine, then $p$ is recognizable by a multi-stack
machine.

articles.title: Unary language of a set of naturals
articles.statement:
For a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the unary
language of $S$ is the language over the one-letter alphabet $\{\ast\}$ consisting of the words
whose length lies in $S$.

articles.title: The halting problem for single-tape machines is undecidable
articles.statement:
There are a finite tape
alphabet $\Gamma$ with a blank symbol, decidable equality and a primitive recursive coding, a type
of states $\Lambda$ with a start state, a single-tape Turing machine $M$ with alphabet $\Gamma$ and
states $\Lambda$, and a finite set $S$ of states that contains the start state and is closed under
the transitions of $M$, such that the set of input words on which $M$ halts is not decidable by a
multi-stack machine.

articles.title: Primitive recursive coding of a finite type
articles.statement:
A finite type $\alpha$ with $n$ elements gets
the primitive recursive coding transported from $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ along a fixed (noncanonically
chosen) bijection between $\alpha$ and $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$.

articles.title: The input encoding of the single-tape emulation is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a
multi-stack machine together with a bijection $e$ from the alphabet of its input stack to the
Booleans, and suppose the tape alphabet $\Gamma'$ of the single-tape emulation of $M$ is finite and
carries a primitive recursive coding. Then the map sending $n \in \mathbb{N}$ to the initial tape
of the emulation on the input word $e^{-1}(b_1) \cdots e^{-1}(b_m)$, where $b_1 \cdots b_m$ is the
binary code of $n$, is primitive recursive.

articles.title: Halting of a single-tape machine
articles.statement:
A single-tape Turing machine $M$ halts on an input word
$l$ when its run, started in its start state with $l$ on the tape, reaches a halting
configuration.

articles.title: Halting agrees with evaluation for multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
A multi-stack machine halts on a
word $l$ over the alphabet of its input stack if and only if the evaluation of its transition
function, started at its main label and initial internal state with $l$ on the input stack and
all other stacks empty, is defined.

articles.title: A code that halts exactly on its own number
articles.statement:
There is a code $c$ of a partial recursive
function on $\mathbb{N}$ such that, for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $c$ halts on input $n$ if and
only if $n$ is the number encoding $c$.

articles.title: A quine
articles.statement:
There is a code $c$ of a partial recursive function on $\mathbb{N}$ that, on
every input $n \in \mathbb{N}$, halts and outputs the number encoding $c$.

articles.title: Description length of a code
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function, the
description length of $c$ is the number of binary digits of the encoding of $c$ as a natural
number, that is, the least $k$ such that this encoding is less than $2^k$ (so it is $0$ when the
encoding is $0$).

articles.title: Codes with singleton domain
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$ there is a code $c$ of a partial
recursive function whose evaluation is defined exactly at $n$, that is, the domain of the partial
function computed by $c$ is $\{n\}$.

articles.title: Every language of a code has a minimal code
articles.statement:
For every code $c$ of a partial recursive
function there is a minimal code $D$ whose domain equals the domain of $c$, where the domain of a
code is the set of inputs on which its evaluation is defined.

articles.title: Minimal codes are unbounded
articles.statement:
For every natural number $N$ there is a minimal code $D$ of a
partial recursive function whose encoding as a natural number is greater than $N$.

articles.title: Minimal codes
articles.statement:
A code $c$ of a partial recursive function is minimal when no code with a
shorter description has the same domain: for every code $d$ whose description length is strictly
less than that of $c$, the domain of $d$ (the set of inputs on which its evaluation is defined)
differs from the domain of $c$. The set of minimal codes is denoted $\mathrm{MIN}$.

articles.title: Minimal codes are not recognizable
articles.statement:
The set $\mathrm{MIN}$ of minimal codes of partial
recursive functions is not recognizable by a multi-stack Turing machine: there is no finite
multi-stack machine that, for every code $c$, halts on the binary encoding of the natural-number
encoding of $c$ exactly when $c$ is minimal.

## Sources

- M. Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed., Theorem 6.7.

articles.title: Rogers's fixed-point theorem for acceptable numberings
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ assign to each
natural number $e$ a partial function $\varphi_e : \mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$, and
suppose that the universal function $(e, n) \mapsto \varphi_e(n)$ is partial computable, that
every partial computable function $f : \mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ equals $\varphi_e$
for some $e$, and that for every partial computable
$g : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ there is a total computable
$s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $\varphi_{s(e)}(n) = g(e, n)$ for all $e$ and $n$. Then for
every total computable $h : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ there is an $e$ with
$\varphi_e(n) = \varphi_{h(e)}(n)$ for all $n$.

articles.title: Rice's theorem for acceptable numberings
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ assign to each natural number $e$
a partial function $\varphi_e : \mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$, and suppose that every
$\varphi_e$ is partial computable, that the universal function $(e, n) \mapsto \varphi_e(n)$ is
partial computable, that every partial computable function
$f : \mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ equals $\varphi_e$ for some $e$, and that for every
partial computable $g : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ there is a total
computable $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $\varphi_{s(e)}(n) = g(e, n)$ for all $e$ and $n$.
Let $C \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a set of indices closed under extensional equality, that is, if
$\varphi_a(n) = \varphi_b(n)$ for all $n$, then $a \in C$ if and only if $b \in C$; and suppose
that $C$ is neither empty nor all of $\mathbb{N}$. Then there is no total computable
$d : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that, for every $e$, $e \in C$ if and only if $d(e) = 1$,
and $e \notin C$ if and only if $d(e) = 0$.

Proof: The standard argument first derives Kleene's recursion theorem for the acceptable
numbering, then diagonalizes a putative decider, following Rice (1953), Rogers §11.2, and
Soare II.3.1.

## Sources

- H. G. Rice, *Classes of recursively enumerable sets and their decision problems*, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 74(2) (1953), 358-366.

articles.title: Effective Rice–Shapiro, necessity
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a class of partial functions
$\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ whose index set, the set of codes $c$ of partial
recursive functions such that the function computed by $c$ is in $C$, is recognizable. Then there
is a recognizable set $B$ of finite lists of pairs of natural numbers, each of which is a graph,
such that a partial recursive function $f$ is in $C$ if and only if some $\theta \in B$
satisfies: for every pair $(x, y)$ in $\theta$, $f(x)$ is defined and equals $y$.

articles.title: Finite-domain partial functions are finite functions
articles.statement:
For every partial function
$g : \mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ with finite domain there is a finite list $\theta$ of
pairs of natural numbers such that the finite function of $\theta$ is $g$ and, for every pair
$(x, y)$ in $\theta$, $g(x)$ is defined and equals $y$.

articles.title: Finite function of a list of pairs
articles.statement:
For a finite list $\theta$ of pairs of natural
numbers, the finite function of $\theta$ is the partial function
$\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ whose value at $x$ is the second component of the first
pair in $\theta$ with first component $x$, and which is undefined at $x$ when $\theta$ has no pair
with first component $x$.

articles.title: Graphs of finite functions
articles.statement:
A finite list $\theta$ of pairs of natural numbers is a graph
when, for every pair $(x, y)$ in $\theta$, the finite function of $\theta$ takes the value $y$ at
$x$; that is, the first pair in $\theta$ with first component $x$ is $(x, y)$.

articles.title: Being a graph is recursively enumerable
articles.statement:
The set of finite lists of pairs of natural
numbers that are graphs is recursively enumerable.

This set is in fact decidable.

articles.title: Extending a finite list of pairs is recursively enumerable
articles.statement:
The set of pairs
$(c, \theta)$, where $c$ is a code of a partial recursive function and $\theta$ is a finite list of
pairs of natural numbers, such that for every pair $(x, y)$ in $\theta$ the function computed by
$c$ is defined at $x$ with value $y$, is recursively enumerable.

articles.title: Rice–Shapiro, finite approximation
articles.statement:
Every partial recursive member of a class with a
recognizable index set has a partial recursive finite subfunction in the class.

articles.title: Rice–Shapiro, upward closure
articles.statement:
In a class with a recognizable index set, every partial
recursive extension of a partial recursive member is a member.

articles.title: The effective Rice–Shapiro theorem
articles.statement:
A class of partial functions has a recognizable index
set iff, among partial recursive functions, its members are exactly the extensions of the finite
functions in some recognizable set of graphs.

articles.title: Effective Rice–Shapiro, sufficiency
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a class of partial functions
$\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ and let $B$ be a recognizable set of finite lists of pairs
of natural numbers. Suppose that a partial recursive function $f$ is in $C$ if and only if some
$\theta \in B$ satisfies: for every pair $(x, y)$ in $\theta$, $f(x)$ is defined and equals $y$.
Then the index set of $C$, the set of codes $c$ of partial recursive functions such that the
function computed by $c$ is in $C$, is recognizable.

articles.title: Halting on zero reduces to totality
articles.statement:
Writing $\varphi_c$ for the partial function on
$\mathbb{N}$ computed by a code $c$ of a partial recursive function, the set of codes $c$ with
$\varphi_c(0)$ defined is many-one reducible to the set of total codes, the codes that halt on
every input: there is a computable function $f$ from codes to codes such that, for every code
$c$, $\varphi_c(0)$ is defined if and only if $f(c)$ is total.

articles.title: Non-halting on zero reduces to totality
articles.statement:
Writing $\varphi_c$ for the partial function on
$\mathbb{N}$ computed by a code $c$ of a partial recursive function, the set of codes $c$ with
$\varphi_c(0)$ undefined is many-one reducible to the set of total codes, the codes that halt on
every input: there is a computable function $f$ from codes to codes such that, for every code
$c$, $\varphi_c(0)$ is undefined if and only if $f(c)$ is total.

articles.title: Totality is not co-recognizable
articles.statement:
The set of total codes, the codes of partial recursive
functions that halt on every input, is not co-recognizable by multi-stack machines: no
multi-stack machine halts on the binary encoding of a code $c$ exactly when $c$ is not total.

articles.title: Totality is undecidable
articles.statement:
The set of total codes, the codes of partial recursive functions
that halt on every input, is not decidable by multi-stack machines: no multi-stack machine
computes a total function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that takes the value $1$ at the number
encoding a code $c$ exactly when $c$ is total.

articles.title: Totality is not recognizable
articles.statement:
The set of total codes, the codes of partial recursive
functions that halt on every input, is not recognizable by multi-stack machines: no multi-stack
machine halts on the binary encoding of a code $c$ exactly when $c$ is total.

articles.title: Total codes
articles.statement:
A code $c$ of a partial recursive function is total when it halts on every
input: writing $\varphi_c$ for the partial function on $\mathbb{N}$ that $c$ computes,
$\varphi_c(n)$ is defined for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Diverging once a code halts on zero
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function, this
is the partial function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that on input $k$ is undefined if $c$ halts
on input $0$ within $k$ steps of bounded evaluation, and equals $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Closure of context-free languages under union
articles.statement:
If $L$ and $M$ are context-free languages
over the same alphabet, then their union $L \cup M$ is context-free.

articles.title: Letter numbering for the substitution grammar
articles.statement:
For a context-free grammar $g$ and a
letter $a$, the number of $a$ is the position (counted from $0$) of the first occurrence of $a$
in the list of terminals occurring in the productions of $g$, or the length of that list when $a$
does not occur in it.

articles.title: Letter decoding for the substitution grammar
articles.statement:
For a context-free grammar $g$ and a natural
number $k$, the letter with number $k$ is the entry at position $k$ (counted from $0$) of the list
of terminals occurring in the productions of $g$; there is no such letter when $k$ is at least the
length of that list.

articles.title: The substitution grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar over $T$ with nonterminals
$N_g$ and start symbol $S$, and let $e$ assign to each letter $a \in T$ an encoded grammar $e(a)$
over $T'$. The substitution grammar is the context-free grammar over $T'$ with nonterminals
$N_g \sqcup (\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N})$, start symbol $S$ taken in the left part, and the
productions of the substitution grammar for $g$ and $e$.

articles.title: Context-free languages are closed under homomorphic images
articles.statement:
Let $T$ and $T'$ be alphabets,
$L$ a context-free language over $T$, and $\varphi$ a map sending each letter of $T$ to a word
over $T'$. Then the language of all words $\varphi(a_1) \cdots \varphi(a_n)$ with
$a_1 \cdots a_n \in L$ is context-free.

A grammar for it replaces every terminal $a$ in every production by the word $\varphi(a)$.

articles.title: Intersection of a context-free language with the language of a DFA
articles.statement:
If $L$ is a
context-free language over an alphabet $T$ and $M$ is a deterministic finite automaton over $T$
with finitely many states, then the intersection of $L$ with the language accepted by $M$ is
context-free.

articles.title: Intersection of a context-free language with a regular language
articles.statement:
If $L$ is a context-free
language and $R$ a regular language over the same alphabet, then $L \cap R$ is context-free.

No finite-alphabet assumption is needed: the grammar built in the proof only mentions terminals
that occur in the productions of the original grammar.

articles.title: Closure of context-free languages under Kleene star
articles.statement:
If $L$ is a context-free language,
then its Kleene star $L^*$ is context-free.

articles.title: Main production of the substitution grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar over $T$
with nonterminals $N_g$, and let $e$ assign to each letter $a \in T$ an encoded grammar $e(a)$
over $T'$. A production $A \to \alpha$ over $T$ with nonterminals in $N_g$ gives the production
$A \to \alpha'$ over $T'$ with nonterminals in $N_g \sqcup (\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N})$, where
$A$ is taken in the left part and $\alpha'$ is obtained from $\alpha$ by replacing each
nonterminal $B$ by $B$ in the left part and each terminal $a$ by the nonterminal $(k, n)$; here
$k$ is the number of $a$ (the position, counted from $0$, of the first occurrence of $a$ in the
list of terminals occurring in the productions of $g$, or the length of that list when $a$ does
not occur in it) and $n$ is the start nonterminal of $e(a)$.

articles.title: Context-free languages are closed under letter maps
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a context-free language
over an alphabet $T$ and let $f \colon T \to T'$ be a map of alphabets. Then the image of $L$
under $f$, the language $\{f(a_1) \cdots f(a_n) \mid a_1 \cdots a_n \in L\}$ over $T'$, is
context-free.

articles.title: Derivations keep the terminals among those of the grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free
grammar and let the sentential form $u$ derive $v$ in $g$ in zero or more steps. If every terminal
occurring in $u$ occurs in some production of $g$, then every terminal occurring in $v$ occurs in
some production of $g$.

articles.title: Closure of context-free languages under concatenation
articles.statement:
If $L$ and $M$ are context-free
languages over the same alphabet, then their concatenation $LM = \{uv : u \in L,\ v \in M\}$ is
context-free.

articles.title: Finite languages are context-free
articles.statement: Every finite language is context-free.

articles.title: Languages of bounded word length are context-free
articles.statement:
Over a finite alphabet, if $n$ is a
natural number and every word of a language $L$ has length at most $n$, then $L$ is
context-free.

articles.title: Powers of a context-free language are context-free
articles.statement:
If $L$ is a context-free language,
then for every natural number $n$ the power $L^n$, the concatenation of $n$ copies of $L$ (with
$L^0$ the language containing only the empty word), is context-free.

articles.title: Productions of the substitution grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar over $T$, and
let $e$ assign to each letter $a \in T$ an encoded grammar $e(a)$ over $T'$. The productions of
the substitution grammar are the main productions obtained from the productions of $g$, together
with, for each terminal $a$ occurring in a production of $g$, the letter productions for $a$
obtained from the productions of $e(a)$.

articles.title: Letter productions of the substitution grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar over
$T$ with nonterminals $N_g$, let $a \in T$ have number $k$ (the position, counted from $0$, of the
first occurrence of $a$ in the list of terminals occurring in the productions of $g$, or the
length of that list when $a$ does not occur in it), and let $n \to w$ be a production over $T'$
whose nonterminals are natural numbers. It gives the production $(k, n) \to w'$ with
nonterminals in $N_g \sqcup (\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N})$, where $w'$ keeps the terminals of $w$
and replaces each nonterminal $m$ by $(k, m)$.

articles.title: Substituting the symbols of a grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar over $T$ with
nonterminals $N_g$, and let $e$ assign to each letter $a \in T$ an encoded grammar $e(a)$ over
$T'$. Each symbol of $g$ becomes a nonterminal in $N_g \sqcup (\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N})$: a
nonterminal $B$ of $g$ becomes $B$ in the left part, and a terminal $a$ becomes the pair $(k, n)$,
where $k$ is the number of $a$ (the position, counted from $0$, of the first occurrence of $a$ in
the list of terminals occurring in the productions of $g$, or the length of that list when $a$
does not occur in it) and $n$ is the start nonterminal of $e(a)$.

articles.title: Context-free languages are closed under substitution by context-free languages
articles.statement: **Context-free languages are closed under substitution by context-free languages.**

articles.title: Intended languages of the substitution grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar over
$T$ with nonterminals $N_g$, let $e$ assign to each letter $a \in T$ an encoded grammar $e(a)$
over $T'$, and let $s$ assign to each letter $a \in T$ a language $s(a)$ over $T'$. Each element
of $N_g \sqcup (\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N})$, the nonterminals of the substitution grammar, is
assigned a language over $T'$. A nonterminal $B \in N_g$ is assigned the substitution of $s$
into the language generated by $g$ from $B$. A pair $(k, n)$ is assigned, when $k$ is less than
the length of the list of terminals occurring in the productions of $g$ and $a$ is the entry at
position $k$ of that list (counted from $0$), the language generated from the nonterminal $n$ by
the grammar that $e(a)$ denotes, and the empty language otherwise.

articles.title: Block of a letter
articles.statement:
For a map $\varphi$ from $T$ to words over $T'$ and a letter
$a \in T$, the block of $a$ is the word over the disjoint union $T \sqcup T'$ that consists of
$a$, as a letter of $T$, followed by the letters of $\varphi(a)$, as letters of $T'$.

articles.title: Erasing right letters
articles.statement:
Erasing right letters is the map from letters of the disjoint
union $T \sqcup T'$ to words over $T$ that sends a letter $a$ of $T$ to the one-letter word $a$
and every letter of $T'$ to the empty word.

articles.title: The marker-insertion grammar simulates the original grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free
grammar over $T'$ and let $T$ be a finite alphabet. If $g$ derives a sentential form $y$ from a
sentential form $x$, then the marker-insertion grammar of $g$ over $T \sqcup T'$ derives the
translation of $y$ from the translation of $x$, where a sentential form is translated by
replacing each of its symbols by its marker translation.

articles.title: Marker loops fill in the left letters
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar over $T'$ and
let $T$ be a finite alphabet. For every word $u$ over $T \sqcup T'$, the marker-insertion grammar
of $g$ derives $u$ from the marked form of $u$, the sentential form that lists the letters of $u$
from $T'$ in order, each preceded by the marker nonterminal $D$, followed by one more $D$.

articles.title: Language of the marker-insertion grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar over $T'$
and let $T$ be a finite alphabet. The marker-insertion grammar of $g$ generates exactly the
words $u$ over $T \sqcup T'$ whose letters from $T'$, read in order, form a word of the language
of $g$.

articles.title: Marker-insertion grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar over $T'$ with start symbol
$A_0$, and let $T$ be a finite alphabet. The marker-insertion grammar of $g$ is the context-free
grammar over $T \sqcup T'$ whose nonterminals are those of $g$ together with a new start symbol
$S$ and a marker $D$, and whose rules are: for each rule $A \to \alpha$ of $g$, the rule
$A \to \alpha'$, where $\alpha'$ is $\alpha$ with $D$ inserted in front of each terminal; the
rule $S \to A_0 D$; the rule $D \to \varepsilon$; and the rule $D \to a D$ for each $a \in T$.

articles.title: Marker translation of a symbol
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar over $T'$ and let $T$ be
an alphabet. Each symbol of $g$ is translated to a string of symbols with terminals in
$T \sqcup T'$ and nonterminals those of $g$ together with two new nonterminals $S$ and $D$: a
terminal $b \in T'$ becomes the marker $D$ followed by $b$, and a nonterminal $A$ of $g$ becomes
$A$.

articles.title: Valuation for the marker-insertion grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar over $T'$
and let $T$ be an alphabet. This valuation assigns a language over $T \sqcup T'$ to each
nonterminal of $g$ and to the two new nonterminals $S$ and $D$ of the marker-insertion grammar
of $g$: to the marker $D$ the words with no letter from $T'$; to the new start symbol $S$ the
words whose letters from $T'$ form a word of the language of $g$; and to a nonterminal $A$ of $g$
the words whose letters from $T'$ form a word that $g$ derives from $A$.

articles.title: Marked form of a word
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar over $T'$, let $T$ be an
alphabet, and let $u$ be a word over $T \sqcup T'$. The marked form of $u$ is the sentential form,
with terminals in $T \sqcup T'$ and nonterminals those of $g$ together with two new nonterminals
$S$ and $D$, that lists the letters of $u$ from $T'$ in order, each preceded by the marker $D$,
followed by one more $D$.

articles.title: Context-free languages are closed under inverse homomorphisms
articles.statement: **Context-free languages are closed under inverse homomorphisms** from a finite alphabet.

articles.title: Context-free languages are closed under inserting letters
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a finite alphabet
and let $L$ be a context-free language over an alphabet $T'$. Then the language of words $u$ over
the disjoint union $T \oplus T'$ whose letters from $T'$, read in order, form a word of $L$ is
context-free.

articles.title: Context-free languages are closed under inverse free-monoid morphisms
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a
finite alphabet, $T'$ an alphabet, $\sigma \colon T^* \to {T'}^*$ a morphism of free monoids and
$L$ a context-free language over $T'$. Then the inverse image
$\sigma^{-1}(L) = \{x \in T^* \mid \sigma(x) \in L\}$ is a context-free language over $T$.

articles.title: Right projection of a word
articles.statement:
For a word $u$ over the disjoint union $T \oplus T'$ of two
alphabets, its right projection is the word over $T'$ obtained from $u$ by deleting every letter
from $T$ and reading each remaining letter as a letter of $T'$, keeping their order.

articles.title: The language $a^n b^n c^n$ is not context-free
articles.statement:
Over the three-letter alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$
(the letters $0, 1, 2$), the language of the words $a^n b^n c^n$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ is not
context-free.

Proof idea: by the pumping lemma, pumping $a^n b^n c^n$ down would keep the three letter counts
equal, so the pumped factor has equal counts of all letters, but a short factor misses $a$ or $c$,
forcing the factor to be empty.

articles.title: The language $a^n b^n c^n$
articles.statement:
Over the three-letter alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$ (the letters
$0, 1, 2$), this is the language of the words $a^n b^n c^n$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$: $n$ copies of
$a$, then $n$ copies of $b$, then $n$ copies of $c$.

articles.title: The grammar $S \to aSb \mid \varepsilon$ generates $a^n b^n$
articles.statement:
For letters $a$ and $b$ of an
alphabet with decidable equality, the language of the context-free grammar with a single
nonterminal $S$, its start symbol, and the two rules $S \to aSb$ and $S \to \varepsilon$ is the
language of the words $a^n b^n$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: The grammar $S \to aSb \mid \varepsilon$
articles.statement:
For letters $a$ and $b$ of an alphabet with
decidable equality, this is the context-free grammar with a single nonterminal $S$, which is its
start symbol, and the two rules $S \to aSb$ and $S \to \varepsilon$.

articles.title: The language $a^n b^n$ is context-free
articles.statement:
For any alphabet and any letters $a$ and $b$ of it,
the language of the words $a^n b^n$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$ is context-free.

articles.title: The language $a^n b^n$
articles.statement:
For letters $a$ and $b$ of an alphabet, this is the language of the
words $a^n b^n$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$: $n$ copies of $a$ followed by $n$ copies of $b$.

articles.title: Context-free languages are not closed under complement
articles.statement:
There is a context-free language
$L$ over the three-letter alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$ whose complement is not context-free.

Closure under complement and union would give closure under intersection.

articles.title: Context-free languages are not closed under intersection
articles.statement:
There are context-free languages
$L$ and $M$ over the three-letter alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$ whose intersection $L \cap M$ is not
context-free.

articles.title: The Kleene star of a one-letter word
articles.statement:
For a letter $a$ of an alphabet, a word $w$ belongs
to the Kleene star of the language $\{a\}$ whose only word is the one-letter word $a$ if and only
if $w = a^k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Complements of context-free languages need not be context-free
articles.statement:
It is not the case that
for every context-free language $L$ over the three-letter alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$, the complement
of $L$ is context-free.

articles.title: Intersections of context-free languages need not be context-free
articles.statement:
Over the three-letter
alphabet $\{0, 1, 2\}$, it is not the case that for all context-free languages $L$ and $M$ the
intersection $L \cap M$ is context-free.

articles.title: Number of marked letters
articles.statement:
A marked word over an alphabet $T$ is a word whose letters are
pairs $(a, b)$ with $a \in T$ and $b$ a Boolean; the letter $(a, b)$ is marked when $b$ is true.
The number of marked letters of a marked word $w$ is the number of letters of $w$ that are
marked, counted with multiplicity.

articles.title: Ogden's lemma for a grammar, with an explicit bound
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar
over an alphabet $T$ and let $R$, $K$, $n$ be natural numbers with $R \ge 2$ such that the
right-hand side of every production of $g$ has length at most $R$, some list of at most $K$
nonterminals contains the left-hand side of every production of $g$, and $R^{K+1} \le n$. A
marked word is a word whose letters are pairs $(a, b)$ with $a \in T$ and $b$ a Boolean, the
letter being marked when $b$ is true; its underlying word is the word of first components. Then
every marked word $w$ whose underlying word lies in the language of $g$ and which has at least
$n$ marked letters can be written as $w = uvxyz$ with marked words $u, v, x, y, z$ such that $vy$
has at least one marked letter, $vxy$ has at most $n$ marked letters, and for every natural
number $i$ the underlying word of $u v^i x y^i z$ lies in the language of $g$, where $v^i$ is the
concatenation of $i$ copies of $v$.

articles.title: Ogden's lemma
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a context-free language over an alphabet $T$. A marked word is a
word whose letters are pairs $(a, b)$ with $a \in T$ and $b$ a Boolean, the letter being marked
when $b$ is true; its underlying word is the word of first components. Then there is a natural
number $n > 0$ such that every marked word $w$ whose underlying word lies in $L$ and which has at
least $n$ marked letters can be written as $w = uvxyz$ with marked words $u, v, x, y, z$ such that
$vy$ has at least one marked letter, $vxy$ has at most $n$ marked letters, and for every natural
number $i$ the underlying word of $u v^i x y^i z$ lies in $L$, where $v^i$ is the concatenation
of $i$ copies of $v$.

articles.title: The pumping lemma for a grammar, with an explicit bound
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar
over an alphabet $T$ and let $R$, $K$, $n$ be natural numbers with $R \ge 2$ such that the
right-hand side of every production of $g$ has length at most $R$, some list of at most $K$
nonterminals contains the left-hand side of every production of $g$, and $R^{K+1} \le n$. Then
every word $w$ in the language of $g$ of length at least $n$ can be written as $w = uvxyz$ with
words $u, v, x, y, z$ over $T$ such that $vy$ is nonempty, $vxy$ has length at most $n$, and
$u v^i x y^i z$ lies in the language of $g$ for every natural number $i$, where $v^i$ is the
concatenation of $i$ copies of $v$.

It follows from Ogden's lemma with every letter marked.

articles.title: A singleton set of vectors is linear
articles.statement:
A singleton set of vectors is linear, with no periods.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Linear set of vectors
articles.statement:
A set of vectors is linear when it consists of a base vector plus
arbitrary nonnegative combinations of finitely many period vectors,
with one coefficient per position in the period list.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Linear sets are semilinear
articles.statement:
Linear sets are semilinear.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: The empty set is semilinear
articles.statement:
The empty set of vectors is semilinear.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: A singleton set of vectors is semilinear
articles.statement:
A singleton set of vectors is semilinear.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Semilinear set of vectors
articles.statement:
A set of vectors is semilinear when it is a finite union of
linear sets.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Duplicate periods get independent coefficients
articles.statement:
Duplicate periods get independent coefficients: with
`P = [p, p]`, the coefficients `(1, 0)` give `p`.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Unguarded linear combination agrees on equal lengths
articles.statement:
The unguarded recursion agrees with `linComb` on equal-length
inputs.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Linear combination with too many coefficients is zero
articles.statement:
Mismatched lengths are rejected: a longer coefficient list
does not silently drop coefficients.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Linear combination with too few coefficients is zero
articles.statement:
Mismatched lengths are rejected: a shorter coefficient list
does not silently truncate.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Linear combination of period vectors
articles.statement:
The linear combination of a list of period vectors with a
coefficient list `c`: pair the two lists position by position and
sum the scaled periods, and reject mismatched lengths by
returning `0` (the length guard is checked up front, before the
recursion, so a shorter coefficient list cannot silently truncate
and a longer one cannot silently drop coefficients). Coefficients
are indexed by *position* in `P`, not by period value, so duplicate
periods get independent coefficients: for `P = [p, p]`,
`linComb P [1, 0] = p`, not `2 • p`.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Parikh image of the empty language is empty
articles.statement:
The Parikh image of the empty language is empty.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Parikh image of a singleton language
articles.statement:
The Parikh image of a singleton language is the singleton of the
Parikh vector.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Parikh image of a union of languages
articles.statement:
The Parikh image of a union is the union of the Parikh images.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Parikh image of a language
articles.statement:
The Parikh image of a language: the set of Parikh vectors of its
words.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Parikh vectors add over concatenation
articles.statement:
Parikh vectors add over concatenation.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Parikh vector of the empty word is zero
articles.statement:
The Parikh vector of the empty word is zero.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Parikh vector of a word
articles.statement:
The Parikh vector of a word: the function counting, for each
letter, how many times it occurs in the word.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Semilinear sets are closed under union
articles.statement:
Semilinear sets are closed under union.

## Sources

- Parikh, "On context-free languages", Journal of the ACM 13 (1966), 570-581.

articles.title: Splitting a height-bounded yield at a concatenation
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar
and $u$, $v$ sentential forms of $g$. If the concatenation $uv$ yields the terminal word $w$
through a derivation forest of height at most $n$, then there are terminal words $w_1$, $w_2$
with $w = w_1 w_2$ such that $u$ yields $w_1$ and $v$ yields $w_2$, each through a derivation
forest of height at most $n$.

articles.title: Concatenating height-bounded yields
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If a sentential
form $u$ yields the terminal word $w_1$ through a derivation forest of height at most $n$, and
a sentential form $v$ yields the terminal word $w_2$ through one of height at most $m$, then the
concatenation $uv$ yields $w_1 w_2$ through a derivation forest of height at most
$\max(n, m)$.

articles.title: Minimal-height derivation forests exist
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If a
sentential form $\alpha$ yields the terminal word $w$, then there is a natural number $n$ such
that $\alpha$ yields $w$ through a derivation forest of height at most $n$, but through no
derivation forest of height at most $m$ for any $m < n$.

articles.title: Pumping through a self-context
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar, $A$ a nonterminal and
$l$, $r$, $x$ terminal words. Suppose that for every terminal word $w$ yielded by $A$ the word
$l w r$ is also yielded by $A$, and that $A$ yields $x$. Then for every natural number $i$ the
nonterminal $A$ yields $l^i x r^i$, where $l^i$ and $r^i$ denote the concatenations of $i$
copies of $l$ and of $r$.

articles.title: Length bound for height-bounded yields
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and $R$ a
natural number such that every production of $g$ has an output of length at most $R$. If a
sentential form $\alpha$ yields the terminal word $w$ through a derivation forest of height at
most $n$, then $|w| \le |\alpha| \cdot \max(2, R)^n$.

articles.title: Raising the height bound of a yield
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If a sentential
form $\alpha$ yields the terminal word $w$ through a derivation forest of height at most $n$,
and $n \le m$, then $\alpha$ yields $w$ through a derivation forest of height at most $m$.

articles.title: A production gives derivation contexts
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and
$A \to \alpha_1 B \alpha_2$ a production of $g$, where $B$ is a nonterminal and $\alpha_1$,
$\alpha_2$ are sentential forms. If $\alpha_1$ yields the terminal word $l$ and $\alpha_2$ yields
the terminal word $r$, then for every terminal word $w$ yielded by $B$ the word $l w r$ is
yielded by $A$; that is, $(l, r)$ is a derivation context from $A$ to $B$.

articles.title: Height-bounded yields are yields
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If a sentential
