form $\alpha$ yields the terminal word $w$ through a derivation forest of height at most $n$,
then $\alpha$ yields $w$.

articles.title: Every yield has a height bound
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If a sentential form
$\alpha$ yields the terminal word $w$, then there is a natural number $n$ such that $\alpha$
yields $w$ through a derivation forest of height at most $n$.

articles.title: Pumping lemma for context-free languages
articles.statement:
For every context-free language $L$ over an
alphabet $T$ there is a natural number $n > 0$ such that every word $w \in L$ with $|w| \ge n$
can be written as $w = uvxyz$ with words $u, v, x, y, z$ over $T$ such that $vy$ is nonempty,
$|vxy| \le n$, and $u v^i x y^i z \in L$ for every natural number $i$, where $v^i$ and $y^i$
denote the concatenations of $i$ copies of $v$ and of $y$.

articles.title: Derivation contexts
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar, let $A$ and $B$ be nonterminals of
$g$, and let $l$ and $r$ be words over the terminal alphabet. Then $(l, r)$ is a derivation
context from $A$ to $B$ when, for every terminal word $w$ that the nonterminal $B$ yields in $g$,
the nonterminal $A$ yields the word $l w r$ in $g$.

This is the language-inclusion form of a one-hole derivation context; it is what pumping
iteration uses, and it holds vacuously when $B$ yields nothing.

articles.title: Height-bounded derivations
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. For a sentential form
$\alpha$ (a list of terminals and nonterminals of $g$), a terminal word $w$ and a natural number
$n$, say that $\alpha$ yields $w$ at height $n$ when this follows from three rules: the empty form
yields the empty word at every height $n$; if $\alpha$ yields $w$ at height $n$, then for every
terminal $a$ the form $a\alpha$ yields $aw$ at height $n$; and if $A \to \beta$ is a production of
$g$, $\beta$ yields $w_1$ at height $n$ and $\alpha$ yields $w_2$ at height $m$, then $A\alpha$
yields $w_1 w_2$ at height $\max(n + 1, m)$.

Thus $n$ bounds the height of a derivation forest, the number of nonterminal expansions along
its longest path; terminals and empty forests contribute nothing.

articles.title: Automaton for words over the left copy
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $T$, write $T \sqcup T$ for the
disjoint union of a left and a right copy of $T$. This is the deterministic automaton over
$T \sqcup T$ with the two states true and false, whose start state and only accepting state are
true, and which moves from state $b$ on a letter $c$ to true exactly when $b$ is true and $c$ lies
in the left copy, and to false otherwise.

articles.title: The left quotient of a context-free language by a regular language is context-free
articles.statement:
**The left quotient of a context-free language by a regular language is context-free**, over
a finite alphabet.

articles.title: Words over the left copy of a doubled alphabet
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $T$, write $T \sqcup T$ for
the disjoint union of a left and a right copy of $T$. This is the language over $T \sqcup T$ of the
words obtained from a word $x$ over $T$ by replacing each letter with its left copy.

articles.title: Automaton running a deterministic automaton on the right copy
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a deterministic
automaton over an alphabet $T$, and write $T \sqcup T$ for the disjoint union of a left and a right
copy of $T$. This is the deterministic automaton over $T \sqcup T$ whose states are the states of
$D$ together with one extra dead state $\bot$. From a state $p$ of $D$, on the right copy of a
letter $a$ it moves to the state that $D$ reaches from $p$ on $a$; on a letter of the left copy,
and from $\bot$ on any letter, it moves to $\bot$. Its start state is the start state of $D$, and
its accepting states are the accepting states of $D$.

articles.title: The right quotient of a context-free language by a regular language is context-free
articles.statement:
**The right quotient of a context-free language by a regular language is context-free**, over
a finite alphabet.

articles.title: Right quotient of a language by a language
articles.statement:
For languages $L$ and $R$ over an alphabet $T$,
the right quotient of $L$ by $R$ is the language of all words $x$ over $T$ such that the
concatenation $xy$ lies in $L$ for some word $y \in R$.

articles.title: Words of a language marked by the right copy
articles.statement:
For a language $R$ over an alphabet $T$, write
$T \sqcup T$ for the disjoint union of a left and a right copy of $T$. This is the language over
$T \sqcup T$ of the words obtained from a word $y \in R$ by replacing each letter with its right
copy.

articles.title: Forgetting the copy of a letter
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $T$, write $T \sqcup T$ for the disjoint
union of a left and a right copy of $T$. This map sends the left copy and the right copy of a
letter $a \in T$ to the one-letter word $a$ over $T$.

articles.title: Leftmost derivations are derivations
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If a sentential
form $u$ has a leftmost derivation in $g$ to a word of terminals $w$, then $u$ derives $w$ in $g$
(by zero or more rewriting steps).

articles.title: Leftmost derivations from a word of terminals are empty
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar
and $u$ a word of terminals. If $u$ has a leftmost derivation in $g$ with list of rules $\rho$ to a
word of terminals $w$, then $\rho$ is the empty list and $w = u$.

articles.title: Inherently ambiguous example as a union of two languages
articles.statement: The example language is the union of `a ^ n b ^ n c ^ *` and `a ^ * b ^ n c ^ n`.

articles.title: The example language is context-free
articles.statement: **The example language is context-free.**

articles.title: Canonical inherently ambiguous context-free language
articles.statement:
The language `{a ^ i b ^ j c ^ k | i = j or j = k}` over the alphabet `Fin 3`
(`0, 1, 2` for `a, b, c`): the standard inherently ambiguous context-free language.

## Sources

- S. Ginsburg, The Mathematical Theory of Context-Free Languages, McGraw-Hill, 1966; J. E. Hopcroft and J. D. Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, Addison-Wesley, 1979, Chapter 7.

articles.title: Ambiguous grammar
articles.statement:
A context-free grammar $g$ is **ambiguous** if some word of terminals
$w$ has two leftmost derivations from the start symbol of $g$ that use different lists of rules.

articles.title: Inherently ambiguous language
articles.statement:
A language is inherently ambiguous when it is context-free and every grammar
generating it is ambiguous.

articles.title: Leftmost derivation
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar, $u$ a sentential form of $g$, $w$ a
word of terminals and $r_1, \dots, r_n$ a list of rules over the terminals and nonterminals of
$g$. The list $r_1, \dots, r_n$ is a leftmost derivation of $w$ from $u$ in $g$ when every $r_i$
is a production of $g$, and, starting from $u$ and for $i = 1, \dots, n$ in turn, the leftmost
nonterminal of the current sentential form is the left-hand side of $r_i$ and is replaced by the
right-hand side of $r_i$, and the sentential form reached after these $n$ steps is $w$, read as a
string of terminals. In particular the empty list is a leftmost derivation of $w$ from $u$
exactly when $u$ is $w$ read as a string of terminals.

articles.title: Words with a leftmost derivation lie in the language
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar.
If a word of terminals $w$ has a leftmost derivation in $g$ from the start symbol of $g$, then $w$
belongs to the language of $g$.

articles.title: Binarization of a reduced grammar is in Chomsky normal form
articles.statement:
If a context-free
grammar $g$ is reduced, then the binarization of $g$ is in Chomsky normal form.

articles.title: Binarization adds no words
articles.statement:
If a context-free grammar $g$ is reduced, then every word
generated by the binarization of $g$ is generated by $g$.

articles.title: Binarization preserves the language
articles.statement:
If a context-free grammar $g$ is reduced, then
the binarization of $g$ generates exactly the language of $g$.

articles.title: Binarization has no empty productions
articles.statement:
If a context-free grammar $g$ is reduced, then
no production of the binarization of $g$ has the empty word as output.

articles.title: Binarization of a grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar with nonterminals $N$ and
initial nonterminal $S$, and let $t_0, \dots, t_{k-1}$ be the list of terminals occurring in the
production outputs of $g$. Encode each symbol of a production output of $g$ as a basic symbol in
$N \sqcup \mathbb{N}$: a nonterminal $A$ as $A$, and a terminal $a$ as the least index $i$ with
$t_i = a$. The binarized grammar of $g$ has as nonterminals the basic symbols together with a
chain nonterminal $\langle\tau\rangle$ for every list $\tau$ of basic symbols, and its initial
nonterminal is $S$. For a list $\sigma$ of basic symbols, its head $h(\sigma)$ is defined by
$h(XY) = XY$ and $h(XYZ\tau) = X\langle YZ\tau\rangle$ for basic symbols $X, Y, Z$ and a list
$\tau$, $h(i) = t_i$ for a single index $i < k$, and $h(\sigma)$ empty in every other case. For
every production $A \to \alpha$ of $g$, with $\sigma$ the encoding of $\alpha$ symbol by symbol,
the binarized grammar has the production $A \to h(\sigma)$, the production
$\langle\tau\rangle \to h(\tau)$ for every suffix $\tau$ of $\sigma$ (including $\sigma$ itself)
with at least two entries, and the production $i \to a$ for every terminal $a$ occurring in
$\alpha$, where $i$ is the encoding of $a$; it has no other productions.

This construction is meant for reduced grammars, which have no empty outputs and no outputs
consisting of a single nonterminal: on other grammars such outputs get the empty head, and in
general neither the language nor Chomsky normal form is preserved.

articles.title: Head of a binarized output
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and let
$a_0, a_1, \dots$ be its list of terminals occurring in production outputs. For a list
$\sigma$ of basic symbols (each a nonterminal of $g$ or a natural number, a terminal wrapper),
the head $h(\sigma)$ is the following form over the nonterminals of the binarized grammar
(basic symbols and chain nonterminals $\langle\tau\rangle$ for lists $\tau$ of basic symbols):
$h(XY) = XY$ for two basic symbols $X, Y$; $h(XYZ\tau) = X\langle YZ\tau\rangle$ for basic
symbols $X, Y, Z$ and a list $\tau$; $h(i) = a_i$ for a single natural number $i$ less than
the length of the list; and $h(\sigma)$ is empty in every other case (the empty list, a single
nonterminal of $g$, or a single out-of-range index).

articles.title: Valuation of the binarized grammar by yields
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and let
$a_0, a_1, \dots$ be its list of terminals occurring in production outputs. A basic symbol is a
nonterminal of $g$ or a natural number (a terminal wrapper); the nonterminals of the binarized
grammar are the basic symbols together with a chain nonterminal $\langle\sigma\rangle$ for every
list $\sigma$ of basic symbols. Decode a basic symbol as a symbol of $g$: a nonterminal $A$ of
$g$ as $A$, a natural number $i$ less than the length of the list as the terminal $a_i$, and any
other natural number as the initial nonterminal of $g$. The valuation assigns to a basic symbol
$X$ the set of words that the decoding of $X$ yields in $g$, and to a chain nonterminal
$\langle\sigma\rangle$ the set of words that the symbolwise decoding of $\sigma$ yields in $g$.

articles.title: The fresh start symbol occurs in no output
articles.statement:
For every context-free grammar $g$, the
fresh initial nonterminal of the fresh-start grammar of $g$ occurs in no production output of
the fresh-start grammar.

articles.title: Adding a fresh start symbol preserves Chomsky normal form
articles.statement:
If a context-free grammar
$g$ is in Chomsky normal form and no production of $g$ has empty output, then the fresh-start
grammar of $g$ is in Chomsky normal form.

The no-empty-outputs hypothesis is essential: an existing empty production would be embedded
with the old initial nonterminal, not the fresh one, on the left.

articles.title: A fresh start symbol is harmless when the empty word is generated
articles.statement:
If the empty word
belongs to the language of a context-free grammar $g$, then the fresh-start grammar of $g$
generates exactly the language of $g$.

articles.title: Language of the grammar with a fresh nullable start symbol
articles.statement:
For every context-free
grammar $G$, the grammar obtained from $G$ by adding a fresh initial nonterminal (with an empty
production and copies of the productions of the old initial nonterminal) generates exactly
$L(G) \cup \{\varepsilon\}$, where $L(G)$ is the language of $G$ and $\varepsilon$ is the
empty word.

articles.title: Grammar with a fresh nullable start symbol
articles.statement:
Given a context-free grammar $G$ with
nonterminals $N$ and initial nonterminal $S$, this is the grammar with nonterminals
$N \cup \{S_0\}$ for a fresh symbol $S_0$, initial nonterminal $S_0$, and the following
productions: every production of $G$; the empty production $S_0 \to \varepsilon$; and
$S_0 \to \alpha$ for every production $S \to \alpha$ of $G$.

The new grammar generates the language of $G$ plus the empty word, and stays in Chomsky normal
form when $G$ is in Chomsky normal form and has no empty outputs.

articles.title: Chomsky normal form for context-free languages
articles.statement:
Every context-free language $L$ is
generated by some context-free grammar in Chomsky normal form.

articles.title: Chomsky normal form theorem
articles.statement:
For every context-free grammar $G$ there is a
context-free grammar in Chomsky normal form that generates the same language as $G$.

articles.title: Decoding basic nonterminals of the binarized grammar
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a context-free
grammar with nonterminals $N$ and initial nonterminal $S$, and let $t_0, \dots, t_{k-1}$ be
the list of terminals occurring in the production outputs of $G$. This map sends an element of
$N \sqcup \mathbb{N}$ (a basic nonterminal of the binarized grammar) to a symbol of $G$: a
nonterminal $A \in N$ goes to $A$, an index $i < k$ goes to the terminal $t_i$, and an index
$i \ge k$ goes to the nonterminal $S$.

Indices $i \ge k$ never arise from encoding nonterminals of $G$ or terminals occurring in the
production outputs of $G$.

articles.title: Terminals of a grammar
articles.statement:
For a context-free grammar $G$, the list of terminals occurring
in the outputs of its productions: going through the productions of $G$ in a fixed but
unspecified order, list the terminals of each output from left to right. A terminal may appear
more than once.

articles.title: Chomsky normal form
articles.statement:
A grammar is in Chomsky normal form when every production has
output either two nonterminals, a single terminal, or the empty word with the initial
nonterminal on the left; and either the initial nonterminal occurs in no output (so an empty
production cannot leak the empty word to other nonterminals) or there are no empty outputs at
all.

articles.title: Encoding symbols as basic nonterminals of the binarized grammar
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a
context-free grammar with nonterminals $N$, and let $t_0, \dots, t_{k-1}$ be the list of
terminals occurring in the production outputs of $G$. This map sends a symbol of $G$ to an
element of $N \sqcup \mathbb{N}$: a nonterminal $A$ goes to $A$, and a terminal $a$ goes to the
least index $i$ with $t_i = a$, or to $k$ if $a$ does not occur in the list.

articles.title: Splitting a yield over a concatenation
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If the
concatenated sentential form $u v$ yields the terminal word $w$, then there are terminal
words $w_1$ and $w_2$ with $w = w_1 w_2$ such that $u$ yields $w_1$ and $v$ yields $w_2$.

articles.title: Concatenation of yields
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If the sentential form
$u$ yields the terminal word $w_1$ and the sentential form $v$ yields the terminal word
$w_2$, then the concatenated form $u v$ yields $w_1 w_2$.

articles.title: Concatenating derivations
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and let $u$, $u'$, $v$, $v'$
be sentential forms of $g$. If $u$ derives $u'$ and $v$ derives $v'$ in $g$ (each in zero or more
steps), then the concatenation $uv$ derives $u'v'$ in $g$.

articles.title: Derivations transfer along a renaming of nonterminals
articles.statement:
Let $g$ and $G$ be context-free
grammars over the same terminal alphabet, and let $f$ map the nonterminals of $g$ to those of $G$.
Extend $f$ to symbols and sentential forms by renaming each nonterminal and keeping each terminal.
Suppose that for every production $A \to \alpha$ of $g$, the renamed production $f(A) \to f(\alpha)$
is a production of $G$. Then whenever a sentential form $u$ derives $v$ in $g$ (in zero or more
steps), $f(u)$ derives $f(v)$ in $G$.

No injectivity of $f$ is needed for this direction.

articles.title: Words of the canonical interpretation are derivable
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and
assign to each nonterminal $A$ of $g$ the language of terminal words that $g$ derives from $A$. If a
terminal word $w$ lies in the language that a sentential form $u$ of $g$ denotes under this
assignment, then $u$ derives $w$ in $g$.

articles.title: Yields are derivable
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If the sentential form $u$
yields the terminal word $w$, then $u$ derives $w$, read as a string of terminal symbols,
in $g$: that is, $u \Rightarrow^* w$ in zero or more rewriting steps.

articles.title: Interpretation of a concatenation
articles.statement:
For every assignment $V$ of languages to nonterminals and
all sentential forms $u$ and $v$, the language that $uv$ denotes under $V$ is the concatenation of
the languages that $u$ and $v$ denote under $V$.

articles.title: Derivations shrink interpretations under a valuation
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and
$V$ a valuation of $g$. If a sentential form $u$ derives $v$ in $g$ (in zero or more steps), then
the language that $v$ denotes under $V$ is contained in the language that $u$ denotes under $V$.

articles.title: A production step shrinks interpretations under a valuation
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free
grammar and $V$ a valuation of $g$. If a sentential form $u$ rewrites to $v$ by one production of
$g$, then the language that $v$ denotes under $V$ is contained in the language that $u$ denotes
under $V$.

articles.title: A terminal word denotes its singleton
articles.statement:
Under every assignment of languages to
nonterminals, a terminal word $w$, read as a sentential form, denotes the singleton language
$\{w\}$.

articles.title: Interpretation after renaming nonterminals
articles.statement:
Let $f \colon N \to N'$ be a map of
nonterminals, extended to sentential forms by renaming each nonterminal and keeping each terminal,
and let $V$ assign a language to each nonterminal in $N'$. For every sentential form $u$ over $N$,
the language that $f(u)$ denotes under $V$ equals the language that $u$ denotes under the
assignment $V \circ f$.

articles.title: Interpretation of a sentential form
articles.statement:
Under an assignment $V$ of languages to nonterminals, a
sentential form denotes the concatenation, in order, of the languages its symbols denote: a
terminal $a$ denotes the language containing only the one-letter word $a$, and a nonterminal $A$
denotes $V(A)$. The empty sentential form denotes the language containing only the empty word.

articles.title: Interpretation of a grammar symbol
articles.statement:
Under an assignment $V$ of languages to nonterminals, a
terminal $a$ denotes the language containing only the one-letter word $a$, and a nonterminal $A$
denotes its assigned language $V(A)$.

articles.title: The languages generated from each nonterminal form a valuation
articles.statement:
For every context-free
grammar $g$, the assignment that sends each nonterminal $A$ of $g$ to the language generated by
$g$ from $A$ is a valuation of $g$.

articles.title: Valuation of a grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar with terminals $T$, and let $V$
assign a language over $T$ to each nonterminal of $g$. Interpret a sentential form under $V$ by
sending each terminal $a$ to the language $\{a\}$ of the one-letter word $a$ and each nonterminal
$B$ to $V(B)$, and concatenating these languages in order (the empty form is interpreted as
$\{\varepsilon\}$). Then $V$ is a *valuation* of $g$ when, for every production $A \to u$
of $g$, the interpretation of $u$ under $V$ is contained in $V(A)$.

articles.title: Language generated from a nonterminal
articles.statement:
For a context-free grammar $g$ and a nonterminal
$A$ of $g$, the language generated by $g$ from $A$ is the set of words $w$ over the terminals of
$g$ such that $g$ derives $w$ from the one-symbol sentential form $A$. It is the language of $g$
with $A$ in place of the initial nonterminal.

articles.title: Valuations bound the language of a grammar
articles.statement:
For every context-free grammar $g$ and every
valuation $V$ of $g$, the language generated by $g$ is contained in $V(S)$, where $S$ is the
initial nonterminal of $g$.

articles.title: Renaming nonterminals fixes terminal words
articles.statement:
Let $f$ map nonterminals $N$ to nonterminals
$N'$, and let $w$ be a word over the terminals. Reading $w$ as a sentential form over $N$ and
renaming its nonterminals by $f$ gives $w$ read as a sentential form over $N'$.

articles.title: Injective renamings are injective on productions
articles.statement:
If $f$ is an injective map from
nonterminals $N$ to nonterminals $N'$, then renaming the nonterminals of productions over $N$ by
$f$ is injective: two productions with the same renaming are equal.

In particular, renaming a finite set of productions by $f$ merges none of them.

articles.title: Renaming the nonterminals of a production
articles.statement:
Given a map $f$ from nonterminals $N$ to
nonterminals $N'$, the renaming by $f$ of a production $A \to u$ is the production
$f(A) \to u'$, where $u'$ is obtained from $u$ by replacing each nonterminal $B$ with $f(B)$ and
leaving each terminal unchanged.

articles.title: Injective renamings are injective on symbols
articles.statement:
If $f$ is an injective map from
nonterminals $N$ to nonterminals $N'$, then renaming grammar symbols by $f$, which fixes each
terminal and sends each nonterminal $A$ to $f(A)$, is injective.

articles.title: Renaming the nonterminals of a symbol
articles.statement:
Given a map $f$ from nonterminals $N$ to
nonterminals $N'$, renaming a grammar symbol by $f$ leaves a terminal $a$ unchanged and sends a
nonterminal $A$ to the nonterminal $f(A)$.

articles.title: Language membership through yields
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar with initial
nonterminal $S$. A terminal word $w$ belongs to the language of $g$ if and only if the
one-symbol sentential form $S$ yields $w$.

articles.title: The language of the empty word is context-free
articles.statement:
For every alphabet $T$, the language
over $T$ whose only word is the empty word is context-free: a grammar with one nonterminal and
a single production erasing it generates this language.

articles.title: Singleton languages are context-free
articles.statement:
For every word $w$ over an alphabet $T$, the
language $\{w\}$ consisting of $w$ alone is context-free: one production spells the word out.

articles.title: Yields coincide with derivations of terminal words
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar,
$u$ a sentential form of $g$ and $w$ a word of terminals. Then $u$ yields $w$ in $g$ if and only
if $u$ derives in $g$, by zero or more rewriting steps, the sentential form consisting of the
letters of $w$ read as terminals.

articles.title: Derivable terminal words are yields
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. If the
sentential form $u$ derives the terminal word $w$, read as a string of terminal symbols,
in $g$, then $u$ yields $w$.

The proof is the valuation argument: the languages yielded by the nonterminals form a
valuation.

articles.title: Yield through one production
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and $A \to \alpha$ a
production of $g$. If $\alpha$ yields the terminal word $w$, then the one-symbol sentential
form $A$ yields $w$.

articles.title: Yield of a sentential form
articles.statement:
For a context-free grammar $g$ with terminal alphabet
$T$, the relation "the sentential form $u$ yields the terminal word $w$" is the smallest
relation such that: the empty form yields the empty word; if $u$ yields $w$, then for every
terminal $a$ the form $a u$ yields $a w$; and if $A \to \alpha$ is a production of $g$,
$\alpha$ yields $w_1$ and $u$ yields $w_2$, then the form $A u$ yields $w_1 w_2$.

articles.title: The empty language is context-free
articles.statement:
The empty language over any alphabet is
context-free: take a grammar with no productions.

articles.title: Correctness of one indexed CYK cell
articles.statement:
A cell is correct once all strictly shorter, valid factors are correct.
The rule enumeration certificate constrains data only, not computation.

articles.title: Correctness of the CYK epsilon scan
articles.statement: Epsilon scanning agrees with existence of a start epsilon production.

articles.title: New CYK table row holds the computed cells
articles.statement: The new length's row contains exactly the cells just computed.

articles.title: CYK table update leaves other lengths' cells unchanged
articles.statement: Updating one length never changes another length's cells.

articles.title: Indexed CYK agrees with the list-table CYK recognizer
articles.statement: Exact Boolean correspondence with the existing list-table recognizer.

articles.title: Correctness of the indexed CYK recognizer
articles.statement: The indexed recognizer decides the existing canonical language.

articles.title: Indexing of a constructed CYK row
articles.statement: Row construction preserves the exact start-position indexing.

articles.title: Correctness of the completed indexed CYK table
articles.statement: Every completed valid cell agrees with canonical grammar derivations.

articles.title: Indexed CYK table keeps its allocated size
articles.statement: The outer table retains its allocated size through every update.

articles.title: Computed CYK cell length bounded by the rule count
articles.statement: Even with duplicates, a cell never exceeds the rule enumeration length.

articles.title: Cost bound for computing one CYK cell
articles.statement: A cell charges every rule, its test, and its possible output cons.

articles.title: Exact cost of the CYK epsilon scan
articles.statement: Exact cost of the empty-input production scan.

articles.title: Cost bound for the CYK production fit test
articles.statement: Output inspection is bounded; only binary productions scan splits.

articles.title: Every CYK table lookup is bounded by the rule count
articles.statement:
All table cells, including invalid/default positions, have bounded
membership-scan length. This invariant is proved from construction.

articles.title: Exact cost of a membership scan
articles.statement: Exact charge for a full membership scan, including a failed scan.

articles.title: Indexed CYK costs a constant times $n^3$ on nonempty words
articles.statement: In the usual nonempty-input form, the bound is a constant times `n³`.

articles.title: Explicit cubic cost bound for indexed CYK
Length of a computed CYK row
articles.statement: The linear row-conversion charge uses the actual number of entries.

articles.title: Cost bound for building one CYK row
articles.statement: Row cost counts all starts, not only successful or distinct factors.

articles.title: Cost bound for the CYK split scan
articles.statement: Each split pays for both indexed cell reads and both membership scans.

articles.title: Cost bound for filling the indexed CYK table
articles.statement:
Table cost includes allocation, every row conversion and every update.
The memory-size hypothesis needed for split costs is discharged internally.

articles.title: Charged rule decoding agrees with the decoded grammar
articles.statement: The charged rule conversion agrees with the existing decoded grammar.

articles.title: Exact cost of grammar rule decoding
articles.statement: Exact grammar-preparation cost, including all production symbols.

articles.title: Charged decoding of encoded grammar rules
articles.statement: Decode every rule, charging all right-hand-side traversals.

articles.title: Charged symbol decoding agrees with canonical decoding
articles.statement: The charged conversion is exactly the canonical symbol decoding.

articles.title: Exact cost of grammar symbol decoding
articles.statement: Exact symbol-decoding traversal cost.

articles.title: Charged decoding of encoded grammar symbols
articles.statement: Decode symbols with a charge for each constructor test and output cons.

articles.title: Correctness of indexed CYK on encoded grammars
articles.statement: Correctness for the canonical encoded language, including epsilon.

articles.title: Cubic cost bound for indexed CYK on encoded grammars
articles.statement:
Cubic word-length bound including canonical grammar preparation.
All dependence on the fixed grammar and symbol-equality model is explicit.

articles.title: Indexed CYK recognizer for encoded grammars
articles.statement: Run indexed CYK on the existing encoded grammar, including preparation.

articles.title: Charged computation of one CYK cell
articles.statement:
Scan every production once, retaining its input exactly when it fits.
Duplicates are allowed; no set insertion or uncharged deduplication occurs.

articles.title: Charged scan for start epsilon productions
articles.statement: Scan start epsilon rules; output emptiness is a single list-tag test.

articles.title: Production-output fit test for indexed CYK
articles.statement:
Test a production output without constructing or comparing substrings.
Pattern inspection is bounded (at most three cons and two symbol tags).

articles.title: CYK table lookup with empty default cells
articles.statement: Two bounded array reads; invalid indices denote an empty cell.

articles.title: CYK cell members come from scanned productions
articles.statement: Membership in a computed cell names an actual scanned production.

articles.title: Charged membership scan agrees with list membership
articles.statement: The charged scan has ordinary list-membership semantics.

articles.title: Charged list-membership scan
articles.statement: Full membership scan, charging equality and list/control operations.

articles.title: Charged indexed CYK recognizer
articles.statement:
The charged indexed recognizer. The nonempty branch pays for the input
length scan, conversion, completed table, final lookup and membership.

articles.title: Charged construction of one CYK row
articles.statement:
Build one row in increasing start-position order. Each cell is evaluated
once against the already completed shorter rows.

articles.title: Successful CYK split scans find a split in range
articles.statement: Every successful scan names a split in exactly the scanned interval.

articles.title: Charged scan of CYK split positions
articles.statement:
Scan split positions `1,...,count`, with two table reads per split.
The 16 units cover four array reads, bounds/default tests, index arithmetic,
Boolean combinations and recursion control.

articles.title: Charged construction of the indexed CYK table
articles.statement:
Fill rows `1,...,depth` in a fixed outer array of size `w.size + 1`.
Row conversion is linear; the outer update is an indexed primitive.

articles.title: Correctness of the CYK recognizer
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar in Chomsky normal
form. For every word $w$ over the terminals of $g$, the CYK recognizer accepts $w$ if and only if
$w$ belongs to the language of $g$.

articles.title: The CYK recognizer
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar with initial nonterminal $S$. The
CYK recognizer accepts the empty word exactly when $g$ has a production $S \to \varepsilon$, and
accepts a nonempty word $w$ exactly when $S$ lies in the cell recorded for $w$ in the CYK table of
$w$ up to length $|w|$.

articles.title: The CYK cell built from given cells
articles.statement:
Given an assignment $f$ of a cell (a finite set of
nonterminals of $g$) to every word, the cell of a word $w$ built from $f$ is the set of left-hand
sides of those productions of $g$ whose outputs fit $w$ with respect to $f$.

articles.title: The unshared CYK recurrence
articles.statement:
The depth-$n$ CYK cell of a word $w$ is defined by recursion
on $n$: at depth $0$ every cell is empty, and the depth-$(n + 1)$ cell of $w$ is the CYK cell of
$w$ built from the depth-$n$ cells of all words. Cells are recomputed without sharing.

articles.title: When a production output fits a word
articles.statement:
Let $f$ assign a cell (a finite set of nonterminals)
to every word. A production output fits a word $w$ with respect to $f$ exactly in two cases: the
output is a single terminal $a$ and $w$ is the one-letter word $a$; or the output is a pair of
nonterminals $B C$ and there is some $i$ with $0 < i < |w|$ such that $B$ lies in the cell of the
first $i$ letters of $w$ and $C$ lies in the cell of the remaining letters. No other output fits
any word.

articles.title: Looking up a word in a CYK table
articles.statement:
In a table listing pairs of a word and a cell, the cell
recorded for a word $u$ is the cell of the first entry whose word is $u$, or the empty set if no
entry has word $u$.

articles.title: Correct CYK tables
articles.statement:
A table listing pairs $(u, X)$ of a word $u$ and a set $X$ of
nonterminals of $g$ is correct when, for every entry $(u, X)$ with $u$ nonempty, $X$ consists
exactly of the nonterminals $B$ such that the one-symbol form $B$ yields $u$.

articles.title: Correctness of the CYK table
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar in Chomsky normal form and
$w$ a word. For every $l$, the CYK table of $w$ up to length $l$ is correct, and for all $j$ and
$m$ with $0 < m \le l$ and $j + m \le |w|$, some entry of the table has as its word the factor of
$w$ of length $m$ starting at position $j$ (positions counted from $0$).

articles.title: The CYK table
articles.statement:
The CYK table of a word $w$ up to length $l$ is a list of pairs of a word
and a cell, defined by recursion on $l$. Up to length $0$ it is empty. The table up to length
$l + 1$ is the table $t$ up to length $l$ followed by one entry for each position $i$ (counted
from $0$) with $i + l + 1 \le |w|$, in increasing order of $i$: the factor $u$ of $w$ of length
$l + 1$ starting at position $i$, together with the CYK cell of $u$ built from the cells recorded
in $t$.

articles.title: Forms yielding the empty word under Chomsky normal form
articles.statement:
If $g$ is in Chomsky normal form,
then every symbol of a sentential form that yields the empty word is a nonterminal $B$ for which
$g$ has a production $B \to \varepsilon$.

articles.title: The CYK step
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar in Chomsky normal form, let $f$ assign to
each word over the terminals a finite set of nonterminals, and let $w$ be a nonempty word. For
$0 < i < |w|$ write $u_i$ for the prefix of $w$ of length $i$ and $v_i$ for the remaining suffix,
so that $w = u_i v_i$. Suppose that for every such $i$ and every nonterminal $B$, $B \in f(u_i)$
if and only if $B$ yields $u_i$, and $B \in f(v_i)$ if and only if $B$ yields $v_i$. Then a
nonterminal $A$ lies in the CYK cell of $w$ built from $f$ if and only if $A$ yields $w$.

articles.title: Correctness of the CYK recurrence
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar in Chomsky normal
form. For every natural number $n$, every nonterminal $A$ and every nonempty word $w$ of length
at most $n$, $A$ lies in the depth-$n$ CYK cell of $w$ if and only if $A$ yields $w$.

articles.title: Nonterminals in outputs have no empty production
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar in
Chomsky normal form. If a nonterminal $B$ occurs in the output of some production of $g$, then
$g$ has no production $B \to \varepsilon$.

Such a production would have the initial nonterminal on the left, which then occurs in an output
while an empty production exists.

articles.title: Shape of yields under Chomsky normal form
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar in Chomsky
normal form, $A$ a nonterminal and $w$ a nonempty word. Then $A$ yields $w$ if and only if $g$
has a production $A \to a$ with $a$ a terminal and $w = a$, or a production $A \to BC$ with
nonterminals $B$ and $C$ and nonempty words $w_1$ and $w_2$ such that $w = w_1 w_2$, $B$ yields
$w_1$ and $C$ yields $w_2$.

articles.title: Language of end-marker encoded words
articles.statement:
The encodings of words over `T`: the words over `T ⊕ Unit`
consisting of left letters followed by a single end marker.

## Sources

- Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3 (deterministic pushdown automata, acceptance by empty stack with an end marker).

articles.title: Encoding DFA after the end marker accepts only the empty input
articles.statement:
After the end marker, the encoding DFA can only be in its
accepting state on empty input.

## Sources

- Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3.

articles.title: Dead state of the encoding DFA is absorbing
articles.statement:
The dead state of the encoding DFA stays dead.

## Sources

- Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3.

articles.title: Encoding DFA accepts every end-marker encoding
articles.statement:
The encoding DFA accepts exactly the encodings: it reaches the
accepting state on an encoding.

## Sources

- Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3.

articles.title: Encoding DFA stays in its start state on left letters
articles.statement:
The encoding DFA stays in its start state while reading left
letters.

## Sources

- Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3.

articles.title: DFA recognizing end-marker encodings
articles.statement:
The DFA for the encodings: state `inl false` while reading left
letters, `inl true` after the end marker (the accepting state), and
`inr ()` dead once anything follows the end marker.

## Sources

- Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3.

articles.title: Injectivity of the end-marker encoding
articles.statement:
Encoding is injective.

## Sources

- Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3.

articles.title: End-marker encoding of a word
articles.statement:
Encode a word by copying it to the left summand and appending the
end marker `Sum.inr ()`.

## Sources

- Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3 (deterministic pushdown automata, acceptance by empty stack with an end marker).

articles.title: Erasing the end-marker encoding recovers the word
articles.statement:
Erasing an encoding recovers the word.

## Sources

- Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3.

articles.title: End-marker erasure
articles.statement:
Erase the end marker: a left letter maps to its one-letter word,
the end marker maps to the empty word.

## Sources

- Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3 (deterministic pushdown automata, acceptance by empty stack with an end marker).

articles.title: Encoding DFA accepts only end-marker encodings
articles.statement:
The encoding DFA reaches the accepting state only on encodings.

## Sources

- Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3.

articles.title: Deterministic context-free languages are context-free
articles.statement:
Every deterministic context-free language is context-free: the
encoded language is accepted by a pushdown automaton, hence
context-free; intersecting with the regular language of encodings and
erasing the end marker recovers the original language.

## Sources

- Ginsburg and Greibach, "Deterministic context free languages", Information and Control 9 (1966), 620-648; Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3.

articles.title: Deterministic context-free language
articles.statement:
A language is deterministic context-free when some deterministic
pushdown automaton with finite state and stack alphabets, whose
transitions consume letters from a finite set, accepts by empty stack
exactly the end-marker encodings of its words.

## Sources

- Ginsburg and Greibach, "Deterministic context free languages", Information and Control 9 (1966), 620-648; Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3.

articles.title: Deterministic pushdown automaton
articles.statement:
A pushdown automaton is deterministic when every transition set
has at most one element, and an available `ε`-transition precludes
every consuming transition from the same state and stack symbol.

## Sources

- Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed., Chapter 2 (deterministic pushdown automata); Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3.

articles.title: End-marker encodings form a regular language
articles.statement:
The encodings of words form a regular language.

## Sources

- Hopcroft, Motwani, and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, 3rd ed., Section 10.3.

articles.title: Earley item dot stays within its production
articles.statement:
The dot of a chart item never passes the end of its production.

## Sources

- Earley, "An efficient context-free parsing algorithm", Communications of the ACM 13 (1970), 94-102.

articles.title: Correctness of the Earley recognizer
articles.statement:
The Earley recognizer accepts exactly the grammar's language.

## Sources

- Earley, "An efficient context-free parsing algorithm", Communications of the ACM 13 (1970), 94-102.

articles.title: Acceptance by the Earley recognizer
articles.statement:
Acceptance by the Earley recognizer: some completed item for a
production of the initial nonterminal consumes the whole input.

## Sources

- Earley, "An efficient context-free parsing algorithm", Communications of the ACM 13 (1970), 94-102.

articles.title: Completeness of the Earley chart
articles.statement:
Completeness: if a chart item waits on a sentential form and that
form yields a word fitting in the remaining input, the chart contains
the item completed by that word.

## Sources

- Earley, "An efficient context-free parsing algorithm", Communications of the ACM 13 (1970), 94-102.

articles.title: Earley chart as a predicate on items
articles.statement:
The chart as a predicate on `EarleyItem`s.

## Sources

- Earley, "An efficient context-free parsing algorithm", Communications of the ACM 13 (1970), 94-102.

articles.title: Earley chart
articles.statement:
The Earley chart for input `w`: the least set of items closed
under initialization, prediction, scanning, and completion.

## Sources

- Earley, "An efficient context-free parsing algorithm", Communications of the ACM 13 (1970), 94-102.

articles.title: Earley item
articles.statement:
An Earley item: a production with a dot after `dot` symbols of its
output, recognizing input that starts at the end of `pre` and whose
recognized prefix is `consumed`. The full input is `pre ++ consumed
++ rest` for some `rest`.

articles.title: A yield from one nonterminal starts with one of its productions
articles.statement:
Inversion of a yield from a single nonterminal: it begins with
one production of that nonterminal.

## Sources

- Earley, "An efficient context-free parsing algorithm", Communications of the ACM 13 (1970), 94-102.

articles.title: Soundness of the Earley chart
articles.statement:
Soundness: the recognized prefix of a chart item yields the input
it consumed.

## Sources

- Earley, "An efficient context-free parsing algorithm", Communications of the ACM 13 (1970), 94-102.

articles.title: Productions of the $\varepsilon$-eliminated grammar come from productions of $g$
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. Every production $A \to \alpha'$ of the grammar obtained
from $g$ by eliminating $\varepsilon$-productions arises from a production $A \to \alpha$ of $g$
with the same left-hand side $A$, such that $\alpha'$ is obtained from $\alpha$ by deleting some
occurrences of nullable nonterminals and $\alpha'$ is nonempty.

articles.title: Productions of the unit-eliminated grammar come from non-unit productions of $g$
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. For every production $A \to \beta$ of the grammar obtained
from $g$ by eliminating unit productions, there are a nonterminal $B$ and a production
$B \to \beta$ of $g$ such that $\beta$ is not a single nonterminal and $B$ is reachable from $A$
by a possibly empty chain of unit productions of $g$.

articles.title: The $\varepsilon$-eliminated grammar generates the nonempty words of $g$
articles.statement:
For a
context-free grammar $g$ and every word $w$ over its terminals, $w$ is generated by the grammar
obtained from $g$ by eliminating $\varepsilon$-productions if and only if $w$ is generated by
$g$ and $w$ is nonempty.

articles.title: The $\varepsilon$-eliminated grammar has no empty productions
articles.statement:
For a context-free
grammar $g$, no production of the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating
$\varepsilon$-productions has empty right-hand side.

articles.title: Elimination of $\varepsilon$-productions
articles.statement:
For a context-free grammar $g$, the grammar
obtained from $g$ by eliminating $\varepsilon$-productions has the same nonterminals and the
same initial nonterminal as $g$. Its productions are the productions $A \to \alpha'$ such that
$g$ has a production $A \to \alpha$, the form $\alpha'$ is obtained from $\alpha$ by deleting
some (possibly no) occurrences of nullable nonterminals (those deriving the empty word in $g$),
and $\alpha'$ is nonempty.

articles.title: Deleting nullable nonterminals shrinks the denoted language
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free
grammar and $V$ an assignment of a language $V(A)$ to each nonterminal $A$ of $g$ such that the
empty word belongs to $V(A)$ whenever $A$ is nullable (derives the empty word in $g$). If a
sentential form $\alpha'$ is obtained from a sentential form $u$ by deleting some occurrences of
nullable nonterminals, then the language denoted by $\alpha'$ under $V$ is contained in the
language denoted by $u$ under $V$.

articles.title: Existence of reduced grammars
articles.statement:
For every context-free grammar $g$ over an alphabet $T$
there is a context-free grammar $g'$ over $T$ that generates exactly the nonempty words
generated by $g$, such that no production of $g'$ has empty right-hand side and no production
of $g'$ has a single nonterminal as its right-hand side.

articles.title: Nonterminals of a sentential form
articles.statement:
For a sentential form $u$, a finite word of terminal
and nonterminal symbols, the nonterminals of $u$ form the finite set of all nonterminals that
occur in $u$.

articles.title: Set of nonterminals mentioned by a grammar
articles.statement:
The nonterminals mentioned by a context-free
grammar $g$ form the finite set consisting of the initial nonterminal of $g$, the left-hand side
of every production of $g$, and every nonterminal occurring in the right-hand side of a
production of $g$.

articles.title: Reduced grammars
articles.statement:
A context-free grammar is reduced when no production has empty
right-hand side and no production has a single nonterminal as its right-hand side.

This is the sense used for the pumping lemma and normal forms. It does not assert that every
nonterminal is reachable or productive.

articles.title: Unit output
articles.statement:
A sentential form is a unit output when it consists of a single
nonterminal.

articles.title: Soundness of ε-production elimination
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and, for each
nonterminal $A$, let $L_g(A)$ be the language of words $g$ derives from $A$. Then $L_g$ is a
valuation of the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating ε-productions: for every production
$A \to \alpha$ of that grammar, the language of $\alpha$ under $L_g$ (the concatenation of the
languages of its symbols, a terminal $a$ denoting $\{a\}$) is contained in $L_g(A)$.

articles.title: Soundness of unit-production elimination
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and, for
each nonterminal $A$, let $L_g(A)$ be the language of words $g$ derives from $A$. Then $L_g$ is a
valuation of the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating unit productions: for every production
$A \to \alpha$ of that grammar, the language of $\alpha$ under $L_g$ (the concatenation of the
languages of its symbols, a terminal $a$ denoting $\{a\}$) is contained in $L_g(A)$.

articles.title: Languages along unit chains
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and, for each nonterminal
$A$, let $L_g(A)$ be the language of words $g$ derives from $A$. If $B$ is reachable from $A$ by
a chain of zero or more unit productions $A \to A_1 \to \dots \to B$ of $g$, then
$L_g(B) \subseteq L_g(A)$.

articles.title: Productions of the ε-free grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar with a production
$A \to u$, and let $\alpha$ be a nonempty form obtained from $u$ by deleting some (possibly no)
occurrences of nullable nonterminals. Then $A \to \alpha$ is a production of the grammar obtained
from $g$ by eliminating ε-productions.

articles.title: Unit chains start at mentioned nonterminals
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar and let $B$
be reachable from $A$ by a chain of zero or more unit productions of $g$. If $B$ is the left-hand
side of some production of $g$, then $A$ is among the nonterminals mentioned by $g$ (its initial
nonterminal, the left-hand sides of its productions, and the nonterminals in their right-hand
sides).

articles.title: Productions of the unit-free grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar, let $B$ be
reachable from $A$ by a chain of zero or more unit productions of $g$, and let $B \to \beta$ be a
production of $g$ whose right-hand side $\beta$ is not a single nonterminal. If $A$ is among the
nonterminals mentioned by $g$, then $A \to \beta$ is a production of the grammar obtained from
$g$ by eliminating unit productions.

articles.title: No empty words without empty productions
articles.statement:
In a context-free grammar in which no
production has an empty right-hand side, every nonempty sentential form yields only nonempty
words.

articles.title: Nullable deletions
articles.statement:
For a context-free grammar $g$ and a sentential form $u$, the nullable
deletions of $u$ are the forms obtained from $u$ by deleting any selection of occurrences of
nullable nonterminals, possibly none and possibly all, keeping the remaining symbols in order.
They form a finite set.

articles.title: Nullable nonterminal
articles.statement:
A nonterminal $A$ of a context-free grammar $g$ is nullable when $g$
derives the empty word from $A$.

articles.title: Eliminating unit productions preserves the language
articles.statement:
For every context-free
grammar $g$, the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating unit productions generates
the same language as $g$.

articles.title: Eliminating unit productions leaves no unit production
articles.statement:
For every context-free
grammar $g$, no production of the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating unit
productions has an output consisting of a single nonterminal.

articles.title: Eliminating unit productions creates no new outputs
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free
grammar. For every production of the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating unit
productions, some production of $g$ has the same output.

In particular, empty outputs are not created.

articles.title: Eliminating unit productions
articles.statement:
A unit production is one whose output is a single
nonterminal. For a context-free grammar $g$, the grammar obtained by eliminating unit
productions has the same nonterminals and the same start symbol as $g$. Its productions
are the $A \to \alpha$ such that $A$ is a nonterminal mentioned by $g$ (its start symbol
or one occurring in a production of $g$), $g$ has a production $B \to \alpha$ that is not
a unit production, and $A$ reaches $B$ by a chain of zero or more unit productions of $g$.

articles.title: Reachability by unit productions
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar. A nonterminal
$A$ of $g$ reaches a nonterminal $B$ by unit productions when there is a chain
$A = A_0, A_1, \dots, A_n = B$ with $n \ge 0$ such that each $A_{i-1} \to A_i$ is a
production of $g$. In particular, every nonterminal reaches itself.

articles.title: Completeness of eliminating empty productions
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar.
If a sentential form $\alpha$ of $g$ yields a terminal word $w$ in $g$, then some form
$\alpha'$ obtained from $\alpha$ by deleting some occurrences of nullable nonterminals
yields $w$ in the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating $\varepsilon$-productions, and
$w$ is empty if $\alpha'$ is empty.

articles.title: Eliminating unit productions keeps every yield
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar.
If a sentential form $\alpha$ of $g$ yields a terminal word $w$ in $g$, then $\alpha$
yields $w$ in the grammar obtained from $g$ by eliminating unit productions.

articles.title: Nonempty Greibach productions begin with a terminal
articles.statement:
In Greibach normal form, every nonempty production output begins
with a terminal followed by nonterminals.

## Sources

- Hopcroft and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, Addison-Wesley, 1979, Chapter 7 (Greibach normal form); Harrison, Introduction to Formal Language Theory, Addison-Wesley, 1978, Chapter 4.

articles.title: Greibach normal form
articles.statement:
A grammar is in Greibach normal form when every production has
output either a single terminal followed by nonterminals, or the
empty word with the initial nonterminal on the left; and either the
initial nonterminal occurs in no output (so an empty production
cannot leak the empty word to other nonterminals) or there are no
empty outputs at all.

## Sources

- Hopcroft and Ullman, Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, Addison-Wesley, 1979, Chapter 7 (Greibach normal form); Harrison, Introduction to Formal Language Theory, Addison-Wesley, 1978, Chapter 4.

articles.title: Regular languages over a finite alphabet are context-free
articles.statement:
Over a finite alphabet,
every regular language is context-free.

Finiteness of the alphabet is necessary: a grammar has finitely many
productions, hence mentions only finitely many terminal symbols, but a DFA
over an infinite alphabet may accept every one-letter word.

articles.title: Productions of the triple grammar
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a pushdown automaton with a finite set of
states, a finite stack alphabet, start state $q_0$ and initial stack symbol $Z_0$, and let $T_0$
be a finite set of input letters. Every production of the triple grammar of $M$ and $T_0$ is of
one of two kinds. Either it is a start production $S \to (q_0, Z_0, q)$ for some state $q$,
where $S$ is the initial nonterminal; or there are states $p$ and $r$, a stack symbol $\gamma$,
an input $a$ that is a letter or $\varepsilon$, a transition of $M$ from $p$ on $a$ popping
$\gamma$ that moves to $r$ and pushes $\gamma_1 \cdots \gamma_k$, and states
$s_1, \dots, s_k$ such that, writing $s_0 = r$, the production is

$$(p, \gamma, s_k) \to a\,(s_0, \gamma_1, s_1)(s_1, \gamma_2, s_2) \cdots (s_{k-1}, \gamma_k, s_k)$$

where $a$ is omitted when it is $\varepsilon$ (for $k = 0$ the production is
$(p, \gamma, r) \to a$).

articles.title: The grammar-simulating pushdown automaton accepts the grammar's language
articles.statement:
For every
context-free grammar $g$ over an alphabet $T$, the language accepted by empty stack by the
one-state pushdown automaton simulating $g$ equals the language generated by $g$.

articles.title: The grammar-simulating pushdown automaton is finitely supported
articles.statement:
For every context-free
grammar $g$ over an alphabet $T$, the one-state pushdown automaton simulating $g$ is finitely
supported.

The finite sets witnessing this are the set containing the single state, the set of stack
symbols consisting of the initial nonterminal of $g$ and all symbols occurring in right-hand
sides of productions of $g$, and the set of terminals occurring in right-hand sides of
productions of $g$.

articles.title: The pushdown automaton simulating a context-free grammar
articles.statement:
For a context-free grammar $g$
over an alphabet $T$, this is the pushdown automaton with input alphabet $T$, a single state, the
terminals and nonterminals of $g$ as stack alphabet, and the initial nonterminal of $g$ as initial
stack symbol. Popping a nonterminal $A$ on an $\varepsilon$-transition, it may push the right-hand
side of any production of $g$ with left-hand side $A$ (whose first symbol becomes the new top);
popping a terminal $a$ while reading the input letter $a$, it pushes nothing. It has no other
transitions.

articles.title: Transitions of the grammar-simulating pushdown automaton
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free
grammar over an alphabet $T$. To the single state, an input option (a letter of $T$, or none for
an $\varepsilon$-transition) and a popped symbol of $g$ (a terminal or a nonterminal), this
assigns a finite set of pairs of the state and a list of symbols of $g$ to push. Popping a
nonterminal $A$ with no input gives, for each production of $g$ with left-hand side $A$, the pair
pushing its right-hand side. Popping a terminal $b$ while reading the letter $a$ gives the single
pair pushing nothing if $a = b$, and the empty set otherwise. Popping a nonterminal while reading
a letter, or a terminal with no input, gives the empty set.

articles.title: Chain of triple nonterminals
articles.statement:
Write $(p, \gamma, q)$ for the nonterminal symbol given by
states $p, q$ and a stack symbol $\gamma$ (the nonterminals of the triple grammar are these
triples and one extra initial nonterminal). The chain form of a list $\gamma_1 \cdots \gamma_k$
of stack symbols along a nonempty list $s_0, s_1, \dots, s_m$ of states is the word
$(s_0, \gamma_1, s_1)(s_1, \gamma_2, s_2) \cdots (s_{j-1}, \gamma_j, s_j)$ with $j = \min(k, m)$:
consecutive states bracket each stack symbol. Along the empty list of states the chain form is
the empty word. In the intended use $m = k$, so every stack symbol is bracketed.

articles.title: Context-free languages are accepted by finitely supported pushdown automata
articles.statement:
For every
context-free language $L$ over an alphabet $T$ there are a context-free grammar $g$ over $T$ and a
finitely supported pushdown automaton with input alphabet $T$, a single state, and the terminals
and nonterminals of $g$ as stack alphabet, whose language accepted by empty stack is $L$.

articles.title: Context-free languages are accepted by pushdown automata
articles.statement:
For every context-free language
$L$ over an alphabet $T$ there are a context-free grammar $g$ over $T$ and a pushdown automaton
with input alphabet $T$, a single state, and the terminals and nonterminals of $g$ as stack
alphabet, whose language accepted by empty stack is $L$.

articles.title: Finite pushdown automata accept context-free languages
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a pushdown automaton
with a finite set of states and a finite stack alphabet, and suppose that there is a finite set
$T_0$ of input letters such that $M$ has no transition, from any state and popping any stack
symbol, that consumes a letter outside $T_0$. Then the language accepted by $M$ by empty stack
is context-free.

articles.title: Context-free languages are exactly the languages of finite pushdown automata
articles.statement:
A language
$L$ over an alphabet $T$ is context-free if and only if there are a pushdown automaton $M$ over
$T$ with a finite set of states and a finite stack alphabet, and a finite set $T_0$ of input
letters such that $M$ has no transition, from any state and popping any stack symbol, that
consumes a letter outside $T_0$, for which the language accepted by $M$ by empty stack is $L$.

Here the alphabet, the states and the stack alphabet are types in the lowest universe.

articles.title: Start productions of the triple grammar
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a pushdown automaton with a finite
set of states, a finite stack alphabet, start state $q_0$ and initial stack symbol $Z_0$, and let
$T_0$ be a finite set of input letters. For every state $q$, the triple grammar of $M$ and $T_0$
contains the production $S \to (q_0, Z_0, q)$, where $S$ is its initial nonterminal.

articles.title: Transition productions of the triple grammar
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a pushdown automaton with a
finite set of states and a finite stack alphabet, and let $T_0$ be a finite set of input
letters. Let $a$ be either $\varepsilon$ or a letter in $T_0$, and suppose that $M$ has a
transition from state $p$ on $a$ popping the stack symbol $\gamma$ that moves to state $r$ and
pushes $\gamma_1 \cdots \gamma_k$. Then for all states $s_1, \dots, s_k$, writing $s_0 = r$,
the triple grammar of $M$ and $T_0$ contains the production

$$(p, \gamma, s_k) \to a\,(s_0, \gamma_1, s_1)(s_1, \gamma_2, s_2) \cdots (s_{k-1}, \gamma_k, s_k)$$

where $a$ is omitted when it is $\varepsilon$.

articles.title: Chain forms consist of nonterminals
articles.statement:
For every list of stack symbols and every list of
states, every symbol of their chain form is a nonterminal.

articles.title: Terminal word of an optional input letter
articles.statement:
As a word of grammar symbols (terminals and
triple nonterminals), an input that is a letter $a$ contributes the one-symbol word consisting of
the terminal $a$, and the empty input $\varepsilon$ contributes the empty word.

articles.title: The triple grammar generates the accepted language
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a pushdown automaton with
a finite set of states and a finite stack alphabet, and let $T_0$ be a finite set of input
letters such that $M$ has no transition, from any state and popping any stack symbol, that
consumes a letter outside $T_0$. Then the language generated by the triple grammar of $M$ and
$T_0$ equals the language accepted by $M$ by empty stack.

articles.title: Triple grammar of a pushdown automaton
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a pushdown automaton over the alphabet
$T$ with a finite set $\sigma$ of states, a finite stack alphabet $\Gamma$, start state $q_0$
and initial stack symbol $Z_0$, and let $T_0$ be a finite set of letters. The triple grammar of
$M$ and $T_0$ is the context-free grammar over $T$ whose nonterminals are an initial
nonterminal $S$ and the triples $(p, \gamma, q)$ with $p, q \in \sigma$ and $\gamma \in \Gamma$.
Its productions are the start productions $S \to (q_0, Z_0, q)$ for every state $q$, and the
transition productions: for every state $p$, stack symbol $\gamma$, input $a$ that is
$\varepsilon$ or a letter of $T_0$, transition of $M$ from $p$ on $a$ popping $\gamma$ that
moves to a state $r$ and pushes $\gamma_1 \cdots \gamma_k$, and all states $s_1, \dots, s_k$,
writing $s_0 = r$, the production

$$(p, \gamma, s_k) \to a\,(s_0, \gamma_1, s_1)(s_1, \gamma_2, s_2) \cdots (s_{k-1}, \gamma_k, s_k)$$

where $a$ is omitted when it is $\varepsilon$ (for $k = 0$ this is $(p, \gamma, r) \to a$).

The nonterminal $(p, \gamma, q)$ is meant to derive the words that take $M$ from state $p$ with
stack $\gamma$ to state $q$ with empty stack; transitions on letters outside $T_0$ are not
used.

articles.title: Lists of states of a given length
articles.statement:
For a finite set $\sigma$ of states and a natural
number $n$, this is the finite set of all lists of length $n$ with entries in $\sigma$. It is
built recursively: for $n = 0$ it contains only the empty list, and for $n + 1$ it consists of
the lists obtained by putting a state $p \in \sigma$ in front of a list from the set for $n$.

articles.title: Production of the triple grammar for a transition
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $r$ be states, $\gamma$ a
stack symbol, $a$ an optional input letter, $\varepsilon_1 \cdots \varepsilon_k$ a list of stack
symbols and $s_1, \dots, s_m$ a list of states. Write $s_0 = r$ and let $q = s_m$ be the last
state of the list $s_0, s_1, \dots, s_m$ (so $q = r$ when $m = 0$). The production has
left-hand side the nonterminal $(p, \gamma, q)$, and its right-hand side is the letter $a$
(nothing if $a$ is absent) followed by the nonterminals $(s_{i-1}, \varepsilon_i, s_i)$ for
$i = 1, \dots, \min(k, m)$ in order.

It encodes a transition that in state $p$, reading $a$ (or no letter), pops $\gamma$, moves to
state $r$ and pushes $\varepsilon_1 \cdots \varepsilon_k$; the triple grammar uses it with
$m = k$.

articles.title: Restricting the stack alphabet preserves the accepted language
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a pushdown
automaton and let $\Gamma_0$ be a finite set of stack symbols of $M$ that contains the initial
stack symbol of $M$ and is closed for $M$. Then the restriction of $M$ to the stack alphabet
$\Gamma_0$ accepts, by empty stack, exactly the same language as $M$.

articles.title: Language accepted by a pushdown automaton
articles.statement:
The language accepted by a pushdown
automaton $M$, by empty stack, consists of the words $w$ for which some computation of $M$
leads from the initial configuration on input $w$ to a configuration, in some state, with no
remaining input and an empty stack.

articles.title: Computations extend by unread input and stack bottom
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a pushdown automaton.
If $M$ can compute from a configuration with state $q$, remaining input $w$ and stack $s$ to a
configuration with state $q'$, remaining input $w'$ and stack $s'$, then for every word $v$ and
every list $t$ of stack symbols, $M$ can compute from the configuration with state $q$,
remaining input $wv$ and stack $st$ to the configuration with state $q'$, remaining input $w'v$
and stack $s't$. Here $st$ is the stack $s$ with $t$ placed below it.

articles.title: Closed sets of stack symbols
articles.statement:
A finite set $\Gamma_0$ of stack symbols is closed for a
pushdown automaton $M$ when every transition of $M$ that pops a symbol in $\Gamma_0$, from any
state and on any input letter or on $\varepsilon$, pushes only symbols in $\Gamma_0$.
Computations starting with a stack inside a closed set keep their stack inside it.

articles.title: Pushdown automaton configuration
articles.statement:
A configuration of a pushdown automaton with input
alphabet $T$, states in $\sigma$ and stack alphabet $\Gamma$ consists of a current state in
$\sigma$, the remaining unread input (a word over $T$), and the stack contents (a list over
$\Gamma$ whose first element is the top of the stack).

articles.title: Computations inside a closed set lift to the restriction
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a pushdown automaton
and let $\Gamma_0$ be a finite set of stack symbols that contains the initial stack symbol of $M$
and is closed for $M$. Suppose $M$ can compute from a configuration with state $q$, remaining
input $w$ and stack $s$ to a configuration with state $q'$, remaining input $w'$ and stack $s'$,
and every symbol of $s$ lies in $\Gamma_0$. Then the symbols of $s'$ also lie in $\Gamma_0$, and
the restriction of $M$ to $\Gamma_0$ can compute from the configuration $(q, w, s)$ to the
configuration $(q', w', s')$, with $s$ and $s'$ read as stacks over $\Gamma_0$.

articles.title: Computations of the restriction are computations of the automaton
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a pushdown
automaton and let $\Gamma_0$ be a finite set of stack symbols that contains the initial stack
symbol of $M$ and is closed for $M$. If the restriction of $M$ to $\Gamma_0$ can compute from a
configuration with state $q$, remaining input $w$ and stack $s$ to a configuration with state
$q'$, remaining input $w'$ and stack $s'$, then $M$ can compute from the configuration
$(q, w, s)$ to the configuration $(q', w', s')$, where the stacks $s$ and $s'$ over $\Gamma_0$ are
read as stacks over the full stack alphabet of $M$.

articles.title: Multi-step computation of a pushdown automaton
articles.statement:
For a pushdown automaton $M$, a
configuration $c$ derives a configuration $c'$ when $M$ can reach $c'$ from $c$ in zero or more
computation steps; that is, derivation is the reflexive transitive closure of the one-step
computation relation of $M$.

articles.title: Finitely supported pushdown automata
articles.statement:
A pushdown automaton $M$ is finitely supported when
there are finite sets $\sigma_0$ of states, $\Gamma_0$ of stack symbols and $T_0$ of input letters
such that the start state lies in $\sigma_0$, the initial stack symbol lies in $\Gamma_0$, every
transition from a state in $\sigma_0$ that pops a symbol in $\Gamma_0$ (on any input letter or on
$\varepsilon$) moves to a state in $\sigma_0$ and pushes only symbols in $\Gamma_0$, and there is
no transition from a state in $\sigma_0$ popping a symbol in $\Gamma_0$ that consumes an input
letter outside $T_0$.

This is the finiteness condition of a standard pushdown automaton; computations from the initial
configuration then only ever visit finitely many states, push finitely many stack symbols, and
respond to finitely many input letters.

articles.title: Initial configuration of a pushdown automaton
articles.statement:
The initial configuration of a pushdown
automaton $M$ on an input word $w$ has the start state of $M$ as its state, all of $w$ as its
remaining input, and the stack consisting of the initial stack symbol of $M$ alone.

articles.title: Lifting a stack to a set of stack symbols
articles.statement:
Given a finite set $\Gamma_0$ of
stack symbols and a stack $s = \gamma_1 \cdots \gamma_n$ all of whose symbols lie in
$\Gamma_0$, the lifted stack is the same list $\gamma_1 \cdots \gamma_n$, in the same
order, regarded as a stack over the alphabet $\Gamma_0$.

articles.title: Transitions of the restricted pushdown automaton
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a pushdown
automaton with stack alphabet $\Gamma$, and let $M|_{\Gamma_0}$ be its restriction to a
finite set $\Gamma_0 \subseteq \Gamma$ of stack symbols that contains the initial stack
symbol and is closed for $M$. Let $q, q'$ be states, $o$ an input option (an input
letter, or none for an $\varepsilon$-transition), $\gamma \in \Gamma_0$ and $s$ a list of
symbols of $\Gamma_0$. Then $(q', s)$ is a transition of $M|_{\Gamma_0}$ from $q$ on $o$
with top symbol $\gamma$ if and only if $(q', s)$, with $s$ read as a list of symbols
of $\Gamma$, is a transition of $M$ from $q$ on $o$ with top symbol $\gamma$.

articles.title: Pushdown automaton
articles.statement:
A pushdown automaton over an input alphabet $T$, with
states in $\sigma$ and stack alphabet $\Gamma$, consists of a transition function, a start
state in $\sigma$ and an initial stack symbol in $\Gamma$. The transition function assigns
to each state $q$, each input option (a letter of $T$, or none for an
$\varepsilon$-transition) and each popped stack symbol $\gamma$ a finite set of pairs
$(q', u)$ of a next state $q'$ and a list $u$ of stack symbols to push.

This is the generalized model: the state and stack types themselves are unrestricted,
and only each transition is finitely branching. A standard (textbook) pushdown
automaton is additionally finitely supported; without that, the language it accepts can
be an arbitrary language, so the conversion from pushdown automata back to context-free
grammars needs finiteness hypotheses.

articles.title: Restricting the stack alphabet of a pushdown automaton
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a pushdown
automaton with stack alphabet $\Gamma$, and let $\Gamma_0 \subseteq \Gamma$ be a finite set
of stack symbols that contains the initial stack symbol of $M$ and is closed for $M$.
The restriction of $M$ to $\Gamma_0$ is the pushdown automaton with the same input
alphabet, states and start state as $M$, stack alphabet $\Gamma_0$, and the initial stack
symbol of $M$ as its initial stack symbol. Its transitions from a state $q$ on an input
option $o$ with top symbol $\gamma \in \Gamma_0$ are the transitions $(q', u)$ of $M$ from
$q$ on $o$ with top symbol $\gamma$, with the pushed list $u$ read as a list over
$\Gamma_0$; closedness guarantees that every symbol of $u$ lies in $\Gamma_0$.

The restricted automaton has a finite stack alphabet and accepts the same language as
$M$.

articles.title: Computations stay inside a closed set of stack symbols
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a pushdown
automaton and $\Gamma_0$ a finite set of stack symbols that is closed for $M$. If a
configuration $c$ derives a configuration $c'$ in zero or more steps of $M$, and every
symbol on the stack of $c$ lies in $\Gamma_0$, then every symbol on the stack of $c'$ lies
in $\Gamma_0$.

articles.title: One step of a pushdown automaton
articles.statement:
Write a configuration of a pushdown automaton
$M$ as $(q, w, s)$: state $q$, remaining input $w$, and stack $s$ listed from the top.
A configuration $(q, w, \gamma s)$ steps to $(q', w, u s)$ whenever $(q', u)$ is an
$\varepsilon$-transition of $M$ from $q$ with top symbol $\gamma$, and a configuration
$(q, a w, \gamma s)$ steps to $(q', w, u s)$ whenever $(q', u)$ is a transition of $M$
from $q$ on the input letter $a$ with top symbol $\gamma$. There are no other steps: a
step pops the top symbol, consumes at most one input letter, and pushes the list $u$
with its head as the new top.

articles.title: The word aabbc is not generated by the $a^n b^n c^n$ grammar
articles.statement: `aabbc` is not generated: its counts are `2 = 2 ≠ 1`.

articles.title: The word aabbcc is generated by the $a^n b^n c^n$ grammar
articles.statement:
`aabbcc` is generated: grow two `a`'s, shuttle the `C`'s right past
the `B`'s, then convert `B`'s and `C`'s to terminals in order.

articles.title: The $a^n b^n c^n$ grammar is context-sensitive
articles.statement:
Every production of the `aⁿbⁿcⁿ` grammar is length-nondecreasing,
so the grammar is context-sensitive.

articles.title: Context-sensitive grammar for $a^n b^n c^n$
articles.statement: The standard context-sensitive grammar for `{aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 1}`.

articles.title: The word abc is generated by the $a^n b^n c^n$ grammar
articles.statement: `abc` is generated.

articles.title: Terminals of the $a^n b^n c^n$ grammar
articles.statement: Terminals of the `aⁿbⁿcⁿ` grammar.

articles.title: Nonterminals of the $a^n b^n c^n$ grammar
articles.statement: Nonterminals of the `aⁿbⁿcⁿ` grammar.

articles.title: The initial sentential form is balanced
articles.statement: The initial form `[S]` is balanced, with all counts zero.

articles.title: Balanced sentential form
articles.statement:
A sentential form is balanced when its `a`-, `b`- and `c`-counts
agree.

articles.title: Count of a's in a sentential form
articles.statement: The `a`-count of a sentential form.

articles.title: Count of b's in a sentential form
articles.statement: The `b`-count: terminal `b`'s plus unborn `B`'s.

articles.title: Count of c's in a sentential form
articles.statement: The `c`-count: terminal `c`'s plus unborn `C`'s.

articles.title: Symbol counts are additive over concatenation
articles.statement: Counting over a concatenation of three forms splits additively.

articles.title: Symbol count of a sentential form
articles.statement:
Count of the symbol `s` in a sentential form (terminals `a`, `b`,
`c`, and the "unborn" `b`/`c` nonterminals `B`, `C`).

articles.title: Unrestricted grammar
articles.statement:
An unrestricted grammar: a finite list of productions and an
initial nonterminal.

articles.title: Derivations preserve balancedness
articles.statement: Derivations preserve balancedness.

articles.title: Derivation in an unrestricted grammar
articles.statement: Derivation: the reflexive-transitive closure of rewriting.

articles.title: Context-sensitive grammar
articles.statement:
A grammar is context-sensitive when every production has a
nonterminal on its left side (so the left side is nonempty and not
terminal-only) and no production shrinks. The standard `S → ε`
exception is not used here: the `aⁿbⁿcⁿ` grammar has `n ≥ 1`.

articles.title: Nonterminal grammar symbols
articles.statement:
Whether a grammar symbol (`Mathlib.Computability.Language.Symbol`,
shared with the context-free development) is a nonterminal.

articles.title: Generated words have equally many a's, b's and c's
articles.statement:
Every generated terminal word has equally many `a`'s, `b`'s and
`c`'s.

articles.title: Language of an unrestricted grammar
articles.statement:
The language of a grammar: terminal words derived from the initial
nonterminal.

articles.title: Rewriting steps preserve balancedness
articles.statement:
One rewriting step preserves balancedness: every production has
the same imbalance on both sides, and the context contributes equally
to all three counts.

articles.title: One rewriting step of a grammar
articles.statement:
One rewriting step: apply a production in a sentential form
context. This is the generic `Cslib.Decidability.Rewriting.Step` at the
grammar's rules, so grammar derivations reuse the string-rewriting API
instead of a second, incompatible copy of it.

articles.title: Applying a production in context is a grammar step
articles.statement: One grammar step: rewrite `lhs` to `rhs` in context `p, q`.

articles.title: Acceptance by a linear bounded automaton
articles.statement:
`M` **accepts** `w` when some run from the initial configuration on `w`
reaches a configuration in the accepting state.

articles.title: Activation rules of the LBA grammar
articles.statement:
The activation rules: an inactive cell becomes active, keeping its
original, current, head state, and boundary tag.

articles.title: All rules of the LBA grammar
articles.statement: All the rules of the grammar.

articles.title: Cell symbol of the LBA grammar
articles.statement: A grammar symbol for the LBA grammar: a cell as a nonterminal.

articles.title: Cell tuple as a grammar symbol
articles.statement: A cell tuple as a grammar symbol.

articles.title: Configuration bound
articles.statement:
For a single-tape machine with state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet
