$\Sigma$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the configuration bound at $k$ is the number
$(|Q| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 2)^{2k}$.

A configuration that uses at most $k$ cells is determined by a state or the halting state, the
symbol or blank under the head, and the first $k$ cells to either side of the head, each a symbol,
a blank, or past the last non-blank cell; so this number bounds how many such configurations
there are.

articles.title: Halting of a linear bounded automaton is decidable
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape machine over
a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, and fix any primitive recursive coding of $\Sigma$. If $M$ is a linear
bounded automaton, then the set of input words over $\Sigma$ on which $M$ halts is computable.

## Sources

- Sipser, *Introduction to the Theory of Computation*, Theorem 5.9, of which this is a fixed-machine halting analogue: Sipser decides acceptance uniformly over machine descriptions, which needs a code type for CSLib machines.

articles.title: Halting of a linear bounded automaton on binary codes is decidable
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a
single-tape machine over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ that is a linear bounded automaton, let
$\alpha$ be a primitive recursively coded type, and let $\iota : \{0, 1\} \to \Sigma$ be any map.
For $a \in \alpha$, let $w_a$ be the word over $\Sigma$ obtained by applying $\iota$ to each bit of
the binary expansion, least significant bit first and without leading zeros, of the
natural-number code of $a$; so $w_a$ is empty when that code is $0$. Then the set of
$a \in \alpha$ such that $M$ halts on $w_a$ is computable.

articles.title: Halting of a machine running in computable space is computable
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape
machine with state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, fix any primitive recursive coding of
$\Sigma$, and let $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be computable. If $M$ runs in space $s$, then the
set of input words over $\Sigma$ on which $M$ halts is computable.

The decision procedure runs $M$ for $(|Q| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 2)^{2 s(n)}$ steps on an
input of length $n$ and checks whether it has halted.

articles.title: Conversion rules of the LBA grammar
articles.statement:
The conversion rules: an active cell becomes its original terminal. The
head cell converts only in the accepting state, so a terminal word is
produced only from an accepting configuration. The boundary tag is
discarded on conversion.

articles.title: Derivations extend by a left context
articles.statement: A derivation may be appended on the left.

articles.title: Derivations extend by a right context
articles.statement: A derivation may be appended on the right.

articles.title: Derivations compose under concatenation
articles.statement: Derivations compose under append.

articles.title: Non-head or accepting cells convert to terminals
articles.statement:
A list of cells, each non-head or accepting, converts to its original
terminals.

articles.title: Runs of an LBA give grammar derivations
articles.statement: Derivations along a run, keeping the tape length and head on the tape.

articles.title: An LBA step is a grammar derivation step on encodings
articles.statement: One machine step is one grammar derivation step on encodings.

articles.title: Generated form derives the initial configuration encoding
articles.statement: The generated form derives the encoding of the initial configuration.

articles.title: The generator derives the full tail of cells
articles.statement: The generator derives the tail cells, ending the generation.

articles.title: The generator derives the middle cells and itself
articles.statement: The generator derives the middle tail cells followed by itself.

articles.title: Replacing a block by a rule is a derivation step
articles.statement:
One grammar step replacing a block: if `u` splits as `p ++ lhs ++ q`
and `(lhs, rhs)` is a rule, then `u` derives `p ++ rhs ++ q`.

articles.title: Setting one list position by a production is a derivation step
articles.statement: A single-cell replacement that is a production is a derivation step.

articles.title: Two-cell replacement at indices $i$ and $j = i + 1$
articles.statement: A two-cell replacement at positions `i` and `j = i + 1`.

articles.title: Setting two adjacent list positions by a production is a derivation step
articles.statement: A two-cell replacement that is a production is a derivation step.

articles.title: Replacing a single cell is a derivation step
articles.statement: One grammar step replacing a single cell by a single cell.

articles.title: Singleton-to-singleton productions are derivation steps
articles.statement: A singleton-to-singleton production is a derivation step.

articles.title: The start symbol derives the generated form of a word
articles.statement: The start symbol derives the generated sentential form of a word.

articles.title: Tail cells derive their activated encoding
articles.statement:
The tail cells, sitting at offset `start ≥ 1` in a word of total length
`start + w.length`, derive their activated encoding. The offset stays
`≥ 1` in the induction step, so the first tail cell is never tagged
`left`: it is `right` when it is the last cell and `middle` otherwise.

articles.title: Transitivity of grammar derivations
articles.statement: Derivations are transitive.

articles.title: Replacing two consecutive cells is a derivation step
articles.statement: One grammar step replacing two consecutive cells.

articles.title: Dropping past an updated list position
articles.statement: Dropping past a set position is unaffected by the set.

articles.title: Configurations of bounded space are finitely many
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape machine with
state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, where a configuration uses the cell under the head
and the cells on either side of it up to the last non-blank one. For every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, at
most $(|Q| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 2)^{2k}$ configurations of $M$ use at most $k$ cells.

articles.title: Every cell of a configuration encoding is active
articles.statement: Every cell of an encoding is active.

articles.title: Head states in a configuration encoding
articles.statement: Every cell of an encoding has head state `none` or the given state.

articles.title: Cell tuples of an LBA configuration from an offset
articles.statement:
The cells of a configuration, as a list of cell tuples: original symbol,
current symbol, head state, active, boundary tag. The head is given as
`some i` for the head position, or `none` once it has been passed. The
`start` index is the position of the first cell in the whole word and
`total` is the whole word's length, so the boundary tag of the cell at
offset `j` is `ofHead (start + j) total`.

articles.title: Configuration encoded as a sentential form
articles.statement:
A configuration as a sentential form: the cells of its tape, with the
original symbols taken from the input word `w`.

articles.title: Space-bounded machines halt within the configuration bound
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape
machine with state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ that runs in space
$s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. If $M$ halts on an input word $w$ of length $n$, then from the
initial configuration on $w$ it reaches a configuration in the halting state in at most
$(|Q| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 1)(|\Sigma| + 2)^{2 s(n)}$ steps.

Its run visits only configurations of space at most $s(n)$, and does not repeat one before
halting.

articles.title: Generated cells of a word
articles.statement:
The generated cells of a word, inactive, with the head state on the first
cell: the sentential form generation produces. The first cell is tagged
`both` for a one-cell word and `left` otherwise; the tail is `tailCells`.

articles.title: Generated sentential form of a word
articles.statement: The generated sentential form of a word.

articles.title: Generation rules of the LBA grammar
articles.statement:
The generation rules: the start symbol produces the first cell and the
generator (or, for a one-cell word, the first cell alone, tagged `both`);
the generator produces a middle non-head cell and itself, or a final
right non-head cell. The first cell of a longer word is tagged `left`.

articles.title: Generator symbol of the LBA grammar
articles.statement: The generator as a grammar symbol.

articles.title: Entries of the cell-tuple encoding
articles.statement:
The `i`-th cell of the encoding: original `w[i]`, current `tape[i]`,
head state exactly at the head position, boundary tag of position
`start + i` in a word of length `total`.

articles.title: Entries of a configuration encoding
articles.statement: The `i`-th cell of the encoding.

articles.title: Initial configuration of a linear bounded automaton
articles.statement:
The initial configuration on the input `w`: the initial state, the tape
`w` itself (no blanks), the head on the first cell.

articles.title: A machine that, on a blank cell, writes a blank and does not move is a linear bounded automaton
articles.statement:
**A machine that, on a blank cell, writes a blank and does not move is a linear bounded
automaton.** Its head never leaves a blank cell, so it stays on the input or on the two blank
cells next to it, and it writes non-blank symbols only on the input. The machine may change state
on a blank cell, or halt there.

articles.title: Linear bounded automaton
articles.statement:
A single-tape machine is a linear bounded automaton when it runs
in space $n + 1$ on inputs of length $n$: every configuration of its run on an input of length $n$
uses at most $n + 1$ cells, whether or not the run halts.

The input itself uses $\max(1, n)$ cells, and the extra cell lets the head step onto a blank cell
next to the input, the analogue of Sipser's endmarkers. With the bound $n$ instead, no machine
would qualify, since the empty input already uses one cell.

articles.title: Language of a linear bounded automaton
articles.statement: The language of `M`: the words it accepts.

articles.title: If the LBA accepts a nonempty word, the grammar derives it
articles.statement:
This is
one inclusion of the LBA-to-grammar direction.

articles.title: The grammar of an LBA is context-sensitive
articles.statement:
Every production has a
nonterminal on its left side and does not shrink.

articles.title: The grammar of an LBA
articles.statement:
The grammar whose rules are the generation,
activation, simulation, and conversion rules above, starting from the start
symbol.

articles.title: Boundary tag of a linear bounded automaton head
articles.statement:
Where the head sits relative to the tape boundaries: strictly inside
the tape, on the first cell, on the last cell, or on the only cell of a
one-cell tape. The transition function observes this tag, so the machine
can tell the two ends of its tape apart from interior cells.

articles.title: Configuration of a linear bounded automaton
articles.statement:
A configuration of a linear bounded automaton: the state, the tape
(a list of cells, one per input cell; `none` is a blank), and the head
position.

articles.title: Head move of a linear bounded automaton
articles.statement: A head move of a linear bounded automaton: left, stay, or right.

articles.title: Nonterminals of the grammar of a linear bounded automaton
articles.statement:
The nonterminals of the grammar of an LBA: a cell, a generator, and the
start symbol. A cell records the original input symbol, the current tape
symbol, the head state if the head is on the cell, whether the cell is
active (simulation acts only on active cells), and the boundary tag of
its position (so simulation can apply the boundary-aware transitions).

articles.title: Legal head move of a linear bounded automaton
articles.statement:
A move is legal from the head position `h` on a tape of length `n` when
the source head is on the tape and the new head position is still on the
tape. In particular a left move from an out-of-bounds head is illegal,
even though the truncated new head `h - 1` would still be out of bounds:
legality requires `h < n` for left moves as well.

articles.title: Length of the cell-tuple encoding
articles.statement:
The encoding has as many cells as the input word, when the tape has the
same length.

articles.title: Length of a configuration encoding
articles.statement: The encoding of a configuration has as many cells as the input word.

articles.title: Linear bounded automaton
articles.statement:
A **linear bounded automaton**: a nondeterministic Turing machine whose
tape is the input word. The transition function gives, for a state, the
symbol under the head (`none` for a blank cell), and the boundary tag of
the head position, the finite set of possible next states, symbols to
write (`none` for a blank), and head moves. The boundary tag is what lets
the machine detect the ends of its tape: without it the model could not
recognize general context-sensitive languages. A move that would take
the head off the tape is not a step.

articles.title: Original symbols of an encoding are the input word
articles.statement: The original symbols of an encoding are the input word.

articles.title: A space bound is at least the space of the input
articles.statement:
If a single-tape machine runs in space
$s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, then $\max(1, n) \le s(n)$ for the length $n$ of every input word,
since the initial configuration on an input of length $n$ uses $\max(1, n)$ cells.

articles.title: The start rule is a generation rule of the LBA grammar
articles.statement: The first generation rule is a rule of the grammar.

articles.title: The activation rule belongs to the LBA grammar
articles.statement: The activation rule is a rule of the grammar.

articles.title: The accepting conversion rule belongs to the LBA grammar
articles.statement: The accepting conversion rule is a rule of the grammar.

articles.title: The non-head conversion rule belongs to the LBA grammar
articles.statement: The non-head conversion rule is a rule of the grammar.

articles.title: The final generation rule belongs to the LBA grammar
articles.statement: The final generation rule is a rule of the grammar.

articles.title: The one-cell generation rule belongs to the LBA grammar
articles.statement: The one-cell generation rule is a rule of the grammar.

articles.title: The first generation rule belongs to the LBA grammar
articles.statement: The first generation rule is a rule of the grammar.

articles.title: The generator step rule belongs to the LBA grammar
articles.statement: The generator step rule is a rule of the grammar.

articles.title: Left transitions give simulation rules
articles.statement: A left transition gives a simulation rule.

articles.title: Right transitions give simulation rules
articles.statement: A right transition gives a simulation rule.

articles.title: Stay transitions give simulation rules
articles.statement: A stay transition gives a simulation rule.

articles.title: Space bounds can be weakened
articles.statement:
If a single-tape machine runs in space
$s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $s' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfies $s(n) \le s'(n)$ for
every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then it runs in space $s'$.

articles.title: Head position after a move
articles.statement:
The head position after a move: left decrements, stay keeps, right
increments.

articles.title: Boundary tag on a one-cell tape
articles.statement: The boundary tag at the head of a one-cell tape.

articles.title: Boundary tag on the first cell of a longer tape
articles.statement: The boundary tag at the head of the first cell of a longer tape.

articles.title: Boundary tag at an interior head position
articles.statement: The boundary tag at an interior head position.

articles.title: Boundary tag on the last cell of a longer tape
articles.statement: The boundary tag at the head of the last cell of a longer tape.

articles.title: Boundary tag of a head position
articles.statement: The boundary tag of head position `h` on a tape of length `n`.

articles.title: Reachable LBA configurations keep the tape length and the head on the tape
articles.statement:
Reachable configurations have the input tape length and the head on the
tape, for a nonempty input word.

articles.title: Simulation rules for a left move
Simulation rules for a right move
articles.statement:
The simulation rules for a right move: the head cell rewrites its current
symbol and loses the head; the neighbouring cell gains the head. Both cells
keep their boundary tags.

articles.title: Simulation rules for a stay move
articles.statement:
The simulation rules for a stay move: the head cell rewrites its current
symbol and state, staying active, keeping its boundary tag.

articles.title: A single-tape machine decides the halting problem of a linear bounded automaton
articles.statement:
Let $M$
be a linear bounded automaton over a finite tape alphabet $\Sigma$, let $\iota$ be any map from
the Booleans to $\Sigma$, and let $\alpha$ be a primitively encodable type. For $a \in \alpha$, let
$w_a$ be the word obtained by writing, letter by letter through $\iota$, the binary expansion
(least significant bit first) of the natural-number code of $a$. Then the predicate on $\alpha$
that holds at $a$ exactly when $M$ halts on the input $w_a$ is decidable by a single-tape
machine.

articles.title: Space-bounded single-tape machines
articles.statement:
Let $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. A single-tape
Turing machine $M$ runs in space $s$ when, for every input word $l$ of length $|l|$, every
configuration reachable from the initial configuration of $M$ on $l$ uses at most $s(|l|)$
cells, whether or not the run halts. The cells used by a configuration are the head cell
together with the cells on each side of it up to the outermost non-blank cell.

articles.title: Start symbol of the LBA grammar
articles.statement: The start symbol as a grammar symbol.

articles.title: LBA steps keep the head on the tape
articles.statement: One step keeps the head on the tape, when the source head is on the tape.

articles.title: LBA steps preserve tape length
articles.statement: One step preserves the tape length.

articles.title: One step of a linear bounded automaton
articles.statement:
One step of the machine: choose a transition for the current state,
the symbol under the head, and its boundary tag, write the symbol, move
the head legally. A step from a configuration whose head is off the
tape is impossible: legality requires the source head to be on the
tape.

articles.title: Middle generated cells of a word
articles.statement:
The middle non-head generated cells of a word, inactive: the cells the
generator produces while the generator remains.

articles.title: Tail generated cells of a word
articles.statement:
The non-head generated cells of a word, inactive, as the tail of a
generated word: middle cells and a final right cell.

articles.title: Middle generated sentential form of a word
articles.statement:
The middle non-head generated sentential form of a word: every cell
tagged `middle`, for the generator's intermediate stage.

articles.title: Tail generated sentential form of a word
articles.statement: The non-head generated sentential form of a word.

articles.title: Splitting a list at two consecutive positions
articles.statement: A list splits at two consecutive positions.

articles.title: Taking past an updated list position
articles.statement: Taking past a set position keeps the new value at that position.

articles.title: Terminal symbol of the LBA grammar
articles.statement: A terminal symbol of the grammar.

articles.title: Jerrum-Sinclair-Vigoda: FPRAS for the permanent
articles.statement:
For a bitstring $x$, let
$\operatorname{perm}(x)$ be the permanent of the 0-1 matrix encoded by $x$: if $x$ decodes, under
the canonical bitstring encoding, to a pair $(k, e)$ of a natural number $k$ and a list $e$ of
$k^2$ natural numbers each at most $1$, then $\operatorname{perm}(x)$ is the permanent of the
$k \times k$ matrix with row-major entries $e$, and otherwise $\operatorname{perm}(x) = 0$. There
are a polynomial $p$ with natural-number coefficients and a polynomial-time computable function
$E$ from triples of bitstrings to natural numbers such that for all bitstrings $x$ and $w$ with
$n = |w| \ge 1$ (the precision, given in unary), at least two thirds of the bitstrings $r$ of
length $p(|x| + n)$ satisfy
$|E(x, r, w) - \operatorname{perm}(x)| \le \operatorname{perm}(x) / n$.

## Sources

- M. Jerrum, A. Sinclair, and E. Vigoda, "A polynomial-time approximation algorithm for the permanent of a matrix with nonnegative entries", Journal of the ACM 51 (2004), 671-697 (STOC 2001); M. Jerrum and A. Sinclair, "Approximating the permanent", SIAM Journal on Computing 18 (1989), 1149-1178 (precursor with restricted guarantees).

articles.title: Permanent of an encoded 0-1 matrix
articles.statement:
For a bitstring $x$ that decodes to a pair $(n, e)$ of
a natural number $n$ and a list $e = (e_0, \dots, e_{m-1})$ of natural numbers with $m = n^2$
and every $e_j \le 1$, the value at $x$ is the permanent
$\sum_{\sigma} \prod_{i < n} e_{in + \sigma(i)}$ of the $n \times n$ matrix with entries $e$ in
row-major order, the sum running over all permutations $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$. For
every other bitstring the value is $0$.

articles.title: Permanent of an encoded 0-1 matrix
articles.statement:
For a bitstring $x$: if $x$ decodes, under the
canonical bitstring encoding, to a pair $(n, e)$ of a natural number $n$ and a list
$e = (e_0, \dots, e_{n^2 - 1})$ of $n^2$ natural numbers each at most $1$, the value at $x$ is the
permanent $\sum_{\sigma} \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} e_{in + \sigma(i)}$ of the $n \times n$ matrix with
row-major entries $e$, where $\sigma$ ranges over the permutations of $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$;
otherwise the value is $0$.

articles.title: The permanent is #P-complete (Valiant)
articles.statement:
The function that sends a bitstring encoding a
square 0-1 matrix to its permanent, and every other bitstring to $0$, is $\#P$-complete.

## Sources

- L. G. Valiant, "The complexity of computing the permanent", Theoretical Computer Science 8 (1979), 189-201.

articles.title: Counting satisfying assignments of a CNF formula
articles.statement:
The counting function $f$ from
bitstrings to natural numbers is defined as follows. If a bitstring $x$ decodes, under the
canonical bitstring encoding of pairs, to a pair $(s, \varphi)$ of a bitstring $s$ of length $n$
and a CNF formula $\varphi$ every literal of which has variable index less than $n$, then $f(x)$
is the number of assignments $a : \{0, \dots, n - 1\} \to \{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$
such that $\varphi$ is satisfied by the assignment sending each variable $v < n$ to $a(v)$ and
every other variable to false. Otherwise $f(x) = 0$.

The bitstring $s$ serves only to give the number of variables $n$ in unary.

articles.title: Counting SAT is #P-complete
articles.statement:
The function counting the satisfying assignments of a CNF
formula is $\#P$-complete: it lies in $\#P$, and every function in $\#P$ is computed from it by
a polynomial-time oracle machine.

## Sources

- L. G. Valiant, "The complexity of enumeration and reliability problems", SIAM Journal on Computing 8 (1979), 410-421.

articles.title: Number of satisfying assignments of an encoded DNF formula
articles.statement:
For a bitstring $x$: if $x$
decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a pair $(u, \varphi)$ of a bitstring $u$ of
length $m$ and a DNF formula $\varphi$ all of whose literals have variables less than $m$, the
value at $x$ is the number of assignments of booleans to the variables $0, \dots, m - 1$ that
satisfy $\varphi$; otherwise the value is $0$.

articles.title: Satisfaction of a DNF formula
articles.statement:
A DNF formula is a list of terms, each a list of literals
$(v, b)$ of a natural number $v$ (the variable) and a boolean $b$ (the polarity). An assignment $a$
of booleans to the natural numbers satisfies the formula when some term of it has $a(v) = b$ for
every literal $(v, b)$ of that term.

articles.title: Karp-Luby: FPRAS for DNF counting
articles.statement:
For a bitstring $x$, let $N(x)$ be the number of
satisfying assignments of the DNF formula encoded by $x$: if $x$ decodes, under the canonical
bitstring encoding, to a pair $(u, \varphi)$ of a bitstring $u$ of length $m$ and a DNF formula
$\varphi$ whose variables are all less than $m$, then $N(x)$ is the number of assignments of
booleans to the variables $0, \dots, m - 1$ that satisfy $\varphi$, and otherwise $N(x) = 0$.
There are a polynomial $p$ with natural-number coefficients and a polynomial-time computable
function $E$ from triples of bitstrings to natural numbers such that for all bitstrings $x$ and
$w$ with $n = |w| \ge 1$ (the precision, given in unary), at least two thirds of the bitstrings
$r$ of length $p(|x| + n)$ satisfy $|E(x, r, w) - N(x)| \le N(x) / n$.

## Sources

- R. M. Karp and M. Luby, "Monte-Carlo algorithms for enumeration and reliability problems", Proceedings of the Twenty-Fourth Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS 1983), 56-64.

articles.title: Stockmeyer: approximate counting of #P functions in BPP^NP
articles.statement:
For every function $f$ in
$\#P$ there are a decision problem $O$ in NP, polynomials $p_r$, $p$ and $q$ with
natural-number coefficients, and polynomial-time computable functions $\mathrm{nextQ}$ and
$\mathrm{final}$, each taking a bitstring and a list of query/answer pairs (bitstring, boolean),
with $\mathrm{nextQ}$ returning a bitstring and $\mathrm{final}$ returning a natural number,
such that the following holds. Let $x$ and $w$ be bitstrings with $n = |w| \ge 1$, where $|\cdot|$
denotes length, and put $m = |x| + n$. For a bitstring $r$ of length $p_r(m)$, let $E(r)$ be the
output of the oracle computation that chooses queries with $\mathrm{nextQ}$ and decides with
$\mathrm{final}$, run with oracle $O$, query-length cap $q(m)$ and $p(m)$ adaptive queries on
the bitstring encoding of the pair $(x, (r, w))$ from the empty history. Then
$f(x)/(1 + 1/n) \le E(r) \le f(x) \cdot (1 + 1/n)$, computed in the rationals, for at least two
thirds of the $2^{p_r(m)}$ bitstrings $r$ of length $p_r(m)$.

The bitstring $w$ gives the precision $n$ in unary; the number of random bits, the number of
queries and the query-length cap are all polynomial in $|x| + n$.

## Sources

- L. J. Stockmeyer, "The complexity of approximate counting", Proceedings of the Fifteenth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 1983), 118-126 (journal version in Information and Computation 1985).

articles.title: Threshold languages of #P functions are in PSPACE
articles.statement:
For every function $f$ in $\#P$,
the threshold language of $f$, which accepts a bitstring exactly when it decodes, under the
canonical bitstring encoding of pairs, to a pair $(x, k)$ of a bitstring $x$ and a natural
number $k$ with $k \le f(x)$, is in PSPACE.

## Sources

- L. G. Valiant, "The complexity of enumeration and reliability problems" (1979); S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Theorem 9.3 (#P ⊆ PSPACE in the threshold-language form).

articles.title: Threshold language of a counting function
articles.statement:
For a function $f$ from bitstrings to
natural numbers, the threshold language of $f$ is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring
$y$ exactly when decoding $y$ with the canonical bitstring encoding of pairs of a bitstring and
a natural number succeeds and gives a pair $(x, k)$ with $k \le f(x)$; bitstrings that do not
decode are rejected.

articles.title: Toda's theorem: PH is contained in $\mathsf{P}^{\#\mathsf{P}}$
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in
the polynomial hierarchy PH lies in $\mathsf{P}^{\#\mathsf{P}}$, the class of decision problems
decidable in polynomial time with a $\#\mathsf{P}$ oracle.

## Sources

- S. Toda, "PP is as hard as the polynomial-time hierarchy", SIAM Journal on Computing 20 (1991), 865-877 (FOCS 1989).

articles.title: The MAJSAT language
articles.statement:
MAJSAT is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly
when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of pairs, to a pair $(u, \varphi)$ of a
bitstring $u$ and a CNF formula $\varphi$ such that, with $n = |u|$, every literal of $\varphi$
has variable index less than $n$, and more than half of the $2^n$ assignments
$a : \{0, \dots, n-1\} \to \{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ satisfy $\varphi$, that is, twice
their number exceeds $2^n$. Only the length of $u$ matters, and a bitstring that does not decode
is rejected.

articles.title: MAJSAT is PP-complete
articles.statement:
The MAJSAT language is in PP, and every decision problem in PP has
a polynomial-time many-one reduction to MAJSAT.

## Sources

- J. Gill, "Computational complexity of probabilistic Turing machines", SIAM Journal on Computing 6 (1977), 675-695.

articles.title: NP is contained in PP
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in NP also belongs to PP, the class of
decision problems decided in probabilistic polynomial time with unbounded error.

## Sources

- J. Gill, "Computational complexity of probabilistic Turing machines" (1977).

articles.title: PP is contained in PSPACE
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in PP, the class of decision problems
decided with unbounded error in probabilistic polynomial time, belongs to PSPACE.

## Sources

- J. Gill, "Computational complexity of probabilistic Turing machines" (1977); S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009 (PP ⊆ PSPACE).

articles.title: Deleting nonterminals from an encoded right-hand side
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a list of natural
numbers and $u$ an encoded right-hand side, that is, a word whose letters are nonterminals
$i \in \mathbb{N}$ or terminals. The result is the list of all words obtained from $u$ by
deleting some of the occurrences of nonterminals that belong to $N$ (possibly none, possibly
all) and keeping every other letter in order; each choice of deleted occurrences contributes one
entry of the list.

articles.title: Computable removal of empty productions agrees with the classical one
articles.statement:
For every encoded
context-free grammar $g$, the grammar denoted by the encoded grammar obtained from $g$ by removing
empty productions is equal to the grammar obtained from the grammar denoted by $g$ by eliminating
empty productions: from each production, all productions obtained by deleting some occurrences of
nullable nonterminals from its output, except those with empty output.

articles.title: Removing empty productions from an encoded grammar
articles.statement:
For an encoded context-free grammar
$g$, the encoded grammar with the same start nonterminal whose productions are, for each
production $A \to u$ of $g$, the productions $A \to v$ for every nonempty word $v$ obtained from
$u$ by deleting some occurrences of nonterminals in the computed list of nullable nonterminals of
$g$.

articles.title: Terminal-free productions yield only the empty word
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an encoded context-free
grammar and consider the grammar of its productions without terminals. If a sentential form
$\alpha$ that contains no terminal yields a word $w$ in that grammar, then $w$ is the empty
word.

articles.title: The reduced grammar has no empty and no unit productions
articles.statement:
For every encoded context-free
grammar $g$, every production of the grammar denoted by the reduction of $g$ (empty productions
removed, then unit productions removed) has a nonempty output, and that output is not a single
nonterminal.

articles.title: Removing empty productions drops only the empty word
articles.statement:
For every encoded context-free
grammar $g$, the language of the encoded grammar obtained from $g$ by removing empty productions
consists of the nonempty words of the language of $g$.

articles.title: The reduced grammar generates the language minus the empty word
articles.statement:
For every encoded
context-free grammar $g$, the language of the reduction of $g$ (empty productions removed, then
unit productions removed) consists of the nonempty words of the language of $g$.

articles.title: Productions of the computable removal of empty productions
articles.statement:
For every encoded context-free
grammar $g$, a production is a production of the grammar denoted by the encoded grammar obtained
from $g$ by removing empty productions if and only if it is a production of the grammar obtained
from the grammar denoted by $g$ by eliminating empty productions.

articles.title: Computed deletions agree with nullable deletions
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an encoded context-free
grammar. For every encoded word $u$ and every sentential form $\alpha$ of the grammar denoted by
$g$, $\alpha$ is obtained from the decoding of $u$ by deleting some occurrences of nullable
nonterminals of the grammar denoted by $g$ if and only if $\alpha$ is the decoding of a word
obtained from $u$ by deleting some occurrences of nonterminals in the computed list of nullable
nonterminals of $g$.

articles.title: The nullable nonterminals are computed
articles.statement:
For every encoded context-free grammar $g$ and
every natural number $A$, $A$ belongs to the computed list of nullable nonterminals of $g$ (the
generating nonterminals of the productions of $g$ without terminals) if and only if $A$ is
nullable in the grammar denoted by $g$, that is, $A$ derives the empty word.

articles.title: Productions of the encoded unit elimination
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an encoded context-free grammar
over terminals $T$ and let $r$ be a production with terminals in $T$ and nonterminals in
$\mathbb{N}$. Then $r$ is a production of the grammar denoted by the encoded unit elimination of
$g$ if and only if $r$ is a production of the grammar obtained from the grammar denoted by $g$ by
eliminating unit productions.

articles.title: Unit reachability is computed
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an encoded context-free grammar and let $A$ and
$B$ be natural numbers. Then $B$ belongs to the computed list of nonterminals reachable from $A$
by unit productions of $g$ if and only if there are $k \ge 0$ and nonterminals
$A = C_0, C_1, \dots, C_k = B$ such that $C_{i-1} \to C_i$ is a production of the grammar denoted
by $g$ for every $i$ with $1 \le i \le k$.

articles.title: Productions without terminals of an encoded grammar
articles.statement:
For an encoded context-free grammar
$g$, the encoded grammar with the same start nonterminal whose productions are the productions
of $g$, in their order, whose right-hand sides contain no terminal.

articles.title: Nonterminals of an encoded grammar
articles.statement:
For an encoded context-free grammar $g$, the list
obtained by duplicate removal from the list made of the start nonterminal of $g$ followed, for
each production of $g$ in order, by its left-hand side and then the nonterminals of its
right-hand side in order. It lists without repetitions the nonterminals that $g$ mentions.

articles.title: Computed nullable nonterminals of an encoded grammar
articles.statement:
For an encoded context-free grammar
$g$, the list of generating nonterminals of the encoded grammar that has the start nonterminal
of $g$ and, as productions, the productions of $g$ whose right-hand sides contain no terminal.

A nonterminal is in this list exactly when it derives the empty word in the grammar denoted by
$g$.

articles.title: Reduction is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a type of terminals with a primitive
recursive encoding. The map sending an encoded context-free grammar $g$ over $T$ to its
reduction, the encoded grammar obtained from $g$ by removing empty productions and then unit
productions, is primitive recursive, where encoded grammars are encoded as pairs of a start
nonterminal and a list of productions.

articles.title: Reduction of an encoded grammar
articles.statement:
For an encoded context-free grammar $g$, the encoded
grammar obtained by first removing the empty productions of $g$ (encoded
$\varepsilon$-elimination) and then removing the unit productions of the result (encoded unit
elimination).

articles.title: A form yielding the empty word contains no terminal
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a context-free grammar
over terminals $T$ and let $\alpha$ be a sentential form of $G$. If $\alpha$ yields the empty
word in $G$, then no terminal symbol $a \in T$ occurs in $\alpha$.

articles.title: The encoded unit elimination denotes the unit-eliminated grammar
articles.statement:
For every encoded
context-free grammar $g$, the grammar denoted by the encoded unit elimination of $g$ is equal to
the grammar obtained from the grammar denoted by $g$ by eliminating unit productions.

articles.title: Unit elimination for encoded grammars
articles.statement:
For an encoded context-free grammar $g$, the
encoded grammar with the start nonterminal of $g$ whose productions are listed as follows: for
each nonterminal $A$ in the list of nonterminals of $g$, and for each production $B \to u$ of $g$
in order such that $B$ is in the computed list of nonterminals reachable from $A$ by unit
productions and $u$ is not a single nonterminal, the production $A \to u$.

articles.title: Nonterminals reachable by unit productions in an encoded grammar
articles.statement:
For an encoded
context-free grammar $g$ and a natural number $A$, let $n$ be the number of distinct nonterminals
mentioned in $g$ (the start, the left-hand sides, and the nonterminals on right-hand sides). The
list is obtained from the empty list by applying one round of unit reachability from $A$
exactly $n + 1$ times.

Its entries are exactly the nonterminals $B$ reachable from $A$ by a possibly empty chain of
unit productions $A \to \dots \to B$ of $g$; in particular $A$ itself is an entry.

articles.title: One round of unit reachability
articles.statement:
For an encoded context-free grammar $g$, a natural number
$A$ and a list $S$ of natural numbers, the list consisting of $A$ followed, for each production of
$g$ in order whose left-hand side lies in $S$ and whose right-hand side is a single nonterminal
$B$, by that nonterminal $B$.

articles.title: Target of a unit right-hand side
articles.statement:
For an encoded right-hand side $u$, a list whose entries
are nonterminals $i \in \mathbb{N}$ or terminals, the optional value is $B$ when $u$ consists of
the single nonterminal $B$, and there is no value otherwise.

articles.title: Yields of the empty word need only terminal-free productions
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an encoded
context-free grammar and $\alpha$ a sentential form of the grammar $g$ denotes. If $\alpha$ yields
the empty word in that grammar, then $\alpha$ also yields the empty word in the grammar denoted by
the encoded grammar consisting of the productions of $g$ that contain no terminal.

articles.title: Yields in the terminal-free subgrammar are yields of the grammar
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an encoded
context-free grammar, $\alpha$ a sentential form and $w$ a word. If $\alpha$ yields $w$ in the
grammar denoted by the encoded grammar consisting of the productions of $g$ that contain no
terminal, then $\alpha$ yields $w$ in the grammar $g$ denotes.

articles.title: Acceptance test for encoded DFAs
articles.statement:
For an encoded DFA $D$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ with
decidable equality and a word $w$ over $\alpha$, the acceptance test is the Boolean that is true
exactly when the state reached by running $D$ on $w$ from its start state is in the list of
accepting states of $D$.

articles.title: Every state of the accessible part is reached
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet
$\alpha$ with a finite state set $\sigma$ with decidable equality, and let $n \ge |\sigma|$. For
every state $p$ of the accessible part of $M$ found with $n$ rounds, some word $w$ leads the
accessible part from its start state to $p$.

articles.title: Accessible part of a DFA, by a bounded search
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet
$\alpha$ with a finite state set $\sigma$ with decidable equality, and let $n \ge |\sigma|$. The
accessible part of $M$ found with $n$ rounds is the DFA over $\alpha$ whose states are the states
found by the reachability search from the empty set with at most $n$ rounds, whose start state is
the start state of $M$, whose transition function is that of $M$ restricted to these states, and
whose accepting states are those of them that $M$ accepts.

Since $n \ge |\sigma|$, the search finds exactly the states that some word leads to from the start
state of $M$, and it stops as soon as a round adds nothing, so a larger bound costs nothing.

articles.title: Accessible part of a DFA
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet $\alpha$ with a finite
state set $\sigma$ with decidable equality. The accessible part of $M$ is its accessible part found
by the reachability search with $|\sigma|$ rounds: the DFA over $\alpha$ whose states are the
states found by the reachability search from the empty set with at most $|\sigma|$ rounds (exactly
the states that some word leads to from the start state of $M$), whose start state is the start
state of $M$, whose transition function is that of $M$ restricted to these states, and whose
accepting states are those of them that $M$ accepts.

articles.title: Equivalence test for encoded DFAs
articles.statement:
Let $D$ and $E$ be encoded DFAs over an alphabet
$\alpha$ with decidable equality. The equivalence test of $D$ and $E$ is the Boolean that is true
exactly when, for every entry $p$ of the list of reachable pairs of states of $D$ and $E$, writing
$p = \langle s, t \rangle$ with Mathlib's pairing function, $s$ is in the accepting list of $D$ if
and only if $t$ is in the accepting list of $E$.

It returns true exactly when $D$ and $E$ have the same language.

articles.title: Correctness of the equivalence test for DFAs
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be DFAs over the same finite
alphabet, with finite state sets with decidable equality and decidable sets of accepting states.
The equivalence test of $M$ and $N$ returns true if and only if $M$ and $N$ accept the same
language.

articles.title: Equivalence test for DFAs
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be DFAs over the same finite alphabet, with
finite state sets with decidable equality and decidable sets of accepting states. Their symmetric
difference is the product DFA on pairs of states that starts at the pair of start states, moves on
a letter by moving both components, and accepts a pair $(p, q)$ when exactly one of the statements
"$M$ accepts $p$" and "$N$ accepts $q$" holds. The equivalence test of $M$ and $N$ is the emptiness
test of their symmetric difference: the Boolean that is true exactly when no pair of states
reachable from the start pair is accepting.

articles.title: Accepted words of length between the number of listed states and twice it
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be an
encoded DFA over an alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality, and let $N$ be the length of its
list of states. For every natural number $n$ and every word $w$ of length $n$ in the language of
$D$ with $N \le n$, the language of $D$ contains a word $v$ whose length $|v|$ satisfies
$N \le |v| < 2N$.

articles.title: Correctness of the infiniteness test for encoded DFAs
articles.statement:
For every encoded DFA $D$ over a
finite alphabet, the infiniteness test returns true on $D$ if and only if the language of $D$ is
infinite.

articles.title: Infiniteness test for encoded DFAs
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be an encoded DFA over a finite alphabet and
let $N$ be the length of its list of states. The infiniteness test is the Boolean that is true
exactly when the language of $D$ contains a word $w$ with $N \le |w| < 2N$; it checks every word
of each length $N + i$ with $0 \le i < N$.

articles.title: A long accepted word makes the language of an encoded DFA infinite
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be an
encoded DFA and let $N$ be the length of the list of states of $D$. If $D$ accepts a word of
length at least $N$, then the language of $D$ is infinite.

The proof pumps the word, using the pumping lemma for DFAs.

articles.title: Emptiness test for encoded DFAs
articles.statement:
For an encoded DFA $D$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ with
decidable equality, the emptiness test is the Boolean that is true exactly when no entry of the
list of reachable states of $D$ is in the accepting list of $D$.

It returns true exactly when the language of $D$ is empty.

articles.title: The emptiness test decides emptiness of DFAs
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet
with finitely many states. The emptiness test applied to $M$ returns true if and only if the
language accepted by $M$ is empty.

articles.title: Emptiness test for DFAs
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states,
the emptiness test returns true exactly when none of the reachable states of $M$ is an
accepting state.

articles.title: Universality test for encoded DFAs
articles.statement:
For an encoded DFA $D$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ with
decidable equality, the universality test is the Boolean that is true exactly when every entry of
the list of reachable states of $D$ is in the accepting list of $D$.

It returns true exactly when the language of $D$ contains every word over $\alpha$.

articles.title: The universality test decides universality of DFAs
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite
alphabet with finitely many states. The universality test applied to $M$ returns true if and
only if $M$ accepts every word over the alphabet.

articles.title: Universality test for DFAs
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many
states, the universality test applied to $M$ is the emptiness test applied to the complement of
$M$: the DFA with the same states, start state and transitions whose accepting states are the
states that $M$ does not accept.

articles.title: Correctness of the bounded reachability search
articles.statement:
Let $s_0 \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$\mathrm{next}$ assign to every natural number a list of natural numbers, its successors, and let
$B$ be a list of natural numbers that contains $s_0$ and is closed under successors: whenever $s$
is in $B$ and $t$ is a successor of $s$, then $t$ is in $B$. Then a natural number $t$ is in the
list computed by the reachability search from $s_0$ through $\mathrm{next}$ within $B$ if and
only if $t$ is reachable from $s_0$ in zero or more successor steps.

articles.title: A state is reachable exactly when some word leads to it
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite
alphabet with finitely many states. A state $s$ of $M$ is in the set of reachable states of $M$
if and only if there is a word $w$ such that running $M$ on $w$ from its start state ends in $s$.

articles.title: Successors of a pair of states
articles.statement:
Let $D$ and $E$ be encoded DFAs over the same alphabet,
and let $p \in \mathbb{N}$ code the pair of states $(s, t)$ under the pairing bijection
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. The successors of $p$ form the list that has, for
each letter $a$ in the letters of $D$ followed by the letters of $E$, the code of the pair made of
the step of $D$ from $s$ on $a$ and the step of $E$ from $t$ on $a$.

articles.title: Reachable pairs of states of two encoded DFAs
articles.statement:
For encoded DFAs $D$ and $E$ over the same
alphabet, code a pair $(s, t)$ of natural numbers by its image $\langle s, t \rangle \in \mathbb{N}$
under Mathlib's pairing function. The reachable pairs of $D$ and $E$ form the list returned by the
bounded reachability search on lists of states started at $\langle s_D, s_E \rangle$, where $s_D$
and $s_E$ are the start states of $D$ and $E$, kept inside the list of coded pairs of states of
$D$ and $E$, and in which the successors of a number $p = \langle s, t \rangle$ are the numbers
$\langle s', t' \rangle$ with $s'$ and $t'$ the states that the transition functions of $D$ and
$E$ take $s$ and $t$ to on the same letter $a$, for $a$ running over the letters of $D$ followed
by the letters of $E$.

A number lies in this list exactly when it is $\langle q, r \rangle$ for the states $q$ and $r$
that $D$ and $E$ reach on some common word.

articles.title: Coded pairs of states of two encoded DFAs
articles.statement:
For encoded DFAs $D$ and $E$ over the same
alphabet, code a pair $(s, t)$ of natural numbers by its image $\langle s, t \rangle \in \mathbb{N}$
under Mathlib's pairing function. This is the list of the numbers $\langle s, t \rangle$ with $s$
running over the states of $D$ in their listed order and, for each $s$, $t$ running over the
states of $E$ in their listed order.

articles.title: Bounded reachability search on lists of states
articles.statement:
Let $s_0 \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$\mathrm{next}$ assign to each $s \in \mathbb{N}$ a list $\mathrm{next}(s)$ of natural numbers, and
let $B$ be a list of natural numbers. One search round sends a list $R$ to the list obtained by
writing $s_0$ followed, for each $s$ in $R$ in order, by $s$ and then the list $\mathrm{next}(s)$,
keeping the entries that lie in $B$, and deleting every entry that occurs again later; its entries
are the elements of $B$ that are $s_0$, an element of $R$, or an element of $\mathrm{next}(s)$ for
some $s$ in $R$, each listed once. The search returns the result of applying this round $|B|$
times to the empty list, where $|B|$ is the length of $B$.

When $B$ contains $s_0$ and is closed under $\mathrm{next}$, a number is an entry of the returned
list exactly when it is reachable from $s_0$ by finitely many, possibly zero, steps from some $s$
to an element of $\mathrm{next}(s)$.

articles.title: One round of the list reachability search
articles.statement:
Let $s_0 \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\mathrm{next}$
assign to each $s \in \mathbb{N}$ a list $\mathrm{next}(s)$ of natural numbers, and let $B$ and $R$
be lists of natural numbers. The round from $s_0$ with successors $\mathrm{next}$ kept inside $B$
sends the list $R$ of states found so far to the following list: write $s_0$ followed, for each
$s$ in $R$ in order, by $s$ and then the list $\mathrm{next}(s)$; keep the entries that lie in $B$;
then delete every entry that occurs again later in the list.

Its entries are therefore the numbers in $B$ that are $s_0$, an element $s$ of $R$, or an element
of $\mathrm{next}(s)$ for some $s$ in $R$, each listed once.

articles.title: One round of the DFA reachability search
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet
$\alpha$. The round sends a finite set $S$ of states of $M$ to the set consisting of the start
state of $M$ and of every state that the transition function of $M$ takes some $s \in S$ to on
some letter $a \in \alpha$.

articles.title: Reachable states of an encoded DFA
articles.statement:
For an encoded DFA $D$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ with
decidable equality, the reachable states of $D$ form the list returned by the bounded reachability
search on lists of states started at the start state of $D$, kept inside the states of $D$, in
which the successors of a state $s$ are the states that the transition function of $D$ takes $s$
to on the letters of $D$, in the order of the letters.

A natural number lies in this list exactly when the automaton denoted by $D$ reaches it from its
start state on some word.

articles.title: The early-stopping search finds exactly the reachable states
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a
finite alphabet with finitely many states. For every natural number $n$ at least the number of
states of $M$, the early-stopping reachability search for $M$ from the empty set with at most $n$
rounds returns the set of reachable states of $M$.

Since the search stops once a round changes nothing, a generous bound costs nothing.

articles.title: Early-stopping DFA reachability search
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet whose set
of states has decidable equality. For a natural number $n$ and a finite set $S$ of states of $M$,
the reachability search from $S$ with at most $n$ rounds returns $S$ when $n = 0$. When
$n = k + 1$, it returns $S$ if one round of the reachability search for $M$ sends $S$ to $S$
itself, and otherwise it returns the search from the image of $S$ under that round with at most
$k$ rounds.

articles.title: Reachable states of a DFA
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet whose set of states
$\sigma$ is finite and has decidable equality. The reachable states of $M$ form the finite set
obtained from the empty set by applying one round of the DFA reachability search for $M$ exactly
$|\sigma|$ times, where $|\sigma|$ is the number of states of $M$.

Since the round is monotone, this set is its least fixed point, and a state lies in it exactly
when $M$ reaches it from its start state on some word.

articles.title: The start state is reachable
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many
states, the start state of $M$ belongs to the reachable states of $M$.

articles.title: Reachable states are closed under transitions
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet whose
set of states is finite and has decidable equality. If a state $s$ of $M$ is reachable from the
start state, then for every letter $a$ the state to which $M$ moves from $s$ on $a$ is also
reachable from the start state.

articles.title: Symmetric difference of two DFAs
articles.statement:
For DFAs $M$ and $N$ over the same alphabet, with sets of
states $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$, this is the product DFA with set of states $\sigma \times \sigma'$
whose start state is the pair of the start states of $M$ and $N$, whose transition takes $(p, q)$
on a letter $a$ to the pair of the state to which $M$ moves from $p$ on $a$ and the state to which
$N$ moves from $q$ on $a$, and whose accepting states are the pairs $(p, q)$ such that $p$ is an
accepting state of $M$ or $q$ is an accepting state of $N$, but not both.

It accepts exactly the words on which $M$ and $N$ disagree.

articles.title: Universality of DFAs is decidable
articles.statement:
For every alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality and
a primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded DFA over $\alpha$ that its language is
the set of all words over $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is the problem
$\mathrm{ALL}_{\mathrm{DFA}}$.

articles.title: Emptiness of DFAs is decidable
articles.statement:
For every alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality and a
primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded DFA over $\alpha$ that its language is
empty is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is the problem $E_{\mathrm{DFA}}$.

## Sources

- Sipser, *Introduction to the Theory of Computation*, Theorem 4.4.

articles.title: Equivalence of DFAs is decidable
articles.statement:
For every alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality and
a primitive recursive encoding, the property of a pair of encoded DFAs over $\alpha$ that their
languages are equal is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is the problem
$\mathrm{EQ}_{\mathrm{DFA}}$.

## Sources

- Sipser, *Introduction to the Theory of Computation*, Theorem 4.5.

articles.title: Infiniteness of DFAs is decidable
articles.statement:
For every finite alphabet $\alpha$, given with an
enumeration of its letters, decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property
of an encoded DFA over $\alpha$ that its language is infinite is decidable by a multi-stack
machine. This is the problem $\mathrm{INFINITE}_{\mathrm{DFA}}$.

articles.title: Acceptance for DFAs is decidable
articles.statement:
For every alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality and
a primitive recursive encoding, the property of a pair $(D, w)$ of an encoded DFA $D$ over
$\alpha$ and a word $w$ over $\alpha$ that $w$ belongs to the language of $D$ is decidable by a
multi-stack machine. This is the problem $A_{\mathrm{DFA}}$.

## Sources

- Sipser, *Introduction to the Theory of Computation*, Theorem 4.1.

articles.title: An encoded DFA on its listed states
articles.statement:
For an encoded DFA $D$, this is the DFA whose set of
states is the finite set of states of $D$ (its start state and the targets of its listed
transitions), whose start state is the start state of $D$, whose transition function is that of
$D$ restricted to these states, and whose accepting states are those in the accepting list of
$D$.

articles.title: Words of a given length
articles.statement:
For a finite alphabet $\alpha$ given with an enumeration of its
letters and for $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the list of the words of length $n$ over $\alpha$: starting
from the list whose only entry is the empty word, it replaces $n$ times each word $w$ of the
current list by the words $a w$ for the letters $a$ of $\alpha$, in their enumeration order.

articles.title: Flags of a concatenation
articles.statement:
For triples of Booleans $b = (b_1, b_2, b_3)$ and
$c = (c_1, c_2, c_3)$, the flags of the product are
$(b_1 \land c_1,\ (b_2 \land c_1) \lor (b_1 \land c_2),\ (b_3 \land c_1) \lor (b_1 \land c_3))$.

If $b$ and $c$ record whether languages $L$ and $M$ are nonempty, contain a nonempty word,
and are infinite, the result records the same for $LM$: in particular $LM$ is infinite when
one factor is infinite and the other nonempty.

articles.title: Productions of a concatenation node
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $i$ and $j$, the
productions of a concatenation node $k$ with arguments $i$ and $j$ are the single production
$k \to i\,j$ (nonterminal $i$ followed by nonterminal $j$) when $i < k$ and $j < k$, and there
are none otherwise.

articles.title: Encoded regular expressions
articles.statement:
An encoded regular expression over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a
list of regular-expression nodes, each a constant ($0$, $1$ or a letter) or an operator (sum,
concatenation or star) whose arguments are node indices; the last node is the root. Any list is
allowed: in the semantics, an argument that is not the index of an earlier node reads as $0$,
and the empty list denotes $0$.

articles.title: The equivalence test is correct
articles.statement:
Over a finite alphabet with decidable equality and a fixed
enumeration of its letters, for all encoded regular expressions $e_1$ and $e_2$, the equivalence
test returns true on $e_1$ and $e_2$ if and only if the regular expressions that $e_1$ and $e_2$
denote have the same language.

articles.title: Equivalence test
articles.statement:
Over a finite alphabet with decidable equality and a fixed enumeration of
its letters, the equivalence test of two encoded regular expressions $e_1$ and $e_2$ returns true
exactly when, for every length $n$ less than the search bound of $e_1$ and $e_2$ and every word $w$
of length $n$, the membership test gives the same answer for $e_1$ on $w$ as for $e_2$ on $w$.

articles.title: Search bound for equivalence
articles.statement:
For encoded regular expressions $e_1$ and $e_2$, the search
bound is $2^{m + n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are the numbers of Thompson states of $e_1$ and $e_2$, each
computed by one pass over the nodes of the encoding.

articles.title: Encodings are lists of nodes
articles.statement:
The map sending an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$
to its list of nodes is a bijection onto the lists of regular-expression nodes over $\alpha$; its
inverse wraps a list of nodes as an encoding.

articles.title: Correctness of the flag pass
articles.statement:
For a list $l$ of nodes and a natural number $k$, let $f_k$
be the entry at position $k$ of the flags of $l$, or the zero flags
$(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$ if $k$ is at least the length of $l$. Then
$f_k$ describes the language of the regular expression at node $k$ of the encoding $l$ when $k$
is less than the length of $l$, and describes the empty language otherwise.

articles.title: Flags of a language
articles.statement:
A triple of Booleans $(b_1, b_2, b_3)$ describes a language $L$ when
$b_1$ is true exactly when $L$ is nonempty, $b_2$ is true exactly when $L$ contains a nonempty
word, and $b_3$ is true exactly when $L$ is infinite.

articles.title: Flags of all nodes
articles.statement:
For a list of nodes $n_0, \dots, n_{m-1}$, the flags
$f_0, \dots, f_{m-1}$ are computed in one left-to-right pass: $f_k$ is the step flags of node
$n_k$ computed from the flags $f_0, \dots, f_{k-1}$ of the nodes before it.

articles.title: Postorder encoding after a prefix
articles.statement:
For a regular expression $r$ and a list $l$ of nodes,
the nodes of $r$ are appended after $l$ in postorder, by recursion on $r$. For $0$, $1$ and a
letter $a$, append the single node $0$, $1$ or $a$. For a sum $s + t$ (respectively a
concatenation $st$), append the nodes of $s$ after $l$, giving $l_1$, then the nodes of $t$ after
$l_1$, giving $l_2$, then a sum (respectively concatenation) node with arguments $|l_1| - 1$ and
$|l_2| - 1$. For a star $s^*$, append the nodes of $s$ after $l$, giving $l_1$, then a star node
with argument $|l_1| - 1$. The root of $r$ is the last node.

articles.title: Encoding of a regular expression
articles.statement:
The encoding of a regular expression $r$ is the list of
nodes obtained by appending the nodes of $r$ in postorder after the empty list, so that the root
of $r$ is the last node.

articles.title: Language of a sentential form
articles.statement:
For an encoded regular expression $e$, the language of a
sentential form $X_1 \cdots X_n$ (terminals in $\alpha$, nonterminals in $\mathbb{N}$) is the
product $L_1 \cdots L_n$, where $L_i$ is $\{a\}$, the language of the one-letter word $a$, when
$X_i$ is the terminal $a$, and the language of the regular expression at node $k$ of $e$ when
$X_i$ is the nonterminal $k$. The empty form has language $\{\varepsilon\}$.

articles.title: The pass computes the Thompson state count of every node
articles.statement:
For every list $l$ of nodes and
every index $k$, the entry at index $k$ of the state counts of $l$ (read as $0$ past the end of the
list) equals the Thompson state count of the regular expression at node $k$ of the encoding with
nodes $l$ when $k$ is less than the length of $l$, and $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Infiniteness test for encoded regular expressions
articles.statement:
Let $e$ be an encoded regular
expression with nodes $n_0, \dots, n_{m-1}$, and let $f_0, \dots, f_{m-1}$ be the flags of all
nodes of $e$, the triples of Booleans computed in one left-to-right pass over the nodes. The
infiniteness test of $e$ is the third component of $f_{m-1}$, the flag triple of the last node
(the root); when $e$ has no nodes it is false.

The three flags of a node say whether its language is nonempty, contains a nonempty word and is
infinite, so the test returns true exactly when the language of $e$ is infinite.

articles.title: Emptiness test for regular expressions
articles.statement:
For an encoded regular expression $e$, the test
returns the answer of the emptiness test for encoded context-free grammars on the grammar of
$e$, which has one nonterminal per node and the root as start symbol.

articles.title: The grammar generates the language of the expression
articles.statement:
For every encoded regular
expression $e$, the language of the context-free grammar of $e$ (one nonterminal per node, the
root as start symbol) equals the language of the regular expression that $e$ denotes.

articles.title: One state count per node
articles.statement:
For every list $l$ of nodes of encoded regular expressions, the
list of state counts of $l$ has the same length as $l$.

articles.title: Short distinguishing words for encoded regular expressions
articles.statement:
Let $e_1$ and $e_2$ be encoded
regular expressions over an alphabet $\alpha$, and let $B$ be their search bound for equivalence.
The regular expressions denoted by $e_1$ and $e_2$ match the same language if and only if every
word $w$ over $\alpha$ of length less than $B$ is matched by the expression denoted by $e_1$
exactly when it is matched by the expression denoted by $e_2$.

articles.title: Short distinguishing words
articles.statement:
Two regular expressions $r$ and $s$ denote the same language if
and only if every word of length less than $2^{n(r) + n(s)}$, where $n$ denotes the Thompson state
count, is matched by $r$ exactly when it is matched by $s$.

The bound is the number of states of the product of the subset-construction DFAs of the Thompson
automata.

articles.title: Membership test for regular expressions
articles.statement:
For an encoded regular expression $e$ and a
word $w$, the test returns the answer of the membership test for encoded context-free grammars
on the word $w$ and the grammar of $e$, which has one nonterminal per node and the root as
start symbol.

articles.title: Soundness of the grammar of a regular expression
articles.statement:
Let $e$ be an encoded regular
expression. If a sentential form $u$ of the context-free grammar of $e$ yields a terminal word
$w$, then $w$ belongs to the language of $u$: the concatenation, over the symbols of $u$, of
$\{a\}$ for a terminal $a$ and of the language of the regular expression at node $k$ for a
nonterminal $k$.

articles.title: A production of a node only produces words of its language
articles.statement:
Let $e$ be an encoded
regular expression, $k$ a natural number and $x$ one of the productions of node $k$ built from
the node of $e$ at index $k$. If a word $w$ belongs to the language of the right-hand side of
$x$ (the concatenation, over its symbols, of $\{a\}$ for a terminal $a$ and of the language of
the regular expression at node $i$ for a nonterminal $i$), then $w$ belongs to the language of
the regular expression at node $k$.

articles.title: Regex nodes as a sum type
articles.statement:
The bijection between the nodes of encoded regular
expressions over $\alpha$ and $1 \oplus 1 \oplus \alpha \oplus (\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}) \oplus
(\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}) \oplus \mathbb{N}$, where $1$ is the one-point type, that sends the
zero node and the empty-word node to the first and second copies of $1$, a character node $a$
to $a$, a sum node with arguments $i, j$ to $(i, j)$ in the first copy of
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, a product node with arguments $i, j$ to $(i, j)$ in the second,
and a star node with argument $i$ to $i$.

articles.title: Productions of a node
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$ and a node $n$, the productions of
node $k$ are the following encoded productions, all with left-hand side $k$, where nonterminal
$i$ stands for node $i$: none if $n$ is the zero node; $k \to \varepsilon$ if $n$ is the
empty-word node; $k \to a$ if $n$ is the character $a$; if $n$ is a sum with arguments $i$ and
$j$, the unit production $k \to i$ when $i < k$ and the unit production $k \to j$ when
$j < k$; if $n$ is a product with arguments $i$ and $j$, the production $k \to i\,j$ when
$i < k$ and $j < k$; if $n$ is a star with argument $i$, the production $k \to \varepsilon$
together with $k \to i\,k$ when $i < k$.

articles.title: Node at an index
articles.statement:
For an encoded regular expression $e$ and a natural number $k$, the
node of $e$ at index $k$ is the entry at position $k$ (counting from $0$) of its list of
nodes, or the zero node when $k$ is at least the length of the list.

articles.title: The pass counts the states of Thompson's automaton
articles.statement:
For every encoded regular expression
$e$, the number of Thompson states of $e$ computed by the pass over its nodes equals the Thompson
state count of the regular expression that $e$ denotes.

This holds even when the expression tree is exponentially larger than the node list.

articles.title: Thompson state count of an encoding
articles.statement:
The number of Thompson states of an encoded regular
expression $e$ is the entry of the state counts of the nodes of $e$ at the last node, the root
(read as $0$ when $e$ has no nodes).

It equals the number of states of Thompson's automaton of the expression that $e$ denotes.

articles.title: Flags of a sum
articles.statement:
For triples of booleans $b = (b_1, b_2, b_3)$ and
$c = (c_1, c_2, c_3)$, the flags of the sum are $(b_1 \lor c_1, b_2 \lor c_2, b_3 \lor c_3)$.

If $b$ and $c$ record whether languages $L$ and $M$ are nonempty, contain a nonempty word and
are infinite, then the flags of the sum record the same for their union $L \cup M$.

articles.title: Productions of a sum node
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$, $i$ and $j$, the productions of a
sum node $k$ with arguments $i$ and $j$ are the unit production $k \to i$ if $i < k$, followed
by the unit production $k \to j$ if $j < k$ (and nothing else). Nonterminals are node indices.

articles.title: The equivalence test is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Over a primitively encodable finite alphabet
with decidable equality and a fixed enumeration of its letters, the equivalence test, as a function
of two encoded regular expressions, is primitive recursive.

articles.title: The equivalence search bound is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a
primitive recursive encoding, the search bound $2^{m+n}$ for equivalence of two encoded regular
expressions over $\alpha$, where $m$ and $n$ are the numbers of states of Thompson's automata of
the two expressions, is a primitive recursive function of the pair of encoded expressions.

articles.title: The Thompson state count of an encoding is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $\alpha$
with a primitive recursive encoding, the number of states of Thompson's automaton of an encoded
regular expression over $\alpha$, computed by one pass over its nodes, is a primitive recursive
function of the encoding.

articles.title: The pass of Thompson state counts is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a
primitive recursive encoding, the map sending a list of regular-expression nodes over $\alpha$ to
the list of their Thompson state counts, computed in one left-to-right pass, is primitive
recursive.

articles.title: One step of the Thompson state count is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $\alpha$
with a primitive recursive encoding, the map sending a list $c$ of natural numbers and a
regular-expression node over $\alpha$ to the Thompson state count of the node computed from $c$
is primitive recursive.

articles.title: Appending nodes does not change earlier expressions
articles.statement:
Let $l$ and $m$ be lists of
regular-expression nodes and let $k$ be smaller than the length of $l$. Then the regular
expression at node $k$ of the encoding with nodes $l$ followed by $m$ equals the regular
expression at node $k$ of the encoding with nodes $l$.

articles.title: Regular expression at a node
articles.statement:
For an encoded regular expression $e$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$,
the regular expression at node $k$ is defined by recursion on $k$ from the node of $e$ at index
$k$ (a zero node when $k$ is past the end): a zero node gives $0$, an epsilon node gives $1$, a
node for a letter $a$ gives $a$, and a sum, product or star node gives the sum, product or star
of the regular expressions at its arguments, where an argument that is not smaller than $k$
reads as $0$.

articles.title: Regular-expression node
articles.statement:
A node of an encoded regular expression over an alphabet
$\alpha$ is one of six kinds: zero, epsilon, a letter $a \in \alpha$, a sum with arguments
$i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, a product (concatenation) with arguments $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, or a star
with argument $i \in \mathbb{N}$, where the arguments are indices of nodes.

articles.title: Flags of a star
articles.statement:
Given a triple of Booleans $(b_1, b_2, b_3)$, the flags of its star are
$(\mathrm{true}, b_2, b_2)$. Read as the flags (nonempty, has a nonempty word, infinite) of a
language, a star is always nonempty, and it has a nonempty word, and is infinite, exactly when
the argument has a nonempty word.

articles.title: Productions of a star node
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $k$ and $i$, the productions of a star
node $k$ with argument $i$ are $k \to \varepsilon$, followed by $k \to i\,k$ if $i < k$ (and
nothing else). Nonterminals are node indices.

articles.title: Appending a node appends its count
articles.statement:
For every list $l$ of regular-expression nodes and
every node $n$, let $l'$ be the list $l$ with $n$ appended at the end. Then the list of Thompson
state counts of $l'$ is the list of counts of $l$ followed by one more entry, the count of $n$
computed from the counts of $l$.

articles.title: Thompson state counts of a node list
articles.statement:
For a list $l$ of regular-expression nodes, the
list of Thompson state counts of $l$ is computed in one left-to-right pass: starting from the
empty list, each node $n$ of $l$ in turn appends the count of $n$ computed from the list of
counts built so far.

articles.title: Flags of the next node
articles.statement:
Given the list $A$ of flag triples of the nodes before it, the
flag triple of a node is $(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$ for a zero node,
$(\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$ for an epsilon node and
$(\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false})$ for a letter node. For a sum, product or star
node it is the flags of a sum, product or star applied to the entries of $A$ at its arguments,
where an argument that is not an index of $A$ reads as
$(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$.

articles.title: One step of the Thompson state count
articles.statement:
Let $c = (c_0, \dots, c_{m-1})$ be a list of
natural numbers, and read $c_i$ as $0$ when $i \ge m$. The Thompson state count of a
regular-expression node from $c$ is $0$ for the node $0$, $1$ for the node $\varepsilon$, $2$ for
a letter, $c_i + c_j$ for a sum node and for a concatenation node with arguments $i$ and $j$, and
$c_i + 1$ for a star node with argument $i$.

When $c$ holds the counts of the nodes before the node, this is the number of states of
Thompson's automaton of its expression; an argument that is not an earlier node counts $0$, as
the expression $0$ does.

articles.title: Inclusion test
articles.statement:
For an encoded regular expression $e$ and an encoded DFA $D$, the
inclusion test returns the Boolean computed by the CFG ⊆ DFA inclusion test on the grammar of
$e$ and the automaton $D$.

articles.title: Emptiness of regular expressions is decidable
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive
recursive encoding, the property of an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ that the
language it denotes is empty (E_REX) is decidable by a multi-stack machine.

articles.title: EQ_REX is decidable
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite alphabet with a primitive recursive
encoding. Then equivalence of encoded regular expressions over $\alpha$ is decidable by a
multi-stack machine: some multi-stack machine decides, for a pair $(e_1, e_2)$ of encoded
regular expressions over $\alpha$, whether the regular expressions that $e_1$ and $e_2$ denote
have the same language.

This is the regular-expression analogue of Sipser, Theorem 4.5 (EQ_DFA). It is proved by
bounded search: the membership decider is run on both expressions for every word shorter than
a bound computed from them, and the answers are compared.

articles.title: Infiniteness of regular expressions is decidable
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a
primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ that
the language it denotes is infinite is decidable by a multi-stack machine.

articles.title: Inclusion of a regular language in a DFA language is decidable
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an
alphabet with decidable equality and a primitive recursive coding by natural numbers. The set of
pairs $(e, D)$ of an encoded regular expression $e$ over $\alpha$ and an encoded DFA $D$ over
$\alpha$ such that the language of the regular expression denoted by $e$ is contained in the
language of $D$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine.

articles.title: Membership for regular expressions is decidable
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with a
primitive recursive coding by natural numbers. The set of pairs $(e, w)$ of an encoded regular
expression $e$ over $\alpha$ and a word $w$ over $\alpha$ such that $w$ belongs to the language of
the regular expression denoted by $e$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine.

## Sources

- Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, Theorem 4.3 ($A_{\mathsf{REX}}$).

articles.title: The grammar of an encoded regular expression
articles.statement:
For an encoded regular expression $e$ with
$n$ nodes, its grammar is the encoded context-free grammar with start nonterminal $n - 1$
(truncated subtraction, so $0$ when $n = 0$), in which nonterminal $k$ stands for node $k$. Its
productions are, for each node $k < n$: none if node $k$ is $0$; $k \to \varepsilon$ if it is
$\varepsilon$; if it is the letter $a$, the production $k \to a$; if it is the sum of nodes $i$
and $j$, the productions $k \to i$ (when $i < k$) and $k \to j$ (when $j < k$); if it is the
product of nodes $i$ and $j$, the production $k \to i\,j$ (when $i < k$ and $j < k$); and if it
is the star of node $i$, the productions $k \to \varepsilon$ and $k \to i\,k$ (when $i < k$).
There are no other productions.

articles.title: Every regular expression has an encoding
articles.statement:
For every regular expression $r$ over an
alphabet $\alpha$, the encoded regular expression obtained by flattening $r$ (listing the nodes of
its subexpressions in postorder, so that the root of $r$ is the last node) denotes $r$.

articles.title: The regular expression denoted by an encoding
articles.statement:
An encoded regular expression $e$ with $n$
nodes denotes the regular expression at its node $n - 1$, the last node. For $n = 0$ this is the
expression at node $0$, which lies past the end of the list and is the empty expression $0$.

articles.title: Completeness of the grammar of an encoded regular expression
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet
with decidable equality, $e$ an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ and $k$ a natural number.
Every word in the language of the regular expression at node $k$ of $e$ is yielded by the
sentential form consisting of the single nonterminal $k$ in the context-free grammar of $e$.

articles.title: Flags of the empty language
articles.statement:
The flag triple of the empty language is
$(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$; the three flags of a language say whether it is
nonempty, whether it has a nonempty word, and whether it is infinite. This triple is also read for
an argument of a node that is not an earlier node.

articles.title: Items found for a grammar and a DFA
articles.statement:
For an encoded grammar $g$ and an encoded DFA $D$,
the found items are the list obtained from the empty list by applying one round of the item
search of $g$ and $D$ as many times as the length of the list of candidate items of $g$ and
$D$.

articles.title: Candidate items for a grammar and a DFA
articles.statement:
For an encoded grammar $g$ and an encoded DFA
$D$, the candidate items form the list of the codes $\langle A, \langle p, q \rangle \rangle$, where
$\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is the natural-number pairing, for every left-hand side $A$ of a
production of $g$ (listed once per production) and all states $p$ and $q$ of $D$.

articles.title: Sound items for a grammar and a DFA
articles.statement:
