For an encoded grammar $g$ and an encoded DFA $D$, a
natural number $x$ is a sound item when there are natural numbers $A$, $p$, $q$ and a word $w$
such that $x = \langle A, \langle p, q \rangle \rangle$, where $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is the
natural-number pairing, the nonterminal $A$ yields $w$ in the grammar denoted by $g$, and the
automaton denoted by $D$, run on $w$ from state $p$, ends in state $q$.

articles.title: Start states of a right-hand side are states of the DFA
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be an encoded DFA, $R$ a
list of natural numbers and $q$ one of the states of $D$. Then for every right-hand side $\beta$,
every start state of $\beta$ for $q$ given $R$ is one of the states of $D$.

articles.title: Start states of a right-hand side in a DFA
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be an encoded DFA, $R$ a list of
natural numbers (the items found so far) and $q \in \mathbb{N}$. The start states of a right-hand
side $\beta$, a list of grammar symbols, for $q$ given $R$ are defined by recursion on $\beta$: for
the empty right-hand side they are the one-element list $[q]$, and for a symbol $X$ followed by
$\beta'$ they are the states of $D$, in order, at which $X$ fits given $R$ and the start states of
$\beta'$ for $q$ given $R$.

articles.title: One round of the item search against a DFA
articles.statement:
For an encoded grammar $g$, an encoded DFA
$D$ and a list $R$ of natural numbers (the items found so far), one round produces the list of the
codes $\langle A, \langle p, q \rangle \rangle$, where $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is the
natural-number pairing, for every production $A \to \beta$ of $g$, every state $q$ of $D$ and
every start state $p$ of $\beta$ for $q$ given $R$.

articles.title: Whether a symbol fits at a DFA state
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be an encoded DFA, $R$ and $S$ lists of
natural numbers (the items found so far and the states where the rest of a right-hand side can
start), $X$ a grammar symbol and $p \in \mathbb{N}$. The test is true exactly when either $X$ is a
terminal $a$ and the step of $D$ from $p$ on $a$ lies in $S$, or $X$ is a nonterminal $B$ and some
$k$ in $S$ has $\langle B, \langle p, k \rangle \rangle$ in $R$, where
$\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is the natural-number pairing.

articles.title: Correctness of the intersection-emptiness test
articles.statement:
For every encoded grammar $g$ and every
encoded DFA $D$, the intersection-emptiness test of $g$ and $D$ returns true if and only if the
intersection of the language of $g$ and the language of $D$ is empty.

articles.title: The intersection-emptiness test for a grammar and a DFA
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an encoded grammar with
start nonterminal $S$, let $D$ be an encoded DFA with start state $s$, and write
$\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ for the natural-number pairing. The test of $g$ and $D$ is true
exactly when there is no accepting state $f$ of $D$ that is also one of the states of $D$ and for
which the code $\langle S, \langle s, f \rangle \rangle$ is among the found items of $g$ and
$D$.

articles.title: Completeness of the start states in a DFA
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an encoded context-free grammar and
$D$ an encoded DFA over an alphabet $T$ with decidable equality, and let $\rho$ be an encoded
right-hand side whose decoding yields a word $u$ in the grammar that $g$ denotes. If $p$ is one
of the states of $D$ and the automaton that $D$ denotes, run on $u$ from state $p$, ends in state
$q$, then $p$ is a start state of $\rho$ for $q$ given the items found for $g$ and $D$.

articles.title: Correctness of the inclusion test
articles.statement:
For every alphabet $T$ with decidable equality, every
encoded context-free grammar $g$ over $T$ and every encoded DFA $D$ over $T$, the inclusion test
on $g$ and $D$ returns true if and only if the language of $g$ is contained in the language of
$D$.

articles.title: The inclusion test for a grammar and a DFA
articles.statement:
For an encoded context-free grammar $g$ and an
encoded DFA $D$ over the same alphabet $T$, where $T$ has decidable equality, the inclusion test on
$g$ and $D$ is the Boolean value of the emptiness test on $g$ and the complement of $D$.

articles.title: Emptiness of the intersection of a context-free and a regular language is decidable
articles.statement:
For
every alphabet $T$ with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property of a
pair $(g, D)$, where $g$ is an encoded context-free grammar over $T$ and $D$ is an encoded DFA
over $T$, that the intersection of the language of $g$ and the language of $D$ is empty is
decidable by a multi-stack machine.

articles.title: Inclusion of a context-free language in a regular language is decidable
articles.statement:
For every
alphabet $T$ with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property of a pair
$(g, D)$, where $g$ is an encoded context-free grammar over $T$ and $D$ is an encoded DFA over
$T$, that the language of $g$ is contained in the language of $D$ is decidable by a multi-stack
machine.

articles.title: Emptiness of context-free grammars is computable
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be an alphabet with decidable
equality and a primitive recursive encoding into the natural numbers. The predicate on encoded
context-free grammars $g$ over $T$ that holds exactly when the language of $g$ is empty is a
computable predicate.

articles.title: A sentential form containing an empty nonterminal denotes the empty language
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be
an alphabet and $N$ a set of nonterminals, and let $V$ assign a language over $T$ to each
nonterminal. A sentential form $X_1 \cdots X_m$ over $T$ and $N$ denotes under $V$ the
concatenation $L_1 \cdots L_m$, where $L_t = V(X_t)$ if $X_t$ is a nonterminal and $L_t = \{X_t\}$
if $X_t$ is a terminal; the empty form denotes $\{\varepsilon\}$. Let $A \in N$ with
$V(A) = \emptyset$. Then every sentential form over $T$ and $N$ in which $A$ occurs denotes the
empty language under $V$.

articles.title: Sentential forms of productive nonterminals derive terminal words
articles.statement:
In a context-free
grammar $G$, if every nonterminal occurring in a sentential form $u$ derives some terminal word,
then $u$ derives some terminal word.

articles.title: Soundness of the productive-nonterminal iteration
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an encoded context-free
grammar. A round sends a list $H$ of nonterminals to the left-hand sides of those productions of
$g$ in whose right-hand side every nonterminal belongs to $H$. For every $k \ge 0$, every
nonterminal obtained after $k$ rounds starting from the empty list derives some terminal word in
the context-free grammar that $g$ denotes.

articles.title: Context-free pumping down below twice the pumping bound
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an encoded
context-free grammar, let $L$ be the largest of $2$ and the lengths of the right-hand sides of
the productions of $g$, let $K$ be the number of distinct left-hand sides of these productions,
and let $N = L^{K+1}$ be the pumping bound of $g$. For every word $w$ in the language of $g$ with
$|w| \ge N$, there is a word $v$ in the language of $g$ with $N \le |v| < 2N$.

articles.title: Splitting a factor
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be a word and $i \le j \le |w|$, and write $w[i, j)$ for the
factor of $w$ from position $i$ to position $j$. If $w[i, j) = uv$, then $i + |u| \le j$,
$w[i, i + |u|) = u$ and $w[i + |u|, j) = v$.

articles.title: Factor of a word
articles.statement:
For a word $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{n-1}$ and natural numbers $i$ and
$j$, the factor of $w$ from position $i$ to position $j$ is obtained by dropping the first $i$
letters of $w$ and keeping at most the first $j - i$ letters of the rest, where $j - i$ is $0$
when $j \le i$. For $i \le j \le n$ it is $w_i w_{i+1} \cdots w_{j-1}$.

articles.title: Items found by the membership procedure
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an encoded context-free grammar and
$w = w_0 \cdots w_{n-1}$ a word. An item is a triple $(A, i, j)$ of natural numbers, coded as a
natural number by nested pairing. A round sends a list $R$ of items to the items $(A, i, j)$ such
that $A \to X_1 \cdots X_m$ is a production of $g$, $j \le n$, and there are positions
$i = k_0, k_1, \ldots, k_m = j$, each at most $n$, such that for every $t$ with $1 \le t \le m$,
either $X_t$ is the terminal $w_{k_{t-1}}$ and $k_t = k_{t-1} + 1$, or $X_t$ is a nonterminal $B$
with $(B, k_{t-1}, k_t)$ in $R$. The items found are the result of applying the round $M$ times
to the empty list, where $M$ is $(n + 1)^2$ times the length of the list of productions of $g$.

articles.title: The generating nonterminals are closed under one more round
articles.statement:
For an encoded grammar $g$,
one more round of the generating-nonterminal computation, applied to the productions of $g$ and
the generating nonterminals of $g$, yields only generating nonterminals of $g$: every left-hand
side of a production of $g$ whose right-hand side has all its nonterminals among the generating
nonterminals of $g$ is itself a generating nonterminal of $g$.

articles.title: One round of the generating-nonterminal computation
articles.statement:
Let a list of productions be given,
each a pair of a nonterminal $A \in \mathbb{N}$ and a right-hand side made of nonterminals and
terminals, together with a list $G$ of nonterminals. One round returns, in order, the left-hand
sides of those productions in whose right-hand side every nonterminal belongs to $G$.

articles.title: Generating nonterminals
articles.statement:
For an encoded grammar $g$, start from the empty list of
nonterminals and, in each round, replace the current list $G$ by the list of left-hand sides of
those productions of $g$ whose right-hand sides contain no nonterminal outside $G$. The
generating nonterminals of $g$ are the list obtained after as many rounds as $g$ has productions.

Every nonterminal in this list derives a terminal word, and the start nonterminal is in it
whenever the grammar generates some word.

articles.title: Correctness of the infiniteness test
articles.statement:
For every encoded context-free grammar $g$, the
infiniteness test returns true on $g$ if and only if the language of $g$ is infinite.

articles.title: The infiniteness test
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an encoded grammar and $N$ its pumping bound. The test
returns true exactly when some word $w$ whose letters all occur as terminals in the productions
of $g$, with $N \le |w| < 2N$, is accepted by the membership test for $g$.

articles.title: Long words make a context-free language infinite
articles.statement:
If the language of an encoded grammar
$g$ contains a word whose length is at least the pumping bound of $g$, then the language of $g$
is infinite.

articles.title: Correctness of the emptiness test
articles.statement:
For every encoded context-free grammar $g$, the
emptiness test returns true on $g$ if and only if the language of $g$ is empty.

articles.title: The emptiness test for context-free grammars
articles.statement:
For an encoded grammar $g$, the test returns
true exactly when the start nonterminal of $g$ is not among the generating nonterminals of $g$.

articles.title: Candidate items for membership
articles.statement:
For an encoded grammar $g$ and a word $w$, the candidate
items are the triples $(A, i, j)$, encoded as natural numbers by pairing, where $A$ is the
left-hand side of a production of $g$ and $i, j \le |w|$; each triple is listed once for every
production whose left-hand side is $A$.

articles.title: Right-hand side length bound
articles.statement:
For an encoded grammar $g$, the length bound is the maximum
of $2$ and the lengths of the right-hand sides of the productions of $g$.

articles.title: Correctness of the membership test
articles.statement:
For every encoded context-free grammar $g$ and every
word $w$, the membership test returns true on $g$ and $w$ if and only if $w$ belongs to the
language of $g$.

articles.title: The membership test for context-free grammars
articles.statement:
For an encoded grammar $g$ with start
nonterminal $S$ and a word $w$, the test returns true exactly when the item $(S, 0, |w|)$ is
among the items found for $g$ and $w$.

articles.title: Completeness of the start positions
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an encoded context-free grammar over an
alphabet $T$ with decidable equality, let $w$ be a word over $T$, and let $\rho$ be an encoded
right-hand side whose decoding yields a word $u$ in the grammar that $g$ denotes. If
$i \le j \le |w|$ and $u$ is the factor of $w$ from position $i$ to position $j$, then $i$ is a
start position of $\rho$ at $j$ for the word $w$ and the list of items found by the membership
procedure on $g$ and $w$.

articles.title: One round of the membership procedure
articles.statement:
Write $\langle s, t \rangle$ for the pairing
bijection $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ given by $\langle s, t \rangle = t^2 + s$
if $s < t$ and $\langle s, t \rangle = s^2 + s + t$ otherwise. Given an encoded grammar $g$, a
word $w$ and a list $R$ of items found so far, the round lists, for every production
$A \to \rho$ of $g$, every position $j \le |w|$ and every start $i$ of $\rho$ for the factor of
$w$ ending at $j$ given $R$, the code $\langle A, \langle i, j \rangle \rangle$ of the item
$(A, i, j)$.

articles.title: Letters of generated words occur in the productions
articles.statement:
If a word $w$ is generated by an
encoded grammar $g$, then every letter of $w$ is among the terminals of $g$, that is, it occurs
in the right-hand side of some production of $g$.

articles.title: Pumping bound of an encoded grammar
articles.statement:
For an encoded grammar $g$, let $L$ be the length
bound of $g$, the larger of $2$ and the largest length of a right-hand side of a production of
$g$, and let $K$ be the number of distinct left-hand sides of the productions of $g$. The
pumping bound of $g$ is $L^{K+1}$.

With this bound, Ogden's lemma with every letter marked gives the pumping lemma for the decoded
grammar.

articles.title: Pumping lemma for encoded grammars
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be an encoded grammar with pumping bound
$N$. Every word $w$ generated by $g$ with $|w| \ge N$ can be written as $w = uvxyz$ with $vy$
nonempty and $|vxy| \le N$, such that $u v^i x y^i z$ is generated by $g$ for every natural
number $i$, including $i = 0$.

articles.title: Acceptable productions
articles.statement:
Given a list $G$ of nonterminals (natural numbers), the test
accepts an encoded production $(A, \rho)$ when every symbol of $\rho$ is acceptable: a
terminal always is, and a nonterminal is when it belongs to $G$. So the production is accepted
exactly when every nonterminal occurring in $\rho$ belongs to $G$.

articles.title: Sound items
articles.statement:
Write $\langle s, t \rangle$ for the pairing bijection
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ given by $\langle s, t \rangle = t^2 + s$ if $s < t$
and $\langle s, t \rangle = s^2 + s + t$ otherwise. Given an encoded grammar $g$ and a word $w$,
a natural number $x$ is a sound item when $x = \langle A, \langle i, j \rangle \rangle$ for some
$A$, $i$, $j$ with $i \le j \le |w|$ such that the nonterminal $A$ yields, in the decoded
grammar of $g$, the factor of $w$ from position $i$ to position $j$.

articles.title: Completeness of the generating-nonterminal computation
articles.statement:
If an encoded grammar $g$
generates some word $w$, then the start nonterminal of $g$ is among the generating nonterminals
of $g$ computed by the emptiness procedure.

articles.title: Start positions of a right-hand side
articles.statement:
Write $\langle s, t \rangle$ for the pairing
bijection $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ given by $\langle s, t \rangle = t^2 + s$
if $s < t$ and $\langle s, t \rangle = s^2 + s + t$ otherwise. Given a word $w$, a list $R$ of
items (natural numbers), a position $j$ and an encoded right-hand side $X_1 \cdots X_m$, a
position $i$ is a start when there are positions $i = p_0, p_1, \ldots, p_m = j$ with
$p_0, \ldots, p_{m-1} \le |w|$ such that for each $l = 1, \ldots, m$: if $X_l$ is a terminal
$a$, then $p_l = p_{l-1} + 1$ and the letter of $w$ at position $p_{l-1}$ (counting from $0$)
is $a$; if $X_l$ is a nonterminal $B$, then $R$ contains the code
$\langle B, \langle p_{l-1}, p_l \rangle \rangle$. The starts are computed from the right, one
symbol at a time, by the symbol-fitting test; for the empty right-hand side the only start is
$j$.

articles.title: Fitting a symbol at a position
articles.statement:
Write $\langle s, t \rangle$ for the pairing bijection
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ given by $\langle s, t \rangle = t^2 + s$ if $s < t$
and $\langle s, t \rangle = s^2 + s + t$ otherwise. Given a word $w$, a list $R$ of items, a
list $S$ of positions and an encoded symbol $X$, the test at a position $i$ succeeds when either
$X$ is a terminal $a$, $i + 1 \in S$ and the letter of $w$ at position $i$ (counting from $0$)
is $a$; or $X$ is a nonterminal $B$ and some $k \in S$ has
$\langle B, \langle i, k \rangle \rangle \in R$.

In use, $S$ holds the positions where the rest of the right-hand side can start.

articles.title: Acceptable symbols
articles.statement:
Given a list $G$ of natural numbers and a symbol $s$ of an encoded
grammar over an alphabet $T$, which is either a nonterminal $i \in \mathbb{N}$ or a terminal in
$T$, $s$ is acceptable when it is a terminal or a nonterminal that occurs in $G$. The test
returns a Boolean.

articles.title: The terminals of an encoded grammar
articles.statement:
For an encoded context-free grammar $g$ over an
alphabet $T$ with decidable equality, the list of the terminals that occur in the right-hand
sides of the productions of $g$, each listed once.

Listing each terminal once keeps the enumeration of the words over these terminals free of
repetitions.

articles.title: Emptiness of context-free grammars is decidable
articles.statement:
For every alphabet $T$ with decidable
equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded context-free grammar $g$
over $T$ that the language of $g$ is empty is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is Sipser,
Theorem 4.8: the problem $E_{\mathrm{CFG}}$ is decidable.

articles.title: Infiniteness of context-free languages is decidable
articles.statement:
For every alphabet $T$ with decidable
equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded context-free grammar $g$
over $T$ that the language of $g$ is infinite is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is the
problem $\mathrm{INFINITE}_{\mathrm{CFG}}$.

articles.title: Membership for context-free grammars is decidable
articles.statement:
For every alphabet $T$ with decidable
equality and a primitive recursive encoding, the property of a pair $(g, w)$, where $g$ is an
encoded context-free grammar over $T$ and $w$ is a word over $T$, that $w$ is in the language of
$g$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is Sipser, Theorem 4.7: the problem
$A_{\mathrm{CFG}}$ is decidable.

articles.title: The words of a given length over a list of letters
articles.statement:
For a list $A$ of letters and a
natural number $n$, the list obtained from the list whose only entry is the empty word by $n$
rounds, each of which replaces every word $w$, in order, by the words $a w$ for the letters $a$
of $A$, in order. Its entries are exactly the words of length $n$ all of whose letters occur in
$A$.

articles.title: Correctness of the NFA membership test
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$ and a word $w$, the
membership test returns true on $w$ if and only if $w$ belongs to the language of $N$.

articles.title: Membership test for encoded NFAs
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$ and a word $w$, the membership
test is the Boolean that is true exactly when some state reached on $w$ is an accepting state of
$N$. The states reached on $w$ are computed from the ε-closure of the start states by, for each
letter of $w$ in turn, following the transitions on that letter and taking the ε-closure.

articles.title: ε-closure of a list of states
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$ and a list $S$ of states, the
ε-closure of $S$ is a list whose members are exactly the states reachable from some state of $S$
by finitely many ε-moves of $N$ (zero moves included), computed by a search from each state of
$S$.

articles.title: Complement of an encoded DFA
articles.statement:
The complement of an encoded DFA $D$ has the same start
state and the same transitions as $D$, and its accepting states are those states of $D$ (its
start state and the targets of its listed transitions) that $D$ does not accept.

articles.title: Encoded DFA
articles.statement:
An encoded deterministic finite automaton over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a
deterministic finite automaton given as data with natural-number states: a start state in
$\mathbb{N}$, a list of accepting states in $\mathbb{N}$, and a list of transitions $((s, a), t)$
with $s, t \in \mathbb{N}$ and $a \in \alpha$, read as "on letter $a$, state $s$ moves to $t$".

articles.title: Encoded NFA
articles.statement:
An encoded NFA over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a nondeterministic finite
automaton with ε-moves given as data, with natural numbers as states: a list of start states, a
list of accepting states, a list of transitions $((s, a), t)$, meaning that on the letter $a$ the
state $s$ may move to $t$, and a list of ε-moves $(s, t)$, meaning that the state $s$ may move to
$t$ without reading a letter.

articles.title: ε-successors of a state
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$ and a state $s$, the ε-successors of $s$
are the list of the targets $t$ of the ε-moves $(s, t)$ of $N$, in the order in which these
ε-moves are listed.

articles.title: ε-move relation
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$, the ε-move relation holds between states $s$ and
$t$ exactly when $(s, t)$ is one of the ε-moves of $N$.

articles.title: Encoded NFAs as tuples
articles.statement:
The bijection between encoded NFAs over $\alpha$ and quadruples
consisting of a list of natural numbers, a list of natural numbers, a list of elements of
$(\mathbb{N} \times \alpha) \times \mathbb{N}$ and a list of pairs of natural numbers, which sends
an encoded NFA to its start states, accepting states, transitions and ε-moves.

articles.title: Encoded DFAs as triples
articles.statement:
Sending an encoded DFA over $\alpha$ to the triple of its start
state, its list of accepting states and its list of transitions is an equivalence (a bijection
with explicit inverse) between encoded DFAs over $\alpha$ and the set
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathrm{List}\,\mathbb{N} \times \mathrm{List}((\mathbb{N} \times \alpha) \times
\mathbb{N})$.

articles.title: The states reached on a word are closed under ε-moves
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be an encoded NFA and $w$ a
word. If $u$ is one of the states that the ε-NFA denoted by $N$ can be in after reading $w$, and
$N$ has an ε-move from $u$ to $v$, then $v$ is also one of these states.

articles.title: Every finite NFA has an encoding
articles.statement:
An NFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states
has an encoded NFA with the same language.

articles.title: Every finite ε-NFA has an encoding
articles.statement:
An `εNFA` over a finite alphabet with finitely many
states has an encoded NFA with the same language.

articles.title: Every finite DFA has an encoding
articles.statement:
A DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many states
has an encoded DFA with the same language.

articles.title: Emptiness test for encoded NFAs
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$, the emptiness test is the
Boolean that is true exactly when no state in the list of reachable states of $N$ is an
accepting state of $N$; the reachable states are those reachable from a start state of $N$ by
zero or more moves, each a transition on some letter or an ε-move.

articles.title: Language of an encoded NFA
articles.statement:
The language of an encoded NFA $N$ over an alphabet $\alpha$
is the language accepted by the ε-NFA that $N$ denotes, whose states are the natural numbers:
the words $w$ over $\alpha$ such that some accepting state of $N$ is among the states reached on
$w$ from the start states of $N$, with ε-moves allowed before, between and after the letters.

articles.title: Language of an encoded DFA
articles.statement:
The language of an encoded DFA $D$ is the set of words $w$
such that the state reached by running $D$ on $w$ from its start state, following its transition
function, is one of its accepting states.

articles.title: Letter step of an encoded NFA
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$, a list $S$ of states and a letter
$a$, the letter step lists the target $t$ of every transition $((s, a), t)$ of $N$ with $s \in S$,
in the order of the transition list of $N$, without taking the ε-closure.

articles.title: Letters of an encoded DFA
articles.statement:
The letters of an encoded DFA $D$ form the list of the letters
$a$ of its listed transitions $((s, a), t)$, in the order the transitions are listed.

articles.title: The ε-closure is reachability along ε-moves
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$, a set $X$ of natural
numbers and a natural number $t$, $t$ lies in the ε-closure of $X$ in the ε-NFA that $N$ denotes
if and only if $t$ is reachable from some $u \in X$ by a sequence of zero or more ε-moves of $N$.

articles.title: The complement DFA accepts the complement language
articles.statement:
For every encoded DFA $D$ and every
word $w$, the complement of $D$ accepts $w$ if and only if $D$ does not accept $w$.

articles.title: The reachable states are those some word can lead to
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$ and a natural
number $t$, $t$ is among the reachable states of $N$ if and only if there is a word $w$ such that
$t$ is among the states that the ε-NFA denoted by $N$ reaches on $w$ from its start states, with
ε-moves allowed before, between and after the letters.

articles.title: The run of an encoded NFA agrees with ε-NFA evaluation
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$, a word $w$
and a natural number $t$, $t$ is among the states in the run of $N$ on $w$ if and only if $t$ is
among the states that the ε-NFA denoted by $N$ reaches on $w$ from its start states, with ε-moves
allowed before, between and after the letters.

articles.title: Successors of a state in an encoded NFA
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$ and a state $s$, this is the
list of the targets $t$ of the transitions $((s, a), t)$ of $N$ on any letter $a$, followed by the
targets $t$ of the ε-moves $(s, t)$ of $N$, each in the order of the corresponding list of $N$.

articles.title: Running an encoded DFA is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with a
primitive recursive encoding and decidable equality, and encode encoded DFAs over $\alpha$
through their start state, accepting states and transitions. The map sending an encoded DFA $D$
and a word $w$ over $\alpha$ to the state reached by running $D$ on $w$ from its start state is
primitive recursive.

articles.title: Assembling an encoded DFA is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with a
primitive recursive encoding, and encode encoded DFAs over $\alpha$ through their start state,
accepting states and transitions. The map sending a triple $(s, F, T)$, where $s \in \mathbb{N}$,
$F$ is a list of natural numbers and $T$ is a list of pairs $((q, a), t)$ with $q, t \in \mathbb{N}$
and $a \in \alpha$, to the encoded DFA over $\alpha$ with start state $s$, accepting states $F$
and transitions $T$ is primitive recursive.

articles.title: The transition function of encoded DFAs is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an
alphabet with a primitive recursive encoding and decidable equality, and encode encoded DFAs over
$\alpha$ through their start state, accepting states and transitions. The map sending an encoded
DFA $D$ over $\alpha$, a state $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and a letter $a \in \alpha$ to the state that
$D$ moves to from $s$ on $a$ (the target of the first transition listed for $(s, a)$, or $s$ if
there is none) is primitive recursive.

articles.title: Reachable states of an encoded NFA
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$, this is the list, found by a
search from each start state of $N$ in turn through the start states of $N$ and the targets of
its transitions and ε-moves, of the states reachable from a start state of $N$ by zero or more
moves, each a transition of $N$ on some letter or an ε-move of $N$.

articles.title: Run of an encoded NFA
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$ and a word $w = a_1 \cdots a_n$, the run of
$N$ on $w$ is the list of states obtained by starting from the ε-closure of the start states of
$N$ and, for each letter $a_i$ in turn, taking the letter step on $a_i$ and then the ε-closure.

articles.title: States an encoded NFA mentions as start states or targets
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$, this is
the list of the start states of $N$, followed by the targets $t$ of its transitions $((s, a), t)$,
followed by the targets $t$ of its ε-moves $(s, t)$.

articles.title: States of an encoded DFA
articles.statement:
The states of an encoded DFA $D$ form the list consisting of its
start state followed by the targets of its listed transitions, in the order they are listed.

articles.title: A step determined by its listed transitions
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be an encoded DFA, let
$s, t \in \mathbb{N}$ be states and let $a$ be a letter. If $D$ lists at least one transition from
$s$ on $a$, and every transition listed from $s$ on $a$ has target $t$, then the transition
function of $D$ takes $s$ on $a$ to $t$.

articles.title: Unlisted transitions fix the state
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be an encoded DFA, $s \in \mathbb{N}$ a state
and $a$ a letter. If $D$ lists no transition from $s$ on $a$, then the transition function of $D$
takes $s$ on $a$ to $s$.

articles.title: One step of an encoded NFA on a list of states
articles.statement:
For an encoded NFA $N$, a list $S$ of
states and a letter $a$, the list of states reached from $S$ on $a$: the ε-closure, computed as a
list, of the list of states $t$ such that $((s, a), t)$ is a transition of $N$ for some $s$ in
$S$.

articles.title: Where a step can lead
articles.statement:
For every encoded DFA $D$, state $s \in \mathbb{N}$ and letter $a$,
the transition function of $D$ takes $s$ on $a$ either to the target of some listed transition of
$D$ or to $s$ itself.

articles.title: The listed states are closed under transitions
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be an encoded DFA and let $s$ be
one of its states, that is, its start state or the target of one of its listed transitions. Then
for every letter $a$ the transition function of $D$ takes $s$ on $a$ to one of the states of $D$.

articles.title: Letters without listed transitions fix every state
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be an encoded DFA and let $a$
be a letter that is not among the letters of $D$, that is, no listed transition of $D$ is labelled
$a$. Then for every state $s \in \mathbb{N}$ the transition function of $D$ takes $s$ on $a$ to
$s$.

articles.title: Transition function of an encoded DFA
articles.statement:
For an encoded DFA $D$, a state $s \in \mathbb{N}$
and a letter $a$, the step of $D$ from $s$ on $a$ is the target of the first transition that $D$
lists from $s$ on $a$, or $s$ itself when $D$ lists no such transition.

articles.title: Emptiness of NFAs is decidable
articles.statement:
For every alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive
encoding, the property of an encoded NFA $N$ (with ε-moves) over $\alpha$ that its language is
empty is decidable by a multi-stack machine. This is the problem $E_{\mathrm{NFA}}$.

articles.title: Membership for NFAs is decidable
articles.statement:
For every alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive
encoding, the property of a pair $(N, w)$, where $N$ is an encoded NFA (with ε-moves) over
$\alpha$ and $w$ is a word over $\alpha$, that $w$ is in the language of $N$ is decidable by a
multi-stack machine. This is Sipser, Theorem 4.2: the problem $A_{\mathrm{NFA}}$ is decidable.

articles.title: The automaton denoted by an encoded DFA
articles.statement:
An encoded DFA $D$ over an alphabet $\alpha$
denotes the deterministic automaton over $\alpha$ with state set $\mathbb{N}$ whose start state is
the start state of $D$, whose transition function is the transition function of $D$, and whose
accepting states are the states in the accepting list of $D$.

articles.title: The ε-NFA of an encoded NFA
articles.statement:
An encoded NFA $N$ over $\alpha$ denotes the ε-NFA over
$\alpha$ with state set $\mathbb{N}$ whose start states are the start states listed in $N$, whose
accepting states are the accepting states listed in $N$, and in which a state $s$ may move to $t$
on a letter $a$ exactly when $((s, a), t)$ is a transition of $N$, and without reading a letter
exactly when $(s, t)$ is an ε-move of $N$.

articles.title: Decoding a production
articles.statement:
Decoding a pair $(A, s)$ of a natural number $A$ and a list $s$
of elements of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$ gives the production, with terminals
$T$ and nonterminals $\mathbb{N}$, whose left-hand side is the nonterminal $A$ and whose
right-hand side is $s$ with each entry decoded as a symbol: a number $i$ from the left summand
becomes the nonterminal $i$ and an element $a$ of $T$ becomes the terminal $a$.

articles.title: Decoding a grammar symbol
articles.statement:
Decoding sends an element of the disjoint union
$\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$ to a grammar symbol with terminals $T$ and nonterminals $\mathbb{N}$:
a natural number $i$ from the left summand goes to the nonterminal $i$, and an element $a$ of
$T$ from the right summand goes to the terminal $a$.

articles.title: Encoding a production
articles.statement:
Encoding a production with terminals $T$ and nonterminals
$\mathbb{N}$ gives the pair $(A, s)$ where $A \in \mathbb{N}$ is its left-hand side and $s$ is
its right-hand side with each symbol encoded as an element of the disjoint union
$\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$: the terminal $a$ becomes $a$ in the right summand and the nonterminal
$i$ becomes $i$ in the left summand.

articles.title: Encoding a grammar symbol
articles.statement:
Encoding sends a grammar symbol with terminals $T$ and
nonterminals $\mathbb{N}$ to an element of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$: the
terminal $a$ goes to $a$ in the right summand $T$, and the nonterminal $i$ goes to $i$ in the
left summand $\mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Encoded context-free grammars
articles.statement:
An encoded context-free grammar over a terminal type $T$
consists of a start nonterminal, which is a natural number, and a list of productions. Each
production is a pair of a left-hand side, a natural number, and a right-hand side, a list of
elements of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$, in which a number $i$ from the left summand
stands for nonterminal $i$ and an element $a$ of $T$ for terminal $a$.

Unlike a general context-free grammar, whose type of nonterminals is part of its data, an
encoded grammar is a concrete object that computable functions can take and return.

articles.title: Encoded grammars as pairs
articles.statement:
Sending an encoded grammar over $T$ to the pair of its start
nonterminal and its list of productions is a bijection from encoded grammars over $T$ onto
pairs $(s, R)$ of a natural number $s$ and a list $R$ of pairs of a natural number and a list
of elements of the disjoint union $\mathbb{N} \sqcup T$.

articles.title: A language is context-free exactly when an encoded grammar generates it
articles.statement:
**A language is context-free exactly when an encoded grammar generates
it.**

articles.title: Grammars with renamings in both directions generate the same language
articles.statement:
Let $g$ and $G$
be context-free grammars over the same terminals. Suppose there are maps $f$ from the
nonterminals of $g$ to those of $G$ and $b$ from the nonterminals of $G$ to those of $g$ such
that renaming the nonterminals of any production of $g$ by $f$ gives a production of $G$,
renaming the nonterminals of any production of $G$ by $b$ gives a production of $g$, $f$ sends
the start nonterminal of $g$ to that of $G$, and $b$ sends the start nonterminal of $G$ to that
of $g$. Then $g$ and $G$ generate the same language. The renamings need not be inverse to each
other.

articles.title: Encoded grammars generate context-free languages
articles.statement:
The language of an encoded grammar is
context-free.

articles.title: The encoding of a grammar generates the same language
articles.statement: **The encoding of a grammar generates the same language.**

articles.title: Language of an encoded grammar
articles.statement:
The language of an encoded context-free grammar $g$ over
$T$ is the language generated by the context-free grammar that $g$ denotes, whose nonterminals
are the natural numbers, whose initial nonterminal is the start nonterminal of $g$ and whose
productions are the decoded productions of $g$.

articles.title: Numbering the nonterminals of a production and back recovers it
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a context-free
grammar over $T$ and $r$ a production of $G$. Replacing each nonterminal $A$ of $r$ by its number,
the position, counting from $0$, of the first occurrence of $A$ in the list of nonterminals that
$G$ mentions, and then replacing each number $n$ by the nonterminal of $G$ with number $n$ (the
entry at position $n$ of that list, or the initial nonterminal of $G$ if the list has no such
entry) gives $r$ again.

articles.title: Renaming the nonterminals of a symbol twice
articles.statement:
For maps $f : N_1 \to N_2$ and
$b : N_2 \to N_3$ and a grammar symbol $s$ with terminals in $T$ and nonterminals in $N_1$,
renaming the nonterminals of $s$ by $f$ and then by $b$ gives the same symbol as renaming them by
$b \circ f$.

articles.title: Numbering of nonterminals
articles.statement:
For a context-free grammar $G$, the number of a nonterminal $A$
of $G$ is the position, counting from $0$, of the first occurrence of $A$ in the list of
nonterminals that $G$ mentions (its initial nonterminal first); if $A$ does not occur in that
list, its number is the length of the list.

articles.title: Nonterminal with a given number
articles.statement:
For a context-free grammar $G$ and a natural number $n$,
the nonterminal of $G$ with number $n$ is the entry at position $n$, counting from $0$, of the
list of nonterminals that $G$ mentions (its initial nonterminal first); if the list has no entry
at position $n$, it is the initial nonterminal of $G$.

articles.title: Nonterminal of a symbol
articles.statement:
The partial map from grammar symbols with terminals in $T$ and
nonterminals in $N$ to $N$ that sends a nonterminal $A$ to $A$ and has no value on terminals.

articles.title: Encoding of a context-free grammar
articles.statement:
For a context-free grammar $G$ over $T$, the encoded
grammar whose start nonterminal is the number of the initial nonterminal of $G$ and whose
productions are the productions of $G$, listed in some fixed order, with every nonterminal $A$
replaced by its number, the position, counting from $0$, of the first occurrence of $A$ in the
list of nonterminals that $G$ mentions (its initial nonterminal first).

articles.title: Grammar denoted by an encoding
articles.statement:
For an encoded context-free grammar $g$ over $T$, the
context-free grammar over $T$ whose nonterminals are the natural numbers, whose initial
nonterminal is the start nonterminal of $g$, and whose productions are the decodings of the
encoded productions of $g$: an encoded production $(i, u)$ becomes the production rewriting the
nonterminal $i$ to the word obtained from $u$ by reading each entry $\mathrm{inl}\, j$ as the
nonterminal $j$ and each entry $\mathrm{inr}\, a$ as the terminal $a$.

articles.title: List of nonterminals mentioned by a grammar
articles.statement:
For a context-free grammar $G$, the list
consisting of the initial nonterminal of $G$ followed, for each production of $G$ in turn (in some
fixed order of its finite set of productions), by the left-hand side of the production and then
the nonterminals of its right-hand side in order. Nonterminals may occur more than once.

articles.title: Predicates with a primitive recursive decision procedure are computable
articles.statement:
Let $\beta$ be a
primcodable type, $p$ a predicate on $\beta$, and $f : \beta \to \mathrm{Bool}$ a primitive
recursive function such that $f(b) = \mathrm{true}$ exactly when $p(b)$ holds, for every
$b \in \beta$. Then $p$ is a computable predicate.

articles.title: Duplicate removal for lists of natural numbers
articles.statement:
For a list $l$ of natural numbers, the list
obtained from $l$ by deleting every entry that occurs again later in $l$: each element of $l$ is
kept once, at its last occurrence, and the kept entries stay in their order in $l$.

articles.title: Bounded monotone rounds on lists close off
articles.statement:
Let $f$ map lists of natural numbers to lists
of natural numbers and be monotone for list inclusion: $f(G) \subseteq f(G')$ whenever
$G \subseteq G'$, where $G \subseteq G'$ means that every entry of $G$ is an entry of $G'$. If $B$
is a list with $f(G) \subseteq B$ for every list $G$, and $n$ is the length of $B$, then
$f(f^n([\,])) \subseteq f^n([\,])$, where $f^n$ is the $n$-fold iterate of $f$ and $[\,]$ is the
empty list.

articles.title: Boolean membership test for lists of natural numbers
articles.statement:
For a list $G$ of natural numbers
and a natural number $j$, the Boolean value that is true exactly when $j$ is an entry of $G$.

articles.title: SAT variable index for a bit of a string variable
articles.statement: A positive SAT index for position `p` of variable `i`; `0` is reserved.

articles.title: Exact clause count of the CNF encoding
articles.statement:
Exact CNF size: one constant-bit clause plus the position clauses for every equation.
This is an output-size count, not a `TimeM` or DPLL runtime bound.

articles.title: CNF encoding uses clauses of width at most two
articles.statement: Every emitted clause has at most two literals, including the constant unit clause.

articles.title: CNF encoding of a word-equation system at fixed lengths
articles.statement: CNF for a system at fixed lengths, with shared variables and one constant bit.

articles.title: Linear size bound for bit-blasted words
articles.statement:
Expanded words are at most linear in source-word length and the supplied bound.
Together with `blastSystem_length`, this bounds CNF output size, not solver time.

articles.title: Bit-blasting a word into literals
articles.statement: Expand a word into literals at a fixed length for each string variable.

articles.title: SAT backend agrees with the bounded formula semantics
articles.statement: The SAT backend decides the same bounded semantics as the existing formula language.

articles.title: Soundness and completeness of the bounded word-equation solver
articles.statement: The bounded SAT-backed solver is sound and complete, including empty strings.

articles.title: Bounded word-equation solver via DPLL
articles.statement: Solve bounded word equations by trying finite length profiles and calling DPLL.

articles.title: Fixed-length bit-blasting is equisatisfiable
articles.statement: Fixed-length bit-blasting is satisfiability-preserving in both directions.

articles.title: Decision procedure for bounded Boolean word equations
articles.statement: An executable decision procedure for bounded Boolean-alphabet word equations.

articles.title: Decidability of Boolean-word pattern matching
articles.statement: Executable decidability for unrestricted Boolean-word pattern matching.

articles.title: Decoding string values from a SAT assignment
articles.statement: Read each string variable's bits from a SAT assignment.

articles.title: Encoding a substitution as a SAT assignment
articles.statement: Encode a substitution as a total SAT assignment, using inverse pairing.

articles.title: Position-wise equality clauses for literal vectors
articles.statement: Compare literal vectors position by position; a length mismatch emits an empty clause.

articles.title: Clause count for one word equation
articles.statement: One empty clause for unequal lengths; otherwise two clauses per bit.

articles.title: Clauses for a word equation with a length check
articles.statement: Short-circuit unequal lengths before emitting position-wise equality clauses.

articles.title: Correctness of the fixed-length SAT-backed solver
articles.statement: The executable SAT-backed procedure accepts exactly the fixed-length solutions.

articles.title: Fixed-length word-equation solver via DPLL
articles.statement: Solve the fixed-length system by bit-blasting and the verified DPLL solver.

articles.title: Clauses forcing two literals to be equal
articles.statement: Two implication clauses forcing equal truth values of two literals.

articles.title: Size of the length-profile search
articles.statement: The complete length-profile search has `(B + 1)^n` entries.

articles.title: Enumeration of bounded length profiles
articles.statement: All bounded length profiles, using Mathlib's finite Cartesian-product enumeration.

articles.title: Membership in the length-profile enumeration
articles.statement: The profile enumeration contains exactly the pointwise-bounded length assignments.

articles.title: Target length bounds the pattern-matching search
articles.statement: The target length is a sufficient search bound for unrestricted pattern matching.

articles.title: Pattern-matching decision against a concrete target
articles.statement: Decide matching against a concrete target, with no bound supplied by the caller.

articles.title: Satisfiability as acceptance by some bounded SAT search
articles.statement:
A source system is satisfiable iff some bounded SAT search accepts.
This does not make failure at one bound a decision of general UNSAT.

articles.title: Enumerated lists over distinct variables are recovered from lookups
articles.statement:
Under `vs.Nodup`, an enumerated association list is recovered from its
lookup function: there is no duplicate key for `getVal` to shadow, so
the list is exactly the association list built from its own lookups.

articles.title: Enumerated lists over distinct variables give distinct assignments
articles.statement:
Under `vs.Nodup`, distinct enumerated association lists denote
distinct assignments: if two enumerated lists agree as lookup functions
on `vs`, they are the same list. Without `Nodup` this fails, since a
duplicate key lets a later entry be shadowed by an earlier one.

articles.title: Size of the bounded assignment enumeration
articles.statement:
Counting the assignment enumeration: the total (worst-case) size of
the candidate search space is `(wordsUpToCount B) ^ |vs|`. This counts
enumerated association lists; see the cost model in the module header
for when it coincides with the number of distinct assignments.

articles.title: Enumeration of bounded assignments as association lists
articles.statement:
All assignments of the variables in `vs` to words of length at most
`B`, as association lists, each occurring once (as in `wordsUpTo`).

articles.title: Soundness and completeness of the bounded-search specification
articles.statement:
Soundness and completeness of the bounded-search specification: it
reports `true` exactly when `φ` has a solution whose values on `vs`
have length at most `B`. The hypothesis is that `vs` covers the
variables of `φ`.

articles.title: Bounded-search satisfiability specification
articles.statement:
The bounded-search specification: enumerate bounded assignments and
check `φ` on each one. This is a classical specification, not an
executable decision procedure: `assignLists` is `noncomputable`, so
this Boolean cannot be evaluated by `decide`.

articles.title: Lookup inherits the length bound on values
articles.statement:
A lookup returns one of the values in the list, so it inherits the
length bound on values.

articles.title: Lookup recovers the assignment from its association list
articles.statement:
Lookup in the association list built from an assignment returns the
assignment.

articles.title: Association-list lookup defaulting to the empty word
articles.statement: Lookup in an association list; unbound variables read as `[]`.

articles.title: Keys of the association list built from an assignment
articles.statement:
The keys of the association list built from an assignment are the
variables themselves.

articles.title: Membership in the bounded assignment enumeration
articles.statement:
Membership in the assignment enumeration: the keys are exactly `vs`
and every value has length at most `B`.

articles.title: Membership in the exact-length word enumeration
articles.statement:
Membership in the exact-length enumeration is exactly the length
equality.

articles.title: Membership in the bounded-length word enumeration
articles.statement: Membership in the enumeration is exactly the length bound.

articles.title: Empty word is in every bounded enumeration
articles.statement: The empty word is enumerated at every bound.

articles.title: Sum of a constant over a list
articles.statement: Summing a constant over a list.

articles.title: Size of the exact-length word enumeration
articles.statement: Counting the exact-length enumeration: `|Σ| ^ n` words.

articles.title: Words of a given length over a finite alphabet
articles.statement:
All words of length exactly `n` over a finite alphabet, each occurring
once: each step extends only the words of the previous length, never the
whole `wordsUpTo` enumeration, so no word is duplicated.

articles.title: Number of words of length at most $B$
articles.statement: The number of words of length at most `B`: `∑_{n ≤ B} |Σ| ^ n`.

articles.title: Size of the bounded-length word enumeration
articles.statement:
Counting the enumeration: `∑_{n ≤ B} |Σ| ^ n` words, the number of
distinct words of length at most `B`.

articles.title: Words of length at most $B$ over a finite alphabet
articles.statement:
All words of length at most `B` over a finite alphabet, each occurring
once: the concatenation of the exact-length layers `0, …, B`.

articles.title: Length-directed Levi's lemma
articles.statement:
Length-directed Levi's lemma: if `u` is no longer than `x`, then
`x` splits as `u ++ w` and the remainders satisfy `v = w ++ y`. The
general form is Mathlib's `List.append_eq_append_iff`, used directly.

articles.title: Word evaluation depends only on occurring variables
articles.statement: Evaluation depends only on variables that occur in the word.

articles.title: Normalization does not change the evaluated word
articles.statement: Removing unused images does not change the evaluated word.

articles.title: Word embedding preserves substitution semantics
articles.statement: The embedding preserves substitution semantics.

articles.title: Substitution of words for variables in a word
articles.statement: Substitute words for variables in a word over constants and variables.

articles.title: Ground test agrees with satisfaction under any substitution
articles.statement: The ground test agrees with satisfaction under any substitution.

articles.title: Ground test decides solvability of ground word equations
articles.statement:
The executable ground test decides existence of a solution, not just
satisfaction of one guessed substitution.

articles.title: Executable satisfaction test for ground word equations
articles.statement:
Executable satisfaction test for a ground equation. Since the variable
type is `Empty`, no substitution search is required.

articles.title: Occurring variable's image is no longer than the evaluated word
articles.statement:
Each occurring variable contributes a contiguous block, so its length cannot
exceed the length of the evaluated word, even when substitutions may be empty.

articles.title: Normalized images are bounded by the evaluation length
articles.statement:
After normalization, every variable image, including unused ones, is
bounded by the length of the original evaluation.

articles.title: Normalization keeps images of occurring variables
articles.statement: Normalization preserves the image of every occurring variable.

articles.title: Normalization empties images of absent variables
articles.statement: Every variable absent from the word has empty normalized image.

articles.title: Word substitution normalized by emptying unused images
articles.statement:
Retain the images of occurring variables and replace every unused image by
`[]`. Only equality of variables, not equality of alphabet symbols, is needed.

articles.title: Bounding variable images by the target loses no pattern matches
articles.statement:
Matching a pattern against a fixed target loses no solutions by bounding
ALL variable images by the target length. Unused variables are normalized to
`[]`; an arbitrary unnormalized solution need not obey this bound.

articles.title: Formula embedding of word equations preserves satisfaction
articles.statement: The formula embedding preserves satisfaction.

articles.title: Satisfiability of a single word equation at a finite length bound
articles.statement:
An equation over `Fin n` is satisfiable iff it is satisfiable at some
finite global length bound. There is no equation-computable bound claimed.

articles.title: Solution of a word equation
articles.statement: A substitution solves a word equation when the substituted sides agree.

articles.title: Word equation as a string-constraint formula
articles.statement: View an ordinary word equation as a string-constraint formula.

articles.title: Ordinary word equation
articles.statement: An ordinary word equation, with no morphisms or language-membership atoms.

articles.title: Solvability of word equation systems at a finite length bound
articles.statement:
A system over finitely many variables has a solution iff one substitution
solves every equation at some finite global length bound. The witness bound is
obtained from the solution; this supplies no terminating general UNSAT test.

articles.title: Embedding of ordinary words into string terms
articles.statement: Embed an ordinary word in the larger string-constraint term language.

articles.title: Domino named by a one-letter block
articles.statement: The domino named by a one-letter block; junk `([], [])` otherwise.

articles.title: Alphabet for the PCP encoding
articles.statement:
The alphabet for the PCP encoding: dominoes (as index letters) and
plain letters.

articles.title: Bottom morphism of the PCP encoding
articles.statement: The bottom morphism.

articles.title: Domino as an index letter
articles.statement: A domino as an index letter.

articles.title: Regular language of domino index words
articles.statement:
The regular language of index words: concatenations of domino
letters.

articles.title: Bottom morphism applied to an index word
articles.statement: The bottom morphism applied to an index word.

articles.title: Top morphism applied to an index word
articles.statement: The top morphism applied to an index word.

articles.title: Flattening a list of one-letter blocks
articles.statement: Flattening a list of one-letter blocks.

articles.title: Membership in the domino index-word language
articles.statement:
Membership in the index-word language: the word is a concatenation
of domino letters.

articles.title: Membership in a sum of regular expressions
articles.statement: Membership in a sum of regular expressions.

articles.title: PCP encoding as a one-variable string constraint
articles.statement: The PCP encoding as a string constraint over one variable.

articles.title: PCP is characterized by string-constraint satisfiability:
articles.statement:
For each
PCP instance `P`, `PCP P` holds iff the encoding constraint is satisfiable.
This is a semantic characterization, not a computable reduction to a
formula-indexed satisfiability predicate (see the module header).

articles.title: Membership atom of the PCP encoding checks index words
articles.statement: The membership atom of the encoding checks index-word membership.

articles.title: Top morphism of the PCP encoding
articles.statement:
The top morphism: a domino letter maps to its top word as plain
letters; plain letters map to `[]` (they never occur in an index word).

articles.title: SAT iff the bounded-search specification holds of the encoding
articles.statement:
**SAT iff the bounded-search specification holds of the encoding** at
length bound `1`, for any variable list covering the variables of the
encoding. This is the bridge from the reduction to the bounded-search
specification: `boundedSatSpec_iff` (soundness / completeness of the
finite search) plus the reduction correctness.

articles.title: Correctness of the SAT-to-string-constraints translation
articles.statement:
**Correctness of the SAT-to-string-constraints translation** at
length bound `1`: Boolean assignments become length-`≤ 1` string
assignments and back.

articles.title: Encoding of CNF formulas as string constraints
articles.statement:
SAT as string constraints: each clause is a disjunction of word
equations `x = [b]`, one per literal.

articles.title: Conjunction of a list of string formulas
articles.statement: Conjunction of a list of formulas.

articles.title: String constraint atom
articles.statement:
A **string atom**: a word equation, a regular-membership test, or a
length bound. Regular languages are represented by the existing
`Cslib.Language.EncodedRegex`.

articles.title: String term evaluation depends only on its variables
articles.statement: Evaluation depends only on the values of the variables in the term.

articles.title: Evaluation of a string term under an assignment
articles.statement: Evaluation of a term under an assignment.

articles.title: String formulas
articles.statement:
Positive Boolean combinations of atoms
(conjunction, disjunction, `true`, `false`; no negation), as in the
positive fragment of SMT-LIB assertions.

articles.title: Disjunction of a list of string formulas
articles.statement: Disjunction of a list of formulas.

articles.title: Satisfaction of a conjunction chain
articles.statement: Satisfaction of a conjunction chain: every member is satisfied.

articles.title: Correctness of the Boolean atom checker
articles.statement: The Boolean checker is correct.

articles.title: Boolean checker for atom satisfaction
articles.statement:
Boolean checker for atom satisfaction. Regular membership uses
`EncodedRegex.memB`.

articles.title: Atom satisfaction depends only on its variables
articles.statement: Satisfaction of an atom depends only on the values of its variables.

articles.title: Satisfaction of a string atom
articles.statement: Satisfaction of an atom under an assignment.

articles.title: Correctness of the Boolean formula checker
articles.statement: The Boolean checker is correct.

articles.title: Boolean checker for formula satisfaction
articles.statement: Boolean checker for formula satisfaction.

articles.title: Formula satisfaction depends only on its variables
articles.statement: Satisfaction depends only on the values of the variables in the formula.

articles.title: Satisfaction of a disjunction chain
articles.statement: Satisfaction of a disjunction chain: one member is satisfied.

articles.title: Satisfaction of a string formula
articles.statement: Satisfaction of a formula under an assignment.

articles.title: String term over variables
articles.statement:
A **string term** over variables `V`: a constant word, a variable,
the concatenation of two terms, or a letter-to-word morphism applied
to a term.

articles.title: Variables occurring in a string atom
articles.statement: The variables occurring in an atom.

articles.title: Variables occurring in a string formula
articles.statement: The variables occurring in a formula.

articles.title: Variables occurring in a string term
articles.statement: The variables occurring in a term, as a list (duplicates allowed).

articles.title: Acyclic closed straight-line system
articles.statement:
A closed straight-line system is **acyclic** when every defining term
mentions only earlier variables, and the query mentions only defined
variables. Hence every variable occurring anywhere in the system is
defined, and unfolding the definitions terminates at ground terms:
there is no free input variable.

articles.title: Satisfiability of a closed acyclic straight-line system is decidable
articles.statement:
The decision procedure checks the query on the unique ground assignment;
it does not search over free inputs, because the closed fragment has none.

articles.title: Satisfying assignments agree with the candidate on defined variables
articles.statement:
Any satisfying assignment agrees with the candidate on defined
variables.

articles.title: Straight-line satisfiability iff the query holds on the candidate
articles.statement:
Satisfiability of a closed straight-line system is equivalent to the query
holding on the candidate assignment.

articles.title: Defining equation for the folded values
articles.statement:
The defining equation for the folded values: the value at position
`acc.length + k` is the `k`-th defining term evaluated under the
folded values. The variable condition says the term only looks at
positions below `acc.length + k`.

articles.title: Straight-line fold appends one value per definition
articles.statement: The fold appends exactly one value per definition.

articles.title: Straight-line fold preserves its initial segment
articles.statement: The fold preserves its initial segment.

articles.title: Lookup in an appended list below the prefix length
articles.statement: Lookup in an appended list agrees with lookup below the prefix length.

articles.title: In-bounds lookup with default equals indexed access
articles.statement: Lookup with a proof of the bound is the `getElem` value.

articles.title: Lookup in a folded list below the starting length
articles.statement:
Lookup in a folded list agrees with lookup in the starting list
below its length.

articles.title: Lookup in a taken prefix agrees with the whole list
articles.statement: Lookup in a taken prefix agrees with lookup in the whole list.

articles.title: One fold step of straight-line evaluation
articles.statement:
One fold step: evaluate the next defining term under the values
computed so far and append the result.

articles.title: Satisfaction of a closed straight-line system
articles.statement:
Satisfaction of a closed straight-line system: the assignment obeys every
definition and satisfies the query.

articles.title: Closed straight-line system
articles.statement:
A **closed straight-line system**: one defining term per variable, plus a
query formula. The definition at position `k` is the definition of
variable `k`. There are no free input variables: every variable the
system talks about must be defined by the system itself.

articles.title: Candidate assignment satisfies every definition
articles.statement: The candidate assignment satisfies every definition.

articles.title: Candidate assignment of a straight-line system
articles.statement: The candidate assignment of a straight-line system.

articles.title: Folded values have one entry per definition
articles.statement: Length of the folded values: one per definition.

articles.title: Folded assignment values of a straight-line system
articles.statement: The folded assignment values, in variable order.

articles.title: The hierarchy is closed under computable precomposition
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number
and let $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be computable. If a set $P$ of natural numbers is in
the class $\Sigma_n$ of the arithmetical hierarchy, then so is $\{w \in \mathbb{N} : g(w) \in P\}$;
and if $P$ is in the class $\Pi_n$, then so is $\{w \in \mathbb{N} : g(w) \in P\}$.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Lemma 4.2.

articles.title: The pairing function is computable
articles.statement:
The pairing bijection
$\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, given by
$\langle a, b \rangle = b^2 + a$ if $a < b$ and $\langle a, b \rangle = a^2 + a + b$ otherwise,
is a computable function of its two arguments.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.3.

articles.title: Computable predicates are closed under precomposition with pairing
articles.statement:
Let
$\langle a, b \rangle$ denote the pairing bijection $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$,
$\langle a, b \rangle = b^2 + a$ if $a < b$ and $\langle a, b \rangle = a^2 + a + b$ otherwise.
If $Q$ is a decidable set of natural numbers, then the set of pairs
$(a, b) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ with $\langle a, b \rangle \in Q$ is decidable.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Lemma 4.2.

articles.title: Computable predicates are closed under computable precomposition
articles.statement:
If $P$ is a decidable
set of natural numbers and $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is a computable function, then the set
$\{w \in \mathbb{N} : g(w) \in P\}$ is decidable.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Lemma 4.2.

articles.title: The first projection of the pairing function is computable
articles.statement:
Let
$\langle a, b \rangle$ denote the pairing bijection $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$,
$\langle a, b \rangle = b^2 + a$ if $a < b$ and $\langle a, b \rangle = a^2 + a + b$ otherwise.
The function sending $z \in \mathbb{N}$ to the first component $a$ of the unique pair $(a, b)$
with $\langle a, b \rangle = z$ is computable.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.3.

articles.title: The second projection of the pairing function is computable
articles.statement:
Let
$\langle a, b \rangle$ denote the pairing bijection $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$,
$\langle a, b \rangle = b^2 + a$ if $a < b$ and $\langle a, b \rangle = a^2 + a + b$ otherwise.
The function sending $z \in \mathbb{N}$ to the second component $b$ of the unique pair $(a, b)$
with $\langle a, b \rangle = z$ is computable.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.3.

articles.title: The class Δₙ of the arithmetical hierarchy
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number. A set $P$ of
natural numbers is in $\Delta_n$ when it is in both classes $\Sigma_n$ and $\Pi_n$ of the
arithmetical hierarchy.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Definition 4.1.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the hierarchy
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, writing $\Sigma_n$ and $\Pi_n$
for the classes of the arithmetical hierarchy, every $\Sigma_n$ set of natural numbers is in
$\Sigma_{n+1}$ and every $\Pi_n$ set of natural numbers is in $\Pi_{n+1}$.

The two inclusions are proved together by induction on $n$: the step case of each uses the
other at the previous level.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Theorem 4.3.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the Π hierarchy
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, every set of natural
numbers in the class $\Pi_n$ of the arithmetical hierarchy is also in $\Pi_{n+1}$; that is,
$\Pi_n \subseteq \Pi_{n+1}$.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Theorem 4.3.

articles.title: Every Πₙ set is Σₙ₊₁
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, every set of natural numbers in the
class $\Pi_n$ of the arithmetical hierarchy is also in $\Sigma_{n+1}$; that is,
$\Pi_n \subseteq \Sigma_{n+1}$, by adding a dummy existential quantifier.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Theorem 4.3.

articles.title: Every Σₙ predicate is Σₙ₊₁
articles.statement:
Let $\Sigma_n$ and $\Pi_n$ be the levels of the arithmetical
hierarchy of predicates on $\mathbb{N}$: $\Sigma_0 = \Pi_0$ is the class of computable predicates,
$P \in \Sigma_{n+1}$ when for some $Q \in \Pi_n$ and all $x$, $P(x)$ holds iff
$Q(\langle x, y \rangle)$ holds for some $y$, and $P \in \Pi_{n+1}$ when for some $Q \in \Sigma_n$
and all $x$, $P(x)$ holds iff $Q(\langle x, y \rangle)$ holds for all $y$; here
$\langle x, y \rangle$ is the standard pairing function of $\mathbb{N}$. Then for every $n$, every
predicate in $\Sigma_n$ is in $\Sigma_{n+1}$.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Theorem 4.3.

articles.title: Σ₁ is the class of recursively enumerable predicates
articles.statement:
A predicate $P$ on $\mathbb{N}$ is
recursively enumerable if and only if it is in $\Sigma_1$, that is, if and only if there is a
computable predicate $Q$ on $\mathbb{N}$ such that for all $x$, $P(x)$ holds iff
$Q(\langle x, y \rangle)$ holds for some $y$, where $\langle x, y \rangle$ is the standard pairing
function of $\mathbb{N}$.

This is the first level of Post's theorem.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Theorem 4.4 (Post).

articles.title: Σₙ and Πₙ predicates are Δₙ₊₁
articles.statement:
Let $\Sigma_n$ and $\Pi_n$ be the levels of the arithmetical
hierarchy of predicates on $\mathbb{N}$: $\Sigma_0 = \Pi_0$ is the class of computable predicates,
$P \in \Sigma_{n+1}$ when for some $Q \in \Pi_n$ and all $x$, $P(x)$ holds iff
$Q(\langle x, y \rangle)$ holds for some $y$, and $P \in \Pi_{n+1}$ when for some $Q \in \Sigma_n$
and all $x$, $P(x)$ holds iff $Q(\langle x, y \rangle)$ holds for all $y$; here
$\langle x, y \rangle$ is the standard pairing function of $\mathbb{N}$. Then for every $n$, every
predicate in $\Sigma_n$ or in $\Pi_n$ is in $\Delta_{n+1}$, that is, in both $\Sigma_{n+1}$ and
$\Pi_{n+1}$.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Theorem 4.3.

articles.title: Every Σₙ predicate is Πₙ₊₁
articles.statement:
Let $\Sigma_n$ and $\Pi_n$ be the levels of the arithmetical
hierarchy of predicates on $\mathbb{N}$: $\Sigma_0 = \Pi_0$ is the class of computable predicates,
$P \in \Sigma_{n+1}$ when for some $Q \in \Pi_n$ and all $x$, $P(x)$ holds iff
$Q(\langle x, y \rangle)$ holds for some $y$, and $P \in \Pi_{n+1}$ when for some $Q \in \Sigma_n$
and all $x$, $P(x)$ holds iff $Q(\langle x, y \rangle)$ holds for all $y$; here
$\langle x, y \rangle$ is the standard pairing function of $\mathbb{N}$. Then for every $n$, every
predicate in $\Sigma_n$ is in $\Pi_{n+1}$.

The proof adds a dummy universal quantifier.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Theorem 4.3.

articles.title: Composing a code with a constant code ignores the input
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code of a partial
recursive function and let $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$. The code that first computes the constant
function with value $n$ and then applies $c$, evaluated at $m$, gives the same partial value as
$c$ evaluated at $n$: one is defined exactly when the other is, and then they are equal.

articles.title: Every recognizable predicate many-one reduces to the halting set
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type
with a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$, and let $p$ be a recognizable (recursively
enumerable) predicate on $\alpha$, that is, the domain of a partial computable function on
$\alpha$. Here the halting set is the set of $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that the partial recursive
function with code number $n$ halts on input $0$. Then there is a computable function
$f : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $a \in \alpha$, $p(a)$ holds if and only if $f(a)$
lies in the halting set.

articles.title: Recognizability transfers down many-one reductions
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be types
with primitive recursive encodings into $\mathbb{N}$, and let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on
$\alpha$ and on $\beta$. Suppose that $p$ many-one reduces to $q$, that is, there is a computable
function $f : \alpha \to \beta$ such that for every $a \in \alpha$, $p(a)$ holds if and only if
$q(f(a))$ holds. If $q$ is recognizable (recursively enumerable: the domain of a partial
computable function on $\beta$), then $p$ is recognizable.

articles.title: Every recognizable predicate one-one reduces to the halting set
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type
with a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$, and let $p$ be a recognizable (recursively
enumerable) predicate on $\alpha$, that is, the domain of a partial computable function on
$\alpha$. Here the halting set is the set of $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that the partial recursive
function with code number $n$ halts on input $0$. Then there is an injective computable function
$f : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $a \in \alpha$, $p(a)$ holds if and only if $f(a)$
lies in the halting set.

The proof takes for $f(a)$ the number of the code that ignores its input and runs a code for $p$
on the number encoding $a$; distinct $a$ give distinct codes.

articles.title: The halting set is recognizable
articles.statement:
The halting set, the set of numbers $n$ such that the
code with number $n$ halts on input $0$, is recursively enumerable: it is the domain of a partial
computable function on $\mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: A predicate is recognizable iff it many-one reduces to the halting set
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
type with a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$ and let $p$ be a predicate on $\alpha$.
Here the halting set is the set of $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that the partial recursive function
with code number $n$ halts on input $0$. Then $p$ is recognizable (recursively enumerable: the
domain of a partial computable function on $\alpha$) if and only if there is a computable function
$f : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $a \in \alpha$, $p(a)$ holds if and only if $f(a)$
lies in the halting set.

articles.title: A predicate is recognizable iff it one-one reduces to the halting set
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
type with a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$ and let $p$ be a predicate on $\alpha$.
Here the halting set is the set of $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that the partial recursive function
with code number $n$ halts on input $0$. Then $p$ is recognizable (recursively enumerable: the
domain of a partial computable function on $\alpha$) if and only if there is an injective
computable function $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for every $a \in \alpha$, $p(a)$ holds
if and only if $f(a)$ lies in the halting set.

articles.title: A creative set is not computable
articles.statement:
Its complement is productive, hence
not RE, but the complement of a computable set is RE.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Theorem 5.7.

articles.title: A creative set is recursively enumerable
articles.statement:
**A creative set is recursively enumerable**, by definition.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Definition 5.2.

articles.title: Creative set
articles.statement:
A set $A$ of natural numbers is creative when it is recursively enumerable
and its complement $\mathbb{N} \setminus A$ is productive.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Definition 5.2.

articles.title: Standard enumeration of the recursively enumerable sets
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $e$ and $n$,
$n$ belongs to $W_e$, the $e$-th recursively enumerable set, when the partial recursive function
$\varphi_e$ computed by the program with index $e$ in the standard numbering of partial recursive
programs is defined at $n$; thus $W_e$ is the domain of $\varphi_e$.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (standard enumeration of the partial recursive functions).

articles.title: An immune set is not recursively enumerable
articles.statement:
It would be an infinite
RE subset of itself.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Theorem 5.6.

articles.title: Immune set
articles.statement:
A set $A$ of natural numbers is immune when it is infinite and every
recursively enumerable set $B \subseteq A$ is finite.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Definition 5.4.

articles.title: A productive set is not recursively enumerable
articles.statement:
No productive set of natural numbers is
recursively enumerable: if it were the $e$-th recursively enumerable set $W_e$, its productive
function would produce a member of it outside $W_e$.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Theorem 5.5.

articles.title: Productive set
articles.statement:
A set $A$ of natural numbers is productive when there is a partial
recursive function $f$ such that for every natural number $e$ with $W_e \subseteq A$, where $W_e$
is the $e$-th recursively enumerable set in the standard enumeration, $f(e)$ is defined,
$f(e) \in A$ and $f(e) \notin W_e$.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Definition 5.1.

articles.title: The complement of a simple set is immune
articles.statement:
**The complement of a simple set is immune**, by definition.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Definition 5.3.

articles.title: A simple set is not computable
articles.statement:
Its complement would be an infinite
RE set, contradicting immunity.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Theorem 5.6.

articles.title: A simple set is recursively enumerable
articles.statement:
**A simple set is recursively enumerable**, by definition.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Definition 5.3.

articles.title: Simple set
articles.statement:
A set $P$ of natural numbers is **simple** when it is recursively enumerable
and its complement $\{n \mid \neg P(n)\}$ is immune.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Definition 5.3.

articles.title: The inverse of a computable bijection is computable
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a computable bijection. Then its inverse function
$f^{-1} : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is computable.

The inverse is computed by unbounded search for the unique preimage.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (inverses of recursive permutations).

articles.title: A recursive isomorphism gives a 1-equivalence
articles.statement:
Let $P$ and $Q$ be predicates on
$\mathbb{N}$. If $P$ and $Q$ are recursively isomorphic, then they are 1-equivalent: $P$ is
one-one reducible to $Q$ and $Q$ is one-one reducible to $P$. Here $P$ is one-one reducible to
$Q$ when there is a computable injective function $g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for
every $n$, $P(n)$ holds if and only if $Q(g(n))$ holds.

This is the easy direction of Myhill's isomorphism theorem.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Theorem 7.1.

articles.title: Recursively isomorphic predicates
articles.statement:
Two predicates $P$ and $Q$ on $\mathbb{N}$ are
recursively isomorphic when there is a computable bijection $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such
that for every $n$, $P(n)$ holds if and only if $Q(f(n))$ holds.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Definition 7.1.

articles.title: The effective enumeration of oracle codes is computable
articles.statement:
**The effective enumeration of oracle codes is computable.**

## Sources
