- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (standard enumerations).

articles.title: The definedness predicate, by cases on the tag
articles.statement:
Write $\langle a, b \rangle$ for the
pairing bijection $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of the Gödel numbering, and say
that a natural number decodes when the computable decoder returns an oracle code on it. Let $t$
and $p$ be natural numbers and write $p = \langle p_1, p_2 \rangle$. Then $\langle t, p \rangle$
decodes if and only if one of the following holds: $t$ is $0$, $1$, $2$, $3$ or $8$ and $p = 0$;
$t$ is $4$, $5$ or $6$ and both $p_1$ and $p_2$ decode; or $t = 7$ and $p$ decodes.

In the recursive cases $t \ge 1$, so $p_1$, $p_2$ and $p$ are strictly smaller than
$\langle t, p \rangle$.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; decoding).

articles.title: The definedness step function is correct
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, let $b_n$ be $1$ if
the computable decoder returns an oracle code on $n$, and $0$ otherwise. For every natural number
$m$, the one-step function of the course-of-values recursion for definedness, applied to the list
$(b_0, b_1, \dots, b_{m-1})$, returns $b_m$.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; decoding).

articles.title: One step of the course-of-values recursion for definedness
articles.statement:
Write $\langle a, b \rangle$
for the pairing bijection $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of the Gödel numbering.
The step takes an argument of the unit type, which it ignores, and a list $L$ of natural numbers;
for $i \in \mathbb{N}$ write $L_i$ for the entry of $L$ at position $i$ (counting from $0$), with
$L_i = 0$ when $i$ is at least the length of $L$. Let $m$ be the length of $L$, and write
$m = \langle t, p \rangle$ and $p = \langle p_1, p_2 \rangle$. The step always returns a value,
namely $1$ if one of the following holds and $0$ otherwise: $t$ is $0$, $1$, $2$, $3$ or $8$ and
$p = 0$; $t$ is $4$, $5$ or $6$ and $L_{p_1} = L_{p_2} = 1$; or $t = 7$ and $L_p = 1$.

Applied to the list whose entry at position $k < m$ is $1$ if $k$ decodes to an oracle code and
$0$ otherwise, it returns the corresponding value for $m$, because in the recursive cases $p_1$,
$p_2$ and $p$ are smaller than $m$.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; decoding).

articles.title: Whether a code number decodes
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, this is the Boolean value that is
true exactly when the computable decoder of oracle codes returns an oracle code on $n$.

By decoder soundness and the inversion of the encoder, this holds exactly when $n$ is the Gödel
number of an oracle code.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; decoding).

articles.title: The computable decoder inverts the encoder
articles.statement:
For every oracle code $c$, the computable
decoder applied to the Gödel number of $c$ returns $c$.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; decoding).

articles.title: The fuel-indexed decoder inverts the encoder
articles.statement:
Write $\langle a, b \rangle$ for the pairing
bijection $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of the Gödel numbering. Let $c$ be an
oracle code with Gödel number $\langle t, p \rangle$. For every fuel $f$ strictly greater than the
depth of $c$, the fuel-indexed decoder with fuel $f$, tag $t$ and payload $p$ returns $c$.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; decoding).

articles.title: The fuel-indexed decoder agrees with the total decoder
articles.statement:
**The fuel-indexed decoder agrees with the total decoder** whenever the
code number is below the fuel: decoding `(tag, payload)` at any fuel above
the code number gives the same result as decoding the code number itself.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; decoding).

articles.title: Decoder soundness
articles.statement:
Write $\langle a, b \rangle$ for the pairing bijection
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of the Gödel numbering. For every fuel $f$, tag
$t$, payload $p$ and oracle code $c$, if the fuel-indexed decoder with fuel $f$, tag $t$ and
payload $p$ returns $c$, then the Gödel number of $c$ is $\langle t, p \rangle$.

Together with the fact that the fuel-indexed decoder inverts the encoder at any fuel above the
code depth, this says that the decoder is exactly the inverse of the Gödel numbering on its image.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; decoding).

articles.title: Fuel-indexed decoder of oracle codes
articles.statement:
Write $\langle a, b \rangle$ for the pairing
bijection $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ of the Gödel numbering. Given a fuel $f$,
a tag $t$ and a payload $p$, the decoder either returns an oracle code or fails; to decode a
number $n = \langle n_1, n_2 \rangle$ with fuel $f$ means to run it with fuel $f$, tag $n_1$ and
payload $n_2$. With fuel $0$ it fails. With fuel $f + 1$, writing $p = \langle p_1, p_2 \rangle$:
if $p = 0$ and $t$ is $0$, $1$, $2$, $3$ or $8$, it returns the instruction zero, successor, left
projection, right projection or oracle query respectively; if $t$ is $4$, $5$ or $6$, it decodes
$p_1$ and $p_2$ with fuel $f$ and, when these give codes $a$ and $b$, returns the pairing,
composition or primitive recursion code built from $a$ and $b$ respectively, failing otherwise;
if $t = 7$, it decodes $p$ with fuel $f$ and, when this gives a code $a$, returns the unbounded
search code built from $a$, failing otherwise; in all other cases it fails.

The recursion is structural in the fuel and uses no classical choice, so the decoder is a
computable function; with enough fuel it inverts the Gödel numbering of oracle codes.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; decoding).

articles.title: The decoder, by cases on the tag
articles.statement:
Write $\langle t, p \rangle$ for the pairing of natural
numbers used by the Gödel numbering of oracle codes, $(p_1, p_2)$ for the unpairing of $p$ (so that
$\langle p_1, p_2 \rangle = p$), and $\mathrm{dec}(n)$ for the result of the computable decoder on
$n$, which is either an oracle code or undefined. Then for all natural numbers $t$ and $p$, the
value $\mathrm{dec}\langle t, p \rangle$ is: $\mathsf{zero}$, $\mathsf{succ}$, $\mathsf{left}$,
$\mathsf{right}$ or $\mathsf{oracle}$ when $p = 0$ and $t$ is $0$, $1$, $2$, $3$ or $8$
respectively; $\mathsf{pair}(a, b)$, $\mathsf{comp}(a, b)$ or $\mathsf{prec}(a, b)$ when $t$ is
$4$, $5$ or $6$ respectively and $\mathrm{dec}(p_1) = a$ and $\mathrm{dec}(p_2) = b$ are both
defined; $\mathsf{rfind}(a)$ when $t = 7$ and $\mathrm{dec}(p) = a$ is defined; and undefined in
every other case.

For $t \in \{4, 5, 6, 7\}$ the numbers decoded on the right, $p_1$, $p_2$ and $p$, are at most $p$
and hence strictly below $\langle t, p \rangle$, so this is a recursion on the code number.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; decoding).

articles.title: Decoding oracle codes
articles.statement:
The computable decoder for the Gödel numbering of oracle codes
sends a natural number $n$ to the result of the fuel-indexed decoder with fuel $n + 1$, tag $n_1$
and payload $n_2$, where $(n_1, n_2)$ is the unpairing of $n$; the result is either an oracle code
or undefined. The fuel $n + 1$ is more than enough, since the depth of an oracle code is at most
its code number.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; decoding).

articles.title: The Gödel numbering of oracle codes is injective
articles.statement:
**The Gödel numbering of oracle codes is injective.**

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings).

articles.title: The Gödel numbering of oracle codes
articles.statement:
Write $\langle a, b \rangle$ for the pairing of
natural numbers equal to $b^2 + a$ if $a < b$ and to $a^2 + a + b$ otherwise. The code number
$\ulcorner c \urcorner$ of an oracle code $c$ is defined by recursion on $c$: $\mathsf{zero}$,
$\mathsf{succ}$, $\mathsf{left}$, $\mathsf{right}$ and $\mathsf{oracle}$ have code numbers
$\langle 0, 0 \rangle$, $\langle 1, 0 \rangle$, $\langle 2, 0 \rangle$, $\langle 3, 0 \rangle$ and
$\langle 8, 0 \rangle$; $\mathsf{pair}(a, b)$, $\mathsf{comp}(a, b)$ and $\mathsf{prec}(a, b)$
have code numbers $\langle 4, \langle \ulcorner a \urcorner, \ulcorner b \urcorner \rangle \rangle$,
$\langle 5, \langle \ulcorner a \urcorner, \ulcorner b \urcorner \rangle \rangle$ and
$\langle 6, \langle \ulcorner a \urcorner, \ulcorner b \urcorner \rangle \rangle$; and
$\mathsf{rfind}(a)$ has code number $\langle 7, \ulcorner a \urcorner \rangle$.

This numbering is an injection into $\mathbb{N}$.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings).

articles.title: The Turing jump
articles.statement:
For a predicate $P$ on $\mathbb{N}$, the Turing jump $P'$ is the
predicate that holds at $n$ exactly when the $n$-th oracle code in the effective enumeration of
oracle codes, evaluated with the oracle that answers $1$ at $m$ if $P(m)$ holds and $0$ otherwise,
halts on input $n$. Thus $P'$ is the diagonal halting set of the universal oracle machine with
oracle $P$.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Definition 2.1 (the jump).

articles.title: The definedness predicate is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
The function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
sending $n$ to $1$ if $n$ decodes to an oracle code under the computable decoder and to $0$
otherwise is primitive recursive.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; decoding).

articles.title: Depth is bounded by the code number
articles.statement:
For every oracle code $c$, the depth of $c$ is at most
the code number of $c$ under the Gödel numbering of oracle codes.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; size bounds).

articles.title: Depth of an oracle code
articles.statement:
Leaves have depth `0`; each constructor adds
one to the maximum depth of its children.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; size bounds).

articles.title: The effective enumeration is a left inverse of the Gödel numbering
articles.statement:
For every oracle code
$c$, the effective enumeration of oracle codes sends the code number of $c$ to $c$.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (standard enumerations).

articles.title: The enumeration of oracle codes is surjective
articles.statement:
**The enumeration of oracle codes is surjective.**

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (standard enumerations).

articles.title: Effective enumeration of oracle codes
articles.statement:
The $n$-th oracle code is the code that the
computable decoder of the Gödel numbering of oracle codes assigns to $n$, or the basic code
$\mathtt{zero}$ (the constant $0$ program) when $n$ is not the number of any code. Because the
decoder inverts the Gödel numbering, this is an effective enumeration tied to that numbering,
not an arbitrary countable encoding.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (standard enumerations).

articles.title: Oracle codes
articles.statement:
Oracle codes are the finite programs built from the basic codes
$\mathtt{zero}$, $\mathtt{succ}$, $\mathtt{left}$, $\mathtt{right}$ and $\mathtt{oracle}$ by the
binary constructors $\mathtt{pair}$, $\mathtt{comp}$ and $\mathtt{prec}$ and the unary constructor
$\mathtt{rfind}$. They are the codes for partial recursive functions (constant zero, successor,
the two unpairing projections, pairing, composition, primitive recursion and unbounded search)
extended by an instruction $\mathtt{oracle}$ that queries the oracle on its input.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, §2 (oracle computations).

articles.title: Evaluation of oracle codes
articles.statement:
Let $o$ be an oracle that assigns to each natural number
either a natural number or no value, $c$ an oracle code and $n$ a natural number. The value of
$c$ on $n$ relative to $o$ is the value returned by the fuel-indexed evaluator of $c$ on $n$
relative to $o$ at the least fuel $k$ for which that evaluator returns a value; it is undefined
when there is no such $k$.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, §2 (oracle computations).

articles.title: Fuel bounds the inputs
articles.statement:
For every oracle $o$, fuel $k$, oracle code $c$ and input $n$,
if the fuel-indexed evaluator with fuel $k$ returns a value on $c$ and $n$ relative to $o$, then
$n < k$.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, §2 (oracle computations).

articles.title: Fuel-indexed evaluation of oracle codes
Pairing with $4$ strictly increases the second argument
articles.statement:
Let $\langle a, b \rangle$ denote
the pairing of natural numbers, equal to $b^2 + a$ if $a < b$ and to $a^2 + a + b$ otherwise.
For every natural number $x$, $x < \langle 4, x \rangle$.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.3 (pairing functions).

articles.title: Pairing is at least its first argument
articles.statement:
Let $\langle a, b \rangle$ denote the pairing of
natural numbers, equal to $b^2 + a$ if $a < b$ and to $a^2 + a + b$ otherwise. For all natural
numbers $a$ and $b$, $a \le \langle a, b \rangle$.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.3 (pairing functions).

articles.title: Pairing is at least its second argument
articles.statement:
Let $\langle a, b \rangle$ denote the pairing of
natural numbers, equal to $b^2 + a$ if $a < b$ and to $a^2 + a + b$ otherwise. For all natural
numbers $a$ and $b$, $b \le \langle a, b \rangle$.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.3 (pairing functions).

articles.title: Pairing with a positive first argument strictly increases the second
articles.statement:
Let
$\langle a, b \rangle$ denote the pairing of natural numbers, equal to $b^2 + a$ if $a < b$ and to
$a^2 + a + b$ otherwise. For all natural numbers $t$ and $x$ with $t \ge 1$,
$x < \langle t, x \rangle$.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.3 (pairing functions).

articles.title: The course-of-values step for definedness is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
One step of the
course-of-values recursion for definedness is primitive recursive as a function of its two
arguments, an element of the unit type and a list of natural numbers.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; decoding).

articles.title: The Gödel decoder of oracle codes is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Regard oracle codes as coded
by their Gödel numbers. Then the computable decoder, which sends a natural number $n$ to the
oracle code with Gödel number $n$ when there is one and to no value otherwise, is primitive
recursive as a map from natural numbers to optional oracle codes.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings; decoding).

articles.title: The Gödel encoding of oracle codes is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Regard oracle codes as coded
by their Gödel numbers, with the computable decoder as decoding. Then the map sending each oracle
code to its Gödel number is primitive recursive.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (Gödel numberings).

articles.title: The effective enumeration of oracle codes is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Regard oracle codes as
coded by their Gödel numbers. Then the effective enumeration of oracle codes, which sends a
natural number $n$ to the oracle code with Gödel number $n$ when there is one and to the zero
code otherwise, is primitive recursive.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.6 (standard enumerations).

articles.title: Turing degree of a predicate
articles.statement:
The Turing degree of a predicate $P$ on the natural numbers
is the Turing degree of its characteristic function, that is, the class of the characteristic
function of $P$ under Turing equivalence of partial functions
$\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Definition 2.3.

articles.title: Turing equivalence of predicates
articles.statement:
Two predicates $P$ and $Q$ on the natural numbers are
Turing equivalent when the characteristic function of $P$ is Turing reducible to the
characteristic function of $Q$ and the characteristic function of $Q$ is Turing reducible to the
characteristic function of $P$.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Definition 2.2.

articles.title: Turing reducibility is reflexive
articles.statement:
Every predicate $P$ on the natural numbers is Turing
reducible to itself.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Theorem 2.4.

articles.title: Turing reducibility is transitive
articles.statement:
For predicates $P$, $Q$ and $R$ on the natural
numbers, if $P$ is Turing reducible to $Q$ and $Q$ is Turing reducible to $R$, then $P$ is Turing
reducible to $R$.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Theorem 2.4.

articles.title: Turing reducibility of predicates
articles.statement:
A predicate $P$ on the natural numbers is Turing
reducible to a predicate $Q$ on the natural numbers when the characteristic function of $P$ is
Turing reducible to the characteristic function of $Q$, that is, partial recursive relative to an
oracle for the characteristic function of $Q$.

## Sources

- Soare, *Recursively Enumerable Sets and Degrees*, Ch. I, Definition 2.2.

articles.title: The first unpairing component is at most the number
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathrm{pair} : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be the pairing bijection with
$\mathrm{pair}(a, b) = b^2 + a$ if $a < b$ and $\mathrm{pair}(a, b) = a^2 + a + b$ otherwise.
For every natural number $n$, the first component of $\mathrm{pair}^{-1}(n)$ is at most $n$.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.3 (pairing functions).

articles.title: The second unpairing component is at most the number
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathrm{pair} : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be the pairing bijection with
$\mathrm{pair}(a, b) = b^2 + a$ if $a < b$ and $\mathrm{pair}(a, b) = a^2 + a + b$ otherwise.
For every natural number $n$, the second component of $\mathrm{pair}^{-1}(n)$ is at most $n$.

## Sources

- Rogers, *Theory of Recursive Functions and Effective Computability*, §1.3 (pairing functions).

articles.title: Characteristic function of a set of naturals
articles.statement:
The characteristic function of a set $p$ of
natural numbers is the partial function $\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$ that is defined at
every $n$, with value $1$ if $n \in p$ and value $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: A set is decidable iff its characteristic function is partial recursive
articles.statement:
A set $p$ of
natural numbers is decidable (computable as a predicate) if and only if its characteristic function
is partial recursive.

articles.title: Halting set
articles.statement:
Fix the standard bijective numbering $n \mapsto c_n$ of the codes of partial
recursive functions $\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$. The halting set is the set of natural
numbers $n$ such that the partial recursive function with code $c_n$ is defined at $0$.

articles.title: The complement of the halting set is not many-one reducible to it
articles.statement:
There is no computable
function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that, for every $n$, $n$ is outside the halting set
if and only if $f(n)$ is in the halting set.

The halting set is recognizable and its complement is not. Since every set is Turing equivalent to
its complement, Turing reducibility is strictly coarser than many-one reducibility.

articles.title: The halting set is not Turing reducible to a decidable set
articles.statement:
For every decidable set $q$ of
natural numbers, the characteristic function of the halting set is not Turing reducible to the
characteristic function of $q$.

articles.title: Decidability transfers down Turing reducibility
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $q$ be sets of natural numbers
such that the characteristic function of $p$ is Turing reducible to the characteristic function of
$q$. If $q$ is decidable, then $p$ is decidable.

articles.title: Every set is Turing equivalent to its complement
articles.statement:
For every set $p$ of natural numbers,
the characteristic function of the complement $\mathbb{N} \setminus p$ and the characteristic
function of $p$ are Turing equivalent: each is Turing reducible to the other.

articles.title: Many-one reducibility implies Turing reducibility
articles.statement:
If $p$ and $q$ are sets of natural
numbers and $p$ is many-one reducible to $q$, that is, there is a computable
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $n \in p \iff f(n) \in q$ for all $n$, then the characteristic
function of $p$ is Turing reducible to the characteristic function of $q$.

articles.title: Interpretation of relation symbols in a graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph and let
$(E_j)_{j \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a family of relations, each a predicate on finite lists of vertices
of $G$. Relation symbol $0$ is interpreted as the edge relation of $G$: it holds of a list exactly
when the list is $[a, b]$ for vertices $a, b$ with an edge from $a$ to $b$. For $i \ge 1$, relation
symbol $i$ is interpreted as $E_{i-1}$.

articles.title: Edge relation of a graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph with vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ and edge table
$t$, a finite list of booleans. For vertices $a, b < n$, there is an edge from $a$ to $b$ exactly
when the entry of $t$ at position $an + b$ (counting from $0$) is true; a position beyond the end
of $t$ counts as false.

articles.title: Encodings of a graph class as a decision problem
articles.statement:
For a class $K$ of graphs, this is the
decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical
bitstring encoding of pairs of a natural number and a list of booleans, to a graph $G \in K$ with
$n$ vertices whose edge table has length exactly $n^2$.

articles.title: Existential second-order definable graph classes
articles.statement:
A class $K$ of graphs is existential
second-order definable if there are a natural number $k$, a first-order formula $\varphi$ and a
boolean $e$ such that every graph $G$ with $n$ vertices whose edge table has length exactly $n^2$
satisfies the following: if $n > 0$, then $G \in K$ if and only if $G$ satisfies the existential
second-order sentence $(k, \varphi)$; if $n = 0$, then $G \in K$ if and only if $e$ is true.

articles.title: Satisfaction of an existential second-order sentence
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph with $n > 0$
vertices, $k$ a natural number and $\varphi$ a first-order formula. Then $G$ satisfies the
existential second-order sentence $(k, \varphi)$ if there are relations $R_0, \dots, R_{k-1}$,
each a predicate on finite lists of vertices of $G$, such that $\varphi$ holds in $G$ when
relation symbol $0$ is interpreted as the edge relation (holding exactly of the lists $[a, b]$
with an edge from $a$ to $b$), relation symbol $j + 1$ as $R_j$ for each $j < k$, every relation
symbol above $k$ as the empty relation, and every variable as vertex $0$.

articles.title: Evaluation of a first-order formula in a graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a graph, let $\rho$ assign a
vertex $\rho(j)$ of $G$ to each variable $x_j$ ($j \in \mathbb{N}$), and let $S$ assign to each
relation symbol $i \in \mathbb{N}$ a predicate $S_i$ on finite lists of vertices of $G$. Truth of a
formula is defined by recursion: $x_a = x_b$ holds when $\rho(a) = \rho(b)$; relation symbol $i$
applied to the variables $x_{a_1}, \dots, x_{a_m}$ holds when $S_i$ holds of the list
$[\rho(a_1), \dots, \rho(a_m)]$; negation, conjunction and disjunction are interpreted as usual;
and $\exists \varphi$ holds when there is a vertex $v$ such that $\varphi$ holds under the
assignment sending $x_0$ to $v$ and $x_{j+1}$ to $\rho(j)$ for each $j$, with $S$ unchanged.

articles.title: First-order formulas over graphs
articles.statement:
Variables and relation symbols are indexed by natural
numbers. Formulas are built from equations $x_a = x_b$ between variables and atomic formulas
applying a relation symbol $i$ to a finite list of variables, by negation, conjunction,
disjunction and existential quantification $\exists \varphi$, which binds variable $0$ of
$\varphi$ (de Bruijn indexing).

articles.title: Finite graphs as edge tables
articles.statement:
A finite graph is a pair $(n, t)$ of a natural number $n$,
the number of vertices, and a finite list $t$ of booleans, read as a row-major edge table. The
length of $t$ is not required to be $n^2$.

articles.title: Isomorphism-closed graph classes
articles.statement:
A class $K$ of graphs is isomorphism-closed if for every
$G_1 \in K$, every graph $G_2$ isomorphic to $G_1$ also belongs to $K$.

articles.title: Isomorphic graphs
articles.statement:
Graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ are isomorphic if they have the same number of
vertices and there is a bijection $\sigma$ from the vertices of $G_1$ to the vertices of $G_2$
such that for all vertices $a, b$ of $G_1$, there is an edge from $a$ to $b$ in $G_1$ if and only
if there is an edge from $\sigma(a)$ to $\sigma(b)$ in $G_2$.

articles.title: Fagin's theorem: NP is existential second-order logic
articles.statement:
Let $K$ be a class of finite
graphs, each given as a pair $(n, t)$ of a number $n$ of vertices and a row-major edge table $t$
(a list of booleans), and suppose that $K$ is closed under graph isomorphism. Then the decision
problem that accepts exactly the bitstrings decoding to a member $(n, t)$ of $K$ whose edge table
has length $n^2$ is in NP if and only if $K$ is definable in existential second-order logic:
there are a first-order formula $\varphi$, a number $k$ and a boolean $b$ such that a graph
$(n, t)$ whose edge table has length $n^2$ belongs to $K$ exactly when either $n > 0$ and some
$k$ relations on its vertices, together with its edge relation, make $\varphi$ true (with every
free variable of $\varphi$ denoting vertex $0$), or $n = 0$ and $b$ is true.

## Sources

- R. Fagin, "Generalized first-order spectra and polynomial-time recognizable sets", in Complexity of Computation, SIAM-AMS Proceedings 7 (1974), 43-73.

articles.title: Formulas whose fixed points are all positive
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a formula of first-order
logic with least fixed points, whose relation symbols are natural numbers. All fixed points of
$\varphi$ are positive when every least-fixed-point subformula of $\varphi$, nested ones included,
binds a relation symbol $R \ge 2$ (so neither the order symbol $0$ nor the edge symbol $1$) and
$R$ occurs only positively in the body of that subformula.

articles.title: Immerman-Vardi: FO + least fixed point is P on ordered structures
articles.statement:
Source: N.
Immerman, "Relational queries definable in polynomial time", Information and Control 68
(1986), 193-243 (STOC 1983); M. Y. Vardi, "The complexity of relational query languages",
Proceedings of the Fourteenth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 1982),
137-146.

articles.title: Negative occurrence of a relation symbol
articles.statement:
A relation symbol $R$ occurs only negatively
in a formula $\varphi$ of first-order logic with least fixed points when every atomic formula
$R(x_{a_1}, \dots, x_{a_k})$ in $\varphi$, including those inside least-fixed-point subformulas,
lies under an odd number of negations.

articles.title: Interpretation of relation symbols in an ordered graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an ordered graph with
vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$ and let $(E_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ be predicates on lists of vertices.
Relation symbol $0$ holds of a list exactly when it is a pair $(a, b)$ with $a < b$, relation
symbol $1$ holds of a list exactly when it is a pair $(a, b)$ with an edge from $a$ to $b$ in $G$,
and relation symbol $i + 2$ is interpreted as $E_i$.

articles.title: Edge relation of an ordered graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an ordered graph with vertices
$0, \dots, n - 1$ and edge table $t$, a list of booleans. There is an edge from $a$ to $b$ when
the entry of $t$ at position $a n + b$ is true; positions beyond the end of $t$ count as false.

articles.title: Encodings of a class of ordered graphs
articles.statement:
For a class $K$ of ordered graphs, this is the
decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical
bitstring encoding of pairs of a natural number and a list of booleans, to some $G \in K$ whose
edge table has length exactly $n^2$, where $n$ is the number of vertices of $G$.

articles.title: Evaluation of FO + LFP formulas in an ordered graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an ordered graph with
vertex set $V = \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, let $\rho$ assign a vertex to each variable
$0, 1, 2, \dots$, and let $S$ assign to each relation symbol $i$ a predicate $S_i$ on lists of
vertices. The truth of a formula is defined by recursion: $x_a = x_b$ holds when
$\rho(a) = \rho(b)$; the atom $R_i(x_{a_1}, \dots, x_{a_k})$ holds when $S_i$ holds of
$(\rho(a_1), \dots, \rho(a_k))$; negation, conjunction and disjunction are evaluated as usual;
$\exists \varphi$ holds when $\varphi$ holds for some $v \in V$ under the assignment sending
variable $0$ to $v$ and variable $j + 1$ to $\rho(j)$. The least-fixed-point formula with bound
symbol $R$, arity $k$, body $\varphi$ and argument variables $a_1, \dots, a_m$ holds when
$(\rho(a_1), \dots, \rho(a_m))$ lies in $X_{n^k}$, where $X_0$ is empty and a list $t$ lies in
$X_{s+1}$ when $\varphi$ holds with $R$ reinterpreted as $X_s$ (the other symbols keeping their
interpretation under $S$) and with variable $j$ assigned the $j$-th entry of $t$ (or $\rho(0)$
if $t$ has no such entry) for $j < k$ and $\rho(j - k)$ for $j \ge k$.

articles.title: Definability in FO + LFP
articles.statement:
A class $K$ of ordered graphs is definable in first-order logic
with least fixed points when there are a formula $\varphi$ and a boolean $b$ such that every
ordered graph $G$ with $n$ vertices whose edge table has length $n^2$ lies in $K$ exactly when
either $n > 0$ and $G$ satisfies $\varphi$, or $n = 0$ and $b$ is true.

articles.title: Satisfaction of an FO + LFP formula by an ordered graph
articles.statement:
An ordered graph $G$ with $n > 0$
vertices satisfies a formula $\varphi$ of first-order logic with least fixed points when $\varphi$
is well-formed in the environment where no relation symbol is bound, all fixed points of
$\varphi$ are positive, and $\varphi$ is true in $G$ with every variable assigned the vertex $0$,
relation symbol $0$ interpreted as the order $<$, relation symbol $1$ as the edge relation, and
every other relation symbol as the empty relation.

articles.title: Formulas of first-order logic with least fixed points
articles.statement:
Variables and relation symbols are
natural numbers. Formulas are built from equalities $x_a = x_b$ and atoms
$R_i(x_{a_1}, \dots, x_{a_k})$ by negation, conjunction, disjunction, existential quantification
and least-fixed-point formulas $\mathrm{lfp}(R, k, \varphi, (a_1, \dots, a_m))$, the least fixed
point of the operator defined by $\varphi$ (with $R$ as the recursive relation, of arity $k$)
applied to the tuple of variables $(a_1, \dots, a_m)$.

articles.title: Well-formed FO + LFP formulas
articles.statement:
Let $e$ assign to each relation symbol (a natural number)
either an arity or nothing. Whether a first-order formula with least fixed points over ordered
graphs is well-formed relative to $e$ is defined by recursion on the formula. An equality of two
variables is well-formed. An atomic formula $R(x_1, \dots, x_k)$ is well-formed when $k = a$ if
$e(R) = a$; when $k = 2$ if $e$ assigns nothing to $R$ and $R$ is $0$ (the order) or $1$ (the edge
relation); and always otherwise. A negation or an existential quantification is well-formed when
its body is, and a conjunction or a disjunction when both of its parts are. A least-fixed-point
formula that binds the symbol $R$ with arity $a$, has body $\varphi$ and is applied to the
variables $y_1, \dots, y_k$ is well-formed when $R \ge 2$, $k = a$, and $\varphi$ is well-formed
relative to the assignment that agrees with $e$ except that it gives $R$ the arity $a$.

articles.title: Finite ordered graphs
articles.statement:
A finite ordered graph is a pair $(n, t)$ of a natural number $n$
and a finite list $t$ of booleans of any length. Here $n$ is the size of the domain
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, ordered numerically, and $t$ is read as a row-major edge table.

articles.title: Positive occurrence of a relation symbol
articles.statement:
A relation symbol $R$ occurs only positively in
a first-order formula with least fixed points over ordered graphs when every atomic formula with
relation symbol $R$ in it, including those inside least-fixed-point subformulas whatever symbol
they bind, lies under an even number of negations.

articles.title: Immerman: FO + transitive closure is NL on ordered structures
articles.statement:
For every set $K$ of
finite ordered graphs, the decision problem of the encodings of $K$ (the bitstrings that decode
to a member $(n, T)$ of $K$ whose edge table $T$ has length exactly $n^2$) belongs to
$\mathrm{NL}$ if and only if $K$ is definable in first-order logic with transitive closure.

## Sources

- N. Immerman, "Languages that capture complexity classes", SIAM Journal on Computing 16 (1987), 760-778 (STOC 1983).

articles.title: Order and edge relations as FO + TC relation symbols
articles.statement:
In an ordered graph with domain
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, relation symbol $0$ holds of a list of elements exactly when the list is
$[a, b]$ with $a < b$, relation symbol $1$ holds exactly when the list is $[a, b]$ and there is
an edge from $a$ to $b$, and every other relation symbol holds of no list.

articles.title: Definability in FO + TC
articles.statement:
A set $K$ of ordered graphs is FO + TC-definable when there
are an FO + TC formula $\varphi$ and a boolean $b$ such that for every ordered graph $(n, T)$
whose edge table $T$ has length exactly $n^2$: if $n > 0$, then $(n, T) \in K$ exactly when
$(n, T)$ satisfies $\varphi$, and if $n = 0$, then $(n, T) \in K$ exactly when $b$ is true.

articles.title: Edge relation of an ordered graph for FO + TC
articles.statement:
For an ordered graph $(n, T)$ with edge
table $T$ and elements $a, b < n$, there is an edge from $a$ to $b$ when the entry of $T$ at
position $a n + b$ is true; positions beyond the end of $T$ count as false.

articles.title: Encodings of a class of ordered graphs
articles.statement:
For a set $K$ of ordered graphs, this is the
decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical
bitstring encoding of pairs of a natural number and a list of booleans, to some ordered graph
$(n, T) \in K$ whose edge table $T$ has length exactly $n^2$.

articles.title: Evaluation of FO + TC formulas
articles.statement:
Fix an ordered graph with domain
$D = \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, an assignment $\rho$ of an element of $D$ to each variable index and
an assignment $S$ of a relation on lists of elements of $D$ to each relation symbol. The truth
value of a formula is defined by recursion. The equation between variables $i$ and $j$ holds
when $\rho(i) = \rho(j)$. Relation symbol $i$ applied to variables $j_1, \dots, j_k$ holds when
$S_i$ holds of the list $[\rho(j_1), \dots, \rho(j_k)]$. Negation, conjunction and disjunction
are interpreted as usual. An existential formula $\exists \varphi$ holds when $\varphi$ holds
under the assignment sending $0$ to some $d \in D$ and $j + 1$ to $\rho(j)$. A transitive
closure $\mathrm{TC}(\varphi; \bar u, \bar v)$ is false when the index lists $\bar u$ and
$\bar v$ have different lengths. Otherwise, with $a$ their common length, it holds when the
tuple $(\rho(v_0), \dots, \rho(v_{a-1}))$ is reachable from $(\rho(u_0), \dots, \rho(u_{a-1}))$
in zero or more steps, where a step from $s \in D^a$ to $t \in D^a$ means that $\varphi$ holds
under the assignment sending $j < a$ to $s_j$, $a \le j < 2a$ to $t_{j - a}$, and $j \ge 2a$ to
$\rho(j - 2a)$.

articles.title: Example: simultaneous reachability of pairs in FO + TC
articles.statement:
The FO + TC formula
$\mathrm{TC}(\varphi; (0, 1), (2, 3))$ of arity $2$ whose body $\varphi$ states that relation
symbol $1$ (the edge relation) holds of variables $0, 2$ and of variables $1, 3$. In the body,
variables $0, 1$ are the source pair and $2, 3$ the target pair, so a step moves both components
along an edge at the same time, and the formula expresses that the pair of outer variables
$(2, 3)$ is reachable from the pair $(0, 1)$ by such steps.

articles.title: Example: parameterized transitive closure in FO + TC
articles.statement:
The FO + TC formula
$\mathrm{TC}(\varphi; (1), (2))$ of arity $1$ whose body $\varphi$ is
$E(0, 1) \lor (E(0, 2) \land E(2, 1))$, where $E$ is relation symbol $1$ (the edge relation).
In the body, variable $0$ is the source, variable $1$ the target, and variable $2$ is outer
variable $0$, shifted by $2$; the endpoint arguments $1$ and $2$ are outer variables, not
shifted. So the formula expresses that outer variable $2$ is reachable from outer variable $1$
by steps that are either an edge or a path of two edges through outer variable $0$.

articles.title: Satisfaction of an FO + TC formula in an ordered graph
articles.statement:
An ordered graph with nonempty
domain $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ satisfies an FO + TC formula $\varphi$ when $\varphi$ evaluates to
true with every variable assigned the element $0$, relation symbol $0$ interpreted as the order
$<$ and relation symbol $1$ as the edge relation (both only on two-element lists), and every
other relation symbol interpreted as the empty relation.

articles.title: Formulas of first-order logic with transitive closure
articles.statement:
FO + TC formulas, with variables
and relation symbols indexed by natural numbers, are built from equations between two variables
and relation symbols applied to lists of variables by negation, conjunction, disjunction,
existential quantification (which binds variable $0$, de Bruijn style) and transitive closure
$\mathrm{TC}(\varphi; \bar u, \bar v)$ of a formula $\varphi$ applied to two lists $\bar u$,
$\bar v$ of variables. With $a = |\bar u| = |\bar v|$, the body $\varphi$ defines a step
relation on $a$-tuples: its variables $0, \dots, a - 1$ are the source tuple, $a, \dots, 2a - 1$
the target tuple, and each variable $j \ge 2a$ is outer variable $j - 2a$.

articles.title: Ordered graphs for first-order logic with transitive closure
articles.statement:
An ordered graph is
encoded as a pair $(n, e)$ of a natural number $n$, the domain size, and a finite list $e$ of
booleans of arbitrary length, the edge table in row-major order. It is read as the graph on
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, ordered numerically, with an edge from $a$ to $b$ when the entry of $e$ at
position $an + b$ is true; a missing entry counts as false.

articles.title: Counter-machine decidable predicates
articles.statement:
A predicate $P$ on the natural numbers is
counter-machine decidable when some counter-machine program computes its characteristic
function: for every natural number $n$, the output of the program on the single input $n$ is
defined and equals $1$ if $P(n)$ holds and $0$ otherwise.

## Sources

- Minsky, *Computation: Finite and Infinite Machines*, 1967, §11.

articles.title: Output of a counter machine
articles.statement:
The output of a counter-machine program $p$ on a list of
inputs is the partial natural number obtained as follows: run $p$ from the initial state on those
inputs; if for some number $t$ of steps the program counter is at least the length of $p$ (the
machine has halted), the output is the content of register $0$ after the least such $t$; if no
such $t$ exists, the output is undefined.

## Sources

- Minsky, *Computation: Finite and Infinite Machines*, 1967, §11.

articles.title: Counter-machine execution is constant after halting
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a counter-machine
program, $s$ a state, and $t_1 \le t_2$ natural numbers. If the state reached from $s$ after
$t_1$ steps of $p$ has program counter at least the length of $p$, then the state reached from $s$
after $t_2$ steps equals the state reached after $t_1$ steps.

## Sources

- Minsky, *Computation: Finite and Infinite Machines*, 1967, §11.

articles.title: Counter-machine execution is stable once halted
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a counter-machine program,
$s$ a state and $t$ a natural number. If the state reached from $s$ after $t$ steps of $p$ has
program counter at least the length of $p$, then the state reached from $s$ after $t + 1$ steps
equals the state reached after $t$ steps.

## Sources

- Minsky, *Computation: Finite and Infinite Machines*, 1967, §11.

articles.title: Bounded execution of a counter machine
articles.statement:
For a counter-machine program $p$, a natural
number $t$ and a state $s$, the execution of $p$ for $t$ steps from $s$ is the state obtained from
$s$ by applying $t$ single steps of $p$.

## Sources

- Minsky, *Computation: Finite and Infinite Machines*, 1967, §11.

articles.title: Initial state of a counter machine
articles.statement:
The initial counter-machine state on a list of inputs
$x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ has program counter $0$, register $i$ holding $x_i$ for each $i < k$, and
every other register holding $0$.

## Sources

- Minsky, *Computation: Finite and Infinite Machines*, 1967, §11.

articles.title: Counter-machine instructions
articles.statement:
A counter-machine instruction is one of: increment register
$r$, decrement register $r$, or jump to instruction $q$ if register $r$ is zero, where the
register index $r$ and the jump target $q$ are natural numbers.

Decrementing a register that holds $0$ leaves it at $0$.

## Sources

- Minsky, *Computation: Finite and Infinite Machines*, 1967, §11.

articles.title: Counter-machine states
articles.statement:
A counter-machine state consists of a program counter, which is a
natural number, and the register contents, a function assigning a natural number to every
register index $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

## Sources

- Minsky, *Computation: Finite and Infinite Machines*, 1967, §11.

articles.title: A counter step is sticky at halting states
articles.statement:
Past the end of the
program the state does not change.

## Sources

- Minsky, *Computation: Finite and Infinite Machines*, 1967, §11.

articles.title: One step of a counter machine
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a counter-machine program, a list of
instructions indexed from $0$, and let $s$ be a state with program counter $c$. If $c$ is at
least the length of $p$ (the machine has halted), the step leaves $s$ unchanged. Otherwise it
executes instruction $c$ of $p$: increment register $r$ adds $1$ to register $r$ and sets the
program counter to $c + 1$; decrement register $r$ subtracts $1$ from register $r$ if it is
positive, leaves it at $0$ otherwise, and sets the program counter to $c + 1$; jump to $q$ if
register $r$ is zero leaves the registers unchanged and sets the program counter to $q$ if
register $r$ holds $0$ and to $c + 1$ otherwise.

Because halted states are fixed, the step can be iterated any number of times.

## Sources

- Minsky, *Computation: Finite and Infinite Machines*, 1967, §11.

articles.title: Output membership for counter machines
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a counter-machine program, let $x$ be
a list of natural-number inputs, and let $t$ and $y$ be natural numbers. If the state reached
after $t$ steps of $P$ from the initial state on $x$ has program counter at least the length
of $P$ (so the machine has halted) and register $0$ holds $y$ in that state, then the output
of $P$ on $x$ is defined and equals $y$.

## Sources

- Minsky, *Computation: Finite and Infinite Machines*, 1967, §11.

articles.title: Value of a little-endian bit list
articles.statement:
The value of a list of bits $b_0, b_1, \dots, b_{m-1}$
is $\sum_{i < m} [b_i]\, 2^i$, where $[b_i]$ is $1$ if $b_i$ is true and $0$ otherwise. So the
first bit is the least significant, and the empty list has value $0$.

articles.title: Bits as stack symbols
articles.statement:
Let
$\Gamma' = \{\mathtt{cons}_l, \mathtt{cons}, \mathtt{bit0}, \mathtt{bit1}\}$ be the stack alphabet
of Mathlib's multi-stack machine $\mathrm{tr}$ that evaluates partial recursive codes. This is
the map from bits to $\Gamma'$ that sends $\mathrm{true}$ to $\mathtt{bit1}$ and $\mathrm{false}$
to $\mathtt{bit0}$.

articles.title: Code of a stack symbol
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack machine, a stack index $k$ and a symbol
$x$ of stack $k$, the code of $x$ is the position of $x$ (counting from $0$) in the chosen
enumeration of the relevant symbols of stack $k$, or the length of that enumeration if $x$ is not
a relevant symbol.

articles.title: Coded configurations of a multi-stack machine
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack machine with label
set $\Lambda$, internal state set $\sigma$ and stack index set $K$, a coded configuration is a
triple consisting of an optional label in $\Lambda$ (no label marks a halted configuration), an
internal state in $\sigma$, and an assignment of a list of natural numbers to each $k \in K$.

articles.title: Turing computable equals recursive
articles.statement:
A function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is
computable (recursive) if and only if some bundled finite multi-stack Turing machine computes it
in binary. Here the binary word of $m \in \mathbb{N}$ is its list of binary digits, least
significant first, with $1$ read as true, $0$ as false and no leading zeros (so the word of $0$
is empty). That is, there are such a machine and identifications of its input and output stack
alphabets with the booleans such that, for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the machine started at its
main label in its initial internal state, with the binary word of $n$ on its input stack and
every other stack empty, reaches the halted configuration whose output stack holds the binary
word of $f(n)$, whose other stacks are empty and whose internal state is the initial one.

articles.title: Turing-computable functions are recursive
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and suppose
that some finite multi-stack Turing machine (finitely many stacks, labels and internal states,
and a finite input alphabet), together with identifications of its input and output stack
alphabets with the booleans, computes $f$ under the binary encoding of natural numbers (least
significant bit first, with $0$ encoded as the empty list): for every $n$, the machine started
at its main label in its initial internal state, with the encoding of $n$ on its input stack and
all other stacks empty, eventually reaches the halted configuration whose output stack holds the
encoding of $f(n)$, whose other stacks are empty and whose internal state is the initial one.
Then $f$ is computable (recursive).

articles.title: Decoding a stack symbol
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack machine, a stack index $k$ and a natural
number $c$, the decoding of $c$ is the entry at position $c$ (counting from $0$) of the chosen
enumeration of the relevant symbols of stack $k$, and is undefined when $c$ is at least the length
of that enumeration.

articles.title: A run halts iff it reaches a configuration without successor
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \sigma \to \mathrm{Option}\ \sigma$ be a step function and $a \in \sigma$, and write
$f^{(k)}(a) \in \mathrm{Option}\ \sigma$ for the result of $k$ steps from $a$: the $k$-th
iterate, applied to $\mathrm{some}\ a$, of the map sending $\mathrm{none}$ to $\mathrm{none}$
and $\mathrm{some}\ x$ to $f(x)$. The evaluation of $f$ from $a$ (the configuration where the run
from $a$ stops) is defined if and only if there are $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $b \in \sigma$ with
$f^{(k)}(a) = \mathrm{some}\ b$ and $f(b) = \mathrm{none}$.

articles.title: Coded stacks after replacing one stack
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack machine, a family $S$ of
stacks, a stack index $k$ and a list $l$ of symbols of stack $k$, the coded stacks of the family
obtained from $S$ by replacing stack $k$ with $l$ are the coded stacks of $S$ with the entry at
$k$ replaced by the list obtained from $l$ by replacing each symbol with its code.

articles.title: Coded stacks
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack machine, the coded stacks of a family $S$ of stacks
assign to each stack index $k$ the list obtained from the stack $S_k$ by replacing each symbol
with its code.

articles.title: Coding a configuration
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack machine, the coded configuration of a
configuration $c$ has the same optional label and internal state as $c$, and the coded stacks of
the stacks of $c$.

articles.title: Binary encoding, least significant bit first
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n \neq 0$, the
binary encoding of $n$ is the list whose first bit is true exactly when $n$ is odd, followed by
the binary encoding of $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$.

articles.title: Every r.e. predicate is the halting set of a machine with finite alphabets
articles.statement:
For every
recursively enumerable predicate $p$ on $\mathbb{N}$ there are a bundled finite multi-stack Turing
machine whose stack alphabets are all finite and an identification of its input alphabet with
the booleans such that, for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $p(n)$ holds if and only if the machine
halts on the binary digits of $n$ (least significant first, with $1$ read as true, $0$ as false
and no leading zeros, so that $0$ gives the empty word).

articles.title: Reachability gives an iteration count
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type, let $\bot \notin \alpha$,
and let $f : \alpha \to \alpha \cup \{\bot\}$ be a partial step function, where $f(x) = \bot$
means that no step is possible from $x$. Extend $f$ to
$\bar f : \alpha \cup \{\bot\} \to \alpha \cup \{\bot\}$ by $\bar f(\bot) = \bot$. If $b \in \alpha$
is reachable from $a \in \alpha$ under $f$, that is, $b$ is obtained from $a$ by finitely many
(possibly zero) steps $x \mapsto f(x)$ none of which gives $\bot$, then there is $N \in \mathbb{N}$
with $\bar f^{N}(a) = b$.

articles.title: A run that stops passes through a configuration without successor
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \sigma \to \mathrm{Option}\ \sigma$ be a step function and $a \in \sigma$, and write
$f^{(k)}(a) \in \mathrm{Option}\ \sigma$ for the result of $k$ steps from $a$: the $k$-th
iterate, applied to $\mathrm{some}\ a$, of the map sending $\mathrm{none}$ to $\mathrm{none}$
and $\mathrm{some}\ x$ to $f(x)$. If $f^{(k)}(a) = \mathrm{none}$ for some $k$, then there are
$j \in \mathbb{N}$ and $b \in \sigma$ with $f^{(j)}(a) = \mathrm{some}\ b$ and
$f(b) = \mathrm{none}$.

articles.title: Every r.e. predicate is the halting set of a multi-stack machine
articles.statement:
For every recursively
enumerable predicate $p$ on $\mathbb{N}$ there are a bundled finite multi-stack Turing machine
and an identification of its input alphabet with the booleans such that, for every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, $p(n)$ holds if and only if the machine halts on the binary digits of $n$
(least significant first, with $1$ read as true, $0$ as false and no leading zeros, so that $0$
gives the empty word).

articles.title: Labels of the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a partial recursive code and let $\mathrm{tr}$ be
Mathlib's multi-stack machine that evaluates such codes. The labels of the wrapped machine for $c$
form the disjoint union $\mathrm{Phase} \sqcup \mathrm{supp}(c)$, where
$\mathrm{Phase} = \{\mathrm{pre}_0, \mathrm{pre}_1, \mathrm{pre}_2, \mathrm{post}_1,
\mathrm{post}_2\}$ is the set of five adapter labels and $\mathrm{supp}(c)$ is Mathlib's support
of $\mathrm{tr}$ for $c$ with the halting continuation: a finite set of labels of $\mathrm{tr}$
that contains the start label for $c$ and is closed under the steps of $\mathrm{tr}$.

articles.title: Stack alphabets of the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{tr}$ be Mathlib's multi-stack machine
that evaluates partial recursive codes, with stacks
$K' = \{\mathrm{main}, \mathrm{rev}, \mathrm{aux}, \mathrm{stack}\}$ and alphabet
$\Gamma' = \{\mathtt{cons}_l, \mathtt{cons}, \mathtt{bit0}, \mathtt{bit1}\}$. The stacks of the
wrapped machine are indexed by $K' \sqcup \{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$: each stack in $K'$
has alphabet $\Gamma'$, and the two stacks $\mathrm{false}$ and $\mathrm{true}$ (the input and
output stacks of the wrapped machine) have the alphabet $\{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$ of
bits.

articles.title: Configurations of the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a partial recursive code, and let
$\Gamma' = \{\mathtt{cons}_l, \mathtt{cons}, \mathtt{bit0}, \mathtt{bit1}\}$ be the alphabet of
Mathlib's multi-stack machine $\mathrm{tr}$ that evaluates such codes. A configuration of the
wrapped machine for $c$ is a configuration of Mathlib's multi-stack (TM2) Turing machine model
with the stack alphabets and labels of the wrapped machine for $c$ and internal states the
optional symbols of $\Gamma'$: it consists of an optional current label (none once the machine
has halted), an internal state that is a symbol of $\Gamma'$ or none, and for each stack $k$ a
finite list of symbols of the alphabet of $k$.

articles.title: The stack set $K'$ is finite
articles.statement:
The set
$K' = \{\mathrm{main}, \mathrm{rev}, \mathrm{aux}, \mathrm{stack}\}$ of the four stacks of
Mathlib's multi-stack machine that evaluates partial recursive codes is a finite type whose
elements are exactly these four stacks.

articles.title: Iterated steps of the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a partial recursive code and let $s$ be
the map that sends none to none and a configuration $d$ of the wrapped machine for $c$ to the
result of one step of the wrapped machine on $d$ (which is none if $d$ has halted). For
$j \in \mathbb{N}$ and $x$ either a configuration of the wrapped machine for $c$ or none, the
$j$-fold run from $x$ is $s^{j}(x)$, the result of applying $s$ to $x$ $j$ times.

articles.title: One step of the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
For a partial recursive code $c$, the step function of the
wrapped machine for $c$ is Mathlib's multi-stack (TM2) step function for the program of the
wrapped machine for $c$. It sends a configuration without a current label (a halted one) to
none, and a configuration with current label $l$ to the configuration obtained by executing the
statement that the program assigns to $l$ on its internal state and stacks.

articles.title: Statements of the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a partial recursive code, and let
$\mathrm{tr}$ be Mathlib's multi-stack machine that evaluates such codes, with stacks
$K' = \{\mathrm{main}, \mathrm{rev}, \mathrm{aux}, \mathrm{stack}\}$ and alphabet
$\Gamma' = \{\mathtt{cons}_l, \mathtt{cons}, \mathtt{bit0}, \mathtt{bit1}\}$. A statement of the
wrapped machine for $c$ is a statement of Mathlib's multi-stack (TM2) Turing machine model whose
stacks are indexed by $K' \sqcup \{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$, where each stack in $K'$ has
alphabet $\Gamma'$ and the stacks $\mathrm{false}$ and $\mathrm{true}$ have the alphabet
$\{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$ of bits, whose labels are the labels of the wrapped machine
for $c$, and whose internal states are the optional symbols of $\Gamma'$ (a symbol of $\Gamma'$,
or none).

articles.title: The program of the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a partial recursive code and let
$\mathrm{tr}$ be Mathlib's multi-stack machine that evaluates such codes, with stacks
$\mathrm{main}, \mathrm{rev}, \mathrm{aux}, \mathrm{stack}$ and alphabet
$\Gamma' = \{\mathtt{cons}_l, \mathtt{cons}, \mathtt{bit0}, \mathtt{bit1}\}$. The program of the
wrapped machine for $c$ assigns a statement to each of its labels, namely the five adapter labels
$\mathrm{pre}_0, \mathrm{pre}_1, \mathrm{pre}_2, \mathrm{post}_1, \mathrm{post}_2$ and the labels
in Mathlib's finite support $\mathrm{supp}(c)$ of $\mathrm{tr}$ for $c$ with the halting
continuation. The internal state $v$ is a symbol of $\Gamma'$ or none, the input stack is the bit
stack $\mathrm{false}$ and the output stack is the bit stack $\mathrm{true}$.

At $\mathrm{pre}_0$: push $\mathtt{cons}$ onto $\mathrm{main}$ and go to $\mathrm{pre}_1$.

At $\mathrm{pre}_1$: pop the input stack and set $v$ to the popped bit as a symbol of $\Gamma'$
($\mathtt{bit1}$ for $\mathrm{true}$, $\mathtt{bit0}$ for $\mathrm{false}$), or to none if the
input stack is empty; if $v$ is a symbol, push it onto $\mathrm{rev}$ and go to $\mathrm{pre}_1$,
otherwise go to $\mathrm{pre}_2$.

At $\mathrm{pre}_2$: pop $\mathrm{rev}$ and set $v$ to the popped symbol (none if $\mathrm{rev}$
is empty); if $v$ is a symbol, push it onto $\mathrm{main}$ and go to $\mathrm{pre}_2$, otherwise
go to the start label of $\mathrm{tr}$ for $c$ with the halting continuation, which lies in
$\mathrm{supp}(c)$.

At a label $l \in \mathrm{supp}(c)$: execute the statement of $\mathrm{tr}$ at $l$, acting on the
stacks of $\mathrm{tr}$, where every jump of $\mathrm{tr}$ becomes a jump to the same label in
$\mathrm{supp}(c)$ and every halt becomes a jump to $\mathrm{post}_1$.

At $\mathrm{post}_1$: pop $\mathrm{main}$ and set $v$ to the popped symbol (none if
$\mathrm{main}$ is empty); if $v$ is none or $\mathtt{cons}$, go to $\mathrm{post}_2$, otherwise
push $v$ onto $\mathrm{rev}$ and go to $\mathrm{post}_1$.

At $\mathrm{post}_2$: pop $\mathrm{rev}$ and set $v$ to the popped symbol (none if $\mathrm{rev}$
is empty); if $v$ is a symbol, push onto the output stack the bit that is $\mathrm{true}$ if
$v = \mathtt{bit1}$ and $\mathrm{false}$ otherwise, and go to $\mathrm{post}_2$; otherwise halt.

articles.title: The wrapped machine of a code
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code for a partial recursive function on lists
of natural numbers, and let $\mathrm{tr}$ be Mathlib's multi-stack machine that evaluates such
codes, with stacks $K' = \{\mathrm{main}, \mathrm{rev}, \mathrm{aux}, \mathrm{stack}\}$ and
alphabet $\Gamma' = \{\mathtt{cons}_l, \mathtt{cons}, \mathtt{bit0}, \mathtt{bit1}\}$. The
wrapped machine of $c$ is the finite multi-stack machine whose stacks are indexed by
$K' \sqcup \{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$, with alphabet $\Gamma'$ on each stack in $K'$ and
the alphabet of bits on the stacks $\mathrm{false}$ and $\mathrm{true}$; its input stack is
$\mathrm{false}$ and its output stack is $\mathrm{true}$; its labels are the labels of the
wrapped machine for $c$, with main label the first pre-phase adapter label $\mathrm{pre}_0$;
its internal states are the optional symbols of $\Gamma'$ (a symbol of $\Gamma'$, or none), with
initial state none; and its program is the program of the wrapped machine for $c$.

articles.title: A run stays stopped after a configuration without successor
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \sigma \to \mathrm{Option}\ \sigma$ be a step function and $a, b \in \sigma$, and write
$f^{(k)}(a) \in \mathrm{Option}\ \sigma$ for the result of $k$ steps from $a$: the $k$-th
iterate, applied to $\mathrm{some}\ a$, of the map sending $\mathrm{none}$ to $\mathrm{none}$
and $\mathrm{some}\ x$ to $f(x)$. If $f^{(k)}(a) = \mathrm{some}\ b$ and $f(b) = \mathrm{none}$,
then $f^{(m)}(a) = \mathrm{none}$ for every $m > k$.

articles.title: Correspondence of labels between the code evaluator and the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a
code for a partial recursive function on lists of natural numbers and let $\mathrm{tr}$ be
Mathlib's multi-stack machine that evaluates such codes. An optional label $o$ of $\mathrm{tr}$
(a label, or none for halting) corresponds to an optional label $o'$ of the wrapped machine for
$c$ when either $o$ is none and $o'$ is the first post-phase label $\mathrm{post}_1$, or $o$ is a
label $l$ of $\mathrm{tr}$ that lies in the support $\mathrm{supp}(c)$ of $c$ and $o'$ is $l$,
read as a label of the wrapped machine.

articles.title: Lifting stacks of tr
articles.statement:
Given contents $s$ of the four stacks main, rev, aux and stack of
Mathlib's code-evaluating machine $\mathrm{tr}$, the stack contents of the wrapped machine that
agree with $s$ on these four stacks and have empty input and output stacks.

articles.title: Main phase of the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code and $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
such that $c$ evaluates to $[f(n)]$ on input $[n]$ for every $n$. Then for every $n$ there is
$N$ such that the wrapped machine, started at the label $\mathrm{trNormal}(c, \mathrm{halt})$ with
empty local state, the encoding $\mathrm{trList}([n])$ on the main stack and all other stacks
empty, is after exactly $N$ steps at the adapter label post1 with empty local state,
$\mathrm{trList}([f(n)])$ on the main stack and all other stacks empty.

articles.title: Stack contents of the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
Given lists $a, b, c, d$ of symbols of $\Gamma'$
and lists $i, o$ of bits, the stack contents of the wrapped machine with $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ on
the stacks main, rev, aux and stack, $i$ on the input stack and $o$ on the output stack.

articles.title: The coded run simulates the machine's run
articles.statement:
Let $o$ be either no configuration or a
configuration of a finite multi-stack machine all of whose stack symbols are relevant. Let
running one step send a running configuration to its successor, and a halted configuration or no
configuration to no configuration. Then for every $j$, applying the coded step on optional
configurations $j$ times to the coding of $o$ gives the coding of the result of running $j$
steps from $o$, and if running $j$ steps from $o$ gives a configuration, all of its stack symbols
are relevant.

articles.title: The coded step on optional configurations
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack machine, the coded
step extended to optional coded configurations: it sends the absent configuration to the absent
configuration, and a coded configuration $c$ to the coded step of $c$, which is itself absent
when $c$ has halted.

articles.title: Running a primitive recursive machine is partial recursive
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$, $\sigma$ and
$\beta$ be primitive recursively encodable types, and let $\mathrm{init} : \alpha \to \sigma$,
$\mathrm{step} : \sigma \to \sigma$, $\mathrm{halted} : \sigma \to \mathrm{Bool}$ and
$\mathrm{out} : \sigma \to \beta$ be primitive recursive. Then the partial function sending $a$
to $\mathrm{out}(\mathrm{step}^k(\mathrm{init}(a)))$, where $k$ is the least natural number for
which $\mathrm{halted}(\mathrm{step}^k(\mathrm{init}(a)))$ is true, and undefined when there is
no such $k$, is partial recursive.

articles.title: Adapter labels
articles.statement:
The type with exactly the five elements pre0, pre1, pre2, post1 and post2,
with decidable equality.

They label the wrapped machine's pre-phase, which copies the input bits onto the main stack of
Mathlib's code-evaluating machine $\mathrm{tr}$, and its post-phase, which copies the result back
to the output stack.

articles.title: The first post-phase loop of the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
Write $\Gamma'$ for the stack alphabet of
Mathlib's code evaluator. Let $c$ be a code, $b$ a list of bits of length $k$, $r$ a list of
symbols of $\Gamma'$, $o$ a list of bits and $v$ an internal state (a symbol of $\Gamma'$ or
none), and write $\beta(b)$ for $b$ with each bit $\mathrm{true}$ replaced by the symbol bit1 and
each bit $\mathrm{false}$ by the symbol bit0 of $\Gamma'$. Started at the adapter label post1
with internal state $v$, $\beta(b)$ followed by the symbol cons on the main stack, $r$ on the rev
stack, $o$ on the output stack and all other stacks empty, the wrapped machine of $c$ is after
exactly $k + 1$ steps at the adapter label post2 with internal state cons, the reversal of
$\beta(b)$ followed by $r$ on the rev stack, $o$ on the output stack and all other stacks
empty.

articles.title: Post-phase of the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code and $b$ a list of bits of length
$k$, and write $\beta(b)$ for $b$ with each bit $0$ replaced by the symbol bit0 and each bit $1$ by
the symbol bit1 of $\Gamma'$. Started at the adapter label post1 with empty local state, $\beta(b)$
followed by the symbol cons on the main stack and all other stacks empty, the wrapped machine is
after exactly $2(k + 1)$ steps in the halting configuration (no label) with empty local state,
$b$ on the output stack and all other stacks empty.

articles.title: The first pre-phase loop of the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
Write $\Gamma'$ for the stack alphabet of
Mathlib's code evaluator. Let $c$ be a code, $a$, $r$, $x$ and $y$ lists of symbols of $\Gamma'$,
$b$ a list of bits of length $k$ and $v$ an internal state (a symbol of $\Gamma'$ or none), and
write $\beta(b)$ for $b$ with each bit $\mathrm{true}$ replaced by the symbol bit1 and each bit
$\mathrm{false}$ by the symbol bit0 of $\Gamma'$. Started at the adapter label pre1 with internal
state $v$, the lists $a$, $r$, $x$ and $y$ on the stacks main, rev, aux and stack, $b$ on the
input stack and the output stack empty, the wrapped machine of $c$ is after exactly $k + 1$ steps
at the adapter label pre2 with internal state none, the reversal of $\beta(b)$ followed by $r$ on
the rev stack, $a$, $x$ and $y$ still on the stacks main, aux and stack, and the input and output
stacks empty.

articles.title: Pre-phase of the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code and $b$ a list of bits of length $k$,
and write $\beta(b)$ for $b$ with each bit $0$ replaced by the symbol bit0 and each bit $1$ by the
symbol bit1 of $\Gamma'$. Started at the adapter label pre0 with empty local state, $b$ on the
input stack and all other stacks empty, the wrapped machine is after exactly $2(k + 1) + 1$ steps
at the label $\mathrm{trNormal}(c, \mathrm{halt})$ at which Mathlib's code-evaluating machine
$\mathrm{tr}$ starts evaluating $c$, with empty local state, $\beta(b)$ followed by the symbol
cons on the main stack and all other stacks empty.

articles.title: Encoding of internal states
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack machine, the primitive recursive
encoding of its finite type of internal states transported from that of $\mathrm{Fin}\, n$, where
$n$ is the number of internal states, along a chosen bijection between the two.

articles.title: Encoding of functions on a finite type
articles.statement:
For a finite type $K$ and a primitive recursively
encodable type $\beta$, the primitive recursive encoding of the functions $K \to \beta$
transported from that of the functions $\mathrm{Fin}\, n \to \beta$, where $n$ is the cardinality
of $K$, along a chosen bijection between $K$ and $\mathrm{Fin}\, n$.

articles.title: Encoding of labels
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack machine, the primitive recursive encoding of
its finite type of labels transported from that of $\mathrm{Fin}\, n$, where $n$ is the number of
labels, along a chosen bijection between the two.

articles.title: Eventually constant functions of a finite parameter are primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$
be a finite primitive recursively encodable type and $\beta$ a primitive recursively encodable
type. If $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{N} \to \beta$ and $N \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfy
$g(a, c) = g(a, N)$ for all $a \in \alpha$ and all $c \ge N$, then $g$ is primitive recursive as
a function of two arguments.

articles.title: Eventually constant functions on ℕ are primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Let $\beta$ be a primitive
recursively encodable type. If $g : \mathbb{N} \to \beta$ and $N \in \mathbb{N}$ satisfy
$g(c) = g(N)$ for all $c \ge N$, then $g$ is primitive recursive.

articles.title: Joint primitive recursion over a finite first argument
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$, $\beta$ and
$\sigma$ be primitive recursively encodable types with $\alpha$ finite, and let
$g : \alpha \to \beta \to \sigma$. If $b \mapsto g(a, b)$ is primitive recursive for every
$a \in \alpha$, then $g$ is primitive recursive as a function of two arguments.

articles.title: Updating the state from the top of a coded stack is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a
stack index of a finite multi-stack machine, write $\Gamma_k$ for the alphabet of stack $k$, and
let $f$ be any function sending an internal state and an optional symbol of $\Gamma_k$ to an
internal state. Then the map sending an internal state $v$ and coded stacks $S$ (a list $S_j$ of
natural numbers for each stack index $j$) to $f(v, t)$, where $t$ is the top of stack $k$ as read
from $S$, is primitive recursive as a function of two arguments, for the encoding of internal
states and the encoding of functions on the finite type of stack indices.

articles.title: Symbols a statement may push
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack machine, a stack $k$ and a
statement $q$ over the machine's stack alphabets, labels and internal states, the set of symbols
of stack $k$ consisting of every value, at every internal state, of the symbol function of every
push instruction onto stack $k$ that occurs in $q$, in either branch of each conditional.

articles.title: R.e. predicates are the halting sets of multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
A predicate $p$ on
$\mathbb{N}$ is recursively enumerable if and only if there are a bundled finite multi-stack
Turing machine and an identification of its input alphabet with the booleans such that, for
every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $p(n)$ holds if and only if the machine halts on the binary digits of
$n$ (least significant first, with $1$ read as true, $0$ as false and no leading zeros, so that
$0$ gives the empty word).

articles.title: The halting set of a multi-stack machine is r.e
articles.statement:
For every bundled finite multi-stack
Turing machine and every identification of its input alphabet with the booleans, the predicate
on $\mathbb{N}$ that holds at $n$ exactly when the machine halts on the binary digits of $n$
(least significant first, with $1$ read as true, $0$ as false and no leading zeros, so that $0$
gives the empty word) is recursively enumerable.

articles.title: Reading the top of a coded stack
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a stack index of the machine and let $S$ assign
to each stack index $j$ a list $S_j$ of natural numbers (codes of symbols). The top of stack $k$ as
read from $S$ is no symbol when $S_k$ is empty. Otherwise, if $c$ is the first entry of $S_k$, it is
the decoding of $c$: the symbol of $\Gamma_k$ at position $c$, counting from $0$, in the list of
relevant symbols of stack $k$, or no symbol when $c$ is at least the length of that list.

articles.title: Stacks with only relevant symbols
articles.statement:
A family of stacks $S$, consisting of a list $S_k$ of
symbols of $\Gamma_k$ for each stack index $k$, has only relevant symbols when for every stack
index $k$, every symbol on $S_k$ is a relevant symbol of stack $k$.

articles.title: The initial stacks have only relevant symbols
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack machine and every
list $s$ of symbols of the input alphabet $\Gamma_{k_0}$, the stacks of the initial configuration
with input $s$ (the list $s$ on the input stack $k_0$ and every other stack empty) have only
relevant symbols.

articles.title: Relevant symbols of a stack
articles.statement:
For a stack index $k$, the relevant symbols of stack $k$ are
the symbols $f(v)$ of $\Gamma_k$, for every internal state $v$, over all statements that push $f$
onto stack $k$ and occur in the program of some label, together with, when $k$ is the input stack
$k_0$, every symbol of $\Gamma_{k_0}$.

Along a run started from an initial configuration, only relevant symbols occur on the stacks.

articles.title: Restricting a statement of the code evaluator to the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
Let $\mathrm{tr}$ be
Mathlib's four-stack machine that evaluates partial recursive codes, and let $S$ be the support
of a code $c$. A statement $q$ of $\mathrm{tr}$ all of whose jump targets lie in $S$ becomes a
statement of the wrapped machine of $c$ with the same structure: each push, peek and pop acts on
the same stack of $\mathrm{tr}$ inside the wrapped machine with the same function, loads and
branches are kept, each jump goes to the same label of $\mathrm{tr}$, now read as an element of
$S$, and halting becomes a jump to the first post-phase label.

articles.title: Configurations before a reached one are running
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{step}$ for the machine's
step map, which is undefined on halted configurations (those with no label), and iterate it as a
partial map. Let $c_0$ and $c$ be configurations and $s$ a natural number such that $s$ steps from
$c_0$ reach $c$. Then for every $j < s$, $j$ steps from $c_0$ reach some configuration $c'$, and
$c'$ is running: its label is defined.

articles.title: The start label lies in the support
articles.statement:
For every code $c$, the label at which Mathlib's code
evaluator $\mathrm{tr}$ begins evaluating $c$ with the halting continuation belongs to the
support of $c$.

articles.title: The coded execution of a statement
articles.statement:
This mirrors the machine's execution of one statement
on stacks of symbol codes. Given a statement $q$, an internal state $v$ and coded stacks $S$ (a list
$S_k$ of natural numbers for each stack index $k$), it returns a coded configuration (an optional
label, an internal state and coded stacks), by recursion on $q$. A push of $f$ onto stack $k$
followed by $q'$ replaces $S_k$ by the code of the symbol $f(v)$ of stack $k$ followed by $S_k$, and
continues with $q'$. A peek at stack $k$ with update $f$ followed by $q'$ continues with $q'$ from
the internal state $f(v, t)$, where $t$ is the top of coded stack $k$ as read from $S$. A pop is
the same as a peek but also removes the first entry of $S_k$ (if there is one). A load of $a$
followed by $q'$ continues with $q'$ from the internal state $a(v)$. A branch on $f$ executes its
first statement if $f(v)$ is true and its second otherwise. A goto $f$ stops with label $f(v)$,
internal state $v$ and stacks $S$, and a halt stops with no label, internal state $v$ and stacks
$S$.

articles.title: The coded step
articles.statement:
For a coded configuration $(l, v, S)$, consisting of an optional label $l$,
an internal state $v$ and coded stacks $S$, the coded step is undefined when $l$ is absent (the
configuration has halted). When $l$ is a label, it is the coded configuration obtained by the coded
execution of the program statement of $l$ from the internal state $v$ on the coded stacks $S$.

articles.title: Support of a code
articles.statement:
For a code $c$, the support of $c$ is the finite set of labels of
Mathlib's code evaluator $\mathrm{tr}$ that Mathlib associates with evaluating $c$ under the
halting continuation.

It contains the label at which this evaluation starts and is closed under the steps of
$\mathrm{tr}$, so it contains every label reachable from there.

articles.title: Enumeration of the relevant symbols of a stack
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack machine and a
stack index $k$, a list without repetitions whose entries are exactly the relevant symbols of
stack $k$, in an order fixed by choice.

articles.title: The wrapped machine computes the function a code evaluates
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code and
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ a function such that, for every $n$, evaluating $c$ on the
one-element list $[n]$ returns $[f(n)]$. Then the wrapped machine of $c$, with input and output
alphabet the booleans, computes $f$ under the binary encoding of natural numbers (least
significant bit first): for every $n$, started with the encoding of $n$ on its input stack and
all other stacks empty, it eventually halts in its initial internal state with the encoding of
$f(n)$ on its output stack and all other stacks empty.

articles.title: Recursive functions are Turing-computable
articles.statement:
Every computable function
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is computed by a finite multi-stack Turing machine (finitely
many stacks, labels and internal states) whose input and output alphabets are identified with
the booleans, under the binary encoding of natural numbers (least significant bit first, with
$0$ encoded as the empty list): for every $n$, the machine started with the encoding of $n$ on
its input stack and all other stacks empty eventually halts in its initial internal state with
the encoding of $f(n)$ on its output stack and all other stacks empty.

articles.title: The wrapped machine of a code halts exactly where the code is defined
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code
for a partial recursive function on lists of natural numbers and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and suppose
that every value of $c$ on the one-element list $[n]$ is itself a one-element list. Then the
wrapped multi-stack machine of $c$ halts on the binary digits of $n$ (least significant first,
with $1$ read as true, $0$ as false and no leading zeros, so that $0$ gives the empty word) if
and only if the evaluation of $c$ at $[n]$ is defined.

articles.title: Halting of a multi-stack machine on an input
articles.statement:
A bundled finite multi-stack Turing
machine halts on a word $l$ over its input alphabet when its evaluation from the initial
configuration on $l$ (the main label, the initial internal state, $l$ on the input stack and
every other stack empty) is defined, that is, its run from that configuration reaches a
configuration without successor.

articles.title: Reading a stack symbol as a bit
articles.statement:
The map from the stack alphabet $\Gamma'$ of Mathlib's code
evaluator (symbols $\mathrm{cons}_l$, $\mathrm{cons}$, $\mathrm{bit0}$, $\mathrm{bit1}$) to the
booleans sends $\mathrm{bit1}$ to true and every other symbol to false.

articles.title: The evaluator's encoding of a one-element list
articles.statement:
For every natural number $m$, the list of
stack symbols by which Mathlib's code evaluator encodes the one-element list $[m]$ is the binary
encoding of $m$ (least significant bit first) with each bit written as $\mathrm{bit1}$ if it is
true and as $\mathrm{bit0}$ if it is false, followed by the symbol $\mathrm{cons}$.

articles.title: The evaluator encodes numbers in binary
articles.statement:
For every natural number $n$, the list of stack
