symbols by which Mathlib's code evaluator encodes $n$ is obtained from the binary encoding of $n$
(least significant bit first) by writing each bit as $\mathrm{bit1}$ if it is true and as
$\mathrm{bit0}$ if it is false.

articles.title: Simulation relation between the code evaluator and the wrapped machine
articles.statement:
A configuration $x$
of Mathlib's code evaluator $\mathrm{tr}$ is related to a configuration $d$ of the wrapped machine
of a code $c$ when $d$ has the same internal state as $x$, the stacks of $d$ are the four stacks
of $x$ together with empty input and output stacks, and the labels correspond: if $x$ has halted
then $d$ is at the first post-phase label, and if $x$ is at a label $l$ then $l$ lies in the
support of $c$ and $d$ is at $l$.

articles.title: Recursive functions are the Turing-computable functions
articles.statement:
A function
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ is computable, that is, total recursive, if and only if some finite
multi-stack Turing machine computes it on binary representations: there are a machine with
finitely many stacks, internal states and program labels and bijections from its input and output
stack alphabets to $\{0, 1\}$ such that, for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the machine started in its
initial state with the binary representation of $n$ (least significant bit first, with $0$
written as the empty word) on its input stack and all other stacks empty halts with the binary
representation of $f(n)$ on its output stack, all other stacks empty and its internal state back
at the initial state.

## Sources

- A. M. Turing, *On Computable Numbers* (1936); S. C. Kleene, *General recursive functions of natural numbers* (1936). Knill, *Some fundamental theorems in mathematics*, §23. Problem `turing_recursive_equiv` of the lean-eval benchmark.

articles.title: A predicate decided by a multi-tape machine is computable
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable
type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive
recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-tape machine, then $p$ is
computable, that is, $p$ is decidable and its Boolean characteristic function
$\alpha \to \mathrm{Bool}$ is computable.

This is Post's theorem applied to $p$ and its complement, both recursively enumerable.

articles.title: Co-recognizability by multi-tape machines
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an
encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A
predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is co-recognizable by a multi-tape machine when its complement
$\neg p$ is recognizable by a multi-tape machine.

articles.title: Multi-tape machines decide no more than multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). Every predicate on $\alpha$ that is decidable by a multi-tape machine is
decidable by a multi-stack machine.

articles.title: Decidability by multi-tape machines
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an
encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A
predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-tape machine when there are a number $k$ and a
deterministic Turing machine $M$ with finitely many states, a read-only input tape, $k$ work tapes
and a write-only output tape, all over the Boolean alphabet, such that for every $a \in \alpha$
there is a Boolean $b$ for which $M$ computes the one-letter word $b$ on the binary word of
$\mathrm{encode}(a)$ (least significant bit first), and $b$ is true exactly when $p(a)$ holds.
Here $M$ computes a word $v$ on an input word $w$ when its run started on $w$ halts with $v$ on
its output tape.

articles.title: Multi-tape machines recognize no more than multi-stack machines
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). Every predicate on $\alpha$ that is recognizable by a multi-tape machine is
recognizable by a multi-stack machine.

articles.title: Recognizability by multi-tape machines
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an
encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive recursive). A
predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a multi-tape machine when there are a number $k$ and
a deterministic Turing machine $M$ with finitely many states, a read-only input tape, $k$ work
tapes and a write-only output tape, all over the Boolean alphabet, such that for every
$a \in \alpha$, the run of $M$ started on the binary word of $\mathrm{encode}(a)$ (least
significant bit first) halts if and only if $p(a)$ holds.

articles.title: A predicate decided by a multi-tape machine is recursively enumerable
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-tape machine, then
$p$ is recursively enumerable, that is, the partial function on $\alpha$ that is defined, with a
trivial value, exactly where $p$ holds is partial recursive.

articles.title: A predicate decided by a multi-tape machine has a recursively enumerable complement
articles.statement:
Let
$\alpha$ be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose
decoding is primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-tape
machine, then its complement $\neg p$ is recursively enumerable, that is, the partial function on
$\alpha$ that is defined, with a trivial value, exactly where $\neg p$ holds is partial
recursive.

articles.title: A predicate recognizable by a multi-tape machine is recursively enumerable
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$
be a primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding
is primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a multi-tape machine,
then $p$ is recursively enumerable, that is, the partial function on $\alpha$ that is defined,
with a trivial value, exactly where $p$ holds is partial recursive.

articles.title: Acceptance is closed under extension on the right
articles.statement:
If a single-tape nondeterministic
Turing machine $m$ accepts a word $x$ over its tape alphabet, then $m$ accepts $xy$ for every word
$y$ over that alphabet.

This is a defect of CSLib's definition of these machines: a transition can only test the cell
under the head for a symbol, never for a blank, so every cell that an accepting run on $x$ reads
holds a letter of $x$ or one the run wrote, and the same run accepts $xy$.

## Sources

- defect of the pinned CSLib definition, fixed upstream by leanprover/cslib#1039.

articles.title: Acceptance as a label list
articles.statement:
A single-tape nondeterministic Turing machine $m$ accepts a
word $x$ if and only if there is a list $\mu$ of transition labels (read a symbol, write a symbol,
move, skip) such that applying the labels of $\mu$ in order to the input tape of $x$ (the tape
holding $x$ from the head cell rightward, every other cell blank) never fails, that is, every read
label finds its symbol in the cell under the head, and $\mu$ leads the automaton of $m$ from some
start state to some accepting state.

articles.title: An NTM that accepts the empty word accepts every word
articles.statement:
If a single-tape nondeterministic
Turing machine $m$ accepts the empty word, then $m$ accepts every word over its tape alphabet.

This is a special case of acceptance being closed under extension on the right, a defect of
CSLib's definition of these machines.

articles.title: A decidable predicate that no single-tape NTM recognizes
articles.statement:
There is a predicate $p$ on the
natural numbers that is decidable by a single-tape deterministic Turing machine but is not
recognizable by any single-tape nondeterministic Turing machine.

The predicate $n = 0$ is such a predicate.

## Sources

- Sipser, Corollary 3.18, whose half "every Turing-recognizable language is recognized by a nondeterministic machine" fails on the pinned CSLib definition; fixed upstream by leanprover/cslib#1039.

articles.title: No NTM accepts exactly the binary code of $0$
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a single-tape nondeterministic
Turing machine with tape alphabet $\Sigma$, and let $\iota$ be any map from the bits to $\Sigma$.
For a natural number $n$, write $w_n$ for the word over $\Sigma$ obtained by applying $\iota$
letter by letter to the little-endian binary code of $n$, in which $0$ is coded by the empty word.
Then it is not the case that, for every natural number $n$, $m$ accepts $w_n$ if and only if
$n = 0$.

The word $w_0$ is empty, and a machine that accepts the empty word accepts every word, in
particular $w_1$.

articles.title: No single-tape NTM recognizes $n = 0$
articles.statement:
The predicate $n = 0$ on the natural numbers is not
recognizable by any single-tape nondeterministic Turing machine.

The binary code of $0$ is the empty word, and a single-tape nondeterministic machine that accepts
the empty word accepts every word.

## Sources

- defect of the pinned CSLib definition, fixed upstream by leanprover/cslib#1039.

articles.title: Acceptance by an NTM with finite state and tape alphabets is r.e
articles.statement:
**Acceptance by an NTM with finite state and tape alphabets is r.e.** in the input word
(Sipser, Theorem 3.16, through recursion theory): search for a label list that applies to the
input tape, checked on coded tapes, and along which the image of the start states, a finite set,
meets the accepting states.

articles.title: Predicates recognizable by a single-tape nondeterministic machine
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type
with a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$. A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable
by a single-tape nondeterministic machine when there are a finite set of states, a finite tape
alphabet $\Sigma$ with decidable equality, an injective map $\iota$ from the bits $\{0, 1\}$ to
$\Sigma$ and a single-tape nondeterministic Turing machine $M$ with these states over $\Sigma$
such that for every $a \in \alpha$, $M$ accepts the input word obtained by writing the binary
encoding of the code of $a$ in $\mathbb{N}$ letter by letter through $\iota$ if and only if
$p(a)$ holds. Here $M$ accepts a word when some run of $M$ from one of its start states on the
tape holding the word, with the head on its first symbol, reaches an accepting state.

In this model a machine cannot test whether a cell is blank, so a machine that accepts a word
accepts every extension of the word on the right. Every such predicate is recognizable by a
single-tape deterministic machine, but not conversely: the predicate $n = 0$ on $\mathbb{N}$ is
decidable by a single-tape deterministic machine and is not recognizable by a single-tape
nondeterministic machine.

## Sources

- the pinned CSLib definition of nondeterministic machines; the upstream PR leanprover/cslib#1039 lets machines read and write blank cells.

articles.title: Deterministic machines recognize NTM acceptance along a computable map
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a
single-tape nondeterministic Turing machine with a finite set of states and a finite tape alphabet
$\Sigma$ that has decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding. Let $\alpha$ be a
primitively encodable type and $f$ a computable map from $\alpha$ to words over $\Sigma$. Then the
predicate on $\alpha$ that holds at $a$ exactly when $m$ accepts $f(a)$ is recognizable by a
single-tape deterministic Turing machine.

## Sources

- Sipser, Theorem 3.16.

articles.title: Deterministic machines recognize NTM acceptance
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a single-tape nondeterministic
Turing machine with a finite set of states and a finite tape alphabet $\Sigma$ that has decidable
equality and a primitive recursive encoding. Then the predicate on words over $\Sigma$ that holds
at a word exactly when $m$ accepts it is recognizable by a single-tape deterministic Turing
machine.

## Sources

- Sipser, Theorem 3.16.

articles.title: A predicate recognized by a single-tape NTM is recognized by a deterministic single-tape machine
articles.statement:
**A predicate recognized by a single-tape NTM is recognized by a deterministic single-tape
machine** (Sipser, Theorem 3.16, through recursion theory).

articles.title: Output membership for RAM machines
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a program of length $\ell$, let
$x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ be inputs and let $t$ and $y$ be natural numbers. If, after $t$ steps of
$P$ from the initial state on these inputs, the program counter is at least $\ell$ and the
accumulator equals $y$, then the output of $P$ on these inputs is defined and equals $y$.

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: Register written by a RAM store
articles.statement:
In a RAM state with register contents $r$, a store
destination resolves to a register index: the direct destination $n$ resolves to $n$, and the
indirect destination $n$ resolves to the contents $r(n)$ of register $n$.

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: Output of a RAM machine
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a program of length $\ell$ and $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$
inputs. Run $P$ from the initial state on these inputs. If for some $t$ the program counter
after $t$ steps is at least $\ell$, the output of $P$ on these inputs is the accumulator after
the least such number of steps; otherwise the output is undefined.

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: RAM execution stays at its halted state
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a program of length $\ell$, $s$ a
state and $t_1 \le t_2$ natural numbers. If the program counter after $t_1$ steps of $P$ from
$s$ is at least $\ell$, then the state after $t_2$ steps of $P$ from $s$ equals the state after
$t_1$ steps.

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: RAM execution is stable once halted
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a program of length $\ell$, $s$ a state
and $t$ a natural number. If the program counter after $t$ steps of $P$ from $s$ is at least
$\ell$, then the state after $t + 1$ steps of $P$ from $s$ equals the state after $t$ steps.

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: Bounded execution of a RAM machine
articles.statement:
For a program $P$, a natural number $t$ and a state
$s$, the state after $t$ steps of $P$ from $s$ is obtained by applying one step of $P$ to $s$
exactly $t$ times.

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: Initial RAM state
articles.statement:
The initial state on inputs $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ has program counter
$0$ and accumulator $0$; register $i$ holds $x_i$ for $i < k$, and every other register holds
$0$.

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: Value of a RAM operand
articles.statement:
In a RAM state with register contents $r$, an operand resolves to
a natural number: the immediate operand $n$ resolves to $n$ itself, the direct operand $n$ to
the contents $r(n)$ of register $n$, and the indirect operand $n$ to $r(r(n))$.

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: A RAM step is sticky at halting states
articles.statement:
If the program counter of a state $s$ is at
least the length of a program $P$, then one step of $P$ leaves $s$ unchanged.

A halt instruction sets the program counter to the length of the program, so once a halt has
been executed the state no longer changes.

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: One step of a RAM machine
articles.statement:
Let $P = (P_0, \dots, P_{\ell-1})$ be a program of length
$\ell$ and $s$ a state with program counter $p$, accumulator $a$ and register contents $r$. If
$p \ge \ell$, the step leaves $s$ unchanged. Otherwise it executes $P_p$, where $v$ denotes
the value of the instruction's operand in $s$: a load sets the accumulator to $v$, an add sets
it to $a + v$, a subtract sets it to $\max(a - v, 0)$, and a store writes $a$ into the
register that its destination resolves to in $s$; each of these also increases the program
counter by $1$. A jump to $q$ sets the program counter to $q$; a jump-if-zero to $q$ sets it
to $q$ if $a = 0$ and to $p + 1$ otherwise; a halt sets it to $\ell$. Nothing else changes.

In particular, once the program counter is at least $\ell$ (for instance after a halt), every
further step leaves the state unchanged.

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: RAM addressing mode
articles.statement:
An addressing mode of a random-access machine specifies an operand
by a natural number $n$ in one of three ways: immediate (the operand is the value $n$ itself),
direct (the operand is the contents of register $n$), or indirect (the operand is the contents
of the register whose index is the contents of register $n$).

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: RAM-decidable predicate
articles.statement:
A predicate $P$ on the natural numbers is RAM decidable when
there is a RAM program, a finite list of RAM instructions, such that for every natural number $n$
the program, started with $n$ in register $0$ and with the accumulator, the program counter and
every other register at $0$, halts (its program counter reaches or passes the end of the
program) with $1$ in the accumulator if $P(n)$ holds and with $0$ in the accumulator otherwise;
that is, its RAM evaluation on the single input $n$ equals the characteristic function of $P$
at $n$.

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: RAM store destination
articles.statement:
A store destination of a random-access machine names, by a
natural number $n$, the register into which the accumulator is stored: either register $n$
itself (direct) or the register whose index is the contents of register $n$ (indirect).

An immediate operand is not a valid store destination.

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: RAM instruction
articles.statement:
An instruction of a random-access machine is one of the following: load
an operand into the accumulator; store the accumulator into a store destination; add an operand
to the accumulator; subtract an operand from the accumulator, truncating at $0$; jump to
instruction $q$; jump to instruction $q$ if the accumulator is $0$; halt. Here an operand is given
by a RAM addressing mode, a store destination is a RAM store destination, and the jump target $q$
is a natural number.

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: RAM state
articles.statement:
A state of a random-access machine consists of a program counter in
$\mathbb{N}$, an accumulator value in $\mathbb{N}$, and register contents, a function
$\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ giving the contents of each register.

## Sources

- Aho–Hopcroft–Ullman, *The Design and Analysis of Computer Algorithms*, 1974, §1.2.

articles.title: Stacks of height at most one give a one-cell tape
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a finite multi-stack
machine, and let $S$ assign to every stack $k$ of $M$ a list $S_k$ of length at most $1$. Let $L'$
be a tape of stack columns whose $k$-th track, for every $k$, is $S_k$ laid out bottom first and
followed by blanks. Then adding the bottom marker to $L'$, as in the translation of $M$ to a
single-tape machine, gives the tape whose first cell is flagged as the bottom and holds the top of
$S_k$ on every stack $k$ (nothing if $S_k$ is empty), followed by blank cells.

articles.title: The answer machine outputs the answer of a one-cell input
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a finite multi-stack
machine whose stack alphabets are all finite, with its input and output stack alphabets
identified with the bits. For every non-blank cell $x$ of the single-tape emulation of $M$, the
answer machine of $M$, started on the one-cell input $x$, halts with the one-cell output holding
the input-bit cell for the answer read from $x$.

articles.title: The answer machine
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a finite multi-stack machine whose stack alphabets are all
finite, with its input and output stack alphabets identified with the bits. The answer machine of
$M$ is the single-tape machine over the non-blank cells of the single-tape emulation of $M$ with a
single state that, in one step, replaces the symbol under the head by the input-bit cell for the
answer read from that cell (the answer $\mathrm{false}$ if the cell is blank), does not move, and
halts.

articles.title: The bottom cell of the start tape
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a finite multi-stack machine whose input
stack alphabet is identified with the bits. The bottom cell of the emulation's start tape is the
cell flagged as the stack bottom that holds the symbol for $\mathrm{true}$ on the input stack and
nothing on every other stack.

articles.title: The answer bit of a cell
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a finite multi-stack machine whose output stack
alphabet is identified with the bits. The answer read from a non-blank cell of the single-tape
emulation of $M$ is $\mathrm{true}$ exactly when the cell holds the symbol for $\mathrm{true}$ on
the output stack.

articles.title: Coded configurations of a single-tape machine
articles.statement:
For a single-tape Turing machine with state
set $Q$ and tape alphabet $\Sigma$, write $\bot$ for an absent value. A coded configuration is a
quadruple $(q, h, L, R)$ where $q \in Q \cup \{\bot\}$ is the state ($\bot$ meaning halted),
$h \in \Sigma \cup \{\bot\}$ is the symbol under the head ($\bot$ being the blank), and $L$ and $R$
are finite lists over $\Sigma \cup \{\bot\}$, meant as the cells to the left and to the right of
the head.

articles.title: Pushing a cell onto a coded tape
articles.statement:
For any type $\Sigma$, an element $x$ of
$\Sigma \cup \{\bot\}$ (with $\bot$ the blank) and a finite list $l$ over $\Sigma \cup \{\bot\}$,
the push of $x$ onto $l$ is the empty list when $x = \bot$ and $l$ is empty, and otherwise the list
obtained by prepending $x$ to $l$.

articles.title: The coded step commutes with coding
articles.statement:
For every configuration $c$ of a single-tape machine
$M$, the code of $c$ has no successor under the coded step exactly when $c$ has no successor
under the step function of $M$, and otherwise the coded step sends the code of $c$ to the code
of the successor of $c$.

articles.title: One step of a single-tape machine on coded configurations
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing
machine with transition function $\delta$, and write $\bot$ both for the halting state and for the
blank. For a finite list $l$ of cells, let $\mathrm{hd}(l)$ be the first entry of $l$, the blank
$\bot$ when $l$ is empty; let $\mathrm{tl}(l)$ be $l$ without its first entry, the empty list when
$l$ is empty; and for a cell $w$ let $w \cdot l$, the push of $w$ onto $l$, be $l$ when $w = \bot$
and $l$ is empty, and $w$ prepended to $l$ otherwise. A coded configuration $(\bot, h, L, R)$ in
the halting state has no successor. For a running state $q$, write $\delta(q, h) = ((w, d), q')$,
where $w$ is the symbol to write, $d$ is either no move or a direction, and $q'$ is the new state,
possibly the halting state $\bot$. The successor of $(q, h, L, R)$ is $(q', w, L, R)$ if $d$ is no
move, $(q', \mathrm{hd}(L), \mathrm{tl}(L), w \cdot R)$ if $d$ is left, and
$(q', \mathrm{hd}(R), w \cdot L, \mathrm{tl}(R))$ if $d$ is right.

articles.title: A predicate decided by a single-tape machine is computable
articles.statement:
The decider's answer is the
symbol under the head of its final tape.

articles.title: Prepending a symbol takes at most two steps
articles.statement:
For every symbol $c$ and every word $l$, the
machine that prepends $c$, started on $l$, halts with output the word $c$ followed by $l$ within
at most two steps.

articles.title: Correctness of the prepending machine
articles.statement:
For every symbol $c$ and every word $l$, the
machine that prepends $c$, started on $l$, halts with output the word $c$ followed by $l$.

articles.title: The machine that prepends a symbol
articles.statement:
For a symbol $c$, this is the single-tape machine
with two states that, from its start state, writes back the symbol under the head, moves left and
enters its second state, and from its second state writes $c$ and halts without moving.

On an input word $l$ it outputs $c$ followed by $l$.

articles.title: The decider outputs the answer bit
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a finite multi-stack machine whose stack
alphabets are all finite, with its input and output stack alphabets identified with the bits, and
let $w$ be a word of bits. Suppose that $M$, started with the input stack holding the reverse of
$w$ followed by $\mathrm{true}$, halts with the output stack holding a list $u$ of length at most
$1$, every other stack empty and its variable back at its initial value. Then there is a bit $b$
such that the decider of $M$, started on the input-bit cells of $w$, halts with the one-cell
output holding the input-bit cell for $b$, and $b = \mathrm{true}$ exactly when $u$ is nonempty
and its first symbol is the symbol for $\mathrm{true}$.

articles.title: The decider of a multi-stack machine
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a finite multi-stack machine whose stack
alphabets are all finite, with its input and output stack alphabets identified with the bits. The
decider of $M$ is the single-tape machine over the non-blank cells of the single-tape emulation of
$M$ that runs the recognizer of $M$ and, once the recognizer halts, runs the answer machine of $M$
on the resulting tape.

articles.title: States of the single-tape emulation
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack machine with finitely many
stacks, labels and internal states and a finite input alphabet. Its plain single-tape emulation
is the translation of $M$ to a single-tape machine with a finite store, followed by the
translation of that machine to a plain single-tape machine, whose states are pairs of a
statement of the intermediate machine, or the halting state, and an internal state. This is the
finite set of those pairs whose first entry is the halting state or a statement occurring in the
program of one of the labels that the first translation produces from the labels of $M$.

The emulation only visits states in this set.

articles.title: Finite single-tape emulation of a multi-stack machine
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack machine
with finitely many stacks, labels and internal states, and with finite stack alphabets. Its
finite single-tape emulation is the single-tape machine that runs the plain single-tape emulation
of $M$ (through a single-tape machine with a finite store) step for step: its states are those in
the finite set of states the emulation visits, and its tape alphabet is the set of non-blank cells
of the emulation, where a cell is a bottom-of-stack flag together with an optional symbol for each
stack.

articles.title: Running the coded step mirrors running the machine
articles.statement:
For every configuration $c$ of a
single-tape machine $M$, iterating the coded step from the code of $c$ until a coded
configuration with no successor is reached terminates exactly when iterating the step function
of $M$ from $c$ until a configuration with no successor is reached does, and then it ends at the
code of the configuration where the run of $M$ from $c$ ends.

articles.title: The emulation's final tape
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack machine with finitely many stacks,
labels and internal states and a finite input alphabet, let $L$ be a list of symbols of its input
stack, and suppose that $M$, started with $L$ on its input stack and every other stack empty,
halts at the configuration $c$. Then its plain single-tape emulation, started on the tape that
holds the symbols of $L$ bottom first on the input stack with the first cell flagged as the
bottom, halts at a configuration $c_0$ for which there is a list $L'$ of columns, each holding an
optional symbol for every stack and padded with blank columns, such that for every stack $k$ the
entries of $L'$ for $k$ are the symbols of stack $k$ of $c$ listed bottom first, followed by
blanks, and the tape of $c_0$ is blank to the left of the head and holds $L'$ from the head
rightwards, with the bottom-of-stack flag set on its first cell and cleared on all others.

articles.title: Halting is termination of the run
articles.statement:
A single-tape machine $M$ halts on an input word $l$ if
and only if iterating the step function of $M$ from the initial configuration on $l$, until a
configuration with no successor is reached, terminates.

articles.title: The recognizer halts iff the multi-stack machine does
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack machine
with finitely many stacks, labels and internal states and with finite stack alphabets, and let
$e$ be a bijection from the alphabet of its input stack to the bits. For every list of bits $w$,
the recognizer built from $M$ and $e$ halts on the word of input cells of the bits of $w$ if and
only if $M$ halts when started on the input stack obtained by applying $e^{-1}$ to each entry of
the reversal of $w$ followed by $\mathsf{true}$.

articles.title: The head of a stack tape is the first entry of its list
articles.statement:
For every one-sided tape $s$ over
an alphabet $\Sigma$, stored as a finite list of cells in $\Sigma \cup \{\bot\}$ (with $\bot$ the
blank) that does not end in $\bot$, the symbol at the head of $s$ is the first entry of that list,
and the blank $\bot$ when the list is empty.

articles.title: Input cell of a bit
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack machine with finitely many stacks, labels
and internal states, and let $e$ be a bijection from the alphabet of its input stack to the bits.
The input cell of a bit $b$ is the non-blank cell of the single-tape emulation of $M$ whose
bottom-of-stack flag is off, whose entry for the input stack is $e^{-1}(b)$, and whose entries for
all other stacks are empty.

articles.title: Input code of a bit word
articles.statement:
For a list of bits $w$, let $b_0, \dots, b_n$ be the reversal of
$w$ followed by $\mathsf{true}$, reading $\mathsf{true}$ as $1$ and $\mathsf{false}$ as $0$. The
input code of $w$ is the natural number $\sum_{i=0}^{n} b_i 2^i$. Its binary expansion, least
significant bit first, is $b_0, \dots, b_n$: the input stack on which the single-tape emulation
starts for the input word $w$.

articles.title: Input decoding
articles.statement:
For a natural number $m > 0$, let $b_0, \dots, b_n$ be its binary
expansion, least significant bit first, without trailing zeros. The input decoding of $m$ is
$\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} b_{n-1-i} 2^i$, the value, least significant bit first, of the reversed
expansion with its first bit dropped. The input decoding of $0$, whose expansion is empty, is $0$.

It undoes the encoding of input words: for every natural number $k$ with binary expansion $w$,
least significant bit first, the input decoding of the number whose binary expansion, least
significant bit first, is the reversal of $w$ followed by $1$ is $k$.

articles.title: The bottom cell followed by the input word is the emulation's start tape
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a
multi-stack machine with finitely many stacks, labels and internal states, and let $e$ be a
bijection from the alphabet of its input stack to the bits. For every list of bits $w$, the bottom
cell followed by the input cells of the bits of $w$, read as cells of the emulation, is the start
tape that the single-tape emulation assigns to the input stack obtained by applying $e^{-1}$ to
each entry of the reversal of $w$ followed by $\mathsf{true}$.

articles.title: The halting problem for partial recursive codes is not co-recognizable on single-tape machines
articles.statement:
**The halting problem for partial recursive codes is not co-recognizable on single-tape
machines.** For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the set of partial recursive codes whose program halts on
input $n$ is not co-recognizable by a single-tape machine: no single-tape machine halts on exactly
the codes whose program does not halt on input $n$.

## Sources

- Sipser, Corollary 4.23 (there for $A_{TM}$), with partial recursive codes run on $n$.

articles.title: The halting problem for partial recursive codes is undecidable on single-tape machines
articles.statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, no single-tape machine decides whether a partial recursive code halts
on input $n$.

## Sources

- Sipser, Theorem 5.1, for codes of partial recursive functions run on $n$.

articles.title: Single-tape decidable predicates are closed under complement
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a single-tape machine, then so
is its complement $\neg p$.

articles.title: Computable predicates are decidable by single-tape machines
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a
primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$, and let $p$ be a computable predicate on $\alpha$,
that is, one whose indicator function $\alpha \to \{0, 1\}$ is computable. Then $p$ is decidable
by a single-tape Turing machine.

articles.title: R.e. predicates are recognizable by single-tape machines
articles.statement: **R.e. predicates are recognizable by single-tape machines.**

articles.title: Outputs are the ends of runs
articles.statement:
A single-tape machine $M$ outputs the word $l'$ on the input
word $l$ if and only if iterating the step function of $M$ from the initial configuration on $l$,
until a configuration with no successor is reached, terminates at the halting configuration for
$l'$: the halting state, with $l'$ written from the head rightwards and every other cell blank.

articles.title: The final tape of a run is partial recursive in the input word
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape
Turing machine whose finite alphabet $\Sigma$ carries a primitive recursive coding. The partial
function sending an input word $l$ over $\Sigma$ to the final tape of the run of $M$ on $l$ (the
symbol under the head, and the lists of cells to the left and to the right of the head), defined
exactly when $M$ halts on $l$, is partial recursive.

articles.title: Pushing a cell onto a coded tape is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Let $\Sigma$ be a type with a
primitive recursive coding, and let $x$ be a cell content, either a symbol of $\Sigma$ or blank.
Then the coded push of $x$, the map on lists of cell contents that prepends $x$ to a list, except
that it sends the empty list to the empty list when $x$ is blank, is primitive recursive.

articles.title: The coded step of a single-tape machine is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape
Turing machine over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, and fix primitive recursive codings of $\Sigma$ and
of the states of $M$. Then the coded step of $M$, which maps a coded configuration to the coded
configuration after one step of $M$ and has no value when the state is the halting state, is
primitive recursive.

articles.title: Binary codes of natural numbers in a tape alphabet are primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Let $\Sigma$ be
a type with a primitive recursive coding and $\iota$ any map from the Booleans to $\Sigma$. Then
the map sending $n \in \mathbb{N}$ to the word over $\Sigma$ obtained by applying $\iota$ letterwise
to the binary code of $n$ (least significant bit first, the empty word for $0$) is primitive
recursive.

articles.title: The code of the initial configuration is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape
Turing machine over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, and fix primitive recursive codings of $\Sigma$ and
of the states of $M$. Then the map sending an input word $w$ over $\Sigma$ to the code of the
initial configuration of $M$ on $w$ is primitive recursive.

articles.title: The halting set of a single-tape machine on binary inputs is r.e
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape
Turing machine over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$ and $\iota$ any map from the Booleans to $\Sigma$.
Then the set of natural numbers $n$ such that $M$ halts on the word obtained by applying $\iota$
letterwise to the binary code of $n$ (least significant bit first, the empty word for $0$) is
recursively enumerable.

articles.title: The halting set of a single-tape machine is r.e
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine
over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, and fix a primitive recursive coding of $\Sigma$. Then the set of
input words over $\Sigma$ on which $M$ halts is recursively enumerable.

articles.title: A predicate recognized by a single-tape machine is r.e
articles.statement: **A predicate recognized by a single-tape machine is r.e.**

articles.title: The recognizer of a multi-stack machine
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a finite multi-stack machine all of
whose stack alphabets are finite, and let $e$ be an identification of the alphabet of its input
stack with the booleans. The recognizer of $M$ is the single-tape machine, over the non-blank
cells of the multi-stack-to-single-tape translation of $M$, that first runs the machine
prepending the bottom cell determined by $M$ and $e$ (the bottom-flagged cell holding
$e^{-1}(\mathrm{true})$ on the input stack and nothing on the other stacks) to its input and, when
that machine halts, runs the single-tape emulation of $M$.

articles.title: Recovering a word from its input code
articles.statement:
For every list of bits $w$, reversing the binary
encoding (least significant bit first) of the input code of $w$ and then dropping the first bit of
the result gives back $w$.

articles.title: Single-tape co-recognizable predicates are those with an r.e. complement
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is co-recognizable by a single-tape machine if
and only if its complement $\neg p$ is recursively enumerable, that is, the partial function on
$\alpha$ that is defined, with a trivial value, exactly where $\neg p$ holds is partial
recursive.

articles.title: Single-tape decidable predicates are co-recognizable
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type
(it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is primitive
recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a single-tape machine, then $p$ is
co-recognizable by a single-tape machine, that is, its complement $\neg p$ is recognizable by a
single-tape machine.

articles.title: Single-tape decidable predicates are exactly the computable predicates
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a single-tape machine if and only
if it is computable, that is, $p$ is decidable and its Boolean characteristic function
$\alpha \to \mathrm{Bool}$ is computable.

articles.title: Post's theorem
articles.statement:
**Post's theorem** for single-tape machines: a predicate is decidable iff it is recognizable
and co-recognizable.

articles.title: Single-tape and multi-stack machines decide the same predicates
articles.statement: **Single-tape and multi-stack machines decide the same predicates.**

articles.title: The halting problem for partial recursive codes is recognizable on single-tape machines
articles.statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the set of partial recursive codes whose program halts on input $n$
is recognizable by a single-tape machine.

articles.title: Single-tape recognizable predicates are exactly the r.e. predicates
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a single-tape machine if and
only if it is recursively enumerable, that is, the partial function on $\alpha$ that is defined,
with a trivial value, exactly where $p$ holds is partial recursive.

articles.title: Single-tape and multi-stack machines recognize the same predicates
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a single-tape machine if and
only if it is recognizable by a multi-stack machine.

articles.title: Decidable predicates are recognizable by single-tape machines
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a
primcodable type (it has an encoding $\mathrm{encode} : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ whose decoding is
primitive recursive). If a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a single-tape machine, then
$p$ is recognizable by a single-tape machine.

articles.title: Code of a single-tape configuration
articles.statement:
The code of a configuration of a single-tape machine
is the quadruple consisting of its state (or the halting state), the symbol under the head (or
blank), and the lists of cells, without trailing blanks, of the tapes to the left and to the right
of the head.

articles.title: Pushing onto a stack tape, on cell lists
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a stack tape, a one-sided tape stored
as its list of cells without trailing blanks, and $x$ a cell content, either a symbol or blank.
Then the cell list of the tape obtained by pushing $x$ onto $s$ is the coded push of $x$ applied to
the cell list of $s$: $x$ prepended to it, except that pushing a blank onto the empty tape gives
the empty list.

articles.title: Tail of a stack tape, on cell lists
articles.statement:
Let $s$ be a stack tape, a one-sided tape stored as
its list of cells without trailing blanks. Then the cell list of the tail of $s$ is the tail of
the cell list of $s$, the tail of the empty list being empty.

articles.title: Prepending a symbol by stepping left
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a symbol and $l$ a list of symbols, and
consider the tape holding $l$ from the head rightwards, all other cells blank. Writing back the
symbol under the head, moving the head one cell left, and then writing $c$ gives the tape holding
the list $c$ followed by $l$ from the head rightwards, all other cells blank.

articles.title: A machine step is a coded step
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a URM program, let $R$ be the sum over the
instructions of $p$ of the largest register index each one mentions, and let $s'$ be a state
that $p$ reaches from the state $s$ in one step. Then the coded step, run on the list of codes of
the instructions of $p$, sends the coded state of $s$ (its program counter together with the list
of the contents of its registers $0, \dots, R$) to the coded state of $s'$.

articles.title: One coded URM step
articles.statement:
A coded state is a program counter $k$ together with a list $r$ of
register contents (in use, the contents of registers $0, \dots, R$, where $R$ is the register bound
of the program), and a program is given by the list $c$ of its instruction codes. Write $c_k$ for
entry $k$ of $c$, and $r_j$ for entry $j$ of $r$, read as $0$ when $j$ is past the end of $r$;
setting an entry past the end of $r$ leaves $r$ unchanged. If $k$ is at least the length of $c$,
the state is halted and has no successor. Otherwise unpair the code $c_k$ as $(i, a)$. If
$i = 0$, the successor is $(k + 1, r')$ where $r'$ is $r$ with entry $a$ set to $0$. If $i = 1$,
it is $(k + 1, r')$ where $r'$ is $r$ with entry $a$ set to $r_a + 1$. If $i = 2$, unpair $a$ as
$(m, n)$; the successor is $(k + 1, r')$ where $r'$ is $r$ with entry $n$ set to $r_m$. If
$i = 3$, unpair $a$ as $(m, b)$ and $b$ as $(n, q)$; the successor is $(q, r)$ if $r_m = r_n$ and
$(k + 1, r)$ otherwise. Any other tag $i$ (which never occurs for a genuine instruction code)
gives no successor.

articles.title: The URM output after a given number of steps is computable
articles.statement:
For every URM program $p$,
the function sending an input $x$ and a step count $t$ to the output of $p$ on $x$ after $t$ steps
(nothing while $p$ is still running, the contents of register $0$ once it has halted) is a
computable function of the pair $(x, t)$.

Unbounded search over $t$ then shows that URM evaluation is partial recursive.

articles.title: A URM-decidable predicate is computable
articles.statement:
If a predicate $P$ on the natural numbers is
URM-decidable, then it is a computable predicate: its Boolean decision function, sending $n$ to
whether $P(n)$ holds, is computable.

articles.title: URM-decidable predicate
articles.statement:
A predicate $P$ on the natural numbers is URM-decidable when
some URM program computes its characteristic function: started on any input $n$ (register $0$
holding $n$, all other registers $0$), the program halts, and register $0$ then holds $1$ if
$P(n)$ holds and $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Tag of an instruction code
articles.statement:
For every URM instruction $I$, unpairing the code of $I$
gives first component $0$ if $I$ is a zero instruction $Z\,n$, $1$ if it is a successor
instruction $S\,n$, $2$ if it is a transfer $T\,m\,n$, and $3$ if it is a jump $J\,m\,n\,q$.

articles.title: Payload of an instruction code
articles.statement:
Write $\langle a, b \rangle$ for the pairing of natural
numbers $a$ and $b$. For every URM instruction $I$, unpairing the code of $I$ gives second
component $n$ if $I$ is $Z\,n$ or $S\,n$, $\langle m, n \rangle$ if $I$ is $T\,m\,n$, and
$\langle m, \langle n, q \rangle \rangle$ if $I$ is $J\,m\,n\,q$.

articles.title: Code of a URM instruction
articles.statement:
**Code of a URM instruction** as a natural number: the instruction tag paired with the
paired arguments, `Z n ↦ pair 0 n`, `S n ↦ pair 1 n`, `T m n ↦ pair 2 (pair m n)`,
`J m n q ↦ pair 3 (pair m (pair n q))`.

articles.title: Bounded URM execution stays at its halted value
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a list of instruction codes,
$s$ a coded state, and $t_1 \le t_2$ natural numbers. If after $t_1$ steps of bounded execution
of $c$ from $s$ the program counter is at least the length of $c$, then $t_2$ steps of bounded
execution of $c$ from $s$ give the same coded state as $t_1$ steps.

articles.title: Bounded URM execution is stable once halted
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a list of instruction codes, $s$
a coded state and $t$ a natural number. If after $t$ steps of bounded execution of $c$ from $s$
the program counter is at least the length of $c$, then $t + 1$ steps of bounded execution of $c$
from $s$ give the same coded state as $t$ steps.

articles.title: Bounded execution unfolds by one step
articles.statement:
For a list of instruction codes, a number $t$
and a coded state $s$, bounded execution for $t + 1$ steps from $s$ is the one-step function
applied to the result of bounded execution for $t$ steps from $s$.

articles.title: Bounded execution only reaches codes of reachable states
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a URM program,
$x$ an input and $t$ a natural number. Then there is a machine state $s'$, reachable from the
initial state with input list $[x]$ by steps of $p$, whose coded state equals the result of
bounded execution for $t$ steps on the instruction codes of $p$ from the initial coded state
for $x$.

articles.title: Bounded execution
articles.statement:
For a list of instruction codes, a number $t$ and a coded state $s$,
bounded execution applies the one-step function for these codes $t$ times, starting from
$s$.

articles.title: Every reachable state is reached by bounded execution
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a URM program and $x$
an input. If a machine state $s$ is reachable from the initial state with input list $[x]$ by
steps of $p$, then for some number $t$, bounded execution for $t$ steps on the instruction codes
of $p$ from the initial coded state for $x$ gives the coded state of $s$.

articles.title: Instruction codes by position
articles.statement:
If the URM program $p$ has instruction $I$ at position
$pc$, then the entry at position $pc$ of the list of instruction codes of $p$, read with
default $0$, is the code of $I$.

articles.title: Reading the register list
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a URM program with register bound $R$ and
$\sigma$ a register state. For every $n$, the entry at position $n$ of the register list of
$\sigma$, read with default $0$, is $\sigma(n)$ if $n \le R$ and $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: Output after a given number of steps
articles.statement:
For a URM program $p$, an input $x$ and a number
$t$, run bounded execution for $t$ steps on the instruction codes of $p$ from the initial coded
state for $x$. If the resulting program counter is less than the length of the list of
instruction codes, the program is still running and there is no output; otherwise the output
is the entry at position $0$ of the resulting register list, read with default $0$.

articles.title: A halted coded state gives a halting machine run
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a URM program, $x$ an input
and $t$ a number. If bounded execution for $t$ steps on the instruction codes of $p$ from the
initial coded state for $x$ reaches a program counter at least the length of the list of
instruction codes, then $p$ halts on the input list $[x]$.

articles.title: The initial coded state codes the initial machine state
articles.statement:
For a URM program $p$ and an
input $x$, the initial coded state for $x$ equals the coded state of the initial machine state
with input list $[x]$.

articles.title: Initial coded state
articles.statement:
For a URM program $p$ with register bound $R$ and an input $x$,
the initial coded state has program counter $0$ and register list $(x, 0, \dots, 0)$ of
length $R + 1$: register $0$ holds $x$ and registers $1, \dots, R$ hold $0$.

articles.title: Length of the register list
articles.statement:
For a URM program $p$ with register bound $R$ and a register
state $\sigma$, the register list of $\sigma$ (the contents of registers $0, \dots, R$) has length
$R + 1$.

articles.title: Instructions stay within the register bound
articles.statement:
For a URM program $p$ with register bound
$R$ and every instruction $I$ of $p$, the largest register index referenced by $I$ is at most
$R$.

articles.title: Decoding a coded state
articles.statement:
A coded state is a pair $(c, \ell)$ of a natural number $c$ and a
list $\ell$ of natural numbers. Its machine state has program counter $c$, and register $n$
holds the $n$-th entry of $\ell$ (counting from $0$) when $n$ is less than the length of $\ell$,
and $0$ otherwise.

articles.title: A URM-computable partial function is partial recursive
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a partial function
from $\mathbb{N}$ to $\mathbb{N}$. Suppose some URM program has the following property for every
natural number $x$: started with $x$ in register $0$ and all other registers $0$, it halts
exactly when $f(x)$ is defined, and then it holds $f(x)$ in register $0$. Then $f$ is partial
recursive.

The URM evaluation is the unbounded search for the first halting step of the coded execution.

articles.title: A state that can step is running
articles.statement:
If a state $s$ of a URM program $p$ makes a step to some
state, then the program counter of $s$ is less than the number of instructions of $p$.

articles.title: The coded step is primitive recursive
articles.statement: **The coded step is primitive recursive**, for any fixed list of instruction codes.

articles.title: Bounded execution is primitive recursive in the input and the step bound
articles.statement:
For a URM
program $p$, the bounded execution of $p$ for $t$ steps ($t$ iterations of the one-step
function on the list of instruction codes of $p$), started from the initial coded state for
input $x$, is a primitive recursive function of the pair $(x, t)$.

articles.title: The initial coded state is primitive recursive in the input
articles.statement: **The initial coded state is primitive recursive in the input.**

articles.title: The one-step function is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
For every list of natural numbers, read as
instruction codes, the function on coded states (pairs of a program counter and a register list)
that sends a coded state to its successor under one coded step, and a coded state with no
successor to itself, is primitive recursive.

articles.title: A URM-recognizable predicate is recursively enumerable
articles.statement: **A URM-recognizable predicate is recursively enumerable.**

articles.title: Registers read by a program lie within the register bound
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a URM program. If
$n$ is a register read by some instruction of $p$, then $n$ is at most the register bound of
$p$.

articles.title: URM-recognizable predicates
articles.statement:
A predicate $P$ on the natural numbers is URM-recognizable
when there is a URM program that, started with input $n$ in register $0$ and every other register
$0$, halts if and only if $P(n)$ holds.

articles.title: Register bound
articles.statement:
The register bound $R$ of a URM program $p$ is the sum, over the
instructions of $p$, of the largest register index each instruction refers to. Every register
that an instruction of $p$ can read or write is at most $R$.

articles.title: A URM-decidable predicate is decidable by a single-tape Turing machine
articles.statement: **A URM-decidable predicate is decidable by a single-tape Turing machine.**

articles.title: A URM-recognizable predicate is recognizable by a single-tape Turing machine
articles.statement: **A URM-recognizable predicate is recognizable by a single-tape Turing machine.**

articles.title: One-step function on coded states
articles.statement:
Given a list of instruction codes, the one-step
function sends a coded state $s$ to the result of one coded URM step from $s$ when that step is
defined, and leaves $s$ unchanged when it is not (in particular when $s$ is halted).

articles.title: A coded step is a machine step
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a URM program and $s$ a machine state. If one
coded URM step, run on the list of codes of the instructions of $p$ from the coded state of $s$,
yields $c'$, then there is a machine state $s'$ such that $p$ steps from $s$ to $s'$ in one step
and the coded state of $s'$ is $c'$.

articles.title: A URM-decidable predicate is decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine
articles.statement: **A URM-decidable predicate is decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine.**

articles.title: A URM-recognizable predicate is recognizable by a multi-stack Turing machine
articles.statement: **A URM-recognizable predicate is recognizable by a multi-stack Turing machine.**

articles.title: Decoding and re-encoding a coded state gives it back
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a URM program with
register bound $R$, and let $c$ be a coded state: a program counter together with a list of
register contents. If the list has length $R + 1$, then the coded state, with respect to $p$, of
the machine state decoded from $c$ is $c$.

articles.title: Coded machine state
articles.statement:
For a URM program $p$ with register bound $R$, the coded state of a
machine state $s$ is the pair consisting of the program counter of $s$ and the register list
$(r_0, \dots, r_R)$ of the contents of registers $0, \dots, R$ of $s$.

articles.title: Updating a register updates the register list
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a URM program with register
bound $R$, let $\sigma$ be a register state, and let $n \le R$ and $v$ be natural numbers. The
register list of the state obtained from $\sigma$ by setting register $n$ to $v$ equals the
register list of $\sigma$ with its entry at position $n$ replaced by $v$.

articles.title: Register list
articles.statement:
For a URM program $p$ with register bound $R$, the register list of a
register state $\sigma$ is the list $(\sigma(0), \sigma(1), \dots, \sigma(R))$ of the contents of
registers $0, \dots, R$.

articles.title: A URM-computable total function is computed by a multi-stack Turing machine
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. Suppose there is a URM program that, for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$,
started with $n$ in register $0$ and all other registers $0$, halts with $f(n)$ in register $0$.
Then there is a multi-stack Turing machine that computes $f$ with input and output numbers
written in binary: started on the binary word of $n$, it halts with the binary word of $f(n)$.

## Sources

- Sipser, *Introduction to the Theory of Computation*, 3rd ed., §3.1 (Church–Turing thesis) and §3.3 (equivalence of models).

articles.title: URM-decidability implies multi-stack decidability
articles.statement:
Every predicate $P$ on $\mathbb{N}$ that is URM-decidable is decidable by a multi-stack Turing
machine.

## Sources

- Sipser, *Introduction to the Theory of Computation*, 3rd ed., §3.1 (Church–Turing thesis).

articles.title: URM-recognizability implies multi-stack recognizability
articles.statement:
Every predicate $P$ on $\mathbb{N}$ that is URM-recognizable is recognizable by a multi-stack
Turing machine.

## Sources

- Sipser, *Introduction to the Theory of Computation*, 3rd ed., §3.1 (Church–Turing thesis).

articles.title: Written registers lie within the register bound
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a URM program with register
bound $R$. If an instruction of $p$ writes to register $n$, then $n \le R$.

articles.title: Babai's theorem: graph isomorphism in quasipolynomial time
articles.statement:
The quasipolynomial graph
isomorphism statement holds: there are a function $D$ from pairs of graph codes to Booleans, an
exponent $c \in \mathbb{N}$, and a deterministic multi-stack Turing machine with a time function
$t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that, on the bit encoding of every pair $(G, H)$, outputs the
single bit $D(G, H)$ within $t(\ell)$ steps, where $\ell$ is the length of the encoding, such that
$t(n) \le 2^{(\lfloor \log_2(n+2) \rfloor + 2)^c}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and $D(G, H)$ is
true if and only if $G$ and $H$ are isomorphic.

Babai (STOC 2016) gave a deterministic quasipolynomial-time graph-isomorphism algorithm; the
corrected proof retains that complexity.

## Sources

- Babai, L., Graph isomorphism in quasipolynomial time, Proc. 48th ACM Symp. Theory Comput. (STOC 2016), 684-697; arXiv:1512.03547, https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03547.

articles.title: The quasipolynomial graph isomorphism statement
articles.statement:
The proposition that graph isomorphism
is decidable in quasipolynomial time: there are a function $D$ from pairs of graph codes to
Booleans, an exponent $c \in \mathbb{N}$, and a deterministic multi-stack Turing machine with a
time function $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that, on the bit encoding of every pair $(G, H)$,
outputs the single bit $D(G, H)$ within $t(\ell)$ steps, where $\ell$ is the length of the
encoding, such that $t(n) \le q_c(n)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, where $q_c$ is the
quasipolynomial time bound with exponent $c$, and $D(G, H)$ is true if and only if $G$ and $H$
are isomorphic.

## Sources

- ALG-016.

articles.title: Bit encoding of a pair of graph codes
articles.statement:
The bit encoding of a pair $(G, H)$ of graph codes
is the bit encoding of $G$ followed by the bit encoding of $H$.

articles.title: Bit encoding of a graph code
articles.statement:
The bit encoding of a graph code with $n$ vertices and
adjacency matrix $A$ is the prefix-free encoding of $n$ followed by the $n^2$ entries of $A$, as
bits, in row-major order: $A_{0,0}, A_{0,1}, \dots, A_{0,n-1}, A_{1,0}, \dots, A_{n-1,n-1}$.

articles.title: Graph codes
articles.statement:
A graph code consists of a vertex count $n \in \mathbb{N}$, with vertices
$0, \dots, n-1$, and a Boolean adjacency matrix $A$ on these vertices that is symmetric
($A_{ij} = A_{ji}$ for all $i, j$) and loop-free ($A_{ii}$ is false for every $i$).

articles.title: Isomorphism of graph codes
articles.statement:
Graph codes $G$ and $H$ with adjacency matrices $A$ and $B$
are isomorphic when they have the same vertex count $n$ and there is a permutation $\sigma$ of
the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that $A_{ij} = B_{\sigma(i)\sigma(j)}$ for all $i, j$.

articles.title: Binary digits of a natural number
articles.statement:
The binary digits of $n \in \mathbb{N}$, most
significant first, as a list of bits with the digit $1$ read as true and $0$ as false; for
$n = 0$ this is the single digit $0$.

articles.title: Prefix-free encoding of a natural number
articles.statement:
The prefix-free encoding of $n \in \mathbb{N}$
consists of $k$ true bits, where $k$ is the number of binary digits of $n$, then one false bit,
then the binary digits of $n$, most significant first.

articles.title: Quasipolynomial time bound
articles.statement:
For an exponent $c \in \mathbb{N}$ and an input length
$n \in \mathbb{N}$, the quasipolynomial time bound is
$q_c(n) = 2^{(\lfloor \log_2(n+2) \rfloor + 2)^c}$.

articles.title: Entry bound for a converted tensor instance
articles.statement:
A converted tensor entry is a sum of at most `2 ^ P` terms, each containing one weight and
`Fintype.card J - 1` off-diagonal factors.

articles.title: Shape bound for contracted tensor networks
articles.statement:
If every contraction class has at most `m` vertices, contraction multiplies the network's
shape parameter by `m`.

articles.title: Size bound for contracted tensor networks
articles.statement:
If every contraction class has at most `m` vertices, contraction multiplies the shape
parameter by `m` and changes the absolute-value exponent from `B` to `B * (m + m * m)`.

articles.title: Capacity bound between grid rows
articles.statement:
The capacity between two grid rows is at most `g²mL` when every active rectangle is
charged at most `2mL` and there are `g` columns.

articles.title: Shape bound for the grid row network
articles.statement:
The grid row network has shape `m g³ L` when both raw-state alphabets have at most
`2^L` elements and every rectangle label set and capacity obeys its declared bound.

articles.title: Size bound for the grid row network
articles.statement:
Under uniform raw tensor and factor bounds, the grid row network has exact source exponents
`m g³ L` for shape and `g B + g² b` for integer magnitudes.

articles.title: Total capacity of the grid row network
articles.statement:
The directed total capacity consists of all vertical row edges plus twice the active
rectangle capacity; diagonal row capacities are excluded.

articles.title: Number of states of a merged vertex
articles.statement: The number of merged states is the product of the state-set sizes in the class.

articles.title: Interaction of merged classes in increasing order
articles.statement:
The interaction of two increasingly ordered classes is the product of all source interactions
crossing between them.

articles.title: Interaction of two distinct merged classes
articles.statement:
The interaction of two distinct classes is the product of all source interactions crossing
between them, oriented from the first class to the second.

articles.title: Merging vertices of a factored tensor network
articles.statement:
Merge vertices along `χ`, retaining source states and labels on their classes and padding all
other coordinates with the supplied defaults.

articles.title: Merging vertices preserves network value
articles.statement: Merging along any map preserves the exact integer-valued network value.

articles.title: Half-edge factored presentation of a tensor instance
articles.statement:
Present an instance as a half-edge network.

A state at `v` chooses one label for every off-diagonal half-edge from `v`; the two sides of
each edge are constrained to agree. The capacities are zero because this construction makes no
size claim.

articles.title: Complete-graph instance of a factored network
articles.statement:
Turn a factored network into a complete-graph tensor instance.

The finite set `D a b` names the source labels on the edge `{a, b}` through `dec a b`.
Labels outside `D a b` make the corresponding directed factor zero.

articles.title: Instance value as a sum over half-edge vectors
articles.statement: Expand an instance value as a sum over directed half-edge vectors with equality factors.

articles.title: Half-edge presentation preserves instance value
articles.statement: The half-edge presentation of an instance has the same value.

articles.title: Converting a factored network to an instance preserves value
articles.statement: Naming every source edge alphabet bijectively inside `labels` preserves network value.

articles.title: Number of ordered grid rectangles
articles.statement: The number of ordered grid rectangles is the product of the two pair counts.

articles.title: Crossing kernel on grid rectangles
articles.statement: The crossing kernel requires opposite directed copies on both rectangle diagonals to agree.

articles.title: Directed labelings of a finite grid
articles.statement: Directed grid labelings with independent finite choices on edges and diagonal entries.

articles.title: Ordered rectangles of a finite grid
articles.statement: Ordered grid rectangles, indexed by an increasing row pair and increasing column pair.

articles.title: Finite grid tensor evaluation
articles.statement:
The finite grid evaluation: local tensors, row and column edge equalities, and one kernel per
ordered rectangle, summed over all directed labelings.

articles.title: Characterization of directed grid labelings
articles.statement:
Membership in `gridLabelings` means precisely that diagonal and edge coordinates use their
respective finite choice sets.

articles.title: Transporting a tensor instance to a grid
articles.statement: Transport an instance to a grid, returning zero unless the self-label is the chosen default.

articles.title: Applying a rectangle kernel to its diagonal ends
articles.statement: Apply a rectangle kernel to its four directed diagonal ends `x`, `y`, `u`, `v`.

articles.title: Complete-graph tensor value as a crossing grid evaluation
articles.statement:
Complete-graph tensor evaluation is the crossing grid evaluation after transport. The
transport gates diagonal entries at `default`; other allowed diagonal labels therefore contribute
zero. The default need not belong to the edge-label set.

articles.title: Row interaction for enumerated left states
articles.statement:
When the left state is enumerated by the row network, the alphabet-membership condition is
automatic, so the interaction recovers the source vertical-equality formula. The right state may
be arbitrary because equality with an allowed left value already forces its vertical value.

articles.title: Interaction between rows of the grid row network
articles.statement:
The interaction between increasing rows is the rectangle-kernel product times vertical
equality indicators. For finite alphabets, an equal vertical value contributes only when it is
in `labels`.

articles.title: Grid row network computes the grid value
articles.statement:
If each rectangle kernel is the finite sum of its top and bottom factors, contracting the
constructed row network gives the canonical finite grid value.

articles.title: Row network of a grid tensor
articles.statement:
Merge every grid row into one vertex of a factored tensor network. The state and label
carriers may be infinite; only the supplied alphabets are enumerated. Capacity metadata charges
`L` per vertical edge and the supplied cut capacity for each active rectangle.

articles.title: Grid value expanded over kernel choices
articles.statement:
If every active rectangle kernel is a finite sum, the grid value is the sum over one kernel
choice for each active rectangle. Raw rectangle indices outside `gridRectangles` retain the
original kernel, which does not affect `gridValue`.

articles.title: Edge labelings of the complete graph
articles.statement: Complete-graph edge labelings, free on `orderedPairs` and default elsewhere.

articles.title: Integer-valued factored tensor network
articles.statement:
An integer-valued factored tensor network.

Only `Θ a b` with `a < b` supplies labels. The factors `f a b` and `f b a` are the two
sides of the same interaction. Capacities `c` are metadata used by `totalCapacity`, `Shaped`,
and `Sized`; `value` does not read them.

articles.title: Edge labels incident to a vertex
articles.statement: Labels incident to `v`, indexed by the other endpoint.

articles.title: Integer-valued complete-graph tensor instance
articles.statement: An integer-valued local tensor at each vertex.

articles.title: Interaction is symmetric under swapping endpoints
articles.statement: Reading an interaction from the other endpoint swaps its states.

articles.title: Interaction of two states in a factored network
articles.statement: The interaction of two states, summed over their shared edge labels.

articles.title: Label set is symmetric in its endpoints
articles.statement: The label set is independent of endpoint order.

articles.title: Label set of an unordered vertex pair
articles.statement: The label set of an unordered vertex pair.

articles.title: Characterization of complete-graph edge labelings
articles.statement:
A labeling belongs to `edgeLabelings` exactly when active edges use allowed labels and all
other coordinates contain the default.

articles.title: Membership in the ordered pairs
articles.statement: Membership in `orderedPairs` is strict ordering of the two coordinates.

articles.title: Ordered pairs representing unordered pairs
articles.statement: Pairs `(a, b)` with `a < b`, representing unordered pairs once.

articles.title: Ordered representative of an unordered pair
articles.statement: The ordered representative `(min a b, max a b)` of the pair `{a, b}`.

articles.title: Factored tensor network with shape parameter
articles.statement:
A network of shape parameter `P`: at most `2 ^ P` states per vertex, symmetric
capacities summing to at most `P` at each vertex, and at most `2 ^ c` labels per edge.

articles.title: Shaped tensor network with bounded entries
articles.statement:
A shaped network whose weights, factors and off-diagonal interactions are bounded by
`2 ^ B` in absolute value.

articles.title: Directed total capacity of a factored network
articles.statement: The directed total capacity `Σ_{a ≠ b} c a b`; both orientations are counted.

articles.title: Value of a factored tensor network
articles.statement: The network value: sum over states of vertex weights times all pair interactions.

articles.title: Value of a complete-graph tensor instance
articles.statement: The sum, over complete-graph edge labelings, of the product of local tensors.

articles.title: State padding of a factored tensor network
articles.statement:
The source's local padding protocol for factored networks. The factor clause is retained
on source states and source labels, even though value preservation uses the interaction clause.
Only capacities between distinct vertices must agree.

articles.title: State padding preserves the weighted pair sum
articles.statement:
Padding the finite state sets preserves the full sum of vertex weights and arbitrary pair
kernels. No factorization, finiteness of the state carriers, or global injectivity is required.

articles.title: State padding preserves value and total capacity
articles.statement: A local state-padding certificate preserves both network value and directed total capacity.

articles.title: Alphabet padding of a tensor instance
articles.statement:
Rename the active edge alphabet of an instance through `dec`, returning zero when any
off-diagonal target label is outside `D`. The diagonal coordinate is replaced by `sourceDefault`.

articles.title: Factoring and unfactoring a tensor instance gives its padding
articles.statement:
Factoring an instance and converting it back through constant edge names gives its padded
version. The decoder must send every admitted target name into the explicit source alphabet.

articles.title: Factoring round trip with the full source alphabet
articles.statement: The source conversion theorem with the full finite source alphabet.

articles.title: Bijective alphabet padding preserves instance value
articles.statement: Padding through a bijective renaming of an explicit source alphabet preserves instance value.

articles.title: Transposition preserves the grid evaluation
articles.statement:
Transposing the grid coordinates, local tensors, and rectangle kernels preserves the finite
grid evaluation. Edge and diagonal label choices remain independent.

articles.title: Transposing a rectangle kernel is an involution
articles.statement: Transposing a rectangle kernel twice recovers the original kernel.

articles.title: Transpose of a rectangle kernel
articles.statement: Transpose a rectangle kernel, exchanging the `y` and `u` directed diagonal ends.

articles.title: Transposing a grid tensor instance is an involution
articles.statement: Transposing a grid tensor instance twice recovers the original instance.

articles.title: Transpose of a grid tensor instance
articles.statement: Swap the row and column coordinates of a grid tensor instance.

articles.title: Aaronson-Wigderson: the algebrization barrier
articles.statement:
Call an oracle a function from bitstrings
to booleans. There are oracles $B$ and $\tilde B$ such that $\tilde B$ is an algebraic extension
of $B$ and $\mathsf{P}^B = \mathsf{NP}^{\tilde B}$. There are also oracles $B$ and $\tilde B$ such
that $\tilde B$ is an algebraic extension of $B$ and $\mathsf{NP}^B$ is not contained in
$\mathsf{P}^{\tilde B}$.

## Sources

- S. Aaronson and A. Wigderson, "Algebrization: A new barrier in complexity theory", Proceedings of the Fortieth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 2008), 731-740 (journal version in ACM Transactions on Computation Theory 1 (2009)).

articles.title: Restriction of an oracle to inputs of length $n$
articles.statement:
For a function $B$ from bitstrings to
booleans and a natural number $n$, the restriction of $B$ to inputs of length $n$ is the function
on $\{0,1\}^n$ sending $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ to $B(a_0 a_1 \cdots a_{n-1})$, the value of
$B$ at the bitstring $a$.

articles.title: Answer bits of the algebraic extension oracle
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $p$ be a
monic irreducible polynomial of degree $n + 1$ over $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, let
$F = \mathbb{F}_2[X]/(p)$ with $\alpha$ the class of $X$, let $B$ be a function from bitstrings to
booleans, and let $\tilde B_n$ be the multilinear extension over $F$ of the restriction of $B$ to
inputs of length $n$. Given a list $(e_0, e_1, \ldots)$ of bitstrings and an index $j$ with
$0 \le j \le n$, let $e_{i,k} \in \{0, 1\}$ be the bit of $e_i$ at position $k$, counting from
$0$, where a missing list entry or a missing bit counts as $0$, and let $x \in F^n$ be the point
with coordinates $x_i = \sum_{k=0}^{n} e_{i,k} \alpha^k$ for $i < n$. The answer bit is true
exactly when the coefficient of $\alpha^j$ in $\tilde B_n(x)$, written in the basis
$1, \alpha, \dots, \alpha^n$ of $F$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$, equals $1$.

The index $j$ ranges over $0, \dots, n$ only: an out-of-range index must be rejected by the
caller, not reduced modulo $n + 1$.

articles.title: Algebraic extension oracles
articles.statement:
Let $B$ and $O$ be oracles, that is, functions from
bitstrings to booleans. Then $O$ is an algebraic extension of $B$ when there are polynomials
$\pi_0, \pi_1, \pi_2, \ldots$ over $\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$, each $\pi_n$ monic and
irreducible of degree $n + 1$, with the following two properties, where $F_n$ is the field
$\mathbb{F}_2[X]/(\pi_n)$, $\alpha_n$ is the class of $X$ in $F_n$, and $\tilde B_n$ is the
multilinear extension over $F_n$ of the restriction of $B$ to inputs of length $n$. First, the
map sending a bitstring $u$ to the coefficient bitstring of $\pi_{|u|}$ with parameter $|u|$
(whose bits say which of the coefficients of $X^0, \dots, X^{|u|+1}$ equal $1$) is
polynomial-time computable. Second, let $y$ be a bitstring. If $y$ decodes, under the canonical
bitstring encoding of triples, to a triple $(u, (e_0, \dots, e_{m-1}), j)$ of a bitstring $u$, a
list of bitstrings and a natural number $j$ such that, writing $n = |u|$, we have $m = n$, every
$e_i$ has length $n + 1$ and $j \le n$, then $O(y)$ is true exactly when the coefficient of
$\alpha_n^j$ in $\tilde B_n(x)$, written in the basis $1, \alpha_n, \dots, \alpha_n^n$ of $F_n$
over $\mathbb{F}_2$, equals $1$. Here $x \in F_n^n$ is the point with coordinates
$x_i = \sum_{k=0}^{n} e_{i,k} \alpha_n^k$, where $e_{i,k} \in \{0, 1\}$ is the bit of $e_i$ at
position $k$, counting from $0$. Otherwise, in particular when $y$ does not decode, $O(y)$ is
false.

Every malformed query is answered false, so an oracle machine cannot route around the algebraic
structure through invalid encodings, and an out-of-range $j$ does not wrap around to
coordinate $0$.

articles.title: Multilinear extension of a Boolean function
articles.statement:
Identify the booleans true and false with $1$
and $0$. Let $F$ be a field, $n$ a natural number and $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$.
The multilinear extension of $f$ at a point $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) \in F^n$ is

$$\sum_{a \in \{0,1\}^n} f(a) \prod_{i=0}^{n-1} \ell_{a_i}(x_i),$$

where $f(a) \in \{0, 1\}$ is read in $F$, $\ell_1(t) = t$ and $\ell_0(t) = 1 - t$.

articles.title: Coefficient bitstring of a polynomial over $\mathbb{F}_2$
articles.statement:
For a polynomial $q$ over
$\mathbb{F}_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ and a natural number $n$, the coefficient bitstring of $q$
with parameter $n$ is the bitstring $b_0 b_1 \cdots b_{n+1}$ of length $n + 2$ in which $b_i$ is
true exactly when the coefficient of $X^i$ in $q$ equals $1$.

articles.title: The decision problem of a family of Boolean functions
articles.statement:
For a family
$f = (f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, where $f_n$ is a Boolean function on $n$ bits, this is the decision
problem that maps a bitstring $x = x_0 x_1 \cdots x_{n-1}$ of length $n$ to
$f_n(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$.

articles.title: Natural property
articles.statement:
Let $C = (C_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, where $C_n$ is a set of Boolean
functions on $n$ bits. Then $C$ is natural when it is constructive and large. Constructive: there
are a polynomial $q$ with natural-number coefficients and, for every $n$, a circuit given as a
list of at most $q(2^n)$ encoded gates, such that a Boolean function $g$ on $n$ bits lies in $C_n$
if and only if the evaluation of the circuit on the truth table of $g$ has last gate value true.
Large: there is a natural number $c$ such that $|C_n| \ge 2^{2^n} / 2^{cn}$ for every $n$, that is,
$C_n$ contains at least a $2^{-cn}$ fraction of the $2^{2^n}$ Boolean functions on $n$ bits.

articles.title: Evaluation of an encoded circuit
