articles.statement:
Given a list of encoded gates $g_0, \dots, g_{m-1}$,
each a (kind, references) pair, and a list of Booleans $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$, this is the
list of the values of all $m$ gates, in order: each pair is decoded to a gate of a flat Boolean
circuit on $n$ inputs, and the resulting circuit is evaluated with input $i$ set to $a_i$. An
input pair $(0, [i])$ with $i \ge n$ decodes to the constant false, so it reads as false.

articles.title: Encoded gates
articles.statement:
An encoded gate of a flat Boolean circuit is a pair $(k, r)$ of a natural
number $k$ (its kind) and a list $r$ of natural numbers (its references), in the shared encoding
of gates as (kind, references) pairs.

articles.title: Keyed function families in P/poly
articles.statement:
Let $F = (F_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a keyed family of
Boolean functions: $F_n(k, x)$ is a Boolean value for every key $k \in \{0,1\}^{n^2}$ and every
input $x \in \{0,1\}^n$. Then $F$ is in P/poly when there is a polynomial $p$ with natural-number
coefficients such that for every $n$ some circuit, given as a list of at most $p(n)$ encoded
gates, computes $F_n$: for all $k$ and $x$, the evaluation of the circuit on the bitstring $kx$ of
length $n^2 + n$ (the bits of $k$ followed by the bits of $x$) has last gate value $F_n(k, x)$.

articles.title: Security of a keyed function family against truth-table distinguishers
articles.statement:
Let
$F = (F_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a keyed family of Boolean functions: $F_n(k, x)$ is a Boolean
value for every key $k \in \{0,1\}^{n^2}$ and every input $x \in \{0,1\}^n$. Write $F_{n,k}$ for the
Boolean function $x \mapsto F_n(k, x)$ on $n$ bits and $T(g)$ for the truth table of a Boolean
function $g$. Then $F$ is secure when the following holds for every polynomial $q$ with
natural-number coefficients and every sequence $(D_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of functions from
bitstrings to Booleans such that, for each $n$, some circuit given as a list of at most $q(2^n)$
encoded gates has last gate value $D_n(t)$ on every bitstring $t$: for every natural number $c$
there is a natural number $N$ such that for every $n \ge N$

$$\left| \frac{|\{k \in \{0,1\}^{n^2} : D_n(T(F_{n,k})) = \mathrm{true}\}|}{2^{n^2}} -
\frac{|\{g : D_n(T(g)) = \mathrm{true}\}|}{2^{2^n}} \right| \le \frac{1}{2^{nc}},$$

where $g$ ranges over all $2^{2^n}$ Boolean functions on $n$ bits. That is, a distinguisher
computed by circuits of size polynomial in the truth-table size $2^n$ tells a uniformly random
member of the family from a uniformly random Boolean function with advantage at most $2^{-cn}$
for all large $n$, for every $c$.

articles.title: Razborov-Rudich: the natural proofs barrier
articles.statement:
Let $F = (F_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a keyed
family of Boolean functions, where $F_n(k, x)$ is a Boolean value for every key
$k \in \{0,1\}^{n^2}$ and every input $x \in \{0,1\}^n$. If $F$ is in P/poly (computed by circuits
of size polynomial in $n$) and is secure against truth-table distinguishers, then there is no
property $C = (C_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, with $C_n$ a set of Boolean functions on $n$ bits, that
is both natural and useful against P/poly.

## Sources

- A. A. Razborov and S. Rudich, "Natural proofs", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 55 (1997), 24-35 (Proceedings of the Twenty-Sixth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing, STOC 1994, 18-27).

articles.title: Truth table
articles.statement:
The truth table of a Boolean function $g$ on $n$ bits is the list of the
$2^n$ values $g(x^{(0)}), g(x^{(1)}), \dots, g(x^{(2^n - 1)})$, where for $i < 2^n$ the input
$x^{(i)}$ has bit $j$ equal to the $j$-th binary digit $\lfloor i / 2^j \rfloor \bmod 2$ of $i$
(bit $0$ being the least significant), for every $j < n$.

articles.title: Usefulness against P/poly
articles.statement:
Let $C = (C_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, where $C_n$ is a set of
Boolean functions on $n$ bits. Then $C$ is useful against P/poly when, for every family
$f = (f_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of Boolean functions $f_n$ on $n$ bits such that $f_n \in C_n$ for
infinitely many $n$, the decision problem of $f$ is not in P/poly. Equivalently, if the decision
problem of a family $f$ is in P/poly, then $f_n \in C_n$ for only finitely many $n$.

articles.title: Nondeterministic time hierarchy
articles.statement:
Source: S. A. Cook, "A hierarchy for nondeterministic
time complexity", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 7 (1973), 343-353; S. Zak, "A
Turing machine time hierarchy", Theoretical Computer Science 26 (1983), 327-333.

articles.title: Baker-Gill-Solovay: oracles separate and collapse P vs NP
articles.statement:
For an oracle $O$, a function
from bitstrings to booleans, write $\mathsf{P}^O$ and $\mathsf{NP}^O$ for the classes of decision
problems decidable in polynomial time, respectively in nondeterministic polynomial time, by
machines that may query $O$. There is an oracle $O$ such that $\mathsf{P}^O \ne \mathsf{NP}^O$,
and there is an oracle $O$ such that $\mathsf{P}^O = \mathsf{NP}^O$.

## Sources

- T. Baker, J. Gill, and R. Solovay, "Relativizations of the P =? NP question", SIAM Journal on Computing 4 (1975), 431-442.

articles.title: An oracle separates NP from coNP
articles.statement:
There is an oracle $O$, a function from bitstrings to
booleans, such that $\mathrm{NP}^O$ differs from the class $\mathrm{coNP}^O$ of decision problems
$L$ whose complement, the decision problem that accepts exactly the bitstrings that $L$ rejects,
belongs to $\mathrm{NP}^O$.

## Sources

- T. Baker, J. Gill, and R. Solovay, "Relativizations of the P =? NP question", SIAM Journal on Computing 4 (1975), 431-442 (oracles separating NP from coNP); S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Chapter 3 (relativization).

articles.title: There is a PSPACE language outside L (space-hierarchy separation)
articles.statement:
There is a decision
problem that belongs to PSPACE but not to the class $\mathsf{L}$ of decision problems decidable
in deterministic logarithmic space.

## Sources

- R. W. Stearns, J. Hartmanis, and P. M. Lewis II, "Hierarchies of memory limited computations" (1965); S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009.

articles.title: Deterministic space hierarchy: quadratic versus linear space
articles.statement:
There is a language $L$
of bitstrings that lies in $\mathrm{DSPACE}(n^2)$ but not in $\mathrm{DSPACE}(n)$, the
deterministic space classes of multi-tape Turing machines for the space bounds $n \mapsto n^2$
and $n \mapsto n$.

## Sources

- R. W. Stearns, J. Hartmanis, and P. M. Lewis II, "Hierarchies of memory limited computations", Proceedings of the Sixth Annual Symposium on Switching Circuit Theory and Logical Design (1965), 179-190.

articles.title: Answer of the checking machine
articles.statement:
For a bit list $x$, the answer is the list $x$ with
the bit $\mathrm{true}$ put in front if the cell-by-cell check of $x$ from the key $(0, 0)$
succeeds, and the one-bit list $[\mathrm{false}]$ otherwise.

articles.title: The readout on raw bits in polynomial time
articles.statement:
A finite multi-stack Turing machine, whose
input and output alphabets are identified with the bits, together with a polynomial time bound,
such that for every bit list $l$, given $l$ as its input, it halts within the bound, evaluated at
$|l|$, with output the one-bit list $[b]$, where $b$ is true if and only if $l$ differs from the
output encoding of the result whose output is the single symbol $2$ of the bit true, that is,
from the list true, true, true, false.

articles.title: Decoding a list of cells
articles.statement:
For a bit list $x$, the list of natural numbers $l$ whose
cells are $x$, if there is one, and nothing otherwise. Here the cells of $l$ are its numbers
written in order, each number $n$ as $n$ copies of $\mathrm{true}$ followed by one
$\mathrm{false}$; distinct lists have distinct cells. The decoder reads one cell at a time
with the unary length reader.

articles.title: The cell-by-cell check recognizes code stacks
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $p_q, p_a$ and
every bit list $x$, the cell-by-cell check of $x$ from the key $(p_q, p_a)$ succeeds if and only
if there is a list of $m \ge 0$ entries $(q_1, a_1, q'_1, s_1), \dots, (q_m, a_m, q'_m, s_m)$ of
natural numbers such that $x$ is the concatenation of the cells of
$q_1, a_1, q'_1, s_1, \dots, q_m, a_m, q'_m, s_m$, in this order, and the keys $(q_i, a_i)$
strictly increase in lexicographic order, starting at $(p_q, p_a)$ or above. Here the cell of a
number $n$ is $n$ bits $\mathrm{true}$ followed by one bit $\mathrm{false}$.

articles.title: The cell-by-cell check agrees with code-stack decoding
articles.statement:
For every bit list $x$, the
cell-by-cell check of $x$ from the key $(0, 0)$ succeeds if and only if the decoding of $x$ as a
code stack returns a code.

articles.title: Cell-by-cell check of a code stack
articles.statement:
The check of a bit list $x$ from a key $(p_q, p_a)$
of natural numbers is defined as follows. The empty list passes. Otherwise, calling the cell of a
number $n$ the $n$ bits $\mathrm{true}$ followed by one bit $\mathrm{false}$, read four cells off
the front of $x$, those of $q$, $a$, $q'$ and $s$ in this order, leaving the rest $r$. The check
fails if one of these cells cannot be read because what remains contains no bit
$\mathrm{false}$, or if the key $(q, a)$ is lexicographically below $(p_q, p_a)$, that is,
unless $p_q < q$, or $p_q = q$ and $p_a \le a$. Otherwise its result is the check of $r$ from
the key $(q, a + 1)$.

The reformatting machine checks its input this way.

articles.title: Decoding inverts the code stack
articles.statement:
For every bit list $x$ and every code $c$, if $x$
decodes to $c$, then the code stack of $c$ is $x$.

articles.title: The code of a list of entries
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a list of entries $(q, a, q', s)$ of natural
numbers, and let $Q$ and $M$ be the sums, over the entries of $E$ counted with multiplicity, of
$q + 1$ and of $a + 1$ respectively. The code of $E$ has a table with $Q$ rows and $M$
columns, and for $q < Q$ and $a < M$ its position $(q, a)$ holds $(q', s)$ for the first entry
$(q, a, q', s)$ of $E$ with key $(q, a)$, and is empty (halting) if $E$ has no entry with that
key.

articles.title: Some step is needed
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $f(0) = 0$. Then no
decision problem is decided by a code within $f(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$: the time class
$\mathrm{CodeTime}(f)$ is empty. With no step on the empty input, the tape stays blank and
holds no answer bit.

articles.title: Monotonicity of time classes on codes
articles.statement:
Let $t, t' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with
$t(n) \le t'(n)$ for every $n$. Then every decision problem that some code decides within
$t(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$ is decided by some code within $t'(|x|)$ steps on every
input $x$: $\mathrm{CodeTime}(t) \subseteq \mathrm{CodeTime}(t')$.

articles.title: A hierarchy within codes, given an upper bound
articles.statement:
Let $f, g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
with $f(n) \le g(n)$ for every $n$, and for a time bound $t$ let $\mathrm{CodeTime}(t)$ be the
class of decision problems that some code decides within $t(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$.
If the diagonal language $\mathrm{diag}(f)$ belongs to $\mathrm{CodeTime}(g)$, then
$\mathrm{CodeTime}(f)$ is a proper subclass of $\mathrm{CodeTime}(g)$.

articles.title: Time classes on codes
articles.statement:
For $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, $\mathrm{CodeTime}(t)$ is
the class of decision problems $L$ such that some code decides $L$ within $t(|x|)$ steps on
every input $x$.

articles.title: The layout machine as a host component
articles.statement:
The component machine with the twelve stacks
$X, Z, P, P_2, U, N, A_2, B_2, D, C, T, O$ of the layout machine, each holding bits, with the
labels and the program of the layout machine, and with its stacks listed in the order
$X, Z, P, P_2, U, N, A_2, B_2, D, C, T, O$.

articles.title: The readout machine as a host component
articles.statement:
The component machine whose stacks are the
input $X$ and the output $O$, each over the alphabet of bits, whose labels and program are
those of the readout machine, which checks whether $X$ holds exactly
$(\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false})$ and pushes $\mathrm{false}$ on
$O$ if so and $\mathrm{true}$ otherwise, and whose list of stacks is $(X, O)$.

articles.title: The checking machine as a host component
articles.statement:
The component machine with the twelve stacks
$X, Y, W, V, Q, A, P_Q, P_A, T_1, T_2, J, O$ of the checking machine, each holding bits, with
the labels and the program of the checking machine, and with its stacks listed in the order
$X, Y, W, V, Q, A, P_Q, P_A, T_1, T_2, J, O$.

articles.title: The constant-false code decides the empty language
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be the code whose table has
one row, for state $0$: on the input symbols $1$ and $2$ it moves right and stays in state $0$,
and on the blank $0$ it writes $1$, the symbol of the bit $\mathrm{false}$, and enters state
$1$, which has no row, so that $c$ halts. Then $c$ decides the empty language within $n + 1$
steps on every input of length $n$.

articles.title: Time classes are not empty once the bound exceeds the input length
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $n + 1 \le f(n)$ for every $n$. Then the empty language, the
decision problem that answers false on every bit list, belongs to the time class of $f$: some code
decides it within $f(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$, where $|x|$ is the length of $x$.

articles.title: The constant-false code
articles.statement:
The code whose table has a single row, for state $0$: on the
blank $0$ it writes the symbol $1$, the symbol of the bit false, and enters state $1$; on the input
symbols $1$ and $2$ it moves right and stays in state $0$; on every other symbol it halts. State $1$
has no row, so the machine halts there. This code answers false on every input.

articles.title: Deciding within a time bound
articles.statement:
A code $c$ decides a decision problem $L$ within the time
bound $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ when, on every bit list $x$, the machine of $c$ started on the
input word of $x$ halts within $t(|x|)$ steps, and its tape from the head rightwards, without
trailing blanks, is the single symbol of the answer $L(x)$: $2$ for true and $1$ for false.

articles.title: Code stacks decode to codes with the same code stack
articles.statement:
For every code $c$, decoding the code
stack of $c$ succeeds and returns a code $c'$ whose code stack equals the code stack of $c$.

articles.title: Decoding a code stack
articles.statement:
For a bit list $x$, the decoding of $x$ as a code is defined as
follows. Write the cell of a number $n$ for the $n$ bits true followed by one bit false, and the
cells of a list of numbers for the cells of its numbers in order. If $x$ is the cells of a list
$l$ of natural numbers (such an $l$ is unique), the length of $l$ is a multiple of $4$, and the
keys $(q, a)$ of the entries $(q, a, q', s)$ formed by the consecutive groups of four numbers of
$l$ strictly increase in lexicographic order, then the decoding of $x$ is the code of these
entries. Otherwise the decoding returns no code.

The code stack of a code is the cells of the numbers $q, a, q', s$ of its entries
$(q, a, q', s)$, listed by increasing key $(q, a)$; codes with the same code stack have the same
clocked evaluator.

articles.title: The diagonal answer read from the encoded output
articles.statement:
For every clocked result $o$, either a
timeout or the output of a halted run, the diagonal answer of $o$ is true exactly when the output
encoding of $o$ differs from the output encoding of the result whose output is the single symbol
$2$ of the bit true, which is the bit list true, true, true, false.

articles.title: The diagonal answer
articles.statement:
For a clocked result $o$, either a timeout or the output of a halted
run, the diagonal answer of $o$ is false if $o$ is the output consisting of the single symbol $2$,
the symbol of the bit true, and true otherwise, including on a timeout.

articles.title: The universal machine's argument for the diagonal language
articles.statement:
For a time bound
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a bit list $x$, the argument is a triple of a code, an input and
a clock. If $x$ decodes to a code $c$, it is $(c, x, f(|x|))$. Otherwise it is the code with the
empty table, the input consisting of the single bit true, and the clock $0$; that code halts at
once with the answer true, so that the diagonal answer is false there.

articles.title: The diagonal language through the universal machine
articles.statement:
For every time bound
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every code $c$ with code stack $x$, the bit list $x$ belongs to
the diagonal language for $f$ iff the output encoding of the result of running $c$ on $x$ for at
most $f(|x|)$ steps differs from the output encoding of the result whose output is the single
symbol $2$ of the bit true.

The clocked universal machine reads the input encoding of a code, an input and a clock $T$ and
writes the output encoding of the result of running the code on the input for at most $T$ steps,
so the condition is read from its output on $c$, $x$ and $f(|x|)$.

articles.title: The diagonal language on a code stack
articles.statement:
For every time bound
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every code $c$ with code stack $x$, the bit list $x$ belongs to
the diagonal language for $f$ iff it is not the case that $c$, run on $x$, halts within $f(|x|)$
steps with output the single symbol $2$ of the bit true.

articles.title: The diagonal language through the clocked evaluator
articles.statement:
For every
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every bit list $x$, let $(c, y, T)$ be the universal machine's
argument for the diagonal language of $f$ on $x$. Then the diagonal language of $f$ holds at $x$
iff the clocked evaluator, running $c$ on $y$ for at most $T$ steps, does not return the output
$[2]$, the symbol of the answer true.

articles.title: Bit lists that encode no code are outside the diagonal language
articles.statement:
For every
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every bit list $x$ that is the code stack of no code, $x$ is not
in the diagonal language of $f$.

articles.title: The diagonal argument
articles.statement:
For every $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the diagonal language of
$f$ is not in the time class of $f$ on codes: no code decides it on every input $x$ within
$f(|x|)$ steps. This is the argument from the proof of Sipser's Theorem 9.10: a code $c$ deciding
it would, on its own code stack, answer the opposite of the diagonal language of $f$.

articles.title: The quadratic diagonal language is in P
articles.statement:
The diagonal language for the time bound
$f(n) = n^2 + 1$, the set of bit lists $x$ that encode a code which does not halt on $x$ within
$|x|^2 + 1$ steps with the answer $\mathrm{true}$, is in the class P of decision problems
decidable in polynomial time.

The decider decodes the canonical encoding of bit lists and then runs a polynomial-time decider
on the raw bits.

articles.title: The diagonal language
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the diagonal language of $f$
holds at a bit list $x$ iff $x$ encodes a code $c$ and the clocked evaluator, running $c$ on $x$
for at most $f(|x|)$ steps, does not return the output $[2]$, the symbol of the answer true:
either $c$ does not halt on $x$ within $f(|x|)$ steps, or it halts with another output. Bit lists
that encode no code are not in the language. This is the diagonal language of the proof of
Sipser's Theorem 9.10.

articles.title: The reformatting function in bits
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a bit list $x$,
the input bits of the clocked universal machine on its argument for the diagonal language of $f$
on $x$ are, when $x$ encodes a code, the cell of $f(|x|)$, then the cells of the input symbols of
$x$, then the bit false, then $x$ reversed; when $x$ encodes no code, they are the fixed list
$[\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}]$.

articles.title: Reading entries from numbers
articles.statement:
A list of natural numbers is read as a list of entries
$(q, a, q', s)$, four consecutive numbers per entry, if possible: the empty list gives no entries;
a list that starts with $q, a, q', s$ and continues with $l$ gives the entry $(q, a, q', s)$
followed by the entries read from $l$, if that succeeds; and the reading fails when the length of
the list is not a multiple of $4$.

articles.title: The code stack determines the clocked semantics
articles.statement:
Codes with the same code stack have the
same clocked evaluator.

articles.title: Diagonalization across models
articles.statement:
There is a decision problem in the class P that no code
decides within $n^2 + 1$ steps: no code halts on every input $x$ within $|x|^2 + 1$ steps with
the answer for $x$ as its output.

The diagonal language for the time bound $n \mapsto n^2 + 1$ is such a problem. The class of
problems that codes decide within $n^2 + 1$ steps is not empty: it contains the problem whose
answer is always $\mathrm{false}$.

articles.title: Expecting a bit in the readout machine
articles.statement:
For a bit $b$ and a label $\ell$, the statement
that pops the top of the input stack $X$ and goes to $\ell$ if the popped symbol is $b$, and to the
label miss otherwise, including when $X$ is empty.

articles.title: Code stacks, entry by entry
articles.statement:
A bit list $x$ encodes a code (its decoding succeeds) iff
there is a list of entries $(q, a, q', s)$ of natural numbers whose keys $(q, a)$ strictly
increase in lexicographic order, such that $x$ is the list of cells of the numbers of these
entries, four numbers per entry.

articles.title: Code stacks are recognized
articles.statement:
For every bit list $x$, the decoding of $x$ as a code
succeeds iff $x$ is the code stack of some code.

articles.title: Stacks of the layout machine
articles.statement:
The layout machine has twelve stacks, named
$X, Z, P, P_2, U, N, A_2, B_2, D, C, T, O$.

articles.title: Stacks of the readout machine
articles.statement:
The readout machine, which reads the answer of the
diagonal language off the output of the clocked universal machine, has exactly two stacks: the
input stack $X$ and the output stack $O$.

articles.title: Stacks of the checking machine
articles.statement:
The checking machine has twelve stacks, named
$X, Y, W, V, Q, A, P_Q, P_A, T_1, T_2, J, O$.

articles.title: Ascending keys of a list of entries
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $p_q$, $p_a$ and a list of
entries $(q, a, q', s) \in \mathbb{N}^4$, this Boolean test is true exactly when the keys
$(q, a)$ of the entries strictly increase in lexicographic order and the first key, if there is
one, is at least $(p_q, p_a)$ in that order.

articles.title: Labels of the layout machine
articles.statement:
The layout machine has 17 labels, named $\mathsf{s0}$,
$\mathsf{mvZ}$, $\mathsf{cp0}$, $\mathsf{cp1}$, $\mathsf{lo0}$, $\mathsf{lo1}$, $\mathsf{lo2}$,
$\mathsf{lo3}$, $\mathsf{lo4}$, $\mathsf{mh}$, $\mathsf{mb}$, $\mathsf{mk}$, $\mathsf{mr}$,
$\mathsf{lo5}$, $\mathsf{lo6}$, $\mathsf{bad}$ and $\mathsf{done}$.

articles.title: Labels of the readout machine
articles.statement:
The readout machine has eight labels: $r_0$, $r_1$,
$r_2$ and $r_3$ read in turn the bits $\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true},
\mathrm{false}$, which encode, at the output of the clocked universal machine, a halt whose
output is the single symbol of the bit $\mathrm{true}$; $r_4$ checks that no bit follows;
$\mathrm{hit}$ and $\mathrm{miss}$ write the answer; and $\mathrm{done}$ stops.

articles.title: Labels of the checking machine
articles.statement:
The labels of the checking machine: 23 labels without
arguments and four families of labels indexed by the outcome of a comparison ($<$, $=$ or $>$),
35 distinct labels in all.

articles.title: Layout after checking gives the universal machine's input
articles.statement:
For every bit list $x$, let
$(c, y, T)$ be the universal machine's argument for the diagonal language of $f(n) = n^2 + 1$ on
$x$. Then the layout function applied to the checking machine's answer on $x$ equals the input
bit list of the clocked universal machine for the code $c$, the input $y$ and the clock $T$.

articles.title: The layout function
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{cell}(n)$ for the bit list of $n$ bits
$\mathrm{true}$ followed by one bit $\mathrm{false}$. On a bit list $\mathrm{true} :: x$, the
layout function returns $\mathrm{cell}(|x|^2 + 1)$, then the cells $\mathrm{cell}(s)$ of the
symbols $s$ of the input word of $x$ (the symbol $2$ for each bit $\mathrm{true}$ and $1$ for
each bit $\mathrm{false}$), then the bit $\mathrm{false}$, then the reverse of $x$. On every other
bit list, that is, the empty list or a list starting with $\mathrm{false}$, it returns the list
$[\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}]$.

articles.title: The code stack determines the table lookups
articles.statement:
If two codes $c$ and $c'$ have the same
code stack, then for every state $q$ and every symbol $a$, the table entry of $c$ at $(q, a)$
equals the table entry of $c'$ at $(q, a)$.

articles.title: Deciding within a larger time bound
articles.statement:
If a code $c$ decides a decision problem $L$
within a time bound $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, and $t' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
satisfies $t(n) \le t'(n)$ for every $n$, then $c$ decides $L$ within $t'$.

articles.title: The diagonal language in polynomial time, given the reformatting machine
articles.statement:
Let
$f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. Suppose that a finite multi-stack Turing machine, the
reformatting machine, computes in polynomial time, from a bit list $x$ given as itself, the
input $\mathrm{encIn}(c, y, T)$ of the clocked universal machine, where
$(c, y, T) = \mathrm{diagArg}_f(x)$ is the argument of the clocked universal function for the
diagonal language $\mathrm{diag}_f$ on $x$. Then a finite multi-stack Turing machine computes
$\mathrm{diag}_f$ in polynomial time: on every bit list $x$, given as itself, it outputs the
one-bit list $[\mathrm{diag}_f(x)]$.

The machine runs the reformatting machine, then the clocked universal machine, then the
readout machine.

articles.title: Deciding the diagonal language on raw bits in polynomial time
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be the diagonal
language for the time bound $f(n) = n^2 + 1$. There is a finite multi-stack Turing machine that,
given a bit list $x$ as its input, halts within a number of steps polynomial in $|x|$ with the
single bit $D(x)$ as its output.

articles.title: Polynomial time is not contained in code time $n^2 + 1$
articles.statement:
Some decision problem in
$\mathsf{P}$ is decided by no code within $n^2 + 1$ steps on every input of length $n$; that is,
$\mathsf{P}$ is not a subset of the class $\mathrm{CodeTime}(n \mapsto n^2 + 1)$.

articles.title: Branch after comparing symbols
articles.statement:
The label the checking machine goes to after comparing
the bound $p$ for the symbol with the symbol $a$ of the current key: if $p > a$, the label
$\mathsf{bad}$, where it rejects; if $p < a$ or $p = a$, the label $\mathsf{sk0}$, where it starts
skipping the rest of the entry.

articles.title: Branch after comparing states
articles.statement:
The label the checking machine goes to after comparing the
bound $p$ for the state (the state of the previous key, or $0$ at the first entry) with the
state $q$ of the current key: if $p < q$, the label $\mathsf{sk0}$, where it starts skipping the
rest of the entry; if $p = q$, the label $\mathsf{ca}$, where it compares the symbols; if
$p > q$, the label $\mathsf{bad}$, where it rejects.

articles.title: There is an EXP language outside P (time-hierarchy separation)
articles.statement:
There is a decision
problem that belongs to the class EXP but not to the complexity class P.

Only this separation is stated; the containment of P in EXP is not part of the statement.

## Sources

- J. Hartmanis and R. E. Stearns, "On the computational complexity of algorithms", Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 117 (1965), 285-306; S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Corollary 3.5.

articles.title: The layout in polynomial time
articles.statement:
A finite multi-stack Turing machine, whose input and
output alphabets are identified with the bits, together with a polynomial time bound, that
computes the layout function: given a bit list $y$ as its input, it halts within the bound,
evaluated at $|y|$, with the layout of $y$ as its output.

articles.title: The readout in polynomial time
articles.statement:
A finite multi-stack Turing machine, given the output
encoding $\mathrm{encOut}(o)$ of a result $o$ of the clocked universal function (a list of
symbols, or a timeout), outputs the one-bit list $[\mathrm{diagAnswer}(o)]$ within a number
of steps polynomial in the length of $\mathrm{encOut}(o)$. Here $\mathrm{diagAnswer}(o)$ is
$\mathrm{true}$ unless $o$ is a halt whose output is the single symbol of the bit
$\mathrm{true}$.

articles.title: The checking machine in polynomial time
articles.statement:
A finite multi-stack Turing machine with a
polynomial time bound that computes the checking answer: given a bit list $x$ as its input, it
halts within the bound, evaluated at $|x|$, with the checking answer on $x$ as its output.

articles.title: Program of the layout machine
articles.statement:
Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, this is the
program of a multi-stack machine whose stacks $X, Z, P, P_2, U, N, A_2, B_2, D, C, T, O$ all hold
bits. To move a stack $S$ onto a stack $S'$ means to pop the bits of $S$ one at a time, pushing
each onto $S'$, until $S$ is empty; to transfer $S$ to some stacks means to pop $S$ until it is
empty, pushing a $1$ on each of these stacks for every bit popped. From the label $\mathsf{s0}$
the program pops $X$. If $X$ was empty or the popped bit is $0$, it pushes $0, 0, 1, 1, 0$ on $O$
in this order and halts. Otherwise it moves $X$ onto $Z$, and then, as long as $Z$ is nonempty,
it pops a bit $b$ from $Z$, pushes $b$ on $U$ and a $1$ on $N$, and pushes $0, 1, 1$ on $P$ in
this order if $b = 1$ and $0, 1$ if $b = 0$. Then it moves $U$ onto $O$, pushes a $0$ on $O$,
moves $P$ onto $P_2$ and then $P_2$ onto $O$, and transfers $N$ to $A_2$ and $B_2$. Then it
loops: it pops $A_2$; if a bit was popped, it pushes a $1$ on $D$, transfers $B_2$ to $C$ and
$T$, transfers $T$ to $B_2$ and loops again; if $A_2$ was empty, it transfers $D$ to $A_2$.
Finally it pushes $0, 1$ on $O$ in this order, transfers $C$ to $O$ and halts.

articles.title: Program of the readout machine
articles.statement:
The readout machine pops the bits of its input stack
$X$ one at a time and compares them with $\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true},
\mathrm{false}$, which encode, at the output of the clocked universal machine, a halt whose
output is the single symbol of the bit $\mathrm{true}$. If the input is exactly this list, it
pushes $\mathrm{false}$ onto its output stack $O$; otherwise (at the first bit that differs,
when the input ends early, or when a fifth bit follows) it pushes $\mathrm{true}$. Then it
halts.

articles.title: Program of the checking machine
articles.statement:
Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, this is the
program of a multi-stack machine whose stacks $X, Y, W, V, Q, A, P_Q, P_A, T_1, T_2, J, O$ all
hold bits. To read a cell from $V$ onto a stack $S$ means to pop the leading $1$s of $V$, pushing
a $1$ on $S$ for each, and then to pop the $0$ that follows; if $V$ is empty at that point, the
machine rejects. From its first label the program pops the bits of $X$ one at a time, pushing
each onto both $Y$ and $W$, and then pops the bits of $W$ one at a time onto $V$. Then it loops.
If $V$ is empty, it pops the bits of $Y$ one at a time onto $O$, pushes a $1$ on $O$ and halts.
Otherwise it reads a cell from $V$ onto $Q$ and then one onto $A$. With $p_Q$, $q$, $p_A$, $a$
the numbers of bits on $P_Q$, $Q$, $P_A$, $A$, it compares $p_Q$ with $q$ and, if they are
equal, $p_A$ with $a$, afterwards pushing back as many $1$s as it popped from each. If
$p_Q > q$, or $p_Q = q$ and $p_A > a$, it rejects; otherwise it reads two more cells from $V$
onto $J$, empties $P_Q$ and $P_A$, moves $Q$ onto $P_Q$ and $A$ onto $P_A$ (pushing a $1$ for
each bit popped), pushes one more $1$ on $P_A$ and loops again. Rejecting pushes a single $0$ on
$O$ and halts.

articles.title: Reading a unary length prefix reads one cell
articles.statement:
For bit lists $x$ and $r$ and a natural
number $n$, reading a unary length prefix of $x$ returns $n$ together with the rest $r$ if and
only if $x$ is the cell of $n$ (that is, $n$ copies of $\mathrm{true}$ followed by
$\mathrm{false}$) followed by $r$.

articles.title: The reformatting machine for $n \mapsto n^2 + 1$
articles.statement:
Let $f(n) = n^2 + 1$. This is a
finite multi-stack Turing machine whose input and output alphabets are identified with the bits,
together with a polynomial $p$, such that for every bit list $x$, started with $x$ on its input
stack it halts within $p(|x|)$ steps with output the clocked universal machine's input bits for
the universal machine's argument $(c, w, T)$ for the diagonal language of $f$ at $x$: the clock
$T$ as a cell, the cells of the input symbols of $w$, a blank cell and the code stack of $c$
reversed. It runs the checking machine and then the layout machine.

articles.title: The layout run
articles.statement:
For every bit list $y$, the layout machine, started at the label
$\mathsf{s0}$ with internal state false, with $y$ on its input stack $X$ and every other stack
empty, reaches the label $\mathsf{done}$ within $18(|y| + 1)^2$ steps, with some internal state
and stacks in which the output stack $O$ holds the layout of $y$.

articles.title: The readout run
articles.statement:
Let $l$ be a bit list, and start the readout machine at the label
$r_0$ with its internal Boolean variable set to $\mathrm{false}$, $l$ on the input stack $X$ and
the output stack $O$ empty. Then the machine reaches the label $\mathrm{done}$ within $6$ steps,
and $O$ then holds exactly one bit, which is $\mathrm{true}$ if and only if
$l \ne [\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}]$, the list that encodes, at
the output of the clocked universal machine, a halt whose output is the single symbol of the bit
$\mathrm{true}$.

articles.title: The checking run
articles.statement:
For every bit list $x$, the checking machine, started at the label
$\mathsf{dupP}$ with internal state false, with $x$ on its input stack $X$ and every other stack
empty, reaches the label $\mathsf{done}$ within $33(|x| + 1)^2$ steps, with some internal state
and stacks in which the output stack $O$ holds the answer of the checking machine on $x$.

articles.title: Deterministic time hierarchy: quadratic versus linear time
articles.statement:
There is a language $L$ of
bitstrings that lies in the multi-tape deterministic time class $\mathrm{DTIME}(n^2)$ but not in
$\mathrm{DTIME}(n)$.

## Sources

- J. Hartmanis and R. E. Stearns, "On the computational complexity of algorithms", Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 117 (1965), 285-306.

articles.title: Stack symbols of the layout machine
articles.statement:
Every stack of the layout machine holds bits: the
alphabet of each of its stacks is the type of Booleans.

articles.title: Stack alphabet of the readout machine
articles.statement:
Every stack of the readout machine, namely
the input stack $X$ and the output stack $O$, has the alphabet of bits.

articles.title: Stack alphabet of the layout machine
articles.statement:
Every stack of the layout machine holds bits: the
alphabet of each stack is the type of Booleans.

articles.title: Description of a code running on an input
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code for a partial recursive
function and let $n$ be its number in the standard encoding of codes as natural numbers. For a
binary string $w$, the description of $c$ running on $w$ is the binary string $1^n 0 w$, that is,
$n$ ones, then a zero, then $w$.

articles.title: Optimality (the invariance theorem)
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a partial recursive function from binary
strings to binary strings, viewed as a description method. Then there is a natural number $c$
such that for all binary strings $x$ and $p$ for which $D(p)$ is defined and equals $x$, the
Kolmogorov complexity of $x$ satisfies $K(x) \le |p| + c$, where $|p|$ is the length of $p$.

articles.title: Shortest descriptions exist
articles.statement:
For every binary string $x$ there is a binary string $p$
whose length is the Kolmogorov complexity $K(x)$ and such that $U(p)$ is defined and equals $x$,
where $U$ is the universal description method.

articles.title: Every partial recursive description method has a code
articles.statement:
Let $D$ be a partial recursive
function from binary strings to binary strings. Then there is a code $c$ for a partial recursive
function such that running $c$ equals $D$ as a partial function: for every binary string $w$,
running $c$ on $w$ is defined exactly when $D(w)$ is, and then has the same value.

articles.title: Most strings are incompressible
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n$ and $c$, fewer than
$2^{n-c}$ binary strings of length $n$ have Kolmogorov complexity less than $n - c$, where
$n - c$ is read as $0$ when $c > n$.

Hence at least $2^n - 2^{n-c} + 1$ strings of length $n$ have complexity at least $n - c$.

articles.title: Few strings have small complexity
articles.statement:
Fewer than `2 ^ m` strings have complexity below `m`.
Padding their shortest descriptions to length `m` maps them injectively to strings of length `m`
other than `0ᵐ`.

articles.title: Incompressible strings exist at every length
articles.statement:
Some string of length `n` has complexity at
least `n`.

articles.title: Kolmogorov complexity is not computable
articles.statement:
The function sending each binary string $x$
to its Kolmogorov complexity $K(x)$ is not computable: no partial recursive function, acting on
binary strings through their encodings as natural numbers, halts on every binary string $x$ with
output $K(x)$.

The proof is a form of Berry's paradox.

articles.title: Padding a string to a given length
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a binary string $p$, the
padding of $p$ to length $n$ is the string $0^k 1 p$ with $k = \max(n - 1 - |p|, 0)$; when
$|p| < n$ it has length $n$.

articles.title: Binary strings of a given length
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the finite set of all binary
strings of length $n$.

articles.title: Concatenation costs at most twice the first part
articles.statement:
There is a natural number $c$ such that
for all binary strings $x$ and $y$, the Kolmogorov complexity of their concatenation $xy$
satisfies $K(xy) \le 2K(x) + K(y) + c$.

articles.title: Doubling costs a constant
articles.statement:
There is a natural number $c$ such that for every binary string
$x$, the Kolmogorov complexity of the concatenation $xx$ of $x$ with itself satisfies
$K(xx) \le K(x) + c$.

articles.title: Complexity is at most the length plus a constant
articles.statement:
There is a natural number $c$ such that
every binary string $x$ satisfies $K(x) \le |x| + c$, where $K(x)$ is the Kolmogorov complexity
of $x$ and $|x|$ is its length.

articles.title: A description bounds the complexity
articles.statement:
Let $x$ and $p$ be binary strings such that $U(p)$ is
defined and equals $x$, where $U$ is the universal description method. Then the Kolmogorov
complexity of $x$ is at most the length of $p$: $K(x) \le |p|$.

articles.title: Kolmogorov complexity
articles.statement:
The Kolmogorov complexity $K(x)$ of a binary string $x$ is the
least length of a binary string $p$ such that $U(p)$ is defined and equals $x$, where $U$ is the
universal description method.

articles.title: Pair description
articles.statement:
For binary strings $p$ and $q$, the pair description of $p$ and $q$ is
the binary string $1^{|p|} 0 p q$, that is, $|p|$ ones, where $|p|$ is the length of $p$, then a
zero, then $p$, then $q$.

The prefix $1^{|p|} 0$ records the length of $p$, so the string splits back into $p$ and $q$.

articles.title: Reading pair descriptions
articles.statement:
Write a binary string $s$ as $1^n s'$, where $n$ is the number
of leading $1$s, and let $r$ be $s'$ without its first letter ($r$ is empty when $s'$ is). Let
$r_1$ be the first $\min(n, |r|)$ letters of $r$ and $r_2$ the remaining ones. The pair reader
maps $s$ to the concatenation $U(r_1)\,U(r_2)$, where $U$ is the universal description method,
and is undefined when $U(r_1)$ or $U(r_2)$ is undefined. On a pair description $1^n 0 r$ with
$|r| \ge n$, this is the concatenation of what the first $n$ letters of $r$ and the rest
describe.

articles.title: The universal description method is partial recursive
articles.statement:
The universal description
method, as a partial function from binary strings to binary strings, is partial recursive.

articles.title: Running a program on a binary string
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ of a partial recursive function on
the natural numbers and a binary string $w$, running $c$ on $w$ evaluates $c$ at the number
encoding $w$; if this halts with output $m$, the result is the binary string encoded by $m$. The
result is undefined when the evaluation does not halt or $m$ encodes no binary string.

articles.title: The universal description method
articles.statement:
A description `1ⁿ 0 w` runs code number `n` on `w`;
a string of `1`s describes nothing.

articles.title: A computable lower bound of Kolmogorov complexity is bounded
articles.statement:
Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov
complexity. If $f$ is a computable function from binary strings to natural numbers with
$f(x) \le K(x)$ for every binary string $x$, then there is a natural number $B$ with $f(x) \le B$
for every binary string $x$.

articles.title: Chaitin's incompleteness theorem
articles.statement:
Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov complexity, and let $S$ be a
recursively enumerable (recognizable) set of pairs $(x, n)$ of a binary string $x$ and a natural
number $n$ such that $n \le K(x)$ for every $(x, n) \in S$. Then there is a natural number $B$
with $n \le B$ for every $(x, n) \in S$.

This is the abstract form of the theorem: think of $S$ as the statements $K(x) \ge n$ that a sound
formal system proves. The proof searches $S$ for a pair with a large bound $n$ and applies
optimality of the universal description method (Berry's paradox).

articles.title: A partial recursive map raises complexity by at most a constant
articles.statement:
Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov
complexity and let $f$ be a partial recursive function from binary strings to binary strings.
Then there is a natural number $c$ such that $K(y) \le K(x) + c$ for all binary strings $x$ and
$y$ such that $f(x)$ is defined and equal to $y$.

articles.title: Shortest descriptions are incompressible
articles.statement:
Let $U$ be the universal description method,
$K$ Kolmogorov complexity, and $|p|$ the length of a binary string $p$. There is a natural number
$b$ such that for all binary strings $x$ and $p$, if $p$ is a shortest description of $x$, that
is, $U(p)$ is defined and equal to $x$ and $|p| = K(x)$, then $|p| \le K(p) + b$.

articles.title: The incompressible strings are not decidable
articles.statement:
Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov complexity and
$|x|$ the length of a binary string $x$. The set of incompressible binary strings, that is, of
binary strings $x$ with $|x| \le K(x)$, is not decidable.

articles.title: The incompressible strings are not recognizable
articles.statement:
Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov complexity
and $|x|$ the length of a binary string $x$. The set of incompressible binary strings, that is,
of binary strings $x$ with $|x| \le K(x)$, is not recursively enumerable (recognizable).

articles.title: Kolmogorov complexity is not lower semicomputable
articles.statement:
Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov complexity.
The set of pairs $(x, n)$ of a binary string $x$ and a natural number $n$ with $n \le K(x)$ is not
recursively enumerable (recognizable).

articles.title: No recognizable set with arbitrarily long members consists of incompressible strings
articles.statement:
Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov complexity and $|x|$ the length of a binary string $x$. There is no
recursively enumerable (recognizable) set $S$ of binary strings such that for every natural
number $n$ some $x \in S$ has $|x| \ge n$, and every $x \in S$ satisfies $|x| \le K(x)$.

articles.title: Kolmogorov complexity is upper semicomputable
articles.statement:
Let $K$ denote Kolmogorov complexity. The
set of pairs $(x, n)$ of a binary string $x$ and a natural number $n$ with $K(x) \le n$ is
recursively enumerable (recognizable).

articles.title: The description relation is recognizable
articles.statement:
Let $U$ be the universal description method.
The set of pairs $(x, p)$ of binary strings such that $U(p)$ is defined and equal to $x$ is
recursively enumerable (recognizable).

articles.title: Decoding a length-prefixed clause
articles.statement:
Given a bit string $w$, writing $1$ for true and $0$
for false, the decoder reads a unary length prefix $1^n 0$ ($n$ ones followed by a zero) from the
front of $w$, then reads exactly $n$ literals from the remaining bits with the literal decoder.
The result is the clause made of these literals, in order, together with the bits left after
them. Decoding fails if $w$ does not begin with such a prefix or one of the literals cannot be
read.

articles.title: Decoding a fixed number of clauses
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a bit string $w$, the
decoder reads $n$ clauses one after another from the front of $w$ with the length-prefixed clause
decoder. The result is the CNF formula made of these clauses, in order, together with the bits
left after them; for $n = 0$ it is the empty formula together with $w$. Decoding fails if one of
the $n$ clauses cannot be read.

articles.title: The CNF decoder inverts the length-prefixed CNF code
articles.statement:
For every bit string $w$ and every
CNF formula $\varphi$, the complete CNF decoder returns $\varphi$ on input $w$ if and only if $w$
is the length-prefixed binary code of $\varphi$.

articles.title: Decoding a complete length-prefixed CNF formula
articles.statement:
Given a bit string $w$, the decoder reads
one CNF formula $\varphi$ from the front of $w$ with the length-prefixed CNF decoder, which also
returns the bits left after $\varphi$. The result is $\varphi$ if no bits are left; decoding fails
if no formula can be read or if bits remain after it.

articles.title: Decoding a length-prefixed CNF formula
articles.statement:
Given a bit string $w$, writing $1$ for true and
$0$ for false, the decoder reads a unary length prefix $1^n 0$ ($n$ ones followed by a zero) from
the front of $w$, then reads exactly $n$ clauses from the remaining bits with the length-prefixed
clause decoder. The result is the CNF formula made of these clauses, in order, together with the
bits left after them. Decoding fails if $w$ does not begin with such a prefix or one of the
clauses cannot be read.

articles.title: Decoding a literal
articles.statement:
Given a bit string $w$, the decoder reads a prefix-coded natural
number $n$ from the front of $w$ and then one more bit $b$. The result is the literal $(n, b)$,
with variable index $n$ and polarity $b$, together with the bits left after $b$. Decoding fails if
no prefix-coded natural number can be read or no bit follows it.

articles.title: Decoding a fixed number of literals
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and a bit string $w$, the
decoder reads $n$ literals one after another from the front of $w$ with the literal decoder. The
result is the clause made of these literals, in order, together with the bits left after them;
for $n = 0$ it is the empty clause together with $w$. Decoding fails if one of the $n$ literals
cannot be read.

articles.title: Decoding a prefix-coded natural number
articles.statement:
Given a bit string $w$, writing $1$ for true and
$0$ for false, the decoder reads one self-delimiting block $1\,b_1\,1\,b_2 \cdots 1\,b_k\,0$ from
the front of $w$, with payload $b_1 \cdots b_k$ and remaining bits $r$. If the payload is the
binary expansion of some natural number $n$, least significant bit first and without trailing
zeros (empty for $n = 0$), the result is $(n, r)$. Decoding fails if $w$ does not begin with such
a block or the payload is not of this form.

articles.title: Length-prefixed binary code of a clause
articles.statement:
Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the code
of a clause $C = (\ell_1, \dots, \ell_k)$ is $1^k 0$ ($k$ ones followed by a zero) followed by the
binary codes of $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_k$ in order, where a literal $(x, b)$ with variable index $x$
and polarity $b$ is coded by the prefix-free code of $x$ followed by the bit $b$.

articles.title: Length-prefixed binary code of a CNF formula
articles.statement:
Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the
code of a CNF formula $\varphi = (C_1, \dots, C_m)$ is $1^m 0$ ($m$ ones followed by a zero)
followed by the length-prefixed binary codes of the clauses $C_1, \dots, C_m$ in order.

articles.title: Binary code of a literal
articles.statement:
A literal $(n, b)$, with variable index $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
polarity $b \in \{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$, is encoded as the prefix-free code of $n$
followed by the single bit $b$.

articles.title: Prefix-free code of a natural number
articles.statement:
The code of $n \in \mathbb{N}$ is the
self-delimiting block of the binary representation of $n$ (least significant bit first, with
$0$ represented by the empty list): each bit $c$ is written as the two bits $\mathrm{true}, c$,
and the block ends with a terminating $\mathrm{false}$.

articles.title: Encodings of satisfiable CNF formulas
articles.statement:
A list $x$ of Booleans encodes a satisfiable CNF
formula when $x$ is the binary code of some CNF formula $\varphi$ and $\varphi$ is
satisfiable.

articles.title: Polynomial-time many-one reduction
articles.statement:
A decision problem $L_1$ reduces to a decision problem
$L_2$ in polynomial time when there is a polynomial-time computable function $f$ from lists of
Booleans to lists of Booleans such that $L_1(x) = L_2(f(x))$ for every list $x$ of Booleans.

articles.title: Reading a unary length prefix
articles.statement:
On a list of Booleans that begins with $k$ copies of
$\mathrm{true}$ followed by $\mathrm{false}$, the reader returns $k$ together with the rest of
the list after that $\mathrm{false}$. On a list containing no $\mathrm{false}$, including the
empty list, it fails.

articles.title: SAT as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The SAT decision problem returns true on a list $x$ of Booleans
when $x$ lies in the SAT language, that is, when $x$ encodes a satisfiable CNF formula, and
false otherwise.

articles.title: The SAT language
articles.statement:
SAT is the set of lists of Booleans that encode a satisfiable CNF
formula.

articles.title: Parsing a self-delimiting block
articles.statement:
For all lists of Booleans $u$, $p$ and $r$, parsing one
self-delimiting block from the front of $u$ succeeds with payload $p$ and remainder $r$ if and
only if $u$ is the self-delimiting block of $p$ followed by $r$.

articles.title: List canonicalizer normalizes a sequence of framed payloads
articles.statement:
Normalize any finite sequence of framed Nat payloads. The payloads
need not be canonical, and previous accumulator/output suffixes survive.

articles.title: List-of-naturals canonicalizer as a host component
articles.statement: The List Nat canonicalizer uses the existing finite Host interface.

articles.title: List canonicalizer normalizes one element
articles.statement:
One list element is normalized and appended to the reverse
accumulator; every scratch stack is ready for the next call.

articles.title: Stack embedding of the number normalizer in the list canonicalizer
articles.statement: Only the Nat workspace is visible to the shared normalizer.

articles.title: Stacks of the list-of-naturals canonicalizer
articles.statement: External input, reverse accumulator, final output, and Nat workspace.

articles.title: Control labels of the list-of-naturals canonicalizer
articles.statement: The normalizer's halt resumes frame emission.

articles.title: Label embedding of the number normalizer in the list canonicalizer
articles.statement: Label embedding of the actual shared Nat normalizer.

articles.title: Program of the list-of-naturals canonicalizer
articles.statement: The concrete canonicalizer program.

articles.title: Embedded list canonicalizer preserves outside stacks
articles.statement:
Embed the concrete normalizer in a caller, preserving every stack
outside its workspace on both success and failure. Entry requires clean
scratch and output stacks. After `bad`, clear partial workspace data
before another invocation.

articles.title: List canonicalizer fails on malformed input
articles.statement:
Every malformed raw List Nat input reaches the failure endpoint.
The accumulator and Nat output may contain partial data; clear the
workspace before reuse. No output claim is made for a failed parse.

articles.title: List canonicalizer runs in linear time on decodable input
articles.statement:
Successful raw List Nat decoding is implemented in linear time,
with canonical output and all private scratch stacks empty.

articles.title: List canonicalizer reaches the decoding outcome with canonical output
articles.statement:
A total success/failure contract at the two actual halt labels.
Success has canonical output; failure exposes no partial-output promise.

articles.title: Workspace layout of the list-of-naturals canonicalizer
articles.statement: Workspace layout for the composition invariant.

articles.title: Payload normalizer as a host component
articles.statement: The normalizer in the canonical component interface.

articles.title: Payload normalization is polynomial-time
articles.statement:
Total binary-payload normalization is polynomial-time in the
canonical encoded machine model.

articles.title: Stacks of the payload normalizer machine
articles.statement: Input, reverse buffer, and output.

articles.title: Control labels of the payload normalizer machine
articles.statement: The reader records the last payload bit; `none` means empty input.

articles.title: Program of the payload normalizer machine
articles.statement: Normalization using only Boolean stack symbols and finite control.

articles.title: Read phase of the payload normalizer consumes each bit once
articles.statement:
The read phase consumes each input bit once and optionally adds the
implicit terminal one. The prefix records already-consumed input.

articles.title: Linear step bound for the payload normalizer machine
articles.statement: The whole component runs in at most `2 |x| + 3` steps.

articles.title: Stack contents for the payload normalizer invariant
articles.statement: The three stack contents used in the run invariant.

articles.title: Pair-list projector main loop emits both lists in reverse
articles.statement:
The main loop emits both lists in reverse, ready for the two
final stack reversals. Order and multiplicity follow the decoded input.

articles.title: Pair-list projector as a host component
articles.statement: The concrete eleven-stack projector uses the existing Host model.

articles.title: Pair-list projector emits one weight and one value frame per item
articles.statement:
One successfully decoded item contributes one canonical weight
frame and one canonical value frame, with pair scratch emptied again.

articles.title: Stacks of the pair-list projector
articles.statement:
Raw outer input, two reversed accumulators, two outputs, and the
existing Nat-pair component's workspace.

articles.title: Control labels of the pair-list projector
articles.statement: Read one outer frame, normalize its pair, emit both fields, repeat.

articles.title: Stack embedding of the pair normalizer in the pair-list projector
articles.statement: The Nat-pair component is embedded without changing its alphabets.

articles.title: Pair-normalizer halt redirection in the pair-list projector
articles.statement: Only the pair component's actual halts are redirected.

articles.title: Program of the pair-list projector
articles.statement: Concrete outer parsing, pair normalization, and two framed streams.

articles.title: Projected pair lists total at most four times the input length
articles.statement:
Both projected canonical lists together are bounded by four times
the original raw list length, including noncanonical input payloads.

articles.title: Embedded pair-list projector preserves outside stacks
articles.statement:
Any stack embedding preserves the external frame on both outcomes.
Only mapped-label reachability is promised: callers establish their own
continuation-label separation. Failed private workspace needs clearing.

articles.title: Pair-list projector fails on malformed input in linear time
articles.statement:
Malformed outer framing or any malformed pair reaches `bad` in
linear time. Failed workspaces may contain partial data and need clearing.

articles.title: Pair-list projector yields canonical weight and value lists
articles.statement:
Successful generic decoding yields the canonical weight and value
lists on separate stacks. All input and scratch stacks are emptied.

articles.title: Pair-list projector always terminates at the decoding outcome
articles.statement:
Total decoder outcome. Success projects canonical lists with empty
scratch; failure promises termination, not reusable workspace contents.

articles.title: Eleven-stack invariant of the pair-list projector
articles.statement: The exact eleven-stack invariant, with caller output suffixes.

articles.title: Successful block parsing reconstructs the input
articles.statement: Successful block parsing reconstructs the entire input.

articles.title: Decoding a list of naturals is block parsing then number decoding
articles.statement:
List Nat decoding is precisely framed-payload parsing followed by
the existing total Nat decoder.

articles.title: Re-encoded decoded list of naturals is linear in raw input
articles.statement:
Re-encoding a successfully decoded List Nat is linear in the raw
input, not in the decoded numeric values.

articles.title: Re-encoding decoded payloads normalizes each one
articles.statement:
Canonical re-encoding normalizes each payload without changing
list order or multiplicity.

articles.title: Decoding natural-number payloads never fails
articles.statement: Nat payload decoding never fails, including on noncanonical bits.

articles.title: Normalizing framed number payloads at most triples the length
articles.statement:
Normalizing every framed Nat payload increases length by at most
threefold, even for noncanonical input.

articles.title: Bit-block copy keeps the order and restores source and scratch
articles.statement:
Copy a bit block in its original order, restoring both the source
and scratch, in exactly `2 * p.length + 2` steps.

articles.title: Two-destination bit transfer takes one step per bit plus one
articles.statement:
Two-destination bit transfer takes one step per bit plus one,
with exact suffix and unrelated-stack preservation.

articles.title: Two-destination bit-block transfer
articles.statement: Pop a bit block onto two distinct destinations, reversing both copies.

articles.title: Frame counter yields the number of raw frames in unary
articles.statement:
Counting a sequence of raw frames yields its length in unary,
with the caller's counter suffix preserved and scratch empty.

articles.title: Frame counter for lists of naturals as a host component
articles.statement: The frame counter is a finite component of the existing Host.

articles.title: One frame adds one unary count bit
articles.statement:
One complete frame contributes exactly one unary count bit and
leaves no payload scratch, independently of the decoded Nat's value.

articles.title: Stacks of the frame counter for lists of naturals
articles.statement: Input, one-block scratch, and a unary element counter.

articles.title: Control labels of the frame counter for lists of naturals
articles.statement: Each complete frame increments the counter and clears its scratch.

articles.title: Program of the frame counter for lists of naturals
articles.statement: Count by repeated shared block reading and shared scratch cleanup.

articles.title: Embedded frame counter preserves caller stacks
articles.statement:
Embedded counting preserves every caller stack outside its
workspace on success and failure. Scratch is empty on success.

articles.title: Frame counter fails on malformed list framing
articles.statement:
Malformed List Nat framing reaches the failure endpoint. The
counter and scratch may be partial and must be cleared before reuse.

articles.title: Frame counter counts every successfully decoded list of naturals
articles.statement:
Count every successfully decoded List Nat, including noncanonical
Nat payloads; the count suffix is preserved exactly.

articles.title: Frame counter decides decodability and counts length in unary
articles.statement: Total List Nat decoding outcome and exact unary length on success.

articles.title: Stack contents of the frame counter for lists of naturals
articles.statement: The three actual stack contents.

articles.title: Frame emitter takes one step per payload bit plus one
articles.statement:
Emit a complete frame in `payload.length + 1` steps, restoring the
input suffix and leaving every unrelated stack unchanged.

articles.title: Reversed self-delimiting frame emitter
articles.statement: Emit one raw payload as a reversed self-delimiting frame.

articles.title: Bit carried by a converter state
articles.statement:
For a state $s$ of the pair-to-canonical converter
(either empty or a symbol of the verifier alphabet), the bit of $s$ is $b$ when $s$ is a
left-tagged bit $\mathrm{inl}\,b$ or a right-tagged bit $\mathrm{inr}(\mathrm{some}\,b)$, and
$\mathrm{false}$ when $s$ is empty or the separator $\mathrm{inr}(\mathrm{none})$.

articles.title: Labels of the bit-list converters
articles.statement:
The two bit-list converters have two program labels,
$\mathrm{read}$ and $\mathrm{emit}$.

articles.title: Stack contents of the bit-list converters
articles.statement:
For bit lists $i$, $o$ and $a$, this assigns
contents to the three stacks of the bit-list converters: $i$ to the input stack, $o$ to the
output stack and $a$ to the stash. Every stack alphabet is $\mathrm{Bool}$.

articles.title: Stacks of the bit-list converters
articles.statement:
The two bit-list converters use three stacks: the
input stack, the output stack and one stash.

articles.title: Polynomial-time decoder of the canonical bit-list encoding
articles.statement:
This is a multi-stack Turing
machine whose input and output alphabets are the bits, together with the polynomial time bound
$t(n) = n + 2$, such that for every bit list $x$, whose canonical bitstring encoding has length
$n$, the machine started with that encoding on its input stack and all other stacks empty halts
within $t(n)$ steps with $x$ on its output stack, all other stacks empty and its internal state
back to the initial one. So the identity on bit lists is computable in polynomial time from the
canonical encoding to the raw bits.

The canonical encoding writes each bit $b$ of $x$ as the three bits true, $b$, false.

articles.title: Polynomial-time encoder to the canonical bit-list encoding
articles.statement:
This is a multi-stack Turing
machine whose input and output alphabets are the bits, together with the polynomial time bound
$t(n) = 2n + 2$, such that for every bit list $x$ of length $n$, the machine started with $x$ on
its input stack and all other stacks empty halts within $t(n)$ steps with the canonical bitstring
encoding of $x$ on its output stack, all other stacks empty and its internal state back to the
initial one. So the identity on bit lists is computable in polynomial time from the raw bits to
the canonical encoding.

The canonical encoding writes each bit $b$ of $x$ as the three bits true, $b$, false.

articles.title: Canonical bit-list decoder
articles.statement:
This is a multi-stack Turing machine over the alphabet
$\mathrm{Bool}$, with time bound $n + 2$, such that for every bit list $x$, started on the
canonical bitstring encoding of $x$, it halts within $n + 2$ steps, where $n$ is the length of
that encoding, with $x$ on its output stack and all other stacks empty. So the identity on bit
lists is computable in polynomial time from the canonical encoding to the raw bits.

articles.title: Run of the pair-to-canonical converter
articles.statement:
Let $x$ and $w$ be bit lists, write $x \# w$ for
the verifier input of the pair $(x, w)$, and read $1$ for true and $0$ for false. Let
$\mathrm{encFst}(x)$ replace each bit $b$ of $x$ by $1, 1, 1, b, 1, 0$ and $\mathrm{encSnd}(w)$
replace each bit $b$ of $w$ by $1, b, 0$. The program of the pair-to-canonical converter goes in
exactly $2|x| + 2|w| + 5$ steps from the configuration at label $\mathrm{readFst}$ with empty
state, $x \# w$ on the input stack and the output stack and both stashes empty, to the halted
configuration with empty state, empty input stack and stashes, and output stack reading
$\mathrm{encFst}(x)$, then $0$, then $\mathrm{encSnd}(w)$ from the top.

articles.title: Left-tagged state test
articles.statement:
For a state $s$ of the pair-to-canonical converter (either empty
or a symbol of the verifier alphabet), the test is true exactly when $s$ is a left-tagged bit
$\mathrm{inl}\,b$ for some bit $b$, and false when $s$ is empty, the separator
$\mathrm{inr}(\mathrm{none})$ or a right-tagged bit.

articles.title: Right-tagged state test
articles.statement:
For a state $s$ of the pair-to-canonical converter (either empty
or a symbol of the verifier alphabet), the test is true exactly when $s$ is a right-tagged bit
$\mathrm{inr}(\mathrm{some}\,b)$ for some bit $b$, and false when $s$ is empty, the separator
$\mathrm{inr}(\mathrm{none})$ or a left-tagged bit.

articles.title: Labels of the converter to the canonical pair encoding
articles.statement:
The machine that turns the
separated form of a pair $(x, w)$ of bit lists (the bits of $x$ tagged left, a separator, then
the bits of $w$ tagged right) into the canonical encoding of the pair has five labels: reading
the first part, reading the second part, emitting the second part, writing the separator, and
emitting the first part.

articles.title: Program of the bit-list decoder
articles.statement:
The program of the machine that decodes the canonical
encoding of a bit list acts on the three stacks of the bit-list converters, all over bits, with an
optional bit as internal state. At label $\mathrm{read}$ it pops a symbol from the input stack into
the state (which becomes empty if the input is empty). If that symbol is true, it pops a second
symbol $b$ into the state, pops and discards a third, pushes $b$ onto the stash (false if the
input ran out before $b$) and returns to $\mathrm{read}$; otherwise it goes to $\mathrm{emit}$. At
label $\mathrm{emit}$ it pops a bit from the stash, pushes it onto the output and returns to
$\mathrm{emit}$, and it halts when the stash is empty.

articles.title: Program of the bit-list encoder
articles.statement:
The program of the machine that writes the canonical
encoding of a bit list acts on the three stacks of the bit-list converters, all over bits, with an
optional bit as internal state. At label $\mathrm{read}$ it pops a bit from the input stack,
pushes it onto the stash and returns to $\mathrm{read}$; when the input is empty it goes to
$\mathrm{emit}$. At label $\mathrm{emit}$ it pops a bit $b$ from the stash, pushes false, $b$ and
true onto the output, so that the output then reads true, $b$, false from the top, and returns to
$\mathrm{emit}$; it halts when the stash is empty.

articles.title: Program of the converter to the canonical pair encoding
articles.statement:
The machine has an input stack
of symbols, each a left-tagged bit, a right-tagged bit or the separator, and three stacks of
bits: the output and two stashes. Its program first pops input symbols and pushes the bit of
each left-tagged one onto the first stash, until the input is empty or the symbol popped is not
a left-tagged bit. It then pops input symbols and pushes the bit of each right-tagged one onto
the second stash, until the input is empty or the symbol popped is not a right-tagged bit. Next
it pops each bit $b$ of the second stash and pushes false, $b$, true onto the output, and then
pushes a single false. Finally it pops each bit $b$ of the first stash and pushes false, true,
$b$, true, true, true onto the output, and halts when the first stash is empty.

Each output block is pushed in reverse, so that it reads true, $b$, false (respectively true,
true, true, $b$, true, false) from the top.

articles.title: Runs of the bit-list decoder
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and configurations $c$ and $d$ of
the machine decoding the canonical encoding of a bit list (each an optional label, an optional bit
as internal state and the contents of the three bit stacks), this is the proposition that $n$
steps of its program lead from $c$ to $d$: applying the step function $n$ times to $c$ is defined
at every step (no configuration before the last one is halted) and gives $d$.

articles.title: Runs of the bit-list encoder
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and configurations $c$ and $d$ of
the machine writing the canonical encoding of a bit list (each an optional label, an optional bit
as internal state and the contents of the three bit stacks), this is the proposition that $n$
steps of its program lead from $c$ to $d$: applying the step function $n$ times to $c$ is defined
at every step (no configuration before the last one is halted) and gives $d$.

articles.title: Runs of the converter to the canonical pair encoding
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$ and
configurations $c$ and $d$ of the converter, this is the proposition that $n$ steps of its
program lead from $c$ to $d$: applying the step function $n$ times to $c$ is defined at every
step (no configuration before the last one is halted) and gives $d$.

articles.title: States of the converter to the canonical pair encoding
articles.statement:
A state of the converter is
either empty or one symbol of the verifier's input alphabet, that is, a left-tagged bit, a
right-tagged bit or the separator.

The state holds the last symbol popped; bits popped from the stashes are stored as left-tagged
bits.

articles.title: Stack contents of the converter to the canonical pair encoding
articles.statement:
Given a list $i$ of input
symbols and bit lists $o$, $a$ and $b$, this is the contents of the four stacks of the converter
with $i$ on the input stack, $o$ on the output stack, $a$ on the first stash and $b$ on the
second stash.

articles.title: Stacks of the converter to the canonical pair encoding
articles.statement:
The converter has four stacks: the
input stack, whose symbols are left-tagged bits, right-tagged bits and the separator (the input
is the bits of a first bit list tagged left, a separator, then the bits of a second bit list
tagged right); the output stack, holding bits; and two stashes, holding the bits of the first
and of the second list.

articles.title: Machine decoding the canonical encoding of a bit list
articles.statement:
The multi-stack Turing machine with
the three stacks of the bit-list converters (input, output and a stash), all over bits, reading
its input from the input stack and leaving its output on the output stack, with the two labels
$\mathrm{read}$ and $\mathrm{emit}$ and start label $\mathrm{read}$, an optional bit as internal
state, initially empty, and the program of the bit-list decoder. It repeatedly pops an input
symbol; while that symbol is true, it pops two more and pushes the first of them onto the stash
(false if the input ran out before it). Then it moves the stash, bit by bit, onto the output, and
halts.

articles.title: Machine writing the canonical encoding of a bit list
articles.statement:
The multi-stack Turing machine with
the three stacks of the bit-list converters (input, output and a stash), all over bits, reading
its input from the input stack and leaving its output on the output stack, with the two labels
$\mathrm{read}$ and $\mathrm{emit}$ and start label $\mathrm{read}$, an optional bit as internal
state, initially empty, and the program of the bit-list encoder. It moves the input, bit by bit,
onto the stash. Then it pops the stash bit by bit, pushing for each bit $b$ the three bits false,
$b$, true onto the output, so that each block reads true, $b$, false from the top, and halts.

articles.title: Machine converting the separator form of a pair to its canonical encoding
articles.statement:
The
multi-stack Turing machine with the four stacks of the converter to the canonical pair encoding
(input, output and two stashes), whose input stack holds symbols of the verifier's alphabet
(left-tagged bits, right-tagged bits and the separator) and whose other stacks hold bits, reading
its input from the input stack and leaving its output on the output stack, with the five labels
of that converter and start label $\mathrm{readFst}$, the converter's states (empty or one
verifier symbol) as internal states, initially empty, and the program of the converter to the
canonical pair encoding. It pops input symbols, pushing the bit of each left-tagged one onto the
first stash, until the input is empty or the symbol popped is not a left-tagged bit. It then pops
input symbols, pushing the bit of each right-tagged one onto the second stash, until the input is
empty or the symbol popped is not a right-tagged bit. Next it pops each bit $b$ of the second
stash and pushes a block reading true, $b$, false from the top onto the output, pushes a single
false, pops each bit $b$ of the first stash and pushes a block reading true, true, true, $b$,
true, false from the top, and halts when the first stash is empty.

articles.title: Stack alphabets of the separator-to-canonical converter
articles.statement:
The input stack of the converter
from the separator form of a pair to its canonical encoding has the verifier's alphabet, and each
of its other three stacks (the output and the two stashes) has the alphabet of bits.

articles.title: Four-output pair-list decoder as a host component
articles.statement: The fixed seventeen-stack decoder in the existing Host interface.

articles.title: List-projector stack embedding in the four-output decoder
articles.statement: The list projector has its own disjoint workspace.

articles.title: Label map from the list projector to the final pair decoder
articles.statement: Successful item projection enters the final pair decoder.

articles.title: Stacks of the four-output pair-list decoder
articles.statement:
Two disjoint existing workspaces; the pair buffer also serves the
initial outer-frame split and is cleared before normalization starts.

articles.title: Control labels of the four-output pair-list decoder
articles.statement: The existing split, list projector, and final pair normalizer.

articles.title: Four-output decoder output is at most twice the input length
articles.statement:
The combined newly emitted output size is at most twice raw input
length, independently of decoded magnitudes and caller output suffixes.

articles.title: Final pair-projector stack embedding in the four-output decoder
articles.statement: The final pair projector has its own disjoint workspace.

articles.title: Label map from final pair halts to the decoder outcomes
articles.statement: The final pair's actual halts are the whole decoder's outcomes.

articles.title: Program of the four-output pair-list decoder
articles.statement: The whole finite program is a composition of existing components.

articles.title: Embedded four-output decoder preserves outside stacks
articles.statement:
Embedded execution preserves every outside stack on both outcomes.
Successful output suffixes survive and private scratch is empty. Failed
workspace may be partial. Callers establish continuation-label separation.

articles.title: Four-output decoder fails on malformed input
articles.statement:
Every failed raw decode reaches `bad` within the same whole-input
bound. Failed owned workspace can be partial and must be discarded
or cleared.

articles.title: Four-output decoder emits four canonical outputs on success
articles.statement:
The entire raw decoder emits four canonical outputs, preserving
caller suffixes and emptying all input and private scratch on success.

articles.title: Four-output decoder reaches exactly the canonical decoding outcome
articles.statement:
Total raw decoder contract with four output suffixes. Exactly the
canonical decoder's success/failure label is reached, with empty
scratch on success.

articles.title: Outer-splitter stack embedding in the four-output decoder
articles.statement: The outer splitter reuses the final pair's input and empty buffer.

articles.title: Label map from the outer splitter to the list projector
articles.statement: Successful outer framing enters the item-list projector.

articles.title: Stack invariant of the four-output pair-list decoder
articles.statement:
Exact raw-field and four-output invariant, with empty private scratch.
At entry the item field is empty and the entire raw input is `pairRaw`.

articles.title: Canonical encoding of a pair of bit lists
articles.statement:
For bit lists $x$ and $w$, the canonical
bitstring encoding of the pair $(x, w)$ is the concatenation of three parts: every bit $b$ of $x$,
in order, written as the six bits true, true, true, $b$, true, false; then a single false; then
every bit $b$ of $w$, in order, written as the three bits true, $b$, false.

articles.title: Polynomial-time conversion to the verifier's pair encoding
articles.statement:
A polynomial-time computation
of the identity map on pairs $(x, w)$ of bit lists, from the canonical bitstring encoding of
$(x, w)$ to the verifier's pair encoding of $(x, w)$ (the bits of $x$, the separator, then the
bits of $w$), by the converter machine, with the bits and the verifier's symbols themselves as
input and output alphabets and time bound $n + 5$: started on the canonical encoding of $(x, w)$,
a list of length $n$, the converter halts within $n + 5$ steps with no bit in its state, the
verifier's pair encoding of $(x, w)$ on its output stack and every other stack empty.

articles.title: Full run of the pair-encoding converter
articles.statement:
For bit lists $x$ and $w$, the converter program
goes in exactly $2|x| + 2|w| + 5$ steps from the configuration at the label *read first*, with
no bit in the state, the input stack holding every bit $b$ of $x$ in order as the six bits true,
true, true, $b$, true, false, then a single false, then every bit $b$ of $w$ in order as the three
bits true, $b$, false, and the other three stacks empty, to the halted configuration with no bit
in the state, the verifier's pair encoding of $(x, w)$ on the output stack and the other three
stacks empty.
