$\ell = (x, s)$, a Boolean $f$ and a list of items, the walk bits are defined by recursion on the
list: there are none for the empty list; for a list starting with a clause marker they are the
walk bits of the rest with $f$ replaced by true; for a list starting with a literal $(x', s')$
they are the bit "$f$ and not ($x = x'$ and $s \ne s'$)" followed by the walk bits of the rest
with the same $f$. For a list $\delta$ of items, the rows of a list of literals are none for the
empty list, and for a list $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_k$ with $k \ge 1$ they are the reverse of the walk
bits of $\ell_1$ with $f$ false over the list $\ell_2, \dots, \ell_k$ followed by $\delta$, then
the rows of $\ell_2, \dots, \ell_k$. The items of a CNF formula $\psi$ are, for each clause of
$\psi$ in order, its literals followed by a clause marker. The row bits of a CNF formula are
defined by recursion on its clauses: the empty formula has none, and for the formula with first
clause $C$ and remaining clauses $\varphi$ they are the rows of the literals of $C$ for $\delta$
the clause marker followed by the items of $\varphi$, followed by the row bits of $\varphi$.

articles.title: CLIQUE emitter: recognizing a standard state
articles.statement:
Let $S$ assign contents to the stacks of
the CLIQUE emitter and let $c, n \in \mathbb{N}$. If the scratch stacks $B$ and $X$ are empty and
the counters $C$ and $N$ hold exactly $c$ and $n$ clause markers, then $S$ is the standard state
whose stacks $T$, $O$, $A$, $D$, $E$ hold what they hold in $S$, whose stacks $B$ and $X$ are
empty and whose counters $C$ and $N$ hold $c$ and $n$ clause markers.

articles.title: Configuration stacks of the CLIQUE emitter
articles.statement:
For a token stack $t$, an output stack $o$
of bits, stacks $a$, $d$, $e$ of token symbols and natural numbers $c$ and $n$, this assigns to
each stack of the CLIQUE emitter its contents: the token stack $T$ holds $t$, the output stack
$O$ holds $o$, the name stack $A$ holds $a$, the walked-occurrence stack $D$ holds $d$, the
walk's other stack $E$ holds $e$, the clause counter $C$ holds $c$ copies of the clause marker,
the occurrence counter $N$ holds $n$ copies of the clause marker, and the scratch stacks $B$ and
$X$ are empty.

articles.title: Start label of the CLIQUE emitter
articles.statement:
The start label of the CLIQUE emitter machine is its
label $\mathsf{start}$.

articles.title: Stack alphabets of the CLIQUE emitter
articles.statement:
In the CLIQUE emitter, the output stack $O$ has
the Booleans as its alphabet, and every other stack has the token symbols as its alphabet.

The counter stacks $C$ and $N$ hold copies of the clause marker.

articles.title: Bits pushed by a walk of the CLIQUE emitter
articles.statement:
Let $l = (x, p)$ be a literal occurrence
with name $x \in \mathbb{N}$ and polarity $p$, let $f$ be a Boolean, and let $ds$ be a list whose
items are literal occurrences or clause markers. The bit list $\mathrm{walkBits}(l, f, ds)$ is
defined by recursion on $ds$: it is empty if $ds$ is empty; if $ds$ is a clause marker followed
by $ds'$, it is $\mathrm{walkBits}(l, \mathrm{true}, ds')$; and if $ds$ is an occurrence $l'$
followed by $ds'$, it is the bit $f \wedge \mathrm{adj}(l, l')$ followed by
$\mathrm{walkBits}(l, f, ds')$. Here $\mathrm{adj}(l, l')$ is the Karp adjacency of literals: it
is false exactly when $l$ and $l'$ have the same name and opposite polarities.

The flag $f$ records whether a clause marker has been passed; while it is false, each occurrence
contributes a false bit.

articles.title: Clique emitter: moving the walk side back
articles.statement:
Let $p$ and $v$ be Booleans, $t$, $a$ and $d$
stack-symbol lists, $o$ a list of bits, $c, n \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $L$ be a list of stack
symbols each of which is a name bit, a polarity marker or a clause marker. From label
$\mathrm{back}(p)$ with flag $v$ and the state with token stack $t$, output $o$, name stack $a$,
walked stack $d$, walk side $L$, clause count $c$, occurrence count $n$ and empty scratch stacks,
the emitter machine reaches in exactly $|L| + 1$ steps, for some flag $v'$, label
$\mathrm{put}(p)$ with flag $v'$ and the same state except that the walked stack is the reverse
of $L$ followed by $d$ and the walk side is empty.

articles.title: Clique emitter: one clause
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a clause, $\varphi$ a CNF formula, $R$ a token list
that is empty or starts with a clause marker, $o$ a list of bits, $c, n, B \in \mathbb{N}$ and $v$
a Boolean. Write $T_C$ for the tokens of $C$ as they lie on the token stack (a clause marker,
then the literals last-first) and $D_\psi$ for the tokens of the items of a formula $\psi$. If
$|T_C| + |D_\varphi| \le B$, then for some flag $v'$ the emitter machine goes in at most
$|T_C| \cdot (7B + 7)$ steps from label start with flag $v$ and the state with token stack $T_C$
followed by $R$, output $o$, walked stack $D_\varphi$, clause count $c$, occurrence count $n$ and
all other stacks empty, to label start with flag $v'$ and the state with token stack $R$, output
the rows pushed for the literals of $C$ walked above a clause marker and the items of $\varphi$,
followed by $o$, walked stack $D_{C \varphi}$ for the formula $C\varphi$ with first clause $C$,
clause count $c + 1$, occurrence count $n + |C|$ and all other stacks empty.

articles.title: Clique emitter: comparing two names
articles.statement:
Let $p$, $q$ and $v$ be Booleans, $u$ and $w$ lists
of bits, $t$, $e$ and $R$ stack-symbol lists with $R$ empty or not starting with a name bit, $o$
a list of bits and $c, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Let $b$ be $(p = q)$ if $u = w$ and true otherwise.
For some flag $v'$, the emitter machine goes in at most $3|w| + 4$ steps from label
$\mathrm{cmp}(p, q)$ with flag $v$ and the state with token stack $t$, output $o$, name stack
$u$, walked stack $w$ followed by $R$, walk side $e$, clause count $c$, occurrence count $n$ and
empty scratch stacks to label $\mathrm{mvN}(p, \mathrm{true})$ with flag $v'$ and the same state
except that the output is $b$ followed by $o$. Here $u$ and $w$ lie on the stacks as name-bit
symbols.

articles.title: Reduction computed in each mode
articles.statement:
The map on bit strings that a mode of the
CLIQUE/VERTEX-COVER reduction machine computes: in the flip mode it is the reduction from CLIQUE
to INDEPENDENT-SET on bit strings, and in the vertex-cover mode it is the reduction from
INDEPENDENT-SET to VERTEX-COVER on bit strings.

articles.title: Pair-bit transform of each mode
articles.statement:
For a mode of the CLIQUE/VERTEX-COVER reduction
machine, the map on booleans applied to each pair bit as it is written to the output: negation in
the flip mode and the identity in the vertex-cover mode.

articles.title: Clique emitter: the instance prefix
articles.statement:
Let $v$ be a Boolean, $d$ and $e$ stack-symbol lists,
$o$ a list of bits and $c, n \in \mathbb{N}$. From label fin with flag $v$ and the state with
empty token stack, output $o$, empty name stack, walked stack $d$, walk side $e$, clause count
$c$, occurrence count $n$ and empty scratch stacks, the emitter machine reaches in exactly
$n + c + 4$ steps label done with some flag and some state whose output, read top-down, is $c$
ones, false, $n$ ones, false, then $o$.

articles.title: Reversing a list preserves the length of a flat map
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be types,
$l$ a list of elements of $\alpha$ and $f$ a function from $\alpha$ to lists of elements of
$\beta$. Concatenating the lists $f(a)$ for $a$ running through the reverse of $l$ gives a list
of the same length as concatenating them for $a$ running through $l$.

articles.title: Emitter run over a formula's clauses
articles.statement:
Write
$\langle \ell, v \mid t, o, a, d, e, c, n\rangle$ for the configuration of the SAT-to-CLIQUE
emitter at label $\ell$ with local bit $v$, stacks $T = t$, $O = o$, $A = a$, $D = d$, $E = e$,
empty scratch stacks $B$ and $X$, and $c$ and $n$ marks on the counters $C$ and $N$;
juxtaposition of lists is concatenation. Let $L \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula
with clauses $C_1, \dots, C_m$ in order, let $R$ be a list of symbols that is empty or starts
with the clause marker, $o$ a list of bits and $v$ a bit. Let $\kappa_i$ be the token list of
$C_i$ as it lies on the token stack and $\tau = \kappa_m \cdots \kappa_1$. If $|\tau| \le L$,
then for some bit $v'$ the machine goes in at most $|\tau| (7L + 7)$ steps from
$\langle \mathsf{start}, v \mid \tau R, o, [], [], [], 0, 0\rangle$ to
$\langle \mathsf{start}, v' \mid R, \rho\, o, [], \delta, [], m, s\rangle$, where $\rho$ is the
row bits of $\varphi$, $\delta$ is the concatenation of the tokens of the items of $\varphi$ and
$s = |C_1| + \dots + |C_m|$ is the total number of literals of $\varphi$.

articles.title: Test for the input bit true
articles.statement:
A test on the result of popping a stack: it is true
exactly when a symbol was popped and that symbol is $\mathrm{bit}(\mathrm{true})$, and false for
every other symbol and for an empty stack.

articles.title: Test for the moved bit true
articles.statement:
A test on the result of popping a stack: it is true
exactly when a symbol was popped and that symbol is $\mathrm{val}(\mathrm{true})$, and false for
every other symbol and for an empty stack.

articles.title: Stacks of the CLIQUE to VERTEX-COVER reduction machine
articles.statement:
Stacks: input `X`, output `O`, counters `A` (`k`), `B` (`n`), `D` (`n`, then `n - k`), and
the reversed pair bits `Y`.

articles.title: Labels of the KG-map machine
articles.statement:
The type of the ten instruction labels of the KG-map
machine: read $k$, read $n$, move the pair bits, subtract, output the pair bits, output $n$, write
the separator, output the last number, the failure label and the halting label.

The machine reaches the subtraction label only in the vertex-cover mode, and at the failure label
it writes the fixed no-instance.

articles.title: Emitter run over one literal occurrence
articles.statement:
Write
$\langle \ell, v \mid t, o, a, d, e, c, n\rangle$ for the configuration of the SAT-to-CLIQUE
emitter at label $\ell$ with local bit $v$, stacks $T = t$, $O = o$, $A = a$, $D = d$, $E = e$,
empty scratch stacks $B$ and $X$, and $c$ and $n$ marks on the counters $C$ and $N$;
juxtaposition of lists is concatenation. Let $l = (x, p)$ be a literal, $R$ a list of symbols that
is empty or does not start with a name-bit symbol, $I$ a list of items, $o$ a list of bits,
$c, n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $v$ a bit. Let $\delta$ be the concatenation of the tokens of the items
of $I$, $\lambda$ the token list of $l$ as it lies on the token stack, $\rho$ the reverse of the
walk bits of $l$ with flag false over $I$, and $\delta'$ the concatenation of the tokens of the
item $l$ followed by those of $I$. Then for some bit $v'$ the machine goes in at most
$7|\delta| + 3|\mathrm{enc}(x)| + 7$ steps, where $\mathrm{enc}(x)$ is the binary encoding of $x$,
from $\langle \mathsf{lits}, v \mid \lambda R, o, [], \delta, [], c, n\rangle$ to
$\langle \mathsf{lits}, v' \mid R, \rho\, o, [], \delta', [], c, n + 1\rangle$.

articles.title: Emitter run over a clause's literals
articles.statement:
Write
$\langle \ell, v \mid t, o, a, d, e, c, n\rangle$ for the configuration of the SAT-to-CLIQUE
emitter at label $\ell$ with local bit $v$, stacks $T = t$, $O = o$, $A = a$, $D = d$, $E = e$,
empty scratch stacks $B$ and $X$, and $c$ and $n$ marks on the counters $C$ and $N$;
juxtaposition of lists is concatenation. Let $L, c \in \mathbb{N}$, let $I$ be a list of items
and $\delta$ the concatenation of their tokens, let $l_1, \dots, l_k$ be literals, $R$ a list of
symbols that is empty or does not start with a name-bit symbol, $o$ a list of bits,
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $v$ a bit. Let $\lambda_i$ be the token list of $l_i$ as it lies on the
token stack and $\Lambda = |\lambda_1| + \dots + |\lambda_k|$. If $\Lambda + |\delta| \le L$, then
for some bit $v'$ the machine goes in at most $\Lambda (7L + 7)$ steps from
$\langle \mathsf{lits}, v \mid \lambda_k \cdots \lambda_1 R, o, [], \delta, [], c, n\rangle$ to
$\langle \mathsf{lits}, v' \mid R, \rho\, o, [], \delta', [], c, n + k\rangle$, where $\rho$ is the
rows pushed for the literals $l_1, \dots, l_k$ above the items $I$ and $\delta'$ is the
concatenation of the tokens of the items $l_1, \dots, l_k$ followed by those of $I$.

articles.title: Modes of the CLIQUE/VERTEX-COVER reduction machine
articles.statement:
A mode is one of two values, the
flip mode and the vertex-cover mode. They select the reduction that the machine of this module
computes: CLIQUE to INDEPENDENT-SET in the flip mode, INDEPENDENT-SET to VERTEX-COVER in the
vertex-cover mode.

articles.title: CLIQUE emitter: putting the current occurrence on the walked stack
articles.statement:
Stacks are listed top
first. Let $p$ be a Boolean, $u$ a list of Booleans and $\bar u$ the list of bit symbols
$\mathrm{bit}(b)$ for $b$ in $u$, let $v$ be a flag, $t$, $d$, $e$ lists of symbols, $o$ a list of
Booleans and $c, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Started at label $\mathrm{put}(p)$ with flag $v$, stacks $T$,
$O$, $A$, $D$, $E$ holding $t$, $o$, $\bar u$, $d$, $e$, empty scratch stacks $B$ and $X$, and $c$
and $n$ clause markers on the counters $C$ and $N$, the CLIQUE emitter reaches, in exactly
$2|u| + 3$ steps and with some flag, the label $\mathrm{lits}$ with $A$ empty, $D$ holding the
literal marker $\mathrm{lit}(p)$ on top of $\bar u$ on top of $d$, and all other stacks as before.

The name goes from $A$ to $D$ through $B$, so it is reversed twice.

articles.title: The CLIQUE emitter computes Karp's instance in cubic time
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula
with token list $\tau$ (in reading order), $o$ a list of Booleans, $v$ a flag, and $S$ stack
contents in which the token stack $T$ holds $\tau$ reversed (stacks are listed top first), the
output stack $O$ holds $o$ and every other stack is empty. Started at its start label with flag
$v$ and stacks $S$, the CLIQUE emitter reaches the label $\mathrm{done}$ in at most
$8(|\tau| + 1)^3$ steps, with some flag and stacks $S'$ such that $O$ holds, in $S'$, Karp's
CLIQUE instance of $\varphi$ followed by $o$.

articles.title: Counter unit symbol of the clique reduction machine
articles.statement:
$U$ is the symbol $\mathsf{cl}$ of
the token alphabet $\mathrm{Sym}$.

It is the unit of the counter stacks $A$, $B$ and $D$, which hold a number $n$ as $n$ copies of
$U$.

articles.title: Stack alphabets of the clique reduction machine
articles.statement:
The alphabet $\Gamma(k)$ of a stack $k$
is the Booleans if $k$ is the output stack $O$, and the token alphabet $\mathrm{Sym}$ for every
other stack ($X$, $A$, $B$, $D$ and $Y$).

articles.title: Walk over the occurrence stack in the CLIQUE emitter
articles.statement:
Let $l = (x, p)$ be a literal
occurrence, $ds$ a list of items (literal occurrences or clause markers), $f$ and $v$ Booleans,
$t$ a token stack, $o$ an output stack of bits, $e$ a stack of token symbols and
$c, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Let $D$ be the concatenation of the tokens of the items of $ds$: a clause
marker for a clause marker, and the polarity marker of $l'$ above the name bits of $l'$ (the
binary encoding of its name as bit symbols) for an occurrence $l'$. Start the CLIQUE emitter at
label $\mathsf{walk}(p, f)$ with internal variable $v$, on the configuration stacks with token
stack $t$, output $o$, name stack the name bits of $x$, walked-occurrence stack $D$, other walk
stack $e$ and counts $c$ and $n$. Then for some Boolean $v'$ the machine reaches, in at most
$6\,|D| + 1$ steps, label $\mathsf{back}(p)$ with internal variable $v'$ on the configuration
stacks with token stack $t$, output stack the reverse of $\mathrm{walkBits}(l, f, ds)$ followed
by $o$, name stack the name bits of $x$, empty walked-occurrence stack, other walk stack the
reverse of $D$ followed by $e$, and counts $c$ and $n$.

articles.title: Counter of the first output number of the KG-map machine
articles.statement:
The map from the modes of the
KG-map machine to its stacks that sends the flip mode to the counter $A$ and the vertex-cover
mode to the counter $D$.

This is the counter the machine drains last, as the first number of its output: $A$ holds $k$,
and in the vertex-cover mode $D$ holds $n - k$ by then.

articles.title: The CLIQUE emitter
articles.statement:
The emitter given by the CLIQUE emitter machine, run from its start
label to its exit label, with token stack $T$ and output stack $O$. Its output on a CNF formula
$\varphi$ is Karp's CLIQUE instance of $\varphi$, its output on undecodable input is the string
$100$, and its step bound on $m$ tokens is $8(m + 1)^3$. Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula with $m$
tokens. Started with the tokens of $\varphi$ on $T$, last token on top, and all other stacks
empty, the machine reaches its exit label within $8(m + 1)^3$ steps, with Karp's CLIQUE instance
of $\varphi$ on $O$, first bit on top.

articles.title: CLIQUE ≤ INDEPENDENT-SET is polynomial-time
articles.statement:
The map on bit strings that sends
$1^k 0 1^n 0 b$, for natural numbers $k$ and $n$ and a bit string $b$, to $1^k 0 1^n 0 \bar b$,
where $\bar b$ is $b$ with every bit complemented, and sends every string not of this form to the
string $100$, is computable in polynomial time.

articles.title: INDEPENDENT-SET ≤ VERTEX-COVER is polynomial-time
articles.statement:
The map on bit strings that sends
$1^k 0 1^n 0 b$, for natural numbers $k \le n$ and a bit string $b$, to $1^{n-k} 0 1^n 0 b$, and
sends every other string (including $1^k 0 1^n 0 b$ with $k > n$) to the string $100$, is
computable in polynomial time.

articles.title: SAT ≤ CLIQUE is polynomial-time
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be the map on bit strings that sends the
binary code of a CNF formula $\varphi$ to the encoding of Karp's CLIQUE instance $(k, G)$ of
$\varphi$, and sends every string that is not the code of a CNF formula to the string $100$.
Here $G$ has one vertex per literal occurrence in $\varphi$, two occurrences are adjacent when
they lie in different clauses and are not complementary, and $k$ is the number of clauses of
$\varphi$. Then $f$ is computable in polynomial time.

articles.title: The CLIQUE-to-INDEPENDENT-SET and INDEPENDENT-SET-to-VERTEX-COVER map as a host component
articles.statement:
**The CLIQUE-to-INDEPENDENT-SET and INDEPENDENT-SET-to-VERTEX-COVER map as a host
component.** For a mode $m$, standing for the reduction from CLIQUE to INDEPENDENT-SET or the one
from INDEPENDENT-SET to VERTEX-COVER, this is the host component whose stacks (listed as
$X, O, A, B, D, Y$), stack alphabets, labels and program are those of the Turing machine that
computes the reduction of mode $m$.

articles.title: Moving the pair bits onto stack $Y$
articles.statement:
Fix a mode $m$ of the CLIQUE/VERTEX-COVER
reduction machine, a list of bits $r$ and a list of symbols $y$. Start the machine for $m$ at the
label for moving the pair bits, with any internal state and any stacks such that stack $X$ holds
$r$ as the symbols $\mathrm{bit}(b)$ and stack $Y$ holds $y$. Then after exactly $|r| + 1$ steps
it is at the label that follows moving the pair bits in mode $m$, with some internal state and
stacks in which $Y$ holds the symbols $\mathrm{val}(b)$ for the bits $b$ of $r$, in reverse
order, on top of $y$, and every stack other than $X$ and $Y$ is unchanged.

articles.title: Label after the move phase of the KG-map machine
articles.statement:
The map from the modes of the KG-map
machine to its labels that sends the flip mode to the label output the pair bits and the
vertex-cover mode to the subtraction label. The machine goes to this label after moving the pair
bits.

articles.title: Output phase of the KG-map machine
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a mode, $r$ a list of bits and $n$ and
$c$ natural numbers. Consider a configuration of the KG-map machine $M_m$ at the label output
pair bits, with any internal bit, in which stack $Y$ holds the symbols $\mathrm{val}(b)$ for the
bits $b$ of $r$ in reverse order (the last bit of $r$ on top), stack $B$ holds $n$ copies of the
unit symbol, the counter of $m$ ($A$ for flip, $D$ for vc) holds $c$ copies of some symbol, and
the output stack $O$ is empty. Then in exactly $|r| + n + c + 4$ steps $M_m$ reaches the halting
label with $O$ equal, top first, to the encoding of the instance with numbers $c$ and $n$ and
pair bits $\beta_m(r)$: $c$ trues, a false, $n$ trues, a false, then $\beta_m(r)$, where
$\beta_m$ negates every bit for flip and leaves the bits unchanged for vc.

articles.title: Output loop for the pair bits of the KG-map machine
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a mode and $y$ and $o$
lists of bits. Consider a configuration of the KG-map machine $M_m$ at the label output pair
bits, with any internal bit, in which stack $Y$ holds the symbols $\mathrm{val}(b)$ for the bits
$b$ of $y$, the first bit of $y$ on top, and the output stack $O$ holds $o$. Then in exactly
$|y| + 1$ steps $M_m$ reaches the label output $n$ with $O$ equal, top first, to false, then the
reverse of $\beta_m(y)$, then $o$, where $\beta_m$ negates every bit for flip and leaves the
bits unchanged for vc; every stack other than $Y$ and $O$ is unchanged.

articles.title: The KG-map machine
articles.statement:
For a mode $m$ (flip or vc), the KG-map machine $M_m$ is the
multi-stack machine with stacks $X$, $A$, $B$, $D$, $Y$ of symbols and an output stack $O$ of
bits, whose labels act as follows; the counters $A$, $B$, $D$ use a fixed unit symbol.

- Read $k$: if $X$ is empty, go to the failure label. Otherwise pop $X$; if the popped symbol is
  the input bit $\mathrm{bit}(\mathit{true})$, push a unit onto $A$ and repeat, else go to read $n$.
- Read $n$: if $X$ is empty, go to the failure label. Otherwise pop $X$; if the popped symbol is
  $\mathrm{bit}(\mathit{true})$, push a unit onto $B$ and onto $D$ and repeat, else go to move.
- Move: if $X$ is empty, go to output pair bits (flip) or subtract (vc). Otherwise pop $X$, push
  $\mathrm{val}(b)$ onto $Y$, where $b$ is true exactly when the popped symbol was
  $\mathrm{bit}(\mathit{true})$, and repeat.
- Subtract: pop $A$. If $A$ was empty, go to output pair bits. Otherwise pop $D$; if $D$ was
  nonempty repeat, else go to the failure label.
- Output pair bits: if $Y$ is empty, push false onto $O$ and go to output $n$. Otherwise pop $Y$,
  push $\beta_m(b)$ onto $O$, where $b$ is true exactly when the popped symbol was
  $\mathrm{val}(\mathit{true})$ and $\beta_m$ is negation for flip and the identity for vc, and
  repeat.
- Output $n$: pop $B$; if $B$ was nonempty, push true onto $O$ and repeat, else go to separator.
- Separator: push false onto $O$ and go to output last number.
- Output last number: as output $n$, but popping the counter of $m$ ($A$ for flip, $D$ for vc)
  and going to the halting label when it is empty.
- Failure: push the bits true, false, false of the fixed no-instance (the encoding of $k = 1$ on
  the empty graph) onto $O$ so that $O$ starts with them, and go to the halting label.
- Halting label: halt.

articles.title: Unterminated first unary number in the KG-map machine
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a mode and $r$ a list
of bits on which reading a unary length prefix fails (this happens exactly when $r$ contains no
false). From any configuration of the KG-map machine $M_m$ at the label read $k$, with any
internal bit, in which stack $X$ holds the input symbols $\mathrm{bit}(b)$ for the bits $b$ of
$r$, top first, $M_m$ reaches the failure label in exactly $|r| + 1$ steps, with every stack
other than $X$ and $A$ unchanged.

articles.title: Reading the first unary number in the KG-map machine
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a mode, $k$ and $i$
natural numbers and $r$ a list of bits. Consider a configuration of the KG-map machine $M_m$ at
the label read $k$, with any internal bit, in which stack $X$ holds the input symbols
$\mathrm{bit}(b)$ for the bits $b$ of the list of $k$ trues, a false and then $r$, top first, and
stack $A$ holds $i$ copies of the unit symbol. Then in exactly $k + 1$ steps $M_m$ reaches the
label read $n$ with $X$ holding $\mathrm{bit}(b)$ for the bits $b$ of $r$, $A$ holding $i + k$
copies of the unit symbol, and every stack other than $X$ and $A$ unchanged.

articles.title: Unterminated second unary number in the KG-map machine
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a mode and $r$ a list
of bits on which reading a unary length prefix fails (this happens exactly when $r$ contains no
false). From any configuration of the KG-map machine $M_m$ at the label read $n$, with any
internal bit, in which stack $X$ holds the input symbols $\mathrm{bit}(b)$ for the bits $b$ of
$r$, top first, $M_m$ reaches the failure label in exactly $|r| + 1$ steps, with every stack
other than $X$, $B$ and $D$ unchanged.

articles.title: Reading the second unary number in the KG-map machine
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a mode, $n$ and $i$
natural numbers and $r$ a list of bits. Consider a configuration of the KG-map machine $M_m$ at
the label read $n$, with any internal bit, in which stack $X$ holds the input symbols
$\mathrm{bit}(b)$ for the bits $b$ of the list of $n$ trues, a false and then $r$, top first, and
stacks $B$ and $D$ each hold $i$ copies of the unit symbol. Then in exactly $n + 1$ steps $M_m$
reaches the label move with $X$ holding $\mathrm{bit}(b)$ for the bits $b$ of $r$, $B$ and $D$
each holding $i + n$ copies of the unit symbol, and every stack other than $X$, $B$ and $D$
unchanged.

articles.title: Correctness and running time of the KG-map machine
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a mode and $x$ a list of
bits, and let $F_m$ be the clique-to-independent-set map on bit strings for flip and the
independent-set-to-vertex-cover map for vc. From any configuration of the KG-map machine $M_m$
at its start label, with any internal bit, in which stack $X$ holds the input symbols
$\mathrm{bit}(b)$ for the bits $b$ of $x$, top first, and every other stack is empty, $M_m$
reaches the halting label in at most $3(|x| + 1)$ steps with the output stack $O$ equal to
$F_m(x)$, top first.

articles.title: Start label of the KG-map machine
articles.statement: The KG-map machine starts at the label read $k$.

articles.title: Failed subtraction in the KG-map machine
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a mode and $n < k$ natural numbers.
From any configuration of the KG-map machine $M_m$ at the label subtract, with any internal bit,
in which stack $A$ holds $k$ copies of the unit symbol and stack $D$ holds $n$ copies, $M_m$
reaches the failure label in exactly $n + 1$ steps, with every stack other than $A$ and $D$
unchanged.

articles.title: Subtraction loop of the clique reduction machine
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a mode of the machine, let
$k \le n$ be natural numbers, and let $S$ be stack contents in which the counter stack $A$ holds
$U^k$ ($k$ copies of the unit symbol $U$) and the counter stack $D$ holds $U^n$. Then for every
Boolean local state $v$ there are a local state $v'$ and stack contents $S'$ such that the machine
of mode $m$ runs in exactly $k + 1$ steps from label $\mathsf{sub}$ with local state $v$ and
stacks $S$ to label $\mathsf{outY}$ with local state $v'$ and stacks $S'$, the stack $D$ of $S'$
holds $U^{n-k}$, and every stack other than $A$ and $D$ has the same contents in $S'$ as in $S$.

articles.title: Number output of the clique reduction machine
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a mode of the machine and $C$
its final counter stack ($A$ for the flip mode, $D$ for the vertex-cover mode). Let $n, c$ be
natural numbers, $u$ a symbol of the alphabet of $C$, and $S$ stack contents in which the stack
$B$ holds $U^n$ ($n$ copies of the unit symbol $U$) and $C$ holds $u^c$. Then for every Boolean
local state $v$ there are a local state $v'$ and stack contents $S'$ such that the machine of
mode $m$ runs in exactly $n + c + 3$ steps from label $\mathsf{outB}$ with local state $v$ and
stacks $S$ to label $\mathsf{done}$ with local state $v'$ and stacks $S'$, and the output stack
$O$ of $S'$ holds, from the top, $c$ copies of $\mathrm{true}$, then $\mathrm{false}$, then $n$
copies of $\mathrm{true}$, then the contents of $O$ in $S$.

articles.title: CLIQUE is in NP
articles.statement: **CLIQUE is in NP**.

articles.title: CLIQUE is NP-complete
articles.statement:
CLIQUE lies in NP, and every decision problem in NP has a
polynomial-time many-one reduction to CLIQUE.

articles.title: CLIQUE is NP-hard
articles.statement:
Every decision problem $L$ in NP has a polynomial-time many-one
reduction to CLIQUE: a polynomial-time computable map $f$ on bit strings such that, for every
bit string $x$, $L$ accepts $x$ exactly when CLIQUE accepts $f(x)$.

articles.title: INDEPENDENT-SET is in NP
articles.statement: **INDEPENDENT-SET is in NP**.

articles.title: INDEPENDENT-SET is NP-complete
articles.statement:
INDEPENDENT-SET lies in NP, and every decision problem
in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to INDEPENDENT-SET.

articles.title: INDEPENDENT-SET is NP-hard
articles.statement:
Every decision problem $L$ in NP has a polynomial-time
many-one reduction to INDEPENDENT-SET: a polynomial-time computable map $f$ on bit strings such
that, for every bit string $x$, $L$ accepts $x$ exactly when INDEPENDENT-SET accepts $f(x)$.

articles.title: The CLIQUE, INDEPENDENT-SET and VERTEX-COVER verifier as a host component
articles.statement:
For a mode $m$
(clique, independent set or vertex cover), this is the host component whose stacks are
$X, W, C, N, V, T$, each over the symbol alphabet of the SAT verifier, and whose labels and
program are those of the verifier machine of mode $m$.

articles.title: NP membership from the CLIQUE, INDEPENDENT-SET and VERTEX-COVER verifier
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a
decision problem, let $m$ be a mode (clique, independent set or vertex cover), and let $V_m$ be
the verifier of mode $m$. If for every bit string $x$, $L$ accepts $x$ exactly when there is a
bit string $w$ with $|w| \le |x|$ such that $V_m$ accepts $(x, w)$, then $L$ is in NP.

articles.title: VERTEX-COVER (exact size `k`) is in NP
articles.statement:
The decision problem VERTEX-COVER, which accepts
exactly the valid encodings of a number $k$ and a graph $G$ such that $G$ has a vertex cover of
exactly $k$ vertices, is in NP.

articles.title: VERTEX-COVER (exact size `k`) is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem VERTEX-COVER, which
accepts exactly the valid encodings of a number $k$ and a graph $G$ such that $G$ has a vertex
cover of exactly $k$ vertices, is in NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a
polynomial-time many-one reduction.

articles.title: VERTEX-COVER (exact size `k`) is NP-hard
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in NP reduces by a
polynomial-time many-one reduction to the decision problem VERTEX-COVER, which accepts exactly
the valid encodings of a number $k$ and a graph $G$ such that $G$ has a vertex cover of exactly
$k$ vertices.

articles.title: The decision problem CONNECTED DOMINATING SET
articles.statement:
CONNECTED DOMINATING SET accepts a bitstring
$x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to an instance of CONNECTED
DOMINATING SET that is well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are
rejected.

articles.title: Feasible CONNECTED DOMINATING SET instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of CONNECTED
DOMINATING SET is feasible when there is a set $S$ of vertices of its graph $G$ with at most $K$
elements such that every vertex of $G$ lies in $S$ or is adjacent in $G$ to a vertex of $S$, and
the subgraph of $G$ induced by $S$ is connected (in particular, $S$ is nonempty).

articles.title: Instances of CONNECTED DOMINATING SET
articles.statement:
An instance of CONNECTED DOMINATING SET is a triple
$(n, E, K)$ of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $E$ of pairs of natural
numbers (the edges) and a natural number $K$ (the bound).

articles.title: CONNECTED DOMINATING SET is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem CONNECTED DOMINATING SET
belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one
reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), CONNECTED DOMINATING SET.

articles.title: Graph of a CONNECTED DOMINATING SET instance
articles.statement:
For an instance $(n, E, K)$ of CONNECTED
DOMINATING SET, its graph is the simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which
distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$.

articles.title: Well-formed CONNECTED DOMINATING SET instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of CONNECTED
DOMINATING SET is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$
in $E$ has $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, with the reversed pair $(v, u)$ not in $E$.

articles.title: DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH accepts
a bitstring $x$ exactly when bitstring decoding of $x$ as a quadruple $(n, E, k, m)$ succeeds and
returns an instance of DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH that is both well formed and feasible; every bitstring
that does not decode is rejected.

articles.title: Feasibility for DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, k, m)$ of DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH is
feasible when there are a finite set $S$ of exactly $k$ natural numbers, each less than $n$, and
a sublist $E'$ of $E$ (obtained by deleting entries and keeping the order) with at least $m$
entries such that both components of every pair in $E'$ lie in $S$.

For a well-formed instance this says that some $k$ vertices of the graph of $E$ on $n$ vertices
induce at least $m$ edges.

articles.title: Instances of DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH
articles.statement:
An instance of DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH is a quadruple
$(n, E, k, m)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $E$ of pairs
of natural numbers (the edges), a natural number $k$ (the size of the vertex set sought) and a
natural number $m$ (the edge threshold).

articles.title: DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH belongs to the
class NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- U. Feige, G. Kortsarz, and D. Peleg, "The dense k-subgraph problem" (2001); M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH.

articles.title: Well-formed DENSEST k-SUBGRAPH instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, k, m)$ of DENSEST
k-SUBGRAPH is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in
$E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, with the reversed pair $(v, u)$ not in $E$.

articles.title: DOMINATING SET as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem DOMINATING SET accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a triple
$(n, E, K)$ of a natural number $n$, a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers and a natural number
$K$ such that $E$ has no repeated entries, every pair $(u, v) \in E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$,
$u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin E$, and there is a set $S$ of at most $K$ vertices with every vertex
in $S$ or adjacent to a vertex of $S$, in the graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ where distinct $i$
and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$. Bitstrings that do not decode are
rejected.

articles.title: Feasibility of a DOMINATING SET instance
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of DOMINATING SET is
feasible when there is a set $S$ of at most $K$ vertices of its graph such that every vertex lies in
$S$ or is adjacent to a vertex of $S$, where the graph has vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ and
distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$.

articles.title: Instances of DOMINATING SET
articles.statement:
An instance of DOMINATING SET is a triple $(n, E, K)$ of a
natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers (the edges)
and a natural number $K$ (the bound).

articles.title: DOMINATING SET is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem DOMINATING SET belongs to NP, and
every decision problem in NP reduces to DOMINATING SET by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), DOMINATING SET.

articles.title: Graph of a DOMINATING SET instance
articles.statement:
For an instance $(n, E, K)$ of DOMINATING SET, its
graph is the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are
adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$.

articles.title: Well-formed DOMINATING SET instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of DOMINATING SET is well
formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v) \in E$ satisfies $u < n$,
$v < n$, $u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin E$.

articles.title: Edge-list adjacency for EDGE DOMINATING SET
articles.statement:
For a list $E$ of ordered pairs of natural
numbers and natural numbers $u$ and $v$, the Boolean adjacency of $u$ and $v$ in $E$ is true
exactly when $(u, v)$ or $(v, u)$ occurs in $E$.

articles.title: The EDGE DOMINATING SET decision problem
articles.statement:
EDGE DOMINATING SET is the decision problem
that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding,
to an EDGE DOMINATING SET instance $(n, E, K)$ that is well formed and feasible, that is, some
sublist of $E$ with at most $K$ entries contains, for every edge of $E$, an edge sharing an
endpoint with it. Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible EDGE DOMINATING SET instances
articles.statement:
An instance with vertex count $n$, edge list $E$
and bound $K$ is feasible when some sublist $D$ of $E$ (its entries taken in order) has at most
$K$ entries and dominates every edge of $E$: for every $e \in E$ there is $d \in D$ such that one
of the two entries of $d$ equals one of the two entries of $e$.

articles.title: EDGE DOMINATING SET instances
articles.statement:
An instance of EDGE DOMINATING SET is a triple
$(n, E, K)$ of a natural number $n$ (the vertex count), a finite list $E$ of ordered pairs of
natural numbers (the edge list) and a natural number $K$ (the bound).

articles.title: EDGE DOMINATING SET is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The EDGE DOMINATING SET decision problem belongs to
NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), EDGE DOMINATING SET; M. Yannakakis and F. Gavril, "Edge dominating sets in graphs" (1980).

articles.title: Well-formed EDGE DOMINATING SET instances
articles.statement:
An instance with vertex count $n$, edge list
$E$ and bound $K$ is well formed when $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(a, b)$ in $E$
satisfies $a < n$, $b < n$ and $a \ne b$, and $(b, a)$ does not occur in $E$. Thus $E$ lists the
edges of a simple graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$, each once and in one orientation.

articles.title: EFFICIENT DOMINATION (PERFECT CODE) as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem
EFFICIENT DOMINATION accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical
bitstring encoding of instances, to an instance $(n, E)$ that is well formed and whose graph has
an efficient dominating set. Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Instances with an efficient dominating set
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E)$ of EFFICIENT DOMINATION
is feasible when its graph has an efficient dominating set (a perfect code): a set $S$ of
vertices such that every vertex $v$ has exactly one vertex $u \in S$ with $u = v$ or $u$
adjacent to $v$.

articles.title: Efficient Domination instances
articles.statement:
An instance of EFFICIENT DOMINATION is a pair $(n, E)$
of a natural number $n$, the number of vertices, and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the
edges.

articles.title: EFFICIENT DOMINATION (PERFECT CODE) is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem EFFICIENT
DOMINATION belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time
many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), EFFICIENT DOMINATION; D. G. Corneil and Y. Perl, "Clustering and domination in perfect graphs" (1984) and the perfect-code literature.

articles.title: Graph of an Efficient Domination instance
articles.statement:
For an instance $(n, E)$, its graph is the
simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which distinct vertices $u$ and $v$ are
adjacent when $(u, v)$ or $(v, u)$ belongs to $E$.

articles.title: Well-formed Efficient Domination instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E)$ is well formed when the
list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(a, b)$ in $E$ satisfies $a < n$, $b < n$ and
$a \ne b$, and $(b, a)$ does not belong to $E$.

articles.title: Directed adjacency for FEEDBACK ARC SET
articles.statement:
For a list $E$ of ordered pairs of natural numbers
and natural numbers $u$ and $v$, the directed adjacency test returns true when the pair $(u, v)$
occurs in $E$, that is, when $E$ contains an arc from $u$ to $v$, and false otherwise.

articles.title: FEEDBACK ARC SET as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem FEEDBACK ARC SET accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of instances, to
an instance $(n, E, K)$ of FEEDBACK ARC SET that is well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do
not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible FEEDBACK ARC SET instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of FEEDBACK ARC SET is
feasible when there is an ordering $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_{n-1}$ of the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, in
which each of them occurs exactly once, such that at most $K$ entries $(u, v)$ of the list $E$,
counted with repetition, are backward, meaning that the position of $v$ in the ordering is
strictly smaller than the position of $u$. Here $v_j$ has position $j$, and a number that is not
among $0, \dots, n-1$ has position $n$.

articles.title: Instances of FEEDBACK ARC SET
articles.statement:
An instance of FEEDBACK ARC SET is a triple $(n, E, K)$
consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a finite list $E$ of ordered pairs
of natural numbers (the arcs) and a natural number $K$ (the bound).

articles.title: FEEDBACK ARC SET is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem FEEDBACK ARC SET belongs to NP, and
every decision problem in NP reduces to FEEDBACK ARC SET by a polynomial-time many-one
reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), FEEDBACK ARC SET; R. M. Karp, "Reducibility among combinatorial problems" (1972).

articles.title: Well-formed FEEDBACK ARC SET instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of FEEDBACK ARC SET is
well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies
$u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$; that is, $E$ lists distinct arcs, without loops, of a directed
graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$.

articles.title: FEEDBACK VERTEX SET as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem FEEDBACK VERTEX SET
accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of
instances, to an instance of FEEDBACK VERTEX SET that is well formed and feasible. Bitstrings
that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feedback vertex sets within the bound
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, es, K)$ of FEEDBACK VERTEX SET is
feasible when there is a set $S$ of at most $K$ vertices of its graph such that the subgraph of
its graph induced on the vertices outside $S$ is acyclic.

articles.title: Instances of FEEDBACK VERTEX SET
articles.statement:
An instance of FEEDBACK VERTEX SET is a triple
$(n, es, K)$ of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $es$ of pairs of natural
numbers (the edges) and a natural number $K$ (the bound).

articles.title: FEEDBACK VERTEX SET is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem FEEDBACK VERTEX SET belongs to
NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to FEEDBACK VERTEX SET by a polynomial-time
many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), FEEDBACK VERTEX SET.

articles.title: Graph of a FEEDBACK VERTEX SET instance
articles.statement:
For an instance $(n, es, K)$ of FEEDBACK VERTEX
SET, its graph is the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and
$j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $es$.

articles.title: Well-formed FEEDBACK VERTEX SET instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, es, K)$ of FEEDBACK VERTEX
SET is well formed when the list $es$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $es$
satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and $(v, u)$ does not belong to $es$.

articles.title: Graph of an independent dominating set instance
articles.statement:
For an independent dominating set
instance with $n$ vertices and edge list $E$, the graph of the instance is the simple graph on
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which distinct vertices $u$ and $v$ are adjacent when $(u, v)$ or
$(v, u)$ belongs to $E$.

articles.title: INDEPENDENT DOMINATING SET as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem INDEPENDENT
DOMINATING SET accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring
encoding, to an independent dominating set instance $(n, E, K)$ that is well formed and whose
graph has an independent dominating set of at most $K$ vertices. It rejects every bitstring
that does not decode to an instance.

articles.title: Instances with a small independent dominating set
articles.statement:
An independent dominating set instance
$(n, E, K)$ has a small independent dominating set when there is a set $S$ of vertices of its
graph with at most $K$ elements such that every vertex lies in $S$ or is adjacent to a vertex of
$S$, and no two distinct vertices of $S$ are adjacent.

articles.title: Independent dominating set instances
articles.statement:
An instance of INDEPENDENT DOMINATING SET is a
triple $(n, E, K)$ of a natural number $n$, the number of vertices, a list $E$ of pairs of
natural numbers, the edges, and a natural number $K$, the bound on the size of the set.

articles.title: INDEPENDENT DOMINATING SET is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem INDEPENDENT DOMINATING
SET belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to
it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), INDEPENDENT DOMINATING SET (a small maximal independent set).

articles.title: Well-formed independent dominating set instances
articles.statement:
An independent dominating set instance
$(n, E, K)$ is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(a, b)$ in
$E$ satisfies $a < n$, $b < n$, $a \ne b$, and $(b, a)$ does not belong to $E$.

articles.title: The MAXIMUM INDUCED MATCHING decision problem
articles.statement:
MAXIMUM INDUCED MATCHING is the decision
problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring
encoding, to a maximum-induced-matching instance $(n, E, K)$ that is well formed and feasible:
the edge list $E$ has no repeated entries, every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$
and $u \ne v$ with $(v, u)$ not in $E$, and some sublist $M$ of $E$ of length at least $K$ is an
induced matching, meaning that any two distinct pairs in $M$ share no endpoint and no pair in $E$
joins an endpoint of one pair in $M$ to an endpoint of a different pair in $M$. Bitstrings that
do not decode are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible maximum-induced-matching instances
articles.statement:
A maximum-induced-matching instance
$(n, E, K)$, with vertex count $n$, edge list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers and bound $K$, is
feasible when there is a sublist $M$ of $E$ of length at least $K$ such that any two distinct
pairs in $M$ share no endpoint, and no pair in $E$ joins an endpoint of one pair in $M$ to an
endpoint of a different pair in $M$.

articles.title: Maximum-induced-matching instances
articles.statement:
A maximum-induced-matching instance is a triple
$(n, E, K)$ of a natural number $n$ (the vertex count), a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers
(the edges) and a natural number $K$ (the bound).

articles.title: MAXIMUM INDUCED MATCHING is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The MAXIMUM INDUCED MATCHING decision problem
belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one
reduction.

## Sources

- L. J. Stockmeyer and V. V. Vazirani, "NP-completeness of some generalizations of the maximum matching problem", Information Processing Letters 15 (1982), 14-19; K. Cameron, "Induced matchings", Discrete Applied Mathematics 24 (1989), 97-102 (NP-completeness for bipartite graphs, polynomial for chordal graphs).

articles.title: Well-formed maximum-induced-matching instances
articles.statement:
A maximum-induced-matching instance
$(n, E, K)$ is well formed when the edge list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$
in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, with the reverse pair $(v, u)$ not in $E$.

articles.title: Graph augmented by added edges
articles.statement:
For an instance $(n, E, K)$ of MINIMUM FILL-IN and a
list $A$ of pairs of natural numbers, the augmented graph is the graph of the edge list $E$
followed by $A$ on $n$ vertices: the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which distinct
vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$ or to $A$.

articles.title: The MINIMUM FILL-IN (CHORDAL COMPLETION) problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem MINIMUM FILL-IN
accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to an
instance $(n, E, K)$ of MINIMUM FILL-IN that is well formed and feasible.

articles.title: Feasible MINIMUM FILL-IN instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of MINIMUM FILL-IN is
feasible when there are an ordering $\sigma$ of the vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$ (a list that
contains each of them exactly once) and a list $A$ of pairs of natural numbers, with no repeated
entries and at most $K$ entries, such that every pair $(u, v)$ in $A$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$
and $u \ne v$, neither $(u, v)$ nor $(v, u)$ belongs to $E$, and $(v, u)$ does not belong to $A$,
and such that, in the graph augmented by $A$, any two distinct vertices $a$ and $b$ that are both
adjacent to a vertex $v$ and both come after $v$ in $\sigma$ are adjacent to each other.

The ordering $\sigma$ is thus a perfect elimination ordering of the augmented graph, so adding
the at most $K$ edges of $A$ to the graph makes it chordal.

articles.title: Instances of MINIMUM FILL-IN
articles.statement:
An instance of MINIMUM FILL-IN is a triple $(n, E, K)$
consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $E$ of pairs of natural
numbers (the edge list) and a natural number $K$ (the bound).

articles.title: MINIMUM FILL-IN (CHORDAL COMPLETION) is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem
MINIMUM FILL-IN lies in NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one
reduction to MINIMUM FILL-IN.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), MINIMUM FILL-IN; M. Yannakakis, "Computing the minimum fill-in is NP-complete" (1981).

articles.title: Well-formed MINIMUM FILL-IN instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of MINIMUM FILL-IN is well
formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies
$u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and its reverse $(v, u)$ does not belong to $E$.

articles.title: Graph of an odd cycle transversal instance
articles.statement:
For an odd cycle transversal instance
$(n, es, K)$, its graph is the graph of the edge list $es$ on $n$ vertices: the simple graph on
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$
belongs to $es$.

articles.title: ODD CYCLE TRANSVERSAL as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem ODD CYCLE TRANSVERSAL
accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to an
odd cycle transversal instance $(n, es, K)$ that is well formed and feasible. Well formed means
that $es$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $es$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$,
$u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin es$; feasible means that some set of at most $K$ vertices can be
removed from the graph of the instance so that the remaining induced subgraph is bipartite.
Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible odd cycle transversal instances
articles.statement:
An odd cycle transversal instance $(n, es, K)$
is feasible when there is a set $S$ of at most $K$ vertices of its graph such that the subgraph
induced on the vertices outside $S$ is bipartite.

articles.title: Odd cycle transversal instances
articles.statement:
An odd cycle transversal instance is a triple
$(n, es, K)$ of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $es$ of pairs of natural
numbers (the edges) and a natural number $K$ (the bound on the number of removed vertices).

articles.title: ODD CYCLE TRANSVERSAL is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem ODD CYCLE TRANSVERSAL, which
accepts a bitstring exactly when it decodes to a well-formed instance $(n, es, K)$ whose graph
becomes bipartite after removing some set of at most $K$ vertices, belongs to NP, and every
decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), ODD CYCLE TRANSVERSAL (vertex deletion to a bipartite graph).

articles.title: Well-formed odd cycle transversal instances
articles.statement:
An odd cycle transversal instance
$(n, es, K)$ is well formed when the list $es$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in
$es$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and $(v, u)$ does not belong to $es$.

articles.title: Graph of a Roman domination instance
articles.statement:
For an instance $(n, E, K)$ of ROMAN DOMINATION,
its graph is the graph of the edge list $E$ on $n$ vertices: the simple graph on
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or
$(j, i)$ belongs to $E$.

articles.title: ROMAN DOMINATION as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem ROMAN DOMINATION accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to an instance
$(n, E, K)$ of ROMAN DOMINATION that is well formed and feasible; it rejects every other
bitstring.

articles.title: Feasible Roman domination instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of ROMAN DOMINATION is
feasible when there is a function $f$ from the vertices $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ of its graph to
$\{0, 1, 2\}$ such that every vertex $v$ with $f(v) = 0$ is adjacent to some vertex $u$ with
$f(u) = 2$, and the total weight $\sum_v f(v)$ is at most $K$.

articles.title: Roman domination instances
articles.statement:
An instance of ROMAN DOMINATION is a triple $(n, E, K)$ of a
natural number $n$, the number of vertices, a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the edges,
and a natural number $K$, the weight bound.

articles.title: ROMAN DOMINATION is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem ROMAN DOMINATION belongs to NP, and
every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- E. J. Cockayne, P. A. Dreyer Jr., S. M. Hedetniemi, and S. T. Hedetniemi, "Roman domination in graphs", Discrete Mathematics 278 (2004), 11-22.

articles.title: Well-formed Roman domination instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of ROMAN DOMINATION is
well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ has
$u < n$, $v < n$, $u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin E$.

articles.title: Graph of a total dominating set instance
articles.statement:
The graph of an instance $(n, E, K)$ of TOTAL
DOMINATING SET is the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$
are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$. Loops are dropped, and pairs with an
endpoint at least $n$ contribute no edge.

articles.title: The decision problem TOTAL DOMINATING SET
articles.statement:
TOTAL DOMINATING SET accepts a bitstring $x$
exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of triples of a natural number,
a list of pairs of natural numbers and a natural number, to an instance $(n, E, K)$ that is well
formed and feasible: some set of at most $K$ vertices of the graph of the instance contains a
neighbor of every vertex. Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasibility of a total dominating set instance
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of TOTAL
DOMINATING SET is feasible when there is a set $S$ of at most $K$ vertices of its graph such that
every vertex $v$ of the graph, including the vertices of $S$, is adjacent to some vertex
$u \in S$.

articles.title: Instances of TOTAL DOMINATING SET
articles.statement:
An instance of TOTAL DOMINATING SET is a triple
$(n, E, K)$ consisting of a natural number $n$, the number of vertices, a list $E$ of pairs of
natural numbers, the edges, and a natural number $K$, the bound.

articles.title: TOTAL DOMINATING SET is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem TOTAL DOMINATING SET belongs to
NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to TOTAL DOMINATING SET by a polynomial-time
many-one reduction.

## Sources

- E. J. Cockayne, R. M. Dawes, and S. T. Hedetniemi, "Total domination in graphs", Networks 10 (1980), 211-219; R. Laskar, J. Pfaff, S. M. Hedetniemi, and S. T. Hedetniemi, "On the algorithmic complexity of total domination", SIAM Journal on Algebraic and Discrete Methods 5 (1984), 420-425.

articles.title: Well-formed total dominating set instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of TOTAL DOMINATING
SET is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$
satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and its reversal $(v, u)$ does not belong to $E$.

articles.title: Well-formed 0-1 integer programming instances
articles.statement:
A 0-1 integer programming instance
$(n, A, b)$ is well formed when the right-hand side list $b$ has as many entries as there are
rows of the coefficient matrix $A$, and every row of $A$ has exactly $n$ entries.

articles.title: 0-1 INTEGER PROGRAMMING FEASIBILITY is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem 0-1 INTEGER
PROGRAMMING FEASIBILITY belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time
many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), 0-1 INTEGER PROGRAMMING; R. M. Karp, "Reducibility among combinatorial problems" (1972).

articles.title: 0-1 integer programming feasibility as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem 0-1
INTEGER PROGRAMMING FEASIBILITY accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the
canonical bitstring encoding, to a 0-1 integer programming instance that is well formed and
feasible; it rejects every bitstring that does not decode to such an instance.

articles.title: Feasible 0-1 integer programs
articles.statement:
Let $(n, A, b)$ be a 0-1 integer programming instance whose
coefficient matrix has the rows $A_0, \dots, A_{m-1}$, with list entries indexed from $0$. For
$r < m$ and $j < n$, let $a_{rj}$ be the integer $p - q$ if row $A_r$ has a $j$-th entry
$(p, q)$, and $a_{rj} = 0$ otherwise; let $b_r$ be the integer $p' - q'$ if $b$ has an $r$-th
entry $(p', q')$, and $b_r = 0$ otherwise. The instance is feasible when there is
$x \in \{0, 1\}^n$ such that $\sum_{j < n} a_{rj} x_j \le b_r$ in $\mathbb{Z}$ for every $r < m$.

articles.title: 0-1 integer programming instances
articles.statement:
A 0-1 integer programming instance is a triple
$(n, A, b)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of variables), a coefficient matrix
$A$ given as a list of rows, each row a list of pairs of natural numbers, and a right-hand side
$b$ given as a list of pairs of natural numbers. A pair $(p, q)$ is read as the integer $p - q$,
so coefficients and right-hand side entries are stored by positive and negative parts.

articles.title: 3-PARTITION as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem 3-PARTITION accepts a bitstring
$x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a 3-partition instance
$(a, B)$ that is well formed (the length of the list $a$ is a multiple of $3$) and feasible (the
entries of $a$ can be split into triples each summing to $B$). Bitstrings that do not decode to
an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible 3-partition instances
articles.statement:
Let $(a, B)$ be a 3-partition instance with
$a = (a_0, \dots, a_{N-1})$, and let $m = \lfloor N/3 \rfloor$. The instance is feasible when
there is a map $g : \{0, \dots, N-1\} \to \{0, \dots, m-1\}$ such that for every $t < m$ exactly
three indices $j$ satisfy $g(j) = t$, and the sum of $a_j$ over these indices equals $B$.

articles.title: 3-partition instances
articles.statement:
An instance of 3-PARTITION is a pair $(a, B)$ of a finite list $a$
of natural numbers and a natural number $B$, the target sum.

articles.title: 3-PARTITION is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem 3-PARTITION on bitstrings is in NP, and
every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), 3-PARTITION (strongly NP-complete).

articles.title: Well-formed 3-partition instances
articles.statement:
A 3-partition instance $(a, B)$ is well formed when the
length of the list $a$ is a multiple of $3$.

articles.title: The bin packing decision problem
articles.statement:
BIN PACKING is the decision problem that accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of bin packing
instances, to a feasible instance; it rejects every bitstring that fails to decode.

articles.title: Feasible bin packing instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(s, B, K)$ of BIN PACKING is feasible when
there is a list of exactly $K$ bins, each a finite list of natural numbers with sum at most $B$,
such that the concatenation of the bins is a permutation of $s$.

Since bins may be empty, this says that the items fit into at most $K$ bins of capacity $B$.

articles.title: Bin packing instances
articles.statement:
An instance of BIN PACKING is a triple $(s, B, K)$ of a finite
list $s$ of natural numbers (the item sizes), a natural number $B$ (the bin capacity) and a
natural number $K$ (the number of bins).

articles.title: BIN PACKING is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The bin packing decision problem belongs to NP, and every
decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), BIN PACKING; D. S. Johnson, "Fast algorithms for bin packing" (1974).

articles.title: Exact-cardinality subset sum as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem
EXACT-CARDINALITY SUBSET SUM accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical
bitstring encoding, to an exact-cardinality subset-sum instance that is feasible; it rejects every
bitstring that does not decode.

articles.title: Feasibility of an exact-cardinality subset-sum instance
articles.statement:
An exact-cardinality subset-sum
instance $(a, K, T)$ is feasible when some subsequence of the list $a$ (entries kept in order, not
necessarily contiguous) has exactly $K$ entries and sum $T$.

articles.title: Exact-cardinality subset-sum instances
articles.statement:
An exact-cardinality subset-sum instance is a
triple $(a, K, T)$ consisting of a list $a$ of natural numbers, a natural number $K$ (the
cardinality) and a natural number $T$ (the target).

articles.title: EXACT-CARDINALITY SUBSET SUM is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem EXACT-CARDINALITY
SUBSET SUM lies in NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction
to it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), SUBSET SUM; NP-completeness via the zero-padding reduction from ordinary subset sum.

articles.title: The KNAPSACK decision problem
articles.statement:
KNAPSACK is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring
$x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a knapsack instance
$(I, C, T)$ for which some subsequence of the item list $I$, possibly empty, has total weight at
most $C$ and total value at least $T$. Bitstrings that do not decode are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible knapsack instances
articles.statement:
A knapsack instance $(I, C, T)$, with item list $I$, capacity
$C$ and target value $T$, is feasible when some subsequence of $I$, possibly empty, has total
weight at most $C$ and total value at least $T$. Repeated items in $I$ are distinct occurrences
that can be selected separately.

articles.title: Knapsack instances
articles.statement:
A 0/1 knapsack instance is a triple $(I, C, T)$ of a list $I$ of items,
each a pair $(w, v)$ of natural numbers giving its weight $w$ and value $v$, a natural-number
capacity $C$, and a natural-number target value $T$.

articles.title: KNAPSACK is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The KNAPSACK decision problem is in NP, and every decision
problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability: A Guide to the Theory of NP-Completeness* (1979), KNAPSACK (MP9).

articles.title: MULTIPLE KNAPSACK as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem MULTIPLE KNAPSACK accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a feasible
multiple-knapsack instance. Bitstrings that do not decode are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible multiple-knapsack instances
articles.statement:
Let a multiple-knapsack instance have items
$(w_0, v_0), \dots, (w_{k-1}, v_{k-1})$ (weight, value), knapsack capacities
$c_0, \dots, c_{m-1}$ and target $V$. The instance is feasible when there are
$a_0, \dots, a_{k-1} \in \{0, \dots, m\}$, where $a_j = b < m$ puts item $j$ in knapsack $b$
and $a_j = m$ leaves item $j$ out, such that for every $b < m$ the total weight
$\sum_{j : a_j = b} w_j$ is at most $c_b$, and the total value $\sum_{j : a_j < m} v_j$ is at
least $V$.

articles.title: Multiple-knapsack instances
articles.statement:
A multiple-knapsack instance consists of a finite list of
items, each a pair $(w, v)$ of natural numbers giving its weight $w$ and value $v$, a finite list
of natural-number knapsack capacities, and a natural-number target value.

articles.title: MULTIPLE KNAPSACK is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem MULTIPLE KNAPSACK belongs to NP,
and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to MULTIPLE KNAPSACK.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), MULTIPLE KNAPSACK.

articles.title: The MULTIWAY NUMBER PARTITION decision problem
articles.statement:
MULTIWAY NUMBER PARTITION is the decision
problem on bitstrings that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical
bitstring encoding, to a multiway number partition instance $(a, K)$ that is feasible. Bitstrings
that do not decode to a multiway number partition instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible multiway number partition instances
articles.statement:
Let $(a, K)$ be a multiway number partition
instance with $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{m-1})$. It is feasible when $K \ge 1$ and there is a map $f$
from $\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ onto $\{0, \dots, K-1\}$ such that the sums
$\sum_{j < m,\, f(j) = p} a_j$ for $p = 0, \dots, K-1$ are all equal. In other words, the entries
of $a$, counted with repetition, can be split into $K$ nonempty parts with equal sums.

articles.title: Multiway number partition instances
articles.statement:
A multiway number partition instance is a pair
$(a, K)$ consisting of a list $a$ of natural numbers and a natural number $K$ (the number of
parts).

articles.title: MULTIWAY NUMBER PARTITION is NP-complete
articles.statement:
Let MULTIWAY NUMBER PARTITION be the decision
problem that accepts exactly the bitstrings decoding to a feasible multiway number partition
instance: a list of natural numbers and a number $K \ge 1$ such that the entries of the list,
counted with repetition, can be split into $K$ nonempty parts with equal sums. Then MULTIWAY
NUMBER PARTITION is in NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time
many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), MULTIWAY NUMBER PARTITION (the `K = 2` slice is PARTITION).

articles.title: NUMERICAL 3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem NUMERICAL
3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a
polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), NUMERICAL 3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING (strongly NP-complete).

articles.title: NUMERICAL 3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem NUMERICAL
3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical
bitstring encoding (natural numbers in binary), to an instance $(A, B, C, t)$ that is well
formed and feasible: the lists $B$ and $C$ have the same length $n$ as the list $A$, and there
are permutations $p$ and $q$ of the numbers $0$ through $n-1$ such that
$A_j + B_{p(j)} + C_{q(j)} = t$ for every $j < n$, with lists indexed from $0$. Every other
bitstring is rejected.

articles.title: Feasible numerical 3-dimensional matching instances
articles.statement:
Let $(A, B, C, t)$ be an instance
and let $n$ be the length of $A$, with lists indexed from $0$. The instance is feasible when
there are permutations $p$ and $q$ of the numbers $0$ through $n-1$ such that
$A_j + B_{p(j)} + C_{q(j)} = t$ for every $j < n$, where an entry of $B$ or $C$ at an index past
the end of its list counts as $0$.

articles.title: Numerical 3-dimensional matching instances
articles.statement:
An instance of NUMERICAL 3-DIMENSIONAL
MATCHING is a quadruple $(A, B, C, t)$ of three finite lists $A$, $B$, $C$ of natural numbers
and a natural number $t$, the target.

articles.title: Well-formed numerical 3-dimensional matching instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(A, B, C, t)$ of
NUMERICAL 3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING is well formed when the lists $B$ and $C$ have the same length
as the list $A$.

articles.title: The STRIP PACKING decision problem
articles.statement:
STRIP PACKING is the decision problem that accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of strip packing
instances, to a strip packing instance that is well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do not
decode to a strip packing instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible strip packings
articles.statement:
A strip packing instance $(R, W, H)$ with
$R = ((w_1, h_1), \dots, (w_n, h_n))$ is feasible when there are natural numbers
$x_1, y_1, \dots, x_n, y_n$ such that $x_j + w_j \le W$ and $y_j + h_j \le H$ for every
$1 \le j \le n$, and for all $1 \le a < b \le n$ at least one of $x_a + w_a \le x_b$,
$x_b + w_b \le x_a$, $y_a + h_a \le y_b$ and $y_b + h_b \le y_a$ holds.

That is, the unrotated rectangles with lower-left corners $(x_j, y_j)$, widths $w_j$ and heights
$h_j$ lie in $[0, W] \times [0, H]$, and any two of them are separated by a vertical or a
horizontal line. When all widths and heights are positive, the latter says that no two of the
rectangles overlap in their interiors.

articles.title: Strip packing instances
articles.statement:
A strip packing instance is a triple $(R, W, H)$ consisting of a
finite list $R = ((w_1, h_1), \dots, (w_n, h_n))$ of pairs of natural numbers, the widths and
heights of the rectangles, a natural number $W$, the width of the strip, and a natural number $H$,
the height bound.

articles.title: STRIP PACKING is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The STRIP PACKING decision problem belongs to NP, and every
decision problem $L$ in NP reduces to STRIP PACKING by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), STRIP PACKING (axis-aligned, no rotations).

articles.title: Well-formed strip packing instances
articles.statement:
A strip packing instance $(R, W, H)$ is well formed
when every rectangle $(w, h)$ in the list $R$ has $w > 0$ and $h > 0$.

articles.title: SUBSET PRODUCT as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem SUBSET PRODUCT accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of pairs of a finite
list of natural numbers and a natural number, to an instance $(a, T)$ that is well formed (every
entry of $a$ is positive) and feasible (some sublist of $a$ has product exactly $T$). It rejects
every bitstring that does not decode to an instance.

articles.title: Feasible SUBSET PRODUCT instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(a, T)$ of SUBSET PRODUCT, with $a$ a
finite list of natural numbers and $T$ a natural number, is feasible when some sublist of $a$ (a
list obtained from $a$ by deleting entries and keeping the order of the rest) has product exactly
$T$.

articles.title: SUBSET PRODUCT instances
articles.statement:
An instance of SUBSET PRODUCT is a pair $(a, T)$ of a finite
list $a$ of natural numbers and a target natural number $T$.

articles.title: SUBSET PRODUCT is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem SUBSET PRODUCT lies in NP, and every
decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to SUBSET PRODUCT.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), SUBSET PRODUCT.

articles.title: Well-formed SUBSET PRODUCT instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(a, T)$ of SUBSET PRODUCT, with $a$ a
finite list of natural numbers and $T$ a natural number, is well formed when every entry of $a$
is positive.

articles.title: Base-4 expansions with digits below $4$ are unique
articles.statement:
Let $m, A, B \in \mathbb{N}$ and let
$d, e : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $d(q) < 4$ and $e(q) < 4$ for every $q < m$. Then
$A \cdot 4^m + \sum_{q < m} d(q) \, 4^q = B \cdot 4^m + \sum_{q < m} e(q) \, 4^q$ holds if and only
if $A = B$ and $d(q) = e(q)$ for every $q < m$.

articles.title: Value of the empty bit list
articles.statement:
The empty bit list, read as a binary number least significant
bit first, has value $0$.

articles.title: Edge numbers of the SUBSET-SUM reduction
articles.statement:
Given a list $b$ of pair bits and a pair index
$q$, the number of pair $q$ is $4^q$ if bit $b_q$ is set and $0$ otherwise; an index past the end
of $b$ counts as an unset bit.

articles.title: Bit-string encoding of SUBSET-SUM instances
articles.statement:
The instance with numbers $a_1, \dots, a_r$
and target $t$ is encoded as the block of $t$ followed by the blocks of $a_1, \dots, a_r$ in
order. The block of a number is its binary expansion, least significant bit first and empty for
the number $0$, made self-delimiting by writing each bit $c$ as $1c$ and appending a final $0$.

articles.title: Vertex covers of size $k$ match subset sums hitting the target
articles.statement:
Let $k, n \in \mathbb{N}$
and let $b$ be a list of booleans with one entry for each pair in the list of vertex pairs
$(i, j)$, $i < j < n$. Let $G$ be the graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$ encoded by the pair
bits $b$. Then $G$ has a vertex cover with exactly $k$ vertices if and only if some sublist (a
subsequence, not necessarily contiguous) of the reduction's numbers for $n$ and $b$ sums to the
reduction's target for $k$, $n$ and $b$.

articles.title: Sublists of the reduction's numbers as vertex and pair sets
articles.statement:
Let $n, t \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$b$ be a list of booleans, and let $m$ be the length of the list of vertex pairs $(i, j)$,
$i < j < n$. Write $x_v$ for the vertex number of $v$ and $y_q$ for the pair number of $q$ defined
from $n$ and $b$. Some sublist (a subsequence, not necessarily contiguous) of the reduction's
numbers for $n$ and $b$ sums to $t$ if and only if there are finite sets $S$ of vertices $v < n$
and $F$ of pair indices $q < m$ with $\sum_{v \in S} x_v + \sum_{q \in F} y_q = t$.

articles.title: Vertex covers in terms of the pair bits
articles.statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $b$ be a list of
booleans with one entry for each pair in the list of vertex pairs $(i, j)$, $i < j < n$, and let
$G$ be the graph on the vertices $0, \dots, n - 1$ encoded by the pair bits $b$. Let $s$ be a
finite set of vertices of $G$ and $S$ a finite set of natural numbers such that each vertex $i$
lies in $s$ exactly when $i \in S$. Then $s$ is a vertex cover of $G$ if and only if, for every
index $q$ (counting from $0$) of the pair list whose entry in $b$ is true, the $q$-th pair
$(i_q, j_q)$ satisfies $i_q \in S$ or $j_q \in S$.

articles.title: Fixed no-instance of SUBSET-SUM
articles.statement:
The encoding of the SUBSET-SUM instance with no numbers
and target $1$. It is a no-instance, because the only sublist of the empty list sums to $0$.

articles.title: Place value of a vertex pair in the SUBSET-SUM reduction
articles.statement:
The place value of pair number
$q$ is $4^q$. The numbers of the reduction from VERTEX-COVER to SUBSET-SUM are written in base
$4$, with the digit at position $q$ belonging to pair $q$.

articles.title: Reduction from VERTEX-COVER to SUBSET-SUM
articles.statement:
The map on bit strings reads $x$ as $k$ ones, a
zero, $n$ ones, a zero and a remaining list $b$ of pair bits. If this parse succeeds and $b$ has
exactly $n(n-1)/2$ bits, one per vertex pair, then $x$ is sent to the encoding of the SUBSET-SUM
instance whose numbers are the numbers of the reduction for $n$ and $b$ and whose target is the
target for $k$, $n$ and $b$. Otherwise $x$ is sent to the fixed no-instance with no numbers and
target $1$.

articles.title: Numbers of the SUBSET-SUM reduction
articles.statement:
For $n$ vertices and a list $b$ of pair bits, with
$m = n(n-1)/2$ vertex pairs, the numbers of the instance are the vertex numbers of
$v = 0, \dots, n - 1$, in this order, followed by the edge numbers of the pairs
$q = 0, \dots, m - 1$, in this order.

articles.title: The target in base 4
articles.statement:
Let $k, n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $b$ be a list of booleans, and let $m$
be the length of the list of vertex pairs $(i, j)$, $i < j < n$. The reduction's target for $k$,
$n$ and $b$ equals $k \cdot 4^m + \sum_{q < m} c_q 4^q$, where $c_q = 2$ if entry $q$ of $b$
(counting from $0$) is true and $c_q = 0$ otherwise, in particular when $b$ has no entry $q$.

articles.title: Target of the SUBSET-SUM reduction
articles.statement:
Let $m = n(n-1)/2$ be the number of vertex pairs
