direction $b$, followed by $t_{i+1}$, is a chain for $R$: every entry is related by $R$ to the
next one.

articles.title: Chain condition for the forward path
articles.statement:
Let $R$ be a relation on $\mathbb{N}$, let $m$ and
$k$ be natural numbers, $c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ a map and $d : \mathbb{N} \to
\{\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}\}$ a choice of directions, and write $t_a = m + a(3m + 2)$ for
the top of diamond $a$. If for every $i < k$ the traversal of diamond $i$ for $c$ in direction
$d(i)$, followed by $t_{i+1}$, is a chain for $R$ (every entry is related by $R$ to the next
one), then the forward path through the first $k$ diamonds for $c$ and $d$ is a chain for
$R$.

articles.title: A satisfying choice gives a Hamiltonian path
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula with $m$
clauses, let $v_0, \dots, v_{k-1}$ be its distinct variables in the order used by the
construction, let $\sigma$ assign a truth value to every variable, and write
$t_a = m + a(3m + 2)$ for the top of diamond $a$. Let $c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be such
that for every $j < m$ we have $c(j) < k$ and clause $j$ of $\varphi$ contains the literal over
$v_{c(j)}$ that $\sigma$ makes true (positive if $\sigma(v_{c(j)})$ is true, negative
otherwise). Then the forward path through the first $k$ diamonds for $c$, with diamond $i$
traversed in direction $\sigma(v_i)$, is a Hamiltonian path from $t_0$ to $t_k$ in the digraph
on the vertices $0, \dots, t_k$ whose arcs are the arcs of the construction for $\varphi$.

articles.title: The frame arcs of a diamond
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula with $m$ clauses, let $i$
and $x$ be natural numbers, and write $t_a = m + a(3m + 2)$ for the top of diamond $a$ and
$r_l = t_i + 1 + l$ for the row vertices of diamond $i$. The four arcs $(t_i, r_0)$,
$(t_i, r_{3m})$, $(r_0, t_{i+1})$ and $(r_{3m}, t_{i+1})$ are arcs of diamond $i$ for the
variable $x$ in the construction for $\varphi$.

articles.title: The detour arcs of a negative occurrence
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula with $m$
clauses, let $i$, $x$ and $j$ be natural numbers with $j < m$, and write
$r_l = m + i(3m + 2) + 1 + l$ for the row vertices of diamond $i$. If the negative literal
$\neg x$ occurs in clause $j$ of $\varphi$, then $(r_{3j+2}, j)$ and $(j, r_{3j+1})$ are arcs
of diamond $i$ for the variable $x$ in the construction for $\varphi$.

articles.title: Positive detour arcs of a diamond
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula with $m$ clauses, let
$i$, $x$, $j$ be natural numbers with $j < m$, and write $r_i(l)$ for row vertex $l$ of diamond
$i$. If the variable $x$ occurs positively in clause $j$ of $\varphi$ (counting clauses from $0$),
then the arcs of diamond $i$ for variable $x$ include both the arc from $r_i(3j+1)$ to clause
vertex $j$ and the arc from clause vertex $j$ to $r_i(3j+2)$.

articles.title: Row arcs of a diamond
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula with $m$ clauses, let $i$ and $x$ be
natural numbers, and write $r_i(l)$ for row vertex $l$ of diamond $i$. For every $l < 3m$, the arcs
of diamond $i$ for variable $x$ include both the arc from $r_i(l)$ to $r_i(l+1)$ and the arc from
$r_i(l+1)$ to $r_i(l)$.

articles.title: Diamond arcs are arcs of the construction
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula, let
$x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ be its distinct variables in the order used by the construction, and let
$i < k$. Every arc of diamond $i$ for variable $x_i$ is an arc of the HAMPATH construction for
$\varphi$.

articles.title: First counter of a HAMPATH-verifier comparison
articles.statement:
The function from the four counter
comparisons of the HAMPATH verifier to its stacks that sends the comparisons of the current
vertex with the vertex count and of the current vertex with the start vertex to the
current-vertex counter $A$, the comparison of the number of vertices seen with the vertex count
to the vertices-seen counter $C$, and the comparison of the previous vertex with the end vertex
to the previous-vertex counter $B$.

articles.title: Step of the HAMPATH verifier's unary comparison loop
articles.statement:
For stacks $\mathit{src}$,
$\mathit{sv}$, $c$ of the HAMPATH verifier, label families $\mathit{self}$ and $\mathit{fin}$
indexed by booleans, and a boolean verdict $\mathit{ok}$, this is the instruction that pops the top
of $\mathit{src}$, reads it as a bit $b$ (false if $\mathit{src}$ is empty or its top is not a bit
symbol), and pushes the bit symbol of $b$ onto $\mathit{sv}$. If $b$ is true, it pops $c$; if $c$
was nonempty it pushes the bit symbol of true onto the scratch stack $R$ and goes to
$\mathit{self}(\mathit{ok})$, and otherwise it goes to $\mathit{self}(\mathrm{false})$. If $b$ is
false, it goes to $\mathit{fin}(\mathit{ok})$ when $c$ is empty and to
$\mathit{fin}(\mathrm{false})$ otherwise.

Iterated, it compares the next unary number of $\mathit{src}$ with the counter $c$, one unit of $c$
per true, parked on $R$: $\mathit{ok}$ is the verdict so far, falsified when $c$ runs out early.

articles.title: Second counter of a HAMPATH-verifier comparison
articles.statement:
The function from the four counter
comparisons of the HAMPATH verifier to its stacks that sends the comparisons of the current
vertex with the vertex count and of the number of vertices seen with the vertex count to the
vertex-count counter $N$, the comparison of the current vertex with the start vertex to the
start-vertex counter $S$, and the comparison of the previous vertex with the end vertex to the
end-vertex counter $T$.

articles.title: Counter comparisons of the HAMPATH verifier
articles.statement:
The four-element type of the comparisons the
verifier makes between its counters: the current vertex $a$ with the vertex count $n$, the
current vertex $a$ with the start vertex $s$, the number $c$ of vertices seen with $n$, and the
previous vertex $b$ with the end vertex $t$.

articles.title: Backward direction of SAT ≤ HAMPATH for paths with normal detours
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a CNF
formula with $m$ clauses and $k$ distinct variables. In Sipser's HAMPATH graph for $\varphi$, clause
$j$ is vertex $j < m$, the top of diamond $i$ is $t_i = m + i(3m + 2)$, and vertex $l \le 3m$ of
its row is $r_{i,l} = t_i + 1 + l$. If $p$ is a Hamiltonian path of this graph (on the vertices
$0, \dots, t_k$) from $t_0$ to $t_k$ whose detours are normal, that is, for every $j < m$ there is
$i < k$ such that $j$ sits in $p$ immediately between $r_{i,3j+1}$ and $r_{i,3j+2}$, in either
order, then $\varphi$ is satisfiable.

The satisfying assignment makes the variable of diamond $i$ true iff row $i$ is traversed from
left to right.

articles.title: Every vertex of the contracted path except its end has a successor
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a CNF
formula with $m$ clauses and $k$ distinct variables. In Sipser's HAMPATH graph for $\varphi$, clause
$j$ is vertex $j < m$ and the top of diamond $i$ is $t_i = m + i(3m + 2)$. Let $p$ be a
Hamiltonian path of this graph (on the vertices $0, \dots, t_k$) from $t_0$ to $t_k$, and let $p'$
be $p$ with the clause vertices deleted. Then every vertex $v \ne t_k$ of $p'$ is immediately
followed in $p'$ by some vertex $w$.

articles.title: The construction has a Hamiltonian path iff the formula is satisfiable
articles.statement:
Let
$\varphi$ be a CNF formula with $m$ clauses and $k$ distinct variables, and let
$t_i = m + i(3m + 2)$ be the top vertex of diamond $i$ in Sipser's construction. The digraph on
the vertices $0, \dots, t_k$ whose arcs are the arcs of the construction for $\varphi$ has a
Hamiltonian path from $t_0$ to $t_k$ if and only if $\varphi$ is satisfiable.

articles.title: Every top but the last is followed by an end of its row
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula
with $m$ clauses and $k$ distinct variables. In Sipser's HAMPATH graph for $\varphi$, clause $j$ is
vertex $j < m$, the top of diamond $i$ is $t_i = m + i(3m + 2)$, and vertex $l \le 3m$ of its row
is $r_{i,l} = t_i + 1 + l$. Let $p$ be a Hamiltonian path of this graph (on the vertices
$0, \dots, t_k$) from $t_0$ to $t_k$ whose detours are normal: for every $j < m$ there is $i < k$
such that $j$ sits in $p$ immediately between $r_{i,3j+1}$ and $r_{i,3j+2}$, in either order. Let
$p'$ be $p$ with the clause vertices deleted. Then for every $i < k$, the top $t_i$ is
immediately followed in $p'$ by $r_{i,0}$ or by $r_{i,3m}$.

articles.title: HAMPATH on an encoded instance
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $s$, $t$, $n$ and every list $E$
of pairs of natural numbers, the HAMPATH decision problem accepts the PATH encoding of
$(s, t, n, E)$ if and only if the digraph on $0, \dots, n - 1$ with edge list $E$ has a
Hamiltonian path from $s$ to $t$.

articles.title: HAMPATH rejects the fixed no-instance
articles.statement:
The HAMPATH decision problem rejects the PATH
encoding of the digraph on the two vertices $0, 1$ with no arcs and $s = t = 0$: a path from $0$
to $0$ that visits both vertices would repeat $0$.

articles.title: Positions in the list of distinct variables
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula, let
$v_0, \dots, v_{k-1}$ be the list of distinct variables of $\varphi$, and let $i < k$. Then the
first position at which $v_i$ occurs in this list is $i$.

articles.title: Emptiness test
articles.statement:
For a stack $k$ and labels $e$ and $ne$, the verifier instruction that
looks at the top of stack $k$ without changing any stack, then goes to $e$ if $k$ is empty and
to $ne$ otherwise.

articles.title: Stacks of the Hamiltonian path verifier
articles.statement:
The verifier has twelve stacks: the input $X$
and the witness $W$; the counters $S$, $T$, $N$ (holding $s$, $t$, $n$), $C$ (the number of
vertices seen), $A$ (the current vertex) and $B$ (the previous one); the save stacks $E$ (for
$X$) and $Z$ (for $W$); and the scratch stacks $R$ and $Q$.

articles.title: Labels of the Hamiltonian path verifier
articles.statement:
The instruction labels of the verifier: reading
$s$, $t$, $n$; validating the edge list and putting it back; validating the witness and putting
it back; the vertex loop, reading a vertex, and the head-or-edge dispatch; for each of the four
counter comparisons, the comparison itself and, for each of its three outcomes, the two loops
restoring the compared counters; the edge scan (comparing an edge's ends, with a flag for the
verdict so far, restoring the counters, putting the edge list back); the repeat scan (likewise
flagged comparisons and restores, then putting the witness back); the final nonzero-count
check; counting the vertex and making it the previous one; accept; and reject.

articles.title: Entering a row and leaving it at once is impossible
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula with
$m > 0$ clauses and $n$ distinct variables. For $k \le n$ let $t_k = m + k(3m + 2)$ be the top
of diamond $k$, and for $k < n$ let row $k$ consist of the vertices $t_k + 1 + l$ with
$0 \le l \le 3m$; its left end is $t_k + 1$ and its right end is $t_k + 1 + 3m$. Let $p$ be a
Hamiltonian path from $t_0$ to $t_n$ in Sipser's digraph for $\varphi$ on the vertices
$0, \dots, t_n$ whose clause detours are normal: every clause vertex $j < m$ occurs in $p$
immediately between the vertices $t_k + 3j + 2$ and $t_k + 3j + 3$ of some row $k < n$, in
either order. Let $q$ be $p$ with the clause vertices $0, \dots, m - 1$ deleted. Then for every
$i < n$ and each end $e$ of row $i$, it is not the case that in $q$ the top $t_i$ is immediately
followed by $e$ and $e$ is immediately followed by $t_{i+1}$.

articles.title: The unary reader of the Hamiltonian path verifier
articles.statement:
For stacks $\mathsf{src}$ and $c$ and
labels $\ell$ (its own) and $m$ (the next one), the statement that goes to label $\mathrm{no}$
if $\mathsf{src}$ is empty; otherwise it pops the top symbol of $\mathsf{src}$ and, if that
symbol is the bit `true`, pushes the bit `true` (one unit) onto $c$ and goes to $\ell$, while
if it is anything else it goes to $m$. Each of the two tests also stores its outcome in the
Boolean variable.

Run in a loop at $\ell$, it reads a unary number off $\mathsf{src}$ onto the counter $c$ and
consumes the terminator.

articles.title: A row entered at one end is run to the other end
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi$ be a CNF formula with
$m$ clauses and $n$ distinct variables. For $k \le n$ let $t_k = m + k(3m + 2)$ be the top of
diamond $k$, and for $k < n$ let row $k$ consist of the vertices $t_k + 1 + l$ with
$0 \le l \le 3m$; its left end is $t_k + 1$ and its right end is $t_k + 1 + 3m$. Let $p$ be a
Hamiltonian path from $t_0$ to $t_n$ in Sipser's digraph for $\varphi$ on the vertices
$0, \dots, t_n$ whose clause detours are normal: every clause vertex $j < m$ occurs in $p$
immediately between the vertices $t_k + 3j + 2$ and $t_k + 3j + 3$ of some row $k < n$, in
either order. Let $q$ be $p$ with the clause vertices $0, \dots, m - 1$ deleted. Let $i < n$,
let $e$ be an end of row $i$, and for $0 \le l \le 3m$ let $r_l$ be the $l$-th vertex of row $i$
counted from $e$, that is $r_l = t_i + 1 + l$ if $e$ is the left end and $r_l = t_i + 1 + 3m - l$
if $e$ is the right end. If the top $t_i$ is immediately followed by $r_0$ in $q$, then for every
$l < 3m$ the vertex $r_l$ is immediately followed by $r_{l+1}$ in $q$.

articles.title: SAT ≤ HAMPATH preserves membership
articles.statement:
For every bit string $x$, SAT accepts $x$ if and only
if HAMPATH accepts the image of $x$ under the SAT-to-HAMPATH reduction map.

articles.title: The unary mover of the Hamiltonian path verifier
articles.statement:
For stacks $\mathsf{src}$ and
$\mathsf{dst}$ and labels $\ell$ (its own) and $m$ (the next one), the statement that goes to
label $\mathrm{no}$ if $\mathsf{src}$ is empty; otherwise it pops the top symbol of
$\mathsf{src}$, reads it as the bit `true` if it is the bit `true` and as `false` otherwise,
pushes that bit onto $\mathsf{dst}$, and goes to $\ell$ if the bit is `true` and to $m$ if it
is `false`. Each of the two tests also stores its outcome in the Boolean variable.

Run in a loop at $\ell$, it moves a unary number, terminator included, from $\mathsf{src}$ to
$\mathsf{dst}$.

articles.title: Statements of the Hamiltonian-path verifier
articles.statement:
A statement of the verifier is a statement of
a multi-stack Turing machine whose stacks are indexed by the verifier's stacks $K$, each stack
over the alphabet $\mathrm{Sym}$, with labels $\mathrm{Lab}$ and a Boolean internal variable.

articles.title: Extending a reversed unary block
articles.statement:
For $a \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\beta_a$ be the list of
symbols obtained by mapping the bit symbol over the reversal of the unary block of $a$ ($a$ copies
of true followed by one false), that is, the bit symbol of false followed by $a$ bit symbols of
true. Then for every list $L$ of symbols, $\beta_a$ followed by the bit symbol of true and then
$L$ equals $\beta_{a+1}$ followed by $L$.

articles.title: Run of the HAMPATH verifier's unary comparison loop
articles.statement:
Let $\mathit{src}$, $\mathit{sv}$, $c$
and the scratch stack $R$ be four distinct stacks of the HAMPATH verifier, and let $\mathrm{cb}$ and
$\mathrm{fin}$ be families of labels indexed by booleans such that for every boolean $\mathit{ok}$
the instruction at $\mathrm{cb}(\mathit{ok})$ is the unary comparison step on $\mathit{src}$,
$\mathit{sv}$, $c$ with loop labels $\mathrm{cb}$, exit labels $\mathrm{fin}$ and verdict
$\mathit{ok}$. Write $1$ and $0$ for the bit symbols of true and false, $1^k$ for $k$ copies of
$1$, and $\bar r$ for the list of bit symbols of a list of booleans $r$; stacks are listed from the
top. Then for all $a, u, j \in \mathbb{N}$, every boolean $\mathit{ok}$, every list of booleans
$r$, every flag $v$ and all stack contents $\sigma$ with $\sigma(\mathit{src}) = 1^a\,0\,\bar r$,
$\sigma(c) = 1^u$ and $\sigma(R) = 1^j$, the verifier runs in exactly $a + 1$ steps from label
$\mathrm{cb}(\mathit{ok})$ with flag $v$ and stacks $\sigma$ to label $\mathrm{fin}(b)$, where $b$
is true exactly when $\mathit{ok}$ is true and $a = u$, with some flag and some stacks $\sigma'$
such that $\sigma'(\mathit{src}) = \bar r$, $\sigma'(\mathit{sv}) = 0\,1^a\,\sigma(\mathit{sv})$,
$\sigma'(c) = 1^{\max(u - a, 0)}$, $\sigma'(R) = 1^{\min(a, u) + j}$, and $\sigma'(k) = \sigma(k)$
for every other stack $k$.

articles.title: Run of a HAMPATH-verifier counter comparison
articles.statement:
Let $i$ be one of the four counter
comparisons of the HAMPATH verifier, with first counter $\mathrm{ca}(i)$ and second counter
$\mathrm{cb}(i)$, and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Suppose the stacks $\sigma$ hold $m$ units (bit
symbols of true) on $\mathrm{ca}(i)$, $n$ units on $\mathrm{cb}(i)$, and nothing on the scratch
stacks $R$ and $Q$. Then for every flag $v$ the verifier goes, in at most
$3 \min(m, n) + 4$ steps, from label $\mathrm{cmp}(i)$ with flag $v$ and stacks $\sigma$ to the
label $\mathrm{cout}(i, o)$ that comparison $i$ picks on the ordering
$o = \mathrm{compare}(m, n) \in \{\mathrm{lt}, \mathrm{eq}, \mathrm{gt}\}$ of $m$ and $n$, with flag
false and the same stacks $\sigma$.

articles.title: HAMPATH-verifier unary comparison with the counter restored
articles.statement:
Let $\mathit{src}$,
$\mathit{sv}$, $c$ and the scratch stack $R$ be four distinct stacks of the HAMPATH verifier, and
let $\mathrm{cb}$, $\mathrm{rs}$ and $\mathrm{nx}$ be families of labels indexed by booleans such
that for every boolean $\mathit{ok}$ the instruction at $\mathrm{cb}(\mathit{ok})$ is the unary
comparison step on $\mathit{src}$, $\mathit{sv}$, $c$ with loop labels $\mathrm{cb}$, exit labels
$\mathrm{rs}$ and verdict $\mathit{ok}$, and the instruction at $\mathrm{rs}(\mathit{ok})$ is the
transfer loop that pops $R$ until it is empty, pushing one unit (the bit symbol of true) on $c$
per symbol popped, and then goes to $\mathrm{nx}(\mathit{ok})$. Write $1$ and $0$ for the bit
symbols of true and false, $1^k$ for $k$ copies of $1$, and $\bar r$ for the list of bit symbols
of a list of booleans $r$; stacks are listed from the top. Let $a, u \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$\mathit{ok}$ be a boolean, $r$ a list of booleans, $v$ a flag, and $\sigma$ stack contents with
$\sigma(\mathit{src}) = 1^a\,0\,\bar r$, $\sigma(c) = 1^u$ and $\sigma(R)$ empty. Then the verifier
runs in exactly $(a + 1) + (\min(a, u) + 1)$ steps from label $\mathrm{cb}(\mathit{ok})$ with flag
$v$ and stacks $\sigma$ to label $\mathrm{nx}(b)$, where $b$ is true exactly when $\mathit{ok}$ is
true and $a = u$, with some flag and with the stacks of $\sigma$ except that $\mathit{src}$ now
holds $\bar r$ and $\mathit{sv}$ holds $0\,1^a$ followed by $\sigma(\mathit{sv})$.

articles.title: Outcome of the HAMPATH verifier's vertex-range comparison
articles.statement:
For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$,
the label that the comparison of the current vertex with the vertex count picks on the ordering
$\mathrm{compare}(m, n)$ of $m$ and $n$ is the head-or-edge dispatch label $\mathrm{hd}$ if
$m < n$, and the reject label $\mathrm{no}$ otherwise.

articles.title: Outcome of a HAMPATH-verifier equality comparison
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{cout}(i, o)$ for the
label that counter comparison $i$ of the HAMPATH verifier picks on the ordering
$o \in \{\mathrm{lt}, \mathrm{eq}, \mathrm{gt}\}$. Let $i$ be a counter comparison and $l$ a label
such that $\mathrm{cout}(i, \mathrm{eq}) = l$ and $\mathrm{cout}(i, o)$ is the reject label
$\mathrm{no}$ for every ordering $o \ne \mathrm{eq}$. Then for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, the label
$\mathrm{cout}(i, \mathrm{compare}(m, n))$ on the ordering of $m$ and $n$ is $l$ if $m = n$ and
$\mathrm{no}$ otherwise.

articles.title: Exit labels of the counter comparisons
articles.statement:
The label the verifier goes to after comparing
two counters, where $a$ is the current vertex, $b$ the previous one, $c$ the number of vertices
seen, $n$ the number of vertices and $s$, $t$ the two ends: after comparing $a$ with $n$ it goes
to the head-or-edge dispatch if $a < n$; after comparing $a$ with $s$ it goes to the repeat scan
if $a = s$; after comparing $c$ with $n$ it goes to the nonzero-count check if $c = n$; after
comparing $b$ with $t$ it goes to the accept label if $b = t$; in every other case it goes to
the reject label.

articles.title: One step of the emptiness test
articles.statement:
If the verifier's instruction at label $l$ is the
emptiness test of stack $k$ with targets $e$ and $ne$, then from label $l$, in any internal state
and on any stacks, exactly one step of the verifier leads to label $e$ if stack $k$ is empty and
to label $ne$ otherwise, in some internal state and with the stacks unchanged.

articles.title: Moving a stack of bits
articles.statement:
Suppose the verifier's instruction at label $p$ is the bit-moving
loop from a stack $a$ to a different stack $b$, continuing at label $p'$ when done. If stack $a$
holds exactly the bits of a list $l$, then from label $p$ in any internal state the verifier
takes exactly $|l| + 1$ steps to reach label $p'$, in some internal state, with stack $a$ empty,
stack $b$ holding the bits of $l$ in reverse order followed by its old contents, and every other
stack unchanged.

articles.title: The Hamiltonian path verifier machine
articles.statement:
The verifier is the program of the multi-stack
machine with the stacks and labels of the Hamiltonian path verifier, every stack over the
alphabet $\mathrm{Sym}$, and a Boolean internal variable, given below label by label. Write
$\mathrm{bit}(x)$ for the bit symbol of a boolean $x$. Write $(a, n)$, $(a, s)$, $(c, n)$ and
$(b, t)$ for the four counter comparisons, and $\alpha(i)$ and $\beta(i)$ for the first and the
second counter of comparison $i$. Every unary reader, unary mover, bit-moving loop and transfer
below has the label it sits at as its own label; the bit-moving loops read bit symbols as bits
and every other symbol as a marker, and push $\mathrm{bit}(x)$ for a bit $x$. The transfer from a
stack $k$ onto a list of stacks with next label $m$ pops $k$; if it popped a symbol, it pushes
$\mathrm{bit}(\mathrm{true})$ onto each listed stack and returns to its own label, and otherwise
it goes to $m$. An emptiness test of a stack "to $e$, else $e'$" goes to $e$ if the stack is
empty and to $e'$ otherwise. A transfer also stores in the Boolean variable whether its pop
found a symbol, and an emptiness test stores there whether the stack is empty.

- $\mathsf{rdS}$, $\mathsf{rdT}$, $\mathsf{rdN}$: the unary reader from $X$ onto $S$, $T$, $N$
  respectively, with next labels $\mathsf{rdT}$, $\mathsf{rdN}$, $\mathsf{vE}$ respectively.
- $\mathsf{vE}$: the emptiness test of $X$ to $\mathsf{vEb}$, else $\mathsf{vEU}$. $\mathsf{vEU}$
  and $\mathsf{vEV}$: the unary mover from $X$ to $E$, with next labels $\mathsf{vEV}$ and
  $\mathsf{vE}$ respectively. $\mathsf{vEb}$: the bit-moving loop from $E$ to $X$ with next label
  $\mathsf{vW}$.
- $\mathsf{vW}$: the emptiness test of $W$ to $\mathsf{vWb}$, else $\mathsf{vWU}$. $\mathsf{vWU}$:
  the unary mover from $W$ to $Z$ with next label $\mathsf{vW}$. $\mathsf{vWb}$: the bit-moving
  loop from $Z$ to $W$ with next label $\mathsf{loop}$.
- $\mathsf{loop}$: the emptiness test of $W$ to $\mathsf{cmp}(c, n)$, else $\mathsf{rdA}$.
  $\mathsf{rdA}$: the unary reader from $W$ onto $A$ with next label $\mathsf{cmp}(a, n)$.
  $\mathsf{hd}$: the emptiness test of $C$ to $\mathsf{cmp}(a, s)$, else $\mathsf{scan}$.
- For each comparison $i$, $\mathsf{cmp}(i)$ is one round of counter comparison of $\alpha(i)$
  and $\beta(i)$, with scratch stacks $R$ (for $\alpha(i)$) and $Q$ (for $\beta(i)$), both units
  $\mathrm{bit}(\mathrm{true})$, own label $\mathsf{cmp}(i)$, and $\mathsf{cr}(i, <)$,
  $\mathsf{cr}(i, =)$, $\mathsf{cr}(i, >)$ as its labels $\mathit{lt}$, $\mathit{eq}$ and
  $\mathit{gt}$. For each ordering $o$, $\mathsf{cr}(i, o)$ is the transfer from $R$ onto
  $\alpha(i)$ with next label $\mathsf{crb}(i, o)$, and $\mathsf{crb}(i, o)$ is the transfer from
  $Q$ onto $\beta(i)$ whose next label is the exit label of the counter comparison $i$ with
  outcome $o$.
- $\mathsf{scan}$: the emptiness test of $X$ to $\mathsf{no}$, else
  $\mathsf{ceU}(\mathrm{true})$. For each boolean $\mathit{ok}$: $\mathsf{ceU}(\mathit{ok})$ is
  the step of the unary comparison loop with source $X$, save stack $E$, counter $B$, label
  families $\mathsf{ceU}$ and $\mathsf{rsU}$, and verdict $\mathit{ok}$; $\mathsf{rsU}(\mathit{ok})$
  is the transfer from $R$ onto $B$ with next label $\mathsf{ceV}(\mathit{ok})$;
  $\mathsf{ceV}(\mathit{ok})$ is the step of the unary comparison loop with source $X$, save stack
  $E$, counter $A$, label families $\mathsf{ceV}$ and $\mathsf{rsV}$, and verdict $\mathit{ok}$;
  and $\mathsf{rsV}(\mathit{ok})$ is the transfer from $R$ onto $A$ with next label $\mathsf{scB}$
  if $\mathit{ok}$ is true and $\mathsf{scan}$ otherwise. $\mathsf{scB}$: the bit-moving loop from
  $E$ to $X$ with next label $\mathsf{nd}$.
- $\mathsf{nd}$: the emptiness test of $W$ to $\mathsf{ndB}$, else $\mathsf{cbN}(\mathrm{true})$.
  For each boolean $\mathit{ok}$: $\mathsf{cbN}(\mathit{ok})$ is the step of the unary comparison
  loop with source $W$, save stack $Z$, counter $A$, label families $\mathsf{cbN}$ and
  $\mathsf{rsN}$, and verdict $\mathit{ok}$; and $\mathsf{rsN}(\mathit{ok})$ is the transfer from
  $R$ onto $A$ with next label $\mathsf{no}$ if $\mathit{ok}$ is true and $\mathsf{nd}$
  otherwise. $\mathsf{ndB}$: the bit-moving loop from $Z$ to $W$ with next label $\mathsf{incC}$.
- $\mathsf{fin}$: the emptiness test of $C$ to $\mathsf{no}$, else $\mathsf{cmp}(b, t)$.
  $\mathsf{incC}$: the counter increment pushing $\mathrm{bit}(\mathrm{true})$ onto $C$ and going
  to $\mathsf{dB}$. $\mathsf{dB}$: the transfer from $B$ onto no stack (it drains $B$) with next
  label $\mathsf{mA}$. $\mathsf{mA}$: the transfer from $A$ onto $B$ with next label
  $\mathsf{loop}$.
- $\mathsf{yes}$ and $\mathsf{no}$: halt.

The verifier parses and validates the input and the witness, then walks the vertices.

articles.title: The unary reader of the Hamiltonian path verifier rejects an unterminated number
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathsf{src} \ne c$ be stacks and $\ell$, $m$ labels such that the verifier's statement at
$\ell$ is the unary reader from $\mathsf{src}$ onto $c$ with own label $\ell$ and next label
$m$. Let $l$ be a bit list from which no unary length can be read (that is, $l$ contains no
`false`), and suppose that $\mathsf{src}$ holds the bits of $l$ (as bit symbols, first bit on
top). Then from label $\ell$, with either value of the Boolean variable and any contents of the
other stacks, the verifier reaches label $\mathrm{no}$ within $|l| + 1$ steps.

articles.title: The unary reader of the Hamiltonian path verifier reads a terminated number
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathsf{src} \ne c$ be stacks and $\ell$, $m$ labels such that the verifier's statement at
$\ell$ is the unary reader from $\mathsf{src}$ onto $c$ with own label $\ell$ and next label
$m$. Let $k, j$ be natural numbers and $r$ a bit list, and suppose that $\mathsf{src}$ holds
$k$ copies of `true`, then `false`, then $r$ (as bit symbols, first bit on top) and that $c$
holds $j$ copies of the bit `true`. Then from label $\ell$, with either value of the Boolean
variable, the verifier reaches label $m$ in exactly $k + 1$ steps, with $\mathsf{src}$ holding
the bits of $r$, $c$ holding $k + j$ copies of the bit `true`, and every other stack
unchanged.

articles.title: The edge scan of the Hamiltonian path verifier
articles.statement:
For a list $e$ of pairs of natural
numbers write $\mathrm{bits}(e)$ for its edge-list encoding, in which each pair $(u, u')$
contributes $u$ copies of `true`, then `false`, then $u'$ copies of `true`, then `false`. Let
$a, b$ be natural numbers and $r$, $d$ lists of pairs of natural numbers. Suppose that the
verifier's stacks hold, as bit symbols with the first bit on top, $\mathrm{bits}(r)$ on
$\mathsf{X}$, $\mathrm{bits}(d)$ in reverse order on $\mathsf{E}$, $a$ copies of the bit `true`
on $\mathsf{A}$, $b$ copies of the bit `true` on $\mathsf{B}$, and nothing on $\mathsf{R}$, the
other stacks being arbitrary. Started at label $\mathrm{scan}$ with either value of its Boolean
variable, the verifier reaches, within $4|\mathrm{bits}(r)| + |\mathrm{bits}(d)| + 2$ steps, the
label $\mathrm{nd}$ if $(b, a)$ is one of the pairs of $r$ and the label $\mathrm{no}$
otherwise. In the first case its stacks are then the initial ones except that $\mathsf{X}$
holds the encoding $\mathrm{bits}$ of the list $d$ followed by $r$, and $\mathsf{E}$ is empty.

articles.title: The unary mover of the Hamiltonian path verifier rejects an unterminated number
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathsf{src} \ne \mathsf{dst}$ be stacks and $\ell$, $m$ labels such that the verifier's
statement at $\ell$ is the unary mover from $\mathsf{src}$ to $\mathsf{dst}$ with own label
$\ell$ and next label $m$. Let $l$ be a bit list from which no unary length can be read (that
is, $l$ contains no `false`), and suppose that $\mathsf{src}$ holds the bits of $l$ (as bit
symbols, first bit on top). Then from label $\ell$, with either value of the Boolean variable
and any contents of the other stacks, the verifier reaches label $\mathrm{no}$ within
$|l| + 1$ steps.

articles.title: The unary mover of the Hamiltonian path verifier moves a terminated number
articles.statement:
Let
$\mathsf{src} \ne \mathsf{dst}$ be stacks and $\ell$, $m$ labels such that the verifier's
statement at $\ell$ is the unary mover from $\mathsf{src}$ to $\mathsf{dst}$ with own label
$\ell$ and next label $m$. Let $k$ be a natural number and $r$ a bit list, and suppose that
$\mathsf{src}$ holds $k$ copies of `true`, then `false`, then $r$ (as bit symbols, first bit on
top). Then from label $\ell$, with either value of the Boolean variable, the verifier reaches
label $m$ in exactly $k + 1$ steps, with $\mathsf{src}$ holding the bits of $r$, with
$\mathsf{dst}$ holding the bit `false` followed by $k$ copies of the bit `true` on top of its
previous contents, and with every other stack unchanged.

articles.title: Start label of the Hamiltonian-path verifier
articles.statement:
The verifier starts at the label
$\mathsf{rdS}$, where it reads the first unary number of the input stack $X$ (the start vertex
$s$) onto the counter stack $S$.

articles.title: A single step of the Hamiltonian-path verifier
articles.statement:
Let $l, l'$ be labels, $v$ a flag value
and $S, S'$ assignments of a list of symbols to each stack. If executing the verifier's statement
at $l$ with flag $v$ and stacks $S$ jumps to the label $l'$ and leaves the stacks $S'$, then the
verifier goes in exactly one step from label $l$, flag $v$ and stacks $S$ to label $l'$ and
stacks $S'$, with some flag value.

articles.title: Interleaved stack updates in the Hamiltonian-path verifier
articles.statement:
Let $a \ne b$ be two stacks of
the verifier, $S$ an assignment of a list of symbols to each stack, and $p, p', t, t'$ lists of
symbols. Setting $a$ to $p$, then $b$ to $t$, then $a$ to $p'$, then $b$ to $t'$ in $S$ gives the
same assignment as setting $a$ to $p'$ and then $b$ to $t'$.

articles.title: The edge-list check of the Hamiltonian-path verifier
articles.statement:
Let $r$ and $acc$ be bit lists, and
let the stacks $St$ hold $r$ on the input stack $X$ and the reverse of $acc$ on the save stack
$E$. Started at the label $\mathsf{vE}$ with any flag value, the verifier reaches within at most
$2|r| + 1$ steps the label $\mathsf{vEb}$ if $r$ decodes as an edge list (a sequence of pairs of
unary numbers, each a block of ones ended by a zero) and the label $\mathsf{no}$ otherwise. When
$r$ decodes, the final stacks are $St$ with $X$ emptied and $E$ holding the reverse of the
concatenation of $acc$ and $r$ (that is, $r$ reversed on top of $acc$ reversed), all other
stacks unchanged.

articles.title: The witness check of the Hamiltonian-path verifier
articles.statement:
Let $w$ and $acc$ be bit lists, and
let the stacks $St$ hold $w$ on the witness stack $W$ and the reverse of $acc$ on the save stack
$Z$. Started at the label $\mathsf{vW}$ with any flag value, the verifier reaches within at most
$2|w| + 1$ steps the label $\mathsf{vWb}$ if $w$ decodes as a vertex list (a sequence of unary
numbers, each a block of ones ended by a zero) and the label $\mathsf{no}$ otherwise. When $w$
decodes, the final stacks are $St$ with $W$ emptied and $Z$ holding the reverse of the
concatenation of $acc$ and $w$ (that is, $w$ reversed on top of $acc$ reversed), all other
stacks unchanged.

articles.title: The HAMPATH emitter
articles.statement:
The emitter whose stacks, alphabets, labels, program and start label
are those of the HAMPATH emitter machine, which exits at the machine's label $\mathsf{done}$,
reads the tokens of a CNF formula from stack $T$ and writes its output bits on stack $O$ (both
symbol maps being the identity), and has step bound $B(n) = 2000 (n + 1)^5$ for $n$ tokens. Its
output for a CNF formula $\varphi$ is Sipser's HAMPATH instance of $\varphi$, and for an
undecodable input the fixed HAMPATH no-instance (two vertices, no arcs, source and target $0$).

articles.title: HAMPATH is in NP
articles.statement: **HAMPATH is in NP**.

articles.title: HAMPATH is NP-complete
articles.statement:
HAMPATH lies in NP, and every decision problem $L$ in NP has a
polynomial-time many-one reduction to HAMPATH: a polynomial-time computable map $f$ on bit
strings such that, for every bit string $x$, $L$ accepts $x$ exactly when HAMPATH accepts $f(x)$.

## Sources

- Sipser, Theorem 7.46.

articles.title: HAMPATH is NP-hard
articles.statement:
Every decision problem $L$ in NP has a polynomial-time many-one
reduction to HAMPATH: a polynomial-time computable map $f$ on bit strings such that, for every
bit string $x$, $L$ accepts $x$ exactly when HAMPATH accepts $f(x)$.

articles.title: The HAMPATH verifier as a host component
articles.statement:
The component machine whose program and labels
are those of the HAMPATH verifier machine, whose stacks are the twelve stacks of that machine (the
input $X$, the witness $W$, the counters $S, T, N, C, A, B$, the save stacks $E, Z$ and the scratch
stacks $R, Q$), each over the symbol alphabet of the SAT verifier.

articles.title: Running the head-or-edge check
articles.statement:
Let $es$ be an edge list, $s, t, n, c, b, a$ numbers and
$q$ a list of vertices, and say the check passes when $a = s$ in case $c = 0$, and
$(b, a) \in es$ in case $c \neq 0$. Started at the head-or-edge dispatch, in any internal state,
on the stack layout during the step on vertex $a$ for $es, s, t, n, c, b, a, q$, the verifier
reaches within $3a + 4\ell + 7$ steps, where $\ell$ is the number of bits of $es$, the repeat
scan if the check passes and the reject label otherwise, in some internal state and with some
stacks; if the check passes, these stacks are the ones it started on.

articles.title: SAT ≤ HAMPATH is polynomial-time
articles.statement:
The map on bit strings that sends a bit string decoding
to a CNF formula $\varphi$ to Sipser's HAMPATH instance for $\varphi$, and every other bit string
to the fixed no-instance with two vertices, no arcs and $s = t = 0$, is computable in polynomial
time.

articles.title: Stack layout between vertex steps
articles.statement:
For an edge list $es$, numbers $s, t, n, c, b$ and a
list $q$ of vertices, the stacks of the verifier between two vertex steps: $X$ holds the bits of
the edge list $es$, $W$ holds the bits of the witness encoding of $q$, the counters $S$, $T$,
$N$, $C$ and $B$ hold $s$, $t$, $n$, $c$ and $b$ in unary, and the stacks $A$, $E$, $Z$, $R$
and $Q$ are empty.

articles.title: Running the vertex loop
articles.statement:
Let $es$ be an edge list, $s, t, n$ numbers and $L$ a bound
with $n \le L$, $t \le L$ and at most $L$ bits in the encoding of $es$. For every list $q$ of
vertices whose witness encoding has at most $L$ bits, every count $c$, every previous vertex
$b \le L$ and every internal state, the verifier started at the vertex loop on the stack layout
between vertex steps for $es, s, t, n, c, b, q$ reaches within $(|q| + 1)(20L + 20)$ steps, with
some internal state and stacks, the accept label if the walk check for $s, t, n, es, c, b, q$
passes and the reject label otherwise.

articles.title: Stack layout during a vertex step
articles.statement:
For an edge list $es$, numbers $s, t, n, c, b, a$ and
a list $q$ of vertices, the stacks of the verifier during the step on vertex $a$: the layout
between vertex steps for $es, s, t, n, c, b, q$, except that stack $A$ holds $a$ in unary.

articles.title: The repeat scan of the Hamiltonian path verifier
articles.statement:
For a list $p$ of natural numbers
write $\mathrm{enc}(p)$ for its witness encoding: each entry in unary (that many copies of
`true`) followed by `false`. Let $a$ be a natural number and $q$, $d$ lists of natural numbers.
Suppose that the verifier's stacks hold, as bit symbols with the first bit on top, the bits of
$\mathrm{enc}(q)$ on $\mathsf{W}$, the bits of $\mathrm{enc}(d)$ in reverse order on
$\mathsf{Z}$, $a$ copies of the bit `true` on $\mathsf{A}$, and nothing on $\mathsf{R}$, the
other stacks being arbitrary. Started at label $\mathrm{nd}$ with either value of its Boolean
variable, the verifier reaches, within $4|\mathrm{enc}(q)| + |\mathrm{enc}(d)| + 2$ steps, the
label $\mathrm{no}$ if $a$ is an entry of $q$ and the label $\mathrm{incC}$ otherwise. In the
second case its stacks are then the initial ones except that $\mathsf{W}$ holds the bits of the
encoding of $d$ followed by $q$, and $\mathsf{Z}$ is empty.

articles.title: Correctness and running time of the Hamiltonian path verifier
articles.statement:
Let $x$ and $w$ be bit
lists. Start the verifier at its start label, with either value of its Boolean variable, with
$x$ on stack $\mathsf{X}$ and $w$ on stack $\mathsf{W}$ (as bit symbols, first bit on top) and
all other stacks empty. Then within $100(|x| + |w| + 1)^4$ steps it reaches the label
$\mathrm{yes}$ if the Hamiltonian path check accepts $x$ and $w$, and the label $\mathrm{no}$
otherwise.

The machine in fact takes quadratically many steps; the theorem states only the quartic bound.

articles.title: One vertex step of the Hamiltonian-path verifier
articles.statement:
Let $es$ be an edge list,
$s, t, n, c, b, a$ natural numbers and $q$ a list of natural numbers. Start the verifier, with
any flag value, at the label $\mathsf{rdA}$ (read the next vertex) with its stacks in the
between-steps layout for $es$, $s$, $t$, $n$, count $c$, previous vertex $b$ and remaining
vertices $a, q$. Let $e$ be the bit encoding of $es$ and $w$ the unary encoding of $q$. Then
within at most $8a + b + 4|e| + 4|w| + 20$ steps it reaches the label $\mathsf{loop}$ if the
step check on $a$ passes and the label $\mathsf{no}$ otherwise. The step check passes when
$a < n$, $a = s$ in case $c = 0$ and $(b, a) \in es$ in case $c \ne 0$, and $a \notin q$. When
it passes, the stacks end in the between-steps layout for $es$, $s$, $t$, $n$, count $c + 1$,
previous vertex $a$ and remaining vertices $q$.

articles.title: The rest of a vertex step in the Hamiltonian-path verifier
articles.statement:
Let $es$ be an edge list,
$s, t, n, c, b, a$ natural numbers and $q$ a list of natural numbers. Start the verifier, with
any flag value, at the label $\mathsf{nd}$ (the repeat scan) with its stacks in the mid-step
layout: the between-steps layout for $es$, $s$, $t$, $n$, count $c$, previous vertex $b$ and
remaining vertices $q$, with $a$ in unary on the stack $A$. Let $w$ be the unary encoding of $q$.
Then within at most $4|w| + a + b + 6$ steps it reaches the label $\mathsf{no}$ if $a \in q$ and
the label $\mathsf{loop}$ if $a \notin q$. In the second case ($a$ has been counted and become
the previous vertex) the stacks end in the between-steps layout for $es$, $s$, $t$, $n$, count
$c + 1$, previous vertex $a$ and remaining vertices $q$.

articles.title: Host graph of an induced-subgraph-isomorphism instance
articles.statement:
For an instance $(n, E, k, F)$,
the host graph is the graph of the edge list $E$ on $n$ vertices: the simple graph on
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or
$(j, i)$ belongs to $E$.

articles.title: Pattern graph of an induced-subgraph-isomorphism instance
articles.statement:
For an instance
$(n, E, k, F)$, the pattern graph is the graph of the edge list $F$ on $k$ vertices: the simple
graph on $\{0, \dots, k - 1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$
or $(j, i)$ belongs to $F$.

articles.title: INDUCED SUBGRAPH ISOMORPHISM as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem INDUCED SUBGRAPH
ISOMORPHISM accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring
encoding, to an instance $(n, E, k, F)$ (host vertex count, host edge list, pattern vertex count,
pattern edge list) that is well-formed and for which there is an injective map $f$ from
$\{0, \dots, k - 1\}$ to $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ such that, for all $a$ and $b$, the vertices $a$
and $b$ are adjacent in the pattern graph if and only if $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ are adjacent in the
host graph. Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Induced embedding of the pattern into the host
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, k, F)$ is feasible
when there is an injective map $f$ from $\{0, \dots, k - 1\}$ to $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ such that,
for all $a, b \in \{0, \dots, k - 1\}$, the vertices $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in the pattern
graph if and only if $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ are adjacent in the host graph.

articles.title: Induced-subgraph-isomorphism instance
articles.statement:
An instance of INDUCED SUBGRAPH ISOMORPHISM is a
quadruple $(n, E, k, F)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of host vertices), a list
$E$ of pairs of natural numbers (the host edges), a natural number $k$ (the number of pattern
vertices) and a list $F$ of pairs of natural numbers (the pattern edges).

articles.title: INDUCED SUBGRAPH ISOMORPHISM is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem INDUCED SUBGRAPH
ISOMORPHISM is in NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time
many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), INDUCED SUBGRAPH ISOMORPHISM.

articles.title: Well-formed induced-subgraph-isomorphism instance
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, k, F)$ is
well-formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies
$u < n$, $v < n$, $u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin E$, and likewise the list $F$ has no repeated
entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $F$ satisfies $u < k$, $v < k$, $u \ne v$ and
$(v, u) \notin F$.

articles.title: Graph of a LONGEST CYCLE instance
articles.statement:
For an instance $(n, E, K)$ of LONGEST CYCLE, its graph
is the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent
when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$. Loops are dropped, and pairs with an endpoint at least
$n$ contribute no edge.

articles.title: The decision problem LONGEST CYCLE
articles.statement:
LONGEST CYCLE accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$
decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of instances, to an instance of LONGEST CYCLE that
is well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode, and bitstrings that decode to
instances that are not well formed, are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible LONGEST CYCLE instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of LONGEST CYCLE is feasible when
there are pairwise distinct vertices $v_1, \dots, v_m$ of the graph of the instance, with $m \ge K$
and $m \ge 3$, such that $v_j$ is adjacent to $v_{j+1}$ for every $1 \le j < m$ and $v_m$ is
adjacent to $v_1$. That is, the graph has a simple cycle with at least $K$ edges and at least
three vertices.

articles.title: Instances of LONGEST CYCLE
articles.statement:
An instance of LONGEST CYCLE is a triple $(n, E, K)$ of a
natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers (the edges),
and a natural number $K$ (the bound).

articles.title: LONGEST CYCLE is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem LONGEST CYCLE belongs to NP, and every
decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to LONGEST CYCLE.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), LONGEST CYCLE.

articles.title: Well-formed LONGEST CYCLE instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of LONGEST CYCLE is well
formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies
$u < n$, $v < n$, $u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin E$.

articles.title: Graph of a longest-path instance
articles.statement:
For a longest-path instance with vertex count $n$ and
edge list $E$, its graph is the graph of the edge list $E$ on $n$ vertices: the simple graph on
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or
$(j, i)$ belongs to $E$.

articles.title: The LONGEST PATH decision problem
articles.statement:
LONGEST PATH is the decision problem that accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a longest-path
instance $(n, E, K, s, t)$ that is well formed and in which the graph of $E$ on $n$ vertices has
a simple path from $s$ to $t$ with at least $K$ edges. Bitstrings that do not decode to a
longest-path instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasibility of a longest-path instance
articles.statement:
A longest-path instance $(n, E, K, s, t)$ is
feasible when the graph of $E$ on $n$ vertices has a simple path from $s$ to $t$ with at least
$K$ edges, that is, a list $v_0, \dots, v_m$ of pairwise distinct vertices with $m \ge K$,
$v_0 = s$ and $v_m = t$, in which $v_j$ and $v_{j+1}$ are adjacent for every $j < m$.

articles.title: Longest-path instances
LONGEST PATH is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The LONGEST PATH decision problem belongs to NP, and every
decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to LONGEST PATH.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), LONGEST PATH.

articles.title: Well-formed longest-path instances
articles.statement:
A longest-path instance $(n, E, K, s, t)$ is well
formed when $s < n$, $t < n$, the list $E$ has no repeated entries, and every pair $(u, v)$ in
$E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and its reverse $(v, u)$ does not belong to $E$.

articles.title: First graph of an instance
articles.statement:
For an instance $(n_1, E_1, n_2, E_2, K)$ of MAXIMUM COMMON
INDUCED SUBGRAPH, the first graph is the graph of the edge list $E_1$ on $n_1$ vertices: the
simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n_1 - 1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when
$(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E_1$.

articles.title: Second graph of an instance
articles.statement:
For an instance $(n_1, E_1, n_2, E_2, K)$ of MAXIMUM COMMON
INDUCED SUBGRAPH, the second graph is the graph of the edge list $E_2$ on $n_2$ vertices: the
simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n_2 - 1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when
$(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E_2$.

articles.title: MAXIMUM COMMON INDUCED SUBGRAPH as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem MAXIMUM
COMMON INDUCED SUBGRAPH accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when the canonical bitstring decoding of
$x$ yields an instance of MAXIMUM COMMON INDUCED SUBGRAPH that is well formed and feasible.
Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible instances of MAXIMUM COMMON INDUCED SUBGRAPH
articles.statement:
An instance
$(n_1, E_1, n_2, E_2, K)$ of MAXIMUM COMMON INDUCED SUBGRAPH is feasible when, writing $G_1$ and
$G_2$ for its first and second graphs, there are a set $A$ of vertices of $G_1$ and a set $B$ of
vertices of $G_2$ with $|A| \ge K$ and $|B| = |A|$, and a bijection $f : A \to B$ such that for
all $a, b \in A$, the vertices $a$ and $b$ are adjacent in $G_1$ if and only if $f(a)$ and $f(b)$
are adjacent in $G_2$.

articles.title: Instances of MAXIMUM COMMON INDUCED SUBGRAPH
articles.statement:
An instance of MAXIMUM COMMON INDUCED
SUBGRAPH is a tuple $(n_1, E_1, n_2, E_2, K)$ in which $n_1$, $n_2$ and $K$ are natural numbers
and $E_1$, $E_2$ are finite lists of pairs of natural numbers: $n_1$ is the vertex count of the
first graph, $E_1$ its edge list, $n_2$ the vertex count of the second graph, $E_2$ its edge
list, and $K$ the bound.

articles.title: MAXIMUM COMMON INDUCED SUBGRAPH is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem MAXIMUM COMMON
INDUCED SUBGRAPH belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a
polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), MAXIMUM COMMON INDUCED SUBGRAPH.

articles.title: Well-formed instances of MAXIMUM COMMON INDUCED SUBGRAPH
articles.statement:
An instance
$(n_1, E_1, n_2, E_2, K)$ of MAXIMUM COMMON INDUCED SUBGRAPH is well formed when, for each
$k \in \{1, 2\}$, the list $E_k$ has no repeated entries and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E_k$ has
$u < n_k$, $v < n_k$, $u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin E_k$.

articles.title: The decision problem MAXIMUM LEAF SPANNING TREE
articles.statement:
The decision problem MAXIMUM LEAF
SPANNING TREE accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring
encoding of instances, to an instance $(n, es, K)$ of MAXIMUM LEAF SPANNING TREE that is well
formed and feasible (its graph has a spanning tree with at least $K$ leaves). Bitstrings that do
not decode are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible MAXIMUM LEAF SPANNING TREE instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, es, K)$ of MAXIMUM LEAF
SPANNING TREE is feasible when there are a sublist $T$ of $es$ (a list obtained from $es$ by
deleting entries) with no repeated entries and exactly $n - 1$ entries, and a set $L$ of at least
$K$ vertices in $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, such that the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in
which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ is an entry of $T$ is
connected, and each vertex in $L$ is an endpoint of exactly one entry of $T$.

articles.title: Instances of MAXIMUM LEAF SPANNING TREE
articles.statement:
An instance of MAXIMUM LEAF SPANNING TREE is a
triple $(n, es, K)$ of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $es$ of pairs of
natural numbers (the edge list) and a natural number $K$ (the bound on the number of leaves).

articles.title: MAXIMUM LEAF SPANNING TREE is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem MAXIMUM LEAF SPANNING TREE
belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one
reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), MAXIMUM LEAF SPANNING TREE.

articles.title: Well-formed MAXIMUM LEAF SPANNING TREE instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, es, K)$ of MAXIMUM LEAF
SPANNING TREE is well formed when $n > 0$, the list $es$ has no repeated entries, and every entry
$(u, v)$ of $es$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and $(v, u)$ is not an entry of
$es$.

articles.title: Directed adjacency for MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH
articles.statement:
For a finite list $E$ of ordered pairs
of natural numbers and natural numbers $u$ and $v$, the directed adjacency test of $E$ at $(u, v)$
returns true when the pair $(u, v)$ occurs in $E$, and false otherwise.

articles.title: MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem MINIMUM
EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical
bitstring encoding, to an instance of MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH that is well formed and
feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of MINIMUM
EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH is feasible when some sublist $F$ of $E$ (obtained by deleting entries of
$E$) has at most $K$ entries and, for all vertices $u < n$ and $v < n$, $v$ is reachable from $u$
within $n$ steps along $E$ if and only if $v$ is reachable from $u$ within $n$ steps along
$F$.

articles.title: Instances of MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH
articles.statement:
An instance of MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH is a
triple $(n, E, K)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a finite list $E$
of ordered pairs of natural numbers (the arcs) and a natural number $K$ (the bound on the number
of arcs).

articles.title: MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem MINIMUM EQUIVALENT
DIGRAPH belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction
to it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH; A. V. Aho, M. R. Garey, and J. D. Ullman, "The transitive reduction of a directed graph", SIAM Journal on Computing 1 (1972), 131-137 (distinguishing transitive reduction from the minimum equivalent subgraph and the hardness connection); D. M. Moyles and G. L. Thompson, "An algorithm for finding a minimum equivalent graph of a digraph", Journal of the ACM 16 (1969), 455-460.

articles.title: Bounded reachability in a digraph
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a finite list of ordered pairs of natural
numbers, read as the arcs of a directed graph, and let $n$, $u$ and $v$ be natural numbers. Then
$v$ is reachable from $u$ within $n$ steps along $E$ when there are natural numbers
$w_0, w_1, \dots, w_k$ with $k \le n$, $w_0 = u$ and $w_k = v$ such that $(w_j, w_{j+1})$ occurs
in $E$ for every $j < k$.

articles.title: Well-formed MINIMUM EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of MINIMUM
EQUIVALENT DIGRAPH is well formed when the list $E$ has no repeated entries and every pair
$(a, b)$ in $E$ satisfies $a < n$, $b < n$ and $a \ne b$; that is, $E$ lists distinct arcs
without loops between vertices among $0, \dots, n - 1$.

articles.title: Directed adjacency in an edge list
articles.statement:
For a list $E$ of ordered pairs of natural numbers
and natural numbers $u$ and $v$, the directed adjacency test of $E$ at $(u, v)$ is the boolean
that is true exactly when the pair $(u, v)$ occurs in $E$, that is, when $E$ contains an edge
from $u$ to $v$.

articles.title: DIRECTED PATH COVER as a decision problem
articles.statement:
DIRECTED PATH COVER is the decision problem
that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding,
to an instance $(n, E, K)$ of DIRECTED PATH COVER that is well formed and feasible; bitstrings
that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible DIRECTED PATH COVER instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of DIRECTED PATH
COVER is feasible when there is a list of at most $K$ paths, each a list of natural numbers,
such that every path has no repeated vertex, every vertex on a path is less than $n$, and
whenever $v$ immediately follows $u$ on a path the pair $(u, v)$ occurs in $E$; and such that
every vertex $v < n$ lies on some path, and all paths containing $v$ are equal.

articles.title: Instances of DIRECTED PATH COVER
articles.statement:
An instance of DIRECTED PATH COVER is a triple
$(n, E, K)$, where the natural number $n$ is the number of vertices, the list $E$ of ordered
pairs of natural numbers lists the directed edges, and the natural number $K$ bounds the number
of paths.

articles.title: DIRECTED PATH COVER is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem DIRECTED PATH COVER is in NP,
and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to
DIRECTED PATH COVER.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), PATH COVER (the `K = 1` slice is Hamiltonian path).

articles.title: Well-formed DIRECTED PATH COVER instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E, K)$ of
DIRECTED PATH COVER is well formed when the edge list $E$ has no repeated entries and every
edge $(a, b)$ in $E$ satisfies $a < n$, $b < n$ and $a \ne b$.

articles.title: Graph of a candidate edge set
articles.statement:
Given a Steiner tree instance with vertex count $n$ and a
list $T$ of triples $(u, v, w)$ of natural numbers, the graph of $T$ is the simple graph on
$\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j, w)$ or
$(j, i, w)$ belongs to $T$ for some natural number $w$. Weights are ignored, and triples with an
endpoint at least $n$ contribute no edge.

articles.title: The STEINER TREE decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem STEINER TREE accepts a bitstring
$x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of Steiner tree instances,
to a Steiner tree instance that is both well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode
are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible Steiner tree instances
articles.statement:
A Steiner tree instance with vertex count $n$, edge list
$E$ of triples $(u, v, w)$, terminal list $R$ and budget $K$ is feasible when every terminal in
$R$ is less than $n$ and there is a sublist $T$ of $E$ (a not necessarily contiguous
subsequence) whose weights $w$ sum to at most $K$ such that any two terminals in $R$ are joined
by a path in the graph of $T$, the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which distinct
vertices are adjacent when they are the endpoints $u, v$ of some triple in $T$.

articles.title: Steiner tree instances
articles.statement:
A Steiner tree instance is a quadruple $(n, E, R, K)$ of a
natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $E$ of triples $(u, v, w)$ of natural numbers
(an edge between $u$ and $v$ of weight $w$), a list $R$ of natural numbers (the terminals) and a
natural number $K$ (the budget).

articles.title: STEINER TREE is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem STEINER TREE belongs to NP, and every
decision problem in NP reduces to STEINER TREE by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), STEINER TREE IN GRAPHS; R. M. Karp, "Reducibility among combinatorial problems" (1972).

articles.title: Well-formed Steiner tree instances
articles.statement:
A Steiner tree instance with vertex count $n$, edge
list $E$ of triples $(u, v, w)$ and terminal list $R$ is well formed when $E$ has no repeated
entries; every $(u, v, w)$ in $E$ has $u < n$, $v < n$, $u \ne v$ and $w > 0$; any two entries
of $E$ with the same endpoints, in the same or the reverse order, are equal; $R$ has no repeated
entries; and every terminal in $R$ is less than $n$.

articles.title: Host graph of a subgraph-isomorphism instance
articles.statement:
For a subgraph-isomorphism instance
$(n, E_G, m, E_H)$, the host graph is the graph of the edge list $E_G$ on $n$ vertices: the simple
graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$
or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E_G$.

articles.title: SUBGRAPH ISOMORPHISM as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem SUBGRAPH ISOMORPHISM
accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of
subgraph-isomorphism instances, to an instance that is well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that
do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible subgraph-isomorphism instances
articles.statement:
A subgraph-isomorphism instance
$(n, E_G, m, E_H)$ is feasible when there is an injective map
$f : \{0, \dots, m - 1\} \to \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ such that for every $(u, v) \in E_H$ with
$u < m$ and $v < m$, the vertices $f(u)$ and $f(v)$ are adjacent in the host graph of the
instance.

articles.title: Subgraph-isomorphism instances
articles.statement:
A subgraph-isomorphism instance is a tuple
$(n, E_G, m, E_H)$ of a natural number $n$ (the number of host vertices), a list $E_G$ of pairs
of natural numbers (the host edges), a natural number $m$ (the number of pattern vertices) and a
list $E_H$ of pairs of natural numbers (the pattern edges).

articles.title: SUBGRAPH ISOMORPHISM is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem SUBGRAPH ISOMORPHISM belongs
to NP, and every decision problem $L$ in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to
SUBGRAPH ISOMORPHISM.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), SUBGRAPH ISOMORPHISM.

articles.title: Well-formed subgraph-isomorphism instances
articles.statement:
A subgraph-isomorphism instance
$(n, E_G, m, E_H)$ is well formed when the list $E_G$ has no repeated entries and every
$(u, v) \in E_G$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$, $u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin E_G$, and likewise the
list $E_H$ has no repeated entries and every $(u, v) \in E_H$ satisfies $u < m$, $v < m$,
$u \ne v$ and $(v, u) \notin E_H$.

articles.title: Costs produced by the Hamiltonian-cycle to TSP converter
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on the
vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $x$ be a Boolean array of length $n^2$ such that for all
$i, j < n$ the cell of $x$ at index $in + j$ exists and is true exactly when $i$ and $j$ are
adjacent in $G$, and let $y$ be the array output by the Hamiltonian-cycle to TSP converter on $x$,
with a Boolean cell read as $1$ if true and $0$ if false. Then for all $i, j < n$ the cell of $y$
at index $in + j$ exists and equals $0$ if $i$ and $j$ are adjacent in $G$ and $1$ otherwise; for
every $i < n$ the cell of $y$ at index $in + i$ exists and equals $1$; and for all $i, j < n$ the
cells of $y$ at indices $in + j$ and $jn + i$ are equal.

articles.title: Hamiltonian cycles of the source graph give zero-cost tours
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on
the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $x$ be a Boolean array of length $n^2$ such that for all
$i, j < n$ the cell of $x$ at index $in + j$ exists and is true exactly when $i$ and $j$ are
adjacent in $G$, and let $y$ be the array output by the Hamiltonian-cycle to TSP converter on $x$,
with a Boolean cell read as $1$ if true and $0$ if false. Let $p$ be a Hamiltonian cycle in $G$
based at a vertex $a$, and let $p'$ be $p$ regarded as a closed walk in the complete graph on
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. Then $p'$ is a Hamiltonian cycle, $p'$ visits the same sequence of vertices
as $p$, and for every directed edge $(u, v)$ traversed by $p'$ the cell of $y$ at index $un + v$
exists, and the sum of these cells over the directed edges of $p'$ is $0$.

articles.title: The Hamiltonian-cycle to TSP converter negates every cell
articles.statement:
For every Boolean array $x$ and
every index $k$, the array output by the Hamiltonian-cycle to TSP converter on $x$ has a cell at
index $k$ exactly when $x$ does, and that cell is the negation of the cell of $x$ at index $k$.

articles.title: Correctness of the Hamiltonian-cycle to TSP reduction
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph on the
vertex set $V = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $x$ be a Boolean array of length $n^2$ such that for all
$i, j < n$ the cell of $x$ at index $in + j$ exists and is true exactly when $i$ and $j$ are
adjacent in $G$, and let $y$ be the array output by the Hamiltonian-cycle to TSP converter on $x$,
with a Boolean cell read as $1$ if true and $0$ if false. Then $G$ has a Hamiltonian cycle if and
only if the complete graph on $V$ has a Hamiltonian cycle $p$ such that for every directed edge
$(u, v)$ traversed by $p$ the cell of $y$ at index $un + v$ exists and the sum of these cells over
the directed edges of $p$ is at most $0$.

articles.title: Tours of cost zero give Hamiltonian cycles of the source graph
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a simple graph
on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, let $x$ be a Boolean array of length $n^2$ such that for
all $i, j < n$ the cell of $x$ at index $in + j$ exists and is true exactly when $i$ and $j$ are
adjacent in $G$, and let $y$ be the array output by the Hamiltonian-cycle to TSP converter on $x$,
with a Boolean cell read as $1$ if true and $0$ if false. Let $p$ be a Hamiltonian cycle based at
a vertex $a$ in the complete graph on $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that for every directed edge
$(u, v)$ traversed by $p$ the cell of $y$ at index $un + v$ exists and the sum of these cells over
the directed edges of $p$ is at most $0$. Then there is a Hamiltonian cycle $q$ in $G$ based at
$a$ that visits the same sequence of vertices as $p$.

articles.title: The Hamiltonian-cycle to TSP converter preserves length
articles.statement:
For every Boolean array $x$, the
array output by the Hamiltonian-cycle to TSP converter on $x$ has the same length as $x$.

No assumption that $x$ encodes a graph is needed.

articles.title: Running time of the Hamiltonian-cycle to TSP converter
articles.statement:
For every Boolean array $x$, the
time charged by the Hamiltonian-cycle to TSP converter on $x$ is $2m$, where $m$ is the length of
$x$: one unit for reading and one unit for writing each cell.

articles.title: Hamiltonian-cycle to TSP converter
articles.statement:
The Hamiltonian-cycle to TSP converter takes a Boolean
array $x$ and, starting from the empty array, scans $x$ from left to right and appends the
negation of each cell, charging one time unit before and one time unit after each append (one
read and one write per cell). It returns the resulting array of negated cells together with the
total time charged.

articles.title: Length of a tour in the symmetric TSP
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be a matrix of natural numbers given as a
list of rows, where an entry $w_{a,b}$ outside the list (no row $a$, or row $a$ too short) is
read as $0$, and rows and columns are numbered from $0$. The length of a list
$(t_0, \dots, t_{k-1})$ of natural numbers with respect to $w$ is
$\sum_{j\lt k} w_{t_j, t_{(j+1) \bmod k}}$, the total weight of the edges along the cycle
$t_0, t_1, \dots, t_{k-1}, t_0$, including the return edge; the empty list has length $0$.

articles.title: Symmetric TSP as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The symmetric traveling salesperson problem is the
decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical
bitstring encoding of symmetric TSP instances, to an instance $(n, w, B)$ that is well formed and
feasible. Bitstrings that fail to decode, and bitstrings that decode to instances that are not
well formed, are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible symmetric TSP instances
articles.statement:
A symmetric TSP instance $(n, w, B)$ is feasible when
there is a list of $n$ pairwise distinct natural numbers containing every $v < n$, that is, an
ordering of the cities $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ visiting each exactly once, whose tour length with
respect to $w$ (the sum of the weights of consecutive edges, including the return edge) is at
most $B$.

articles.title: Symmetric TSP instances
articles.statement:
An instance of the symmetric traveling salesperson problem is a
triple $(n, w, B)$ of a natural number $n$, the number of cities, a weight matrix $w$ given as a
finite list of rows, each a finite list of natural numbers, and a natural number $B$, the bound.

The type itself does not require $w$ to be an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix with zero diagonal.

articles.title: TRAVELING SALESPERSON (SYMMETRIC) is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The symmetric traveling salesperson
decision problem belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a
polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), TRAVELING SALESPERSON PROBLEM.

articles.title: Well-formed symmetric TSP instances
articles.statement:
A symmetric TSP instance $(n, w, B)$ is well formed
when $n > 0$, the weight matrix $w$ has exactly $n$ rows and each row has exactly $n$ entries, $w$
is symmetric, that is $w_{a,b} = w_{b,a}$ for all $a, b < n$, and $w$ has zero diagonal, that is
$w_{a,a} = 0$ for all $a < n$. Rows and columns are numbered from $0$.

articles.title: Graph of a HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (UNDIRECTED) instance
articles.statement:
For an instance $(n, E)$, its graph
is the simple graph on the vertices $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$
are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$.

articles.title: HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (UNDIRECTED) as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem HAMILTONIAN
CYCLE (UNDIRECTED) accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring
encoding, to a well-formed instance $(n, E)$ with $n \ge 3$ whose graph has a Hamiltonian cycle.
It rejects every bitstring that does not decode to an instance.

articles.title: Feasible HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (UNDIRECTED) instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E)$ is feasible when
$n \ge 3$ and its graph has a Hamiltonian cycle, that is, a cycle that visits every vertex exactly
once.

articles.title: Instances of HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (UNDIRECTED)
articles.statement:
An instance of HAMILTONIAN CYCLE
(UNDIRECTED) is a pair $(n, E)$ of a natural number $n$, the number of vertices, and a finite
list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the edges.

articles.title: HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (UNDIRECTED) is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem HAMILTONIAN CYCLE
(UNDIRECTED) belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one
reduction to it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), HAMILTONIAN CIRCUIT; R. M. Karp, "Reducibility among combinatorial problems" (1972).

articles.title: Size of an accepted Hamiltonian-cycle certificate
articles.statement:
If the Hamiltonian-cycle verifier
accepts the bit strings $x$ and $y$, then $|y| = mw$, where $m = \lfloor \sqrt{|x|} \rfloor$ and
$w$ is the least natural number with $m \le 2^w$, and moreover $|y| \le |x|$.

articles.title: Completeness of the Hamiltonian-cycle verifier
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a bit string and
$m = \lfloor \sqrt{|x|} \rfloor$, suppose $|x| = m^2$, and let $G$ be a simple graph on the
vertices $0, \dots, m - 1$ in which $i$ and $j$ are adjacent exactly when entry $im + j$ of $x$
(counting from $0$) is true. If $G$ has a Hamiltonian cycle, then there is a bit string $y$ of
length $mw$, where $w$ is the least natural number with $m \le 2^w$, such that the
Hamiltonian-cycle verifier accepts $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Acceptance condition of the Hamiltonian-cycle verifier
articles.statement:
Let $x$ and $y$ be bit strings,
$m = \lfloor \sqrt{|x|} \rfloor$, and $w$ the least natural number with $m \le 2^w$. For each $i$
let $d_i$ be the number whose binary digits, least significant first, are the bits of $y$ at
positions $iw, \dots, iw + w - 1$ (counting from $0$; positions past the end of $y$ are
omitted). The Hamiltonian-cycle verifier accepts $x$ and $y$ if and only if $|x| = m^2$,
$m \ge 3$, $|y| = mw$, and for all $i, j < m$: entry $im + i$ of $x$ is false, entries $im + j$
and $jm + i$ of $x$ are equal, $d_i < m$, $d_i = d_j$ implies $i = j$, and entry
$d_i m + d_{(i+1) \bmod m}$ of $x$ exists and is true.

articles.title: Certificates exist exactly for Hamiltonian graphs
articles.statement:
For every bit string $x$, with
$m = \lfloor \sqrt{|x|} \rfloor$, some bit string $y$ makes the Hamiltonian-cycle verifier accept
$x$ and $y$ if and only if $|x| = m^2$, $m \ge 3$, and there is a simple graph $G$ on the vertices
$0, \dots, m - 1$ in which $i$ and $j$ are adjacent exactly when entry $im + j$ of $x$ (counting
from $0$) is true, and $G$ has a Hamiltonian cycle.

articles.title: Soundness of the Hamiltonian-cycle verifier
articles.statement:
If the Hamiltonian-cycle verifier accepts
the bit strings $x$ and $y$, then, with $m = \lfloor \sqrt{|x|} \rfloor$, we have $|x| = m^2$ and
$m \ge 3$, and there is a simple graph $G$ on the vertices $0, \dots, m - 1$ in which $i$ and $j$
are adjacent exactly when entry $im + j$ of $x$ (counting from $0$) is true, and $G$ has a
Hamiltonian cycle.

articles.title: Step bound for accepted Hamiltonian-cycle certificates
articles.statement:
There is a constant $c > 0$ such
that for all bit strings $x$ and $y$ that the Hamiltonian-cycle verifier accepts, its step count
on $x$ and $y$ is at most $c\,(|x| + 1)^2$.

articles.title: Quadratic step bound for the Hamiltonian-cycle verifier
articles.statement:
There is a constant $c > 0$ such
that for all bit strings $x$ and $y$, the step count of the Hamiltonian-cycle verifier on $x$ and
$y$ is at most $c\,(|x| + |y| + 1)^2$.

articles.title: Hamiltonian-cycle verifier
articles.statement:
Given bit strings $x$ and $y$, let
$m = \lfloor \sqrt{|x|} \rfloor$ and let $w$ be the least natural number with $m \le 2^w$. The
verifier reads $x$ as the adjacency matrix of a graph on the vertices $0, \dots, m - 1$, stored
row by row, and $y$ as $m$ words of $w$ bits, the $i$-th word giving a number $v_i$ in binary,
least significant bit first. It accepts exactly when $|x| = m^2$, every diagonal entry of the
matrix is false, the matrix is symmetric, $m \ge 3$, $|y| = mw$, the numbers
$v_0, \dots, v_{m-1}$ are distinct and less than $m$, and $v_i$ is adjacent to
$v_{(i+1) \bmod m}$ for every $i < m$. Along with the answer it returns a step count of the
operations it performs: bit reads from $x$ and $y$, checks and updates.

articles.title: Well-formed HAMILTONIAN CYCLE (UNDIRECTED) instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E)$ is well formed
when $0 < n$, the list $E$ has no repeated entries, and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies
$u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and its reversal $(v, u)$ does not belong to $E$.

articles.title: Graph of an undirected Hamiltonian path instance
articles.statement:
For an instance $(n, E)$ of undirected
Hamiltonian path, its graph is the simple graph on the vertex set $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which
distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$.

articles.title: HAMILTONIAN PATH (UNDIRECTED) as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem HAMILTONIAN PATH
(UNDIRECTED) accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring
encoding, to an instance $(n, E)$ of undirected Hamiltonian path that is well formed and feasible;
bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible undirected Hamiltonian path instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E)$ of undirected
Hamiltonian path is feasible when its graph has a Hamiltonian path: a list of length $n$ of
vertices of the graph, with no repeated entries and containing every vertex, in which any two
consecutive entries are adjacent.

articles.title: Instances of undirected Hamiltonian path
articles.statement:
An instance of undirected Hamiltonian path is a
pair $(n, E)$ of a natural number $n$, the number of vertices, and a finite list $E$ of pairs of
natural numbers, the edge list.

articles.title: HAMILTONIAN PATH (UNDIRECTED) is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem HAMILTONIAN PATH
(UNDIRECTED) belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time
many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), HAMILTONIAN PATH.

articles.title: Well-formed undirected Hamiltonian path instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, E)$ of undirected
Hamiltonian path is well formed when $n > 0$, the list $E$ has no repeated entries, and every pair
$(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and the reversed pair $(v, u)$ does not
belong to $E$.

articles.title: Directed adjacency for DIRECTED DISJOINT PATHS
articles.statement:
For a finite list $E$ of ordered pairs of
natural numbers and natural numbers $u$ and $v$, the directed adjacency of $u$ to $v$ in $E$ is
the boolean value that is true exactly when the pair $(u, v)$ occurs in $E$.

articles.title: DIRECTED DISJOINT PATHS as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem DIRECTED DISJOINT
PATHS accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding,
to an instance of DIRECTED DISJOINT PATHS that is well formed and feasible; bitstrings that do
not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible directed disjoint paths instances
articles.statement:
Let $(n, A, P)$ be an instance of DIRECTED
DISJOINT PATHS whose list of source-target pairs is
$P = ((s_0, t_0), \dots, (s_{k-1}, t_{k-1}))$. The instance is feasible when there are lists
$\pi_0, \dots, \pi_{k-1}$ of natural numbers such that, for every $p < k$, the list $\pi_p$ is
nonempty, has no repeated entries, has first entry $s_p$ and last entry $t_p$, has all its
entries less than $n$, and every two consecutive entries $u, v$ of $\pi_p$ form an arc $(u, v)$
occurring in $A$; and such that, for all distinct $p, q < k$, no $v < n$ is an entry of both
$\pi_p$ and $\pi_q$.

articles.title: Directed disjoint paths instances
articles.statement:
An instance of DIRECTED DISJOINT PATHS is a triple
$(n, A, P)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a finite list $A$ of
ordered pairs of natural numbers (the arcs) and a finite list $P$ of ordered pairs of natural
numbers (the source-target pairs).

articles.title: DIRECTED DISJOINT PATHS is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem DIRECTED DISJOINT PATHS
belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one
reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), DISJOINT PATHS; S. Fortune, J. Hopcroft, and J. Wyllie, "The directed subgraph homeomorphism problem" (1980).

articles.title: Well-formed directed disjoint paths instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, A, P)$ of DIRECTED
DISJOINT PATHS is well formed when the arc list $A$ has no repeated entries, every arc $(u, v)$
in $A$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and every source-target pair $(s, t)$ in $P$
satisfies $s < n$ and $t < n$.

articles.title: The 1-in-3-SAT decision problem
articles.statement:
The 1-in-3-SAT decision problem accepts a bitstring $x$
exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a pair $(n, \varphi)$ of a
natural number $n$ and a CNF formula $\varphi$ such that every clause of $\varphi$ has exactly
three literals, every literal $(y, b)$ of $\varphi$ has variable index $y < n$, and some
assignment $v$ of truth values to the variables $0, \dots, n - 1$ makes exactly one position
of every clause hold a literal $(y, b)$ with $v(y) = b$. It rejects every bitstring that does
not decode.

articles.title: Feasible 1-in-3-SAT instances
articles.statement:
A 1-in-3-SAT instance $(n, \varphi)$ is feasible when
there is an assignment $v$ of truth values to the variables $0, \dots, n - 1$, with variables
$y \ge n$ read as false, such that every clause of $\varphi$ has exactly one position holding a
literal $(y, b)$ with $v(y) = b$.

articles.title: 1-in-3-SAT instances
articles.statement:
A 1-in-3-SAT instance is a pair $(n, \varphi)$ of a natural number
$n$, the number of variables, and a CNF formula $\varphi$.

Any CNF formula is allowed here; that $\varphi$ has three literals per clause, all over the
variables below $n$, is required separately by well-formedness.

articles.title: 1-IN-3-SAT is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The 1-in-3-SAT decision problem belongs to NP, and every
decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources
