feasible when there is a list of $n$ truth values $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ such that the assignment
sending each variable $x < n$ to $a_x$ and every variable $x \ge n$ to false satisfies the CNF
formula $\varphi$.

articles.title: Monotone 3-SAT instances
articles.statement:
A monotone 3-SAT instance is a pair $(n, \varphi)$ of a
natural number $n$, the number of variables, and a CNF formula $\varphi$.

articles.title: MONOTONE 3-SAT is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem MONOTONE 3-SAT belongs to NP, and
every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to MONOTONE 3-SAT.

## Sources

- T. J. Schaefer, "The complexity of satisfiability problems", Proceedings of the Tenth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 1978), ACM, 1978, 216-226 (dichotomy theorem).

articles.title: Well-formed monotone 3-SAT instances
articles.statement:
A monotone 3-SAT instance $(n, \varphi)$ is well
formed when every clause of the CNF formula $\varphi$ is a list of exactly three literals
(repetitions allowed), each with a variable below $n$, and the literals of each clause are all
positive or all negative.

articles.title: NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT
accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a
NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT instance $(n, \varphi)$ that is well-formed and not-all-equal satisfiable.
Every bitstring that decodes to no instance is rejected.

articles.title: Not-all-equal satisfiability of an instance
articles.statement:
A NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT instance
$(n, \varphi)$, with $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\varphi$ a CNF formula, is not-all-equal satisfiable
when there are truth values $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ such that, for the assignment $v$ with
$v(x) = a_x$ for $x < n$ and $v(x) = \mathrm{false}$ for $x \ge n$, every clause of $\varphi$
contains a literal satisfied by $v$ and a literal not satisfied by $v$.

articles.title: NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT instances
articles.statement:
A NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT instance is a pair $(n, \varphi)$ of
a natural number $n$, the number of variables, and a CNF formula $\varphi$. The formula is not
required to have three literals per clause; that is part of well-formedness.

articles.title: NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT over
bitstrings belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one
reduction to it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability: A Guide to the Theory of NP-Completeness* (1979), NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT; T. J. Schaefer, "The complexity of satisfiability problems" (1978).

articles.title: Well-formed NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT instances
articles.statement:
A NOT-ALL-EQUAL 3-SAT instance $(n, \varphi)$
is well-formed when every clause of $\varphi$ is a list of exactly three literals, repetitions
allowed, and every literal $(x, b)$ in it has variable index $x < n$.

articles.title: Job sequencing with deadlines, processing times and profits as a decision problem
articles.statement:
This
decision problem accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring
encoding, to a job-sequencing instance that is feasible; bitstrings that do not decode to an
instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible job-sequencing instances
articles.statement:
Let $(J, K)$ be a job-sequencing instance with jobs
$J = (p_0, d_0, w_0), \dots, (p_{n-1}, d_{n-1}, w_{n-1})$. The instance is feasible when there
are distinct indices $j_1, \dots, j_m < n$, for some $m \ge 0$, such that
$w_{j_1} + \dots + w_{j_m} \ge K$ and, for every $t$ with $1 \le t \le m$,
$p_{j_1} + \dots + p_{j_t} \le d_{j_t}$: the selected jobs, run one after another in this order
from time $0$, each finish by their deadlines, and their total profit is at least $K$.

articles.title: Job-sequencing instances
articles.statement:
An instance of job sequencing with deadlines, processing times
and profits is a pair $(J, K)$ of a finite list $J$ of jobs, each a triple $(p, d, w)$ of natural
numbers giving its processing time $p$, deadline $d$ and profit $w$, and a natural number $K$,
the profit bound.

articles.title: JOB SEQUENCING WITH DEADLINES, PROCESSING TIMES, AND PROFITS is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision
problem of job sequencing with deadlines, processing times and profits on bitstrings is
NP-complete: it belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one
reduction to it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), SEQUENCING WITH DEADLINES AND PROFITS (arbitrary processing times); R. M. Karp, "Reducibility among combinatorial problems" (1972).

articles.title: The PARALLEL MACHINES WITH DEADLINES decision problem
articles.statement:
This decision problem accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to jobs
$(p_1, d_1), \dots, (p_k, d_k)$ of natural numbers (processing times and deadlines) and a number
$m$ of machines for which there are start times $s_1, \dots, s_k \in \mathbb{N}$ and machines
$\mu_1, \dots, \mu_k \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ such that $s_j + p_j \le d_j$ for every $j$, and
for all $a \ne b$ with $\mu_a = \mu_b$, either $s_a + p_a \le s_b$ or $s_b + p_b \le s_a$. It
rejects every bitstring that does not decode.

articles.title: Feasible schedules on parallel machines with deadlines
articles.statement:
An instance consisting of jobs
$(p_1, d_1), \dots, (p_k, d_k)$, where job $j$ has processing time $p_j$ and deadline $d_j$, and
a number $m$ of machines is feasible when there are start times $s_1, \dots, s_k \in \mathbb{N}$
and machines $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_k \in \{0, \dots, m - 1\}$ such that $s_j + p_j \le d_j$ for
every $j$, and for all $a \ne b$ with $\mu_a = \mu_b$, either $s_a + p_a \le s_b$ or
$s_b + p_b \le s_a$.

articles.title: Parallel machine scheduling instances
articles.statement:
An instance of parallel machine scheduling with
deadlines is a pair consisting of a finite list of jobs, each a pair $(p, d)$ of natural numbers
giving its processing time $p$ and deadline $d$, and a natural number $m$, the number of
machines.

articles.title: PARALLEL MACHINES WITH DEADLINES is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The PARALLEL MACHINES WITH DEADLINES
decision problem belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a
polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), PARALLEL MACHINE SCHEDULING WITH DEADLINES.

articles.title: The precedence-constrained multiprocessor scheduling decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision
problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring
encoding, to a precedence-multiprocessor scheduling instance that is well formed and feasible.
Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible precedence-multiprocessor scheduling instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(d, P, m, D)$ with
job durations $d = (d_0, \dots, d_{n-1})$ is feasible when there are start times
$s_0, \dots, s_{n-1} \in \mathbb{N}$ and machines $\mu_0, \dots, \mu_{n-1} \in \mathbb{N}$ such
that $\mu_j < m$ and $s_j + d_j \le D$ for every $j < n$, $s_a + d_a \le s_b$ for every
precedence pair $(a, b) \in P$, and for all jobs $a < b < n$ with $\mu_a = \mu_b$, either
$s_a + d_a \le s_b$ or $s_b + d_b \le s_a$. Here $s_j$ and $d_j$ are read as $0$ when
$j \ge n$.

articles.title: Instances of precedence-constrained multiprocessor scheduling
articles.statement:
An instance is a tuple
$(d, P, m, D)$ in which $d = (d_0, \dots, d_{n-1})$ is a list of natural numbers, $d_j$ being the
duration of job $j$; $P$ is a list of pairs $(a, b)$ of natural numbers, each read as the
precedence constraint that job $a$ precedes job $b$; $m$ is a natural number, the number of
machines; and $D$ is a natural number, the deadline.

articles.title: PRECEDENCE-CONSTRAINED MULTIPROCESSOR SCHEDULING is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The
precedence-constrained multiprocessor scheduling decision problem is in NP, and every decision
problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), PRECEDENCE-CONSTRAINED MULTIPROCESSOR SCHEDULING; J. D. Ullman, "NP-complete scheduling problems" (1975).

articles.title: Well-formed precedence-multiprocessor scheduling instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(d, P, m, D)$
whose list of job durations $d$ has length $n$ is well formed when every precedence pair
$(a, b) \in P$ satisfies $a < n$, $b < n$ and $a \ne b$, and there is an ordering of the jobs
$0, \dots, n-1$ (a permutation of this list) in which $a$ comes before $b$ for every
$(a, b) \in P$.

articles.title: Resource-constrained project scheduling as a decision problem
articles.statement:
RESOURCE-CONSTRAINED
PROJECT SCHEDULING is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes,
under the canonical bitstring encoding of RCPSP instances, to an RCPSP instance that is well
formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: RESOURCE-CONSTRAINED PROJECT SCHEDULING is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem
RESOURCE-CONSTRAINED PROJECT SCHEDULING belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a
polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), BIN PACKING; J. Blazewicz, J. K. Lenstra, and A. H. G. Rinnooy Kan, "Scheduling subject to resource constraints: classification and complexity", Discrete Applied Mathematics 5 (1983), 11-24 (classification).

articles.title: Feasible RCPSP instances
articles.statement:
Let $(J, P, C, D)$ be an RCPSP instance with $n$ jobs, where
job $j < n$ has duration $p_j$ and resource demand $r_j$, and set $p_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$. The
instance is feasible when there are start times $s_0, \dots, s_{n-1} \in \mathbb{N}$, with
$s_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, such that every job finishes by the deadline ($s_j + p_j \le D$ for all
$j < n$), every precedence pair $(a, b) \in P$ satisfies $s_a + p_a \le s_b$, and at every time
$t < D$ the total demand of the jobs active at $t$ (the jobs $j < n$ with
$s_j \le t < s_j + p_j$) is at most $C$.

articles.title: Instances of resource-constrained project scheduling
articles.statement:
An instance of
resource-constrained project scheduling (an RCPSP instance) is a quadruple $(J, P, C, D)$: a list
$J$ of jobs, each a pair $(p, r) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ of a duration $p$ and a
resource demand $r$; a list $P$ of precedence pairs $(a, b) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ of
job indices; a resource capacity $C \in \mathbb{N}$; and a deadline $D \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Well-formed RCPSP instances
articles.statement:
An RCPSP instance $(J, P, C, D)$ whose job list $J$ has
$n$ jobs is well formed when every precedence pair $(a, b) \in P$ satisfies $a < n$, $b < n$ and
$a \ne b$, and there is a listing of $0, 1, \dots, n-1$, each exactly once, in which $a$ comes
before $b$ for every $(a, b) \in P$.

articles.title: Single-machine scheduling with release times and deadlines as a decision problem
articles.statement:
SINGLE-MACHINE SCHEDULING WITH RELEASE TIMES AND DEADLINES is the decision problem that accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of
release-deadlines instances, to a feasible instance. Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance
are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible single-machine schedules with release times and deadlines
articles.statement:
A release-deadlines
instance with jobs $(p_j, r_j, d_j)$ for $j < n$ is feasible when there are start times
$s_0, \dots, s_{n-1} \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $r_j \le s_j$ and $s_j + p_j \le d_j$ for every
$j < n$, and for all $a < b < n$ either $s_a + p_a \le s_b$ or $s_b + p_b \le s_a$.

articles.title: Instances of single-machine scheduling with release times and deadlines
articles.statement:
A
release-deadlines instance is a list of jobs $(p_0, r_0, d_0), \dots, (p_{n-1}, r_{n-1}, d_{n-1})$
of triples of natural numbers, where $p_j$ is the processing time, $r_j$ the release time and
$d_j$ the deadline of job $j$.

articles.title: SINGLE-MACHINE SCHEDULING WITH RELEASE TIMES AND DEADLINES is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The
decision problem SINGLE-MACHINE SCHEDULING WITH RELEASE TIMES AND DEADLINES belongs to NP, and
every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- J. K. Lenstra, A. H. G. Rinnooy Kan, and P. Brucker, "Complexity of machine scheduling problems", Annals of Discrete Mathematics 1 (1977), 343-362 (strong NP-hardness of nonpreemptive 1|r_j|L_max; feasibility is L_max <= 0).

articles.title: The 3-machine flow shop scheduling decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem
3-MACHINE FLOW SHOP SCHEDULING accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the
canonical bitstring encoding of flow-shop instances, to an instance that is well formed and
feasible. Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible flow-shop schedules
articles.statement:
Let an instance consist of jobs $1, \dots, n$, where job $j$
is a list of natural numbers whose $k$-th entry $p_{j,k}$ is its processing time on machine $k$
(read as $0$ if the list has fewer than $k$ entries), and a deadline $D$. The instance is
feasible when there are natural numbers $s_{j,k}$, for each job $j$ and each $k \in \{1, 2, 3\}$,
such that for every job $j$ we have $s_{j,1} + p_{j,1} \le s_{j,2}$,
$s_{j,2} + p_{j,2} \le s_{j,3}$ and $s_{j,3} + p_{j,3} \le D$, and for every machine
$k \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ and all jobs $a < b$ we have $s_{a,k} + p_{a,k} \le s_{b,k}$ or
$s_{b,k} + p_{b,k} \le s_{a,k}$.

Here $s_{j,k}$ is the start time of job $j$ on machine $k$: each job visits machines 1, 2, 3 in
that order, no machine processes two jobs at once, and every job finishes by $D$.

articles.title: Flow-shop instances
articles.statement:
A flow-shop instance is a pair consisting of a finite list of jobs,
each a finite list of natural numbers (its processing times on machines 1, 2 and 3, in that
order), and a natural number $D$, the deadline. The type does not force a job to have exactly
three entries; that is part of well-formedness.

articles.title: 3-MACHINE FLOW SHOP SCHEDULING is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The 3-machine flow shop scheduling
decision problem belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a
polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey, D. S. Johnson, and R. Sethi, "The complexity of flowshop and jobshop scheduling", Mathematics of Operations Research 1 (1976), 117-129; T. F. Gonzalez and S. Sahni, "Flowshop and jobshop schedules: complexity and approximation", Operations Research 26 (1978), 36-52.

articles.title: Well-formed flow-shop instances
articles.statement:
A flow-shop instance is well formed when every job in
it is a list of exactly three natural numbers.

articles.title: One step of the tardiness computation
articles.statement:
Let $J = ((p_0, d_0), \dots, (p_{n-1}, d_{n-1}))$
be a list of jobs with processing times $p_i \in \mathbb{N}$ and due dates $d_i \in \mathbb{N}$,
let $j \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $(p, d) = (p_j, d_j)$ if $j < n$ and $(p, d) = (0, 0)$ otherwise.
Running job $j$ from the state $(t, s) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, where $t$ is the elapsed
time and $s$ the accumulated tardiness, gives the state $(t + p, \, s + \max(t + p - d, 0))$.

articles.title: The TOTAL TARDINESS decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem TOTAL TARDINESS accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding (natural numbers in
binary), to an instance of TOTAL TARDINESS that is feasible, that is, whose jobs admit an ordering
of total tardiness at most its bound. It rejects every bitstring that does not decode to an
instance.

articles.title: Feasible TOTAL TARDINESS instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(J, K)$ of TOTAL TARDINESS with $n$ jobs
is feasible when some ordering of its jobs, that is, some permutation $(j_1, \dots, j_n)$ of
$(0, 1, \dots, n - 1)$, has total tardiness at most $K$.

articles.title: Instances of TOTAL TARDINESS
articles.statement:
An instance of TOTAL TARDINESS is a pair $(J, K)$ consisting
of a finite list $J = ((p_0, d_0), \dots, (p_{n-1}, d_{n-1}))$ of jobs, where job $j$ has
processing time $p_j \in \mathbb{N}$ and due date $d_j \in \mathbb{N}$, and a bound
$K \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: TOTAL TARDINESS is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The TOTAL TARDINESS decision problem belongs to NP, and
every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), TOTAL TARDINESS (1||sum T_j); J. Du and J. Y.-T. Leung, "Minimizing total tardiness on one machine is NP-hard" (1990).

articles.title: Total tardiness of a job order
articles.statement:
Let $J = ((p_0, d_0), \dots, (p_{n-1}, d_{n-1}))$ be a
list of jobs with processing times $p_i \in \mathbb{N}$ and due dates $d_i \in \mathbb{N}$, and
set $(p_i, d_i) = (0, 0)$ for $i \ge n$. For a list $(j_1, \dots, j_m)$ of natural numbers (job
indices), let $C_k = p_{j_1} + \dots + p_{j_k}$ be the completion time of the $k$-th job when the
jobs are run in this order. The total tardiness of the order is
$\sum_{k=1}^{m} \max(C_k - d_{j_k}, 0)$.

articles.title: SINGLE-MACHINE WEIGHTED COMPLETION WITH PRECEDENCE as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision
problem accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding,
to an instance $(J, P, K)$ that is well formed and feasible: every precedence pair in $P$ consists
of two distinct job indices of $J$, and some ordering of all the jobs that puts the first job of
every precedence pair before the second has total weighted completion time at most $K$.
Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible weighted completion instances
articles.statement:
Let $(J, P, K)$ be an instance whose job list $J$
consists of $n$ jobs $(p_0, w_0), \dots, (p_{n-1}, w_{n-1})$ (processing time, weight). It is
feasible when there is an ordering $j_1, \dots, j_n$ of the indices $0, \dots, n-1$, each listed
exactly once, such that for every pair $(a, b)$ in $P$ the position of $a$ in the ordering is
smaller than the position of $b$, where an index that does not occur gets position $n + 1$, and
$\sum_{k=1}^{n} w_{j_k} (p_{j_1} + \dots + p_{j_k}) \le K$.

articles.title: Instances of single-machine weighted completion with precedence
articles.statement:
An instance of the
scheduling problem $1 \mid \mathrm{prec} \mid \sum w_j C_j$ (one machine, precedence constraints,
objective the sum over jobs $j$ of the weight $w_j$ times the completion time $C_j$) is a triple
$(J, P, K)$: a list $J$ of jobs, each a pair $(p, w)$ of natural numbers giving its processing
time and weight; a list $P$ of pairs of natural numbers, read as precedence constraints between
job indices; and a natural number bound $K$.

articles.title: SINGLE-MACHINE WEIGHTED COMPLETION WITH PRECEDENCE is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem
SINGLE-MACHINE WEIGHTED COMPLETION WITH PRECEDENCE on bitstrings belongs to NP, and every
decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), 1|prec|sum w_j C_j; E. L. Lawler, "Sequencing jobs to minimize total weighted completion time subject to precedence constraints", Annals of Discrete Mathematics 2 (1978), 75-90; J. K. Lenstra and A. H. G. Rinnooy Kan, "Complexity of scheduling under precedence constraints", Operations Research 26 (1978), 22-35.

articles.title: One step of the weighted completion time computation
articles.statement:
Let $J$ be a list of jobs, each a
pair (processing time, weight), let $(t, s)$ be a state consisting of the elapsed time $t$ and the
accumulated weighted completion time $s$, and let $j$ be a job index. With $(p, w)$ the job at
position $j$ of $J$ counting from $0$, or $(0, 0)$ if $J$ has no such position, the step sends
$(t, s)$ to $(t + p, s + w (t + p))$.

articles.title: Total weighted completion time of a job order
articles.statement:
Let $J$ be a list of jobs, each a pair
$(p_i, w_i)$ of processing time and weight indexed from $0$, with $(p_i, w_i) = (0, 0)$ for $i$
outside the list. For a list $j_1, \dots, j_m$ of job indices, the total weighted completion time
is $\sum_{k=1}^{m} w_{j_k} C_k$, where $C_k = p_{j_1} + \dots + p_{j_k}$ is the completion time of
the $k$-th job in the order.

articles.title: Well-formed weighted completion instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(J, P, K)$ whose job list $J$ has
$n$ jobs is well formed when every precedence pair $(a, b)$ in $P$ satisfies $a < n$, $b < n$ and
$a \ne b$.

articles.title: The weighted number of tardy jobs decision problem
articles.statement:
WEIGHTED NUMBER OF TARDY JOBS is the
decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical
bitstring encoding of weighted tardy jobs instances, to a feasible instance, that is, an instance
having an ordering of its jobs whose weighted number of tardy jobs is at most its bound. A
bitstring that decodes to no instance is rejected.

articles.title: Feasible weighted tardy jobs instances
articles.statement:
A weighted tardy jobs instance, consisting of a
list of $n$ jobs and a bound $K$, is feasible when there is an ordering of its jobs, that is, a
list of the job indices $0, 1, \dots, n - 1$ in which each index occurs exactly once, whose
weighted number of tardy jobs is at most $K$.

articles.title: Weighted tardy jobs instances
articles.statement:
An instance of WEIGHTED NUMBER OF TARDY JOBS is a pair
consisting of a finite list of jobs, each a triple $(p, d, w)$ of natural numbers giving its
processing time $p$, due date $d$ and weight $w$, and a natural number $K$, the bound.

articles.title: WEIGHTED NUMBER OF TARDY JOBS is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The weighted number of tardy jobs decision
problem lies in NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to
it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), WEIGHTED NUMBER OF TARDY JOBS (1||sum w_j U_j).

articles.title: One step of the weighted tardy jobs computation
articles.statement:
Let $J$ be a list of jobs, each a triple
$(p, d, w)$ of natural numbers (processing time, due date, weight). Given a state $(t, s)$ and a
natural number $j$, let $(p, d, w)$ be the job at position $j$ of $J$, counting from $0$, or
$(0, 0, 0)$ if $J$ has no position $j$, and let $t' = t + p$. The step returns $(t', s + w)$ if
$d < t'$, and $(t', s)$ otherwise.

articles.title: Weighted number of tardy jobs of an ordering
articles.statement:
Let $J$ be a list of jobs, each a triple of
natural numbers (processing time, due date, weight), and write $(p_i, d_i, w_i)$ for the job at
position $i$ of $J$, counting from $0$, with $(p_i, d_i, w_i) = (0, 0, 0)$ when $J$ has no
position $i$. For a list $(j_1, \dots, j_m)$ of natural numbers, the weighted number of tardy
jobs of this order is the sum of $w_{j_k}$ over all $k$ with $d_{j_k} < C_k$, where
$C_k = p_{j_1} + \dots + p_{j_k}$ is the completion time of the $k$-th job.

articles.title: 3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem 3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING
accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a
3-dimensional matching instance $(n, T)$ that is well formed (every coordinate of every triple in
$T$ is less than $n$) and feasible (it has a perfect matching). Bitstrings that do not decode to
an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible 3-dimensional matching instances
articles.statement:
A 3-dimensional matching instance $(n, T)$ is
feasible, or has a perfect matching, when there is a list $M$ of length $n$, obtained from the
list of triples $T$ by deleting some of its entries, such that for each of the three coordinate
positions, every natural number $a < n$ occurs in that position in exactly one triple of $M$.

articles.title: 3-dimensional matching instances
articles.statement:
An instance of 3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING is a pair $(n, T)$
of a natural number $n$, the part size, and a finite list $T$ of triples of natural numbers.

articles.title: 3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem 3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING on
bitstrings is in NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one
reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), 3-DIMENSIONAL MATCHING; R. M. Karp, "Reducibility among combinatorial problems" (1972).

articles.title: Well-formed 3-dimensional matching instances
articles.statement:
A 3-dimensional matching instance $(n, T)$
is well formed when each of the three coordinates of every triple in $T$ is less than $n$.

articles.title: EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS
accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of pairs
of a natural number and a list of lists of natural numbers, to an instance of EXACT COVER BY
3-SETS that is well formed and feasible; bitstrings that do not decode are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(q, C)$ of EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS
is feasible when $C$ has a sublist $S$, obtained by deleting some entries of $C$, such that for
every natural number $x < 3q$ there is exactly one list that occurs in $S$ and contains $x$.

articles.title: Instances of EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS
articles.statement:
An instance of EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS is a pair
$(q, C)$ of a natural number $q$ and a finite list $C$ of finite lists of natural numbers. The
intended universe is $\{0, \dots, 3q - 1\}$ and the entries of $C$ are the candidate
three-element subsets; that each entry lists three distinct elements of the universe is
required by well-formedness, not by the type of instances.

articles.title: EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS is in
NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS.

articles.title: Well-formed EXACT COVER BY 3-SETS instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(q, C)$ of EXACT COVER BY
3-SETS is well formed when every entry of $C$ is a list of exactly three pairwise distinct
natural numbers, each less than $3q$.

articles.title: EXACT COVER as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem EXACT COVER accepts a bitstring
$x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of pairs of a natural number
and a list of lists of natural numbers, to an instance of EXACT COVER that is well formed and
feasible; bitstrings that do not decode are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible EXACT COVER instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, C)$ of EXACT COVER is feasible when $C$
has a sublist $S$, obtained by deleting some entries of $C$, such that for every natural number
$x < n$ there is exactly one list that occurs in $S$ and contains $x$.

articles.title: Instances of EXACT COVER
articles.statement:
An instance of EXACT COVER is a pair $(n, C)$ of a natural
number $n$, the size of the universe $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$, and a finite list $C$ of finite lists
of natural numbers, the candidate subsets. That each entry of $C$ lists distinct elements of the
universe is required by well-formedness, not by the type of instances.

articles.title: EXACT COVER is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem EXACT COVER is in NP, and every decision
problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), EXACT COVER; R. M. Karp, "Reducibility among combinatorial problems" (1972).

articles.title: Well-formed EXACT COVER instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, C)$ of EXACT COVER is well formed
when every entry of $C$ is a list of pairwise distinct natural numbers, each less than $n$.

articles.title: The FACILITY LOCATION decision problem
articles.statement:
FACILITY LOCATION is the decision problem that
accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a
facility location instance that is well-formed and feasible; bitstrings that do not decode to an
instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible facility location instances
articles.statement:
Let $(o, D, B)$ be a facility location instance
with opening costs $o = (o_0, \dots, o_{n-1})$, assignment-cost rows $D = (D_0, \dots, D_{m-1})$
and budget $B$, and write $D_{c,j}$ for the $j$-th entry of the row $D_c$, read as $0$ when $D_c$
has no $j$-th entry. The instance is feasible when there is a map $\sigma$ from the clients
$\{0, \dots, m-1\}$ to the facilities $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ such that the opening costs of the
facilities in the image of $\sigma$ plus the assignment costs stay within the budget:
$\sum_{j \in \sigma(\{0, \dots, m-1\})} o_j + \sum_{c=0}^{m-1} D_{c,\sigma(c)} \le B$.

articles.title: Facility location instances
articles.statement:
A facility location instance is a triple $(o, D, B)$ made of
a finite list $o$ of natural numbers (the opening costs of the facilities), a finite list $D$ of
finite lists of natural numbers (the $c$-th list holds the costs of assigning client $c$ to each
facility), and a natural number $B$ (the budget).

articles.title: FACILITY LOCATION is NP-complete
articles.statement:
FACILITY LOCATION belongs to NP, and every decision
problem $L$ in NP reduces to FACILITY LOCATION by a polynomial-time many-one reduction: there is
a polynomial-time computable map $f$ on bitstrings such that, for every bitstring $x$, $L$
accepts $x$ exactly when FACILITY LOCATION accepts $f(x)$.

## Sources

- G. Cornuéjols, G. L. Nemhauser, and L. A. Wolsey, "The uncapacitated facility location problem", in P. B. Mirchandani and R. L. Francis, eds., Discrete Location Theory, Wiley, 1990, 119-171.

articles.title: Well-formed facility location instances
articles.statement:
A facility location instance $(o, D, B)$, with
opening costs $o$ and assignment-cost rows $D$, is well-formed when every row of $D$ has the same
length as $o$.

articles.title: The generalized assignment decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem GENERALIZED
ASSIGNMENT accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring
encoding of generalized-assignment instances, to an instance that is well formed and feasible.
Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible generalized assignments
articles.statement:
Let $(R, C, c, K)$ be a generalized-assignment instance,
let $n$ be the number of rows of $R$ (the jobs) and $m$ the length of $c$ (the machines), and
read entries missing from $R$ or $C$ as $0$. The instance is feasible when there are machines
$a_1, \dots, a_n \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ such that for every machine $i$ the sum of $R_{j,i}$
over the jobs $j$ with $a_j = i$ is at most $c_i$, and $\sum_{j=1}^{n} C_{j,a_j} \le K$.

articles.title: Generalized-assignment instances
articles.statement:
A generalized-assignment instance is a tuple
$(R, C, c, K)$ where $R$ and $C$ are finite lists of finite lists of natural numbers, read as
matrices indexed by job and machine ($R_{j,i}$ is the resource job $j$ consumes on machine $i$
and $C_{j,i}$ is the cost of assigning job $j$ to machine $i$), $c$ is a finite list of natural
numbers (the machine capacities $c_i$), and $K$ is a natural number (the cost bound).

articles.title: GENERALIZED ASSIGNMENT is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The generalized assignment decision problem
belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one
reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), GENERALIZED ASSIGNMENT PROBLEM.

articles.title: Well-formed generalized-assignment instances
articles.statement:
A generalized-assignment instance
$(R, C, c, K)$ is well formed when $R$ and $C$ have the same number of rows and every row of $R$
and every row of $C$ has as many entries as $c$ (one per machine).

articles.title: The MAXIMUM COVERAGE decision problem
articles.statement:
MAXIMUM COVERAGE is the decision problem that
accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a
maximum-coverage instance $(n, S, K, M)$ that is well formed and feasible: every subset in the
list $S$ has no repeated elements and only elements less than $n$, and some sublist of $S$ with
at most $K$ entries covers at least $M$ distinct elements less than $n$. Bitstrings that do not
decode are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible maximum-coverage instances
articles.statement:
A maximum-coverage instance $(n, S, K, M)$, with
universe size $n$, list of subsets $S$, set budget $K$ and coverage target $M$, is feasible when
there are a sublist $T$ of $S$ with at most $K$ entries and a list of at least $M$ pairwise
distinct natural numbers, each less than $n$ and each belonging to some subset in $T$.

articles.title: Maximum-coverage instances
articles.statement:
A maximum-coverage instance is a tuple $(n, S, K, M)$ of a
natural number $n$ (the universe size), a list $S$ of lists of natural numbers (the subsets), a
natural number $K$ (the set budget) and a natural number $M$ (the coverage target).

articles.title: MAXIMUM COVERAGE is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The MAXIMUM COVERAGE decision problem belongs to NP,
and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), SET COVER: maximum coverage with target `M = n` is exactly set cover (at most `K` sets covering all `n` elements).

articles.title: Well-formed maximum-coverage instances
articles.statement:
A maximum-coverage instance $(n, S, K, M)$ is
well formed when every subset in the list $S$ has no repeated elements and all of its elements
are less than $n$.

articles.title: Weight covered at least n times
articles.statement: The weight of the elements covered at least `n` times by the rows `sub`.

articles.title: Feasibility for maximum n-times coverage
articles.statement: At most `k` overlays cover weight at least `τ` at least `n` times.

articles.title: Instance of maximum n-times coverage
articles.statement: An instance: `n`, the coverage rows of the overlays, element weights, `k`, `τ`.

articles.title: Maximum n-times coverage decision problem
articles.statement: MAXIMUM n-TIMES COVERAGE as a decision problem over bitstrings.

articles.title: MAXIMUM n-TIMES COVERAGE is NP-complete
articles.statement: **MAXIMUM n-TIMES COVERAGE is NP-complete** (Liu, Dimitrakakis, Carter and Gifford 2022).

articles.title: Well-formed maximum n-times coverage instance
articles.statement: Well-formedness: every row has one entry per element.

articles.title: The MINIMUM TEST SET decision problem
articles.statement:
It accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes,
under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a triple $(n, C, K)$ of a natural number $n$, a list
$C$ of lists of natural numbers (the tests) and a natural number $K$ with the following
properties: every test is a list of numbers below $n$ without repeated entries, and some sublist
$T$ of $C$, obtained by deleting entries of $C$, has length at most $K$ and distinguishes every
pair, that is, for all distinct $a, b < n$ some test in $T$ contains exactly one of $a$ and $b$.
Bitstrings that do not decode are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible minimum test set instance
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, C, K)$ of MINIMUM TEST SET is feasible
when some sublist $T$ of $C$ (obtained by deleting entries of $C$) has length at most $K$ and
distinguishes every pair: for all distinct $a, b < n$ some test in $T$ contains exactly one of
$a$ and $b$.

articles.title: Minimum test set instance
articles.statement:
An instance of MINIMUM TEST SET is a triple $(n, C, K)$ of a
natural number $n$ (the number of elements), a finite list $C$ of finite lists of natural numbers
(the tests) and a natural number $K$ (the bound).

articles.title: MINIMUM TEST SET is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The MINIMUM TEST SET decision problem lies in NP, and
every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), MINIMUM TEST COLLECTION; A. De Bonis, L. Gargano, and U. Vaccaro, "Generalized framework for test set problems" (1997).

articles.title: Well-formed minimum test set instance
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, C, K)$ of MINIMUM TEST SET is well
formed when every test in the list $C$ is a list of numbers below $n$ without repeated entries,
so that each test lists a subset of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, each element once.

articles.title: Generalized nonmetric k-center as a decision problem
articles.statement:
This decision problem accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a k-center
instance that is well formed and feasible; bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are
rejected.

articles.title: k-CENTER (GENERALIZED, NONMETRIC) is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem of generalized
nonmetric k-center on bitstrings is NP-complete: it belongs to NP, and every decision problem in
NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- O. Kariv and S. L. Hakimi, "An algorithmic approach to network location problems. I: The p-centers", SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics 37 (1979), 513-538.

articles.title: Feasible k-center instances
articles.statement:
Let $(D, K, B)$ be a k-center instance with rows
$D_0, \dots, D_{m-1}$, and let $n$ be the length of $D_0$, with $n = 0$ if $m = 0$. For $c < m$
and a natural number $f$, write $D_c(f)$ for the entry of $D_c$ at position $f$, counting from
$0$, and set $D_c(f) = 0$ if $D_c$ has at most $f$ entries. The instance is feasible when there
is a set $S$ of at most $K$ locations $f < n$ such that every client $c < m$ has some $f \in S$
with $D_c(f) \le B$.

articles.title: k-center instances
articles.statement:
An instance of generalized nonmetric k-center is a triple $(D, K, B)$
of a finite list $D$ of rows, each a finite list of natural numbers (row $c$ lists the costs from
client $c$ to the locations), and natural numbers $K$, the bound on the number of locations, and
$B$, the radius.

articles.title: Well-formed k-center instances
articles.statement:
A k-center instance $(D, K, B)$ is well formed when all
rows of $D$ have the same length.

articles.title: The k-MEDIAN decision problem
articles.statement:
**The k-MEDIAN decision problem.** k-MEDIAN (generalized, nonmetric) is the decision problem
that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to
a k-median instance $(d, K, B)$ that is well formed and feasible. That is, $d$ has rows
$d_0, \dots, d_{n-1}$ (the clients) of a common length $m$ (the locations), and there are a set
$S \subseteq \{0, \dots, m-1\}$ of at most $K$ locations and a choice of $a(c) \in S$ for each
client $c < n$ with $\sum_{c < n} d_{c, a(c)} \le B$. Bitstrings that do not decode are
rejected.

articles.title: k-MEDIAN (GENERALIZED, NONMETRIC) is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The k-MEDIAN decision problem is in NP,
and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- O. Kariv and S. L. Hakimi, "An algorithmic approach to network location problems. II: The p-medians", SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics 37 (1979), 539-560.

articles.title: Feasible k-median instances
articles.statement:
Let $(d, K, B)$ be a k-median instance whose cost matrix $d$
has rows $d_0, \dots, d_{n-1}$, one per client, and let $m$ be the length of $d_0$, or $m = 0$
when $n = 0$. The instance is feasible when there are a set $S \subseteq \{0, \dots, m-1\}$ of at
most $K$ locations and a choice of $a(c) \in S$ for each client $c < n$ such that
$\sum_{c < n} d_c(a(c)) \le B$, where $d_c(j)$ is the entry of $d_c$ at index $j$ (counting from
$0$), read as $0$ when $d_c$ has fewer than $j + 1$ entries.

articles.title: k-median instances
articles.statement:
A k-median instance is a triple $(d, K, B)$ of a cost matrix $d$, given
as a list of rows of natural numbers (one row per client, one entry per location; the rows need
not have equal length), a natural number $K$ bounding the number of open locations, and a
natural-number budget $B$.

articles.title: Well-formed k-median instances
articles.statement:
A k-median instance $(d, K, B)$ is well formed when all
rows of its cost matrix $d$ have the same length.

articles.title: QUADRATIC ASSIGNMENT as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem QUADRATIC ASSIGNMENT
accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a
quadratic assignment instance that is well formed and feasible; bitstrings that do not decode
are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible quadratic assignment instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, F, D, K)$ of quadratic
assignment is feasible when there is a permutation $\pi$ of the numbers $0, \dots, n - 1$ such
that

$$
\sum_{a < n} \sum_{b < n} F_{a b} \, D_{\pi(a) \pi(b)} \le K.
$$

Here $F_{a b}$ is entry $b$ of row $a$ of $F$, and likewise for $D$; an entry that is missing,
because the matrix has too few rows or the row is too short, is read as $0$.

articles.title: Instances of QUADRATIC ASSIGNMENT
articles.statement:
An instance of quadratic assignment is a tuple
$(n, F, D, K)$ consisting of a natural number $n$ (the size), a flow matrix $F$ and a distance
matrix $D$, each given as a list of rows that are lists of natural numbers, and a natural
number $K$ (the cost bound).

articles.title: QUADRATIC ASSIGNMENT is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem QUADRATIC ASSIGNMENT lies in NP,
and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), QUADRATIC ASSIGNMENT PROBLEM; S. Sahni and T. Gonzalez, "P-complete approximation problems" (1976).

articles.title: Well-formed quadratic assignment instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, F, D, K)$ of quadratic
assignment is well formed when the flow matrix $F$ and the distance matrix $D$ each have
exactly $n$ rows and every row of each has length $n$.

articles.title: The SET COVER decision problem
articles.statement:
SET COVER is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring
$x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a set-cover instance
$(n, C, K)$ that is both well formed and feasible: every list in $C$ has no repeated entries and
only entries less than $n$, and some sublist of $C$ with at most $K$ entries contains every natural
number $y < n$ in one of its lists. Bitstrings that do not decode to a set-cover instance are
rejected.

articles.title: Feasible set-cover instances
articles.statement:
A set-cover instance $(n, C, K)$ is feasible when there is a
sublist $D$ of $C$ (a list obtained from $C$ by deleting entries while keeping their order) with
at most $K$ entries such that every natural number $x < n$ belongs to some list in $D$.

articles.title: Set-cover instances
articles.statement:
A set-cover instance is a triple $(n, C, K)$ consisting of a natural
number $n$, the size of the universe, a finite list $C$ of finite lists of natural numbers, the
subsets, and a natural number $K$, the bound.

articles.title: SET COVER is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The SET COVER decision problem lies in NP, and every decision
problem $L$ in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to SET COVER.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), SET COVER; R. M. Karp, "Reducibility among combinatorial problems" (1972).

articles.title: Well-formed set-cover instances
articles.statement:
A set-cover instance $(n, C, K)$ is well formed when every
list $s$ in $C$ has no repeated entries and every entry of $s$ is less than $n$, that is, each
member of $C$ lists the elements of a subset of $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ without repetition.

articles.title: The SET PACKING decision problem
articles.statement:
SET PACKING is the decision problem that accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a set-packing
instance $(n, C, K)$ that is both well formed and feasible: every list in $C$ has no repeated
entries and only entries less than $n$, and some sublist of $C$ with no repeated entries and at
least $K$ entries has no element in common between any two of its distinct entries. Bitstrings
that do not decode to a set-packing instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible set-packing instances
articles.statement:
A set-packing instance $(n, C, K)$ is feasible when there
is a sublist $D$ of $C$ (a list obtained from $C$ by deleting entries while keeping their order)
with no repeated entries and at least $K$ entries such that any two distinct entries of $D$ have
no element in common.

In particular two copies of the same list, even of the empty list, cannot both be chosen.

articles.title: Set-packing instances
articles.statement:
A set-packing instance is a triple $(n, C, K)$ consisting of a
natural number $n$, the size of the universe, a finite list $C$ of finite lists of natural numbers,
the subsets, and a natural number $K$, the bound.

articles.title: SET PACKING is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The SET PACKING decision problem lies in NP, and every
decision problem $L$ in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to SET PACKING.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), SET PACKING; R. M. Karp, "Reducibility among combinatorial problems" (1972).

articles.title: Well-formed set-packing instances
articles.statement:
A set-packing instance $(n, C, K)$ is well formed when
every list $s$ in $C$ has no repeated entries and every entry of $s$ is less than $n$, that is,
each member of $C$ lists the elements of a subset of $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ without repetition.

articles.title: The SET SPLITTING decision problem
articles.statement:
SET SPLITTING is the decision problem that accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a pair
$(n, C)$ of a natural number $n$ and a list $C$ of lists of natural numbers such that every list
in $C$ has no repeated entries and only entries less than $n$, and some finite set $S$ of natural
numbers less than $n$ contains an entry of every list in $C$ and misses an entry of every list in
$C$. Bitstrings that do not decode to such a pair are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible set-splitting instances
articles.statement:
A set-splitting instance $(n, C)$, a natural number $n$
together with a list $C$ of lists of natural numbers, is feasible when there is a finite set $S$
of natural numbers, all less than $n$, such that every list in $C$ has an entry in $S$ and an
entry not in $S$.

articles.title: Set-splitting instances
articles.statement:
A set-splitting instance is a pair $(n, C)$ of a natural number
$n$, the size of the universe, and a list $C$ of lists of natural numbers, the subsets to be
split.

articles.title: SET SPLITTING is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The SET SPLITTING decision problem belongs to NP, and every
decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), SET SPLITTING (hypergraph 2-coloring); S. Lovasz, "Coverings and colorings of hypergraphs" (1973).

articles.title: Well-formed set-splitting instances
articles.statement:
A set-splitting instance $(n, C)$, a natural number
$n$ together with a list $C$ of lists of natural numbers, is well formed when every list in $C$
has no repeated entries and all its entries are less than $n$.

articles.title: The Akari decision problem
articles.statement:
The Akari (Light Up) decision problem accepts a list of
booleans $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of lists of lists of
natural numbers, to an Akari board that is well formed and feasible; it rejects every list that
does not decode.

articles.title: Feasible Akari boards
articles.statement:
Let $B$ be an Akari board with $m$ rows, let $n$ be the length of its
first row ($n = 0$ when there are no rows), and write $B_{r,c}$ for the entry in row $r$ and column
$c$, read as $1$ when there is no such entry. The board $B$ is feasible when there is a finite set
$S$ of pairs of natural numbers (the bulbs) such that every bulb $(r, c) \in S$ has $r < m$,
$c < n$ and $B_{r,c} = 0$; every cell $(r, c)$ with $r < m$, $c < n$ and $B_{r,c} = 0$ is
illuminated by some bulb in $S$; no bulb in $S$ illuminates a different bulb in $S$; and for every
$(r, c)$ with $r < m$, $c < n$ and $B_{r,c} \ge 2$, the number of bulbs $(r', c') \in S$ with
$|r - r'| + |c - c'| = 1$ equals $B_{r,c} - 2$.

articles.title: Akari boards
articles.statement:
An Akari instance is a board given as a list of rows, each row a list of
natural numbers: the entry $0$ is an empty cell, $1$ is a wall, and $2 + k$ is a wall numbered $k$.
The rows need not have the same length; that is part of well-formedness.

articles.title: AKARI (LIGHT UP) is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The Akari decision problem belongs to NP, and every
decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- Brandon McPhail, "Light Up is NP-complete", unpublished manuscript, 2005.

articles.title: Illumination on an Akari board
articles.statement:
Let $B$ be a board, a list of rows of natural numbers, and
write $B_{r,c}$ for the entry in row $r$ and column $c$, read as $1$ when there is no such entry. A
bulb at $(b_r, b_c)$ illuminates the cell $(r, c)$ when either $b_r = r$ and $B_{r,c'} = 0$ for
every column $c'$ strictly between $b_c$ and $c$, or $b_c = c$ and $B_{r',c} = 0$ for every row
$r'$ strictly between $b_r$ and $r$. In particular, a bulb illuminates its own cell.

articles.title: Well-formed Akari boards
articles.statement:
An Akari board is well formed when every entry is at most $6$
and all its rows have the same length.

articles.title: The CLOSEST STRING decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem CLOSEST STRING accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of
closest-string instances, to an instance that is well formed and feasible. Bitstrings that do
not decode to a closest-string instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible closest-string instances
articles.statement:
Write $\ell(x)$ for the length of a bitstring $x$.
A closest-string instance $(S, d)$ is feasible when there is a bitstring $c$ with
$\ell(c) = \ell(s_1)$, where $s_1$ is the first bitstring of $S$ (and $\ell(c) = 0$ if $S$ is
empty), such that for every $s$ in $S$ the number of positions $j < \min(\ell(c), \ell(s))$ at
which $c$ and $s$ differ is at most $d$.

If all bitstrings of $S$ have length $\ell(c)$, this number is the Hamming distance between $c$
and $s$.

articles.title: Closest-string instances
articles.statement:
A closest-string instance is a pair $(S, d)$ of a finite list
$S$ of bitstrings (finite lists of booleans) and a natural number $d$, the distance bound.

The bitstrings are not required to have equal length; that is the well-formedness condition.

articles.title: CLOSEST STRING is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The CLOSEST STRING decision problem belongs to NP, and
every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- J. K. Lanctot et al., "Distinguishing string selection problems" (2003); M. Frances and A. Litman, "On covering problems of codes" (1997).

articles.title: Well-formed closest-string instances
articles.statement:
A closest-string instance $(S, d)$ is well formed
when all bitstrings in the list $S$ have the same length.

articles.title: LATIN SQUARE COMPLETION as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem LATIN SQUARE
COMPLETION accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring
encoding of pairs of a natural number and a list of lists of natural numbers, to an instance
$(n, G)$ that is well formed ($n > 0$ and $G$ consists of $n$ rows of length $n$ with entries at
most $n$) and feasible ($G$ can be completed to an $n \times n$ grid whose rows and columns are
permutations of $1, \dots, n$ and which agrees with $G$ on its nonzero entries). Bitstrings that
do not decode, or that decode to a malformed instance, are rejected.

articles.title: Completable partial Latin squares
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, G)$ of LATIN SQUARE COMPLETION is
feasible when there is a grid $C$ consisting of $n$ rows of length $n$ such that for all
$r, c < n$ the entry $G_{rc}$ is either $0$ or equal to $C_{rc}$, every row of $C$ is a
permutation of $1, \dots, n$, and every column of $C$ is a permutation of $1, \dots, n$. Here
$G_{rc}$ is taken to be $0$ when $G$ has no entry in row $r$ and column $c$.

articles.title: Latin square completion instances
articles.statement:
An instance of LATIN SQUARE COMPLETION is a pair
$(n, G)$ of a natural number $n$, the intended size, and a list $G$ of lists of natural numbers,
read as the rows of a partial grid in which the entry $0$ marks a blank cell.

articles.title: LATIN SQUARE COMPLETION is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem LATIN SQUARE COMPLETION on
bitstrings lies in NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time
many-one reduction.

## Sources

- C. J. Colbourn, "The complexity of completing partial Latin squares" (1984).

articles.title: Well-formed Latin square completion instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(n, G)$ of LATIN SQUARE
COMPLETION is well formed when $n > 0$, $G$ has exactly $n$ rows, every row of $G$ has length
$n$, and every entry of $G$ is at most $n$.

articles.title: The LONGEST COMMON SUBSEQUENCE decision problem
articles.statement:
LONGEST COMMON SUBSEQUENCE is the
decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical
bitstring encoding, to a feasible longest-common-subsequence instance. Bitstrings that do not
decode are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible longest-common-subsequence instances
articles.statement:
A longest-common-subsequence instance
$(R, K)$ is feasible when there is a binary string $w$ of length at least $K$ that is a
subsequence of every string in $R$, that is, $w$ is obtained from each string in $R$ by deleting
some of its entries.

articles.title: Longest-common-subsequence instances
articles.statement:
A longest-common-subsequence instance is a pair
$(R, K)$ of a finite list $R$ of binary strings (finite lists of booleans) and a natural number
$K$.

articles.title: LONGEST COMMON SUBSEQUENCE is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The LONGEST COMMON SUBSEQUENCE decision
problem, over binary strings, belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a
polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- M. R. Garey and D. S. Johnson, *Computers and Intractability* (1979), LONGEST COMMON SUBSEQUENCE; D. Maier, "The complexity of some problems on subsequences and supersequences" (1978).

articles.title: Minesweeper consistency as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The Minesweeper consistency decision
problem accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding,
to a Minesweeper instance that is well formed and feasible, that is, admits a mine placement
consistent with all of its clues. It rejects every bitstring that does not decode to a Minesweeper
instance.

articles.title: Feasible Minesweeper instances
articles.statement:
Index rows and columns by natural numbers, and call a cell
$(r', c') \ne (r, c)$ a neighbour of $(r, c)$ when $|r' - r| \le 1$ and $|c' - c| \le 1$. A
Minesweeper instance with $R$ rows, $C$ columns and a list of clues is feasible when there is a
finite set $M$ of cells $(r, c)$ with $r < R$ and $c < C$ (the mines) such that for every clue
$(r, c, k)$ in the list the cell $(r, c)$ is not in $M$ and exactly $k$ cells of $M$ are
neighbours of $(r, c)$.

articles.title: Minesweeper instances
articles.statement:
A Minesweeper instance consists of a number of rows $R$, a number of
columns $C$ and a finite list of clues, where $R$ and $C$ are natural numbers and each clue is a
triple $(r, c, k)$ of natural numbers giving a row $r$, a column $c$ and the number $k$ shown.

articles.title: MINESWEEPER CONSISTENCY is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The Minesweeper consistency decision problem lies
in NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

## Sources

- R. Kaye, "Minesweeper is NP-complete" (2000).

articles.title: Well-formed Minesweeper instances
articles.statement:
A Minesweeper instance with $R$ rows, $C$ columns and a
list of clues is well formed when every clue $(r, c, k)$ in the list satisfies $r < R$, $c < C$
and $k \le 8$.

articles.title: The NONOGRAM decision problem
articles.statement:
NONOGRAM is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring
$x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of nonogram instances, to a
feasible nonogram instance. Bitstrings that do not decode to an instance are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible nonogram instances
articles.statement:
A nonogram instance with row clues $R_0, \dots, R_{m-1}$ and
column clues $C_0, \dots, C_{n-1}$ is feasible when there is a picture, a list of $m$ rows of
Booleans each of length $n$, such that for every $r < m$ the run list of row $r$ equals $R_r$,
and for every $c < n$ the run list of column $c$, read from row $0$ to row $m - 1$, equals $C_c$.

articles.title: Nonogram instances
articles.statement:
A nonogram instance is a pair $(R, C)$ of finite lists, the row clues
$R$ and the column clues $C$, where each clue is a finite list of natural numbers.

articles.title: NONOGRAM is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The NONOGRAM decision problem belongs to NP, and every decision
problem in NP reduces to NONOGRAM by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- N. Ueda and T. Nagao, "NP-completeness results for nonogram via parsimonious reductions" (1996).

articles.title: One step of the run-length computation
articles.statement:
For a Boolean $b$ and a pair $(k, R)$ of a
natural number $k$ and a finite list $R$ of natural numbers, the step returns $(k + 1, R)$ if $b$
is true. If $b$ is false it returns $(0, R)$ when $k = 0$, and $(0, R')$ when $k > 0$, where $R'$
is the list $R$ with $k$ prepended.

Here $k$ is the length of the current run of true cells and $R$ is the list of completed runs.

articles.title: Run lengths of a row
articles.statement:
For a finite list $l$ of Booleans, the runs of $l$ are its maximal
blocks of consecutive true entries. The run list of $l$ is the list of the lengths of these
blocks, in order from left to right; it is empty when $l$ has no true entry.

articles.title: The SHORTEST COMMON SUPERSEQUENCE decision problem
articles.statement:
SHORTEST COMMON SUPERSEQUENCE is the
decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical
bitstring encoding, to a pair $(R, K)$ of a list $R$ of lists of booleans and a natural number
$K$ for which some list of booleans of length at most $K$ has every list in $R$ as a subsequence.
Bitstrings that do not decode to such a pair are rejected.

articles.title: Feasible shortest common supersequence instances
articles.statement:
An instance $(R, K)$ of SHORTEST COMMON
SUPERSEQUENCE, a list $R$ of lists of booleans together with a natural number $K$, is feasible
when there is a list $w$ of booleans of length at most $K$ such that every list in $R$ is a
subsequence of $w$ (its entries occur in $w$ in the same order, not necessarily consecutively).

articles.title: Shortest common supersequence instances
articles.statement:
An instance of SHORTEST COMMON SUPERSEQUENCE is a
pair $(R, K)$ of a list $R$ of binary strings (lists of booleans) and a natural number $K$, the
length bound.

articles.title: SHORTEST COMMON SUPERSEQUENCE is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The SHORTEST COMMON SUPERSEQUENCE decision
problem over binary strings belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a
polynomial-time many-one reduction.

## Sources

- K.-J. Räihä and E. Ukkonen, "The shortest common supersequence problem over binary alphabet is NP-complete", Theoretical Computer Science 16 (1981), 187-198. (D. Maier, "The complexity of some problems on subsequences and supersequences", JACM 25 (1978), 322-336, proves SCS only for a five- symbol alphabet; the binary case is Räihä-Ukkonen.)

articles.title: SUDOKU as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem SUDOKU accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly
when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of pairs of a natural number and a finite
list of finite lists of natural numbers, to a Sudoku instance that is well formed and feasible.
It rejects every bitstring that does not decode to an instance.

articles.title: Feasible Sudoku instances
articles.statement:
A Sudoku instance $(n, G)$, with block size $n$ and grid $G$ a
list of rows of natural numbers, is feasible when there is a grid $C$ of natural numbers with
exactly $n^2$ rows, each of exactly $n^2$ entries, such that, indexing rows and columns from $0$:
for all $r, c < n^2$ the entry $G_{rc}$ is $0$ or equals $C_{rc}$, where an entry missing from
$G$ counts as $0$; every row of $C$ and every column of $C$ lists each of $1, \dots, n^2$ exactly
once; and for all $b, b' < n$ the $n^2$ entries $C_{bn + i,\, b'n + j}$ with $i, j < n$ list each
of $1, \dots, n^2$ exactly once.

articles.title: Sudoku instances
SUDOKU is NP-complete
articles.statement:
The decision problem SUDOKU lies in NP, and every decision problem
in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to SUDOKU.

## Sources

- T. Yato and T. Seta, "Complexity and completeness of finding another solution and its application to puzzles" (2003).

articles.title: Well-formed Sudoku instances
articles.statement:
A Sudoku instance $(n, G)$, with block size $n$ and grid $G$
a list of rows of natural numbers, is well formed when $n > 0$, $G$ has exactly $n^2$ rows, every
row of $G$ has exactly $n^2$ entries, and every entry of $G$ is at most $n^2$.

articles.title: Complement of “infinitely often”
articles.statement:
For every set $p$ of symbols, the complement of the
ω-language of infinite words with infinitely many letters in $p$ is the ω-language of infinite
words whose letters are eventually all in the complement of $p$.

articles.title: Two-state Büchi automaton for “eventually always”
articles.statement:
For a set $p$ of symbols, this is the
nondeterministic Büchi automaton over the alphabet of symbols with states $\mathsf{false}$ and
$\mathsf{true}$, single start state $\mathsf{false}$ and single accepting state $\mathsf{true}$.
From $\mathsf{false}$ it may read any letter and move to either state; from $\mathsf{true}$ it
may read only letters in $p$, and then it stays in $\mathsf{true}$.

articles.title: Eventually always
articles.statement:
For a set $p$ of symbols, the ω-language “eventually always $p$”
consists of the infinite words $x_0 x_1 x_2 \ldots$ for which there is an $N$ with $x_k \in p$
for all $k \ge N$.

articles.title: Two-state Büchi automaton for “infinitely often”
articles.statement:
For a set $p$ of symbols, this is the
nondeterministic Büchi automaton over the alphabet of symbols with states $\mathsf{true}$ and
$\mathsf{false}$, single start state $\mathsf{true}$ and single accepting state $\mathsf{true}$,
in which reading a letter $x$ from either state leads to exactly one state: $\mathsf{true}$ if
$x \in p$ and $\mathsf{false}$ otherwise. So the state records whether the last letter read was
in $p$.

articles.title: Infinitely often
articles.statement:
For a set $p$ of symbols, the ω-language “infinitely often $p$”
consists of the infinite words $x_0 x_1 x_2 \ldots$ with $x_k \in p$ for infinitely many $k$.

articles.title: Nonempty Büchi languages contain ultimately periodic words
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a
nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states over a nonempty alphabet. If $A$
accepts some infinite word, then there are finite words $u$ and $v$ with $v$ nonempty such that
$A$ accepts the ultimately periodic word $u v^\omega = u v v v \cdots$.

articles.title: Reachability by words is reachability in the transition graph
articles.statement:
For states $s$ and $t$ of
a nondeterministic Büchi automaton, the automaton can move from $s$ to $t$ by reading some finite
word (possibly empty) if and only if $t$ is reachable from $s$ in zero or more steps of the
transition graph, which has an edge from $p$ to $q$ when some symbol takes $p$ to $q$.

articles.title: Nonempty words and paths of positive length
articles.statement:
For states $s$ and $t$ of a
nondeterministic Büchi automaton, the automaton can move from $s$ to $t$ by reading some nonempty
finite word if and only if $t$ is reachable from $s$ in one or more steps of the transition
graph, which has an edge from $p$ to $q$ when some symbol takes $p$ to $q$.

articles.title: Lasso detection by finite reachability
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a nondeterministic Büchi automaton
with finitely many states and finitely many symbols, with decidable equality of states, and whose
transitions, start states and accepting states are decidable. Then $A$ has a lasso if and only if
its set of lasso states, computed by finite reachability closures as the accepting states that are
reachable from a start state and lie on a nonempty cycle, is nonempty.

articles.title: The lasso condition in the transition graph
articles.statement:
A nondeterministic Büchi automaton has a
lasso if and only if there are a start state $s_0$ and an accepting state $s$ such that $s$ is
reachable from $s_0$ in zero or more steps of the transition graph and $s$ is reachable from
itself in one or more steps; the transition graph has an edge from $p$ to $q$ when some symbol
takes $p$ to $q$.

articles.title: An accepted word yields a lasso
articles.statement:
If a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many
states accepts some infinite word, then it has a lasso: some accepting state is visited twice
along an accepting run, and the run between the two visits is the cycle.

articles.title: Lasso of a Büchi automaton
articles.statement:
A nondeterministic Büchi automaton has a lasso if there are a
start state $s_0$ and an accepting state $s$ such that the automaton can move from $s_0$ to $s$ by
reading some finite word $u$, and from $s$ back to $s$ by reading some nonempty finite word
$v$.

articles.title: Correctness of the Büchi emptiness test
articles.statement:
For a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with
finitely many states and finitely many symbols, with decidable equality of states, and whose
transitions, start states and accepting states are decidable, the emptiness test returns true if
and only if the automaton accepts no infinite word.

articles.title: Büchi emptiness test
articles.statement:
For a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states and
finitely many symbols, with decidable equality of states, and whose transitions, start states and
accepting states are decidable, the emptiness test returns true exactly when the automaton has no
lasso. It decides this by computing the set of lasso states; by the lasso characterization, it
returns true iff no infinite word is accepted.

With $n$ states, $f$ reachable accepting states and $k$ symbols, the computation performs at most
$f + 1$ reachability closures of $O(n^3 k)$ transition tests each.

articles.title: Lasso characterization of Büchi nonemptiness
articles.statement:
For finitely many states, the language
of a nondeterministic Büchi automaton is nonempty iff some accepting state is reachable from a
start state and lies on a nonempty cycle.

articles.title: Lassos give accepted ultimately periodic words
articles.statement:
Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a nondeterministic
Büchi automaton over a nonempty alphabet. Suppose $s_0$ is a start state and $s$ an accepting
state of $\mathcal{A}$, that reading the finite word $u$ the automaton can move from $s_0$ to $s$,
and that reading a nonempty finite word $v$ it can move from $s$ back to $s$. Then $\mathcal{A}$
accepts the infinite word $u v^\omega = u v v v \cdots$.

articles.title: Lasso states of a finite Büchi automaton
articles.statement:
For a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with
finitely many states, decidable equality of states, a finite alphabet, and decidable transitions,
start set and accepting set, the lasso states form the finite set of accepting states $s$ that are
reachable from some start state in zero or more transitions and lie on a nonempty cycle, that is,
$s$ is reachable from itself in one or more transitions.

The set is computed by one reachability closure from all start states, then one cycle closure for
each reachable accepting state; each closure takes as many rounds as there are states.

articles.title: Büchi acceptance condition
articles.statement:
A nondeterministic Büchi automaton accepts an infinite word
$x = x_0 x_1 x_2 \cdots$ if and only if it has a run on $x$, that is, a sequence of states
$s_0 s_1 s_2 \cdots$ with $s_0$ a start state and a transition from $s_k$ to $s_{k+1}$ reading
$x_k$ for every $k$, such that $s_k$ is an accepting state for infinitely many $k$.

articles.title: Finite set of start states
articles.statement:
For a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many
states and a decidable start set, this is the set of its start states, viewed as a finite set.

articles.title: Symbol-forgetting transition graph of a Büchi automaton
articles.statement:
For a nondeterministic Büchi
automaton, the transition graph has an edge from a state $s$ to a state $t$ exactly when the
automaton has a transition from $s$ to $t$ reading some symbol.

articles.title: The degeneralization counter reaches every higher value
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi
automaton with acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1}$, and let $s$ be an infinite sequence of
states that visits every $F_j$ infinitely often, with counter sequence $c_0, c_1, \dots$. Then
for every time $n$ and every $j$ with $c_n \le j \le k$ there is a time $m \ge n$ with $c_m = j$.

The distance $d = j - c_n$ appears in the statement as a separate variable, and the proof is by
induction on $d$: the first visit to the awaited set after time $n$ advances the counter by one
(the counter stays put until then).

articles.title: The degeneralization counter waits for the awaited set
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi
automaton with acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1}$, let $s$ be an infinite sequence of states
with counter sequence $c_0, c_1, \dots$, and let $i < k$ and $n$ satisfy $c_n = i$. If $m \ge n$
and $s_{j+1} \notin F_i$ for every $j$ with $n \le j < m$, then $c_m = i$.

articles.title: Recursion step of the counter sequence
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton, $s$ an
infinite sequence of states, and $c_0, c_1, \dots$ the counter sequence of $s$. For every $n$,
$c_{n+1} = \mathrm{next}(c_n, s_{n+1})$, where $\mathrm{next}$ is the counter update of $g$.

articles.title: The counter sequence starts at zero
articles.statement:
For every generalized Büchi automaton $g$ and every
infinite sequence of states $s$, the counter sequence of $s$ has value $0$ at time $0$.

articles.title: Counter sequence of a state sequence
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton with $k$
acceptance sets and let $s = (s_0, s_1, \dots)$ be an infinite sequence of states. The counter
sequence $c_0, c_1, \dots$ of $s$, with values in $\{0, \dots, k\}$, is defined by $c_0 = 0$ and
$c_{n+1} = \mathrm{next}(c_n, s_{n+1})$, where $\mathrm{next}$ is the counter update of $g$. So
$c_n$ is the counter after reading the states $s_1, \dots, s_n$; the state $s_0$ is not read.

articles.title: The degeneralization counter crosses every value below its target
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a
generalized Büchi automaton with acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1}$ and counter update
$\mathrm{next}$, let $s$ be an infinite sequence of states, and let $c_0, c_1, \dots$ be any
sequence in $\{0, \dots, k\}$ with $c_{n+1} = \mathrm{next}(c_n, s_{n+1})$ for every $n$. Let
$a \le b$ be times with $c_a = 0$ and $c_b = d \le k$, and suppose $c_t \ne k$ for every $t$ with
$a < t < b$. Then for every $j < d$ there is a time $t$ with $a \le t < b$ such that $c_t = j$,
$c_{t+1} = j + 1$ and $s_{t+1} \in F_j$.

The proof is by induction on $b$, case-splitting the last counter step into stay, advance, or
the impossible reset.

articles.title: Generalized Büchi automaton
articles.statement:
A generalized Büchi automaton with states $S$ and symbols
$\Sigma$ is a nondeterministic automaton (a labelled transition relation on $S$ together with a
set of start states) equipped with a natural number $k$ and $k$ acceptance sets
$F_0, \dots, F_{k-1} \subseteq S$. A run is accepting when it visits every acceptance set
infinitely often.

articles.title: Degeneralization preserves the language
articles.statement:
A word is accepted by the
degeneralized Büchi automaton iff it is accepted by the generalized Büchi
automaton.

articles.title: Language of a generalized Büchi automaton
articles.statement:
An infinite word $x$ belongs to the language of
a generalized Büchi automaton $g$ with acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1}$ iff there is a run
$s$ of $g$ on $x$ such that for every $j < k$ there are infinitely many times $t$ with
$s_t \in F_j$. Here a run of $g$ on $x$ is an infinite sequence of states $s_0, s_1, \dots$ with
$s_0$ a start state and a transition from $s_i$ to $s_{i+1}$ labelled $x_i$ for every $i$.

articles.title: The degeneralization counter stays when the awaited set is missed
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a
generalized Büchi automaton with acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1}$ and counter update
$\mathrm{next}$. If $i \in \{0, \dots, k\}$ satisfies $i < k$ and the state $t$ is not in $F_i$,
then $\mathrm{next}(i, t) = i$.

articles.title: The degeneralization counter advances on a hit
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton
with acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1}$, let $i \in \{0, \dots, k\}$ be a counter value and let
$t$ be a state of $g$. If $i < k$ and $t \in F_i$, then the counter update of $i$ at $t$ is
$i + 1$.

articles.title: The degeneralization counter resets at the top
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton
with $k$ acceptance sets and let $i \in \{0, \dots, k\}$ be a counter value. If $i = k$, then for
every state $t$ of $g$ the counter update of $i$ at $t$ is $0$.

articles.title: Counter update for degeneralization
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi automaton with
acceptance sets $F_0, \dots, F_{k-1}$. The counter update takes a counter value
$i \in \{0, \dots, k\}$ and a state $t$ of $g$ and returns a counter value in $\{0, \dots, k\}$:
if $i < k$, it returns $i + 1$ when $t \in F_i$ and $i$ when $t \notin F_i$; if $i = k$, it
returns $0$.

articles.title: Degeneralization of a generalized Büchi automaton
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a generalized Büchi
automaton with $k$ acceptance sets. Its degeneralization is the Büchi automaton over the same
alphabet whose states are the pairs $(s, i)$ of a state $s$ of $g$ and a counter value
$i \in \{0, \dots, k\}$. On a symbol $x$ there is a transition from $(s, i)$ to $(s', i')$ iff $g$
has a transition from $s$ to $s'$ on $x$ and $i'$ is the counter update of $i$ at the state $s'$.
The start states are the pairs $(s, 0)$ with $s$ a start state of $g$, and the accepting states
are the pairs $(s, k)$.

articles.title: Büchi-to-parity conversion preserves the language
articles.statement:
Every nondeterministic Büchi automaton
accepts the same language of infinite words as its presentation as a parity automaton (priority
$2$ on accepting states, $1$ elsewhere).

articles.title: Nondeterministic parity automaton
articles.statement:
A nondeterministic parity automaton with states in $Q$
and symbols in $\Sigma$ is a nondeterministic automaton (a transition relation labelled by
symbols on $Q$, together with a set of start states) with a priority $p(q) \in \mathbb{N}$
assigned to each state $q \in Q$.

articles.title: Every state sequence of a finite parity automaton has a parity winner
articles.statement:
Let $\mathcal{A}$
be a nondeterministic parity automaton with finitely many states and priority function $p$. For
every infinite sequence of states $s_0, s_1, s_2, \dots$, the priority sequence
$p(s_0), p(s_1), p(s_2), \dots$ satisfies the even or the odd max-parity condition: the largest
priority occurring infinitely often exists and is even, or it exists and is odd.

articles.title: Büchi automata as parity automata
articles.statement:
A nondeterministic Büchi automaton is turned into the
nondeterministic parity automaton with the same states, transitions and start states, in which
every accepting state has priority $2$ and every other state has priority $1$.

articles.title: The tail of a bounded sequence is bounded by its largest infinitely occurring value
articles.statement:
Let
$d \in \mathbb{N}$, let $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of natural numbers with $p_k \le d$
for all $k$, and let $n$ be the largest value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$. Then
$p_k \le n$ for all sufficiently large $k$.

articles.title: Bounded sequences have a largest infinitely occurring value
articles.statement:
Let $d \in \mathbb{N}$. If a
sequence $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of natural numbers satisfies $p_k \le d$ for all $k$, then some
natural number $n \le d$ is the largest value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$.

articles.title: Prefix independence of the largest infinitely occurring value
articles.statement:
Let
$(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of natural numbers and let $j, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then
$n$ is the largest value occurring infinitely often in the shifted sequence
$(p_{j+k})_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ if and only if $n$ is the largest value occurring infinitely often
in $(p_k)$.

articles.title: Largest infinitely occurring value
articles.statement:
Let $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of natural
numbers and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Then $n$ is the largest value occurring infinitely often in
$(p_k)$ if $p_k = n$ for infinitely many $k$, and every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $p_k = m$ for
infinitely many $k$ satisfies $m \le n$.

Larger values may still occur, each only finitely often; for bounded sequences they eventually
stop occurring.

articles.title: Max-parity with priorities 1 and 2 is the Büchi condition
articles.statement:
Let $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ be
a sequence of natural numbers with $p_k \in \{1, 2\}$ for every $k$. Then $(p_k)$ satisfies the even
