max-parity condition if and only if $p_k = 2$ for infinitely many $k$.

articles.title: Even max-parity condition
articles.statement:
A sequence $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of natural numbers
(priorities) satisfies the even max-parity condition if there is an even $n$ that is the largest
value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$.

This is the winning condition of the even player under the max-parity convention.

articles.title: For bounded sequences the odd parity condition is the negation of the even one
articles.statement:
Let
$d \in \mathbb{N}$. If a sequence $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of natural numbers satisfies
$p_k \le d$ for all $k$, then it satisfies the odd max-parity condition if and only if it does not
satisfy the even max-parity condition.

articles.title: Odd max-parity condition
articles.statement:
A sequence $(p_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ of natural numbers
(priorities) satisfies the odd max-parity condition if there is an odd $n$ that is the largest
value occurring infinitely often in $(p_k)$.

This is the winning condition of the odd player under the max-parity convention.

articles.title: The attractor stabilizes after as many stages as there are positions
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity
game with finitely many positions, $N$ of them, let $p$ be a player and $T$ a set of positions.
Then the attractor of $T$ for $p$ equals the $N$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$, that is, the
result of applying the attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ $N$ times to
$\emptyset$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$.

articles.title: Attractor inside a set of positions
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an encoded parity game on $n$ positions,
$p$ a player (encoded as a Boolean: false for even, true for odd), and $T$, $U$ sets of
positions. The attractor of $T$ for $p$ inside $U$ is the set obtained from $\emptyset$ by
applying $n$ times the map $X \mapsto (T \cap U) \cup \mathrm{CPre}_p^U(X)$, where
$\mathrm{CPre}_p^U(X)$ is the controllable predecessor of $X$ for $p$ inside $U$.

articles.title: Attractor stages
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions and $n$ a
natural number. The $n$-th attractor stage $S_n$ of $T$ for $p$ is the set obtained by applying the
attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ $n$ times to $\emptyset$, where
$\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$; thus $S_0 = \emptyset$ and
$S_{n+1} = T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(S_n)$.

The $n$-th stage consists of the positions from which $p$ can force a visit to $T$ within fewer
than $n$ moves.

articles.title: Attractor operator
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The
attractor operator of $T$ for $p$ is the monotone map on sets of positions sending $X$ to
$T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$.

articles.title: The attractor strategy moves into the stage from its controllable predecessor
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be
a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions, $n$ a natural number and $S_n$ the $n$-th
attractor stage of $T$ for $p$. If a position $v$ owned by $p$ lies in the controllable
predecessor $\mathrm{cpre}_p(S_n)$ of $S_n$ for $p$, then the successor that the attractor
strategy of $p$ for $T$ chooses at $v$ lies in $S_n$.

articles.title: The attractor strategy reaches the target from the attractor
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game
with finitely many positions, $N$ of them, let $p$ be a player and $T$ a set of positions. If
$\pi$ is a play of $G$ that conforms to the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ and whose initial
position $\pi_0$ lies in the attractor of $T$ for $p$, then $\pi_i \in T$ for some $i < N$.

articles.title: The attractor strategy reaches the target from an attractor stage
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity
game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of positions and $n$ a natural number. If $\pi$ is a play of $G$
that conforms to the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ and whose initial position $\pi_0$ lies in
the $n$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$, then $\pi_i \in T$ for some $i < n$.

articles.title: Attractor strategy
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The
attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ is the positional strategy of $p$ that at a position $v$ moves
to a successor of $v$ lying in the $n$-th attractor stage of $T$ for $p$, for the least $n$ for
which $v$ has such a successor, and to an arbitrary successor of $v$ if no successor of $v$ lies
in any attractor stage.

articles.title: The attractor lies in every closed set
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a
set of positions. If a set $X$ of positions satisfies $T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X) \subseteq X$,
where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the controllable predecessor for $p$, then the attractor of $T$ for $p$
is contained in $X$.

articles.title: Attractor
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. The
attractor of $T$ for $p$ is the least fixed point of the attractor operator
$X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ on sets of positions, where $\mathrm{cpre}_p$ is the
controllable predecessor for $p$.

articles.title: Plays conforming to a strategy
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a positional strategy of player $p$ in a
parity game. An infinite sequence of positions $\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots$ (not necessarily a play)
conforms to $\sigma$ if $\pi_{i+1} = \sigma(\pi_i)$ for every $i$ such that $p$ owns $\pi_i$.

articles.title: Controllable predecessor inside a set of positions
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an encoded parity game,
$p$ a player (encoded as a Boolean: false for even, true for odd), and $U$, $X$ sets of
positions. The controllable predecessor of $X$ for $p$ inside $U$ is the set of positions
$v \in U$ such that either $v$ is owned by $p$ and some move of $G$ goes from $v$ to a position
of $U \cap X$, or $v$ is not owned by $p$ and every move of $G$ from $v$ to a position of $U$
ends in $X$.

Moves leaving $U$ are ignored; in particular a position of $U$ not owned by $p$ with no move into
$U$ belongs to the set.

articles.title: Controllable predecessor
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $X$ a set of
positions. The controllable predecessor $\mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$ of $X$ for $p$ is the set of
positions $v$ such that either $v$ is owned by $p$ and some move from $v$ leads into $X$, or $v$
is not owned by $p$ and every move from $v$ leads into $X$.

articles.title: Traps disjoint from a set avoid its attractor
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and
$T$ a set of positions. If a set $U$ of positions is a trap for $p$ and is disjoint from $T$, then
$U$ is disjoint from the attractor of $T$ for $p$.

Since the complement of the attractor is itself a trap for $p$ disjoint from $T$, it is the
largest such trap.

articles.title: The winning regions of the two players are disjoint
articles.statement:
In a parity game, for every player
$p$, no position lies both in the winning region of $p$ and in the winning region of the
opponent of $p$.

articles.title: Dual parity game
articles.statement:
The dual of an encoded parity game $G$ is the encoded parity game with
the same positions and moves in which every position is owned by the other player than in $G$
and has priority one more than in $G$.

Since incrementing priorities flips every parity, the even player wins the dual game exactly
where the odd player wins the original.

articles.title: Encoded parity game
articles.statement:
An encoded finite parity game on the $n$ positions
$0, \dots, n - 1$ consists of an owner for each position, given as a Boolean (false for the even
player, true for the odd player), a move relation, given as a Boolean-valued $n \times n$
matrix, and a priority for each position, given as a natural number.

No seriality is assumed: a position may have no move, since restricted subgames need not be
serial on the whole arena.

articles.title: Every player is $p$ or the opponent of $p$
articles.statement:
For all players $p$ and $q$ of a parity game,
$q = p$ or $q$ is the opponent of $p$.

articles.title: The attractor strategy forces a visit
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game with finitely many
positions, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. From every position $v$ of the attractor of
$T$ for $p$, the attractor strategy of $p$ for $T$ forces a visit to $T$: every play from $v$
conforming to it visits $T$.

articles.title: Forcing a visit to a set
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $\sigma$ a positional
strategy of $p$, $T$ a set of positions and $v$ a position. The strategy $\sigma$ forces a visit
to $T$ from $v$ when every play $\pi$ of $G$ with $\pi_0 = v$ that conforms to $\sigma$ visits
$T$, that is, $\pi_i \in T$ for some $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Plays of a parity game
articles.statement:
An infinite sequence of positions $\pi_0, \pi_1, \dots$ of a
parity game is a play if for every $i$ there is a move from $\pi_i$ to $\pi_{i+1}$.

articles.title: The complement of an attractor is a trap
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$
a set of positions. The complement of the attractor of $T$ for $p$ is a trap for $p$.

articles.title: Winning regions are traps for the opponent
articles.statement:
In a parity game $G$, the winning region of a
player $p$, the set of positions from which $p$ has a winning positional strategy, is a trap for
the opponent of $p$.

articles.title: Trap for a player
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game and $p$ a player. A set $U$ of positions is a
trap for $p$ when, for every position $v \in U$, every move from $v$ leads into $U$ if $v$
belongs to $p$, and some move from $v$ leads into $U$ if $v$ does not belong to $p$. Thus $p$
cannot force the play out of $U$.

articles.title: Joint successor of two strategies
articles.statement:
Let $\sigma$ be a positional strategy of player $p$
and $\tau$ a positional strategy of the opponent of $p$ in a parity game. The joint successor of
a position $v$ is $\sigma(v)$ if $p$ owns $v$, and $\tau(v)$ otherwise.

articles.title: Positions of maximal priority
articles.statement:
For an encoded parity game $G$ and a set $U$ of positions,
the positions of maximal priority in $U$ are the positions $v \in U$ whose priority equals the
maximal priority of $G$ on $U$.

articles.title: Maximal priority on a set of positions
articles.statement:
For an encoded parity game $G$ and a set $U$ of
positions, the maximal priority on $U$ is the largest priority of $G$ at a position of $U$, or
$0$ if $U$ is empty.

articles.title: Characterization of the attractor
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game with finitely many positions,
$p$ a player and $T$ a set of positions. A position $v$ lies in the attractor of $T$ for $p$ if
and only if some positional strategy of $p$ forces a visit to $T$ from $v$.

articles.title: Opponent moves stay in the winning region
articles.statement:
In a parity game, let $v$ be a position in the
winning region of player $p$ that is owned by the opponent of $p$. Then every position $w$ with a
move from $v$ to $w$ is in the winning region of $p$.

articles.title: A winning strategy's move stays in the winning region
articles.statement:
In a parity game, let $\sigma$ be a
positional strategy of player $p$ that wins from a position $v$ owned by $p$. Then the successor
$\sigma(v)$ chosen by $\sigma$ is in the winning region of $p$.

articles.title: Positional strategies exist
articles.statement:
In a parity game, every player has a positional strategy,
since every position has a move.

articles.title: No strategy forces a visit from outside the attractor
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a
player and $T$ a set of positions. If a position $v$ is not in the attractor of $T$ for $p$, then
no positional strategy of $p$ forces a visit to $T$ from $v$.

articles.title: No play is won by both players
articles.statement:
In a parity game, for every player $p$, no infinite
sequence of positions (play or not) is won both by $p$ and by the opponent of $p$.

articles.title: Winning strategies keep winning along allowed moves
articles.statement:
In a parity game, let $\sigma$ be a
positional strategy of player $p$ that wins from a position $v$, and let $w$ be a position with a
move from $v$ to $w$ such that $w = \sigma(v)$ if $p$ owns $v$. Then $\sigma$ wins from $w$.

articles.title: Opponent
articles.statement:
The opponent of a player of a parity game is the other player: the opponent
of the even player is the odd player, and the opponent of the odd player is the even player.

articles.title: Outcome of two positional strategies
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a player of a parity game, $\sigma$ a
positional strategy of $p$ and $\tau$ a positional strategy of the opponent of $p$. The outcome
of $\sigma$ and $\tau$ from a position $v$ is the infinite sequence of positions
$v_0, v_1, v_2, \dots$ with $v_0 = v$ in which $v_{i+1}$ is the successor chosen by $\sigma$ at
$v_i$ if $p$ owns $v_i$, and the successor chosen by $\tau$ at $v_i$ otherwise. It is the play
from $v$ in which $p$ follows $\sigma$ and the opponent follows $\tau$.

articles.title: Parity game
articles.statement:
A parity game on a type of positions consists of an owner for each
position, which is one of the two players, a move relation between positions, where the owner of
$v$ may move from $v$ to $w$ when $v$ is related to $w$, and a natural-number priority for each
position, such that every position has at least one move (there are no dead ends).

As in the usual infinite-play model, the absence of dead ends means that both players always
have positional strategies.

articles.title: Players of a parity game
articles.statement:
A parity game has exactly two players, the even player and the
odd player.

The even player is the one who wins the plays whose largest priority occurring infinitely often
is even, and the odd player the one who wins those where it is odd.

articles.title: Positional strategy in a parity game
articles.statement:
A positional (memoryless) strategy for player `p`: a choice of successor at each position,
legal at the positions `p` owns. Its values elsewhere are irrelevant.

articles.title: Priority compression
articles.statement:
For an encoded parity game $G$ on $n$ positions, the compressed game
has the same owners and moves as $G$ and gives each position $v$ the priority $2r + (q \bmod 2)$,
where $q$ is the priority of $v$ in $G$ and $r$ is the number of distinct priorities occurring
in $G$ that are smaller than $q$.

Since at most $n$ distinct priorities occur, every compressed priority is strictly below $2n$.

articles.title: Priority compression preserves and reflects the order of priorities
articles.statement:
For an encoded
parity game $G$ and positions $v$, $w$, the priority of $v$ is smaller than the priority of $w$
in the priority-compressed game of $G$ if and only if it is smaller in $G$.

articles.title: Bound on compressed priorities
articles.statement:
For an encoded parity game $G$ on $n$ positions, every
priority of the priority-compressed game of $G$ is strictly less than $2n$.

This holds because at most $n$ distinct priorities occur in $G$.

articles.title: Priority compression preserves parity
articles.statement:
For an encoded parity game $G$ and every position
$v$, the priority of $v$ in the priority-compressed game of $G$ has the same parity as the
priority of $v$ in $G$.

articles.title: Compressed priority
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an encoded parity game on the positions
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$. The compressed priority of a natural number $p$ is $2r + (p \bmod 2)$, where
$r$ is the rank of $p$ in $G$: the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur in $G$.

The compressed priority of $p$ is congruent to $p$ modulo $2$. On the priorities that occur in
$G$, compression is injective and strictly increasing.

articles.title: Monotonicity of priority ranks
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an encoded parity game, and for a natural
number $p$ let the rank of $p$ be the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur in $G$. If
$v$ and $w$ are positions of $G$ and the priority of $w$ is at most the priority of $v$, then the
rank of the priority of $w$ is at most the rank of the priority of $v$.

## Sources

- M. Jurdziński, "Small progress measures for solving parity games", *Proceedings of STACS 2000*, LNCS 1770, 290-301.

articles.title: Priority ranks are below the number of priorities
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an encoded parity game,
and for a natural number $p$ let the rank of $p$ be the number of distinct priorities $q < p$
that occur in $G$. For every position $v$ of $G$, the rank of the priority of $v$ is strictly
less than the number of distinct priorities that occur in $G$.

The priorities below the priority of $v$ form a proper subset of the occurring priorities, since
the priority of $v$ occurs but is not below itself.

## Sources

- M. Jurdziński, "Small progress measures for solving parity games", *Proceedings of STACS 2000*, LNCS 1770, 290-301.

articles.title: Strict monotonicity of priority ranks
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an encoded parity game, and for a
natural number $p$ let the rank of $p$ be the number of distinct priorities $q < p$ that occur
in $G$. If $v$ and $w$ are positions of $G$ and the priority of $w$ is strictly less than the
priority of $v$, then the rank of the priority of $w$ is strictly less than the rank of the
priority of $v$.

The priority of $w$ is counted in the rank of the priority of $v$ but not in its own rank.

## Sources

- M. Jurdziński, "Small progress measures for solving parity games", *Proceedings of STACS 2000*, LNCS 1770, 290-301.

articles.title: Rank of a priority in a parity game
articles.statement:
The rank of a priority `p` among the distinct priorities occurring in
the game: the number of distinct priorities `q < p` that occur.

articles.title: The parity game of a serial encoded game
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be an encoded parity game on the
positions $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ in which every position has a move to some position. The associated
parity game has the same positions, moves and priorities, and a position is owned by the odd
player if $G$ assigns it to the odd player and by the even player otherwise; every position has
a move by the hypothesis on $G$.

articles.title: The trap strategy avoids the target
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player, $T$ a set of
positions and $A$ the attractor of $T$ for $p$. If $\pi$ is a play starting at a position outside
$A$ that conforms to the trap strategy of the opponent of $p$ for the complement of $A$, then
$\pi_i \notin T$ for every $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: The trap strategy stays in the trap
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $U$ a trap
for $p$. If $\pi$ is a play with $\pi_0 \in U$ that conforms to the trap strategy of the opponent
of $p$ for $U$, then $\pi_i \in U$ for every $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Trap strategy
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $U$ a set of positions. The trap
strategy for $U$ is the positional strategy of the opponent of $p$ that, at each position $v$,
moves to some position $w \in U$ with a move from $v$ to $w$ if there is one, and to an arbitrary
position reachable from $v$ in one move otherwise.

articles.title: The attractor is a fixed point
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, $p$ a player and $T$ a set of
positions, and let $A$ be the attractor of $T$ for $p$. Then $T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(A) = A$, where
$\mathrm{cpre}_p(A)$ is the controllable predecessor of $A$ for $p$; that is, $A$ is a fixed point
of the attractor operator $X \mapsto T \cup \mathrm{cpre}_p(X)$.

articles.title: Winning region of a parity game
articles.statement: The positions from which player `p` has a winning positional strategy.

articles.title: Winning strategy from a position
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a player of a parity game. A positional
strategy $\sigma$ of $p$ wins from a position $v$ when every play starting at $v$ that conforms
to $\sigma$ (at every position owned by $p$, the play moves to the successor chosen by $\sigma$)
is won by $p$.

articles.title: Parity winning condition of a player
articles.statement:
A player wins an infinite sequence of
natural-number priorities when the sequence satisfies that player's parity condition: the even
player wins it when the largest priority occurring infinitely often exists and is even, and the
odd player wins it when the largest priority occurring infinitely often exists and is odd.

articles.title: Winning is prefix independent
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a player of a parity game, $\pi = (\pi_0,
\pi_1, \dots)$ an infinite sequence of positions and $j$ a natural number. Then the sequence
$(\pi_j, \pi_{j+1}, \dots)$, obtained by dropping the first $j$ positions of $\pi$, is won by $p$
if and only if $\pi$ is won by $p$.

articles.title: Bounded priorities give every play a winner
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a player of a parity game in
which every position has priority at most $d$, for some natural number $d$. Then every infinite
sequence of positions, in particular every play, is won by $p$ or by the opponent of $p$.

articles.title: Winner of a play in a parity game
articles.statement:
Let $G$ be a parity game, write $\Omega(v)$ for the
priority of a position $v$, and let $p$ be a player. An infinite sequence
$\pi = \pi_0 \pi_1 \pi_2 \dots$ of positions of $G$ is won by $p$ when its priority sequence
$\Omega(\pi_0) \Omega(\pi_1) \Omega(\pi_2) \dots$ satisfies the parity condition of $p$: among
the priorities occurring infinitely often there is a largest one, and it is even if $p$ is the
even player and odd if $p$ is the odd player.

The definition applies to every infinite sequence of positions, whether or not it follows the
moves of $G$.

articles.title: Run-wise Rabin/Streett duality
articles.statement:
Let $r$ be a Rabin automaton and let $s$ be an infinite
sequence of states. Then $s$ satisfies the Rabin condition of $r$, that is, for some Rabin pair
$(E, F)$ of $r$ the sequence $s$ visits $E$ infinitely often and $F$ only finitely often, if and
only if $s$ fails the Streett condition with the same pairs, that is, it is not the case that for
every Rabin pair $(E, F)$ of $r$, if $s$ visits $E$ infinitely often then $s$ visits $F$
infinitely often.

The sequence $s$ need not be a run of $r$. (For languages of nondeterministic automata there is
no such complementation statement, since complementation also swaps the run quantifier.)

articles.title: Streett-to-Muller conversion preserves the language
articles.statement:
If the state space is finite, then a
Streett automaton $r$ accepts the same language as its Muller presentation: the Muller automaton
with the same transitions and initial states as $r$ whose acceptance sets are the sets $S$ of
states such that, for every Streett pair $(E, F)$ of $r$, if $S$ meets $E$ then $S$ meets $F$.

articles.title: Parity-to-Muller conversion preserves the language
articles.statement:
If the state space is finite, then a
parity automaton accepts the same language as its Muller presentation, the Muller automaton
obtained by converting it to its Rabin presentation and that to a Muller automaton.

articles.title: Rabin-to-Muller conversion preserves the language
articles.statement:
If the state space is finite, then a
Rabin automaton $r$ accepts the same language as its Muller presentation: the Muller automaton
with the same transitions and initial states as $r$ whose acceptance sets are the sets $S$ of
states such that, for some Rabin pair $(E, F)$ of $r$, $S$ meets $E$ and is disjoint from $F$.

articles.title: Parity-to-Rabin conversion preserves the language
articles.statement:
If the state space is finite, then a
parity automaton $a$ accepts the same language as its Rabin presentation: the Rabin automaton
with the same transitions and initial states as $a$ whose Rabin pairs are the pairs
$(E_i, F_i)$ for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, where $E_i$ is the set of states of priority $2i$ and
$F_i$ the set of states of priority greater than $2i$.

articles.title: Parity-to-Streett conversion preserves the language
articles.statement:
If the state space is finite, then
a parity automaton $a$ accepts the same language as its Streett presentation: the Streett
automaton with the same transitions and initial states as $a$ whose Streett pairs are the pairs
$(E_i, F_i)$ for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, where $E_i$ is the set of states of priority $2i + 1$ and
$F_i$ the set of states of priority greater than $2i + 1$.

articles.title: Membership in the language of a Streett automaton
articles.statement:
An infinite word $x$ is accepted by a
Streett automaton $r$ if and only if there is a run $s$ of $r$ on $x$ such that for every Streett
pair $(E, F)$ of $r$, if $s$ visits $E$ infinitely often then $s$ visits $F$ infinitely often.

articles.title: Membership in the language of a Rabin automaton
articles.statement:
An infinite word $x$ is accepted by a
Rabin automaton $r$ if and only if there is a run $s$ of $r$ on $x$ and a Rabin pair $(E, F)$ of
$r$ such that $s$ visits $E$ infinitely often and visits $F$ only finitely often.

articles.title: Rabin automaton
articles.statement:
A Rabin automaton is a nondeterministic automaton together with a set
of Rabin pairs $(E, F)$, each a pair of sets of states. A run is accepting when some pair is
hit: the run visits $E$ infinitely often and $F$ only finitely often.

articles.title: Streett automaton
articles.statement:
A Streett automaton is a nondeterministic automaton together with a
set of Streett pairs $(E, F)$, each a pair of sets of states. A run is accepting when every pair
is respected: if the run visits $E$ infinitely often then it also visits $F$ infinitely often.

articles.title: Muller presentation of a Streett automaton
articles.statement:
Given a Streett automaton with set of
Streett pairs $\mathcal{P}$, this is the Muller automaton with the same states, initial states
and transitions whose accepting family consists of the sets $S$ of states such that every pair
$(E, F) \in \mathcal{P}$ with $S \cap E \neq \emptyset$ also satisfies $S \cap F \neq \emptyset$.
A Muller automaton accepts a run when the set of states that the run visits infinitely often
belongs to its accepting family.

articles.title: Muller presentation of a parity automaton
articles.statement:
The Muller automaton of a parity automaton
is the Muller presentation of its Rabin presentation. It has the same states, initial states
and transitions, and its accepting family consists of the sets $S$ of states for which there
is a natural number $i$ such that $S$ contains a state of priority $2i$ and no state of
priority greater than $2i$. A Muller automaton accepts a run when the set of states that the
run visits infinitely often belongs to its accepting family.

articles.title: Muller presentation of a Rabin automaton
articles.statement:
Given a Rabin automaton with set of Rabin
pairs $\mathcal{R}$, this is the Muller automaton with the same states, initial states and
transitions whose accepting family consists of the sets $S$ of states for which some pair
$(E, F) \in \mathcal{R}$ satisfies $S \cap E \neq \emptyset$ and $S \cap F = \emptyset$. A
Muller automaton accepts a run when the set of states that the run visits infinitely often
belongs to its accepting family.

articles.title: Rabin presentation of a parity automaton
articles.statement:
Given a parity automaton with priority
function $\Omega$ from states to natural numbers, this is the Rabin automaton with the same
states, initial states and transitions whose Rabin pairs are the pairs $(E_i, F_i)$ for
$i \in \mathbb{N}$, where $E_i = \{s : \Omega(s) = 2i\}$ and $F_i = \{s : \Omega(s) > 2i\}$.

articles.title: Streett automaton with the pairs of a Rabin automaton
articles.statement:
Given a Rabin automaton, this is
the Streett automaton with the same states, initial states and transitions and the same set
of pairs.

For a fixed run and a pair $(E, F)$, the Streett condition (if the run visits $E$ infinitely
often, then it visits $F$ infinitely often) is the negation of the Rabin condition (the run
visits $E$ infinitely often and $F$ only finitely often).

articles.title: Streett presentation of a parity automaton
articles.statement:
Given a parity automaton with priority
function $\Omega$ from states to natural numbers, this is the Streett automaton with the same
states, initial states and transitions whose Streett pairs are the pairs $(E_i, F_i)$ for
$i \in \mathbb{N}$, where $E_i = \{s : \Omega(s) = 2i + 1\}$ and
$F_i = \{s : \Omega(s) > 2i + 1\}$.

articles.title: Membership in APX
articles.statement:
An NPO problem $M$ is in APX when there are a rational number
$\rho \ge 1$ and a polynomial-time computable map $A$ from bitstrings to bitstrings such that, for
every instance $x$, the solution $A(x)$ is feasible for $x$ in $M$ and its value is at least
$\mathrm{opt}_M(x) / \rho$, where $\mathrm{opt}_M(x)$ is the optimum of $M$ on $x$.

articles.title: Hastad: optimal inapproximability of MAX-3SAT
articles.statement:
If $\mathsf{P} \ne \mathsf{NP}$, then for
every rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is no polynomial-time function $A$ from bitstrings to
bitstrings such that, for every bitstring $x$, the bitstring $A(x)$ has the same length as $x$
and the MAX-3SAT value of the assignment $A(x)$ on $x$ is at least $(7/8 + \varepsilon)$ times
the MAX-3SAT optimum of $x$.

## Sources

- J. Håstad, "Some optimal inapproximability results", Journal of the ACM 48 (2001), 798-859 (STOC 1997).

articles.title: Nondegenerate 3-clauses
articles.statement:
A clause, given as a list of literals $(v, s)$ with variable
index $v \in \mathbb{N}$ and polarity $s$, is nondegenerate if it has exactly three literals,
its variable indices are pairwise distinct, and it contains no complementary pair, that is, no
two literals $(v, s)$ and $(v, \lnot s)$.

articles.title: Optimum of a MAX-3SAT instance
articles.statement:
The MAX-3SAT optimum of a bitstring $x$ is the maximum,
over all bitstrings $a$ of length $|x|$, of the MAX-3SAT value of $a$ on $x$.

articles.title: Value of a MAX-3SAT assignment
articles.statement:
For bitstrings $x$ and $a$, read $a$ as the assignment
giving variable $v$ the value $a_v$ if $v < |a|$ and false otherwise. If $x$ decodes, under the
canonical bitstring decoding, to a pair $(u, \varphi)$ of a bitstring $u$ and a CNF formula
$\varphi$ in which every variable index is less than $|u|$ and every clause is nondegenerate,
then the MAX-3SAT value of $a$ on $x$ is the number of clauses of $\varphi$, counted with
multiplicity, that contain a literal $(v, s)$ whose variable gets the value $s$. Otherwise the
value is $0$.

The bitstring $u$ gives the number of variables in unary. Since degenerate and malformed
instances get value $0$, the $7/8$ random-assignment bound holds on every instance with nonzero
value.

articles.title: L-reductions
articles.statement:
Write $\mathrm{opt}_M(x)$ for the optimum of an NPO problem $M$ on an
instance $x$ and $v_M(x, s)$ for the value of a solution $s$ for $x$. An NPO problem $M_1$
L-reduces to an NPO problem $M_2$ when there are polynomial-time computable maps $f$, from
bitstrings to bitstrings, and $g$, from pairs of bitstrings to bitstrings, and rational numbers
$\alpha > 0$ and $\beta > 0$, such that for every instance $x$ the following hold. First,
$\mathrm{opt}_{M_2}(f(x)) \le \alpha \, \mathrm{opt}_{M_1}(x)$. Second, for every solution $s$
that is feasible for $f(x)$ in $M_2$, the solution $g(x, s)$ is feasible for $x$ in $M_1$ and
$\mathrm{opt}_{M_1}(x) - v_{M_1}(x, g(x, s)) \le
\beta \, (\mathrm{opt}_{M_2}(f(x)) - v_{M_2}(f(x), s))$.

This is the L-reduction of Papadimitriou and Yannakakis, with polynomial-time maps $f$ and $g$.

articles.title: The MAX-3SAT objective
articles.statement:
The value of MAX-3SAT on an instance $x$ under an assignment $a$,
both bitstrings, is defined as follows. Suppose $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring
encoding, to a pair $(u, \varphi)$ of a bitstring $u$ and a CNF formula $\varphi$, and suppose
moreover that $|a| \le |x|$, that every literal of $\varphi$ has variable index less than $|u|$
and that every clause of $\varphi$ has at most $3$ literals. Then the value is the number of
clauses of $\varphi$, counted with multiplicity, that contain a literal $(v, b)$ with $a_v = b$,
where $a_v$ is the bit of $a$ at position $v$ (counting from $0$), read as false when
$v \ge |a|$. In every other case the value is $0$.

The length of $u$ is the number of variables, so the value reads only $a_v$ for $v < |u|$:
padding an assignment with trailing false bits, or padding an assignment of length at least
$|u|$ with arbitrary trailing bits, does not change its value as long as its length stays at
most $|x|$.

articles.title: MAX-3SAT is MAXSNP-complete
articles.statement:
There is a MAXSNP problem whose value function is the
MAX-3SAT value function and which is MAXSNP-complete: its underlying NPO problem is in APX, and
the underlying NPO problem of every MAXSNP problem L-reduces to it.

## Sources

- C. H. Papadimitriou and M. Yannakakis, "Optimization, approximation, and complexity classes", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 43 (1991), 425-440.

articles.title: MAXSNP-completeness
articles.statement:
A MAXSNP problem $M$ is MAXSNP-complete when its underlying NPO
problem is in APX and, for every MAXSNP problem $M'$, the underlying NPO problem of $M'$
L-reduces to the underlying NPO problem of $M$.

articles.title: MAXSNP problems
articles.statement:
A MAXSNP problem, in the normal form of Papadimitriou and
Yannakakis, is an NPO problem $M$, with value function $v$ and solution length bound $b$,
together with natural numbers $k$ and $N$, a polynomial-time computable map $W$ sending each
instance $x$ to a list $W(x)$ of windows, each a pair $(w, j)$ of a list
$w = (w_1, \dots, w_m)$ of natural numbers (variable indices) and a natural number $j$ (a
pattern index), and a function $\mathrm{acc}$ assigning a truth value to each pair of a natural
number and a bitstring, such that the following hold. There is a polynomial $q$ with
natural-number coefficients such that $W(x)$ has at most $q(|x|)$ entries for every instance
$x$. Every window $(w, j)$ in $W(x)$ has $|w| \le k$ and $j < N$. A bitstring $s$ is a feasible
solution for $x$ exactly when $|s| \le b(|x|)$. For every feasible solution $s$ for $x$, the
value $v(x, s)$ is the number of entries $(w, j)$ of the list $W(x)$, counted with
multiplicity, for which $\mathrm{acc}(j, (s_{w_1}, \dots, s_{w_m}))$ is true, where $s_i$ is
the bit of $s$ at position $i$ (counting from $0$), read as false when $i \ge |s|$.

The windows depend only on the instance, never on the candidate solution: only the fixed
predicate $\mathrm{acc}$ inspects bits of the solution. The counting equation is required only
for feasible solutions, because padding a solution with false bits preserves the window count
while sufficiently long paddings are infeasible.

articles.title: NPO problems
articles.statement:
An NPO (NP optimization) problem consists of a rational-valued value
function $v$, a Boolean feasibility predicate $F$ and an objective encoding $e$, each taking an
instance $x$ and a solution $s$ (both bitstrings), together with a polynomial $b$ with
natural-number coefficients, such that the following hold. $F$ and $e$ are polynomial-time
computable. For all $x$ and $s$, $e(x, s)$ is a triple $(\sigma, p, q)$ of a Boolean $\sigma$
and natural numbers $p$ and $q$ with $q \ne 0$; if $s$ is feasible for $x$ (that is,
$F(x, s)$ is true), then $v(x, s) = -p/q$ when $\sigma$ is true and $v(x, s) = p/q$ when
$\sigma$ is false, and otherwise $v(x, s) = 0$; and $v(x, s) \ge 0$. Every feasible solution
$s$ for $x$ has $|s| \le b(|x|)$, and every instance $x$ has a feasible solution.

Feasible solutions on every instance are needed for completeness: an L-reduction to a problem
with no feasible solutions on some instance would have to map a feasible target output back to
a feasible source solution that does not exist.

articles.title: Optimum of an NPO problem
articles.statement:
The optimum of an NPO problem $M$, with value function $v$ and
solution length bound $b$, on an instance $x$ is the maximum of $v(x, s)$ over all bitstrings $s$
with $|s| \le b(|x|)$.

Since every feasible solution has length at most $b(|x|)$, every instance has a feasible
solution, and $v$ is nonnegative and equals $0$ on infeasible solutions, this is the maximum of
$v(x, s)$ over the feasible solutions $s$ for $x$.

articles.title: Alphabet reduction with given constants
articles.statement:
Let $S_0, e, d', V$ be natural numbers and
$c', \alpha'$ rationals. A map $T$ from 2CSP instances to 2CSP instances is an alphabet reduction
with constants $S_0, e, c', \alpha', d', V$ when $S_0 \ge 2$, $e \ge 2$, $0 < c' \le 1$,
$0 < \alpha' < 1$, $d' \ge 1$, $V \ge 1$, and for every 2CSP instance $I$ with $n$ variables,
alphabet size at most $S_0^e$ and $m$ constraints: $T(I)$ has at most $V(n + 1)$ variables,
alphabet size at most $S_0$ and at most $d' m$ constraints; if $I$ is well-formed then so is
$T(I)$; if some assignment gives $I$ value $1$ then some assignment gives $T(I)$ value $1$; and
for every rational $\delta$ with $0 < \delta \le 1$, if every assignment gives $I$ value at most
$1 - \delta$, then every assignment gives $T(I)$ value at most $1 - \min(\alpha', c'\delta)$.

The bounds $S_0 \ge 2$ and $e \ge 2$ give $S_0^e > S_0$, so the reduction must genuinely shrink
the alphabet.

articles.title: Satisfied constraint of a 2CSP instance
articles.statement:
Let $I = (n, \Sigma, C)$ be a 2CSP instance and
$\sigma$ an assignment of a label less than $\Sigma$ to each variable less than $n$. A constraint
$(u, v, P)$ is satisfied by $\sigma$ when $u < n$, $v < n$ and the pair $(\sigma(u), \sigma(v))$
belongs to $P$.

articles.title: Degree of a variable in a 2CSP instance
articles.statement:
For a 2CSP instance $(n, \Sigma, C)$ and a
natural number $v$, the degree of $v$ is the number of entries $(u, w, P)$ of the list $C$ with
$u = v$ or $w = v$.

articles.title: Value of a 2CSP instance under an assignment
articles.statement:
Let $I = (n, \Sigma, C)$ be a 2CSP
instance and $\sigma$ an assignment of a label less than $\Sigma$ to each variable less than $n$.
The value of $I$ under $\sigma$ is the rational number $1$ if $C$ is empty, and otherwise the
number of entries of the list $C$ that are constraints satisfied by $\sigma$, divided by the
length of $C$.

articles.title: 2CSP instances
articles.statement:
A 2CSP instance is a triple $(n, \Sigma, C)$ of a natural number $n$ (the
number of variables), a natural number $\Sigma$ (the alphabet size) and a finite list $C$ of
constraints, where each constraint is a triple $(u, v, P)$ of natural numbers $u$ and $v$ (the
variables it mentions) and a finite list $P$ of pairs of natural numbers (the allowed label
pairs).

articles.title: Well-formed 2CSP instances
articles.statement:
A 2CSP instance $(n, \Sigma, C)$ is well-formed when every
constraint $(u, v, P)$ in $C$ satisfies $u < n$ and $v < n$, and every allowed pair $(a, b)$ in
$P$ satisfies $a < \Sigma$ and $b < \Sigma$.

articles.title: Dinur's gap amplification and alphabet reduction
articles.statement:
There exist natural numbers
$S_0, e, d, D, d', V$ and rationals $c, \alpha, c', \alpha'$ with $S_0 \ge 2$, $e \ge 2$, $c > 1$,
$0 < \alpha < 1$, $d \ge 1$, $D \ge 1$, $0 < c' \le 1$, $0 < \alpha' < 1$, $d' \ge 1$ and $V \ge 1$,
and maps $A$ and $R$ from 2CSP instances to 2CSP instances, with the following properties.
Both maps are polynomial-time computable: for each $T \in \{A, R\}$ there is a polynomial-time
computable function $f$ from lists of booleans to lists of booleans such that, for every 2CSP
instance $I$, decoding $f$ applied to the bitstring encoding of $I$ succeeds and returns $T(I)$.
The map $A$ is a gap amplification with constants $c, \alpha, d, D, e$, and $R$ is an alphabet
reduction with constants $S_0, e, c', \alpha', d', V$. Finally, for every 2CSP instance $I$ with
alphabet size at most $S_0$, the instance $J = R(A(I))$ has alphabet size at most $S_0$; if $I$
is well-formed then so is $J$; if some assignment gives $I$ value $1$ then some assignment gives
$J$ value $1$; and for every rational $\delta$ with $0 < \delta \le 1$, if every assignment gives
$I$ value at most $1 - \delta$, then every assignment gives $J$ value at most
$1 - \min(\alpha', c' \min(\alpha, c\delta))$.

The constants $c$ and $c'$ are not tied together: the statement does not assert $c' c > 1$, so
the composed map $R \circ A$ need not enlarge the gap.

## Sources

- I. Dinur, "The PCP theorem by gap amplification", Journal of the ACM 54 (2007), 12:1-12:44 (Proceedings of the Thirty-Eighth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing, STOC 2006, 241-250).

articles.title: Gap amplification with given constants
articles.statement:
Let $c, \alpha$ be rationals and $d, D, e$ natural
numbers. A map $T$ from 2CSP instances to 2CSP instances is a gap amplification with constants
$c, \alpha, d, D, e$ when $c > 1$, $0 < \alpha < 1$, $d \ge 1$, $D \ge 1$, and for every 2CSP
instance $I$ with $n$ variables, alphabet size $\Sigma$ and $m$ constraints: $T(I)$ has exactly $n$
variables, alphabet size at most $\Sigma^e$ and at most $d m$ constraints; if $I$ is well-formed
then so is $T(I)$; for every natural number $v$, if $v$ has degree $k$ in $I$, then $v$ has degree
at most $D(k + 1)$ in $T(I)$; if some assignment gives $I$ value $1$ then some assignment
gives $T(I)$ value $1$; and for every rational $\delta$ with $0 < \delta \le 1$, if every assignment
gives $I$ value at most $1 - \delta$, then every assignment gives $T(I)$ value at most
$1 - \min(\alpha, c\delta)$.

articles.title: Feasible MAX-CUT solutions
articles.statement:
A bitstring $s$ is a feasible solution of a MAX-CUT instance
$x$ exactly when the length of $s$ equals the vertex count $\lfloor \sqrt{|x|} \rfloor$ of $x$,
so that $s$ has one bit per vertex.

## Sources

- C. H. Papadimitriou and M. Yannakakis, "Optimization, approximation, and complexity classes", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 43 (1991), 425-440.

articles.title: Vertex count of a MAX-CUT instance
articles.statement:
The vertex count of a MAX-CUT instance, a bitstring
$x$ of length $|x|$, is $\lfloor \sqrt{|x|} \rfloor$.

## Sources

- C. H. Papadimitriou and M. Yannakakis, "Optimization, approximation, and complexity classes", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 43 (1991), 425-440.

articles.title: MAX-CUT has no PTAS unless P = NP
articles.statement:
If $\mathsf{P} \neq \mathsf{NP}$, then the
optimization problem MAX-CUT does not admit a polynomial-time approximation scheme.

## Sources

- C. H. Papadimitriou and M. Yannakakis, "Optimization, approximation, and complexity classes", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 43 (1991), 425-440 (MAX-CUT is MAXSNP-complete, hence APX-hard); S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Chapter 11 (APX-hardness rules out a PTAS unless P = NP).

articles.title: Value of a MAX-CUT solution
articles.statement:
Let $x$ be a MAX-CUT instance with vertex count
$n = \lfloor \sqrt{|x|} \rfloor$ and let $s$ be a bitstring, with bits indexed from $0$. If $s$
is a feasible solution of $x$ (its length is $n$), the value of $s$ is the number, as a rational
number, of pairs $(i, j)$ with $i < j < n$ such that bit $i n + j$ of $x$ is true and bits $i$
and $j$ of $s$ differ; otherwise the value is $0$.

## Sources

- C. H. Papadimitriou and M. Yannakakis, "Optimization, approximation, and complexity classes", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 43 (1991), 425-440.

articles.title: MAX-CUT as an optimization problem
articles.statement:
MAX-CUT is the optimization problem whose instances
are bitstrings $x$, read as an adjacency matrix on $n = \lfloor \sqrt{|x|} \rfloor$ vertices in
which, for $i < j < n$, bit $i n + j$ of $x$ (bits indexed from $0$) says whether $\{i, j\}$ is
an edge. Its feasible solutions for $x$ are the bitstrings of length $n$, one bit per vertex;
the value of a feasible solution $s$ is the number of pairs $i < j < n$ that are edges and
whose bits in $s$ differ, the value of an infeasible solution is $0$, and the polynomial bound
on the length of feasible solutions is $p(m) = m$.

## Sources

- C. H. Papadimitriou and M. Yannakakis, "Optimization, approximation, and complexity classes", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 43 (1991), 425-440.

articles.title: The PCP theorem: NP = PCP(O(log n), O(1))
articles.statement:
A decision problem belongs to NP if and only
if, for some natural numbers $c$ and $q$, it belongs to $\mathrm{PCP}(r, s)$, where the
randomness bound is $r(n) = c \lfloor \log_2(n + 1) \rfloor$ and the query bound is the constant
function $s(n) = q$.

## Sources

- S. Arora, C. Lund, R. Motwani, M. Sudan, and M. Szegedy, "Proof verification and the hardness of approximation problems", Journal of the ACM 45 (1998), 501-555 (FOCS 1992); S. Arora and S. Safra, "Probabilistic checking of proofs: a new characterization of NP", Journal of the ACM 45 (1998), 70-122.

articles.title: 2-SAT as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The 2-SAT decision problem accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly
when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a pair $(n, \varphi)$ of a natural
number $n$ and a CNF formula $\varphi$ such that every clause of $\varphi$ has at most two
literals, every variable occurring in $\varphi$ is less than $n$, and there is a list
$(a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ of booleans such that $\varphi$ is satisfied by the assignment that
sends each variable $v < n$ to $a_v$ and every other variable to false.

articles.title: 2-SAT is in P
articles.statement:
The 2-SAT decision problem lies in the complexity class P.

## Sources

- M. Davis, G. Logemann, and D. Loveland, "A machine program for theorem-proving", Communications of the ACM 5 (1962), 394-397; B. Aspvall, M. F. Plass, and R. E. Tarjan, "A linear-time algorithm for testing the truth of certain quantified Boolean formulas", Information Processing Letters 8 (1979), 121-123.

articles.title: The primality decision problem
articles.statement:
The primality decision problem is the decision problem
that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when decoding $x$ with the canonical bitstring encoding of
the natural numbers (Mathlib's binary encoding) yields a prime number, and rejects $x$ otherwise.

articles.title: PRIMES is in P
articles.statement:
The primality decision problem, which accepts a bitstring exactly when it
decodes to a prime number under the canonical bitstring encoding of the natural numbers, belongs
to the complexity class P.

## Sources

- M. Agrawal, N. Kayal, and N. Saxena, "PRIMES is in P", Annals of Mathematics 160 (2004), 781-793.

articles.title: Out-of-range arcs need no guard
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a list of $n$ Boolean marks and let $u$, $v$
be natural numbers; write $m_u$ for the entry of $m$ at position $u$ (counting from $0$), taken to
be false when $u \ge n$. If $u < n$, $v < n$ and $m_u$ is true, set position $v$ of $m$ to true,
and otherwise keep $m$; the result is the same as setting position $v$ of $m$ to true when $m_u$ is
true and keeping $m$ otherwise.

Setting a position $v \ge n$ leaves the list unchanged, so the machine, which reads the mark of $u$
and then sets the mark of $v$, ignores an arc with an end past the last vertex, as the marking
algorithm does.

articles.title: Arcs of the PATH digraph
Reading the mark of vertex $j$
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a list of Boolean marks and $j$ a natural
number. Drop the first $j$ marks of $m$ and write the rest as bit symbols; reading the top symbol
as a bit, with false when there is no top symbol, gives the entry of $m$ at position $j$ (counting
from $0$), or false when $j$ is at least the length of $m$.

articles.title: Counting true entries of pointwise dominated boolean lists
articles.statement:
Let $l_1$ and $l_2$ be lists
of booleans of the same length such that every position holding $\mathrm{true}$ in $l_1$ also
holds $\mathrm{true}$ in $l_2$. Then $l_1$ has at most as many $\mathrm{true}$ entries as $l_2$,
and strictly fewer if $l_1 \ne l_2$.

articles.title: Decoding inverts the PATH instance encoding
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $s, t, n$ and a list $E$
of pairs of natural numbers, the PATH instance parser applied to the PATH instance encoding of
$(s, t, n, E)$ succeeds and returns $(s, t, n, E)$.

articles.title: The PATH instance parser succeeds exactly on encodings
articles.statement:
For a bit string $x$, natural
numbers $s, t, n$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the PATH instance parser applied to
$x$ succeeds with result $(s, t, n, E)$ if and only if $x$ is the PATH instance encoding of
$(s, t, n, E)$.

articles.title: Decoding a PATH instance
articles.statement:
Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, a bit string $x$ is parsed
by reading a unary number $s$ (a run of ones ended by a zero), then a unary number $t$ from the
rest, then a graph from what remains: a unary number $n$ followed by pairs $(u, v)$ of unary
numbers until the input ends. The result is $(s, t, n, E)$, with $E$ the list of these pairs in
order; there is no result unless the input ends right after $n$ or right after a complete pair.

articles.title: The edge loop of a pass
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, $es$ a list of arcs $(u, w)$ of
natural numbers and $m$ a list of $n$ Boolean marks. Encode an arc $(u, w)$ by $u$ ones, a zero,
$w$ ones and a zero, and $es$ by the concatenation of the codes of its arcs; let $\ell$ be the
length of this code. Suppose the marking machine is at the edge-loop label, in any internal state,
with stacks $S$ such that the input stack $X$ holds the code of $es$ and the mark stack $M$ holds
$m$ (vertex $0$ on top), as bit symbols, and the parked-mark stack $P$ and the arc counters $U$
and $V$ are empty. Then within $4\ell + 1$ steps it reaches the pass-loop label with stacks $S'$
in which $X$ is empty, the edge stack $E$ holds the code of $es$ in reverse order on top of its
contents in $S$, $M$ holds the marks that one pass of the marking algorithm with $n$ vertices over
$es$ (Mark Pass) produces from $m$, and $P$, $U$, $V$ are empty; every stack other than $X$, $E$,
$M$, $U$, $V$ and $P$ holds the same list in $S'$ as in $S$.

articles.title: The PATH instance encoding is injective
articles.statement:
Let $s, t, n, s', t', n'$ be natural numbers and
$E, E'$ lists of pairs of natural numbers. If the PATH instance encodings of $(s, t, n, E)$ and
$(s', t', n', E')$ are equal, then $s = s'$, $t = t'$, $n = n'$ and $E = E'$.

articles.title: Encoding of a PATH instance
articles.statement:
Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the instance with
source $s$, target $t$ and the digraph given by $n$ and the edge list $E$ is encoded as $s$ ones,
a zero, $t$ ones, a zero, then $n$ ones and a zero, followed, for each pair $(u, v)$ of $E$ in
order, by $u$ ones, a zero, $v$ ones and a zero.

articles.title: The frame of a read
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a stack of the marking machine, $ps$ a list of pairs of a
stack and a symbol, $i$ a natural number, and $S$, $S'$ two contents of the stacks. Suppose every
stack $q$ other than the input $X$ and $d$ holds in $S'$ the list it holds in $S$ with $i$ further
copies of the symbol of the first entry for $q$ in $ps$ pushed on top (and unchanged if $ps$ has
no entry for $q$). Then $S'$ agrees with $S$ on every stack other than $X$, $d$ and the stacks
that have an entry in $ps$.

articles.title: Agreement off a set of stacks
articles.statement:
For a list $A$ of stacks of the marking machine and two
contents $S$, $S'$ of its stacks, $S'$ agrees with $S$ off $A$ when every stack not in $A$ holds
the same list in $S'$ as in $S$.

articles.title: A cleared mark or nothing reads as cleared
articles.statement:
For every decidable proposition $p$, the
optional mark that is a cleared mark (false) when $p$ holds and absent otherwise, read with
default false, is false.

articles.title: Setting an entry of a boolean list to true
articles.statement:
Let $m$ be a list of booleans and $v, w$
natural numbers, and read a position at or beyond the end of a list as $\mathrm{false}$. Set
the entry of $m$ at position $w$ to $\mathrm{true}$, leaving $m$ unchanged if $w$ is not less
than the length of $m$. Then position $v$ of the result holds $\mathrm{true}$ if and only if
position $v$ of $m$ holds $\mathrm{true}$, or $v = w$ and $w$ is less than the length of $m$.

articles.title: The initial marks mark exactly the source, if it is a vertex
articles.statement:
Let $n, s, v$ be natural
numbers, and read a position at or beyond the end of a list as $\mathrm{false}$. Position $v$ of
the initial marks for $n$ vertices and source $s$ holds $\mathrm{true}$ if and only if $v < n$
and $v = s$.

articles.title: Initial marks
articles.statement:
For $n, s \in \mathbb{N}$, the initial marks are the list of $n$ booleans
whose entry at position $i < n$ is true exactly when $i = s$; all entries are false when
$s \ge n$.

articles.title: The marking algorithm is polynomial-time
articles.statement:
The marking algorithm for PATH, as a function
from bit strings to booleans, is computable in polynomial time by a Turing machine with respect
to the canonical bitstring encodings of lists of booleans and of booleans.

articles.title: Marks survive repeated passes
articles.statement:
Let $n$ and $v$ be natural numbers, $E$ a list of pairs of
natural numbers and $m$ a list of booleans whose position $v$ holds $\mathrm{true}$ (positions at
or beyond the end read as $\mathrm{false}$). Then for every natural number $k$, position $v$
still holds $\mathrm{true}$ after $k$ marking passes over $E$ for $n$ vertices, starting from
$m$.

articles.title: Stacks of the PATH marking machine
articles.statement:
The PATH marking machine, run on an instance with
source $s$, target $t$ and $n$ vertices, has eleven stacks: the input stack $X$, the output stack
$O$, the stack $E$ of the edge bits (reversed between passes), the junk stack $J$, the counters
$S$, $T$ and $N$ for $s$, $t$ and $n$ ($N$ counts the passes left), the counters $U$ and $V$ for
the endpoints $u$ and $v$ of an arc, the mark stack $M$ (with the mark of vertex $0$ on top) and
the stack $P$ of parked marks.

articles.title: Labels of the PATH marking machine
articles.statement:
For an instance with source $s$, target $t$, $n$
vertices and arcs $(u, v)$, the labels of the PATH marking machine are $\mathsf{rdS}$,
$\mathsf{rdT}$ and $\mathsf{rdN}$ (read $s$, $t$ and $n$); $\mathsf{val0}$, $\mathsf{valU}$ and
$\mathsf{valV}$ (validate the edge list: at a pair, inside $u$, inside $v$); $\mathsf{goS}$ and
$\mathsf{backS}$ (walk to $s$ and set its mark, then restore); $\mathsf{pass}$ (the pass loop),
$\mathsf{ld}$ (reload the edges) and $\mathsf{edge}$ (the edge loop); $\mathsf{rdU}$ and
$\mathsf{rdV}$ (read $u$ and $v$); $\mathsf{go1}$ and, for each bit $b$, $\mathsf{back1}(b)$
(walk to $u$, then restore holding its mark $b$); $\mathsf{go2}$ and $\mathsf{back2}$ (walk to
$v$ and set its mark, then restore); $\mathsf{drV}$ (drain the counter stack $V$);
$\mathsf{goT}$ (walk to $t$ and answer); $\mathsf{bad}$ (answer false); and $\mathsf{done}$
(halt).

articles.title: Repeated marking passes preserve the length
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, $E$ a list of
pairs of natural numbers and $m$ a list of booleans. For every natural number $k$, applying $k$
marking passes over $E$ for $n$ vertices to $m$ gives a list of the same length as $m$.

articles.title: A marking pass preserves the length
articles.statement:
Let $n$ be a natural number, $E$ a list of pairs of
natural numbers and $m$ a list of booleans. A marking pass over $E$ for $n$ vertices, applied to
$m$, gives a list of the same length as $m$.

articles.title: The final marks have one entry per vertex
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n, s$ and a list $E$ of
pairs of natural numbers, the marks after $n$ marking passes over $E$ for $n$ vertices, starting
from the initial marks for source $s$, form a list of length $n$.

articles.title: A pass marks the heads of arcs with marked tails
articles.statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $E$ be a
list of pairs of natural numbers and let $m$ be a list of booleans, where $m$ marks $w$ when
$w < |m|$ and the $w$-th entry of $m$ (counting from $0$) is true. If $(u, v) \in E$ with $u < n$
and $v < n$, $v < |m|$ and $m$ marks $u$, then the result of the marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$
on $m$ marks $v$.

articles.title: A pass either changes nothing or adds a mark
articles.statement:
For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $E$
of pairs of natural numbers and every list $m$ of booleans, let $m'$ be the result of the marking
pass of $E$ with bound $n$ on $m$. Then $m' = m$, or $m'$ has strictly more entries equal to true
than $m$.

articles.title: Marks persist through a pass
articles.statement:
Let $n, v \in \mathbb{N}$, let $E$ be a list of pairs of
natural numbers and let $m$ be a list of booleans. If $v < |m|$ and the $v$-th entry of $m$
(counting from $0$) is true, then the same holds for the result of the marking pass of $E$ with
bound $n$ on $m$.

articles.title: Repeated passes reach a fixpoint
articles.statement:
Let $n, s \in \mathbb{N}$ with $s < n$ and let $E$ be a
list of pairs of natural numbers. Let $r$ be the list obtained from the initial marks (only $s$
marked among $0, \dots, n - 1$) by $n$ marking passes of $E$ with bound $n$. Then one more
marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ leaves $r$ unchanged.

Each pass that changes the marks adds at least one mark, the initial marks contain one mark, and
there are at most $n$ marks.

articles.title: A pass sets no mark when none is set
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$ and every list
$es$ of arcs of natural numbers, one pass of the marking algorithm with $n$ vertices over $es$
(Mark Pass) maps the list of $k$ cleared marks to itself.

articles.title: Soundness of a pass
articles.statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $P$ be a property of natural numbers and
let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers such that $P(u)$ implies $P(v)$ whenever
$(u, v) \in E$, $u < n$ and $v < n$. If $m$ is a list of booleans such that $P(v)$ holds for every
$v < |m|$ whose entry in $m$ is true, then $P(v)$ holds for every $v$ whose entry is true in the
result of the marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ on $m$.

articles.title: One marking pass
articles.statement:
Given $n \in \mathbb{N}$, an edge list $E$ and a list $m$ of booleans
(the marks), the pass scans the pairs $(u, v)$ of $E$ in order and, whenever $u < n$, $v < n$
and position $u$ of the current marks is true, sets position $v$ to true. A position beyond the
end of the list counts as false and setting it changes nothing. Marks set earlier in the pass
are seen by later pairs.

articles.title: The counter unit of the PATH marking machine
articles.statement:
The unit symbol of the counters of the PATH
marking machine is the clause-end symbol $\mathrm{cl}$ of the SAT verifier's symbol alphabet.

articles.title: The pass loop of the marking machine
articles.statement:
Let $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$, let $es$ be a list of
pairs of natural numbers with edge bits $b$, and let $m$ be a list of $n$ marks. Start the marking
machine at the label `pass`, with any flag, from stacks on which $N$ holds $k$ counter units, $X$,
$P$, $U$ and $V$ are empty, $E$ holds the reverse of $b$ and $M$ holds $m$, both as bit symbols.
Then within $k(5|b| + 3) + 1$ steps the machine reaches the label `goT`, with $M$ holding
$p^k(m)$ as bit symbols, where $p$ is one marking pass over $es$ on $n$ vertices, with $P$ empty,
and with every stack other than $N$, $X$, $E$, $M$, $U$, $V$ and $P$ unchanged.

articles.title: The marking algorithm reads the mark of the target
articles.statement:
If a bit string $x$ parses as a PATH
instance with source $s$, target $t$, $n$ vertices and edge list $es$, then the marking algorithm
on $x$ returns the mark of $t$ in the reach marks of $s$ (the marks after $n$ marking passes over
$es$, starting from the marks on $0, \dots, n - 1$ with only $s$ marked, and none if $s \ge n$),
where a vertex $t \ge n$ counts as unmarked.

So the checks $s < n$ and $t < n$ of the marking algorithm are implied: a vertex $t \ge n$ has no
mark, and for $s \ge n$ every mark stays cleared.

articles.title: The marking algorithm for PATH
articles.statement:
On a bit string $x$, the check decodes $x$ as a PATH
instance. If decoding fails it returns false; if it yields $(s, t, n, E)$ it returns true exactly
when $s < n$, $t < n$ and position $t$ of the marks after $n$ marking passes from $s$ over $E$
is true.

articles.title: The marking machine as a host component
articles.statement:
The component machine whose stack indices,
stack alphabets, labels and program are those of the marking machine, with its eleven stacks
listed once each, in the order: input, output, edge bits, junk, the counters for the source, the
target and the number of vertices, the counters for the two ends of an arc, the marks and the
parked marks.

articles.title: The marking algorithm decides PATH
articles.statement:
For every bit string $x$, the marking algorithm
returns the same answer on $x$ as the decision problem PATH.

articles.title: PATH ∈ P
articles.statement:
**PATH ∈ P** (Sipser, Theorem 7.14). The decision problem PATH belongs to the class P of
decision problems decidable in polynomial time. Here PATH accepts a bit string exactly when it
encodes natural numbers $s$, $t$, $n$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers such that
$s < n$, $t < n$ and $t$ is reachable from $s$ in zero or more steps along the arcs of $E$ below
$n$, the pairs $(u, v) \in E$ with $u < n$ and $v < n$.

articles.title: The PATH problem
articles.statement:
PATH is the decision problem that accepts a bit string $x$ exactly when
$x$ is the encoding of some instance $(s, t, n, E)$ with $s < n$, $t < n$ and a sequence
$s = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k = t$ with $k \ge 0$ such that each $(v_i, v_{i+1})$ is an arc, that is,
a pair listed in $E$ with both ends below $n$.

articles.title: The marking machine for PATH
articles.statement:
The multi-stack machine program whose input lies on the
stack $X$ and whose answer is pushed on the Boolean stack $O$. To read a unary number off $X$ onto
a stack $d$, it pops a bit off $X$ and pushes it on $d$, repeating while the bit is true and
moving on after the first false bit; an empty $X$ jumps to `bad`. To walk along a counter $c$, it
pops units off $c$ one at a time, each time moving the top mark of $M$ (if there is one) onto $P$,
until $c$ is empty. To restore, it moves the bits on top of $P$ back onto $M$ one at a time.

At `rdS`, `rdT` and `rdN` it reads $s$, $t$ and $n$ in turn off $X$ onto $J$, pushing a counter
unit on $S$, $T$ or $N$ respectively for each true bit, and at `rdN` also a cleared mark on $M$;
then it goes to `val0`. At `val0` it goes to `goS` if $X$ is empty, and otherwise reads two unary
numbers off $X$ onto $E$ (at `valU` and `valV`) and returns to `val0`. At `goS` it walks along $S$
and then sets the top mark of $M$ (if any); at `backS` it restores and goes to `pass`. At `pass`
it pops a unit off $N$ and goes to `ld`, or to `goT` if $N$ is empty. At `ld` it moves the bits on
top of $E$ onto $X$, then goes to `edge`. At `edge` it goes to `pass` if $X$ is empty, and
otherwise reads $u$ and $v$ off $X$ onto $E$ (at `rdU` and `rdV`), pushing a counter unit on $U$,
respectively $V$, for each true bit, and then goes to `go1`. At `go1` it walks along $U$ and reads
the top mark $b$ of $M$ (false if there is none); at `back1 b` it restores and goes to `go2` if $b$
is true and to `drV` otherwise. At `go2` it walks along $V$ and sets the top mark of $M$ (if any);
at `back2` it restores and goes to `edge`. At `drV` it empties $V$ and goes to `edge`. At `goT` it
walks along $T$, pushes the top mark of $M$ (false if there is none) on $O$ and goes to `done`. At
`bad` it pushes false on $O$ and goes to `done`. At `done` it halts.

articles.title: The final marks are exactly the reachable vertices
articles.statement:
Let $n, s, t \in \mathbb{N}$ with
$s < n$ and $t < n$, and let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers. Start from the marks on
$0, \dots, n - 1$ in which only $s$ is marked and apply $n$ marking passes of $E$ with bound $n$.
Then $t$ is marked if and only if $t$ is reachable from $s$ in zero or more steps along the arcs
of $E$ below $n$, the pairs $(u, v) \in E$ with $u < n$ and $v < n$.

articles.title: Reach marks
articles.statement:
For $n, s \in \mathbb{N}$ and an edge list $E$, the reach marks are obtained
from the initial marks of $s$ among $0, \dots, n - 1$ by applying the marking pass over $E$ with
bound $n$ exactly $n$ times.

articles.title: Reading a cut-off unary number
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a stack other than $X$ and $O$, let $g$ encode
bits as symbols of $d$, and let $ps$ be a list of stack–symbol pairs whose stacks are distinct and
differ from $X$ and $O$. Suppose the instruction of the marking machine at a label $\ell$ is the
unary read off $X$ onto $d$ through $g$ that pushes $ps$ for each true bit, repeats at $\ell$ and
continues at $\ell'$. If a bit list $l$ has no unary length prefix (every bit of $l$ is true) and
$X$ holds $l$ as bit symbols, then from $\ell$, with any flag, the machine reaches the label `bad`
within $|l| + 1$ steps, leaving the output stack $O$ unchanged.

articles.title: Reading a unary number
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a stack other than $X$, let $g$ encode bits as symbols
of $d$, and let $ps$ be a list of stack–symbol pairs whose stacks are distinct and differ from $X$
and $d$. Suppose the instruction of the marking machine at a label $\ell$ is the unary read off
$X$ onto $d$ through $g$ that pushes $ps$ for each true bit, repeats at $\ell$ and continues at
$\ell'$. If $X$ holds, as bit symbols, $k$ true bits, then a false bit, then a bit list $r$, then
in exactly $k + 1$ steps the machine goes from $\ell$, with any flag, to $\ell'$; afterwards $X$
holds $r$, $d$ has received $k$ copies of $g(\mathrm{true})$ and then $g(\mathrm{false})$ on top,
each stack $q$ with a pair $(q, a)$ in $ps$ has received $k$ copies of $a$ on top, and every
other stack is unchanged.

articles.title: The unary read instruction
articles.statement:
Given a stack $d$, an encoding $g$ of bits as symbols of $d$,
a list $ps$ of stack–symbol pairs and labels $\ell$ and $\ell'$, the instruction of the marking
machine that jumps to `bad` if $X$ is empty, and otherwise pops the top of $X$ as a bit $b$ (a
symbol that is not a bit counts as false) and pushes $g(b)$ on $d$; then, if $b$ is true, it
pushes $a$ on $q$ for each pair $(q, a)$ of $ps$, in order, and jumps to $\ell$, and if $b$ is
false it jumps to $\ell'$. Run at its own label $\ell$, it reads a unary number off $X$.

articles.title: Reading the mark of a vertex
articles.statement:
Let $u \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $m$ be a list of marks.
Start the marking machine at the label `go1`, with any flag, from stacks on which $U$ holds $u$
counter units, $M$ holds $m$ as bit symbols and $P$ is empty. Then within $2u + 2$ steps it
reaches `go2` if the mark of vertex $u$ in $m$ is set and `drV` otherwise (a vertex past the end
of $m$ counts as unmarked), with $U$ and $P$ empty, $M$ holding $m$ again, and every other
stack unchanged.

articles.title: Frames are reflexive
articles.statement:
For every list $A$ of stacks of the marking machine and every
assignment $S$ of contents to its stacks, $S$ agrees with itself off $A$.

articles.title: Restoring the parked marks
articles.statement:
Suppose the instruction of the marking machine at a label
$\ell$ moves the bits on top of $P$ onto $M$ one at a time, repeating at $\ell$ and continuing at
$\ell'$ once $P$ is empty or its top is not a bit. If $P$ holds the reverse of a bit list $p$ and
$M$ holds a bit list $q$, both as bit symbols, then in exactly $|p| + 1$ steps the machine goes
from $\ell$, with any flag, to $\ell'$, leaving $P$ empty, $M$ holding $p$ followed by $q$, and
every other stack unchanged.

articles.title: Running time and output of the marking machine
articles.statement:
For every bit string $x$, the marking
machine started at its start label, with any flag, with $x$ on the input stack $X$ as bit symbols
and every other stack empty, reaches the label `done` within $8(|x| + 1)^4$ steps, with the
output stack $O$ holding exactly one entry: the answer of the marking algorithm on $x$.

articles.title: Setting the first mark
articles.statement:
For a list of booleans, the list obtained by setting its first
entry: the empty list is left unchanged, and a list $b :: r$ with first entry $b$ and remaining
entries $r$ becomes $\mathrm{true} :: r$.

articles.title: Initial marks by setting one entry
articles.statement:
For all natural numbers $n$ and $s$, setting entry $s$
of the list of $n$ copies of false to true (which changes nothing when $s \ge n$) gives the
initial marks of $n$ vertices from $s$: the list of length $n$ whose entry $i$ is true exactly
when $i = s$.

articles.title: Mark-setting step
articles.statement:
For a label $\ell$, the statement of the marking machine that pops the
top cell of the mark stack $M$ and, if there was one, pushes the set mark (the bit true) onto $M$
in its place; in either case it then goes to $\ell$.

articles.title: Walking to a vertex and setting its mark
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a stack other than the mark stack $M$
and the parking stack $P$, and let $\mathit{self}$, $\mathit{back}$, $\mathit{next}$ be labels
such that the marking machine at $\mathit{self}$ is the walk step counted by $c$ that loops at
$\mathit{self}$ and finishes with the mark-setting step to $\mathit{back}$, and at
$\mathit{back}$ it moves the bit block of $P$ onto $M$, looping at $\mathit{back}$ and then
going to $\mathit{next}$. Let $S$ be stacks in which $c$ holds the counter value $j$ (for some
unit symbol), $M$ holds the bits of a list $m$ of booleans, and $P$ is empty. Then from label
$\mathit{self}$ with stacks $S$ and any internal state, the machine reaches label
$\mathit{next}$ in at most $2j + 2$ steps, with some internal state and stacks $S'$ such that
$c$ and $P$ are empty, $M$ holds the bits of $m$ with entry $j$ set to true (unchanged when
$j \ge |m|$), and $S'$ agrees with $S$ on every stack other than $c$, $M$ and $P$.

articles.title: Start label of the PATH marking machine
articles.statement:
The marking machine for PATH starts at the label
that reads the source vertex $s$, in unary, off the input.

articles.title: Effect of the mark-setting step
articles.statement:
Let $\ell$ be a label, $v$ an internal state and $S$
stacks whose mark stack $M$ holds the bits of a list $l$ of booleans. Executing the mark-setting
step to $\ell$ from internal state $v$ and stacks $S$ ends at label $\ell$ with some internal
state and the stacks $S$ with $M$ replaced by the bits of $l$ with its first entry set to true
(the empty list stays empty); every other stack is unchanged.

articles.title: A walk step with an exhausted counter
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a stack, $\mathit{self}$ a label,
$\mathit{fin}$ a statement and $S$ stacks in which $c$ is empty. For every internal state $v$,
executing from $v$ and $S$ the walk step counted by $c$ that loops at $\mathit{self}$ and
finishes with $\mathit{fin}$ gives the same result as executing $\mathit{fin}$ from internal
state false and the same stacks $S$.

articles.title: Statements of the PATH marking machine
articles.statement:
The statements of the multi-stack Turing machine
(TM2) model whose stacks carry the stack alphabets $\Gamma$ of the marking machine, whose labels
are the labels of the marking machine, and whose internal state is a boolean.

articles.title: Setting an entry by splitting the list
articles.statement:
For every list $m$ of booleans and every natural
number $j$, the first $j$ entries of $m$ followed by the remaining entries with their first entry
set to true (the empty list stays empty) equal $m$ with entry $j$ set to true (which is $m$
itself when $j \ge |m|$).

articles.title: Frames compose
articles.statement:
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be lists of stacks such that every stack in $A$ or in
$B$ is in $C$. If stacks $S_2$ agree with $S_1$ on every stack outside $A$, and $S_3$ agree with
$S_2$ on every stack outside $B$, then $S_3$ agree with $S_1$ on every stack outside $C$.

articles.title: Stack alphabets of the PATH marking machine
articles.statement:
The output stack $O$ of the PATH marking
machine holds Booleans, and every other stack holds symbols of the SAT verifier's symbol
alphabet.

articles.title: Updating a framed stack preserves the frame
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a list of stacks of the PATH
marking machine, and let $S$ and $S'$ be stack contents such that $S'$ agrees with $S$ on every
stack outside $A$. Then for every stack $k \in A$ and every list $l$ over the alphabet of $k$,
the contents obtained from $S'$ by replacing stack $k$ with $l$ still agree with $S$ on every
stack outside $A$.

articles.title: Validation phase of the PATH marking machine
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be a list of bits, $v$ a Boolean
and $S$ stack contents whose input stack $X$ holds $w$ as bit symbols. Then there are a Boolean
$v'$ and stack contents $S'$ such that, in at most $2|w| + 1$ steps, the machine goes from the
validation label (at a pair) with state $v$ and stacks $S$ to state $v'$ and stacks $S'$ at the
label that walks to the source vertex if $w$ decodes as an edge list, and at the label that
answers false otherwise. The output stack $O$ of $S'$ equals that of $S$. Moreover, if $w$
decodes as an edge list, then $X$ is empty in $S'$, the edge stack $E$ of $S'$ is the reverse
of $w$ as bit symbols followed by the old contents of $E$, and $S'$ agrees with $S$ on every
stack other than $X$ and $E$.

articles.title: Walking along the marks of the PATH marking machine
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a stack other than the
marks stack $M$ and the parked stack $P$, let $u$ be a symbol of the alphabet of $c$, and let
$\ell$ be a label at which the program is the walk step counted by $c$ that returns to $\ell$
(with some final statement). Let $j$ be a natural number, $p$ and $q$ lists of bits, $v$ a
Boolean, and $S$ stack contents in which $c$ holds exactly $j$ copies of $u$, $M$ holds $q$ as
bit symbols, and $P$ holds the reverse of $p$ as bit symbols. Then there are a Boolean $v'$ and
stack contents $S'$ such that the machine goes in exactly $j$ steps from label $\ell$ with state
$v$ and stacks $S$ to label $\ell$ with state $v'$ and stacks $S'$, where $c$ is empty in $S'$,
$M$ holds $q$ with its first $j$ entries dropped, $P$ holds the reverse of the concatenation of
$p$ with the first $j$ entries of $q$, all as bit symbols, and $S'$ agrees with $S$ on every
stack other than $c$, $M$ and $P$.

articles.title: Walk step of the PATH marking machine
articles.statement:
Given a counter stack $c$, a label $\ell$ and a
final statement $f$, the walk step pops the top of $c$. If $c$ was nonempty, it goes to $\ell$
after moving the top mark of the marks stack $M$, if there is one, onto the parked stack $P$:
the mark is popped, read as a bit (a symbol that is not a bit reads as false), and pushed on
$P$ as that bit. If $c$ was empty, it runs $f$.

articles.title: Decision version of hypergraph $k$-cut
articles.statement:
For a natural number $k$, this is the decision
problem on bitstrings that decodes an input as a triple $(n, E, B)$: a number $n$ of vertices
$0, \dots, n-1$, a list $E$ of hyperedges, each a list of vertices with a natural-number cost, and
a natural-number budget $B$. It accepts the input iff every hyperedge lists only vertices below
$n$ and there is a partition of the vertices into $k$ non-empty parts, given by a map $f$ from
$\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ onto $\{0, \dots, k-1\}$, such that the total cost of the hyperedges in $E$
(counted with multiplicity) that meet two different parts is at most $B$. Inputs that do not
decode are rejected.

articles.title: Hypergraph $k$-cut for fixed $k$ is in P
articles.statement:
For every natural number $k$, the decision version
of hypergraph $k$-cut is in the complexity class P. That problem accepts a hypergraph on the
vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, given by hyperedges with natural-number costs, and a budget $B$ iff every
hyperedge lists only vertices below $n$ and some partition of the vertices into $k$ non-empty parts
has total cost of the hyperedges meeting two parts at most $B$; inputs that do not decode are
rejected.

Chandrasekaran and Chekuri give, for every fixed $k$, a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for
hypergraph $k$-cut with non-negative hyperedge costs, which decides this problem.

## Sources

- EGRES Open (Egerváry Research Group), list of open problems, Minimum k-way cut in a hypergraph, https://oldlemon.cs.elte.hu/egres/open/Minimum_k-way_cut_in_a_hypergraph; resolution: K. Chandrasekaran and C. Chekuri, Hypergraph k-cut for fixed k in deterministic polynomial time, FOCS 2020; arXiv:2009.12442, abstract: for hypergraphs with non-negative hyperedge costs and fixed k, a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for Hypergraph-k-cut (a least-cost F ⊆ E such that G - F has at least k components, equivalently a partition of V into k non-empty parts minimizing the cost of crossing hyperedges), https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.12442.

articles.title: The EGRES question on hypergraph $k$-cut for fixed $k$
articles.statement:
The statement that for every natural
number $k$, the decision version of hypergraph $k$-cut is in the complexity class P. That problem
accepts a hypergraph on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$, given by hyperedges with natural-number
costs, and a budget $B$ iff every hyperedge lists only vertices below $n$ and some partition of the
vertices into $k$ non-empty parts has total cost of the hyperedges meeting two parts at most $B$;
inputs that do not decode are rejected.

articles.title: Integer from magnitude and sign
articles.statement:
A pair $(n, s)$ of a natural number $n$ and a Boolean
sign $s$ decodes to the integer $n$ if $s$ is true and to $-n$ if $s$ is false.

articles.title: Integer linear-programming feasibility in fixed dimension
articles.statement:
For a natural number $d$, this
decision problem accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring
decoding, to a pair $(A, b)$ such that $A$ is a list of rows, each a list of exactly $d$ integers,
$b$ is a list of integers with as many entries as $A$ has rows, and there is an integer vector
$y \in \mathbb{Z}^d$ with $\sum_{j < d} A_{rj} y_j \le b_r$ for every row index $r$. Each integer
entry is given as a pair $(n, s)$ of a natural number and a sign, standing for $n$ if $s$ is true
and $-n$ otherwise. Every other bitstring is rejected.

articles.title: Integer linear programming in fixed dimension is in P (Lenstra)
articles.statement:
For every natural number
$d$, integer linear-programming feasibility in dimension $d$ is in the complexity class P.

## Sources

- H. W. Lenstra Jr., "Integer programming with a fixed number of variables", Mathematics of Operations Research 8 (1983), 538-548.

articles.title: Signed integer from a magnitude–sign pair
articles.statement:
The integer decoded from a pair $(k, s)$ of a
