natural number $k$ and a boolean $s$ is $k$ if $s$ is true and $-k$ if $s$ is false.

articles.title: Rational linear-program feasibility
articles.statement:
The decision problem of rational linear-program
feasibility accepts a bitstring $w$ exactly when $w$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring
encoding, to a pair $(A, b)$ of a list $A$ of $m$ rows, each a list of magnitude–sign pairs, and
a list $b$ of $m'$ magnitude–sign pairs, such that every row of $A$ has the length $n$ of the
first row ($n = 0$ when $m = 0$), $m' = m$, and some $x \in \mathbb{Q}^n$ satisfies
$\sum_{j\lt n} A_{rj} x_j \le b_r$ for every $r < m$. Here a magnitude–sign pair $(k, s)$ of a
natural number $k$ and a boolean $s$ stands for the integer $k$ if $s$ is true and $-k$ if $s$ is
false, $A_{rj}$ is the integer given by the $j$-th entry of the $r$-th row and $b_r$ is the
integer given by the $r$-th entry of $b$. Bitstrings that do not decode are rejected.

articles.title: Linear programming is in P (Khachiyan)
articles.statement:
The decision problem of rational linear-program
feasibility is in the complexity class P. This problem accepts exactly the bitstrings that decode,
under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a list $A$ of $m$ rows of integers, all of the same
length $n$, and a list $b$ of $m$ integers, for which some $x \in \mathbb{Q}^n$ satisfies
$\sum_{j\lt n} A_{rj} x_j \le b_r$ for every $r < m$, where $A_{rj}$ is the $j$-th entry of the
$r$-th row of $A$ and $b_r$ is the $r$-th entry of $b$. Each integer is given as a magnitude–sign
pair $(k, s)$ of a natural number $k$ and a boolean $s$, standing for $k$ if $s$ is true and $-k$
if $s$ is false.

## Sources

- L. G. Khachiyan, "A polynomial algorithm in linear programming", Soviet Mathematics Doklady 20 (1979), 191-194.

articles.title: General matching decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$
exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a triple $(n, E, K)$ of a
natural number $n$, a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers and a natural number $K$ such that
every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ has $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \neq v$, and some sublist $M$ of $E$
(a subsequence, keeping the order of $E$) with no repeated entries and length at least $K$ has
the property that any two different pairs $(u_1, v_1)$ and $(u_2, v_2)$ in $M$ share no
element: $u_1, v_1 \notin \{u_2, v_2\}$. Bitstrings that do not decode are rejected.

articles.title: General matching is in P (Edmonds' blossom algorithm)
articles.statement:
The general matching decision
problem belongs to the complexity class P. This is the problem of deciding, for a vertex count
$n$, a list $E$ of edges joining distinct vertices below $n$ and a target $K$, encoded as a
bitstring, whether $E$ contains at least $K$ distinct pairwise vertex-disjoint edges.

## Sources

- J. Edmonds, "Paths, trees, and flowers", Canadian Journal of Mathematics 17 (1965), 449-467.

articles.title: Max-flow decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when
$x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a tuple $(n, E, s, t, K)$ of a natural
number $n$, a list $E = (e_0, \dots, e_{m-1})$ of triples $e_j = (u_j, v_j, c_j)$ of natural
numbers and natural numbers $s$, $t$ and $K$ such that $u_j < n$, $v_j < n$ and $u_j \neq v_j$
for every $j < m$, $s < n$, $t < n$ and $s \neq t$, and there are natural numbers
$f_0, \dots, f_{m-1}$ with $f_j \le c_j$ for every $j < m$, with
$\sum_{j : v_j = v} f_j = \sum_{j : u_j = v} f_j$ for every $v < n$ other than $s$ and $t$, and
with $\sum_{j : u_j = s} f_j - \sum_{j : v_j = s} f_j \ge K$, where the subtraction is
truncated at $0$. Bitstrings that do not decode are rejected.

articles.title: Max flow is in P (Edmonds-Karp)
articles.statement:
The max-flow decision problem belongs to the complexity
class P. This is the problem of deciding, for a vertex count $n$, a list of edges joining
distinct vertices below $n$ with natural-number capacities, distinct vertices $s, t < n$ and a
target $K$, encoded as a bitstring, whether some flow in natural numbers that respects the
capacities and is conserved at every vertex other than $s$ and $t$ has net outflow from $s$ at
least $K$.

## Sources

- J. Edmonds and R. M. Karp, "Theoretical improvements in algorithmic efficiency for network flow problems", Journal of the ACM 19 (1972), 248-264; L. R. Ford Jr. and D. R. Fulkerson, Flows in Networks, Princeton University Press, 1962.

articles.title: Perfect matchings in dense hypergraphs are decidable in polynomial time
articles.statement:
Resolved true: Keevash, Knox and Mycroft give a polynomial-time algorithm when the minimum codegree
is at least `n/k + γn` for a fixed `γ > 0`, and Han extends it to minimum codegree at least `n/k`,
so the problem is in `P` for every `1/k ≤ c < 1/2`. Inputs whose edge count is below what the
codegree condition forces are rejected first, so `n` is polynomial in the input size whenever the
remaining checks run. Source: A. Ruciński, in Combinatorics, Probability and Computing, Oberwolfach
Reports 3 (2006), no. 48, p. 2929, Problem 5, DOI 10.4171/OWR/2006/48; resolution: P. Keevash, F.
Knox and R. Mycroft, Polynomial-time perfect matchings in dense hypergraphs, Adv. Math. 269 (2015),
265-334, arXiv:1307.2608 (c > 1/k); J. Han, Decision problem for perfect matchings in dense
k-uniform hypergraphs, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 369 (2017), 5197-5218, arXiv:1409.5931 (c = 1/k), KKM
main theorem (codegree ≥ n/k + γn) and Han main theorem (codegree ≥ n/k): polynomial-time decision,
https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.5931.

articles.title: Ruciński's question on perfect matchings in dense hypergraphs
articles.statement:
The statement that for every
natural number $k \ge 2$ and every rational $c$ with $1/k \le c < 1/2$, the decision problem
$\mathrm{PM}(k, c)$ is in the complexity class P. Here $\mathrm{PM}(k, c)$ accepts a list of edges
of a $k$-uniform hypergraph $H$ on the vertices $0, \dots, n-1$ iff every edge consists of $k$
distinct vertices below $n$, $k \mid n$, every $(k-1)$-element set of vertices lies in at least
$cn$ edges of $H$, and $H$ has a perfect matching; inputs that do not decode are rejected. This is
the positive answer to Ruciński's question (Oberwolfach Combinatorics, Probability and Computing,
2006, Problem 5).

articles.title: Perfect matching in uniform hypergraphs with a codegree condition
articles.statement:
For a natural number
$k$ and a rational $c$, $\mathrm{PM}(k, c)$ is the decision problem on bitstrings that decodes an
input as a pair $(n, E)$ of a natural number $n$ and a list $E$ of lists of natural numbers, and
accepts it iff every list in $E$ consists of $k$ distinct vertices below $n$, $k \mid n$, every
$(k-1)$-element subset of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ is contained in at least $cn$ edges of the
hypergraph $H$ whose edges are the vertex sets of the lists in $E$, and $H$ has a perfect
matching, that is, $n/k$ pairwise disjoint edges. Inputs that do not decode are rejected.

articles.title: Undirected s-t connectivity as a decision problem
articles.statement:
A bitstring $x$ is a yes-instance
exactly when bitstring decoding of $x$, as a tuple $(n, E, s, t)$ of natural numbers $n$, $s$, $t$
and a finite list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, succeeds and returns $(n, E, s, t)$ such that
$s < n$, $t < n$, and there are pairwise distinct natural numbers $v_0, \dots, v_k$, all less than
$n$, with $v_0 = s$, $v_k = t$ and, for every $i < k$, $(v_i, v_{i+1}) \in E$ or
$(v_{i+1}, v_i) \in E$.

articles.title: Undirected ST-connectivity is in L (Reingold)
articles.statement:
The undirected $s$-$t$ connectivity
decision problem lies in the class $\mathsf{L}$ of decision problems decidable in deterministic
logarithmic space.

## Sources

- O. Reingold, "Undirected connectivity in log-space", Journal of the ACM 55 (2008), 1-24 (STOC 2005).

articles.title: Gate values of a serialized circuit
articles.statement:
For a list $C = (g_0, \dots, g_{m-1})$ of serialized
gates and a list $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{n-1})$ of Booleans, the gate values of $C$ on $a$ are the
list of gate values of the flat Boolean circuit on $n$ inputs whose $j$-th gate is decoded from the
(kind, references) pair $g_j$, evaluated on the assignment that gives input $i$ the value $a_i$.

A pair $(0, [i])$ with $i \ge n$ decodes to the constant false, so an input index out of range
reads as false.

articles.title: Outputs of a serialized circuit
articles.statement:
For a list $C$ of serialized gates, a list $a$ of Booleans
and a natural number $k$, the outputs of $C$ on $a$ are the last $k$ entries of the gate values of
$C$ on $a$, or all of them when $C$ has fewer than $k$ gates.

articles.title: Concatenation of two bitstrings
articles.statement:
For $n$-bit strings $y$ and $r$, their concatenation is the
$2n$-bit string whose bit $i$ is $y_i$ for $i < n$ and $r_{i - n}$ for $n \le i < 2n$.

articles.title: Serialized circuit gates
articles.statement:
A serialized gate is a pair $(k, r)$ of a natural number $k$, the
kind of the gate, and a list $r$ of natural numbers, its references.

These pairs are read through the shared (kind, references) encoding of gates of flat Boolean
circuits.

articles.title: Goldreich-Levin: hardcore predicate from one-way permutations
articles.statement:
Let $\pi$ be a family of
bijections $\pi_n$ of the set of $n$-bit strings, one for each natural number $n$. Suppose that
$\pi$ is computable by polynomial-size circuits: there is a polynomial $q$ with natural number
coefficients such that for every $n$ some list of at most $q(n)$ serialized gates has, on every
$n$-bit string $x$, outputs (its last $n$ gate values) equal to $\pi_n(x)$. Suppose also that $\pi$
is one-way: for every polynomial $p$ with natural number coefficients and every family $(C_n)$ of
lists of serialized gates with at most $p(n)$ gates in $C_n$ for all $n$, the inversion success
probability of $C_n$ against $\pi_n$ is a negligible function of $n$. Then for every polynomial
$p$ with natural number coefficients and every family $(C'_n)$ of lists of serialized gates with
at most $p(n)$ gates in $C'_n$ for all $n$, the function $n \mapsto \max(0, s_n - 1/2)$ is
negligible, where $s_n$ is the prediction success probability of $C'_n$ against $\pi_n$ for the
inner product modulo 2.

## Sources

- O. Goldreich and L. A. Levin, "A hard-core predicate for all one-way functions", Proceedings of the Twenty-First Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 1989), 25-32.

articles.title: Inversion success probability of a circuit
articles.statement:
For a list $C$ of serialized gates and a map
$\pi$ from $n$-bit strings to $n$-bit strings, the inversion success probability of $C$ against
$\pi$ is the rational number $N / 2^n$, where $N$ is the number of $n$-bit strings $x$ such that
the outputs of $C$ on input $\pi(x)$, taken as its last $n$ gate values, are exactly $x$.

articles.title: Prediction success probability for the inner-product bit
articles.statement:
For a list $C$ of serialized
gates and a map $\pi$ from $n$-bit strings to $n$-bit strings, the prediction success probability
of $C$ against $\pi$ is the rational number $N / 2^{2n}$, where $N$ is the number of pairs
$(x, r)$ of $n$-bit strings such that $C$ has at least one gate and the value of its last gate on
the concatenation of $\pi(x)$ and $r$, a $2n$-bit input, equals the inner product of $x$ and $r$
modulo 2.

articles.title: Inner product modulo 2
articles.statement:
For $n$-bit strings $x$ and $r$, their inner product modulo 2 is
true if and only if the number of indices $i < n$ with $x_i$ and $r_i$ both true is odd, that is,
$\langle x, r \rangle = \sum_{i < n} x_i r_i \bmod 2$.

articles.title: Algorithmica
articles.statement:
Algorithmica is the statement that the complexity classes $\mathrm{P}$ and
$\mathrm{NP}$ are equal.

articles.title: Easy on average
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a polynomial with natural-number coefficients, $L$ a
decision problem, and $S$ a family of samplers, where $S_n$ sends each string $r$ of $p(n)$
random bits to a bitstring $S_n(r)$. The pair $(L, S)$ is easy on average when there is a
polynomial-time computable function $A$ from bitstrings to booleans such that for every natural
number $c$ there is $N$ such that for all $n \ge N$

$$1 - \frac{1}{n^c + 1} \le \frac{\#\{r \in \{0,1\}^{p(n)} : A(S_n(r)) = L(S_n(r))\}}{2^{p(n)}},$$

that is, $A$ agrees with $L$ on $S_n(r)$ for at least a fraction $1 - 1/(n^c + 1)$ of the
coin strings $r$.

The algorithm $A$ does not depend on $c$, so its error is negligible. Requiring the bound
$1 - 1/(q(n) + 1)$ for a single polynomial $q$ instead would be vacuous: the zero polynomial
gives the lower bound $0$, which every algorithm meets.

articles.title: Hard on average
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a polynomial with natural-number coefficients, $L$ a
decision problem, and $S$ a family of samplers, where $S_n$ sends each string $r$ of $p(n)$
random bits to a bitstring $S_n(r)$. The pair $(L, S)$ is hard on average when it is not easy
on average: there is no polynomial-time computable function $A$ from bitstrings to booleans
such that for every natural number $c$ and all sufficiently large $n$, $A$ agrees with $L$ on
$S_n(r)$ for at least a fraction $1 - 1/(n^c + 1)$ of the $2^{p(n)}$ coin strings $r$.

Since hardness is the logical complement of easiness, if $\mathrm{P} \ne \mathrm{NP}$ and
Heuristica fails, then some NP problem is hard on average for some samplable ensemble.

articles.title: Cryptomania
articles.statement:
Cryptomania is the statement that public-key cryptography exists: there
are a polynomial $\ell$ with natural-number coefficients and polynomial-time computable maps
$G$ (key generation), $E$ (encryption) and $D$ (decryption) from bitstrings to bitstrings with
the following two properties. First, decryption is correct: for every natural number $n$, all
key coins $r$ and encryption coins $s$ that are bitstrings of length $\ell(n)$, and every bit
$b$, if $(pk, sk)$ is the key pair of $G$ on $r$ and the ciphertext $e$ is $E$ applied to the
bitstring encoding of the triple $(pk, (b), s)$, where $(b)$ is the one-bit list, then $D$
applied to the bitstring encoding of the pair $(sk, e)$ is $(b)$. Second, the scheme is secure:
for every family $(C_n)$ of encoded flat Boolean circuits and every polynomial $q$ with
natural-number coefficients such that each $C_n$ has at most $q(n)$ gates, and for every natural
number $c$, there is $N$ such that for all $n \ge N$ the eavesdropping advantage of $C_n$
against $(G, E)$ with polynomial $\ell$ at length $n$ is at most $1/n^c$.

articles.title: Exactly one of Impagliazzo's five worlds holds
articles.statement:
Exactly one of the statements
Algorithmica, Heuristica, Pessiland, Minicrypt and Cryptomania is true: one of them holds and
the other four fail.

articles.title: Evaluation of an encoded flat circuit
articles.statement:
Let $C$ be a flat Boolean circuit given as a list
of gates, each encoded as a (kind, references) pair, and let $a = (a_0, \dots, a_{k-1})$ be a
list of booleans. The gate values of $C$ on $a$ are the gate values, in order, of the circuit on
$k$ inputs obtained by decoding each gate of $C$, evaluated on the assignment that sends input
$i$ to $a_i$.

Decoding turns an input variable $x_i$ with $i \ge k$ into the constant false.

articles.title: Outputs of an encoded flat circuit
articles.statement:
For an encoded flat Boolean circuit $C$, a list of
booleans $a$ and a natural number $k$, the outputs of $C$ on $a$ are the last $k$ entries of the
list of gate values of $C$ on $a$, or the whole list if $C$ has fewer than $k$ gates.

articles.title: Inversion success probability of a circuit
articles.statement:
Let $f$ map $n$-bit strings to bitstrings
and let $C$ be an encoded flat Boolean circuit. For an $n$-bit string $x$, the candidate preimage
$x'$ consists of the last $n$ gate values of $C$ on input $f(x)$ (all of them if $C$ has fewer
than $n$ gates), padded with false to length $n$. The inversion success probability of $C$
against $f$ is the fraction of the $2^n$ strings $x$ for which $f(x') = f(x)$.

articles.title: Key pair produced by a key generator
articles.statement:
For a map $G$ from bitstrings to bitstrings (the key
generator) and a bitstring $r$ of coins, the key pair of $G$ on $r$ is the pair of bitstrings
obtained by decoding $G(r)$ with the canonical bitstring encoding of pairs of bitstrings, or the
pair of empty bitstrings if this decoding fails.

articles.title: Eavesdropping advantage against a public-key scheme
articles.statement:
Let $G$ (key generation) and $E$
(encryption) be maps from bitstrings to bitstrings, let $C$ be an encoded flat Boolean circuit,
let $\ell$ be a polynomial with natural-number coefficients and let $n$ be a natural number. For
key coins $r$ and encryption coins $s$, each a string of $\ell(n)$ bits, and a bit $b$, let $pk$
be the first component of the key pair of $G$ on $r$, and let the ciphertext $e$ be $E$ applied
to the bitstring encoding of the triple $(pk, (b), s)$, where $(b)$ is the one-bit list. The
circuit $C$ succeeds on $(r, s, b)$ when it has a last gate value on the bitstring encoding of
the pair $(pk, e)$ and that value equals $b$. If $N$ is the number of triples $(r, s, b)$ on
which $C$ succeeds, the advantage of $C$ at length $n$ is $|N / 2^{2\ell(n) + 1} - 1/2|$.

articles.title: Serialized gates of five-worlds circuits
articles.statement:
A serialized gate of a flat Boolean circuit is a
pair $(k, r)$ of a natural number $k$ (the gate kind) and a list $r$ of natural numbers (its
references, depending on the kind: an input index, a constant bit, or indices of other gates), in
the shared encoding of gates as (kind, references) pairs.

articles.title: Heuristica
articles.statement:
Heuristica: `P ≠ NP`, but every NP problem is easy on average for every samplable
distribution.

articles.title: Impagliazzo's five worlds
articles.statement:
The following four statements hold. First, if public-key
encryption exists, then one-way functions exist. Second, if one-way functions exist, then some
decision problem $L$ in NP is hard on average for some samplable distribution: there are a
polynomial $p$ with natural-number coefficients and a family $S$ of maps $S_n$ from $p(n)$-bit
coin strings to bitstrings such that $(p, S)$ is samplable and $L$ is hard on average with
respect to $S$. Third, if some decision problem in NP is hard on average for some samplable
distribution in this sense, then $\mathsf{P} \ne \mathsf{NP}$. Fourth, exactly one of the five
worlds Algorithmica, Heuristica, Pessiland, Minicrypt and Cryptomania holds.

## Sources

- R. Impagliazzo, "A personal view of average-case complexity", Proceedings of the Tenth Annual Structure in Complexities Theory Conference (1995), 134-147.

articles.title: Minicrypt
articles.statement: Minicrypt: one-way functions exist, but public-key cryptography does not.

articles.title: One-way functions exist
articles.statement:
There are a family of functions $f_n$, each mapping $n$-bit strings
to bitstrings, and a polynomial $q$ with natural-number coefficients such that the following hold:
$|f_n(x)| \le q(n)$ for every $n$ and every $n$-bit string $x$; some polynomial-time computable
function on bitstrings maps the canonical bitstring encoding of every pair $(n, x)$ to $f_n(x)$;
and for every family of flat Boolean circuits $C_n$, given as lists of serialized gates, with at
most $p(n)$ gates for some polynomial $p$ with natural-number coefficients, the fraction of
$n$-bit strings $x$ with $f_n(x') = f_n(x)$ is a negligible function of $n$. Here $x'$ is the
$n$-bit string whose $i$-th bit is the $i$-th of the last $n$ gate values of $C_n$ on input
$f_n(x)$, or false when there is no such value.

The functions need not be injective, and they are computed by a single uniform polynomial-time
algorithm: per-length polynomial-size circuits would admit noncomputable $\mathsf{P/poly}$
families.

articles.title: Pessiland
articles.statement:
Pessiland is the statement that $\mathsf{P} \ne \mathsf{NP}$, that one-way
functions do not exist, and that some decision problem $L$ in NP is hard on average for some
samplable distribution: there are a polynomial $p$ with natural-number coefficients and a family
$S$ of maps $S_n$ from $p(n)$-bit coin strings to bitstrings such that $(p, S)$ is samplable and
$L$ is hard on average with respect to $S$.

articles.title: Public-key encryption exists
articles.statement:
There are a polynomial $\ell$ with natural-number
coefficients and polynomial-time computable functions $G$ (key generation), $E$ (encryption) and
$D$ (decryption) on bitstrings with the following two properties. Here tuples are passed to
these functions and to circuits through their canonical bitstring encodings, and for a bitstring
$r$ the keys $(\mathit{pk}, \mathit{sk})$ are the decoding of $G(r)$ as a pair of bitstrings,
both empty when decoding fails. Correctness: for every $n$, all bitstrings $r$ and $s$ of length
$\ell(n)$ and every bit $b$, $D(\mathit{sk}, E(\mathit{pk}, [b], s)) = [b]$. Security: for every
family of flat Boolean circuits $C_n$, given as lists of serialized gates, with at most $p(n)$
gates for some polynomial $p$ with natural-number coefficients, and for every natural number
$c$, the advantage of $C_n$ is at most $1 / n^c$ for all sufficiently large $n$. The advantage
of $C_n$ is $|P_n - 1/2|$, where $P_n$ is the fraction of triples $(r, s, b)$ of bitstrings $r$
and $s$ of length $\ell(n)$ and a bit $b$ for which the last gate value of $C_n$ on input
$(\mathit{pk}, E(\mathit{pk}, [b], s))$ is $b$.

articles.title: Samplable distributions
articles.statement:
Let $p$ be a polynomial with natural-number coefficients and let
$S$ be a family of maps $S_n$ from $p(n)$-bit coin strings to bitstrings. The pair $(p, S)$ is
samplable when every $S_n(r)$ has length exactly $n$ and some polynomial-time computable function
on bitstrings maps the canonical bitstring encoding of every pair $(n, r)$ to $S_n(r)$.

The distribution sampled at length $n$ is that of $S_n(r)$ for a uniformly random coin string
$r$. The sampler is a single uniform polynomial-time algorithm: per-length circuits would admit
noncomputable $\mathsf{P/poly}$ samplers. The coin count is a polynomial rather than $n$: a
distribution giving probability $2^{-(n+1)}$ to one output is samplable with $n + 1$ coins but
not from $n$ uniform coins.

articles.title: Nisan-Wigderson: exponential hardness in E derandomizes BPP
articles.statement:
Suppose there are a decision
problem $f$ in E and a natural number $c > 0$ such that, for every $n$, every well-formed flat
Boolean circuit $C$ on $n$ inputs without mod gates that computes $f$ on all bitstrings of length
$n$ (for every bitstring $x$ of length $n$, the value of its last gate on input $x$ is $f(x)$)
satisfies $|C|^c \ge 2^n$, where $|C|$ is its number of gates; that is, $C$ has at least $2^{n/c}$
gates. Then BPP equals P.

## Sources

- N. Nisan and A. Wigderson, "Hardness vs randomness", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 49 (1994), 149-167 (FOCS 1988).

articles.title: One-way functions imply P ≠ NP
articles.statement:
If some family $f$, assigning to each natural number $n$
and each $n$-bit string $x$ a bitstring $f_n(x)$, is a one-way function family, then
$\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP}$.

## Sources

- O. Goldreich, Foundations of Cryptography, Vol. 1, Cambridge University Press, 2001, Section 2.2 (one-way functions imply P ≠ NP); R. Impagliazzo, "A personal view of average-case complexity", Proceedings of the Tenth Annual Structure in Complexities Theory Conference (1995), 134-147 (five worlds).

articles.title: Agreement of a circuit with a Boolean function
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a finite type, let $C$
be a circuit given as a list of encoded gates, let $g$ assign a Boolean to each $a \in \alpha$,
and let $\mathrm{enc}$ encode each $a \in \alpha$ as a list of Booleans. The agreement of $C$
with $g$ is the rational number $N / |\alpha|$ (which is $0$ when $\alpha$ is empty), where $N$
is the number of $a \in \alpha$ such that $C$ has at least one gate and the value of its last
gate, when $C$ is evaluated on the input list $\mathrm{enc}(a)$, equals $g(a)$.

articles.title: Gate values of an encoded circuit
articles.statement:
For a list $C$ of encoded gates and a list $x$ of
Booleans of length $\ell$, the gate values of $C$ on $x$ are obtained by decoding each pair of $C$
to a gate of a flat Boolean circuit on $\ell$ inputs and evaluating the decoded circuit with the
assignment that gives input $i$ the value $x_i$; the result lists the values of all gates in
order. A pair referring to an input index $i \ge \ell$ decodes to the constant false.

articles.title: Flattening blocks of bits
articles.statement:
For $n > 0$ and $k$ blocks $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$ of $n$ bits
each, the flattened string has $nk$ bits, and its bit $i$ is bit $i \bmod n$ of the block
$x_{\lfloor i/n \rfloor}$.

articles.title: XOR of finitely many bits
articles.statement:
For $k$ bits $b_0, \dots, b_{k-1}$, their XOR is true if and
only if an odd number of the $b_i$ are true.

articles.title: XOR of independent copies of a function
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $n$ and $k$ and a Boolean
function $f$ on $n$ bits, the function $f^{\oplus k}$ takes $k$ blocks $x_0, \dots, x_{k-1}$
of $n$ bits each to $f(x_0) \oplus \cdots \oplus f(x_{k-1})$, which is true if and only if an
odd number of the values $f(x_i)$ are true.

articles.title: Encoded gates
articles.statement:
An encoded gate is a pair $(k, r)$ of a natural number $k$ (the gate kind)
and a list $r$ of natural numbers (its references), the shared (kind, references) encoding of
gates of flat Boolean circuits.

articles.title: Yao's XOR lemma: hardness amplification by XOR
articles.statement:
There is a natural number $c$ such that
the following holds for all natural numbers $n \ge 1$ and $k$, every rational $\delta$ with
$0 < \delta \le 1/2$, every Boolean function $f$ on $n$ bits and every natural number $s$.
Suppose every circuit given as a list of at most $s$ encoded gates has agreement at most
$1 - \delta$ with $f$, where an input $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ is given to the circuit as its $n$ bits.
Then every circuit $C$ given as a list of encoded gates, whose number of gates $|C|$ satisfies
$|C| \cdot (k + 1)^c \le s$, has agreement at most $1/2 + (1 - 2\delta)^k / 2 + 1/(k + 1)$ with
the XOR $f^{\oplus k}$ of $k$ independent copies of $f$, where a $k$-tuple of $n$-bit blocks is
given to the circuit as its $nk$-bit flattening.

## Sources

- A. C. Yao, "Theory and applications of trapdoor functions", Proceedings of the Twenty-Third Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS 1982), 80-91.

articles.title: Adleman's theorem: BPP is contained in P/poly
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in BPP lies in
P/poly.

## Sources

- L. Adleman, "Two theorems on random polynomial time", Proceedings of the Nineteenth Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS 1978), 75-83.

articles.title: AM is contained in $\Pi_2^p$ (Babai)
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in the Arthur–Merlin class
$\mathsf{AM}$ lies in $\Pi_2^p$, the second universal level of the polynomial hierarchy.

## Sources

- L. Babai, "Trading group theory for randomness", Proceedings of the Seventeenth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 1985), 421-429; see also O. Goldreich and D. Zuckerman and the set lower-bound protocol of Goldwasser-Sipser.

articles.title: MA is contained in AM
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in the class $\mathsf{MA}$ is in the class
$\mathsf{AM}$.

## Sources

- L. Babai, "Trading group theory for randomness", Proceedings of the Seventeenth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 1985), 421-429; S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Theorem 8.2 (MA ⊆ AM).

articles.title: MA is contained in PH
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in the class $\mathsf{MA}$ is in the
polynomial hierarchy $\mathsf{PH}$.

## Sources

- L. Babai, "Trading group theory for randomness", Proceedings of the Seventeenth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 1985), 421-429 (MA ⊆ AM, AM ⊆ Π₂); L. J. Stockmeyer, "The polynomial-time hierarchy", Theoretical Computer Science 3 (1977), 1-22 (PH); S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Theorem 5.4 (PH ⊆ PSPACE) and Chapter 8.

articles.title: BPP is contained in PSPACE
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in BPP lies in PSPACE.

## Sources

- S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009 (BPP ⊆ PSPACE).

articles.title: RP is contained in BPP
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in the class $\mathsf{RP}$ of
one-sided-error randomized polynomial-time decision problems also belongs to the class
$\mathsf{BPP}$ of bounded-error probabilistic polynomial-time decision problems.

## Sources

- S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Chapter 7 (error reduction for RP); M. Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed., 2013, Theorem 10.13 (RP ⊆ BPP via amplification).

articles.title: RP is contained in NP
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in the class $\mathsf{RP}$ of
one-sided-error randomized polynomial-time decision problems also belongs to the class
$\mathsf{NP}$.

## Sources

- S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Theorem 7.3 (RP ⊆ NP); M. Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed., 2013, Theorem 10.13.

articles.title: BQP is contained in PP
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in BQP lies in PP.

## Sources

- E. Bernstein and U. Vazirani, "Quantum complexity theory", SIAM Journal on Computing 26 (1997), 1411-1473 (BQP ⊆ PP); L. Adleman, J. DeMarrais, and M.-D. Huang, "Quantum computability", SIAM Journal on Computing 26 (1997), 1524-1540; S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Theorem 10.2.

articles.title: BQP is contained in PSPACE
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in BQP, the class of bounded-error
quantum polynomial-time decision problems, lies in PSPACE, the class of decision problems
decidable in polynomial space.

## Sources

- E. Bernstein and U. Vazirani, "Quantum complexity theory", SIAM Journal on Computing 26 (1997), 1411-1473 (BQP ⊆ PSPACE); S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Theorem 10.2.

articles.title: Goldwasser-Sipser: private coins add no power to interactive proofs
articles.statement:
The class
$\mathsf{IP}$ of decision problems with (private-coin) interactive proofs equals the class
$\mathsf{PubIP}$ of decision problems with public-coin interactive proofs with polynomially many
rounds.

## Sources

- S. Goldwasser and M. Sipser, "Private coins versus public coins in interactive proof systems", Proceedings of the Eighteenth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 1986), 59-68 (journal version in Advances in Computing Research 5 (1989), 73-90).

articles.title: Public-coin interactive proofs
articles.statement:
A decision problem $L$ is in $\mathsf{PubIP}$ when there
are polynomials $r$, $q$ and $k$ with natural-number coefficients and polynomial-time functions
$V_{\mathrm{msg}}$ (the verifier's message function) and $V_{\mathrm{dec}}$ (its decision
function) with the following property. For a bitstring $x$, a prover $P$ (an arbitrary function
from pairs of a coin prefix and a transcript to bitstrings) and a coin string $c$, let $G(P, c)$
be the outcome of the public-coin interactive-proof game with message length cap $q(|x|)$,
$k(|x|)$ fresh coins per round, verifier $V_{\mathrm{msg}}$ and $V_{\mathrm{dec}}$, prover $P$,
input $x$, coins $c$, $r(|x|)$ remaining rounds out of $r(|x|)$ total rounds and the empty
initial transcript. Then for every bitstring $x$: if $L(x)$ is true, some prover $P$ makes
$G(P, c)$ true for at least $2/3$ of the coin strings $c \in \{0,1\}^{r(|x|) k(|x|)}$; and if
$L(x)$ is false, every prover $P$ makes $G(P, c)$ true for at most $1/3$ of them.

articles.title: Public-coin interactive-proof game
articles.statement:
The game takes a length cap $c$, a number $k$ of
fresh coins per round, a verifier message function $V_{\mathrm{msg}}$, a verifier decision
function $V_{\mathrm{dec}}$, a prover $P$ mapping pairs of a coin prefix and a transcript (a list
of bitstrings) to bitstrings, an input $x$, a coin string $\rho$, a number $j$ of remaining
rounds, a total number $T$ of rounds and a transcript $t$, and returns a Boolean outcome. If
$j = 0$, the outcome is $V_{\mathrm{dec}}(x, \rho, t)$. Otherwise let $\pi$ be the first
$(T - j + 1) k$ coins of $\rho$ (all of $\rho$ if it is shorter), where $T - j$ is truncated
subtraction ($0$ when $j > T$). The verifier sends $m = V_{\mathrm{msg}}(x, \pi, t)$ and the
prover replies $a = P(\pi, t')$, where $t'$ is $t$ extended by $m$. If both $m$ and $a$ have
length at most $c$, the outcome is that of the game with $j - 1$ remaining rounds, the same
$T$, and transcript $t$ extended by $m$ and then $a$; otherwise the outcome is false.

So the verifier's message and the prover's reply in a round see only the coins revealed up to
that round, while the final decision may use the whole coin string.

articles.title: Directed graph isomorphism as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem accepts a bitstring
$x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a triple $(n, E_1, E_2)$
of a natural number $n$ and two lists $E_1$ and $E_2$ of pairs of natural numbers for which
there is a bijection $f$ of $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ such that for all $a, b < n$, $(a, b) \in E_1$
if and only if $(f(a), f(b)) \in E_2$. Bitstrings that do not decode to such a triple are
rejected.

Pairs in $E_1$ or $E_2$ with an entry at least $n$ play no role.

articles.title: Graph isomorphism is in NP and coAM
articles.statement:
The directed graph isomorphism decision problem
belongs to NP and to coAM.

## Sources

- O. Goldreich, "On the complexity of graph isomorphism" and the Goldreich-Micali-Wigderson interactive proof for graph non- isomorphism; see J. Köbler, U. Schöning, and J. Torán, The Graph Isomorphism Problem: Its Structural Complexity, Birkhäuser, 1993.

articles.title: Directed graph non-isomorphism as a decision problem
articles.statement:
The decision problem accepts a
bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of triples
$(n, E_1, E_2)$ of a natural number and two lists of pairs of natural numbers, to a triple for
which there is no bijection $f$ from $\{0, \ldots, n - 1\}$ to itself such that, for all
$a, b < n$, $(a, b) \in E_1$ if and only if $(f(a), f(b)) \in E_2$. Bitstrings that do not
decode are rejected.

Pairs in $E_1$ or $E_2$ with an entry at least $n$ play no role, so $E_1$ and $E_2$ are read as
directed graphs on the vertex set $\{0, \ldots, n - 1\}$.

articles.title: Graph non-isomorphism is in AM
articles.statement:
The directed graph non-isomorphism decision problem
belongs to the class $\mathsf{AM}$ of decision problems decided by Arthur–Merlin protocols.

## Sources

- O. Goldreich, S. Micali, and A. Wigderson, "Proofs that yield nothing but their validity, or all languages in NP have zero-knowledge proof systems", Journal of the ACM 38 (1991), 691-729 (FOCS 1986); O. Goldwasser and M. Sipser, "Private coins versus public coins in interactive proof systems", Advances in Computing Research 5 (1989), 73-90.

articles.title: IP = PSPACE (Shamir)
articles.statement:
The class $\mathsf{IP}$ of decision problems that have
interactive proofs (a polynomial-time verifier using polynomially many rounds and random coins,
with completeness at least $2/3$ and soundness at most $1/3$ against every prover) equals the
class $\mathrm{PSPACE}$ of decision problems whose languages are decided by multi-tape Turing
machines in polynomial space.

## Sources

- A. Shamir, "IP = PSPACE", Journal of the ACM 39 (1992), 869-877 (FOCS 1990); see also C. Lund, L. Fortnow, H. Karloff, and N. Nisan, "Algebraic methods for interactive proof systems", Journal of the ACM 39 (1992), 859-868.

articles.title: Embedding of a 2-local term into $n$ qubits
articles.statement:
Let a 2-local term act on qubits $i$ and $j$,
and let $M$ be the $4 \times 4$ complex matrix encoded by its list of entries, with rows and
columns indexed by pairs of bits. Its embedding into $n$ qubits is the $2^n \times 2^n$ complex
matrix whose entry at basis indices $s, t \in \{0, \dots, 2^n - 1\}$ is
$M_{(s_i, s_j), (t_i, t_j)}$ if $s_k = t_k$ for every $k \ne i, j$, and $0$ otherwise, where
$s_k = \lfloor s / 2^k \rfloor \bmod 2$ is bit $k$ of $s$.

When $i \ne j$ and $i, j < n$, this is $M$ acting on qubits $i$ and $j$, tensored with the
identity on the other qubits.

articles.title: Ground energy of a Hermitian matrix
articles.statement:
For a natural number $n$, the ground energy of a
Hermitian $2^n \times 2^n$ complex matrix $H$ is the smallest eigenvalue of $H$.

articles.title: Hamiltonian of a list of 2-local terms
articles.statement:
For a number $n$ of qubits and a list
$h_1, \dots, h_m$ of 2-local terms, the Hamiltonian is the $2^n \times 2^n$ complex matrix
$\tilde h_1 + \dots + \tilde h_m$, where $\tilde h_l$ is the embedding of $h_l$ into $n$ qubits;
for the empty list it is the zero matrix.

articles.title: Initial state of a QMA verifier
articles.statement:
For a bitstring $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1})$, with true
read as $1$ and false as $0$, numbers $m$ and $a$, and a vector $\psi \in \mathbb{C}^{2^m}$ (the
witness on $m$ qubits), the initial state is the tensor product of the computational basis state
of $x$, the vector $\psi$ and the all-zero state on $a$ ancilla qubits, in this order. It is the
vector on $\{0, \dots, 2^{n+m+a} - 1\}$ whose value at $s$ is $\psi(\lfloor s / 2^n \rfloor)$ if
$s < 2^{n+m}$ and $s \bmod 2^n = \sum_{k < n} x_k 2^k$, and $0$ otherwise. So $x$ occupies the
$n$ low-order bits of the index, the witness the next $m$ bits and the ancillas the $a$
high-order bits.

articles.title: No-instances of the 2-local Hamiltonian problem
articles.statement:
A bitstring $x$ is a no-instance when
decoding it under the canonical bitstring encoding gives a tuple $(n, (h_1, \dots, h_m), a, b)$ of
a natural number $n$, a list of 2-local terms $h_1, \dots, h_m$ and two encoded rational numbers,
whose values we also write $a$ and $b$, such that every $h_l$ is valid on $n$ qubits,
$b - a \ge 1/(m + 1)$, and the Hamiltonian $H$ of $h_1, \dots, h_m$ on $n$ qubits is Hermitian
and has ground energy at least $b$.

articles.title: Yes-instances of the 2-local Hamiltonian problem
articles.statement:
A bitstring $x$ is a yes-instance when
decoding it under the canonical bitstring encoding gives a tuple $(n, (h_1, \dots, h_m), a, b)$ of
a natural number $n$, a list of 2-local terms $h_1, \dots, h_m$ and two encoded rational numbers,
whose values we also write $a$ and $b$, such that every $h_l$ is valid on $n$ qubits,
$b - a \ge 1/(m + 1)$, and the Hamiltonian $H$ of $h_1, \dots, h_m$ on $n$ qubits is Hermitian
and has ground energy at most $a$.

articles.title: The 2-local Hamiltonian problem is QMA-complete
articles.statement:
The 2-local Hamiltonian promise
problem, given by its yes-instances and no-instances, is in QMA, and every promise problem in QMA
whose sets of yes-instances and no-instances are disjoint sets of bitstrings has a polynomial-time
reduction to it.

Here an instance encodes a number $n$ of qubits, a list of $m$ valid 2-local terms on $n$ qubits
and encoded rationals $a$ and $b$ with $b - a \ge 1/(m + 1)$; it is a yes-instance when the
Hamiltonian of the terms on $n$ qubits is Hermitian with ground energy at most $a$, and a
no-instance when it is Hermitian with ground energy at least $b$.

## Sources

- A. Y. Kitaev, "Quantum NP", talk at AQIP 1999; A. Y. Kitaev, A. H. Shen, and M. N. Vyalyi, Classical and Quantum Computation, American Mathematical Society, 2002, Section 14.4; J. Kempe, A. Y. Kitaev, and O. Regev, "The complexity of the local Hamiltonian problem", SIAM Journal on Computing 35 (2006), 1070-1097 (the 2-local reduction); A. D. Bookatz, "QMA-complete problems", arXiv:1212.6312 (2012), Section 2 (survey of the QMA-completeness of the local Hamiltonian problem); S. Arora and B. Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, 2009, Chapter 10, for the QMA-completeness of 2-local Hamiltonian.

articles.title: Valid 2-local Hamiltonian term
articles.statement:
A 2-local term acting on qubits $i$ and $j$ with entry
list $e$ is valid on $n$ qubits when $i < j < n$, the list $e$ has exactly $16$ entries, each
entry has nonzero denominators in the encodings of both its real and its imaginary part, the
$4 \times 4$ complex matrix $M$ encoded by $e$ is positive semidefinite, and
$\sum_{p, q} |M_{pq}|^2 \le 1$, that is, $M$ has Frobenius norm at most $1$.

In particular $M$ is Hermitian and has operator norm at most $1$.

articles.title: Encoded 2-local Hamiltonian term
articles.statement:
A 2-local Hamiltonian term is encoded as a triple
$(i, j, e)$ of natural numbers $i$ and $j$, the qubits it acts on, and a list $e$ of pairs of
encoded rational numbers, the real and imaginary parts of the entries of its $4 \times 4$ matrix
in row-major order.

The encoding itself does not require $e$ to have $16$ entries or the matrix to be Hermitian; the
qubit bounds, the number of entries and positive semidefiniteness (hence Hermiticity) are part of
the validity of a term.

articles.title: Polynomial-time reduction between promise problems
articles.statement:
A promise problem $(Y_1, N_1)$,
given by sets $Y_1$ and $N_1$ of bitstrings, reduces to another such promise problem $(Y_2, N_2)$
when there is a polynomial-time computable map $f$ from bitstrings to bitstrings with
$f(x) \in Y_2$ for every $x \in Y_1$ and $f(x) \in N_2$ for every $x \in N_1$.

articles.title: QMA for promise problems
articles.statement:
A pair $(\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}}, \Pi_{\mathrm{no}})$ of sets of
bitstrings is in QMA when there are polynomials $m$, $a$ and $s$ with natural-number coefficients
and a polynomial-time computable map sending each bitstring $x$ to a list of encoded 2-local
quantum gates such that, for every bitstring $x$, writing $N = |x| + m(|x|) + a(|x|)$: the list
has at most $s(|x|)$ gates, each well-formed on $N$ qubits; if $x \in \Pi_{\mathrm{yes}}$, some
state $\psi$ on $m(|x|)$ qubits with squared norm $1$ makes the acceptance probability of the
circuit, applied to the tensor product of the basis state of $x$, $\psi$ and the all-zero state
on $a(|x|)$ qubits, at least $2/3$; and if $x \in \Pi_{\mathrm{no}}$, every state $\psi$ on
$m(|x|)$ qubits with squared norm $1$ makes this acceptance probability at most $1/3$.

No condition is imposed on bitstrings outside $\Pi_{\mathrm{yes}} \cup \Pi_{\mathrm{no}}$.

articles.title: Sipser-Gács-Lautemann: BPP is in $\Sigma_2^p$ and $\Pi_2^p$
articles.statement:
Every decision problem in
BPP lies in $\Sigma_2^p$ and in $\Pi_2^p$, the classes of the polynomial hierarchy defined by two
alternating blocks of polynomially bounded quantifiers, beginning with $\exists$ and with
$\forall$ respectively.

## Sources

- M. Sipser, "A complexity theoretic approach to randomness", Proceedings of the Fifteenth Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 1983), 330-335; P. Gács (unpublished); C. Lautemann, "BPP and the polynomial hierarchy", Information Processing Letters 17 (1983), 215-217.

articles.title: SAT with a unary variable count as a decision problem
articles.statement:
A bitstring $x$ is a yes-instance
exactly when bitstring decoding of $x$, as a pair of a list of booleans and a CNF formula,
succeeds and returns a pair $(u, \varphi)$ such that, writing $m$ for the length of $u$, every
variable occurring in $\varphi$ is less than $m$ and some assignment of booleans to the variables
$0, \dots, m - 1$ satisfies $\varphi$ once it is extended by assigning false to every variable
$v \ge m$.

articles.title: UniqueSAT with a unary variable count as a decision problem
articles.statement:
A bitstring $x$ is a
yes-instance exactly when bitstring decoding of $x$, as a pair of a list of booleans and a CNF
formula, succeeds and returns a pair $(u, \varphi)$ such that, writing $m$ for the length of $u$,
every variable occurring in $\varphi$ is less than $m$ and exactly one assignment of booleans to
the variables $0, \dots, m - 1$ satisfies $\varphi$ once it is extended by assigning false to
every variable $v \ge m$.

articles.title: Valiant-Vazirani: SAT reduces to UniqueSAT
articles.statement:
There are a polynomial $p$ with
natural-number coefficients and a polynomial-time computable function $R$ from pairs of
bitstrings to bitstrings such that, for every bitstring $x$ of length $n$: if $x$ is not in SAT,
then for every bitstring $r$ of length $p(n)$ the bitstring $R(x, r)$ is in neither SAT nor
UniqueSAT; and if $x$ is in SAT, then the number $N$ of bitstrings $r$ of length $p(n)$ for which
$R(x, r)$ is in UniqueSAT satisfies $8(n + 1) N \ge 2^{p(n)}$.

Here SAT and UniqueSAT are the bitstring decision problems for CNF formulas with the variable
count given in unary.

## Sources

- L. G. Valiant and V. V. Vazirani, "NP is as easy as detecting unique solutions", Theoretical Computer Science 47 (1986), 85-93 (STOC 1985).

articles.title: Next state while spelling out a letter's image
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet $T$
with transition function $\delta$, and let $\varphi$ map each letter of $T$ to a word over $T'$. For
a state $q$ of $M$, a letter $a$ and a natural number $i$, the state reached after emitting position
$i$ (counted from $0$) of $\varphi(a)$ from $q$ is the intermediate state $(q, a, i + 1)$ of the
ε-NFA if $i + 1 < |\varphi(a)|$, and the state $\delta(q, a)$ of $M$ otherwise.

articles.title: Maximal length of the image of a letter
articles.statement:
For a map $\varphi$ from a finite alphabet $T$ to
words over $T'$, the bound is the maximum of the lengths $|\varphi(a)|$ over all letters $a \in T$
(and $0$ when $T$ is empty).

articles.title: Edge labels for a letter's image
articles.statement:
For a map $\varphi$ from letters of $T$ to words over $T'$
and a letter $a$, the label sequence of $a$ is a single ε-label when $\varphi(a)$ is empty, and
otherwise the letters of $\varphi(a)$ in order, each as a non-ε label.

articles.title: The cyclic shifts of the words of a regular language form a regular language
articles.statement: **The cyclic shifts of the words of a regular language form a regular language.**

articles.title: Cyclic shift of a language
articles.statement:
For a language $L$ over $\alpha$, the cyclic shift of $L$ is
the language of all words $yx$ over $\alpha$ such that $xy \in L$ for some words $x$ and $y$; that
is, the language of all rotations of the words of $L$.

articles.title: Detour labels
articles.statement:
For a word $y = b_1 \cdots b_n$ over $T'$, the detour labels of $y$ are
the sequence of ε-NFA labels $\varepsilon, b_1, \ldots, b_n, \varepsilon$: an ε-move, the letters
of $y$ in order, and a final ε-move.

They label the detour that the substitution ε-NFA takes through a copy of the automaton for one
letter.

articles.title: Soundness of the paths of the substitution ε-NFA
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over $T$ with start
state $q_0$, and for each letter $a \in T$ let $N_a$ be a DFA over $T'$, with accepted language
$L(N_a)$; for a word $w = a_1 \cdots a_n$ over $T$ write $L_w = L(N_{a_1}) \cdots L(N_{a_n})$,
which is $\{\varepsilon\}$ when $w$ is empty. Let $x$ be a sequence of labels, each a letter of
$T'$ or $\varepsilon$, let $\bar x$ be the word over $T'$ obtained from $x$ by deleting the
$\varepsilon$'s, and suppose the ε-NFA built from $M$ and the $N_a$ has a path reading $x$ from
the state $q_0$ of $M$ to a state $u$. If $u$ is a state $q$ of $M$, then there is a word $w$
over $T$ such that $M$ reaches $q$ from $q_0$ on $w$ and $\bar x \in L_w$. If $u$ is the state
$p$ of the copy of $N_a$ entered from the state $q$ of $M$, then there are a word $w$ over $T$
such that $M$ reaches $q$ from $q_0$ on $w$, a word $y_1 \in L_w$ and a word $y_2$ over $T'$
such that $\bar x = y_1 y_2$ and $N_a$ reaches $p$ from its start state on $y_2$.

articles.title: Soundness of the homomorphic-image ε-NFA
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet $T$ with
start state $q_0$, and let $\varphi$ map letters of $T$ to words over $T'$; for a word $w$ over $T$,
write $\varphi(w)$ for the concatenation of the images of its letters. Suppose the ε-NFA of $M$ and
$\varphi$ has a path from the state $q_0$ of $M$ to a state $u$, with label sequence $x$, and let
$\bar x$ be the word formed by the non-ε labels of $x$. If $u$ is a state $q$ of $M$, then there is
a word $w$ over $T$ on which $M$ reaches $q$ from $q_0$ and $\varphi(w) = \bar x$. If $u$ is the
intermediate state $(q, a, i)$, then there is a word $w$ over $T$ on which $M$ reaches $q$ from
$q_0$ and $\varphi(w)$ followed by the first $i$ letters of $\varphi(a)$ (all of $\varphi(a)$ if it
is shorter) equals $\bar x$.

articles.title: Words leading a DFA from a state into a set of states
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ over $\alpha$ with
state type $\sigma$, a state $p \in \sigma$ and a set $S \subseteq \sigma$ of states, this is the
language of all words $w$ over $\alpha$ such that the run of $M$ started in $p$ on $w$ ends in a
state of $S$.

articles.title: Homomorphic images of regular languages over finite alphabets are regular
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a
finite alphabet, $T'$ an arbitrary (possibly infinite) alphabet, and $\varphi$ a map from $T$ to
words over $T'$, extended to words by $\varphi(a_1 \cdots a_n) = \varphi(a_1) \cdots \varphi(a_n)$.
If $L$ is a regular language over $T$, then its image $\{\varphi(w) : w \in L\}$ is a regular
language over $T'$.

articles.title: Finishing a letter's image in the image ε-NFA
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet $T$
with transition function $\delta$, and let $\varphi$ map letters of $T$ to words over $T'$. For
every state $q$ of $M$, letter $a$ and natural number $i$, the ε-NFA of $M$ and $\varphi$ has a path
to the state $\delta(q, a)$ of $M$ from the state $(q, a, i + 1)$ if $i + 1 < |\varphi(a)|$, and
from $\delta(q, a)$ otherwise, whose labels are the letters of $\varphi(a)$ after position $i$
(positions counted from $0$), in order and all non-ε.

articles.title: Spelling out a letter's image in the image ε-NFA
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet
$T$ with transition function $\delta$, and let $\varphi$ map letters of $T$ to words over $T'$. For
every state $q$ of $M$ and letter $a$, the ε-NFA of $M$ and $\varphi$ has a path from the state $q$
to the state $\delta(q, a)$ whose label sequence is a single ε-label if $\varphi(a)$ is empty, and
the letters of $\varphi(a)$ in order, all non-ε, otherwise.

articles.title: Paths inside one copy of a letter automaton
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over $T$, and for each
letter $a \in T$ let $N_a$ be a DFA over $T'$. For every state $q$ of $M$, letter $a \in T$,
state $p$ of $N_a$ and word $y$ over $T'$, the ε-NFA built from $M$ and the $N_a$ has a path
reading the letters of $y$, with no ε-moves, from the state $p$ of the copy of $N_a$ entered from
$q$ to the state of the same copy that $N_a$ reaches from $p$ on $y$.

articles.title: Shuffle of two words
articles.statement:
The relation "$w$ is a shuffle of $u$ and $v$" on words over $\alpha$
is defined inductively: the empty word is a shuffle of the empty word and the empty word, and if
$w$ is a shuffle of $u$ and $v$, then for every letter $a$ the word $aw$ is a shuffle of $au$ and
$v$, and a shuffle of $u$ and $av$. Thus $w$ interleaves the letters of $u$ and of $v$, keeping
their order within each word.

articles.title: NFA for the left quotient by a language
articles.statement:
Given a DFA $M$ over an alphabet $T$ with state
set $\sigma$ and a language $R$ over $T$, this is the NFA with state set $\sigma$ and the same
accepting states as $M$, in which from a state $q$ on a letter $a$ the only possible move is to
the state $M$ reaches from $q$ on $a$, and whose start states are the states that $M$ reaches from
its start state on the words of $R$.

The set of start states is defined by quantifying over $R$, so it is not computable in general.

articles.title: Regular languages are closed under left quotients by arbitrary languages
articles.statement:
If $L$ is a
regular language over an alphabet $T$ and $R$ is any language over $T$, then the left quotient
$\{y \mid \exists x \in R,\ xy \in L\}$ of $L$ by $R$ is regular.

articles.title: The ε-NFA for a substitution
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over $T$ with states $\sigma$, and for each
letter $a \in T$ let $N_a$ be a DFA over $T'$ with states $\tau_a$. This ε-NFA over $T'$ has as
states the states $q$ of $M$ and the triples $(q, a, p)$ with $q$ a state of $M$, $a \in T$ and
$p$ a state of $N_a$, read as the state $p$ of the copy of $N_a$ entered from $q$. A state $q$ of
$M$ has an ε-move to $(q, a, s_a)$ for every $a \in T$, where $s_a$ is the start state of $N_a$,
and no letter moves. A state $(q, a, p)$ moves on a letter $b$ to $(q, a, \delta_a(p, b))$, where
$\delta_a$ is the transition function of $N_a$, and has an ε-move, to the state $\delta_M(q, a)$
of $M$, exactly when $p$ is an accepting state of $N_a$; here $\delta_M$ is the transition
function of $M$. The start state is the start state of $M$, and the accepting states are the
accepting states of $M$.

articles.title: The ε-NFA for the homomorphic image
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet $T$ with start
state $q_0$, transition function $\delta$ and accepting states $F$, let $\varphi$ map letters of $T$
to words over $T'$, and let $N$ be the maximum of the lengths $|\varphi(a)|$ over $a \in T$. The
ε-NFA over $T'$ has as states the states of $M$ together with the triples $(q, a, i)$ with $q$ a
state of $M$, $a \in T$ and $0 \le i < N$. Write $\mathrm{next}(q, a, i)$ for $(q, a, i + 1)$ if
$i + 1 < |\varphi(a)|$ and for $\delta(q, a)$ otherwise. From a state $q$ of $M$, reading $b$ leads
to $\mathrm{next}(q, a, 0)$ for each letter $a$ whose image starts with $b$, and an ε-move leads to
$\delta(q, a)$ for each letter $a$ with $\varphi(a)$ empty. From $(q, a, i)$, reading $b$ leads to
$\mathrm{next}(q, a, i)$ if the letter of $\varphi(a)$ at position $i$ (counted from $0$) is $b$,
and there are no ε-moves. The only start state is $q_0$ and the accepting states are those in
$F$.

articles.title: DFA for the right quotient by a language
articles.statement:
Given a DFA $M$ over an alphabet $T$ with state
set $\sigma$ and a language $R$ over $T$, this is the DFA with the same states, transition function
and start state as $M$, whose accepting states are the states $q$ from which some word of $R$
leads $M$ to an accepting state of $M$.

The accepting set is defined by quantifying over $R$, so it is not computable in general.

articles.title: Regular languages are closed under right quotients by arbitrary languages
articles.statement:
If $L$ is a
regular language over an alphabet $T$ and $R$ is any language over $T$, then the right quotient
$\{x \mid \exists y \in R,\ xy \in L\}$ of $L$ by $R$ is regular.

articles.title: The shuffle of two regular languages is regular
articles.statement: **The shuffle of two regular languages is regular.**

articles.title: Shuffle automaton of two DFAs
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be DFAs over $\alpha$ with state types
$\sigma$ and $\tau$, start states $s_M$ and $s_N$, sets of accepting states $F_M$ and $F_N$, and
transition functions $\delta_M$ and $\delta_N$. Their shuffle automaton is the NFA over $\alpha$
with state type $\sigma \times \tau$, the single start state $(s_M, s_N)$ and accepting states
$F_M \times F_N$, which on a letter $a$ moves from a state $(p, q)$ to the two states
$(\delta_M(p, a), q)$ and $(p, \delta_N(q, a))$.

articles.title: Shuffle of two languages
articles.statement:
For languages $L$ and $M$ over $\alpha$, the shuffle of $L$ and
$M$ is the language of all words $w$ over $\alpha$ such that $w$ is a shuffle of some word $u \in L$
and some word $v \in M$, that is, $w$ interleaves $u$ and $v$.

articles.title: States of the homomorphic-image ε-NFA
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a finite alphabet, let $\varphi$ map
letters of $T$ to words over $T'$, let $\sigma$ be a set (the states of a DFA), and let $N$ be the
maximum of the lengths $|\varphi(a)|$ over $a \in T$. The states of the ε-NFA form the disjoint
union of $\sigma$ and the set of triples $(q, a, i)$ with $q \in \sigma$, $a \in T$ and
$0 \le i < N$.

articles.title: Substitution of languages for letters
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $T$, and let
$s$ assign to each letter $a \in T$ a language $s(a)$ over an alphabet $T'$. The substitution of
$s$ into $L$ is the language over $T'$ of all words $y_1 y_2 \cdots y_n$ for which there is a word
$a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n \in L$ with $y_i \in s(a_i)$ for every $i$.

articles.title: Regular languages are closed under substitution over a finite alphabet
articles.statement:
Let $T$ be a
finite alphabet and $T'$ any alphabet. If $L$ is a regular language over $T$ and $s(a)$ is a
regular language over $T'$ for every letter $a \in T$, then the substitution of $s$ into $L$ is a
regular language over $T'$.

articles.title: Finite languages are regular
articles.statement: Every finite language over any alphabet is regular.

articles.title: Languages of bounded word length are regular
articles.statement:
Over a finite alphabet, if every word of a
language $L$ has length at most $n$, for some natural number $n$, then $L$ is regular.

articles.title: Single-word languages are regular
articles.statement:
For every word $w$ over any alphabet, the language
whose only word is $w$ is regular.

articles.title: Regex-denoted languages are closed under union
articles.statement: Denoted languages are closed under union.

articles.title: Single-letter languages are regex-denoted
articles.statement: A singleton `{[a]}` is denoted by `char a`.

articles.title: Coefficient in the equation system of a DFA
articles.statement:
The system of equations of a DFA at a state: the coefficient of `X j` in the
equation for `X q`, the finite union of the singletons `{[a]}` over the letters taking
`q` to `j`.

articles.title: Constant term in the equation system of a DFA
articles.statement: The constant term of the equation for `X q`: `1` on accepting states, `0` otherwise.

articles.title: DFA equation coefficients are regex-denoted
articles.statement: Every coefficient is denoted by a regular expression.

articles.title: DFA equation constant terms are regex-denoted
articles.statement: Every constant term is denoted by a regular expression.

articles.title: Coefficient after eliminating the last state
articles.statement:
The coefficient of the reduced system obtained by eliminating the last state: the old
coefficient, plus the detour through the last state, which may loop there any number of
times.

articles.title: Constant term after eliminating the last state
articles.statement: The constant term of the reduced system obtained by eliminating the last state.

articles.title: Languages of DFAs on finitely many numbered states are regex-denoted
articles.statement: The language of a DFA with `Fin n` states is denoted by a regular expression.

articles.title: Kleene's theorem: DFA languages are regex-denoted
articles.statement: The language of a DFA over a finite state type is denoted by a regular expression.

articles.title: Solving a system of language equations
articles.statement:
If the languages `X i` satisfy
`X i = (∑ j, A i j * X j) + B i` with every coefficient `A i j` excluding the empty word
and every coefficient and constant term denoted by a regular expression, then every `X i`
is denoted by a regular expression. The proof eliminates the last state with Arden's lemma
and applies the induction hypothesis to the reduced system.

articles.title: Kleene's theorem, converse direction
articles.statement:
**Kleene's theorem, converse direction** (Sipser, *Introduction to the Theory of
Computation*, 3rd ed., Theorem 1.54): every regular language over a finite alphabet is denoted
by a regular expression. Source: M. Sipser, *Introduction to the Theory of Computation*, 3rd
ed., Theorem 1.54.

articles.title: Sharpness of the finite-alphabet hypothesis
articles.statement:
Over an infinite alphabet, the language
of one-letter words is regular but is denoted by no regular expression, since a regular
expression mentions only finitely many letters. Source: M. Sipser, *Introduction to the
Theory of Computation*, 3rd ed., Theorem 1.54 (finite alphabet).

articles.title: Equation system satisfied by DFA state languages
articles.statement:
The DFA equations: from `q`, either step on a letter and continue, or stop if `q`
accepts.

articles.title: Language accepted from a DFA state
articles.statement: The language accepted from a state: the unknown `X q` of the system.

articles.title: Language denoted by a regular expression
articles.statement: A language is denoted by a regular expression when it is `r.matches'` for some `r`.

articles.title: Kleene's theorem
articles.statement:
**Kleene's theorem** (Sipser, 3rd ed., Theorem 1.54): over a finite alphabet, a language
is regular if and only if it is denoted by a regular expression. Source: M. Sipser,
*Introduction to the Theory of Computation*, 3rd ed., Theorem 1.54.

articles.title: Regex-denoted languages are closed under Kleene star
articles.statement: Denoted languages are closed under Kleene star.

articles.title: Membership in a DFA equation coefficient
articles.statement: Membership in a coefficient: the word is a single letter taking `q` to `j`.

articles.title: Letters of matched words occur in the regular expression
articles.statement: Every letter of a word matched by `r` occurs in `r`.

articles.title: Membership in a finite union of languages
articles.statement: Membership in a finite union of languages.

articles.title: Regex-denoted languages are closed under concatenation
articles.statement: Denoted languages are closed under concatenation.

articles.title: DFA equation coefficients exclude the empty word
articles.statement: No coefficient contains the empty word.

articles.title: Empty word outside a concatenation
articles.statement: The empty word is not in a concatenation whose right factor excludes it.

articles.title: The language of the empty word is regex-denoted
articles.statement: The language `{[]}` is denoted by `1`.

articles.title: Letters occurring in a regular expression
articles.statement: The letters occurring in a regular expression.

articles.title: The one-letter-word DFA accepts exactly words of length one
articles.statement: The one-letter-word DFA accepts exactly the words of length one.

articles.title: DFA accepting the one-letter words
articles.statement: The three-state DFA accepting exactly the one-letter words.

articles.title: Regex-denoted languages are closed under finite unions
articles.statement: Denoted languages are closed under finite unions.

articles.title: The empty language is regex-denoted
articles.statement: The empty language is denoted by `0`.

articles.title: Total output of a composite sequential transducer
articles.statement:
Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer
from $I$ to $M$, $S_2$ one from $M$ to $O$, and $C$ their composition. For a sequential
transducer $S$ with start state $s$, initial output $\iota$ and final output map $\phi$, and a
word $x$, let $\delta_S(s, x)$ be the state $S$ reaches by reading $x$ from $s$ and
$\lambda_S(s, x)$ the concatenation of the words it emits along the way, and call the
concatenation $\iota \, \lambda_S(s, x) \, \phi(\delta_S(s, x))$ the whole output of $S$ on $x$
(acceptance plays no role). Then for every word $x$ over $I$, the whole output of $C$ on $x$
equals the whole output of $S_2$ on the whole output of $S_1$ on $x$.

articles.title: Output of the second transducer on the first one's whole output
articles.statement:
Let $S_1$ be a
sequential transducer from $I$ to $M$ and $S_2$ one from $M$ to $O$, with start states $s_1$ and
$s_2$. For a transducer $S$, a state $q$ and a word $w$, write $\delta_S(q, w)$ for the state $S$
reaches by reading $w$ from $q$ and $\lambda_S(q, w)$ for the concatenation of the words it emits
along the way (without initial or final output); juxtaposition of words is concatenation. For a
word $x$ over $I$, let $\iota$ be the initial output of $S_1$, let $u = \lambda_{S_1}(s_1, x)$,
let $f$ be the final output of $S_1$ at $\delta_{S_1}(s_1, x)$, and let
$r = \delta_{S_2}(s_2, \iota)$. Then
$\lambda_{S_2}(s_2, \iota u f) = \lambda_{S_2}(s_2, \iota) \, \lambda_{S_2}(r, u) \,
\lambda_{S_2}(\delta_{S_2}(r, u), f)$.

articles.title: Output of a composite sequential transducer
articles.statement:
Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer from
$I$ to $M$, $S_2$ one from $M$ to $O$, and $C$ their composition. For a transducer $S$, a state
$q$ and a word $w$, write $\lambda_S(q, w)$ for the concatenation of the words $S$ emits while
reading $w$ from $q$ (without initial or final output). Then for all states $q_1$ of $S_1$ and
$q_2$ of $S_2$ and every word $x$ over $I$,
$\lambda_C((q_1, q_2), x) = \lambda_{S_2}(q_2, \lambda_{S_1}(q_1, x))$.

articles.title: State of the second transducer after the first one's whole output
articles.statement:
Let $S_1$ be a
sequential transducer from $I$ to $M$ and $S_2$ one from $M$ to $O$, with start states $s_1$ and
$s_2$. For a transducer $S$, a state $q$ and a word $w$, write $\delta_S(q, w)$ for the state $S$
reaches by reading $w$ from $q$ and $\lambda_S(q, w)$ for the concatenation of the words it emits
along the way (without initial or final output); juxtaposition of words is concatenation. For a
word $x$ over $I$, let $\iota$ be the initial output of $S_1$, let $u = \lambda_{S_1}(s_1, x)$,
and let $f$ be the final output of $S_1$ at $\delta_{S_1}(s_1, x)$. Then
$\delta_{S_2}(s_2, \iota u f) = \delta_{S_2}(\delta_{S_2}(\delta_{S_2}(s_2, \iota), u), f)$.

articles.title: States reached by a composite sequential transducer
articles.statement:
Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer
from $I$ to $M$, $S_2$ one from $M$ to $O$, and $C$ their composition. For a transducer $S$, a
state $q$ and a word $w$, write $\delta_S(q, w)$ for the state $S$ reaches by reading $w$ from
$q$ and $\lambda_S(q, w)$ for the concatenation of the words it emits along the way (without
initial or final output). Then for all states $q_1$ of $S_1$ and $q_2$ of $S_2$ and every word
$x$ over $I$,
$\delta_C((q_1, q_2), x) = (\delta_{S_1}(q_1, x), \delta_{S_2}(q_2, \lambda_{S_1}(q_1, x)))$.

articles.title: One step of a composite transducer: the successor state
articles.statement:
Let $S_1$ be a sequential
transducer from $I$ to $M$, $S_2$ one from $M$ to $O$, and $C$ their composition. Let $q_1$ be a
state of $S_1$, $q_2$ a state of $S_2$ and $a \in I$ a letter, and suppose that $S_1$, reading
$a$ in state $q_1$, moves to $q_1'$ and emits the word $w$. Then $C$, reading $a$ in state
$(q_1, q_2)$, moves to $(q_1', q_2')$, where $q_2'$ is the state $S_2$ reaches by reading $w$
from $q_2$.

articles.title: One step of a composite transducer: the output
articles.statement:
Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer from
$I$ to $M$, $S_2$ one from $M$ to $O$, and $C$ their composition. Let $q_1$ be a state of $S_1$,
$q_2$ a state of $S_2$ and $a \in I$ a letter, and let $w$ be the word $S_1$ emits when it reads
$a$ in state $q_1$. Then the word $C$ emits when it reads $a$ in state $(q_1, q_2)$ is the
concatenation of the words $S_2$ emits while reading $w$ from $q_2$.

articles.title: Composition of sequential transducers
articles.statement:
Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer from $I$ to
$M$ with start state $s_1$, initial output $\iota_1$ and final output map $\phi_1$, and let $S_2$
be one from $M$ to $O$ with start state $s_2$, initial output $\iota_2$ and final output map
$\phi_2$. For a transducer $S$, a state $q$ and a word $w$, write $\delta_S(q, w)$ for the state
$S$ reaches by reading $w$ from $q$ and $\lambda_S(q, w)$ for the concatenation of the words it
emits along the way. The composition of $S_1$ and $S_2$ is the sequential transducer from $I$ to
$O$ whose states are the pairs $(q_1, q_2)$ of a state of $S_1$ and a state of $S_2$, where:
reading a letter $a$ in state $(q_1, q_2)$, if $S_1$ reading $a$ in $q_1$ moves to $q_1'$ and
emits $w$, the composition moves to $(q_1', \delta_{S_2}(q_2, w))$ and emits
$\lambda_{S_2}(q_2, w)$; the start state is $(s_1, \delta_{S_2}(s_2, \iota_1))$; the initial
output is $\iota_2$ followed by $\lambda_{S_2}(s_2, \iota_1)$; a state $(q_1, q_2)$ is accepting
when $q_1$ is accepting for $S_1$ and $\delta_{S_2}(q_2, \phi_1(q_1))$ is accepting for $S_2$; and
the final output at $(q_1, q_2)$ is $\lambda_{S_2}(q_2, \phi_1(q_1))$ followed by
$\phi_2(\delta_{S_2}(q_2, \phi_1(q_1)))$.

In words: run $S_1$ and feed its output, including its initial output (fed through $S_2$ before
any input is read) and its final output, through $S_2$.

articles.title: Inverse sequential transduction preserves regular languages
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a sequential
transducer with finitely many states, input alphabet $I$ and output alphabet $O$, and let $L$ be
a regular language over $O$. Then the preimage of $L$ under $S$, the set of words over $I$ that
$S$ translates to some word of $L$, is regular.

The proof is the product of $S$ with a DFA for $L$, started in the DFA state reached on the
initial output of $S$.

articles.title: Mealy machine
articles.statement:
A Mealy machine with state set $Q$, input alphabet $I$ and output
alphabet $O$ consists of a start state in $Q$ and a transition function that, given a state
$q \in Q$ and an input letter $a \in I$, returns a successor state in $Q$ and a single output
letter in $O$; thus the output of a transition depends on the state and the input letter.

articles.title: Moore machine
articles.statement:
A Moore machine with state type $Q$, input alphabet $\Sigma$ and output
alphabet $\Gamma$ consists of a transition function, assigning to each state $q$ and input
letter $a$ a successor state $\delta(q, a) \in Q$, an output function $\lambda : Q \to \Gamma$,
and a start state $q_0 \in Q$. The output depends only on the state.

articles.title: The product DFA recognizes the preimage
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a sequential transducer with output
alphabet $\Gamma$ and let $M$ be a DFA over $\Gamma$. The language accepted by the product DFA
of $S$ and $M$ equals the preimage under $S$ of the language accepted by $M$, that is, the set
of input words that $S$ translates to some word accepted by $M$.

articles.title: Runs of the product DFA
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a sequential transducer and $M$ a DFA over the
output alphabet of $S$. For every input word $x$, state $q$ of $S$ and state $r$ of $M$, the
product DFA of $S$ and $M$, started in $(q, r)$ and run on $x$, ends in the state $(q', r')$,
where $q'$ is the final state of the run of $S$ from $q$ on $x$ and $r'$ is the state that $M$
reaches from $r$ on the output word of that run.

articles.title: Product DFA of a sequential transducer and a DFA
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a sequential transducer
with state type $Q$, input alphabet $\Sigma$ and output alphabet $\Gamma$, and let $M$ be a DFA
over $\Gamma$ with state type $P$. The product DFA of $S$ and $M$ is the DFA over $\Sigma$ with
state type $Q \times P$ defined as follows. In state $(q, r)$ on a letter $a$, if $S$ moves from
$q$ to $q'$ emitting the word $w$, it moves to $(q', r')$, where $r'$ is the state $M$ reaches
from $r$ on $w$. Its start state is $(q_0, r_0)$, where $q_0$ is the start state of $S$ and
$r_0$ is the state $M$ reaches from its start state on the initial output of $S$. A state
$(q, r)$ is accepting when $q$ is an accepting state of $S$ and the state $M$ reaches from $r$
on the final output of $S$ at $q$ is an accepting state of $M$.

articles.title: Preimage of a language under a sequential transducer
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a sequential transducer
with input alphabet $\Sigma$ and output alphabet $\Gamma$, and let $L$ be a language over
$\Gamma$. The preimage of $L$ under $S$ is the language over $\Sigma$ consisting of the words $x$
for which there is a word $y \in L$ such that $S$ translates $x$ to $y$.

articles.title: Run of a Mealy machine
articles.statement:
The run of a Mealy machine $M$ from a state $q$ on an input
word $a_1 \cdots a_n$ is the pair $(q_n, o_1 \cdots o_n)$, where $q_0 = q$ and, for each
$1 \le i \le n$, $M$ moves from $q_{i-1}$ on $a_i$ to $q_i$ emitting the output letter $o_i$.

articles.title: Run of a Moore machine
articles.statement:
The run of a Moore machine $M$ with output function $\lambda$
from a state $q$ on an input word $a_1 \cdots a_n$ is the pair
$(q_n, \lambda(q_0) \lambda(q_1) \cdots \lambda(q_n))$, where $q_0 = q$ and, for each
$1 \le i \le n$, $q_i$ is the successor of $q_{i-1}$ on $a_i$. The output word has $n + 1$
letters and begins with the output of the starting state.

articles.title: Run of a sequential transducer
articles.statement:
The run of a sequential transducer $S$ from a state $q$
on an input word $a_1 \cdots a_n$ is the pair $(q_n, w_1 w_2 \cdots w_n)$, where $q_0 = q$ and,
for each $1 \le i \le n$, $S$ moves from $q_{i-1}$ on $a_i$ to $q_i$ emitting the word $w_i$.
The initial output and the final outputs of $S$ are not included.

articles.title: Output word of a Mealy machine run
articles.statement:
For a Mealy machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input
word $x$, the output word of $M$ from $q$ on $x$ is the second component of the run of $M$ from
$q$ on $x$: the word of output letters emitted along that run, one per input letter.

articles.title: Output word of a Moore machine run
articles.statement:
For a Moore machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input
word $x$, the output word of $M$ from $q$ on $x$ is the second component of the run of $M$ from
$q$ on $x$: the outputs of the states visited along that run, starting with the output of $q$;
it has one more letter than $x$.

articles.title: Output of a sequential transducer on a concatenation
articles.statement:
For a sequential transducer $S$,
a state $q$ and input words $x$ and $y$, the output word of the run of $S$ from $q$ on $xy$ is
the output word of the run from $q$ on $x$ followed by the output word of the run on $y$ from
the final state of the run from $q$ on $x$.

articles.title: Output of a Mealy machine on a nonempty word
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Mealy machine, $q$ a state,
$a$ an input letter and $x$ an input word, and let $q'$ and $o$ be the successor state and the
output letter of $M$ in state $q$ on letter $a$. The output word of the run of $M$ from $q$ on
$ax$ is $o$ followed by the output word of the run from $q'$ on $x$.

articles.title: Output of a Moore machine on a nonempty word
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Moore machine, $q$ a state,
$a$ an input letter and $x$ an input word, and let $q'$ be the successor state of $M$ in state
$q$ on letter $a$. The output word of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $ax$ is the output of $q$
followed by the output word of the run from $q'$ on $x$.

articles.title: Output of a sequential transducer on a nonempty word
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a sequential
transducer, $q$ a state, $a$ an input letter and $x$ an input word, and let $q'$ and $w$ be the
successor state and the output word of $S$ in state $q$ on letter $a$. The output word of the
run of $S$ from $q$ on $ax$ is $w$ followed by the output word of the run from $q'$ on $x$.

articles.title: Moore machine output via its sequential rendering
articles.statement:
For a Moore machine $M$, a state $q$
and an input word $x$, the output word of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $x$ is the output of $q$
followed by the output word of the run of the sequential rendering of $M$ from $q$ on $x$.

articles.title: Output word of a sequential transducer run
articles.statement:
For a sequential transducer $S$, a state $q$
and an input word $x$, the output word of the run from $q$ on $x$ is the concatenation of the
output words that $S$ emits on the successive letters of $x$, starting in $q$ and moving to the
successor state after each letter; the initial and final outputs are not included.

articles.title: Final state of a Mealy machine run
articles.statement:
For a Mealy machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input
word $x$, the final state of the run from $q$ on $x$ is the state reached by starting in $q$
and moving, on each successive letter of $x$, to the successor state given by the transition
function of $M$; on the empty word it is $q$.

articles.title: Final state of a Moore machine run
articles.statement:
For a Moore machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input
word $x$, the final state of the run from $q$ on $x$ is the state reached by starting in $q$
and moving, on each successive letter of $x$, to the successor state given by the transition
function of $M$; on the empty word it is $q$.

articles.title: Final state of a sequential transducer on a concatenation
articles.statement:
For a sequential transducer
$S$, a state $q$ and input words $x$ and $y$, the final state of the run of $S$ from $q$ on $xy$
is the final state of the run on $y$ from the final state of the run from $q$ on $x$.

articles.title: Final state of a Mealy machine on a nonempty word
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Mealy machine, $q$ a
state, $a$ an input letter and $x$ an input word, and let $q'$ be the successor state of $M$ in
state $q$ on letter $a$. The final state of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $ax$ is the final state of
the run from $q'$ on $x$.

articles.title: Final state of a Moore machine run on a nonempty word
articles.statement:
For a Moore machine $M$ with
transition function $\delta$, a state $q$, an input letter $a$ and an input word $w$, the final
state of the run of $M$ from $q$ on the word $aw$ equals the final state of the run of $M$ from
$\delta(q, a)$ on $w$.

articles.title: Final state of a sequential transducer run on a nonempty word
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a sequential
transducer, $q$ a state, $a$ an input letter and $w$ an input word, and let $q'$ be the successor
state of $q$ on $a$ under the transition function of $S$. Then the final state of the run of $S$
from $q$ on the word $aw$ equals the final state of the run of $S$ from $q'$ on $w$.

articles.title: Final state of a sequential transducer run
articles.statement:
For a sequential transducer $S$, a state $q$
and an input word $w$, the final state of the run of $S$ from $q$ on $w$ is obtained by starting
in $q$, reading the letters of $w$ in order, moving at each letter to the successor state given
by the transition function of $S$, and taking the state reached at the end.

articles.title: The sequential transducer of a Mealy machine has the same run outputs
articles.statement:
For a Mealy
machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $w$, the output word of the run from $q$ on $w$ of the
sequential transducer associated with $M$ (excluding its initial and final outputs) equals the
output word of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $w$.

articles.title: The sequential transducer of a Mealy machine has the same final states
articles.statement:
For a Mealy
machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $w$, the final state of the run from $q$ on $w$ of the
