sequential transducer associated with $M$ equals the final state of the run of $M$ from $q$ on
$w$.

articles.title: Sequential transducer
articles.statement:
A sequential transducer with states in a type $Q$, input letters in
a type $\Sigma$ and output letters in a type $\Gamma$ consists of a transition function assigning
to each state $q \in Q$ and input letter $a \in \Sigma$ a successor state in $Q$ and an output
word over $\Gamma$, a start state in $Q$, a set of accepting states $F \subseteq Q$, an initial
output word over $\Gamma$, and, for each state in $Q$, a final output word over $\Gamma$.

No finiteness is assumed of $Q$, $\Sigma$ or $\Gamma$.

articles.title: The sequential transducer of a Moore machine
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Moore machine with transition
function $\delta$, output function $\lambda$ and start state $q_0$. Its sequential transducer has
the same states and the start state $q_0$; reading a letter $a$ in state $q$ it moves to
$\delta(q, a)$ and emits the one-letter word $\lambda(\delta(q, a))$; every state is accepting;
the initial output is the one-letter word $\lambda(q_0)$; and every final output is empty.

articles.title: Every state of the sequential transducer of a Moore machine is accepting
articles.statement:
For a Moore
machine $M$, the set of accepting states of the sequential transducer associated with $M$ is the
set of all states.

articles.title: Every state of the sequential transducer of a Mealy machine is accepting
articles.statement:
For a Mealy
machine $M$, the set of accepting states of the sequential transducer associated with $M$ is the
set of all states.

articles.title: Final outputs of the sequential transducer of a Moore machine
articles.statement:
For a Moore machine $M$
and every state $q$, the final output word at $q$ of the sequential transducer associated with
$M$ is empty.

articles.title: Final outputs of the sequential transducer of a Mealy machine
articles.statement:
For every Mealy machine
$M$ and every state $q$, the final output of the sequential transducer of $M$ at $q$ is the
empty word.

articles.title: Initial output of the sequential transducer of a Moore machine
articles.statement:
For every Moore machine
$M$, the initial output of the sequential transducer of $M$ is the one-letter word consisting of
the output of the start state of $M$.

articles.title: Initial output of the sequential transducer of a Mealy machine
articles.statement:
For every Mealy machine
$M$, the initial output of the sequential transducer of $M$ is the empty word.

articles.title: Mealy machine as a sequential transducer
articles.statement:
The sequential transducer of a Mealy machine
$M$ has the states and the start state of $M$; on an input letter $a$ in a state $q$ it moves
to the state that $M$ moves to and emits the one-letter word consisting of the letter that $M$
outputs on this transition. Every state accepts, and the initial and final outputs are empty.

articles.title: Transduction of a Moore machine
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Moore machine with start state $q_0$, and
write $o(q)$ for the output of a state $q$. On an input word $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$, let $q_i$ be
the state that $M$ moves to from $q_{i-1}$ on $a_i$. The transduction of $M$ on this word is the
output word $o(q_0)\, o(q_1) \cdots o(q_n)$, of length $n + 1$.

articles.title: Transduction of a Mealy machine
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a Mealy machine with start state $q_0$. On
an input word $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$, for each $i$ let $q_i$ and $b_i$ be the state that $M$ moves
to and the letter that it outputs when it reads $a_i$ in state $q_{i-1}$. The transduction of
$M$ on this word is the output word $b_1 b_2 \cdots b_n$.

articles.title: Translations of a composite sequential transducer
articles.statement:
Let $S_1$ be a sequential transducer
from an alphabet $A$ to an alphabet $B$, and $S_2$ one from $B$ to an alphabet $C$. For every word
$x$ over $A$ and every word $y$ over $C$, the composition of $S_1$ and $S_2$ translates $x$ to $y$
if and only if there is a word $z$ over $B$ such that $S_1$ translates $x$ to $z$ and $S_2$
translates $z$ to $y$.

articles.title: The sequential transducer of a Moore machine computes its transduction
articles.statement:
For every Moore
machine $M$, input word $x$ and output word $y$, the sequential transducer of $M$ translates $x$
to $y$ if and only if the transduction of $M$ on $x$ is $y$.

articles.title: The sequential transducer of a Mealy machine computes its transduction
articles.statement:
For every Mealy
machine $M$, input word $x$ and output word $y$, the sequential transducer of $M$ translates $x$
to $y$ if and only if the transduction of $M$ on $x$ is $y$.

articles.title: Translation by a sequential transducer
articles.statement:
A sequential transducer $S$ translates an input
word $x$ to an output word $y$ when the run of $S$ on $x$ from its start state ends in an
accepting state $q$ and $y$ is the concatenation of the initial output of $S$, the output words
emitted by the transitions along the run, and the final output of $S$ at $q$.

articles.title: Language of a generalized regular expression
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $\alpha$, the language over
$\alpha$ denoted by a generalized regular expression over $\alpha$ is defined recursively, for
generalized regular expressions $e$, $e_1$, $e_2$: an ordinary regular expression denotes the
language it matches; the complement $\neg e$ denotes the complement, in the set of all words over
$\alpha$, of the language of $e$; the union $e_1 + e_2$ denotes the union and the concatenation
$e_1 e_2$ the concatenation of the languages of $e_1$ and $e_2$; and the star $e^*$ denotes the
Kleene star of the language of $e$.

articles.title: Generalized regular expressions
articles.statement:
A generalized regular expression over an alphabet
$\alpha$ is built from ordinary regular expressions over $\alpha$ by complement, union,
concatenation and Kleene star: every ordinary regular expression over $\alpha$ is one, and if
$e$, $e_1$, $e_2$ are generalized regular expressions, then so are the complement $\neg e$, the
union $e_1 + e_2$, the concatenation $e_1 e_2$ and the star $e^*$.

articles.title: Bounded generalized star height
articles.statement:
A language $L$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ has generalized
star height at most $n$, for a natural number $n$, if some generalized regular expression over
$\alpha$ whose generalized star height is at most $n$ denotes $L$.

articles.title: Star height of a regular expression
articles.statement:
The star height of an ordinary regular expression
is the nesting depth of the Kleene star in it: the expressions for the empty language and the
empty word and the single letters have star height $0$; a union $e_1 + e_2$ and a concatenation
$e_1 e_2$ have the larger of the star heights of $e_1$ and $e_2$; and $e^*$ has star height one
more than $e$.

articles.title: Generalized star height
articles.statement:
The generalized star height of a generalized regular expression
is the nesting depth of the Kleene star in it, counting the stars inside its ordinary regular
subexpressions: for generalized regular expressions $e$, $e_1$, $e_2$, an ordinary regular
expression has its usual star height; the complement $\neg e$ has the star height of $e$; the
union $e_1 + e_2$ and the concatenation $e_1 e_2$ have the larger of the star heights of $e_1$
and $e_2$; and the star $e^*$ has star height one more than $e$.

articles.title: Correctness of Thompson's construction
articles.statement:
The automaton accepts exactly the words the
regular expression matches.

articles.title: Number of states of Thompson's automaton
articles.statement:
For every regular expression $r$, the number of
states of Thompson's automaton of $r$ is $n(r)$, the Thompson state count of $r$: $n(0) = 0$,
$n(\varepsilon) = 1$, $n(a) = 2$ for a letter $a$, $n(P + Q) = n(P) + n(Q)$, $n(PQ) = n(P) + n(Q)$
and $n(P^*) = n(P) + 1$.

articles.title: Single-letter automaton
articles.statement:
For a letter $a$ of the alphabet $\alpha$, this is the ε-NFA over
$\alpha$ with two states, a start state and an accepting state, and a single move, which reads $a$
and goes from the start state to the accepting state; it has no other moves and no ε-moves.

articles.title: Concatenation of ε-NFAs
articles.statement:
Given ε-NFAs $M$ with state set $\sigma$ and $N$ with state set
$\tau$ over the same alphabet, their concatenation is the ε-NFA on the disjoint union
$\sigma \sqcup \tau$ whose moves are the moves of $M$, the moves of $N$, and an ε-move from every
accepting state of $M$ to every start state of $N$. Its start states are the start states of $M$
and its accepting states are the accepting states of $N$.

articles.title: Thompson state count
articles.statement:
The state count $n(r)$ of a regular expression $r$ is defined by
structural recursion: $n(0) = 0$, $n(\varepsilon) = 1$, $n(a) = 2$ for a letter $a$,
$n(P + Q) = n(P) + n(Q)$, $n(PQ) = n(P) + n(Q)$ and $n(P^*) = n(P) + 1$.

It is the number of states of Thompson's automaton of $r$.

articles.title: One-state automaton
articles.statement:
The ε-NFA over the alphabet $\alpha$ with a single state, which is both
its start state and its accepting state, and no moves at all (neither letter moves nor
ε-moves).

articles.title: Kleene star of an ε-NFA
articles.statement:
Given an ε-NFA $M$ with state set $\sigma$, its star automaton has
the states of $M$ together with one new state $q_0$, which is its only start state and its only
accepting state. Its moves are the moves of $M$, an ε-move from $q_0$ to every start state of $M$,
and an ε-move from every accepting state of $M$ to $q_0$.

articles.title: States of Thompson's automaton
articles.statement:
The state set $S(r)$ of Thompson's automaton of a regular
expression $r$ is defined by structural recursion: $S(0)$ is empty, $S(\varepsilon)$ has one
element, $S(a)$ has two elements for a letter $a$, both $S(P + Q)$ and $S(PQ)$ are the disjoint
union $S(P) \sqcup S(Q)$, and $S(P^*)$ is $S(P)$ together with one new element.

articles.title: Thompson's construction
articles.statement:
To each regular expression $r$ over an alphabet $\alpha$ it assigns
an ε-NFA over $\alpha$ with state set $S(r)$, the states of Thompson's automaton of $r$, by
structural recursion: $0$ goes to the automaton with no states, $\varepsilon$ to the one-state
automaton, a letter $a$ to the single-letter automaton of $a$, $P + Q$ to the union of the
automata of $P$ and $Q$, $PQ$ to their concatenation, and $P^*$ to the star automaton of the
automaton of $P$.

articles.title: Union of ε-NFAs
articles.statement:
Given ε-NFAs $M$ with state set $\sigma$ and $N$ with state set $\tau$ over
the same alphabet, their union is the ε-NFA on the disjoint union $\sigma \sqcup \tau$ whose moves
are the moves of $M$ and the moves of $N$, whose start states are the start states of $M$ and of
$N$, and whose accepting states are the accepting states of $M$ and of $N$.

articles.title: The ε-NFA with no states
articles.statement:
Over an alphabet $\alpha$, this is the ε-NFA whose set of
states is empty; consequently it has no start states, no accepting states and no transitions.

articles.title: Regular languages are accepted by two-way deterministic automata
articles.statement:
For every regular
language $L$ over an alphabet, there is a deterministic two-way automaton with finitely many
states whose language is exactly $L$.

articles.title: Regular languages are accepted by two-way nondeterministic automata
articles.statement:
For every
regular language $L$ over an alphabet, there is a nondeterministic two-way automaton with
finitely many states that accepts exactly the words of $L$.

A run of such an automaton on a word starts in a start state with the head at the first
position; each step reads the symbol under the head, changes the state and moves the head one
position left, keeps it in place, or moves it one position right, and the run is stuck if the
head would move left of the first position. A word is accepted when some run ends in an
accepting state with the head just past the last symbol.

articles.title: Finite two-way nondeterministic automata accept regular languages
articles.statement:
Every
nondeterministic two-way automaton with finitely many states accepts a regular language.

A run of such an automaton on a word starts in a start state with the head at the first
position; each step reads the symbol under the head, changes the state and moves the head one
position left, keeps it in place, or moves it one position right, and the run is stuck if the
head would move left of the first position. A word is accepted when some run ends in an
accepting state with the head just past the last symbol.

articles.title: Finite two-way deterministic automata accept regular languages
articles.statement:
The language of every
deterministic two-way automaton with finitely many states is regular.

articles.title: The two-way simulation of a DFA accepts the same language
articles.statement:
For every DFA $M$, the
deterministic two-way automaton that simulates $M$ by always moving its head one symbol to the
right has exactly the language accepted by $M$.

articles.title: Language of a deterministic two-way automaton
articles.statement:
The language of a deterministic two-way
automaton $A$ is the set of words accepted by $A$ viewed as a nondeterministic two-way
automaton: a word $w$ belongs to it when, starting in the start state with the head at the
first position of $w$ and following the step function of $A$ (which moves the head one
position left, keeps it in place, or moves it one position right, and gets stuck when it is
undefined or would move the head left of the first position), the automaton reaches an
accepting state with the head just past the last symbol of $w$.

articles.title: Membership in the language of a two-way deterministic automaton
articles.statement:
For every
deterministic two-way automaton $A$ and every word $w$, $w$ belongs to the language of $A$ if
and only if $w$ is accepted by $A$ viewed as a nondeterministic two-way automaton.

articles.title: A DFA as a two-way deterministic automaton
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ with transition function
$\delta$, this is the deterministic two-way automaton with the same states, start state and
accepting states as $M$ which, in state $q$ reading a symbol $a$, goes to state $\delta(q, a)$
and moves its head one symbol to the right.

articles.title: The two-way simulation of a DFA agrees with that of its NFA
articles.statement:
For every DFA $M$, the
deterministic two-way automaton that simulates $M$, viewed as a nondeterministic two-way
automaton, equals the nondeterministic two-way automaton obtained by viewing $M$ as an NFA and
letting that NFA always move its head one symbol to the right.

articles.title: A deterministic two-way automaton as a nondeterministic one
articles.statement:
A deterministic two-way
automaton $A$ is viewed as the nondeterministic two-way automaton with the same states and
accepting states, whose only start state is the start state of $A$, and which can go from state
$q$ reading a symbol $a$ to state $q'$ with head move $m$ exactly when the step function of $A$
at $q$ and $a$ returns $q'$ and $m$.

articles.title: Deterministic two-way automata have unique transitions
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a deterministic
two-way automaton, viewed as a nondeterministic two-way automaton. If, on reading the symbol
$x$ in state $q$, it has a transition to state $q'$ with head move $m$ and a transition to
state $q''$ with head move $m'$, then $m = m'$ and $q' = q''$.

articles.title: Transition relation of a deterministic two-way automaton
articles.statement:
Let $A$ be a deterministic
two-way automaton, viewed as a nondeterministic two-way automaton. On reading the symbol $x$ in
state $q$, it has a transition to state $q'$ with head move $m$ if and only if the transition
function of $A$ sends $(q, x)$ to the pair $(q', m)$.

articles.title: Deterministic two-way automaton
articles.statement:
A deterministic two-way automaton with state set $Q$
over the alphabet $\Sigma$ consists of a partial transition function, which assigns to each
state $q \in Q$ and input symbol $a \in \Sigma$ at most one pair of a successor state and a head
move (left, stay or right), together with a single start state and a set of accepting states.

articles.title: Brzozowski's automaton accepts the language of the original automaton
articles.statement:
For a deterministic
finite automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, Brzozowski's automaton of
$M$ accepts exactly the language of $M$.

articles.title: States of Brzozowski's automaton as residual languages
articles.statement:
For a deterministic finite
automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, the bijection from the states of
Brzozowski's automaton of $M$ to the residual languages of the reachable states of $M$ that sends
each state $p$ to the language accepted by $M$ from the state that $M$ reaches on $w$, where $w$
is a chosen word leading Brzozowski's automaton from its start state to $p$.

articles.title: Brzozowski's automaton identifies exactly the Nerode equivalent words
articles.statement:
For a deterministic
finite automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states and words $w$ and $w'$,
Brzozowski's automaton of $M$ reaches the same state on $w$ as on $w'$ if and only if $w$ and $w'$
are Nerode equivalent for the language of $M$, that is, have the same left quotient.

articles.title: Every state of the intermediate Brzozowski automaton is reachable
articles.statement:
For a deterministic
finite automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, every state of the
intermediate Brzozowski automaton of $M$ (the subset construction of the reversal of $M$
restricted to its reachable subsets) is reached from its start state by some word.

articles.title: The intermediate Brzozowski automaton
articles.statement:
For a deterministic finite automaton $M$ over a
finite alphabet with finitely many states, the subset construction of the reversal of $M$,
restricted to the subsets reachable from its start state.

articles.title: Residual language of a state of Brzozowski's automaton
articles.statement:
For a deterministic finite
automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, the map that sends a state $p$ of
Brzozowski's automaton of $M$ to the language accepted by $M$ from the state that $M$ reaches on
$w$, where $w$ is a chosen word leading Brzozowski's automaton from its start state to $p$; this
language is one of the residual languages of the reachable states of $M$.

articles.title: States of Brzozowski's automaton
articles.statement:
For a deterministic finite automaton $M$ over a finite
alphabet with finitely many states, the subsets of states of the intermediate Brzozowski automaton
of $M$ that are reachable from the start state in the subset construction of its reversal.

articles.title: Every state of Brzozowski's automaton is reachable
articles.statement:
For a deterministic finite automaton
$M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states, every state of Brzozowski's automaton of $M$
is reached from its start state by some word.

articles.title: Brzozowski's automaton
articles.statement:
For a deterministic finite automaton $M$ over a finite alphabet
with finitely many states, the subset construction of the reversal of the intermediate Brzozowski
automaton of $M$, restricted to the subsets reachable from its start state. Equivalently: reverse,
determinize by the subset construction and keep the reachable subsets, twice.

articles.title: States of the intermediate Brzozowski automaton
articles.statement:
For a deterministic finite automaton $M$
over a finite alphabet with finite state set $Q$, the subsets of $Q$ reachable from the start state
in the subset construction of the reversal of $M$.

They are found by a reachability search of at most $2^{|Q|}$ rounds, the number of subsets, which
stops as soon as a round adds nothing.

articles.title: Brzozowski's automaton is the minimal automaton
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet
with finitely many states, and let $L$ be its language. For a language $K$ and a word $w$, write
$w^{-1}K = \{v \mid wv \in K\}$ for the left quotient of $K$ by $w$. Every state of Brzozowski's
automaton of $M$ is reached by some word $w$; rename that state to $w^{-1}L$, which does not
depend on the choice of $w$. The renamed automaton is exactly the minimized DFA of $M$: its states
are the left quotients of $L$ by words, its start state is $L$, reading a letter $a$ (a word of
length one) sends $K$ to $a^{-1}K$, and it accepts the $K$ that contain the empty word.

articles.title: The determinized reversal accepts the reversed language
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA with finitely
many states and $L$ its language, and write $w^R$ for the word $w$ read backwards. The
determinized reversal of $M$ accepts exactly the reversed language $L^R = \{w \mid w^R \in L\}$.

articles.title: Brzozowski's lemma
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA with finitely many states in which every state is
reached from the start state by some word, and let $L$ be its language. Write $u^R$ for the word
$u$ read backwards, $L^R = \{u \mid u^R \in L\}$ for the reversed language, and
$w^{-1}K = \{v \mid wv \in K\}$ for the left quotient of a language $K$ by a word $w$. Then two
words $w$ and $w'$ lead the determinized reversal of $M$ from its start state to the same set of
states if and only if $w^{-1}L^R = w'^{-1}L^R$.

articles.title: States reached in the determinized reversal
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA with finitely many states
and $w$ a word. On input $w$, the determinized reversal of $M$ reaches the set of states $q$ of
$M$ from which $M$, reading $w$ backwards starting at $q$, ends in an accepting state.

articles.title: Determinized reversal of a DFA
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ with finitely many states, the determinized
reversal of $M$ is the subset construction applied to the reversal of $M$: its states are the sets
of states of $M$; reading a letter $a$ from a set $S$ leads to the set of states $q$ whose
$a$-successor in $M$ lies in $S$; its start state is the set of accepting states of $M$; and it
accepts exactly the sets that contain the start state of $M$.

articles.title: Block of accepting states
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ with finite state set $Q$, this is the set
$F \subseteq Q$ of accepting states of $M$, as a finite set.

articles.title: Predecessor-work bound for the complete Hopcroft run
Hopcroft predecessor-work as splitter counts plus pops
articles.statement:
Double counting visits by source state and letter, retaining every
incoming transition even when many sources have the same successor.

articles.title: Zero Hopcroft predecessor-work over an empty alphabet
articles.statement: An empty alphabet causes no predecessor-work, for any state count.

articles.title: Zero Hopcroft predecessor-work with at most one state
articles.statement:
Zero predecessor-work for zero/one-state boundary parameters.
This does not assert that constructing the initial partition costs zero.

articles.title: $O(|\Sigma| n \log n)$ bound on Hopcroft predecessor-work
articles.statement:
A uniform `O(|Σ| n log n)` bound, with the explicit constant `4`.
The condition `n ≥ 2` is essential when absorbing the additive unit
into the logarithm. This concerns predecessor-work, not scan runtime.

articles.title: Total predecessor-work bound
articles.statement:
**Total predecessor-work bound**, including one unit for every pop,
for every prefix of the initialized execution. No runtime claim is made
for the scanning implementation or for initialization.

articles.title: Predecessor cost of a Hopcroft splitter trace
articles.statement:
The predecessor cost of a splitter trace: for each popped splitter `(C, a)`, one
predecessor visit per state in the preimage `preimage M C a`, plus `1` per-splitter
overhead. This is the quantity the total-work bound constrains
to `O(|Σ| n log n)`. Charging splitter size `C.card` instead
would undercount: if all `n` states transition on `a` to one state `q`, processing the
singleton splitter `({q}, a)` costs `n` predecessor visits while `C.card` charges
only `1`.

articles.title: Hopcroft splitter trace length equals loop fuel
articles.statement:
The trace and the loop take the same number of steps: the trace length is the fuel
the loop consumed, i.e. the loop would stop after exactly that many rounds if run with
only that much fuel.

articles.title: Termination of Hopcroft's loop
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA with finite state set $Q$ over a finite
alphabet $\Sigma$, let $P$ be a partition of the states given as a list of blocks, let $W$ be a
waiting list of splitters, and let $k$ be a natural number. If $P$ and $W$ satisfy the invariants
of Hopcroft's loop and $|W| + |\Sigma| \cdot (|Q| - |P|) \le k$, where $|P|$ and $|W|$ are the
lengths of the lists, then Hopcroft's loop run from $(P, W)$ with a budget of $k$ rounds ends with
an empty waiting list, and the partition and waiting list it returns again satisfy the invariants.

The invariants make $P$ a partition into nonempty blocks, so $|P| \le |Q|$ and the difference
$|Q| - |P|$ is not truncated.

articles.title: Hopcroft's waiting list is exhausted
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA with finite state set $Q$ over a
finite alphabet $\Sigma$. Hopcroft's loop, run from the initial partition and the initial waiting
list with a budget of $|\Sigma| \cdot (|Q| + 1)$ rounds, ends with an empty waiting list.

articles.title: Instrumented complete Hopcroft run returns the minimization partition
articles.statement:
At the proved terminating fuel, instrumentation returns the original
correct minimization partition and an empty waiting list.

articles.title: Recorded Hopcroft cost obeys the predecessor-work bound
articles.statement:
The canonical cost monad records the proved total predecessor-work
bound for every initialized execution prefix.

articles.title: Instrumented Hopcroft loop returns the original result
articles.statement: Instrumentation preserves the exact loop result.

articles.title: Recorded Hopcroft cost equals the work of the popped trace
articles.statement: The recorded cost is exactly the work of the actual popped trace.

articles.title: Hopcroft loop with recorded predecessor-work
articles.statement:
The actual loop with predecessor-visit and pop events recorded in
CSLib's `TimeM`. Pure scans are not charged in this event model.

articles.title: Hopcroft's refinement loop
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA. Given a round budget $k$, a partition $P$
of the states of $M$ (a list of blocks) and a waiting list $W$ of splitters $(C, a)$, each a block
$C$ with a letter $a$, the loop returns the pair $(P, W)$ unchanged if $k = 0$ or $W$ is empty.
Otherwise it removes the first splitter $(C, a)$ from $W$, replaces $P$ by the partition after the
splitter $(C, a)$ and the remaining waiting list by the waiting list after the splitter $(C, a)$,
and continues with budget $k - 1$.

articles.title: Hopcroft's partition
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA with finite state set $Q$ over a finite alphabet
$\Sigma$. Hopcroft's partition of $M$ is the partition returned by Hopcroft's loop run from the
initial partition and the initial waiting list with a budget of $|\Sigma| \cdot (|Q| + 1)$
rounds.

articles.title: Hopcroft's partition is Moore's relation
articles.statement:
For every DFA $M$ with finitely many states over
a finite alphabet, Hopcroft's relation of $M$, the set of pairs of states lying in a common block
of Hopcroft's partition, equals Moore's state equivalence of $M$ as a set of pairs of states.

articles.title: Hopcroft's relation
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ with finitely many states, Hopcroft's relation is the
set of pairs $(p, q)$ of states of $M$ such that $p$ and $q$ lie in a common block of Hopcroft's
partition.

articles.title: The splitter trace records exactly the splitters the loop pops
articles.statement:
The loop and the
trace recurse on the same state, so they take the same number of steps. The two
theorems below make the correspondence usable: the trace length is at most `k`, and
running the loop for exactly the trace's length gives the full loop result, so the trace
contains every splitter the loop pops and no others.

articles.title: Trace of splitters popped by Hopcroft's algorithm
articles.statement:
The splitters popped by Hopcroft's loop, in order: the same recursion as
`DFA.hopcroftLoop`, collecting each popped splitter. The cost of processing one popped
splitter `(C, a)` is `(preimage M C a).card + 1`: one predecessor visit per state whose
`a`-successor lies in `C`, plus `O(1)` per-splitter overhead. See `hopcroftCost`.
`hopcroftLoop_eq_hopcroftLoop_of_length` proves this trace records exactly the
splitters the loop pops, so the trace cannot drift from the loop.

articles.title: Hopcroft's initial partition
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ with finite state set $Q$ and set of accepting
states $F$, the initial partition is the list of blocks $F$, $Q \setminus F$, in this order, with
any empty block removed.

articles.title: No initial Hopcroft splitters with at most one state
articles.statement:
With at most one state, the accepting/rejecting split has an empty
side, so the algorithm has no initial splitters.

articles.title: Hopcroft's initial waiting list
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA with finite state set $Q$, set of
accepting states $F$ and finite alphabet $\Sigma$. If $F$ and $Q \setminus F$ are both nonempty,
the initial waiting list consists of the splitters $(S, b)$ for every letter $b \in \Sigma$, where
$S = F$ if $|F| \le |Q \setminus F|$ and $S = Q \setminus F$ otherwise; if one of $F$ and
$Q \setminus F$ is empty, the initial waiting list is empty.

articles.title: The invariants hold initially
articles.statement:
For every DFA $M$ with finitely many states over a finite
alphabet, Hopcroft's initial partition and initial waiting list satisfy the invariants of
Hopcroft's loop.

articles.title: Invariants of Hopcroft's loop
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA with transition function $\delta$. A list
$P$ of sets of states and a waiting list $W$ of pairs $(C, b)$ of a set of states $C$ and a letter
$b$ satisfy the invariants when: (i) $P$ is a partition of the states into nonempty blocks;
(ii) for every $(C, b)$ in $W$, $C$ is an entry of $P$; (iii) for every letter $b$ and all states
$p$, $q$ lying in a common entry of $P$, if for every $C$ with $(C, b)$ in $W$ the states
$\delta(p, b)$ and $\delta(q, b)$ are both in $C$ or both outside $C$, then $\delta(p, b)$ and
$\delta(q, b)$ lie in a common entry of $P$; (iv) any two states lying in a common entry of $P$
are both accepting or both rejecting; and (v) any two states from which $M$ accepts the same
language lie in a common entry of $P$.

articles.title: Hopcroft's final partition is a partition
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$, Hopcroft's final partition of
$M$ is a partition of the states of $M$ into nonempty blocks.

articles.title: Partitions of the states
articles.statement:
A list $P$ of sets of states is a partition into nonempty
blocks when entries of $P$ at different positions are disjoint, every entry of $P$ is nonempty,
and every state lies in some entry of $P$.

articles.title: Number of pops bounded by the total splitter count
articles.statement:
A nonempty popped block pays for its pop, even if its preimage is
empty. This bounds the `+1` term independently of predecessor visits.

articles.title: A partition has at most as many blocks as there are states
articles.statement:
If a list $P$ of sets of
states is a partition into nonempty blocks, then the length of $P$ is at most the number $|Q|$ of
states.

articles.title: Number of blocks after one round
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA with transition function $\delta$, let
$P$ be a list of sets of states, $C$ a set of states and $a$ a letter, and let
$\mathrm{pre} = \{q : \delta(q, a) \in C\}$. The partition after the splitter $(C, a)$, which
replaces each entry $D$ of $P$ meeting both $\mathrm{pre}$ and its complement by
$D \cap \mathrm{pre}$ and $D \setminus \mathrm{pre}$, has length equal to the length of $P$ plus
the number of entries of $P$ (counted with repetition) that meet both $\mathrm{pre}$ and its
complement.

articles.title: Growth of the waiting list in one round
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA with transition function
$\delta$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$, let $P$ be a list of sets of states with no repeated
entries, let $W$ be a list of pairs of a set of states and a letter, let $C$ be a set of states
and $a$ a letter, and let $S = \{q : \delta(q, a) \in C\}$ be the preimage of $C$ under $a$. Then
the waiting list after the splitter $(C, a)$, computed from the blocks $P$ and the rest $W$ of the
waiting list, has length at most $|W| + |\Sigma| \cdot k$, where $k$ is the number of entries of
$P$ split by $S$, that is, meeting both $S$ and its complement.

articles.title: Blocks of Hopcroft's partition are language classes
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA, $D$ a block of
Hopcroft's final partition of $M$ and $p$ a state in $D$. Then a state $q$ lies in $D$ if and only
if the language accepted by $M$ from $q$ equals the language accepted by $M$ from $p$.

articles.title: Correctness of Hopcroft's algorithm
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$, two states $p$ and $q$ share a block
of Hopcroft's final partition of $M$ exactly when the language accepted by $M$ from $p$ equals the
language accepted by $M$ from $q$.

articles.title: A block contains both or neither of two related states
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a list of sets of
states that is a partition into nonempty blocks, let $C$ be an entry of $P$, and let $p$ and $q$
be states lying in a common entry of $P$. Then $p \in C$ if and only if $q \in C$.

articles.title: New splitters are halves of the split block
articles.statement:
Every entry `newSplitters` adds for a block `D` is a half of `D` (one of the two sides
of the split by `pre`), or the smaller half.

articles.title: Moore classes are Hopcroft blocks
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ and reachable states $p$ and $q$ of $M$,
the classes of $p$ and $q$ under Moore's equivalence on reachable states (the states of Moore's
minimal automaton) are equal if and only if $p$ and $q$ share a block of Hopcroft's final
partition of $M$.

articles.title: Halving chains shrink blocks by a factor of at least $2^k$
articles.statement:
After `k` halving steps, the initial block is at least `2 ^ k` times the final block.
The halving hypothesis is stated for the cardinalities only; no subset hypothesis is
needed.

articles.title: New splitters for a split block
articles.statement:
Given a waiting list $W$ of pairs of a set of states and a
letter and sets $S$ and $D$ of states, write $D_1 = D \cap S$ and $D_2 = D \setminus S$. The new
waiting entries for $D$ consist, for each letter $b$ in the enumeration order of the alphabet,
of both $(D_1, b)$ and $(D_2, b)$ if $(D, b)$ is in $W$, and otherwise of the single entry
$(E, b)$, where $E$ is the smaller of $D_1$ and $D_2$ by cardinality ($D_1$ on a tie).

articles.title: Popped Hopcroft splitters are nonempty
articles.statement:
Every popped splitter has a nonempty block, including splitters whose
predecessor set is empty.

articles.title: Preimage of a set under a letter
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ with transition function $\delta$, a set
$C$ of states and a letter $a$, the preimage of $C$ under $a$ is the set of states $q$ with
$\delta(q, a) \in C$.

articles.title: Rejecting states
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ with state set $Q$ and set of accepting states $F$, the
rejecting block is the set $Q \setminus F$ of states of $M$ that are not accepting.

articles.title: With an empty waiting list, blocks are the classes of equal continuation languages
articles.statement:
Let
$M$ be a DFA and $P$ a list of blocks of states such that $P$ with the empty waiting list
satisfies the invariants of Hopcroft's loop. Then two states $p$ and $q$ lie in a common block of
$P$ if and only if they accept the same continuation languages, that is, $M$ accepts a word from
$p$ exactly when it accepts it from $q$.

With an empty waiting list the invariants say that $P$ is a right congruence refining acceptance.

articles.title: Effect of one splitter on the common-block relation
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA with transition
function $\delta$, $P$ a list of blocks of states, $C$ a set of states and $a$ a letter. Two states
$p$ and $q$ lie in a common block after the splitter $(C, a)$ is applied to $P$ if and only if
they lie in a common block of $P$ and $\delta(p, a) \in C \iff \delta(q, a) \in C$.

articles.title: Lying in a common block
articles.statement:
For a list $P$ of sets of states, two states $p$ and $q$ are
related by $P$ when some block $D$ of $P$ contains both $p$ and $q$.

articles.title: One refinement round of the partition
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ with transition function $\delta$, a
list $P$ of blocks of states, a set $C$ of states and a letter $a$, let
$S = \{q : \delta(q, a) \in C\}$ be the preimage of $C$ under $a$. The partition after the
splitter $(C, a)$ replaces each block $D$ of $P$, in order, by the two blocks $D \cap S$ and
$D \setminus S$ when both are nonempty, and keeps $D$ otherwise.

articles.title: One update of the waiting list
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ with transition function $\delta$, a list $P$
of blocks of states, a list $W$ of pairs of a set of states and a letter, a set $C$ of states and a
letter $a$, let $S = \{q : \delta(q, a) \in C\}$ be the preimage of $C$ under $a$, and say that $S$
splits a set $D$ when $D$ meets both $S$ and its complement. The waiting list after the splitter
$(C, a)$, from the rest $W$ of the waiting list, consists of the entries of $W$ whose set is not
split by $S$, followed, for each block $D$ of $P$ split by $S$ in order, by the new splitters for
$D$: for each letter $b$ in the enumeration order of the alphabet, both $(D \cap S, b)$ and
$(D \setminus S, b)$ if $(D, b)$ is in $W$, and otherwise the single entry $(E, b)$, where $E$ is
the smaller of $D \cap S$ and $D \setminus S$ by cardinality ($D \cap S$ on a tie).

articles.title: One round preserves the invariants
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA, $P$ a list of blocks of states, $W$
a list of pairs of a set of states and a letter, $C$ a set of states and $a$ a letter. If $P$ and
the waiting list obtained by putting $(C, a)$ in front of $W$ satisfy the invariants of
Hopcroft's loop, then so do the partition after the splitter $(C, a)$ and the waiting list after
the splitter $(C, a)$ from the rest $W$.

articles.title: Pieces of a split block lie on one side
articles.statement:
Let $S$ and $D$ be sets of states. Every piece of
$D$ split by $S$ (the two sets $D \cap S$ and $D \setminus S$ if $D$ meets both $S$ and its
complement, and $D$ itself otherwise) is contained in $S$ or disjoint from $S$: any two states
$x$ and $y$ of the piece satisfy $x \in S \iff y \in S$.

articles.title: The smaller-half counting lemma
articles.statement:
In a chain of blocks where each step at least
halves the size, a block containing a given state can occur at most `Nat.log 2 n` times
past the start, where `n` is the number of states. In Hopcroft's algorithm, the successive
smaller halves containing one fixed state form such a chain: each of them is the smaller
half of a split of the previous block containing that state.

## Sources

- J. E. Hopcroft, "An `n log n` algorithm for minimizing states in a finite automaton", Theory of Machines and Computations, 1971; the counting argument is presented in J. Berstel, L. Boasson, O. Carton and I. Fagnot, "Minimization of automata", 2010.

articles.title: Smaller of two finite sets of states
articles.statement:
For finite sets $A$ and $B$ of states, the
smaller one is $A$ if $|A| \le |B|$ and $B$ otherwise; on a tie in cardinality it is $A$.

articles.title: Splitting a block by a set
articles.statement:
For sets $P$ and $D$ of states, splitting $D$ by $P$ gives
the two-element list $[D \cap P,\ D \setminus P]$ if both of these sets are nonempty, and the
one-element list $[D]$ otherwise.

articles.title: A set of states split by another
articles.statement:
A set $D$ of states is split by a set $P$ of states
when $D$ contains both a state in $P$ and a state not in $P$, that is, when $D \cap P$ and
$D \setminus P$ are both nonempty.

articles.title: Splitter count bound along a Hopcroft execution
articles.statement:
Total state/letter charging along the actual execution. The bound
includes initial tokens and tokens still pending through replacements.
No amortized bound is assumed in the execution invariant.

articles.title: Hopcroft visits each of $n$ states at most $\log_2 n + 1$ times per letter
articles.statement:
Each state is processed with a fixed letter at most `log₂ n + 1`
times during any prefix of the actual initialized Hopcroft execution.

articles.title: Initial splitter count is at most one
articles.statement: Initially there is at most one token for each state and letter.

articles.title: Splitter count of newly added splitters
articles.statement:
Replacement contributes one token at a state in the parent block;
otherwise only membership in the smaller half contributes a token.

articles.title: Waiting entries give positive splitter count
articles.statement: A waiting entry supplies a token; duplicate entries remain counted.

articles.title: Potential inequality for one Hopcroft refinement round
Splitter count update after one Hopcroft round
articles.statement:
The exact token update at a state. Only its unique parent block can
contribute a new token, even when other blocks split in the same round.

articles.title: Splitter count of a state and letter
articles.statement:
Number of splitters with letter `b` containing `q`, with multiplicity.
This applies both to the waiting list and to the actual popped trace.

articles.title: Refined Hopcroft blocks lie inside their old blocks
articles.statement:
A refined block containing `q` is a subset of the old block
containing `q`. Both partitions are the canonical Hopcroft partitions.

articles.title: Smaller-half splitters have at most half the block size
articles.statement:
A smaller-half entry added by `newSplitters` for a block `D` has at most half the size
of `D`: the two halves are disjoint and union to `D`. No split hypothesis is needed: the
halves of any block partition it.

articles.title: The smaller part of a split has at most half the size
articles.statement:
If two disjoint sets union to `D`, the smaller of them has at most half the size of
`D`.

articles.title: The smaller of two sets has at most half their total size
articles.statement:
The smaller of two sets has at most half their combined size: it is one of the two
sets, so twice its size is at most the sum of the two sizes.

articles.title: DFA morphisms preserve the accepted language
articles.statement:
If $f$ is a morphism from a DFA $M$ to a DFA
$N$ over the same alphabet, then $M$ and $N$ accept the same language.

articles.title: Injectivity of the canonical residual map
articles.statement:
For an accessible DFA $M$, the canonical
residual map from $M$ to the residual-language DFA of its accepted language is injective if and
only if $M$ is state-separated, that is, any two states of $M$ with the same continuation
language are equal.

articles.title: The canonical residual map is surjective
articles.statement:
For an accessible DFA $M$, every state of the
residual-language DFA of the language accepted by $M$ is the image of some state of $M$ under
the canonical residual map.

articles.title: Uniqueness of the canonical residual map
articles.statement:
For an accessible DFA $M$ accepting the
language $L$, every DFA morphism from $M$ to the residual-language DFA of $L$ equals the
canonical residual map.

articles.title: The canonical residual map
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an accessible DFA accepting the language $L$. The
residual-language DFA of $L$ has as states the left quotients $x^{-1}L = \{y \mid xy \in L\}$
for words $x$, start state $L$, transitions $K \mapsto a^{-1}K$ on a symbol $a$, and a state $K$
is accepting when it contains the empty word. The canonical residual map is the DFA morphism from
$M$ to this DFA that sends each state $q$ of $M$ to its continuation language, the set of words
$z$ such that running $M$ from $q$ on $z$ ends in an accepting state.

articles.title: Composition of DFA morphisms
articles.statement:
If $f$ is a DFA morphism from $M$ to $N$ and $g$ is a DFA
morphism from $N$ to $P$, where $M$, $N$, $P$ are DFAs over the same alphabet, then the composite
of $g$ and $f$ is the DFA morphism from $M$ to $P$ whose state map is $g \circ f$.

articles.title: Morphisms of DFAs
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $N$ be DFAs over the same alphabet with transition
functions $\delta_M$ and $\delta_N$. A morphism from $M$ to $N$ is a map $f$ from the states of
$M$ to the states of $N$ that sends the start state of $M$ to the start state of $N$, satisfies
$f(\delta_M(q, a)) = \delta_N(f(q), a)$ for every state $q$ of $M$ and every symbol $a$, and
such that each state $q$ of $M$ is accepting if and only if $f(q)$ is accepting in $N$.

articles.title: Converting a CSLib automaton to a Mathlib DFA preserves its language
articles.statement:
For every
deterministic automaton $M$ on finite words, the DFA with the same states, transition function,
start state and accepting states as $M$ accepts exactly the language of $M$.

articles.title: Left quotients of continuation languages
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA, write $\delta^*(q, x)$ for
the state $M$ reaches from the state $q$ by reading the word $x$, and let $L_M(q)$ be the
language of words accepted by $M$ when started in $q$. For every state $q$ and every word $x$,
the left quotient $\{z : xz \in L_M(q)\}$ of $L_M(q)$ by $x$ equals $L_M(\delta^*(q, x))$.

articles.title: Left quotients as reachable residuals
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA accepting the language $L$. The
set of left quotients $\{z : xz \in L\}$ of $L$ by words $x$ equals the set of reachable
residuals of $M$ (the languages accepted by $M$ from the states it reaches from its start
state). The bijection from the first set to the second sends each language to itself.

articles.title: DFA morphisms commute with evaluation from a state
articles.statement:
If $f$ is a morphism from a DFA $M$
to a DFA $N$, then for every state $q$ of $M$ and every word $x$, running $N$ on $x$ from $f(q)$
ends in the image under $f$ of the state reached by running $M$ on $x$ from $q$.

articles.title: DFA morphisms commute with evaluation
articles.statement:
If $f$ is a morphism from a DFA $M$ to a DFA $N$,
then for every word $x$, the state that $N$ reaches on input $x$ from its start state is the
image under $f$ of the state that $M$ reaches on input $x$ from its start state.

articles.title: The minimized DFA accepts the same language
articles.statement:
For every DFA $M$, the minimized DFA of $M$
accepts exactly the language accepted by $M$.

articles.title: The minimized DFA is accessible
articles.statement:
For every DFA $M$, every state of the minimized DFA of
$M$ is reached from its start state by reading some word.

articles.title: When finite, the minimized DFA has as many states as there are Nerode classes
articles.statement:
Let $M$
be a DFA accepting the language $L$. If the set of reachable residuals of $M$ (the states of the
minimized DFA of $M$) and the set of Nerode classes of $L$ are both finite, then they have the
same number of elements.

articles.title: Evaluation in the minimized DFA agrees with the left-quotient automaton
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a
DFA accepting the language $L$, and consider the automaton whose states are the left quotients
of $L$, with start state $L$, moving from $K$ on a letter $a$ to $\{z : az \in K\}$. For every
word $x$, the state that the minimized DFA of $M$ reaches on $x$, carried to the left quotients
of $L$ by the bijection that sends each language to itself, is the state that this automaton
reaches on $x$.

articles.title: States reached in the minimized DFA
articles.statement:
For every DFA $M$ and every word $x$, the state that
the minimized DFA of $M$ reaches on $x$ is the language accepted by $M$ from the state that $M$
reaches on $x$.

articles.title: Transitions of the minimized DFA on reached states
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA, and for a word $x$
let $[x]$ be the language accepted by $M$ from the state that $M$ reaches on $x$. For every word
$x$ and every letter $a$, the minimized DFA of $M$ moves from the state $[x]$ on input $a$ to the
state $[xa]$.

articles.title: Transitions of the minimized DFA
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA. For every reachable residual $K$ of
$M$ (a state of the minimized DFA of $M$) and every letter $a$, the minimized DFA of $M$ moves
from $K$ on input $a$ to the left quotient $\{z : az \in K\}$ of $K$ by $a$.

articles.title: Minimized DFA
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA accepting the language $L$. The minimized DFA of $M$
has as states the reachable residuals of $M$, that is, the languages accepted by $M$ from the
states it reaches from its start state. Its start state is $L$; on a letter $a$ it moves from
a state $K$ to the left quotient $\{z : az \in K\}$; and its accepting states are those that
contain the empty word.

It is the canonical automaton of $L$, whose states are the left quotients of $L$, with each
state renamed to the same language viewed as a reachable residual of $M$.

articles.title: Reachable residuals of the minimized DFA
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA accepting the language $L$.
The reachable residuals of the minimized DFA of $M$ and the reachable residuals of $M$ both form
the set of left quotients $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ of $L$ by words $x$, and this is the
bijection from the first set to the second that sends each language to itself.

It is built as the composite of the bijections from the Nerode classes of $L$ to both sets, each
sending the class of a word $x$ to $x^{-1}L$; so minimizing the minimized DFA again gives the
same state space.

articles.title: Residual reached by a word
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ and a word $x$, the minimized state of $x$ is the
language accepted by $M$ starting from the state that $M$ reaches on reading $x$ from its start
state, viewed as an element of the reachable residuals of $M$.

articles.title: Nerode classes and reachable residuals
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ accepting the language $L$, there is a
bijection from the Nerode classes of $L$ to the reachable residuals of $M$; it sends the class of a
word $x$ to the left quotient $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$.

articles.title: The Nerode congruence relates words with equal left quotients
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language
over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $x, y \in \Sigma^*$. Then $x$ and $y$ are related by the Nerode
congruence of $L$, that is, $xz \in L \iff yz \in L$ for every word $z$, if and only if they are
Nerode equivalent for $L$, that is, their left quotients $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ and
$y^{-1}L$ are equal.

articles.title: Nerode classes are the residual languages
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet
$\Sigma$, and write $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ for the left quotient of $L$ by a word $x$. This
is the bijection from the classes of the Nerode congruence of $L$ onto the set
$\{x^{-1}L : x \in \Sigma^*\}$ of residual languages of $L$ that sends the class of each word $x$
to $x^{-1}L$.

The residual languages are the states of Mathlib's residual-language DFA of $L$.

articles.title: The residual language of a Nerode class
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet
$\Sigma$, and write $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ for the left quotient of $L$ by a word $x$. This
is the map from the classes of the Nerode congruence of $L$ to the set
$\{w^{-1}L : w \in \Sigma^*\}$ of residual languages of $L$ that sends the class of each word $x$
to $x^{-1}L$; it is well defined because Nerode-congruent words have the same left quotient.

articles.title: Mathlib DFAs as CSLib automata
articles.statement:
A Mathlib DFA $M$ is viewed as a CSLib deterministic
automaton on finite words with the same states, the same transition function, the same start state
and the same set of accepting states as $M$.

articles.title: Identity DFA morphism
articles.statement:
For every DFA $M$, the identity map on the states of $M$ is a DFA
morphism from $M$ to itself.

articles.title: The canonical automaton of a DFA's language is its minimized DFA
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over
an alphabet $\Sigma$ accepting the language $L$, and write $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ for the
left quotient of $L$ by a word $x$. Consider the canonical automaton of $L$ as a DFA: its states
are the classes $[x]$ of the Nerode congruence of $L$, its start state is the class of the empty
word, on a letter $a$ it goes from $[x]$ to $[xa]$, and its accepting states are the classes of
words of $L$. Renaming each class $[x]$ to $x^{-1}L$, regarded as one of the languages accepted
from the states of $M$ reachable from its start state, gives exactly the minimized DFA of $M$.

articles.title: The Nerode automaton is the residual-language automaton
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an
alphabet $\Sigma$, and write $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$ for the left quotient of $L$ by a word
$x$. Consider the canonical automaton of $L$ as a DFA: its states are the classes $[x]$ of the
Nerode congruence of $L$, its start state is the class of the empty word, on a letter $a$ it goes
from $[x]$ to $[xa]$, and its accepting states are the classes of words of $L$. Renaming each
class $[x]$ to $x^{-1}L$ gives exactly Mathlib's residual-language DFA of $L$: its states are the
residual languages $x^{-1}L$ for $x \in \Sigma^*$, its start state is $L$, on a letter $a$ it goes
from $K$ to $a^{-1}K$, and its accepting states are the residual languages that contain the empty
word.

articles.title: States of an accessible, state-separated DFA correspond to residuals
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA
that is accessible and state-separated, and let $L$ be the language it accepts. The map sending
each state $q$ of $M$ to the language of words accepted by $M$ starting from $q$ is a bijection
from the states of $M$ onto the set of left quotients $\{z : xz \in L\}$ of $L$ by words $x$.

articles.title: State-separated DFA
articles.statement:
A DFA $M$ is state-separated when any two equivalent states of $M$
are equal: if $p \ne q$, then the languages of words accepted by $M$ starting from $p$ and from
$q$ are different.

articles.title: The residual-language DFA is accessible
articles.statement:
For every language $L$, the residual-language DFA
of $L$ is accessible. This automaton has as states the left quotients $x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$
for words $x$, start state $L$, transition from $K$ on a letter $a$ to $a^{-1}K$, and accepts $K$
when $K$ contains the empty word.

articles.title: States reached in the residual-language DFA
articles.statement:
For every language $L$ and every word $x$, the
state that the residual-language DFA of $L$ reaches on reading $x$ is the left quotient
$x^{-1}L = \{z : xz \in L\}$. This automaton has the left quotients of $L$ as states, start state
$L$, transition from $K$ on a letter $a$ to $a^{-1}K$, and accepts $K$ when $K$ contains the empty
word.

articles.title: CSLib automata as Mathlib DFAs
articles.statement:
A CSLib deterministic automaton $M$ on finite words is
viewed as a Mathlib DFA with the same states, the same transition function, the same start state
and the same set of accepting states as $M$.

articles.title: Moore's automaton has one state per Nerode class
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet
with finitely many states, Moore's minimal automaton of $M$ has exactly as many states as there
are Nerode classes of the language accepted by $M$.

articles.title: Correctness of Moore's refinement
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely
many states, two states $p$ and $q$ of $M$ are related by Moore's relation if and only if they
have the same continuation language: for every word $w$, $M$ started at $p$ accepts $w$ exactly
when $M$ started at $q$ accepts $w$.

articles.title: Moore class of a reachable state
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely
many states. For a reachable state $s$ of $M$, its Moore class is the equivalence class of $s$
among the reachable states of $M$ under Moore's relation; it is a state of Moore's minimal
automaton of $M$.

articles.title: Moore's automaton accepts the same language
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with
finitely many states, Moore's minimal automaton of $M$ accepts exactly the language accepted by
$M$.

articles.title: Moore's minimal automaton
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finitely many states,
Moore's minimal automaton of $M$ has as states the classes of reachable states of $M$ under
Moore's relation. Its start state is the class of the start state of $M$; reading a letter $a$
sends the class of a reachable state $s$ to the class of the state that $M$ reaches from $s$ on
$a$; and the class of $s$ is accepting exactly when $s$ is an accepting state of $M$.

These do not depend on the chosen member $s$, because Moore-related states agree on acceptance
and their successors on each letter are again Moore-related.

articles.title: Moore classes are the reachable residuals
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with
finitely many states. The states of Moore's minimal automaton of $M$ are in bijection with the
reachable residual languages of $M$: the bijection sends the class of a reachable state $s$ to
the continuation language of $s$, the set of words that $M$ accepts when started at $s$.

articles.title: Output of the stopping Moore iteration
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with
finitely many states, and write $R$ for one round of Moore's refinement. For every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every set $E$ of pairs of states of $M$, there is $k \le n$ such that the
stopping Moore iteration from $E$ with budget $n$ returns $R^k(E)$, and if $k < n$ then $R^k(E)$
is a fixed point of $R$, that is, $R(R^k(E)) = R^k(E)$.

articles.title: Stopping Moore iteration
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with finitely many
states, and write $R$ for one round of Moore's refinement. For a set $E$ of pairs of states of
$M$ and a budget $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the stopping Moore iteration is defined by recursion on $n$:
with budget $0$ it returns $E$; with budget $n + 1$ it returns $E$ if $R(E) = E$, and otherwise
the stopping Moore iteration from $R(E)$ with budget $n$.

articles.title: Moore's relation
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ over a finite alphabet with finite set of states $Q$,
Moore's relation is the set of pairs of states obtained from $Q \times Q$ by repeating rounds of
Moore's refinement until a round changes nothing, for at most $|Q \times Q|$ rounds.

articles.title: Continuation language of a Moore class
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over a finite alphabet with
finitely many states. Each state of Moore's minimal automaton of $M$, a class of reachable states
of $M$, is sent to the continuation language of any member $s$, the set of words that $M$
accepts when started at $s$; this is a reachable residual language of $M$. It does not depend on
the choice of $s$, because Moore-related states have the same continuation language.

articles.title: Moore equivalence on reachable states
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$, two reachable states $p$ and $q$
of $M$ are related when the pair $(p, q)$ lies in Moore's relation of $M$; this relation is an
equivalence relation on the reachable states of $M$.

articles.title: States of Moore's automaton
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$, these are the equivalence classes of the
reachable states of $M$ under Moore equivalence, that is, under Moore's relation of $M$
restricted to reachable states. They are the states of Moore's minimal automaton.

articles.title: Moore refinement step
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA with state set $S$ and transition function
$\delta$. One round of Moore's refinement sends a set $E \subseteq S \times S$ of pairs of
states to the set of pairs $(p, q) \in S \times S$ such that $p$ is accepting if and only if
$q$ is accepting and, for every letter $a$, the pair $(\delta(p, a), \delta(q, a))$ lies in
$E$.

articles.title: Moore's automaton is the minimal automaton
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA. Renaming each state of
Moore's minimal automaton of $M$, a class of reachable states, to the continuation language
accepted from its members turns Moore's automaton into exactly the minimized DFA of $M$, whose
states are the reachable continuation languages of $M$.

articles.title: Moore's relation contains every post-fixed point
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA. If a set $Z$ of
pairs of states of $M$ is contained in its image under one round of Moore's refinement, then
$Z$ is contained in Moore's relation of $M$.

articles.title: Accepting Nerode classes
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language. The accepting Nerode classes of $L$ are
those whose words belong to $L$: the Nerode class $[x]$ of a word $x$ is accepting if and only if
$x \in L$. This is well-defined because Nerode equivalent words are either both in $L$ or both
outside $L$.

articles.title: The Nerode automaton recognizes its language
articles.statement:
For every language $L$, the language accepted
by the Nerode automaton of $L$ is exactly $L$.

articles.title: Accessible DFA
articles.statement: A DFA is accessible when every state is reachable.

articles.title: Equality case of the Nerode state bound
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language with finitely many
Nerode classes, and let $M$ be a DFA with a finite set of states $Q$ that accepts exactly $L$.
Send each Nerode class of $L$ to the state that $M$ reaches from its start state on the chosen
representative word of the class. Then the number of Nerode classes of $L$ equals $|Q|$ if and
only if every state in $Q$ is the image of some Nerode class under this map.

articles.title: Nerode classes bound the number of DFA states
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language with finitely many
Nerode classes, and let $M$ be a DFA with a finite set of states $Q$ that accepts exactly $L$.
Then the number of Nerode classes of $L$ is at most $|Q|$.

articles.title: Strict Nerode state bound
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language with finitely many Nerode classes, and
let $M$ be a DFA with a finite set of states $Q$ that accepts exactly $L$. Send each Nerode
class of $L$ to the state that $M$ reaches from its start state on the chosen representative
word of the class. If some state in $Q$ is not the image of any Nerode class under this map,
then the number of Nerode classes of $L$ is strictly less than $|Q|$.

articles.title: Residual map on Nerode classes
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language. The residual map sends the Nerode
class $[x]$ of a word $x$ to the left quotient $x^{-1}L = \{ y \mid xy \in L \}$, viewed as an
element of the set $\{ w^{-1}L \mid w \text{ a word} \}$ of left quotients of $L$. It is
well-defined because Nerode equivalent words have the same left quotient.

articles.title: Distinguishable words
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Two words $x$ and
$y$ over $\Sigma$ are distinguishable by $L$ when there is a word $z$ over $\Sigma$ such that
exactly one of $xz$ and $yz$ belongs to $L$.

articles.title: Distinguishable words reach different DFA states
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language and let $M$ be
a DFA that accepts exactly $L$. If two words $x$ and $y$ are distinguishable by $L$, then the
states that $M$ reaches from its start state on reading $x$ and on reading $y$ are different.

articles.title: Finitely many Nerode classes iff finitely many left quotients
articles.statement:
For every language $L$,
writing $x^{-1}L = \{ y \mid xy \in L \}$ for the left quotient of $L$ by a word $x$, there are
finitely many Nerode classes of $L$ if and only if the set $\{ x^{-1}L \mid x \text{ a word} \}$
of left quotients of $L$ is finite.

This is the quotient formulation of the Myhill--Nerode criterion.

articles.title: Myhill–Nerode theorem, quotient form
articles.statement:
A language $L$ is regular, that is, accepted by some
deterministic finite automaton, if and only if $L$ has finitely many Nerode classes.

articles.title: Nerode equivalent words agree on membership
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language. If two words $x$ and
$y$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$, then $x \in L$ if and only if $y \in L$.

articles.title: Myhill–Nerode lower bound via left quotients
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language and let $M$ be a DFA
with a finite set of states $Q$ that accepts exactly $L$. For a word $x$, the left quotient of
$L$ by $x$ is the language $\{z \mid xz \in L\}$. Then the number of distinct left quotients of
$L$ is at most $|Q|$.

articles.title: Nerode class of a word
articles.statement:
For a language $L$ and a word $x$, the Nerode class $[x]$ of $x$
is the equivalence class of $x$ under Nerode equivalence for $L$.

articles.title: Nerode classes correspond to reachable residuals
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language and let $M$ be
a DFA that accepts exactly $L$. This is the bijection from the Nerode classes of $L$ to the
reachable residuals of $M$, the languages accepted by $M$ from states it reaches from its start
state. It sends the Nerode class of a word $x$ to the left quotient $\{z \mid xz \in L\}$, which
is the language $M$ accepts from the state it reaches on reading $x$.

articles.title: Bijection between Nerode classes and left quotients
articles.statement:
For every language $L$, the map
sending the Nerode class $[x]$ of a word $x$ to the left quotient
$x^{-1}L = \{ y \mid xy \in L \}$ is a bijection from the set of Nerode classes of $L$ onto the
set $\{ w^{-1}L \mid w \text{ a word} \}$ of left quotients of $L$.

articles.title: Nerode classes
articles.statement:
For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the Nerode classes of $L$
are the elements of the quotient of the set of words over $\Sigma$ by Nerode equivalence for
$L$, under which two words $x$ and $y$ are equivalent when they have the same left quotient,
that is, when for every word $z$ we have $xz \in L$ if and only if $yz \in L$.

articles.title: Every state of the Nerode automaton is reachable
articles.statement:
For every language $L$ and every
Nerode class $q$ of $L$, there is a word $x$ such that the Nerode automaton of $L$, started in
its start state and reading $x$, ends in the state $q$.

articles.title: The Nerode automaton
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. The Nerode
automaton of $L$ is the deterministic automaton over $\Sigma$, not necessarily finite, whose
states are the Nerode classes of words for $L$, whose start state is the class of the empty
word, which on reading a symbol $a \in \Sigma$ moves from the class of a word $x$ to the class
of $xa$, and whose accepting states are the classes of the words in $L$.

articles.title: Appending the empty word preserves the Nerode class
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an
alphabet $\Sigma$. For every word $x \in \Sigma^*$, the word $x\varepsilon$ obtained by appending
the empty word $\varepsilon$ is Nerode equivalent to $x$ for $L$.

articles.title: Nerode equivalence is a right congruence
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet
$\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$, then for every word
$z \in \Sigma^*$ the words $xz$ and $yz$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$.

articles.title: Appending a symbol preserves Nerode equivalence
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet
$\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$, then for every symbol
$a \in \Sigma$ the words $xa$ and $ya$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$.

articles.title: Nerode equivalence is equivalence of the reached states
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA and let $L$ be
the language it accepts. Two words $x$ and $y$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$ if and only if the
states that $M$ reaches from its start state on reading $x$ and on reading $y$ are
observationally equivalent, that is, $M$ accepts the same language from both states.

articles.title: Continuation characterization of Nerode equivalence
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an
alphabet $\Sigma$. Two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$ if and only if,
for every word $z \in \Sigma^*$, $xz \in L$ holds exactly when $yz \in L$.

articles.title: Words reaching the same DFA state are Nerode equivalent
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA and let $L$ be
the language it accepts. If $M$ reaches the same state from its start state on reading the words
$x$ and $y$, then $x$ and $y$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$.

articles.title: Nerode equivalence
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Two words
$x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$ when they have the same left quotient, that is,
$\{z \in \Sigma^* \mid xz \in L\} = \{z \in \Sigma^* \mid yz \in L\}$.

articles.title: The Nerode setoid
articles.statement:
For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the Nerode setoid of $L$
is the set $\Sigma^*$ of words equipped with Nerode equivalence for $L$, which is reflexive,
symmetric and transitive.

articles.title: Residual languages of reachable states
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ and a state $q$ of $M$, let $L_q$
be the language of words $z$ such that running $M$ from $q$ on $z$ ends in an accepting state.
The reachable residuals of $M$ form the set of the languages $L_q$ over all states $q$ that $M$
reaches from its start state on some input word.

This semantic state space forgets duplicate DFA states that accept the same continuations.

articles.title: Reachable state of a DFA
articles.statement: A state is reachable when some input word reaches it from the start state.

articles.title: Representative of a Nerode class
articles.statement:
For a language $L$ and a Nerode class $q$ of $L$,
the representative of $q$ is a word whose Nerode class is $q$, chosen once and for all.

articles.title: Equivalent states of a DFA
articles.statement:
Two states $p$ and $q$ of a DFA $M$ are equivalent when
they accept the same continuation language: for every word $z$, running $M$ from $p$ on $z$
ends in an accepting state if and only if running $M$ from $q$ on $z$ does.

articles.title: Transition on Nerode classes
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and
$a \in \Sigma$ a symbol. Appending $a$ sends the Nerode class of a word $x$ to the Nerode class
of $xa$; this is well defined because Nerode equivalence is preserved by appending a symbol.

articles.title: Distinct Nerode classes reach distinct states
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA that accepts exactly
the language $L$. Then the map sending each Nerode class of $L$ to the state that $M$ reaches
from its start state on the chosen representative of the class is injective. In particular, $M$
has at least one distinct state for each Nerode class.

articles.title: Nerode classes to DFA states
articles.statement:
For a language $L$ and a DFA $M$ over the same alphabet,
this map sends each Nerode class $q$ of $L$ to the state that $M$ reaches from its start
state on the chosen representative of $q$.

Unlike the canonical map from words to states, this does not claim that equivalent words reach
equal states in a nonminimal DFA.

articles.title: Regular languages are closed under alphabet preimages
articles.statement:
Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$
be a map between alphabets. If $L$ is a regular language over $\Gamma$, then its alphabet
preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$ is regular, where $f^*(w)$ is the word obtained
by applying $f$ to each letter of $w$.

articles.title: Alphabet preimages are inverse images under word morphisms
articles.statement:
Let
$f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets, $f^* \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ the
monoid morphism that applies $f$ to each letter of a word, and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. Then
the alphabet preimage of $L$ under $f$ equals the inverse image
$(f^*)^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$ of $L$ under $f^*$.

articles.title: The alphabet preimage morphism refines the preimage's syntactic congruence
articles.statement:
Let
$f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets, $L$ a language over $\Gamma$ with
syntactic monoid $M(L)$, and $\varphi \colon \Sigma^* \to M(L)$ the alphabet preimage morphism,
which sends a word $w$ to the class in $M(L)$ of the word $f^*(w)$ obtained by applying $f$ to
each letter of $w$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ satisfy $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$, then $x$
and $y$ are syntactically congruent for the alphabet preimage
$\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$. In other words, the kernel congruence of $\varphi$ is
contained in the syntactic congruence of the alphabet preimage.

articles.title: Alphabet preimage morphism
articles.statement:
Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets
and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. The alphabet preimage morphism of $f$ and $L$ is the monoid
morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$ that sends a word $w$ to
the syntactic class of $f^*(w)$, the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of $w$. It is
the composite of the letterwise map $f^* \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ with the syntactic
morphism of $L$.

articles.title: Division map for the syntactic monoid of an alphabet preimage
articles.statement:
Let
$f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. Write
$f^*(w)$ for the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of a word $w$, $[u]_L$ for the
class of a word $u$ in the syntactic monoid $M(L)$ of $L$, $K$ for the alphabet preimage
$\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$, and $\varphi \colon \Sigma^* \to M(L)$ for the alphabet
preimage morphism $w \mapsto [f^*(w)]_L$. This is the monoid morphism from the submonoid
$\varphi(\Sigma^*)$ of $M(L)$ to the syntactic monoid $M(K)$ that sends $\varphi(w)$ to $[w]_K$;
it is well defined because $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$ implies $[x]_K = [y]_K$.

This morphism is surjective, so $M(K)$ is a quotient of a submonoid of $M(L)$.

articles.title: Alphabet preimage
articles.statement:
Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets and $L$ a
language over $\Gamma$. The alphabet preimage of $L$ under $f$ is the language over $\Sigma$
consisting of the words $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$ such that $f(a_1) f(a_2) \cdots f(a_n) \in L$.

articles.title: Finiteness of the syntactic monoid is invariant under renaming letters
articles.statement:
Let
$e \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a bijection between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$.
The syntactic monoid of the alphabet preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid e^*(w) \in L\}$, where
$e^*(w)$ is the word obtained by applying $e$ to each letter of $w$, is finite if and only if
the syntactic monoid of $L$ is finite.

articles.title: Alphabet preimages preserve finiteness of the syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
Let
$f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$ whose
syntactic monoid is finite. Then the syntactic monoid of the alphabet preimage
$\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$ is finite, where $f^*(w)$ is the word obtained by applying
$f$ to each letter of $w$.

articles.title: Inverse images under word morphisms preserve finiteness of the syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
Let
$h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids and $L$ a language over
$\Gamma$ whose syntactic monoid is finite. Then the syntactic monoid of the inverse image
$h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ is finite.

articles.title: Renaming letters by a bijection preserves and reflects regularity
articles.statement:
Let
$e \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a bijection between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$.
The alphabet preimage $\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid e^*(w) \in L\}$, where $e^*(w)$ is the word
obtained by applying $e$ to each letter of $w$, is regular if and only if $L$ is regular.

articles.title: The alphabet preimage morphism recognizes the alphabet preimage
articles.statement:
Let
$f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$ be a map between alphabets and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$. Write
$f^*(w)$ for the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter of a word $w$, $[u]_L$ for the
class of a word $u$ in the syntactic monoid $M(L)$ of $L$, $A_L \subseteq M(L)$ for the
accepting set of classes of words in $L$, and $\varphi \colon \Sigma^* \to M(L)$ for the alphabet
preimage morphism $w \mapsto [f^*(w)]_L$. Then $\varphi$ recognizes the alphabet preimage
$\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$ through $A_L$: for every word $w \in \Sigma^*$, we have
$f^*(w) \in L$ if and only if $\varphi(w) \in A_L$.

articles.title: Syntactic equivalence pulls back along an alphabet map
articles.statement:
Let $f \colon \Sigma \to \Gamma$
be a map between alphabets, $L$ a language over $\Gamma$, and $K$ the alphabet preimage
$\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid f^*(w) \in L\}$, where $f^*(w)$ is the word obtained by applying $f$ to
each letter of $w$. If $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are words such that $f^*(x)$ and $f^*(y)$ are
syntactically equivalent for $L$, then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for $K$.

articles.title: Syntactic equivalence pulls back along a word morphism
articles.statement:
Let
$h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids, $L$ a language over
$\Gamma$, and $K = h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ its inverse image. If
$x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are words such that $h(x)$ and $h(y)$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$,
then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for $K$.

articles.title: Word morphisms act letter by letter
articles.statement:
Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid
morphism between free monoids. For every word $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n \in \Sigma^*$ (including the
empty word, $n = 0$), we have $h(a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n) = h(a_1) h(a_2) \cdots h(a_n)$, the
concatenation of the images of its letters.

articles.title: Regular languages are closed under inverse word morphisms
articles.statement:
Let
$h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids. If $L$ is a regular
language over $\Gamma$, then its inverse image $h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ is
regular.

articles.title: Letterwise description of the inverse image under a word morphism
articles.statement:
Let
$h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids and $L$ a language over
$\Gamma$. The inverse image $h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ consists exactly of
the words $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n \in \Sigma^*$ such that the concatenation
$h(a_1) h(a_2) \cdots h(a_n)$ of the images of their letters lies in $L$.

articles.title: Division map for the syntactic monoid of an inverse image
articles.statement:
Let
$h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid morphism between free monoids and $L$ a language over
