$\Gamma$. Write $[u]_L$ for the class of a word $u$ in the syntactic monoid $M(L)$ of $L$, $K$ for
the inverse image $h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$, and
$\varphi \colon \Sigma^* \to M(L)$ for the recognizing morphism $w \mapsto [h(w)]_L$. This is the
monoid morphism from the submonoid $\varphi(\Sigma^*)$ of $M(L)$ to the syntactic monoid $M(K)$
that sends $\varphi(w)$ to $[w]_K$; it is well defined because $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$ implies
$[x]_K = [y]_K$.

This morphism is surjective, so $M(K)$ is a quotient of a submonoid of $M(L)$.

articles.title: Inverse image under a word morphism
articles.statement:
Let $\Sigma$ and $\Gamma$ be alphabets,
$h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ a monoid morphism between their free monoids of words, and $L$ a
language over $\Gamma$. The inverse image of $L$ under $h$ is the language
$h^{-1}(L) = \{w \in \Sigma^* \mid h(w) \in L\}$ over $\Sigma$.

articles.title: Recognizing morphism of an inverse image
articles.statement:
Let $h \colon \Sigma^* \to \Gamma^*$ be a monoid
morphism between free monoids and $L$ a language over $\Gamma$ with syntactic monoid $M(L)$. The
recognizing morphism of $h$ and $L$ is the monoid morphism $\Sigma^* \to M(L)$ that sends a word
$w$ to the syntactic class $[h(w)]_L$ of $h(w)$; it is the composite of $h$ with the syntactic
morphism of $L$.

articles.title: Size bound for the syntactic monoid of a context quotient
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an
alphabet $A$, let $u, v$ be words over $A$, and write $u^{-1} L v^{-1} = \{x \mid uxv \in L\}$
for the context quotient. If the image of the syntactic morphism of $L$ and the syntactic monoid
of $u^{-1} L v^{-1}$ are both finite, then the syntactic monoid of $u^{-1} L v^{-1}$ has at most
as many elements as the image of the syntactic morphism of $L$.

articles.title: Accepting set for a context quotient
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi \colon A^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism
from the free monoid on an alphabet $A$ to a monoid $M$, let $P \subseteq M$, and let $u, v$ be
words over $A$. The accepting set for the context $(u, v)$ is
$\{m \in M \mid \varphi(u)\, m\, \varphi(v) \in P\}$.

articles.title: Recognizers recognize context quotients
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi \colon A^* \to M$ be a monoid
morphism from the free monoid on an alphabet $A$ to a monoid $M$ that recognizes a language $L$
over $A$ through $P \subseteq M$, that is, a word $x$ lies in $L$ exactly when $\varphi(x) \in P$.
Then for all words $u, v$ over $A$, $\varphi$ recognizes the context quotient
$\{x \mid uxv \in L\}$ through the set $\{m \in M \mid \varphi(u)\, m\, \varphi(v) \in P\}$.

articles.title: Regular languages are closed under context quotients
articles.statement:
If $L$ is a regular language over
an alphabet $A$, then for all words $u, v$ over $A$, the context quotient
$u^{-1} L v^{-1} = \{x \mid uxv \in L\}$ is regular.

articles.title: Composing context quotients
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $A$, and for words
$u, v$ over $A$ write $u^{-1} L v^{-1} = \{x \mid uxv \in L\}$. Then for all words
$u_1, v_1, u_2, v_2$ over $A$,
$u_2^{-1} (u_1^{-1} L v_1^{-1}) v_2^{-1} = (u_1 u_2)^{-1} L (v_2 v_1)^{-1}$.

articles.title: The canonical map to the syntactic monoid of a context quotient
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language
over an alphabet $A$, let $u, v$ be words over $A$, and write
$u^{-1} L v^{-1} = \{x \mid uxv \in L\}$. Let $\eta$ be the syntactic morphism of $L$ and
$\eta'$ the syntactic morphism of $u^{-1} L v^{-1}$. This is the monoid morphism from the image
of $\eta$ to the syntactic monoid of $u^{-1} L v^{-1}$ that sends $\eta(x)$ to $\eta'(x)$ for
every word $x$ over $A$.

articles.title: Context quotient
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $A$ and let $u, v$ be words over
$A$. The context quotient of $L$ by $(u, v)$ is the language
$u^{-1} L v^{-1} = \{x \in A^* \mid uxv \in L\}$ of words that land in $L$ when placed between
$u$ and $v$.

articles.title: Context quotients preserve finiteness of the syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over
an alphabet $A$ whose syntactic monoid is finite. Then for all words $u, v$ over $A$, the
syntactic monoid of the context quotient $u^{-1} L v^{-1} = \{x \mid uxv \in L\}$ is finite.

articles.title: Left quotients preserve finiteness of the syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an
alphabet $A$ whose syntactic monoid is finite. Then for every word $u$ over $A$, the syntactic
monoid of the left quotient $u^{-1} L = \{x \mid ux \in L\}$ is finite.

articles.title: Right quotients preserve finiteness of the syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over
an alphabet $A$ whose syntactic monoid is finite. Then for every word $u$ over $A$, the syntactic
monoid of the right quotient $L u^{-1} = \{x \mid xu \in L\}$ is finite.

articles.title: Regular languages are closed under left quotients by fixed words
articles.statement:
If $L$ is a regular
language over an alphabet $A$, then for every word $u$ over $A$, the left quotient
$u^{-1} L = \{x \mid ux \in L\}$ is regular.

The proof starts a DFA for $L$ in the state it reaches on $u$.

articles.title: Accepting set for a left quotient
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi \colon A^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism
from the free monoid on an alphabet $A$ to a monoid $M$, let $P \subseteq M$, and let $u$ be a
word over $A$. The accepting set for the left quotient by $u$ is
$\{m \in M \mid \varphi(u)\, m \in P\}$.

articles.title: The canonical map to the syntactic monoid of a left quotient
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over
an alphabet $A$, let $u$ be a word over $A$, and write $u^{-1} L = \{x \mid ux \in L\}$. Let
$\eta$ be the syntactic morphism of $L$ and $\eta'$ the syntactic morphism of $u^{-1} L$. This
is the monoid morphism from the image of $\eta$ to the syntactic monoid of $u^{-1} L$ that sends
$\eta(x)$ to $\eta'(x)$ for every word $x$ over $A$.

articles.title: Recognizers recognize left quotients
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi \colon A^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism
from the free monoid on an alphabet $A$ to a monoid $M$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $A$
through $P \subseteq M$, that is, a word $x$ lies in $L$ exactly when $\varphi(x) \in P$. Then
for every word $u$ over $A$, $\varphi$ recognizes the left quotient $\{x \mid ux \in L\}$ through
the set $\{m \in M \mid \varphi(u)\, m \in P\}$.

articles.title: Recognizers recognize right quotients
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi \colon A^* \to M$ be a monoid
morphism from the free monoid on an alphabet $A$ to a monoid $M$ that recognizes a language $L$
over $A$ through $P \subseteq M$, that is, a word $x$ lies in $L$ exactly when $\varphi(x) \in P$.
Then for every word $u$ over $A$, $\varphi$ recognizes the right quotient $\{x \mid xu \in L\}$
through the set $\{m \in M \mid m\, \varphi(u) \in P\}$.

articles.title: Regular languages are closed under right quotients by fixed words
articles.statement:
If $L$ is a regular
language over an alphabet $A$, then for every word $u$ over $A$, the right quotient
$L u^{-1} = \{x \mid xu \in L\}$ is regular.

articles.title: Accepting set for a right quotient
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi \colon A^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism
from the free monoid on an alphabet $A$ to a monoid $M$, let $P \subseteq M$, and let $u$ be a
word over $A$. The accepting set for the right quotient by $u$ is
$\{m \in M \mid m\, \varphi(u) \in P\}$.

articles.title: The canonical map to the syntactic monoid of a right quotient
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over
an alphabet $A$, let $u$ be a word over $A$, and write $L u^{-1} = \{x \mid xu \in L\}$. Let
$\eta$ be the syntactic morphism of $L$ and $\eta'$ the syntactic morphism of $L u^{-1}$. This
is the monoid morphism from the image of $\eta$ to the syntactic monoid of $L u^{-1}$ that sends
$\eta(x)$ to $\eta'(x)$ for every word $x$ over $A$.

articles.title: Right quotient of a language by a word
articles.statement:
For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and a
word $w \in \Sigma^*$, the right quotient of $L$ by $w$ is the language
$\{x \in \Sigma^* : xw \in L\}$ of all words $x$ whose concatenation $xw$ with $w$ lies in $L$.

articles.title: Syntactic equivalence via context quotients
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $A$.
Two words $x, y$ over $A$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$ if and only if, for all words
$u, v$ over $A$, $x$ lies in the context quotient $u^{-1} L v^{-1} = \{w \mid uwv \in L\}$
exactly when $y$ does.

articles.title: Recognition pulls back along a factorization
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an
alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to C$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid
$\Sigma^*$ that recognizes $L$ through a subset $A \subseteq C$. If $\varphi = f \circ \psi$ for
monoid morphisms $\psi : \Sigma^* \to T$ and $f : T \to C$, then $\psi$ recognizes $L$ through the
preimage $f^{-1}(A)$.

articles.title: Changing the accepting set off the image of a recognizer
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be
a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$
through a subset $A_1 \subseteq M$. If $A_2 \subseteq M$ satisfies
$\varphi(x) \in A_1 \iff \varphi(x) \in A_2$ for every word $x$, then $\varphi$ also recognizes $L$
through $A_2$.

articles.title: The syntactic DFA of a language with finite syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
If the syntactic monoid of a
language $L$ is finite, then the syntactic DFA of $L$ has finitely many states and accepts exactly
$L$.

This gives a specific finite recognizer, the syntactic DFA, rather than merely the existence of
some finite DFA.

articles.title: Languages of finite automata have finite syntactic monoids
articles.statement:
Every language accepted by a
DFA with finitely many states has a finite syntactic monoid.

articles.title: Finite recognizers give finite syntactic monoids
articles.statement:
If a monoid morphism from the free monoid
$\Sigma^*$ to a finite monoid $M$ recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through some subset of
$M$, then the syntactic monoid of $L$ is finite.

articles.title: Finite syntactic monoid implies regularity
articles.statement:
Every language whose syntactic monoid is
finite is regular.

articles.title: The syntactic morphism recognizes the language
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet
$\Sigma$. For every word $x \in \Sigma^*$, $x \in L$ if and only if the image of $x$ under the
syntactic morphism of $L$ lies in the accepting set of the syntactic monoid of $L$, the set of
syntactic classes of words of $L$.

articles.title: Equal syntactic classes give equal Nerode classes
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language. For all words
$x$ and $y$, if the syntactic morphism of $L$ sends $x$ and $y$ to the same element of the
syntactic monoid of $L$, then $x$ and $y$ have the same Nerode class with respect to $L$.

articles.title: The image of a recognizer maps onto the syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be
a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$
through a subset $A \subseteq M$. Then the canonical monoid morphism from the image
$\varphi(\Sigma^*)$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$, which sends $\varphi(x)$ to the syntactic class
of $x$, is surjective.

articles.title: Map from a recognizer's image to the syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a
monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$
through a subset $A \subseteq M$. This is the monoid morphism from the image $\varphi(\Sigma^*)$
to the syntactic monoid of $L$ that sends $\varphi(x)$ to the syntactic class of $x$ for every
word $x$. It is well defined because words with the same image under $\varphi$ are syntactically
equivalent for $L$.

articles.title: Recognizer kernels refine the syntactic congruence
articles.statement:
If a monoid morphism $\varphi$ from the
free monoid $\Sigma^*$ recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A$ of its
codomain, then the kernel congruence of $\varphi$ is contained in the syntactic congruence of $L$:
any words $x, y$ with $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.

articles.title: The kernel quotient of a recognizer maps onto the syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
If a monoid morphism
$\varphi$ from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset
$A$ of its codomain, then the canonical monoid morphism from the quotient of $\Sigma^*$ by the
kernel congruence of $\varphi$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$, which sends the class of a word
$x$ to its syntactic class, is surjective.

articles.title: Canonical map from a recognizer's kernel quotient to the syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a
language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the
free monoid on $\Sigma$ into a monoid $M$, and let $A \subseteq M$ be such that $\varphi$
recognizes $L$ through $A$. Since the kernel congruence of $\varphi$ (words $x, y$ with
$\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$) is contained in the syntactic congruence of $L$, there is a monoid
morphism from the quotient of $\Sigma^*$ by the kernel of $\varphi$ to the syntactic monoid of
$L$ sending the class of each word $w$ to the syntactic class of $w$.

This is the algebraic minimality map before identifying the kernel quotient with the image of
the recognizer.

articles.title: Recognition as an inverse image
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, let
$\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on $\Sigma$ into a monoid
$M$, and let $A \subseteq M$. Then $\varphi$ recognizes $L$ through $A$ if and only if the set
of words of $\Sigma^*$ that belong to $L$ equals $\varphi^{-1}(A)$.

articles.title: The syntactic morphism recognizes its language
articles.statement:
For every language $L$ over an alphabet
$\Sigma$, the syntactic morphism of $L$, from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ to the syntactic monoid
of $L$, recognizes $L$ through the accepting subset of the syntactic monoid, namely the set of
syntactic classes of words in $L$.

articles.title: The transition morphism of a DFA recognizes its language
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over an
alphabet $\Sigma$ with state set $Q$, start state $q_0$ and set of accepting states $F$. The
transition morphism of $M$, from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ to the monoid of state
transformations of $Q$, recognizes the language accepted by $M$ through the set of
transformations $f$ with $f(q_0) \in F$.

No accessibility or state-separation hypothesis on $M$ is needed.

articles.title: Recognition of a language by a monoid morphism
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet
$\Sigma$, let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on $\Sigma$
into a monoid $M$, and let $A \subseteq M$. Then $\varphi$ recognizes $L$ through $A$ when, for
every word $w \in \Sigma^*$, $w \in L$ if and only if $\varphi(w) \in A$.

articles.title: State transformations as functions
articles.statement:
For a type $Q$ of states, the bijection from the
state transformations of $Q$ to the functions $Q \to Q$ that sends each transformation to its
underlying function; it forgets the multiplication of state transformations.

articles.title: State transformation monoid
articles.statement:
For a type $Q$ of states, the state transformation monoid
of $Q$ consists of all functions $Q \to Q$, multiplied by composition in the opposite order: the
product $fg$ first applies $f$ and then $g$, so $(fg)(q) = g(f(q))$, and the unit is the
identity function.

articles.title: Accepting set of the syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
For a language $L$, the accepting set of the
syntactic monoid of $L$ is the set of syntactic classes of words of $L$: a class belongs to it
when its representatives lie in $L$, which does not depend on the representative chosen.

articles.title: Image of the syntactic action
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an accessible, state-separated DFA and let $L$
be the language $M$ accepts. The image of the action of the syntactic monoid of $L$ on the states
of $M$, the monoid homomorphism sending the syntactic class of each word $x$ to the state
transformation induced by reading $x$, is exactly the transition monoid of $M$.

articles.title: Action of the syntactic monoid on states
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an accessible, state-separated DFA
with state type $Q$, and let $L$ be the language $M$ accepts. This is the monoid homomorphism
from the syntactic monoid of $L$ to the state transformation monoid of $Q$ that sends the
syntactic class of each word $x$ to the map taking each state $q$ to the state $M$ reaches from
$q$ by reading $x$. It is well defined because syntactically equivalent words act identically on
the states of such a DFA.

articles.title: Syntactic congruence as a kernel
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be an accessible, state-separated DFA and let
$L$ be the language $M$ accepts. The syntactic congruence of $L$ equals the kernel of the
transition morphism of $M$: two words are syntactically equivalent for $L$ if and only if they
induce the same transformation of the states of $M$.

articles.title: Syntactic congruence
articles.statement:
For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic
congruence of $L$ is the monoid congruence on the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that relates words $x$
and $y$ when, for all words $u$ and $v$, $uxv \in L$ if and only if $uyv \in L$.

articles.title: The syntactic DFA accepts its language
articles.statement:
For every language $L$, the syntactic DFA of $L$
accepts exactly $L$.

articles.title: The syntactic DFA is accessible
articles.statement:
For every language $L$, every state of the syntactic DFA
of $L$ is reachable: some word leads to it from the start state.

articles.title: Runs of the syntactic DFA
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. For every
state $q$ of the syntactic DFA of $L$ (an element of the syntactic monoid of $L$) and every word
$x \in \Sigma^*$, the state reached from $q$ by reading $x$ is $q \cdot [x]$, where $[x]$ is the
image of $x$ under the syntactic morphism of $L$.

articles.title: The syntactic DFA
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. The syntactic DFA of
$L$ has the syntactic monoid of $L$ as its set of states, the identity $1$ as start state, and
the syntactic classes of the words of $L$ as accepting states; from a state $q$, reading a
letter $a \in \Sigma$ leads to $q \cdot [a]$, where $[a]$ is the syntactic class of the
one-letter word $a$.

It is the direct automata-theoretic presentation of the canonical syntactic recognizer.

articles.title: Syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic monoid of
$L$ is the quotient of the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ of words by the syntactic congruence of $L$,
which relates words $x$ and $y$ when $uxv \in L \iff uyv \in L$ for all words $u$ and $v$.

articles.title: Syntactic morphism
articles.statement:
For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic morphism
of $L$ is the monoid homomorphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ of words to the syntactic
monoid of $L$ that sends each word to its class under the syntactic congruence of $L$.

articles.title: Syntactic equivalence is compatible with concatenation
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an
alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $w, x, y, z \in \Sigma^*$ be words. If $w$ and $x$ are syntactically
equivalent for $L$, and $y$ and $z$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then $wy$ and $xz$ are
syntactically equivalent for $L$.

articles.title: Syntactic equivalence via transition actions
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$
that is accessible (every state is reached from the start state by some word) and
state-separated (distinct states have distinct continuation languages), and let $L$ be the
language accepted by $M$. Then two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$
if and only if they have the same transition action on $M$: for every state $q$, running $M$
from $q$ on $x$ ends in the same state as running $M$ from $q$ on $y$.

articles.title: Syntactically equivalent words agree on membership
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an
alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then
$x \in L$ if and only if $y \in L$.

articles.title: Syntactic equivalence refines Nerode equivalence
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet
$\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then they are
Nerode equivalent for $L$: the sets $\{z : xz \in L\}$ and $\{z : yz \in L\}$ are equal.

articles.title: Words with equal recognizer images are syntactically equivalent
articles.statement:
Let
$\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on an alphabet $\Sigma$ into
a monoid $M$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a set $A \subseteq M$. If two
words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ satisfy $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$, then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically
equivalent for $L$: for all words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$, $uxv \in L$ if and only if $uyv \in L$.

articles.title: Words with the same transition action are syntactically equivalent
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over
an alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $L$ be the language accepted by $M$. If two words
$x, y \in \Sigma^*$ have the same transition action on $M$, that is, for every state $q$, running
$M$ from $q$ on $x$ ends in the same state as running $M$ from $q$ on $y$, then $x$ and $y$ are
syntactically equivalent for $L$.

articles.title: Syntactic equivalence is stable under left multiplication
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an
alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then
for every word $w \in \Sigma^*$ the words $wx$ and $wy$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.

articles.title: Syntactic equivalence is stable under right multiplication
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an
alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then
for every word $w \in \Sigma^*$ the words $xw$ and $yw$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.

articles.title: Syntactic equivalence
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Two words
$x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$ when, for all words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$,
$uxv \in L$ if and only if $uyv \in L$.

articles.title: Transition monoid element of a word
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Each word
$x \in \Sigma^*$ determines the element of the transition monoid of $M$ given by the state
transformation that sends each state $q$ to the state $M$ reaches from $q$ after reading $x$.

articles.title: Syntactically equivalent words act identically
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA that is accessible
(every state is reachable from the start state) and state-separated (two states with the same
continuation language are equal). If two words $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for the
language accepted by $M$, then $x$ and $y$ have the same transition action on $M$: for every
state $q$, reading $x$ from $q$ and reading $y$ from $q$ lead to the same state.

articles.title: Transition action of a word
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ and a word $x$, the transition action of $x$ is
the map sending each state $q$ of $M$ to the state that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ starting
from $q$.

articles.title: Transition monoid of a DFA
articles.statement:
The transition monoid of a DFA $M$ is the image of the
transition morphism of $M$: the submonoid of state transformations of $M$ consisting of the
transition actions of all words, where a word $x$ acts by sending each state $q$ to the state
that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ from $q$. State transformations are multiplied in reading
order, so the product $fg$ applies $f$ first and then $g$.

articles.title: Transition morphism of a DFA
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$, the transition morphism is the monoid
homomorphism from the free monoid of words to the state transformations of $M$ that sends each
word $x$ to its transition action, the map taking each state $q$ to the state that $M$ reaches
by reading $x$ from $q$. State transformations are multiplied in reading order, so the product
$fg$ applies $f$ first and then $g$; with this order, the word $xy$ is sent to the product of
the images of $x$ and $y$.

articles.title: Transition transformation of a word
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ and a word $x$, the transition
transformation of $x$ is the transition action of $x$, the map sending each state $q$ to the
state that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ from $q$, regarded as an element of the monoid of state
transformations of $M$ (multiplied in reading order: $fg$ applies $f$ first, then $g$).

articles.title: Endofunction bound for the syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA with a finite
set of states $Q$, and suppose the syntactic monoid of the language accepted by $M$ is
finite. Then that syntactic monoid has at most $|Q|^{|Q|}$ elements.

articles.title: The syntactic monoid is no larger than the transition monoid
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA
accepting the language $L$, and suppose that the transition monoid of $M$ and the syntactic
monoid of $L$ are both finite. Then the syntactic monoid of $L$ has at most as many elements as
the transition monoid of $M$.

articles.title: Finitely many state transformations
articles.statement:
If $Q$ is a finite set, then the monoid of state
transformations of $Q$, consisting of all functions $Q \to Q$ multiplied in diagrammatic order,
is finite.

articles.title: Regular languages have finite syntactic monoids
articles.statement:
If $L$ is a regular language, then the
syntactic monoid of $L$ is finite.

articles.title: Transition monoids of finite automata are finite
articles.statement:
For every DFA $M$ with a finite set of
states, the transition monoid of $M$ is finite.

articles.title: Regular languages are those with finite syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
A language $L$ is regular if
and only if the syntactic monoid of $L$ is finite.

articles.title: The transition monoid recognizes the accepted language
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA with start
state $q_0$ and accepting states $F$. The map sending each word to the element of the transition
monoid of $M$ that it induces recognizes the language accepted by $M$, with accepting set the
elements $f$ of the transition monoid such that $f(q_0) \in F$: a word is accepted by $M$ exactly
when the transformation it induces sends $q_0$ into $F$.

articles.title: The transition morphism recognizes through accepting transformations
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a DFA
with start state $q_0$ and accepting states $F$. The transition morphism of $M$, from words to
state transformations, recognizes the language accepted by $M$ through the accepting
transformations of $M$: a word is accepted by $M$ exactly when the transformation it induces
sends $q_0$ into $F$.

articles.title: Accepting transformations of a DFA
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ with set of states $Q$, start state
$q_0$ and accepting states $F$, the accepting transformations of $M$ are the state
transformations $f$ of $Q$ with $f(q_0) \in F$.

articles.title: The transition monoid maps to the syntactic monoid
articles.statement:
For a DFA $M$ accepting the language
$L$, this is the monoid homomorphism from the transition monoid of $M$ to the syntactic monoid of
$L$ that sends the transformation induced by each word $w$ to the syntactic class of $w$.

articles.title: Labels of the composite machine
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be finite multi-stack Turing
machines with label sets $\Lambda_1$ and $\Lambda_2$, and let $X$ be the alphabet of the input
stack of $M_2$. The label set of their composite machine is the disjoint union of $\Lambda_1$,
$\Lambda_2$ and two copies of $X \sqcup \{\bot\}$, one for each copy loop: in each copy, $\bot$
labels the step that pops and $x \in X$ labels the step that pushes $x$.

articles.title: States of the composite machine
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be finite multi-stack Turing machines
with internal state sets $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$, and let $X$ be the alphabet of the input stack
of $M_2$. The internal states of their composite machine are the triples in
$\sigma_1 \times \sigma_2 \times (X \sqcup \{\bot\})$: a state of $M_1$, a state of $M_2$, and
either the symbol just popped by a copy loop or $\bot$ when there is none.

articles.title: Stack alphabets of the composite machine
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be finite multi-stack Turing
machines and let $X$ be the alphabet of the input stack of $M_2$. The stacks of their composite
machine are the stacks of $M_1$, the stacks of $M_2$ and one scratch stack. Each stack of $M_1$
keeps its alphabet from $M_1$, each stack of $M_2$ keeps its alphabet from $M_2$, and the scratch
stack has alphabet $X$.

articles.title: Stack indices of the composite machine
articles.statement:
For finite multi-stack Turing machines $M_1$ and
$M_2$ with stack index sets $K_1$ and $K_2$, the stacks of their composite machine are indexed by
the disjoint union $K_1 \sqcup K_2 \sqcup \{\ast\}$: the stacks of $M_1$, the stacks of $M_2$, and
one scratch stack $\ast$.

articles.title: Polynomial-time functions are closed under composition
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ be
types with canonical bitstring encodings. If $f : \alpha \to \beta$ and $g : \beta \to \gamma$ are
polynomial-time computable, then so is $g \circ f$.

articles.title: The composite polynomial-time TM2 computation
articles.statement:
Let $h_1$ be a polynomial-time TM2
computation of $f : \alpha \to \beta$ with respect to encodings $e_\alpha$ and $e_\beta$, and
let $h_2$ be one of $g : \beta \to \gamma$ with respect to $e_\beta$ and $e_\gamma$. This is the
polynomial-time TM2 computation of $g \circ f$ with respect to $e_\alpha$ and $e_\gamma$ whose
machine is the composite machine of the machines of $h_1$ and $h_2$ with the glue map between
them, whose input alphabet bijection is that of $h_1$, whose output alphabet bijection is that of
$h_2$, and whose time bound is the composite time bound of $h_1$ and $h_2$.

It witnesses that polynomial-time TM2 computability is closed under composition.

articles.title: P is closed under polynomial-time preimages
The composite machine computes the composite function in time
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ compute
$f : \alpha \to \beta$ in polynomial time from the encoding $e_\alpha$ to $e_\beta$, and let $M_2$
compute $g : \beta \to \gamma$ in polynomial time from $e_\beta$ to $e_\gamma$. For every
$a \in \alpha$, let $n$ be the length of $e_\alpha(a)$ and $T$ the composite time bound. Started on
$e_\alpha(a)$, written in the input alphabet of $M_1$, the composite machine of $M_1$ and $M_2$
(with the glue map from output symbols of $M_1$ to input symbols of $M_2$) reaches within
$T(n)$ steps the halted configuration whose output stack holds $e_\gamma(g(f(a)))$, written in the
output alphabet of $M_2$, whose other stacks are empty and whose internal state is the initial
one.

articles.title: Time bound of the composite machine
articles.statement:
Let $p_1, p_2 \in \mathbb{N}[X]$ be the polynomial time
bounds of a machine $M_1$ computing $f$ and a machine $M_2$ computing $g$, and let $c$ be the sum,
over the labels of $M_1$, of the number of push instructions in the statement at that label. The
composite time bound is the polynomial $p_1 + 4(X + c\,p_1) + 2 + p_2 \circ (X + c\,p_1)$.

The two copy loops take $2m + 1$ steps each on an intermediate string of length
$m \le n + c\,p_1(n)$, where $n$ is the input length.

articles.title: The composite machine
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be finite multi-stack Turing machines, let $X$ be
the alphabet of the input stack of $M_2$, and let $\varphi$ map the output alphabet of $M_1$ to $X$.
The composite machine has the stacks of $M_1$, the stacks of $M_2$ and one scratch stack with
alphabet $X$; its input stack is that of $M_1$ and its output stack is that of $M_2$. It starts
at the main label of $M_1$, in the state made of the initial states of $M_1$ and $M_2$ and no held
symbol. It runs $M_1$; when $M_1$ halts, it pops the output stack of $M_1$ onto the scratch stack,
translating each symbol by $\varphi$, then pops the scratch stack onto the input stack of $M_2$,
then runs $M_2$ from its main label, and it halts when $M_2$ halts.

articles.title: Composition of polynomial-time functions under encodings
articles.statement:
Let $e_\alpha$, $e_\beta$,
$e_\gamma$ be encodings of types $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$ as lists over alphabets
$\Gamma_\alpha$, $\Gamma_\beta$, $\Gamma_\gamma$. If $f : \alpha \to \beta$ is polynomial-time
computable with respect to $e_\alpha$ and $e_\beta$, and $g : \beta \to \gamma$ is polynomial-time
computable with respect to $e_\beta$ and $e_\gamma$, then $g \circ f$ is polynomial-time
computable with respect to $e_\alpha$ and $e_\gamma$.

articles.title: Second copy loop of the composite machine
articles.statement:
Consider the composite program of machines
$M_1$ and $M_2$ with symbol translation $\varphi$. Suppose it is at the label that pops the
scratch stack, with state $(v_1, v_2, o)$, with $M_1$'s stacks holding $S_1$, $M_2$'s stacks
holding $S_2$, and the scratch stack holding the list $t$. Then after exactly $2|t| + 1$ steps it
is at the start label of $M_2$, with state $(v_1, v_2, \mathrm{none})$, $M_1$'s stacks still
$S_1$, $M_2$'s input stack holding the reverse of $t$ followed by its previous contents, $M_2$'s
other stacks unchanged, and the scratch stack empty.

articles.title: First copy loop of the composite machine
articles.statement:
Consider the composite program of machines $M_1$
and $M_2$ with symbol translation $\varphi$. Suppose it is at the label that pops $M_1$'s output
stack, with state $(v_1, v_2, o)$, with $M_1$'s stacks holding $S_1$, $M_2$'s stacks holding $S_2$,
the scratch stack holding $t$, and $M_1$'s output stack holding the list $y$. Then after exactly
$2|y| + 1$ steps it is at the label that pops the scratch stack, with state
$(v_1, v_2, \mathrm{none})$, $M_1$'s output stack empty and its other stacks unchanged, $M_2$'s
stacks still $S_2$, and the scratch stack holding the reverse of the list obtained by applying
$\varphi$ to each symbol of $y$, followed by $t$.

articles.title: Embedding of $M_2$'s configurations into the composite machine
articles.statement:
A configuration $c$ of $M_2$
is sent to the configuration of the composite of $M_1$ and $M_2$ whose label is the label of $c$
viewed as a label of the $M_2$ part (halted if $c$ is halted), whose state is
$(q_1, v, \mathrm{none})$ with $q_1$ the initial state of $M_1$ and $v$ the state of $c$, and whose
stacks are the stacks of $c$ on $M_2$'s stacks, with $M_1$'s stacks and the scratch stack
empty.

articles.title: Embedding of $M_1$'s configurations into the composite machine
articles.statement:
A configuration $c$ of $M_1$
is sent to the configuration of the composite of $M_1$ and $M_2$ whose label is the label of $c$
viewed as a label of the $M_1$ part, or the label that pops $M_1$'s output stack (the start of the
first copy loop) if $c$ is halted, whose state is $(v, q_2, \mathrm{none})$ with $v$ the state of
$c$ and $q_2$ the initial state of $M_2$, and whose stacks are the stacks of $c$ on $M_1$'s stacks,
with $M_2$'s stacks and the scratch stack empty.

articles.title: Evaluation of a natural-number polynomial is monotone
articles.statement:
For every polynomial $p$ with
coefficients in $\mathbb{N}$ and all natural numbers $a \le b$, we have $p(a) \le p(b)$.

articles.title: Symbol translation between composed machines
articles.statement:
Let $h_1$ be a polynomial-time TM2
computation of $f : \alpha \to \beta$ and $h_2$ one of $g : \beta \to \gamma$, where $\beta$ is
encoded by lists over an alphabet $\Gamma_\beta$. A symbol $y$ of the output-stack alphabet of
$h_1$'s machine is sent to the symbol of the input-stack alphabet of $h_2$'s machine that
corresponds, under $h_2$'s input alphabet bijection with $\Gamma_\beta$, to the letter that $y$
corresponds to under $h_1$'s output alphabet bijection with $\Gamma_\beta$.

articles.title: Stacks of the initial configuration are no longer than the input
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a finite
multi-stack Turing machine (Mathlib's TM2 model with finitely many stacks, function labels and
internal states, and a finite input alphabet) with input stack $k_0$, and let $l$ be a list of
symbols from the alphabet of stack $k_0$. Then for every stack $k$ of $M$, the stack $k$ in the
initial configuration of $M$ on input $l$ has length at most the length of $l$.

The initial configuration holds $l$ on stack $k_0$ and leaves every other stack empty.

articles.title: Simulation transports runs
articles.statement:
Let $f : \alpha \to \mathrm{Option}\,\alpha$ and
$g : \beta \to \mathrm{Option}\,\beta$ be partial step functions (a value $\mathrm{none}$ means
halting) and $e : \alpha \to \beta$ a map such that $f(c) = c'$ implies $g(e(c)) = e(c')$ for all
$c, c'$. Then for every $n$ and all $c, d \in \alpha$, if $n$ steps of $f$ starting from $c$ end
at $d$, then $n$ steps of $g$ starting from $e(c)$ end at $e(d)$.

Halted configurations are absorbing, so every intermediate configuration of such a run is live.

articles.title: Composite label of an $M_1$ label
articles.statement:
A label $l$ of $M_1$ is sent to $l$ viewed as a label of
the $M_1$ part of the composite of $M_1$ and $M_2$, and the halted label is sent to the label that
pops $M_1$'s output stack, which starts the first copy loop.

articles.title: Lifting a statement of the second machine
articles.statement:
Given finite multi-stack Turing machines
$M_1$ and $M_2$, a statement of $M_2$ is translated into a statement of their composite
machine, whose state is a triple $(v_1, v_2, o)$, by recursion on the statement: an operation
on a stack $k$ of $M_2$ acts on the copy of $k$ among the composite stacks, every read or update
of $M_2$'s state reads or updates the component $v_2$ and leaves $v_1$ and $o$ unchanged, a
branch tests $v_2$, a jump to a label $l$ of $M_2$ becomes a jump to the copy of $l$, and
halting stays halting.

articles.title: Lifting a statement of the first machine
articles.statement:
Given finite multi-stack Turing machines
$M_1$ and $M_2$, a statement of $M_1$ is translated into a statement of their composite
machine, whose state is a triple $(v_1, v_2, o)$, by recursion on the statement: an operation
on a stack $k$ of $M_1$ acts on the copy of $k$ among the composite stacks, every read or update
of $M_1$'s state reads or updates the component $v_1$ and leaves $v_2$ and $o$ unchanged, a
branch tests $v_1$, a jump to a label $l$ of $M_1$ becomes a jump to the copy of $l$, and
halting becomes a jump to the pop label of the first copy loop, which moves $M_1$'s output.

articles.title: Intermediate length bound of the composite machine
articles.statement:
Let $h_1$ be a polynomial-time TM2
computation of $f : \alpha \to \beta$ with polynomial time bound $p_1 \in \mathbb{N}[X]$, and let
$c$ be the push bound of the machine of $h_1$. This is the polynomial
$X + c\,p_1 \in \mathbb{N}[X]$.

Evaluated at the length $n$ of an input, its value $n + c\,p_1(n)$ bounds the length of the
intermediate string that the machine of $h_1$ writes for the composite machine.

articles.title: Assembling the stacks of the composite machine
articles.statement:
Given finite multi-stack Turing machines
$M_1$ and $M_2$, contents $S_1$ for the stacks of $M_1$, contents $S_2$ for the stacks of $M_2$,
and a list $t$ of symbols of $M_2$'s input alphabet, the stack contents of their composite
machine put $S_1(k)$ on the copy of each stack $k$ of $M_1$, $S_2(k)$ on the copy of each stack
$k$ of $M_2$, and $t$ on the scratch stack.

articles.title: Pop label of the first copy loop
articles.statement:
In the composite machine of $M_1$ and $M_2$, this is
the label $\mathrm{none}$ in the first copy-loop part of the label set; the composite program
uses it to pop a symbol from $M_1$'s output stack.

articles.title: Pop label of the second copy loop
articles.statement:
In the composite machine of $M_1$ and $M_2$, this is
the label $\mathrm{none}$ in the second copy-loop part of the label set; the composite program
uses it to pop a symbol from the scratch stack.

articles.title: The program of the composite machine
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be finite multi-stack Turing
machines and $\varphi$ a map from $M_1$'s output alphabet to $M_2$'s input alphabet. At a label
of $M_1$ or of $M_2$ the composite program runs the lifted statement of that machine at that
label. At the pop label of the first copy loop it pops $M_1$'s output stack, stores the image
under $\varphi$ of the popped symbol (or nothing) in the third state component, and jumps to the
push label of the first loop for that image, or to the pop label of the second loop if the
stack was empty. At the push label of the first loop for $x$ it pushes $x$ on the scratch stack
and jumps to the first pop label. At the pop label of the second loop it pops the scratch
stack, stores the popped symbol (or nothing) in the third state component, and jumps to the
push label of the second loop for that symbol, or to the copy of $M_2$'s main label if the
scratch stack was empty. At the push label of the second loop for $x$ it pushes $x$ on $M_2$'s
input stack and jumps to the second pop label.

articles.title: Push labels of the first copy loop
articles.statement:
In the composite machine of $M_1$ and $M_2$, for a
symbol $x$ of $M_2$'s input alphabet, this is the label $\mathrm{some}\ x$ in the first copy-loop
part of the label set; the composite program uses it to push $x$ on the scratch stack.

articles.title: Push labels of the second copy loop
articles.statement:
In the composite machine of $M_1$ and $M_2$, for a
symbol $x$ of $M_2$'s input alphabet, this is the label $\mathrm{some}\ x$ in the second
copy-loop part of the label set; the composite program uses it to push $x$ on $M_2$'s input
stack.

articles.title: Push bound of a finite multi-stack Turing machine
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack Turing
machine $M$ (Mathlib's TM2 model with finitely many labels), the push bound of $M$ is the sum,
over all labels $l$ of $M$, of the number of push instructions in the statement that $M$
assigns to $l$.

No stack of $M$ grows by more than the push bound in a single step.

articles.title: Number of push instructions in a TM2 statement
articles.statement:
For a statement $q$ of a multi-stack
Turing machine (Mathlib's TM2 model), this is the number of push nodes in $q$: a push node counts
$1$ plus the count of its continuation; peek, pop and load nodes count as their continuation; a
branch counts the sum of its two branches; goto and halt count $0$.

It is an upper bound on the number of symbols pushed in one step.

articles.title: Polynomial-time TM2-computable functions are closed under composition
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$,
$\beta$, $\gamma$ be types encoded as lists over alphabets by $e_\alpha$, $e_\beta$, $e_\gamma$.
If $f : \alpha \to \beta$ is computable in polynomial time by a multi-stack Turing machine (a
TM2 machine) with respect to $e_\alpha$ and $e_\beta$, and $g : \beta \to \gamma$ is computable
in polynomial time by a TM2 machine with respect to $e_\beta$ and $e_\gamma$, then there is a TM2
machine computing $g \circ f$ in polynomial time with respect to $e_\alpha$ and $e_\gamma$.

## Sources

- Mathlib PR #44441 states the same result as `TM2ComputableInPolyTime.comp`.

articles.title: Scratch stack of the composite machine
articles.statement:
For multi-stack Turing machines (TM2 machines)
$M_1$ and $M_2$ with stack index types $K_1$ and $K_2$, the composite machine has stack indices
$K_1 \oplus K_2 \oplus \mathrm{Unit}$; its scratch stack is the index given by the unique element
of the $\mathrm{Unit}$ summand.

articles.title: Intermediate alphabet of the composite machine
articles.statement:
For a multi-stack Turing machine (a TM2
machine) $M_2$ with input stack $k_0$, this is the alphabet of the symbols on stack $k_0$ of $M_2$.

When a machine $M_1$ is composed with $M_2$, the composite machine uses this alphabet for its
scratch stack and for the symbol held in its control state.

articles.title: Applying a relabelled action
articles.statement:
Let $f : Q \to Q'$ be a map of states; relabelling by $f$
replaces a state $q$ by $f(q)$ and keeps the halting state. For every action $a$ of a machine with
$k$ work tapes and states $Q$ and every configuration $c$ of such a machine, applying $a$ with its
successor state relabelled by $f$ to $c$ with its state relabelled by $f$ gives the configuration
obtained by applying $a$ to $c$ and then relabelling its state by $f$.

articles.title: Relabelling preserves computing a function within time and space bounds
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $M'$
be deterministic machines with $k$ work tapes over the same alphabet such that $M'$ simulates $M$
up to a state relabelling $f$. Let $e_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $e_{\mathrm{out}}$ be injective encodings
of types $\alpha$ and $\beta$ as words over the alphabet, $g : \alpha \to \beta$ a function and
$t, s : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$ bounds. Then $M'$ computes $g$ with respect to these encodings in
time $t$ and space $s$ if and only if $M$ does. Here a machine does so when, for every
$a \in \alpha$, on input $e_{\mathrm{in}}(a)$ it eventually halts with output
$e_{\mathrm{out}}(g(a))$, every computation path of at least $t(a)$ steps ends halted, and every
computation path visits at most $s(a)$ work-tape cells.

articles.title: Computing an output means halting with it
articles.statement:
A deterministic multi-tape Turing machine
computes the output $o$ on input $w$ if and only if there is a step $t$ at which the run from the
initial configuration on $w$ halts (it is halted after $t$ steps and not halted after any $s < t$
steps) and the configuration it reaches after $t$ steps has output tape $o$.

articles.title: Output at a time bound
articles.statement:
If a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine runs in time $t$ on
input $w$, then for every word $o$ the machine computes $o$ on $w$ if and only if the
configuration reached from the initial configuration on $w$ after $t$ steps has output tape $o$.

articles.title: Relabelling preserves what a machine computes
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $M'$ be deterministic machines
with $k$ work tapes over the same alphabet such that $M'$ simulates $M$ up to a state relabelling
$f$. Then for all words $x$ and $o$ over the alphabet, $M'$ started on input $x$ eventually halts
with output $o$ if and only if $M$ does.

articles.title: Output determinism
articles.statement: A deterministic machine computes at most one output on an input.

articles.title: Relabelling preserves deciding a language
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $M'$ be deterministic machines with
$k$ work tapes over the alphabet $\{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$ such that $M'$ simulates $M$
up to a state relabelling $f$. Then for every set $L$ of binary words, $M'$ decides $L$ if and only
if $M$ decides $L$.

articles.title: Relabelling preserves halting
articles.statement:
Let $f$ be a map of states. For every configuration $c$,
the configuration obtained from $c$ by replacing its state $q$ by $f(q)$, and keeping the halting
state, is halted if and only if $c$ is halted.

articles.title: Halting persists along a run
articles.statement:
For a configuration $c$ of a deterministic multi-tape Turing
machine and steps $s \le t$, if the run from $c$ is halted after $s$ steps, then it is halted after
$t$ steps.

articles.title: A time bound forces halting
articles.statement:
If a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine runs in time $t$
on input $w$, then the run from the initial configuration on $w$ is halted after $t$ steps.

articles.title: Run composition for halting
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a configuration of a deterministic multi-tape
Turing machine and let $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. If the run from $c$ is not halted after any $s < m$
steps, and the run from the configuration reached after $m$ steps halts at step $n$ (it is halted
after $n$ steps and not halted after fewer), then the run from $c$ halts at step $m + n$.

articles.title: Halting at step zero
articles.statement:
A deterministic multi-tape Turing machine started in a
configuration $c$ halts at step $0$ if and only if $c$ is halted.

articles.title: Initial configurations under relabelling
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $M'$ be deterministic machines with
$k$ work tapes over the same alphabet such that $M'$ simulates $M$ up to a state relabelling $f$.
Then for every input word $x$, the initial configuration of $M'$ on $x$ is the initial
configuration of $M$ on $x$ with its state $q$ replaced by $f(q)$.

articles.title: Simulation up to a state relabelling
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $M'$ be deterministic machines with $k$
work tapes over the same alphabet, with state sets $Q$ and $Q'$, and let $f : Q \to Q'$. Then $M'$
simulates $M$ up to the relabelling $f$ when the initial state of $M'$ is $f(q_0)$, where $q_0$ is
the initial state of $M$, and for every state $q \in Q$, every possibly blank symbol $a$ under the
input head and every tuple $w$ of possibly blank symbols under the work heads, the action of $M'$
in state $f(q)$ reading $a$ and $w$ is the action of $M$ in state $q$ reading $a$ and $w$ with its
successor state relabelled by $f$ (a successor state $q'$ becomes $f(q')$, and halting stays
halting).

Nothing is required of $M'$ in states outside the range of $f$, and $f$ need not be injective.

articles.title: Every machine is a relabelling of itself
articles.statement:
Every deterministic machine with $k$ work tapes
simulates itself up to the identity relabelling of its states.

articles.title: Relabelling the successor state of an action
articles.statement:
For a map $f : Q \to Q'$ of states and an
action $a$ of a machine with $k$ work tapes and states $Q$, the relabelled action is the action
with states $Q'$ that moves the input head, writes and moves on the work tapes and outputs exactly
as $a$ does, and whose successor state is $f(q)$ when $a$ goes to state $q$ and is halting when $a$
halts.

articles.title: Lockstep runs
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $M'$ be multi-tape Turing machines with the same number of
work tapes and the same alphabet, with state sets $Q$ and $Q'$, such that $M'$ simulates $M$ up
to the state relabelling $f : Q \to Q'$. For a configuration $c$ of $M$, write $f_*(c)$ for the
configuration of $M'$ obtained by replacing the state $q$ of $c$ by $f(q)$ and keeping the input
head, the work tapes, the work heads and the output (a halted configuration stays halted). Then
for every configuration $c$ of $M$ and every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, running $M'$ for $t$ steps from
$f_*(c)$ gives $f_*(c_t)$, where $c_t$ is the configuration reached by running $M$ for $t$ steps
from $c$.

articles.title: Lockstep runs from the initial configuration
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $M'$ be deterministic machines
with $k$ work tapes over the same alphabet such that $M'$ simulates $M$ up to a state relabelling
$f$. Then for every input word $x$ and every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the configuration of $M'$ after
$t$ steps on input $x$ is the configuration of $M$ after $t$ steps on input $x$ with its state
relabelled by $f$: a state $q$ becomes $f(q)$ and the halting state stays halting.

articles.title: Halted configurations are fixed
articles.statement:
If a configuration $c$ of a deterministic multi-tape
Turing machine is halted, then for every $t \in \mathbb{N}$ the run from $c$ is in configuration
$c$ after $t$ steps.

articles.title: Runs of a machine given by a transition function
articles.statement:
Let $\delta$ be a transition function
that assigns an action to every state, symbol or blank read on the input tape, and tuple of
symbols or blanks read on the work tapes, and let $M$ be the deterministic multi-tape Turing
machine with initial state $q_0$ and transition function $\delta$. Let $S_\delta$ be the map on
configurations that fixes every halted configuration and sends a running configuration in state
$q$ to the result of applying to it the action that $\delta$ selects for $q$ and the symbols or
blanks under its heads. For every configuration $c$ and every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the run of $M$
from $c$ is in configuration $S_\delta^t(c)$ after $t$ steps, where $S_\delta^t$ is the $t$-fold
iterate of $S_\delta$.

articles.title: Peeling off the first step of a run
articles.statement:
For a configuration $c$ of a deterministic
multi-tape Turing machine and every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, the run from $c$ after $t + 1$ steps is in
the same configuration as the run from the successor of $c$ after $t$ steps.

articles.title: Halting step after a run prefix
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine,
$c$ a configuration of $M$ and $m, n$ natural numbers. If $M$ started in $c$ halts at step
$m + n$, that is, it is halted after $m + n$ steps and not halted after any fewer, then $M$
started in the configuration reached from $c$ after $m$ steps halts at step $n$.

articles.title: Space bounds of deterministic machines
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a deterministic multi-tape Turing
machine, $x$ an input and $s \in \mathbb{N}$. Then $M$ runs in space $s$ on $x$, that is, every
computation path of $M$ on $x$ visits at most $s$ work-tape cells, if and only if for every
$t \in \mathbb{N}$ the run of $M$ from the initial configuration on $x$ visits at most $s$
work-tape cells within its first $t$ steps. Visited cells are counted on each work tape
separately and summed over the work tapes.

articles.title: Relabelling preserves space bounds
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $M'$ be multi-tape Turing machines with
the same number of work tapes and the same alphabet such that $M'$ simulates $M$ up to a state
relabelling $f$. Then for every input $x$ and every $s \in \mathbb{N}$, $M'$ runs in space $s$
on $x$ if and only if $M$ runs in space $s$ on $x$.

articles.title: Time bounds of deterministic machines
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a deterministic multi-tape Turing
machine, $w$ an input and $t$ a natural number. Then $M$ runs in time $t$ on $w$, that is, every
computation path of $M$ on $w$ with at least $t$ steps ends in a halted configuration, if and only
if $M$ started in its initial configuration on $w$ is halted after $t$ steps.

articles.title: Relabelling preserves time bounds
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $M'$ be multi-tape Turing machines with
the same number of work tapes and the same alphabet such that $M'$ simulates $M$ up to a state
relabelling $f$. Then for every input $x$ and every $t \in \mathbb{N}$, $M'$ runs in time $t$ on
$x$ if and only if $M$ runs in time $t$ on $x$.

articles.title: Space of the deterministic computation path
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a deterministic multi-tape
Turing machine, $x$ an input and $t \in \mathbb{N}$. The number of work-tape cells visited along
the computation path of $M$ on $x$ made of the first $t$ steps from the initial configuration
equals the space used by the run of $M$ from the initial configuration on $x$ up to step $t$.
Both count the visited cells on each work tape separately and sum over the work tapes.

articles.title: Step determinism
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a deterministic multi-tape Turing machine, with the one-step
relation it inherits as a nondeterministic machine. If a configuration $c$ steps to both $c_1$
and $c_2$, then $c_1 = c_2$.

articles.title: Step of a machine given by a transition function
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be the deterministic multi-tape
Turing machine with initial state $q_0$ and transition function $\delta$. For every configuration
$c$, the step of $M$ from $c$ is the successor of $c$ under $\delta$: $c$ itself if $c$ is halted,
and otherwise the result of applying to $c$ the action that $\delta$ selects for the state of $c$
and the symbols under its input and work tape heads.

articles.title: Successor under a transition function
articles.statement:
Let $\delta$ be a transition function of a
multi-tape Turing machine with $k$ work tapes, assigning an action to each state, input symbol
and tuple of $k$ work tape symbols, where a symbol may be blank. The successor of a configuration
$c$ under $\delta$ is $c$ itself if $c$ is halted, and otherwise the configuration obtained by
applying to $c$ the action $\delta(q, a, b)$, where $q$ is the state of $c$, $a$ the symbol under
its input head and $b$ the symbols under its work tape heads.

articles.title: Relabelled machines step in lockstep
articles.statement:
Let $M$ and $M'$ be multi-tape Turing machines
with the same number of work tapes and the same alphabet, with state sets $Q$ and $Q'$, such that
$M'$ simulates $M$ up to the state relabelling $f : Q \to Q'$. For a configuration $c$ of $M$,
write $f_*(c)$ for the configuration of $M'$ obtained by replacing the state $q$ of $c$ by
$f(q)$ and keeping the input head, the work tapes, the work heads and the output (a halted
configuration stays halted). Then for every configuration $c$ of $M$, one step of $M'$ from
$f_*(c)$ gives $f_*(c')$, where $c'$ is the result of one step of $M$ from $c$.

articles.title: Relabellings compose
articles.statement:
Let $M$, $M'$ and $M''$ be multi-tape Turing machines with the same
number of work tapes and the same alphabet, with state sets $Q$, $Q'$ and $Q''$. If $M'$
simulates $M$ up to the state relabelling $f : Q \to Q'$ and $M''$ simulates $M'$ up to the
state relabelling $g : Q' \to Q''$, then $M''$ simulates $M$ up to the state relabelling
$g \circ f$.

articles.title: Adding two counters into a third
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, c, t$ be stacks with $a \ne c$, $a \ne t$,
$b \ne c$, $b \ne t$ and $c \ne t$, with unit symbols $u_a, u_b, u_c, u_t$. Write
$\mathrm{xfer}(k, ps, \ell, \ell')$ for the transfer loop at label $\ell$ that pops stack $k$ until
it is empty, pushing $x$ onto stack $j$ for each pair $(j, x)$ in $ps$ per popped symbol, and then
goes to $\ell'$. Suppose the machine $M$ has
$M(l_1) = \mathrm{xfer}(a, [(c, u_c), (t, u_t)], l_1, l_2)$,
$M(l_2) = \mathrm{xfer}(t, [(a, u_a)], l_2, l_3)$,
$M(l_3) = \mathrm{xfer}(b, [(c, u_c), (t, u_t)], l_3, l_4)$ and
$M(l_4) = \mathrm{xfer}(t, [(b, u_b)], l_4, \mathit{next})$. Let $m, n, p \in \mathbb{N}$, let $v$
be a state and let $S$ be stacks in which $a$ holds exactly $u_a^m$, $b$ holds $u_b^n$, $c$ holds
$u_c^p$ and $t$ is empty. Then exactly $2m + 2n + 4$ steps of $M$ lead from label $l_1$ with
state $v$ and stacks $S$ to label $\mathit{next}$ with the state storing the flag false and the
stacks $S$ with $c$ replaced by $u_c^{m+n+p}$.

articles.title: Adding units to target stacks
articles.statement:
Let $ps$ be a list of pairs $(j, x)$ of a stack $j$ and a
symbol $x$ of stack $j$, let $i \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $S$ be stacks. The resulting stacks are
as follows: if $(k, x)$ is the first pair in $ps$ whose stack is $k$, stack $k$ holds $i$ copies
of $x$ followed by $S_k$ (so the copies are on top); if no pair in $ps$ has stack $k$, stack $k$
holds $S_k$.

When the stacks in the pairs of $ps$ are distinct, the first pair with stack $k$ is the only one.

articles.title: Agreement of host and sub-machine stacks
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a stack embedding with stack
renaming $e$ and alphabet bijections $\iota_k$. Stack contents $S$ of the sub-machine and $S'$
of the host agree when, for every sub-machine stack $k$, the host stack $e(k)$ holds the list
obtained from $S(k)$ by applying $\iota_k$ to each symbol.

articles.title: Bit on top of a stack
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a decoder that reads each symbol either as a bit or as
a marker. For an optional symbol $o$ (the top of a stack, absent when the stack is empty), the
bit of $o$ under $d$ is $x$ when $o$ is a symbol that $d$ reads as the bit $x$, and false when $o$
is absent or $d$ reads it as a marker.

articles.title: Budgeted run
articles.statement:
For a machine $M$, numbers $K, X \in \mathbb{N}$ and configurations $c$ and
$d$, the budgeted run from $c$ to $d$ with $K$ steps already spent and budget $X$ holds when there
is an $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $K + n \le X$ such that $n$ steps of $M$ lead from $c$ to $d$.

It is used for goal-directed chaining of runs: the chaining lemmas only increase $K$.

articles.title: Cleanup empties its stacks
articles.statement:
Let $ks$ be a list of pairwise distinct stacks of a program
$M$ whose state carries a flag bit, and $\mathit{self}$, $\mathit{next}$ labels such that $M$
runs at $\mathit{self}$ the cleanup round for $ks$, looping at $\mathit{self}$ and exiting to
$\mathit{next}$. Let $m$ be a natural number and $S$ stack contents in which every stack of $ks$
holds at most $m$ symbols. Then for every state $v$, $M$ runs in at most $m + 1$ steps from label
$\mathit{self}$, state $v$ and stacks $S$ to label $\mathit{next}$, the state storing the flag
value false, and the stacks $S'$ with $S'(k)$ empty for every $k$ in $ks$ and $S'(k) = S(k)$ for
every other stack $k$.

articles.title: Cleanup round
articles.statement:
For a list $ks$ of stacks and labels $\mathit{self}$ and $\mathit{next}$,
the cleanup round is the statement that sets the state to the one storing the flag value false,
pops the stacks listed in $ks$ in order, once per entry (an empty stack stays empty), while
recording in the flag whether some pop found a symbol, and then goes to $\mathit{self}$ if one
did and to $\mathit{next}$ otherwise.

articles.title: Deciding step of the comparison
articles.statement:
Suppose the program has at label $\ell$ the bit-block
comparison statement of stacks $a$ and $b$ (decoders $d_a$, $d_b$; scratch stacks arbitrary) with
loop label $\ell$, equality label $\ell_=$ and mismatch label $\ell_{\ne}$. From a configuration
at label $\ell$, with any state, in which the tops of $a$ and $b$ are not the same bit, the
program takes one step to a configuration with the same stacks and some state, at label $\ell_=$
if neither top is a bit (each of $a$ and $b$ is empty or has a marker on top) and at label
$\ell_{\ne}$ otherwise.

articles.title: Comparison pops a common prefix
articles.statement:
Suppose the program has at label $\ell$ the bit-block
comparison statement of stacks $a$ and $b$ (decoders $d_a$, $d_b$) with scratch stacks $t_a$ and
$t_b$ (encoders $e_a$, $e_b$) and loop label $\ell$, and that $a$, $b$, $t_a$, $t_b$ are pairwise
distinct. Let $p = p_1 \dots p_n$ be a bit string, and take a configuration at label $\ell$, with
any state, in which stack $a$ holds a list $X$ on top of $A$ and stack $b$ holds a list $Y$ on
top of $B$, where $X$ is the bit block $p$ under $d_a$ and $Y$ is the bit block $p$ under $d_b$.
Then in exactly $n$ steps the program reaches a configuration at label $\ell$, with some state,
in which stack $a$ is $A$, stack $b$ is $B$, stack $t_a$ holds $e_a(p_n), \dots, e_a(p_1)$ on top
of its old contents, stack $t_b$ holds $e_b(p_n), \dots, e_b(p_1)$ on top of its old contents,
and every other stack is unchanged.

articles.title: Correctness of the bit-block comparison
articles.statement:
Suppose the program has at label $\ell$ the
bit-block comparison statement of stacks $a$ and $b$ (decoders $d_a$, $d_b$) with scratch stacks
$t_a$ and $t_b$ (encoders $e_a$, $e_b$), loop label $\ell$, equality label $\ell_=$ and mismatch
label $\ell_{\ne}$, and that $a$, $b$, $t_a$, $t_b$ are pairwise distinct. Let $u$ and $w$ be bit
strings, and take a configuration at label $\ell$, with any state, in which stack $a$ holds a
list $X$ on top of $A$ and stack $b$ holds a list $Y$ on top of $B$, where $X$ is the bit block
$u$ under $d_a$, $Y$ is the bit block $w$ under $d_b$, $A$ ends a bit block under $d_a$ and $B$
ends a bit block under $d_b$. Then there is a common prefix $c = c_1 \dots c_m$ of $u$ and $w$,
after which $u$ and $w$ do not continue with the same bit, such that in exactly $m + 1$ steps the
program reaches a configuration, with some state, at label $\ell_=$ if $u = w$ and at label
$\ell_{\ne}$ otherwise, in which stack $a$ holds $X$ without its first $m$ symbols on top of $A$,
stack $b$ holds $Y$ without its first $m$ symbols on top of $B$, stack $t_a$ holds
$e_a(c_m), \dots, e_a(c_1)$ on top of its old contents, stack $t_b$ holds
$e_b(c_m), \dots, e_b(c_1)$ on top of its old contents, and every other stack is unchanged.

articles.title: Bit-block comparison statement
articles.statement:
Let $a$ and $b$ be stacks with decoders $d_a$ and $d_b$
that read each symbol either as a bit or as a marker, let $t_a$ and $t_b$ be scratch stacks with
bit encoders $e_a$ and $e_b$, and let $\ell$, $\ell_=$ and $\ell_{\ne}$ be labels. The comparison
statement with loop label $\ell$ performs one round of comparison: if the tops of $a$ and $b$ are
the same bit $x$, it pops both, pushes $e_a(x)$ onto $t_a$ and $e_b(x)$ onto $t_b$, and goes to
$\ell$. Otherwise it changes no stack: it goes to $\ell_=$ if neither top is a bit (each of $a$
and $b$ is empty or has a marker on top), and to $\ell_{\ne}$ if the tops are different bits or
exactly one of them is a bit. It records its tests in the one-bit flag of the machine state.

articles.title: The comparison loop
articles.statement:
Let $a, b, t_a, t_b$ be pairwise distinct stacks with unit symbols
$u_a, u_b, u_{t_a}, u_{t_b}$, and let $r$ map each ordering to a label. Suppose the machine $M$
has at label $\ell$ the comparison round of $a$ and $b$ with scratch stacks $t_a, t_b$ and units
$u_{t_a}, u_{t_b}$ that repeats at $\ell$ and exits to $r(\mathrm{lt})$, $r(\mathrm{eq})$ and
$r(\mathrm{gt})$: it pops $a$ and $b$, pushes $u_{t_a}$ onto $t_a$ if $a$ was non-empty and
$u_{t_b}$ onto $t_b$ if $b$ was non-empty, and goes to $\ell$ if both were non-empty, to
$r(\mathrm{lt})$ if only $b$ was, to $r(\mathrm{eq})$ if neither was and to $r(\mathrm{gt})$ if
only $a$ was. Then for all $m, n, p, q \in \mathbb{N}$, every state $v$ and all stacks $S$ in
which $a, b, t_a, t_b$ hold exactly $u_a^m, u_b^n, u_{t_a}^p, u_{t_b}^q$ respectively, there are
a state $v'$ and stacks $S'$ such that exactly $\min(m, n) + 1$ steps of $M$ lead from label
$\ell$ with state $v$ and stacks $S$ to label $r(\mathrm{compare}(m, n))$ with state $v'$ and
stacks $S'$, where in $S'$ the stack $a$ holds $u_a^{m - \min(m, n+1)}$, $b$ holds
$u_b^{n - \min(n, m+1)}$, $t_a$ holds $u_{t_a}^{p + \min(m, n+1)}$, $t_b$ holds
$u_{t_b}^{q + \min(n, m+1)}$, and every other stack is as in $S$.

articles.title: Non-destructive comparison of two counters
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a TM2 machine whose state type
carries a flag bit, let $a, b, t_a, t_b$ be pairwise distinct stacks with symbols $u_a$, $u_b$,
$u_{t_a}$, $u_{t_b}$ of their alphabets, let $\ell$ be a label and let $r$, $r'$, $o$ map each
ordering to a label. Suppose that $M$ has at $\ell$ the comparison round of $a$ and $b$ with
scratch stacks $t_a, t_b$ and units $u_{t_a}, u_{t_b}$ that goes to $\ell$ again and exits to
$r(\mathrm{lt})$, $r(\mathrm{eq})$ and $r(\mathrm{gt})$, and that for every ordering $\omega$,
$M$ has at $r(\omega)$ the counter transfer loop of $t_a$ into the single target $(a, u_a)$ that
repeats at $r(\omega)$ and exits to $r'(\omega)$, and has at $r'(\omega)$ the counter transfer
loop of $t_b$ into the single target $(b, u_b)$ that repeats at $r'(\omega)$ and exits to
$o(\omega)$. Write $\mathrm{compare}(m, n)$ for the ordering of natural numbers $m$ and $n$, and
$[m \ne n]$ for $1$ if $m \ne n$ and $0$ otherwise. Then for all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, every
state $v$ and all stacks $S$ in which $a$ holds exactly $u_a^m$, $b$ holds exactly $u_b^n$ and
$t_a$ and $t_b$ are empty, $M$ runs in exactly $3\min(m, n) + 3 + [m \ne n]$ steps from label
$\ell$ with state $v$ and stacks $S$ to label $o(\mathrm{compare}(m, n))$ with the state that
stores the flag value false and with the same stacks $S$.

articles.title: One round of counter comparison
articles.statement:
For stacks $a, b, t_a, t_b$, symbols $u_{t_a}$ of stack
$t_a$ and $u_{t_b}$ of stack $t_b$, and labels $\mathit{self}$, $\mathit{lt}$, $\mathit{eq}$ and
$\mathit{gt}$, this machine statement pops stack $a$ and then stack $b$; after each pop it stores
in the state whether the pop found a symbol and branches on it. If both pops found a symbol, it
pushes $u_{t_a}$ onto $t_a$, then $u_{t_b}$ onto $t_b$, and goes to $\mathit{self}$. If only the
pop of $a$ found a symbol, it pushes $u_{t_a}$ onto $t_a$ and goes to $\mathit{gt}$; if only the
pop of $b$ found one, it pushes $u_{t_b}$ onto $t_b$ and goes to $\mathit{lt}$; if neither did,
it goes to $\mathit{eq}$.

articles.title: Unary counter
articles.statement:
The unary counter with unit symbol $u$ and value $n \in \mathbb{N}$ is the
list $u^n$ consisting of exactly $n$ copies of $u$.

articles.title: Copying a counter through a scratch stack
articles.statement:
Let $a, c, t$ be pairwise distinct stacks with
unit symbols $u_a, u_c, u_t$. Write $\mathrm{xfer}(k, ps, \ell, \ell')$ for the transfer loop at
label $\ell$ that pops stack $k$ until it is empty, pushing $x$ onto stack $j$ for each pair
$(j, x)$ in $ps$ per popped symbol, and then goes to $\ell'$. Suppose the machine $M$ has
$M(l_1) = \mathrm{xfer}(a, [(c, u_c), (t, u_t)], l_1, l_2)$ and
$M(l_2) = \mathrm{xfer}(t, [(a, u_a)], l_2, \mathit{next})$. Let $m, p \in \mathbb{N}$, let $v$
be a state and let $S$ be stacks in which $a$ holds exactly $u_a^m$, $c$ holds $u_c^p$ and $t$ is
empty. Then exactly $2m + 2$ steps of $M$ lead from label $l_1$ with state $v$ and stacks $S$ to
label $\mathit{next}$ with the state storing the flag false and the stacks $S$ with $c$ replaced
by $u_c^{m+p}$.

articles.title: Decrement
articles.statement:
For a stack $k$ and labels $\ell_0$ and $\ell_+$, this machine statement pops
stack $k$, stores in the state whether a symbol was popped, and goes to $\ell_+$ if a symbol was
popped and to $\ell_0$ if stack $k$ was empty.

articles.title: Four pairwise distinct stacks
articles.statement:
Four stack indices $a$, $b$, $t_a$, $t_b$ are pairwise
distinct: $a 
e b$, $a 
e t_a$, $a 
e t_b$, $b 
e t_a$, $b 
e t_b$ and $t_a 
e t_b$.

These are the two compared stacks and the two scratch stacks of the bit-block comparison.

articles.title: Embedding of a machine in a host
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a stack embedding and $\varphi$ a map from
the labels of a machine $M$ to the labels of a host machine $M'$ over the same internal states.
Then $M$ embeds in $M'$ along $E$ and $\varphi$ when, for every label $\ell$ of $M$, either the
statement of $M'$ at $\varphi(\ell)$ is the statement of $M$ at $\ell$ translated along $E$ and
$\varphi$, or the statement of $M$ at $\ell$ is the halt statement (in which case $M'$ may do
anything at $\varphi(\ell)$).

articles.title: Gap emission
articles.statement:
Let $P, Q, T_1, T_2, o$ be pairwise distinct stacks, with unit symbols
$u_P, u_Q, u_{T_1}, u_{T_2}$ for the first four, and let $ys$ be a list of symbols of stack $o$.
Write $\mathrm{xfer}(k, ps, \ell, \ell')$ for the transfer loop at label $\ell$ that pops stack
$k$ until it is empty, pushing $x$ onto stack $j$ for each pair $(j, x)$ in $ps$ per popped
symbol, and then goes to $\ell'$. Let $r, r_B, \mathit{out}$ map each ordering to a label, with
$\mathit{out}(\mathrm{eq}) = \mathit{next}$ and $\mathit{out}(\omega) = \mathit{emit}$ for every
ordering $\omega \ne \mathrm{eq}$. Suppose the machine $M$ has: at label $\mathit{dec}$ the
decrement of $P$ that goes to $\mathit{cmp}$ if a symbol was popped and to $\mathit{ifZero}$ if
$P$ was empty; at label $\mathit{cmp}$ the comparison round of $P$ and $Q$ with scratch stacks
$T_1, T_2$ and units $u_{T_1}, u_{T_2}$ that repeats at $\mathit{cmp}$ and exits to
$r(\mathrm{lt})$, $r(\mathrm{eq})$ and $r(\mathrm{gt})$; for every ordering $\omega$,
$M(r(\omega)) = \mathrm{xfer}(T_1, [(P, u_P)], r(\omega), r_B(\omega))$ and
$M(r_B(\omega)) = \mathrm{xfer}(T_2, [(Q, u_Q)], r_B(\omega), \mathit{out}(\omega))$; and at
label $\mathit{emit}$ the statement that prepends $ys$ to stack $o$ (so that $ys$ reads top-down)
and goes to $\mathit{dec}$. Let $q \in \mathbb{N}$. Then for every $g \in \mathbb{N}$, every
state $v$ and all stacks $S$ in which $P$ holds exactly $u_P^{q+g+1}$, $Q$ holds $u_Q^q$, and
$T_1$ and $T_2$ are empty, exactly $g(3q + 6) + 3q + 4$ steps of $M$ lead from label
$\mathit{dec}$ with state $v$ and stacks $S$ to label $\mathit{next}$ with the state storing the
flag false and the stacks $S$ with $P$ replaced by $u_P^q$ and $o$ replaced by $g$ copies of $ys$
concatenated, followed by the old contents of $o$.

articles.title: Prepending a constant list
articles.statement:
For a stack $k$, a list $(y_1, \dots, y_m)$ of symbols of
stack $k$ and a label $\ell$, this statement pushes $y_m, \dots, y_1$ onto stack $k$ in this order
and then goes to label $\ell$; it is the constant-list push of the reversed list. Afterwards
$y_1, \dots, y_m$ sit on top of stack $k$, read from the top down.

articles.title: Pushing a constant list
articles.statement:
For a stack $k$, a list $(x_1, \dots, x_m)$ of symbols of
stack $k$ and a label $\ell$, this statement pushes $x_1, \dots, x_m$ onto stack $k$ in this order,
so that $x_m$ ends on top, and then goes to label $\ell$. The machine executes it in a single
step.

articles.title: End of a bit block
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a decoder that reads each symbol either as a bit or as a
marker. A list of symbols $A$ (the rest of a stack below a block) ends a bit block under $d$ when
$A$ is empty or $d$ reads its first symbol as a marker.

articles.title: Flag bit of a machine state
articles.statement:
A flag on a type $\sigma$ of machine states consists of a map
$\mathrm{tag} : \mathrm{Bool} \to \sigma$ that stores a bit in a state and a map
$\mathrm{untag} : \sigma \to \mathrm{Bool}$ that reads it back, such that
$\mathrm{untag}(\mathrm{tag}(\beta)) = \beta$ for every bit $\beta$. The program primitives use it
to branch on whether a pop found a symbol.

articles.title: Loop head of a for loop over a counter
articles.statement:
For stacks $c$ and $c'$, a symbol $u'$ of stack
$c'$ and labels $b$ and $r$, the loop head is the statement that pops stack $c$, replaces the
machine state by the state whose flag bit records whether a symbol was popped, and branches on
that bit: if a symbol was popped, it pushes $u'$ onto the index stack $c'$ and goes to label $b$
(the loop body); if $c$ was empty, it goes to label $r$.

articles.title: Time bound for a for loop over a counter
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack machine whose states
carry a flag bit, with $\mathrm{tag}(\beta)$ the state storing the bit $\beta$; write $(\ell, v, S)$
for the configuration at label $\ell$ with state $v$ and stack contents $S$, and $u^m$ for a stack
holding exactly $m$ copies of the symbol $u$. Let $c \ne c'$ be stacks with a symbol $u$ of stack
$c$ and a symbol $u'$ of stack $c'$, and let $h, b, r, e$ be labels such that at $h$ the machine
runs the loop head on $c$ with index stack $c'$ (pop $c$; if a symbol was popped, push $u'$ onto
$c'$ and go to $b$, otherwise go to $r$), and at $r$ it runs the transfer that drains $c'$, pushing
one $u$ onto $c$ per popped symbol, and then goes to $e$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $B \in
\mathbb{N}$, and let $P(i, S)$ be a predicate such that $P(i, S)$ implies $P(i, S')$ whenever $S$
and $S'$ agree on every stack other than $c$ and $c'$. Assume that for every $i < n$ and all stack
contents $S$ with $S_c = u^{n-1-i}$, $S_{c'} = u'^{\,i+1}$ and $P(i, S)$, there are a state $v'$ and
stack contents $S'$ such that $M$ goes from $(b, \mathrm{tag}(\mathrm{true}), S)$ to $(h, v', S')$
in at most $B$ steps, with $S'_c = S_c$, $S'_{c'} = S_{c'}$ and $P(i + 1, S')$. Then for every state
$v$ and all stack contents $S$ with $S_c = u^n$, $S_{c'}$ empty and $P(0, S)$, there are stack
contents $S'$ such that $M$ goes from $(h, v, S)$ to $(e, \mathrm{tag}(\mathrm{false}), S')$ in at
most $n(B + 1) + n + 2$ steps, with $S'_c = u^n$, $S'_{c'}$ empty and $P(n, S')$.

articles.title: A for loop over a counter reaches its exit
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack machine whose states
carry a flag bit, with $\mathrm{tag}(\beta)$ the state storing the bit $\beta$; write $(\ell, v, S)$
for the configuration at label $\ell$ with state $v$ and stack contents $S$, and $u^m$ for a stack
holding exactly $m$ copies of the symbol $u$. Let $c \ne c'$ be stacks with a symbol $u$ of stack
$c$ and a symbol $u'$ of stack $c'$, and let $h, b, r, e$ be labels such that at $h$ the machine
runs the loop head on $c$ with index stack $c'$ (pop $c$; if a symbol was popped, push $u'$ onto
$c'$ and go to $b$, otherwise go to $r$), and at $r$ it runs the transfer that drains $c'$, pushing
one $u$ onto $c$ per popped symbol, and then goes to $e$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $P(i, S)$
be a predicate such that $P(i, S)$ implies $P(i, S')$ whenever $S$ and $S'$ agree on every stack
other than $c$ and $c'$. Assume that for every $i < n$ and all stack contents $S$ with $S_c =
u^{n-1-i}$, $S_{c'} = u'^{\,i+1}$ and $P(i, S)$, there are a state $v'$ and stack contents $S'$ such
that $M$ goes from $(b, \mathrm{tag}(\mathrm{true}), S)$ to $(h, v', S')$ in finitely many steps,
with $S'_c = S_c$, $S'_{c'} = S_{c'}$ and $P(i + 1, S')$. Then for every state $v$ and all stack
contents $S$ with $S_c = u^n$, $S_{c'}$ empty and $P(0, S)$, there are stack contents $S'$ such that
$M$ goes from $(h, v, S)$ to $(e, \mathrm{tag}(\mathrm{false}), S')$ in finitely many steps, with
$S'_c = u^n$, $S'_{c'}$ empty and $P(n, S')$.

articles.title: Exact running time of a for loop over a counter
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack machine whose
states carry a flag bit, with $\mathrm{tag}(\beta)$ the state storing the bit $\beta$; write $(\ell,
v, S)$ for the configuration at label $\ell$ with state $v$ and stack contents $S$, and $u^m$ for a
stack holding exactly $m$ copies of the symbol $u$. Let $c \ne c'$ be stacks with a symbol $u$ of
stack $c$ and a symbol $u'$ of stack $c'$, and let $h, b, r, e$ be labels such that at $h$ the
machine runs the loop head on $c$ with index stack $c'$ (pop $c$; if a symbol was popped, push $u'$
onto $c'$ and go to $b$, otherwise go to $r$), and at $r$ it runs the transfer that drains $c'$,
pushing one $u$ onto $c$ per popped symbol, and then goes to $e$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let
$\mathrm{cost} : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, and let $P(i, S)$ be a predicate such that $P(i, S)$
implies $P(i, S')$ whenever $S$ and $S'$ agree on every stack other than $c$ and $c'$. Assume that
for every $i < n$ and all stack contents $S$ with $S_c = u^{n-1-i}$, $S_{c'} = u'^{\,i+1}$ and $P(i,
S)$, there are a state $v'$ and stack contents $S'$ such that $M$ goes from $(b,
\mathrm{tag}(\mathrm{true}), S)$ to $(h, v', S')$ in exactly $\mathrm{cost}(i)$ steps, with $S'_c =
S_c$, $S'_{c'} = S_{c'}$ and $P(i + 1, S')$. Then for every state $v$ and all stack contents $S$
with $S_c = u^n$, $S_{c'}$ empty and $P(0, S)$, there are stack contents $S'$ such that $M$ goes
from $(h, v, S)$ to $(e, \mathrm{tag}(\mathrm{false}), S')$ in exactly $\sum_{i < n}
(\mathrm{cost}(i) + 1) + n + 2$ steps, with $S'_c = u^n$, $S'_{c'}$ empty and $P(n, S')$.
