articles.title: Frame condition for a stack embedding
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a stack embedding with stack renaming
$e$. Two contents $S'$ and $S''$ of the host's stacks satisfy the frame condition when every host
stack $k'$ outside the image of $e$ has the same contents in both: $S''(k') = S'(k')$ whenever
$e(k) \ne k'$ for every sub-machine stack $k$.

articles.title: Counter increment
articles.statement:
For a stack $k$, a symbol $u$ of stack $k$ (the unit of a unary
counter) and a label $\ell$, this statement pushes $u$ onto stack $k$ and then goes to label
$\ell$.

articles.title: Bit blocks
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a decoder that reads each symbol either as a bit or as a marker. A
list of symbols $s_1, \dots, s_n$ is the bit block of a bit string $p$ under $d$ when $p$ has the
same length $n$ and, for each $i$, $d$ reads $s_i$ as the $i$-th bit of $p$.

articles.title: Bit test for the top of a stack
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a decoder that reads each symbol either as a
bit or as a marker. For an optional symbol $o$ (the top of a stack, absent when the stack is
empty), the test is true when $o$ is a symbol that $d$ reads as a bit, and false when $o$ is
absent or $d$ reads it as a marker.

articles.title: A halted run stays halted
articles.statement:
Let $f : \sigma \to \mathrm{Option}\,\sigma$ be a partial step
function and let $\hat f$ be its lift to $\mathrm{Option}\,\sigma$, which sends $\mathrm{none}$ to
$\mathrm{none}$ and $\mathrm{some}\,x$ to $f(x)$. Then $\hat f^{\,n}(\mathrm{none}) = \mathrm{none}$
for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

articles.title: Translating a statement along a stack embedding
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a stack embedding with stack
renaming $e$ and alphabet bijections $\iota_k$, and let $\varphi$ map the sub-machine's labels to
the host's labels. The translation of a sub-machine statement is the host statement obtained
recursively, where $s$ denotes the current state. A push of the symbol $f(s)$ on stack $k$
becomes a push of $\iota_k(f(s))$ on stack $e(k)$. A peek or pop on stack $k$ becomes a peek or
pop on stack $e(k)$ whose result is mapped back by $\iota_k^{-1}$ before the state update. A jump
to label $f(s)$ becomes a jump to $\varphi(f(s))$. State updates, branches and halt are kept, with
their sub-statements translated.

articles.title: Restoring a stack after a comparison
articles.statement:
Let $t \ne a$ be stacks with decoders $d_t$ and
$d_a$ that read each symbol either as a bit or as a marker. Let $e_t$ be a bit encoder for $t$
that $d_t$ reads back ($d_t$ reads $e_t(x)$ as the bit $x$), and let $g_a$ be a bit encoder for
$a$ that inverts $d_a$ ($g_a(x) = s$ whenever $d_a$ reads the symbol $s$ as the bit $x$). Suppose
the program has at label $\ell$ the bit-block move statement from $t$ (decoder $d_t$) onto $a$
(re-encoding $g_a$) with loop label $\ell$ and exit label $\ell'$. Let $X$ be the bit block of a
bit string $u$ under $d_a$ and let $c = c_1 \dots c_m$ be a prefix of $u$. From a configuration
at label $\ell$, with any state, in which stack $t$ holds $e_t(c_m), \dots, e_t(c_1)$ on top of a
list $R$ that ends a bit block under $d_t$, and stack $a$ holds $X$ without its first $m$ symbols
on top of a list $A$, the program reaches in exactly $m + 1$ steps a configuration at label
$\ell'$, with some state, in which stack $t$ is $R$, stack $a$ holds $X$ on top of $A$, and every
other stack is unchanged.

articles.title: Running the bit-moving loop
articles.statement:
Let $a \ne b$ be stacks of a program $M$ whose state carries
a flag bit, $d$ a decoder reading each symbol of $a$ as a bit or a marker, $g$ an encoder from bits
to symbols of $b$, and $\mathit{self}$, $\mathit{next}$ labels such that $M$ runs at
$\mathit{self}$ the bit-moving loop from $a$ to $b$ with decoder $d$ and encoder $g$, looping at
$\mathit{self}$ and exiting to $\mathit{next}$. Let $p = p_1 \cdots p_n$ be a bit list and $S$
stack contents in which $a$ holds a bit block for $p$ under $d$ followed by a rest $A$ that ends a
bit block under $d$. Then for every state $v$ there are a state $v'$ and stack contents $S'$ such
that $M$ runs in exactly $n + 1$ steps from label $\mathit{self}$, state $v$ and stacks $S$ to
label $\mathit{next}$, state $v'$ and stacks $S'$, where $S'(a) = A$, $S'(b)$ is
$g(p_n), \dots, g(p_1)$ (top first) followed by $S(b)$, and $S'(k) = S(k)$ for every other stack
$k$.

articles.title: Bit-moving loop
articles.statement:
For stacks $a$ and $b$, a decoder $d$ reading each symbol of $a$ as a bit
or a marker, an encoder $g$ from bits to symbols of $b$, and labels $\mathit{self}$ and
$\mathit{next}$, the bit-moving loop from $a$ to $b$ is the statement that looks at the top of
$a$: if it is a symbol that $d$ reads as a bit $x$, it pops it, pushes $g(x)$ onto $b$ and goes to
$\mathit{self}$; if it is a marker or $a$ is empty, it goes to $\mathit{next}$. It overwrites the
state with a flag bit, used as scratch.

articles.title: Multiplying unary counters
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack machine whose states carry a flag
bit, with $\mathrm{tag}(\mathrm{false})$ the state storing the bit false; write $(\ell, v, S)$ for
the configuration at label $\ell$ with state $v$ and stack contents $S$, and $u^m$ for a stack
holding exactly $m$ copies of the symbol $u$. Let $a, a', b, c, t$ be pairwise distinct stacks
with symbols $u_a, u_{a'}, u_b, u_c, u_t$ of the respective stacks, and let $h, \ell_1, \ell_2, r,
e$ be labels such that: at $h$ the machine runs the loop head on $a$ with index stack $a'$ (pop
$a$; if a symbol was popped, push $u_{a'}$ onto $a'$ and go to $\ell_1$, otherwise go to $r$); at
$\ell_1$ it runs the transfer that drains $b$, pushing $u_c$ onto $c$ and $u_t$ onto $t$ per
popped symbol, and then goes to $\ell_2$; at $\ell_2$ it runs the transfer that drains $t$,
pushing $u_b$ onto $b$ per popped symbol, and then goes to $h$; and at $r$ it runs the transfer
that drains $a'$, pushing $u_a$ onto $a$ per popped symbol, and then goes to $e$. Then for all
$m, n, p \in \mathbb{N}$, every state $v$ and all stack contents $S$ with $S_a = u_a^m$, $S_{a'}$
empty, $S_b = u_b^n$, $S_c = u_c^p$ and $S_t$ empty, $M$ goes from $(h, v, S)$ to
$(e, \mathrm{tag}(\mathrm{false}), S')$ in exactly $m(2n + 3) + m + 2$ steps, where $S'$ agrees
with $S$ on every stack except $c$ and $S'_c = u_c^{mn + p}$.

articles.title: Popping a list of stacks
articles.statement:
For a list $ks$ of stacks and a statement $q$, this is the
statement that pops the stacks listed in $ks$ in order, once per entry (an empty stack stays
empty), after each pop replacing the state by the one storing the old flag or-ed with whether
that pop found a symbol, and then continues with $q$.

articles.title: Pushing symbols onto several stacks
articles.statement:
Let $ps$ be a list of pairs $(k, x)$ of a stack index
$k$ and a symbol $x$ of the alphabet of stack $k$, and let $q$ be a statement of a TM2 machine.
This is the statement that, for each pair $(k, x)$ of $ps$ in list order, pushes $x$ onto stack
$k$, and then continues with $q$.

articles.title: Pushing a list of symbols onto one stack
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a stack index, $xs = [x_1, \dots, x_m]$
a list of symbols of the alphabet of stack $k$, and $q$ a statement of a TM2 machine. This is the
statement that pushes $x_1, \dots, x_m$ onto stack $k$ in that order, so that $x_m$ ends on top
when $m \ge 1$, and then continues with $q$.

articles.title: Reachability for a TM2 machine
articles.statement:
For a TM2 machine $M$ and configurations $c$ and $d$, $d$
is reachable from $c$ when there is some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $M$ runs from $c$ to $d$
in exactly $n$ steps.

articles.title: Repeated block
articles.statement:
For a list $ys$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\mathrm{rep}(ys, n)$ is the
concatenation of $n$ copies of $ys$; it is the empty list when $n = 0$.

articles.title: Exact run transport to supplied host final stacks
articles.statement:
Source-shaped transport to supplied host final stacks: agreement fixes embedded slots
and the frame condition fixes every other slot, so the host endpoint is exact.

articles.title: Exact program matching transports a run with its step count
articles.statement:
Exact program matching transports a run, including a halted endpoint, while preserving
the local state, embedded stacks, untouched host stacks, and exact number of steps.

articles.title: Run embedding
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a stack embedding with stack renaming $e$, let $\varphi$ map the
labels of a machine $M$ to those of a host machine $M'$, and suppose $M$ embeds in $M'$ along $E$
and $\varphi$. Suppose $M$ goes in exactly $n$ steps from label $\ell$, state $v$ and stacks $S$ to
a live label $\ell'$, state $v'$ and stacks $T$, where the start may also be the halted
configuration with no label (whose image under $\varphi$ again has no label). If host stacks $S'$
agree with $S$, then there are host stacks $T'$ such that $M'$ goes in exactly $n$ steps from
label $\varphi(\ell)$, state $v$ and stacks $S'$ to label $\varphi(\ell')$, state $v'$ and stacks
$T'$. Moreover $T'$ agrees with $T$, and $S'$, $T'$ satisfy the frame condition: host stacks
outside the image of $e$ are unchanged.

articles.title: Exact matching transports a bounded run
articles.statement:
Exact matching transports a bounded run with arbitrary optional endpoints, retaining
the same step witness and budget as well as agreement and the host frame.

articles.title: Run embedding for bounded runs
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a stack embedding with stack renaming $e$, let
$\varphi$ map the labels of a machine $M$ to those of a host machine $M'$, and suppose $M$ embeds
in $M'$ along $E$ and $\varphi$. Suppose $M$ goes in at most $B$ steps from label $\ell$, state $v$
and stacks $S$ to label $\ell'$, state $v'$ and stacks $T$, and host stacks $S'$ agree with $S$.
Then there are host stacks $T'$ such that $M'$ goes in at most $B$ steps from label
$\varphi(\ell)$, state $v$ and stacks $S'$ to label $\varphi(\ell')$, state $v'$ and stacks $T'$.
Moreover $T'$ agrees with $T$, and $S'$, $T'$ satisfy the frame condition: host stacks outside
the image of $e$ are unchanged.

articles.title: Runs within a step budget
articles.statement:
For a TM2 machine $M$, a bound $B \in \mathbb{N}$ and
configurations $c$ and $d$, $M$ runs from $c$ to $d$ within $B$ steps when there is some
$n \le B$ such that $M$ runs from $c$ to $d$ in exactly $n$ steps.

articles.title: Exact-length runs of a TM2 machine
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a TM2 machine, given by a statement for
each label, and let $c$ and $d$ be configurations. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $M$ runs from $c$ to
$d$ in exactly $n$ steps when applying the step function of $M$ $n$ times, starting at $c$, is
defined at every step (no configuration before the last one has halted) and ends at $d$.

articles.title: Stack embedding
articles.statement:
Given a family of stack alphabets $\Gamma$ indexed by the stacks $K$ of a
sub-machine and a family $\Gamma'$ indexed by the stacks $K'$ of a host, a stack embedding
consists of an injective map $e : K \to K'$ renaming the stacks together with, for each stack
$k \in K$, a bijection $\iota_k : \Gamma_k \to \Gamma'_{e(k)}$ from the alphabet of $k$ onto the
alphabet of its image.

articles.title: A single step executes the statement at the current label
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a TM2 machine, $l$
a label, $v$ an internal state, $S$ an assignment of a list of symbols to each stack, and $d$ a
configuration. If executing the statement $M(l)$ from state $v$ and stacks $S$ yields $d$, then
$M$ runs in exactly one step from the configuration with label $l$, state $v$ and stacks $S$ to
$d$.

articles.title: Executing a translated statement
articles.statement:
Let $E$ be a stack embedding with stack renaming $e$, and
let $\varphi$ map sub-machine labels to host labels. Let $q$ be a sub-machine statement, $v$ a
state, $S$ sub-machine stacks and $S'$ host stacks that agree with $S$. Let executing $q$ from
state $v$ and stacks $S$ yield the next label $\ell$ (possibly none), state $w$ and stacks $T$.
Then there are host stacks $T'$ such that executing the translation of $q$ along $E$ and
$\varphi$ from state $v$ and stacks $S'$ yields the next label $\varphi(\ell)$ (none if $\ell$ is
none), state $w$ and stacks $T'$. Moreover $T'$ agrees with $T$, and $S'$, $T'$ satisfy the frame
condition.

articles.title: Termwise bound on a sum of consecutive values
articles.statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and
$c, i, j \in \mathbb{N}$. If $f(t) \le c$ for every $t$ with $i \le t < i + j$, then
$\mathrm{sumFrom}(f, i, j) = f(i) + f(i+1) + \dots + f(i+j-1)$ is at most $j \cdot c$.

articles.title: Sum of consecutive values
articles.statement:
For $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$,
$\mathrm{sumFrom}(f, i, j) = f(i) + f(i+1) + \dots + f(i+j-1)$ is the sum of $f(t)$ over the
$j$ indices $t$ with $i \le t < i + j$; it is $0$ when $j = 0$.

articles.title: Recovering a bit block from its bits
articles.statement:
Let $d$ be a decoder reading symbols as bits or
markers and $g$ an encoder from bits to symbols such that $g(b) = x$ whenever $d$ reads $x$ as the
bit $b$. If the symbol list $xs$ is a bit block for the bit list $u$ under $d$ and
$c = c_1 \cdots c_m$ is a prefix of $u$, then the first $m$ symbols of $xs$ are
$g(c_1), \dots, g(c_m)$.

articles.title: Draining a counter while prepending a block
articles.statement:
Let $k$ and $o$ be stack indices, $ys$ a list
of symbols of the alphabet of stack $o$, and $\ell$ and $\ell'$ labels. This is the TM2 statement
that pops stack $k$ and sets the internal state to the flag bit recording whether a symbol was
popped. If one was, it prepends $ys$ to stack $o$ (so that $ys$ reads from the top down) and goes
to $\ell$; if stack $k$ was empty, it goes to $\ell'$.

Used as the statement at label $\ell$ with $k \ne o$, it empties a unary counter on stack $k$ and
prepends one copy of $ys$ to stack $o$ per unit removed, then goes to $\ell'$.

articles.title: Running a counter transfer
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack machine whose state carries a
flag bit, and suppose that at label $\ell$ it executes the transfer loop that empties stack $k$
into the targets $p_1, \dots, p_m$ and then goes to label $\ell'$. Here each target $p_i$ is a
pair of a stack $t_i$ and a symbol $x_i$ of its alphabet, the stacks $t_1, \dots, t_m$ are
distinct, and $k$ is none of them. Let $u$ be a symbol of stack $k$. Then for every $n$, every
state $v$ and all stack contents $S$ in which stack $k$ holds exactly $u^n$, the machine goes in
exactly $n + 1$ steps from label $\ell$ with state $v$ and stacks $S$ to label $\ell'$ with the
state that stores the flag value false and the stacks obtained from $S$ by emptying stack $k$
and then pushing $n$ copies of $x_i$ on each stack $t_i$.

articles.title: Counter transfer loop
articles.statement:
For a stack $k$, a list $ps$ of pairs $(t, x)$ of a stack $t$ and a
symbol $x$ of stack $t$, and labels $\ell$ and $\ell'$, this machine statement pops stack $k$,
stores in the state whether a symbol was popped, and branches on it: if a symbol was popped, it
pushes $x$ onto $t$ for each pair $(t, x)$ of $ps$ in list order and goes to $\ell$; if stack $k$
was empty, it goes to $\ell'$.

Placed at label $\ell$, it pops $k$ until $k$ is empty and pushes one copy of every target symbol
per popped symbol: with $ps$ empty it drains $k$, with one target it moves the counter, and with
two targets it copies it.

articles.title: Agreement with the embedded component
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component machine and $\alpha$ an
input alphabet. For stack contents $S$ of $c$ and stack contents $T$ of the host over $\alpha$,
$T$ agrees with $S$ under the embedding of the component's stacks into the host if and only if,
for every stack $k$ of $c$, the host's copy of $k$ holds exactly $S(k)$.

articles.title: The list of host stacks
articles.statement:
For a component machine $c$, the host stacks are listed as the
input stack, the output stack, the two buffer stacks $X_1$ and $W_1$, and then the host's copies
of the stacks of $c$, in the order of the list of stacks that $c$ carries.

articles.title: Cleanup stacks of the generic host
articles.statement:
For a component machine $c$ and a host stack $o$, the
cleanup stacks are the list of all host stacks with $o$ removed, in the order of the list of
host stacks. The cleanup empties these stacks and leaves the output stack $o$.

articles.title: Cleanup in a host
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component machine, $\alpha$ an input alphabet, $o$ a host
stack, $a$ a bit, and $M$ a host program with Boolean state whose statement at the cleanup label
for $a$ is the cleanup round on the list of all host stacks with $o$ removed, kept in the order
of the list of host stacks, repeating at the cleanup label for $a$ and exiting to the output
label for $a$. If $S$ assigns to every host stack at most $m$ symbols, then for every state $v$,
$M$ runs from the cleanup label for $a$ with state $v$ and stacks $S$ to the output label for $a$
in at most $m + 1$ steps, ending with state false, stack $o$ holding $S(o)$ and every other stack
empty.

articles.title: Component machine
articles.statement:
A component machine consists of a finite type $K$ of stacks with
decidable equality, a finite alphabet $\Gamma_k$ for each stack $k$, a finite type $L$ of labels
with decidable equality, a multi-stack Turing machine program assigning to each label in $L$ a
statement over the alphabets $\Gamma$ and the labels $L$ with Boolean internal state, and a list
of the stacks in which every stack occurs exactly once, so that a host can empty all of them.

articles.title: Reading a bit of $w$
articles.statement:
On the pair alphabet of the $x \# w$ input, the symbol that
encodes a bit $b$ of $w$ (the right injection of $\mathrm{some}\,b$) is read as the bit $b$;
every other symbol, a bit of $x$ (a left injection) or the separator $\#$ (the right injection
of $\mathrm{none}$), is read as no bit.

articles.title: Reading a bit of $x$
articles.statement:
On the pair alphabet of the $x \# w$ input, the symbol that
encodes a bit $b$ of $x$ (the left injection of $b$) is read as the bit $b$; every other symbol,
the separator $\#$ or a bit of $w$ (both right injections), is read as no bit.

articles.title: The component's stacks inside a host
articles.statement:
For a component machine $c$ and an input alphabet
$\alpha$, the stack embedding of $c$ into the host over $\alpha$ sends each stack $k$ of $c$ to
the host's copy of $k$, whose alphabet is the alphabet $\Gamma_k$ of $k$, and identifies the two
alphabets by the identity. Distinct stacks have distinct copies, so the embedding is injective.

articles.title: The reduction host embeds the component
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component machine with stacks
$c_X$ and $c_O$, a map $g_X$ from bits to the alphabet of $c_X$, and labels $s$ and $d$,
and suppose that $c$ halts at $d$. Rename the labels of $c$ by sending $d$ to the cleanup label
with answer false and every other label $l$ to the host's copy of $l$, and embed the stacks of
$c$ as the host's copies over the bit input alphabet. Then the reduction host built from
$c_X$, $c_O$, $g_X$, $s$ and $d$ embeds $c$: for every label $l$ of $c$, either $c$ halts at
$l$, or the host's statement at the renamed label of $l$ is the statement of $c$ at $l$ with
stacks and labels translated.

articles.title: The verifier host embeds the component
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component machine with stacks $c_X$
and $c_W$, maps $g_X$ and $g_W$ from bits to the alphabets of $c_X$ and $c_W$, and labels
$\mathit{start}$, $\mathit{yes}$ and $\mathit{no}$, and suppose that the statement of $c$ at
$\mathit{yes}$ and the statement of $c$ at $\mathit{no}$ are the halt statement. Rename the labels
of $c$ by sending $\mathit{yes}$ to the cleanup label with answer true, $\mathit{no}$ (when it
differs from $\mathit{yes}$) to the cleanup label with answer false, and every other label $l$ to
the host's copy of $l$, and embed the stacks of $c$ as the host's copies over the work alphabet
of the dense-SAT verifier. Then the verifier host program built from $c_X$, $c_W$, $g_X$, $g_W$,
$\mathit{start}$, $\mathit{yes}$ and $\mathit{no}$ embeds $c$: for every label $l$ of $c$, either
the statement of $c$ at $l$ is the halt statement, or the host's statement at the renamed label
of $l$ is the statement of $c$ at $l$ with stacks and labels translated.

articles.title: Labels of the generic host as a sum type
articles.statement:
For a component machine $c$ with labels $L$, let
$P_0$ be the set of phase-0 labels and $B = \{\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{true}\}$. The host labels of
$c$ are in bijection with the disjoint union $P_0 \sqcup L \sqcup B \sqcup B$: the phase-0 label
$p$ corresponds to $p$, the host copy of the component label $l$ to $l$, the cleanup label with
answer $a$ to $a$ in the first copy of $B$, and the output label with answer $a$ to $a$ in the
second copy of $B$.

The bijection shows that there are finitely many host labels.

articles.title: Alphabets of the generic host
articles.statement:
For a component machine $c$ with stack alphabets
$(\Gamma_k)_k$ and a type $\alpha$, the alphabet of a host stack is $\alpha$ on the input stack,
$\Gamma_k$ on the host copy of the component's stack $k$, and the booleans on the output stack and
on the two phase-0 buffers.

articles.title: Halting configuration of a finite multi-stack machine
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack Turing
machine $M$ with output stack $k_1$ and initial internal state $\sigma_0$, and a list $l$ over the
alphabet of $k_1$, the halting configuration of $M$ with output $l$ has no current label, internal
state $\sigma_0$, the list $l$ on $k_1$ and every other stack empty.

articles.title: Stacks of the generic host
articles.statement:
For a component machine $c$ with stack indices $K$, the host
stacks are an input stack, an output stack, two buffers $X_1$ and $W_1$ used in phase 0 (which
moves the input onto the component's stacks), and one copy of each component stack $k \in K$.

articles.title: Labels of the generic host
articles.statement:
For a component machine $c$ with labels $L$, and with $P_0$ the
set of phase-0 labels, the host labels are one label for each $p \in P_0$, one copy of each
component label $l \in L$, and, for each boolean answer $a$, a cleanup label and an output label
carrying $a$.

articles.title: Initial configuration of a finite multi-stack machine
articles.statement:
For a finite multi-stack Turing
machine $M$ with input stack $k_0$, main label $\lambda_0$ and initial internal state $\sigma_0$,
and a list $l$ over the alphabet of $k_0$, the initial configuration of $M$ on $l$ has current
label $\lambda_0$, internal state $\sigma_0$, the list $l$ on $k_0$ and every other stack empty.

articles.title: Decider host
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component machine with stacks $c_X$ and $c_O$ and labels
$\mathit{start}$ and $\mathit{done}$, where the statement at $\mathit{done}$ is the halting
statement. Let $g_X$ map bits to symbols of $c_X$, let $e_O$ be a bijection from the alphabet of
$c_O$ to the booleans, let $L$ map bit lists to booleans, and let $p$ be a polynomial with
coefficients in $\mathbb{N}$. Suppose that for every bit list $x$, the component started at
$\mathit{start}$ with internal state false, with $g_X$ applied to each bit of $x$ on $c_X$ and
every other stack empty, reaches the label $\mathit{done}$ in at most $p(|x|)$ steps with exactly
the one symbol $e_O^{-1}(L(x))$ on $c_O$. Then $L$ is polynomial-time computable for the
canonical bitstring encodings, that is, $L$ belongs to the class $\mathrm{P}$ of decision
problems decidable in polynomial time.

The proof applies the reduction host to $x \mapsto [L(x)]$, read with the one-bit encoding of the
booleans.

articles.title: Reduction host, canonical form
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component machine with stacks $c_X$ and
$c_O$ and labels $\mathit{start}$ and $\mathit{done}$, where the statement at $\mathit{done}$ is
the halting statement. Let $g_X$ map bits to symbols of $c_X$, let $e_O$ be a bijection from the
alphabet of $c_O$ to the booleans, let $f$ map bit lists to bit lists, and let $p$ be a polynomial
with coefficients in $\mathbb{N}$. Suppose that for every bit list $x$, the component started at
$\mathit{start}$ with internal state false, with $g_X$ applied to each bit of $x$ on $c_X$ and
every other stack empty, reaches the label $\mathit{done}$ in at most $p(|x|)$ steps with stack
$c_O$ holding exactly $e_O^{-1}$ applied to each bit of $f(x)$. Then $f$ is polynomial-time
computable for the canonical bitstring encodings.

articles.title: Verifier host, canonical form
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component machine with distinct stacks $c_X$
and $c_W$ and labels $\mathit{start}$, $\mathit{yes}$ and $\mathit{no}$, where
$\mathit{yes} \ne \mathit{no}$ and the statements at $\mathit{yes}$ and $\mathit{no}$ are the
halting statement. Let $g_X$ and $g_W$ map bits to symbols of $c_X$ and $c_W$, let $f$ assign a
boolean $f(x, w)$ to all bit lists $x$ and $w$, and let $p$ be a polynomial with coefficients in
$\mathbb{N}$. Suppose that for all bit lists $x$ and $w$, the component started at
$\mathit{start}$ with internal state false, with $g_X$ applied to each bit of $x$ on $c_X$, $g_W$
applied to each bit of $w$ on $c_W$ and every other stack empty, reaches in at most
$p(|x| + |w|)$ steps the label $\mathit{yes}$ if $f(x, w)$ is true and the label $\mathit{no}$ if
it is false. Then the map $(x, w) \mapsto f(x, w)$ on pairs of bit lists is polynomial-time
computable for the canonical bitstring encodings.

articles.title: Membership in the cleanup stacks of the generic host
articles.statement:
For a component machine $c$ and host
stacks $o$ and $k$, the stack $k$ belongs to the list of stacks that the cleanup for the output
stack $o$ empties if and only if $k \ne o$.

articles.title: Moving a bit block through a buffer
articles.statement:
Let $a$, $t$, $b$ be pairwise distinct stacks of a
program $M$ with Boolean state, and let $l_1$, $l_2$, $l_3$ be labels such that $M$ runs at $l_1$
the bit-moving loop from $a$ to $t$ with decoder $d$ and encoder $g_t$, looping at $l_1$ and
exiting to $l_2$, and at $l_2$ the bit-moving loop from $t$ to $b$ with decoder $d_t$ and encoder
$g$, looping at $l_2$ and exiting to $l_3$, where $d_t$ decodes $g_t(y)$ to $y$ for every bit $y$.
Let $x = x_1 \cdots x_n$ be a bit list and $S$ stack contents in which $a$ holds a bit block for
$x$ under $d$ followed by a rest $A$ that ends a bit block under $d$, and $t$ is empty. Then for
every state $v$ there are a state $v'$ and stack contents $S'$ such that $M$ runs in exactly
$2n + 2$ steps from label $l_1$, state $v$ and stacks $S$ to label $l_3$, state $v'$ and stacks
$S'$, where $S'(a) = A$, $S'(t)$ is empty, $S'(b)$ is $g(x_1), \dots, g(x_n)$ (top first)
followed by $S(b)$, and $S'(k) = S(k)$ for every other stack $k$.

articles.title: Phase-0 labels of the generic host
articles.statement:
The six labels of a host's phase 0, which moves the
input onto the component's stacks: two for the two passes that move the first block $x$, one that
drops the separator, two for the two passes that move the second block $w$, and one that resets
the state and starts the component.

articles.title: Component labels in the reduction host
articles.statement:
For a component with exit label $\mathit{done}$,
the label $\mathit{done}$ is sent to the host's cleanup label with answer false, and every other
component label $l$ to the host label that runs the component at $l$.

articles.title: Reduction host
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component with stacks $c_X$ and $c_O$, an encoding $g_X$ of
bits as symbols of $c_X$, an identification $e_O$ of the alphabet of $c_O$ with the bits, and
labels $\mathit{start}$ and $\mathit{done}$, where the component halts at $\mathit{done}$. Let $f$
be a function from bit lists to bit lists and $p$ a polynomial with natural-number coefficients.
Suppose that for every bit list $x$ the component, started at $\mathit{start}$ with state false,
with $x$ encoded by $g_X$ on $c_X$ and every other stack empty, reaches $\mathit{done}$ within
$p(|x|)$ steps with some state and stacks in which $c_O$ holds $f(x)$ translated symbol by symbol
by $e_O^{-1}$. Then $f$ is computable in polynomial time on raw bit lists (the identity as input
and output encoding): by the reduction host machine, with the bits as input alphabet, $e_O$ as
output alphabet and the reduction host's step bound for $p$ as time bound.

articles.title: The reduction host's run on one input
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component with stacks $c_X$ and $c_O$,
an encoding $g_X$ of bits as symbols of $c_X$, an identification $e_O$ of the alphabet of $c_O$
with the bits, and labels $\mathit{start}$ and $\mathit{done}$, where the component halts at
$\mathit{done}$. Let $p$ be a polynomial with natural-number coefficients and $x$, $o$ bit lists,
and suppose that the component, started at $\mathit{start}$ with state false, with $x$ encoded by
$g_X$ on $c_X$ and every other stack empty, reaches $\mathit{done}$ within $p(|x|)$ steps with
some state and stacks in which $c_O$ holds $o$ translated symbol by symbol by $e_O^{-1}$. Then the
reduction host program, started at its first phase-0 label with state false, $x$ on the input
stack and every other stack empty, halts within $T(|x|)$ steps, where $T$ is the reduction host's
step bound for $p$, with state false, $o$ translated by $e_O^{-1}$ on the host's copy of $c_O$ and
every other stack empty.

articles.title: The reduction host's run
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component with stacks $c_X$ and $c_O$, an encoding
$g_X$ of bits as symbols of $c_X$, an identification $e_O$ of the alphabet of $c_O$ with the bits,
and labels $\mathit{start}$ and $\mathit{done}$, where the component halts at $\mathit{done}$. Let
$f$ be a function from bit lists to bit lists and $p$ a polynomial with natural-number
coefficients, and suppose that for every bit list $y$ the component, started at $\mathit{start}$
with state false, with $y$ encoded by $g_X$ on $c_X$ and every other stack empty, reaches
$\mathit{done}$ within $p(|y|)$ steps with some state and stacks in which $c_O$ holds $f(y)$
translated symbol by symbol by $e_O^{-1}$. Then for every bit list $x$ the reduction host program,
started at its first phase-0 label with state false, $x$ on the input stack and every other stack
empty, halts within $T(|x|)$ steps, where $T$ is the reduction host's step bound for $p$, with
state false, $f(x)$ translated by $e_O^{-1}$ on the host's copy of $c_O$ and every other stack
empty.

articles.title: Reduction host program
articles.statement:
The program of the reduction host for a component with stacks
$c_X$ and $c_O$, an encoding $g_X$ of bits as symbols of $c_X$ and labels $\mathit{start}$ and
$\mathit{done}$. Phase 0 moves the whole input stack onto the buffer $X_1$ with the bit-moving
loop, then moves $X_1$ onto the host's copy of $c_X$ re-encoded by $g_X$ (so in the original
order), then sets the state to false and goes to $\mathit{start}$, or to the cleanup if
$\mathit{start} = \mathit{done}$. At the host label of a component label $l$ it runs the
component's statement at $l$ on the host's copies of the component stacks, with every jump to
$\mathit{done}$ sent to the cleanup. The cleanup pops every stack other than the copy of $c_O$
once per round, repeating while something was popped, and then goes to the final label, which
halts. The phase-0 labels for a separator and a second block halt.

articles.title: Step bound of the reduction host
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component machine with stacks $c_X$ and
$c_O$, an encoding $g_X$ of bits as symbols of $c_X$ and labels $\mathit{start}$ and
$\mathit{done}$, and let $B$ be the push bound of the reduction host machine built from these
data. For a polynomial $p$ with natural-number coefficients, the step bound of the reduction host
is the polynomial in the variable $X$

$$(B + 1)(2X + 3 + p) + X + 2.$$

At an input length $n$ it counts phase 0 and the component, at most $2n + 3 + p(n)$ steps, then
the cleanup, which takes at most one step more than the longest stack, of length at most $n$
plus $B$ times the steps so far, and the halt.

articles.title: Reduction host machine
articles.statement:
The reduction host as a finite multi-stack Turing machine: its
stacks are the host stacks with the host alphabets for bit input, its labels are the host labels,
its state is a bit starting at false, its program is the reduction host program started at the
first phase-0 label, its input stack is the input stack (raw bits) and its output stack is the
host's copy of the component's stack $c_O$.

articles.title: Stack lengths grow by at most the push bound per step
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a finite multi-stack
Turing machine with push bound $B$. If every stack of $S$ has length at most $N$ and $M$ runs in
$n$ steps from a configuration with some label, state $v$ and stacks $S$ to a configuration with
some label, state $v'$ and stacks $S'$, then every stack of $S'$ has length at most $N + Bn$.

articles.title: Stack lengths when only one stack is filled
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component machine and consider
its host with input alphabet $\alpha$. If a host stack $o$ holds a list $l$ and every other host
stack is empty, then every host stack has length at most the length of $l$.

articles.title: Relabelling in the verifier host
articles.statement:
Given labels $\mathit{yes}$ and $\mathit{no}$ of a
component machine $c$, a label $l$ of $c$ is sent to the host label that starts the cleanup with
answer true if $l = \mathit{yes}$, to the host label that starts the cleanup with answer false if
$l \ne \mathit{yes}$ and $l = \mathit{no}$, and to the host label that runs the component at $l$
otherwise.

articles.title: Verifier host
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component machine with stacks $c_X \ne c_W$, maps $g_X$ and
$g_W$ from bits to the alphabets of $c_X$ and $c_W$, and labels $\mathit{start}$, $\mathit{yes}$
and $\mathit{no}$ with $\mathit{yes} \ne \mathit{no}$, where the program halts at $\mathit{yes}$
and at $\mathit{no}$. Let $f$ assign a boolean to each pair of bit lists and let $p$ be a
polynomial with natural number coefficients. Suppose that for all bit lists $x$ and $w$, the
component started at $\mathit{start}$ with state false, the bits of $x$ mapped by $g_X$ on $c_X$,
the bits of $w$ mapped by $g_W$ on $c_W$ and every other stack empty reaches the label
$\mathit{yes}$ if $f(x, w)$ is true and $\mathit{no}$ otherwise within $p(|x| + |w|)$ steps. Then
the verifier host machine computes $(x, w) \mapsto f(x, w)$ in polynomial time, with the verifier
host's step bound for $p$ as time bound: on the pair encoding of $(x, w)$, over the pair alphabet,
it outputs the one-element bit list $[f(x, w)]$.

articles.title: The verifier host's run
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component machine with stacks $c_X \ne c_W$, maps
$g_X$ and $g_W$ from bits to the alphabets of $c_X$ and $c_W$, and labels $\mathit{start}$,
$\mathit{yes}$ and $\mathit{no}$ with $\mathit{yes} \ne \mathit{no}$, where the program halts at
$\mathit{yes}$ and at $\mathit{no}$. Let $f$ assign a boolean to each pair of bit lists and let
$p$ be a polynomial with natural number coefficients. Suppose that for all bit lists $x$ and $w$,
the component started at $\mathit{start}$ with state false, the bits of $x$ mapped by $g_X$ on
$c_X$, the bits of $w$ mapped by $g_W$ on $c_W$ and every other stack empty reaches the label
$\mathit{yes}$ if $f(x, w)$ is true and $\mathit{no}$ otherwise within $p(|x| + |w|)$ steps. Then
for all bit lists $x$ and $w$, with $n$ the length of the pair encoding of $(x, w)$, the verifier
host program started at its first phase-0 label with state false, the pair encoding of $(x, w)$
on the input stack and every other stack empty halts within $T(n)$ steps, where $T$ is the
verifier host's step bound for $p$, with state false, the one-element list $[f(x, w)]$ on the
output stack and every other stack empty.

articles.title: Verifier host program
articles.statement:
The program of the verifier host for a component machine $c$ with
stacks $c_X$ and $c_W$, encodings $g_X$ and $g_W$ of bits as symbols of $c_X$ and $c_W$, and
labels $\mathit{start}$, $\mathit{yes}$ and $\mathit{no}$, on the host stacks with the work
alphabet of the dense-SAT verifier on the input stack. On an input $x \# w$ in the pair encoding,
phase 0 moves the symbols on top of the input stack that encode bits of $x$ onto the buffer $X_1$
with the bit-moving loop, then moves $X_1$ onto the host's copy of $c_X$ re-encoded by $g_X$ (so
in the original order); it pops one symbol off the input stack (the separator $\#$); it moves
the symbols that encode bits of $w$ onto the buffer $W_1$ and then $W_1$ onto the host's copy of
$c_W$ re-encoded by $g_W$; then it sets the state to false and goes to the renamed label of
$\mathit{start}$. Here a label of $c$ is renamed to the cleanup label with answer true if it is
$\mathit{yes}$, to the cleanup label with answer false if it is $\mathit{no}$ but not
$\mathit{yes}$, and to the host's copy of itself otherwise. At the host's copy of a component
label $l$ it runs the component's statement at $l$ on the host's copies of the component stacks,
with every jump target renamed. The cleanup label with answer $a$ pops every stack other than the
output stack once per round, repeating while something was popped, and then goes to the output
label with answer $a$, which pushes $a$ on the output stack and halts.

articles.title: Step bound of the verifier host
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a component machine with stacks $c_X$ and
$c_W$, encodings $g_X$ and $g_W$ of bits as symbols of $c_X$ and $c_W$, and labels
$\mathit{start}$, $\mathit{yes}$ and $\mathit{no}$, and let $B$ be the push bound of the verifier
host machine built from these data. For a polynomial $p$ with natural-number coefficients, the
step bound of the verifier host is the polynomial in the variable $X$

$$(B + 1)(2X + 4 + p) + X + 2.$$

At an input length $n$ it counts phase 0 and the component, at most $2n + 4 + p(n)$ steps, then
the cleanup, which takes at most one step more than the longest stack, of length at most $n$
plus $B$ times the steps so far, and the output step.

articles.title: The verifier host machine
articles.statement:
The verifier host as a finite multi-stack Turing machine for a
component machine $c$: its stacks are the host stacks, with the pair alphabet on the input stack,
the alphabets of $c$ on the component's stacks and bits on the other stacks; its labels are the
host labels and its program is the verifier host program; it starts at the first phase-0 label
with a boolean internal state, initially false; it reads its input from the input stack and leaves
its output on the output stack.

articles.title: Halting from a configuration is normalizability
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine
and $c$ a configuration of $M$. Then $M$ halts from $c$ if and only if $c$ is normalizable for
the transition relation of $M$, that is, the run of $M$ from $c$ reaches, in finitely many steps
(possibly none), a configuration that has no successor.

The configurations without a successor are exactly those in the halting state.

articles.title: Halting from a configuration is invariant along a run
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing
machine and let $a$ and $b$ be configurations of $M$ such that the run of $M$ from $a$ reaches $b$
in finitely many steps (possibly none). Then $M$ halts from $a$ if and only if $M$ halts from $b$.

The backward direction holds for any relation; the forward direction uses that $M$ is
deterministic.

articles.title: Configurations with the same successor halt together
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing
machine and let $a$ and $b$ be configurations of $M$ that have the same successor, or that both
have no successor. Then $M$ halts from $a$ if and only if $M$ halts from $b$.

articles.title: Halting from a configuration
articles.statement:
A single-tape Turing machine $M$ halts from a configuration
$c$ when its run from $c$ reaches, in finitely many steps (possibly none), a configuration in the
halting state.

Equivalently, $c$ is normalizable for the transition relation of $M$, since the configurations in
the halting state are exactly those without a successor; the same holds for CSLib's register
machines.

articles.title: A machine that produces an output halts
articles.statement:
If a single-tape Turing machine $M$ outputs a word
$w'$ on an input word $w$, then $M$ halts on $w$.

articles.title: Halting on an input is halting from the initial configuration
articles.statement:
A single-tape Turing machine
$M$ halts on an input word $w$ if and only if $M$ halts from the initial configuration on $w$.

articles.title: Halting on an input
articles.statement:
A single-tape Turing machine $M$ halts on an input word $w$ when its
run from the initial configuration on $w$ (the start state, with $w$ written from the head
position rightwards on an otherwise blank tape) reaches, in finitely many steps (possibly none), a
configuration in the halting state.

articles.title: Distinct words give distinct tapes
articles.statement:
The map sending a word $w$ to the tape that holds $w$
from the head position rightwards, every other cell blank, is injective.

articles.title: Single-tape Turing machines are deterministic
articles.statement:
For a single-tape Turing machine $M$, every
configuration of $M$ has at most one successor under the transition relation of $M$.

articles.title: Co-recognizability by single-tape machines
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a primcodable type. A predicate
$p$ on $\alpha$ is co-recognizable by a single-tape Turing machine when its complement $\neg p$ is
recognizable by a single-tape Turing machine.

articles.title: Predicates decidable by a single-tape Turing machine
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a
primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$. A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is decidable by a
single-tape machine when there are a finite, nonempty tape alphabet $\Sigma$, an injective map
$\iota$ from the bits $\{0, 1\}$ to $\Sigma$ and a single-tape Turing machine $M$ over $\Sigma$
such that for every $a \in \alpha$ there is a bit $b$ for which $M$ outputs the one-symbol word
$\iota(b)$ on the input word obtained by writing the binary encoding of the code of $a$ in
$\mathbb{N}$ letter by letter through $\iota$, and $b = 1$ exactly when $p(a)$ holds. Here $M$
outputs a word $w$ on an input when its run from the input halts with exactly $w$ on the tape,
every other cell blank and the head on the first symbol of $w$.

articles.title: Predicates recognizable by a single-tape Turing machine
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be a type with a
primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$. A predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ is recognizable by a
single-tape machine when there are a finite, nonempty tape alphabet $\Sigma$, an injective map
$\iota$ from the bits $\{0, 1\}$ to $\Sigma$ and a single-tape Turing machine $M$ over $\Sigma$
such that for every $a \in \alpha$, the run of $M$ on the input word obtained by writing the
binary encoding of the code of $a$ in $\mathbb{N}$ letter by letter through $\iota$ reaches the
halting state if and only if $p(a)$ holds.

articles.title: Halting configurations are exactly those without a successor
articles.statement:
For a single-tape Turing
machine $M$ and a configuration $c$ of $M$, one step of $M$ from $c$ gives no configuration if
and only if $c$ is in the halting state.

articles.title: One step of a single-tape Turing machine
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine, $q$ a
state of $M$ other than the halting state and $t$ a tape, and let the transition function of $M$
at $q$ and the symbol under the head of $t$ (possibly blank) give the symbol $s$ to write
(possibly blank), the head movement $d$ (left, right or none) and the next state $q'$ (possibly
the halting state). Then the configuration in state $q$ with tape $t$ has a successor, namely the
configuration in state $q'$ whose tape is obtained from $t$ by writing $s$ under the head and
then moving the head by $d$.

articles.title: Outputs are unique
articles.statement:
If a single-tape Turing machine $M$ outputs the word $l_1$ on the
input $l$ and also outputs the word $l_2$ on the input $l$, then $l_1 = l_2$. Here $M$ outputs a
word $w$ on $l$ when its run from the initial configuration on $l$ halts with exactly $w$ on the
tape, every other cell blank and the head on the first symbol of $w$ (an all-blank tape if $w$ is
empty).

The run of a machine is determined by its input, and a halting configuration has no successor.

articles.title: Value of the cell-symbol map
articles.statement:
For every cell $o$ over the non-blank symbols of an alphabet
$\Gamma_0$ with blank symbol $b$, the cell symbol of $o$ is $b$ when $o$ is the blank cell and is
$x$ when $o$ holds the non-blank symbol $x$.

articles.title: The cell-symbol map is injective
articles.statement:
Distinct cells over the non-blank symbols of an alphabet
$\Gamma_0$ have distinct cell symbols in $\Gamma_0$.

articles.title: Cell symbol
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma_0$ be an alphabet with blank symbol $b$. A tape cell over the
non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$ is either blank or holds a symbol $x \ne b$ of $\Gamma_0$. Its cell
symbol is $b$ for the blank cell and $x$ for the cell holding $x$. This map from cells to
$\Gamma_0$ sends the blank cell to the blank symbol, so it is a pointed map.

articles.title: The simulating machine halts exactly when the Post–Turing machine halts
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma_0$
be a finite alphabet with at least one non-blank symbol, let $M$ be a Post–Turing machine over
$\Gamma_0$ supported by the finite set of states $S$, and let $l$ be a word of non-blank symbols
of $\Gamma_0$. The single-tape machine simulating $M$ halts on the input $l$ if and only if $M$,
started on $l$, halts.

articles.title: First cell of the half-tape view of a stack tape
articles.statement:
For every stack tape $s$ over $\Gamma$
(a finite list of cells, each a symbol of $\Gamma$ or the blank, that does not end in a blank), the
first cell of the half-tape view of $s$ (its cells followed by infinitely many blanks) is the
first cell of $s$, which is the blank if $s$ is empty.

articles.title: First symbol of a half-tape read from non-blank cells
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma_0$ be an alphabet with
blank symbol $b$. For every stack tape $s$ of cells over the non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$ (a
finite list of cells, blank beyond its end), the first symbol of the half-tape over $\Gamma_0$
read from $s$ is the cell symbol of the first cell of $s$; when $s$ is empty this is $b$.

articles.title: Head cell of the view of a two-way tape
articles.statement:
For every two-way tape $t$ over $\Gamma$ (a head
cell with a left and a right stack tape), the head cell of the view of $t$ as a tape of cells is
the head cell of $t$.

articles.title: Head symbol of a tape read from non-blank cells
articles.statement:
For every two-way tape $t$ of cells over
the non-blank symbols of an alphabet $\Gamma_0$, the symbol under the head of the tape over
$\Gamma_0$ read from $t$ is the cell symbol of the cell under the head of $t$.

articles.title: Left half of the view of a two-way tape
articles.statement:
For every two-way tape $t$ over $\Gamma$ (a head
cell with a left and a right stack tape), the left half of the view of $t$ as a tape of cells is
the half-tape view of the left stack tape of $t$.

articles.title: Non-blank symbols
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $\Gamma_0$ with a distinguished blank symbol $b$, the
non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$ are the elements $x \in \Gamma_0$ with $x \ne b$. They form the
tape alphabet of the single-tape machine that simulates a Post–Turing machine over $\Gamma_0$.

articles.title: Cells of the half-tape view of a stack tape
articles.statement:
For every stack tape $s$ over $\Gamma$ (a
finite list of cells, each a symbol of $\Gamma$ or the blank, that does not end in a blank) and
every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the cell at position $n$ of the half-tape view of $s$ (its cells followed
by infinitely many blanks) is the $n$-th cell of $s$, counting from $0$, if $n$ is less than the
length of $s$, and the blank otherwise.

articles.title: Cells of an input tape
articles.statement:
For every word $w = w_0 \cdots w_{m-1}$ over $\Gamma$ and every
integer $i$, the cell at position $i$ of the view of the input tape of $w$ is $w_i$ if
$0 \le i < m$, and the blank otherwise.

articles.title: Cells after $n$ moves to the right
articles.statement:
For every two-way tape $t$ over $\Gamma$, every
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and every integer $i$, the cell at position $i$ of the view of the tape obtained
from $t$ by moving the head $n$ times to the right is the cell at position $i + n$ of the view
of $t$.

articles.title: Cells after an optional move
articles.statement:
For an optional direction $d$, let $\delta(d)$ be $0$ if $d$
is no move, $-1$ if $d$ is a move to the left and $1$ if $d$ is a move to the right. For every
two-way tape $t$ over $\Gamma$ and every integer $i$, the cell at position $i$ of the view of the
tape obtained from $t$ by the optional move $d$ is the cell at position $i + \delta(d)$ of the view
of $t$.

articles.title: Cells after a write and an optional move
articles.statement:
For an optional direction $d$, let $\delta(d)$ be
$0$ if $d$ is no move, $-1$ if $d$ is a move to the left and $1$ if $d$ is a move to the right. For
every two-way tape $t$ over $\Gamma$, every cell $a$ (a symbol of $\Gamma$ or the blank) and every
integer $i$, the cell at position $i$ of the view of the tape obtained from $t$ by writing $a$
under the head and then performing the optional move $d$ is $a$ if $i + \delta(d) = 0$, and the
cell at position $i + \delta(d)$ of the view of $t$ otherwise.

articles.title: Cells after a write
articles.statement:
For every two-way tape $t$ over $\Gamma$, every cell $a$ (a symbol of
$\Gamma$ or the blank) and every integer $i$, the cell at position $i$ of the view of the tape
obtained from $t$ by writing $a$ under the head is $a$ if $i = 0$, and the cell at position $i$
of the view of $t$ otherwise.

articles.title: The cells of the view
articles.statement:
Let $t$ be a two-way tape over $\Gamma$ with head cell $h$, left
stack tape $(\ell_0, \dots, \ell_{p-1})$ and right stack tape $(r_0, \dots, r_{q-1})$. For every
integer $i$, the cell at position $i$ of the view of $t$ as a tape of cells is $h$ if $i = 0$,
$r_{i-1}$ if $0 < i \le q$, $\ell_{-i-1}$ if $-p \le i < 0$, and the blank otherwise.

articles.title: Single-tape simulation of a Post–Turing machine
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma_0$ be a finite alphabet with
blank symbol $b$ and at least one non-blank symbol, and let $M$ be a Post–Turing machine over
$\Gamma_0$ with start state $q_0$, supported by the finite set of states $S$ (so $q_0 \in S$, and
from a state in $S$ the machine $M$ only enters states in $S$). The single-tape machine simulating
$M$ has the non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$ as tape alphabet, $S$ as set of states and $q_0$ as
start state. In a state $q$, reading a cell $s$ whose cell symbol is $a$, it acts as follows. If
$M$ halts in $q$ on $a$, it writes $s$ back and halts. If $M$ moves the head in direction $d$ and
enters $q'$, it writes $s$ back, moves in direction $d$ and enters $q'$. If $M$ writes $a'$ and
enters $q'$, it writes the blank cell when $a' = b$ and otherwise the cell holding $a'$, does not
move, and enters $q'$.

CSLib machines need a chosen symbol of their alphabet, so an alphabet whose only symbol is the
blank is excluded.

articles.title: The offset of an optional move is at most one
articles.statement:
For every optional head move $d$ (no move,
a move to the left, or a move to the right), the offset of $d$ lies between $-1$ and $1$, that is,
$-1 \le \mathrm{offset}(d) \le 1$.

articles.title: Offset of an optional head move
articles.statement:
The offset of an optional head move $d$ is $0$ if $d$ is
no move, $-1$ if $d$ is a move to the left and $1$ if $d$ is a move to the right.

After the move $d$, the cell at position $i$ relative to the head is the cell that was at
position $i$ plus the offset of $d$.

articles.title: The single-tape simulation has the same output
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma_0$ be a finite alphabet with
at least one non-blank symbol, let $M$ be a Post–Turing machine over $\Gamma_0$ supported by the
finite set of states $S$, and let $l$ and $l'$ be words of non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$. If
$M$, started on $l$, halts in a configuration whose tape holds $l'$ starting at the head, with
blanks everywhere else, then the single-tape machine simulating $M$ outputs $l'$ on the input
$l$: its run from the initial configuration on $l$ reaches the halting state with the tape
holding exactly $l'$, starting at the head.

articles.title: The single-tape simulation outputs within one extra step
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma_0$ be a finite
alphabet with at least one non-blank symbol, let $M$ be a Post–Turing machine over $\Gamma_0$
supported by the finite set of states $S$, and let $l$ and $l'$ be words of non-blank symbols of
$\Gamma_0$. If $M$, started on $l$, reaches in exactly $n$ steps a configuration $c$ in which it
halts, and the tape of $c$ holds $l'$ starting at the head with blanks everywhere else, then the
single-tape machine simulating $M$ outputs $l'$ on the input $l$ within $n + 1$ steps: its run
from the initial configuration on $l$ reaches, in at most $n + 1$ steps, the halting state with
the tape holding exactly $l'$, starting at the head.

articles.title: Runs of a TM0 machine are runs of its single-tape simulation
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a TM0 machine
over a finite alphabet $\Gamma_0$ with blank symbol $b$ and at least one non-blank symbol,
supported by a finite set $S$ of states, and let $\widehat{M}$ be the single-tape machine over
the non-blank symbols $N = \Gamma_0 \setminus \{b\}$ simulating $M$. For a tape $t$ over $N$,
write $\tau(t)$ for the TM0 tape read from $t$ cell by cell. If $M$ goes from a configuration
$(q, T)$ to a configuration $(q', T')$ in exactly $n$ steps, $q \in S$, and $\tau(t) = T$, then
$q' \in S$ and there is a tape $t'$ over $N$ with $\tau(t') = T'$ such that $\widehat{M}$ goes
from the configuration $(q, t)$ to the configuration $(q', t')$ in exactly $n$ steps.

articles.title: Right half of the tape view
articles.statement:
For every two-sided tape $t$ over $\Gamma$ (a head cell
together with a left and a right stack tape), the right half of the tape view of $t$ is the
half-tape view of the right half of $t$.

articles.title: The simulation halts one step after the TM0 machine
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a TM0 machine over a
finite alphabet $\Gamma_0$ with blank symbol $b$ and at least one non-blank symbol, supported by a
finite set $S$ of states, and let $\widehat{M}$ be the single-tape machine over the non-blank
symbols $N = \Gamma_0 \setminus \{b\}$ simulating $M$. For a tape $t$ over $N$, write $\tau(t)$
for the TM0 tape read from $t$ cell by cell. If $q \in S$ and $M$ has no step from the
configuration $(q, \tau(t))$, then one step of $\widehat{M}$ from the configuration $(q, t)$
leads to its halting state with the tape $t$ unchanged.

articles.title: Each TM0 step is one step of the simulation
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a TM0 machine over a finite
alphabet $\Gamma_0$ with blank symbol $b$ and at least one non-blank symbol, supported by a finite
set $S$ of states, and let $\widehat{M}$ be the single-tape machine over the non-blank symbols
$N = \Gamma_0 \setminus \{b\}$ simulating $M$. For a tape $t$ over $N$, write $\tau(t)$ for the
TM0 tape read from $t$ cell by cell. If $q \in S$ and one step of $M$ takes the configuration
$(q, \tau(t))$ to a configuration $(q', T')$, then $q' \in S$ and there is a tape $t'$ over $N$
with $\tau(t') = T'$ such that one step of $\widehat{M}$ takes the configuration $(q, t)$ to the
configuration $(q', t')$.

articles.title: Tail of the half-tape view of a stack tape
articles.statement:
For every stack tape $s$ over $\Gamma$ (a list
of cells, each a symbol of $\Gamma$ or the blank cell, not ending in a blank cell), the tail of
the half-tape view of $s$ is the half-tape view of the tail of $s$: dropping the first cell of
$s$ drops the first cell of its half-tape.

articles.title: Dropping the first cell of a stack tape of non-blank symbols
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $\Gamma_0$
with blank symbol $b$ and every stack tape $s$ over the non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$, dropping
the first symbol of the half-tape read from $s$ gives the half-tape read from $s$ with its first
cell removed (the empty stack tape staying empty).

articles.title: Half-tape view of a stack tape
articles.statement:
A stack tape $s$ over an alphabet $\Gamma$ is a finite list
of cells, each a symbol of $\Gamma$ or the blank cell, that does not end in a blank cell. Its
half-tape view is the half-tape of cells (a sequence of cells taken up to trailing blanks, the
blank cell being the default) whose cells are those of $s$ in order, followed by blank cells.

articles.title: Pushing a cell onto a stack tape
articles.statement:
For every cell $c$ (a symbol of $\Gamma$ or the blank
cell) and every stack tape $s$ over $\Gamma$, the half-tape view of the stack tape obtained by
pushing $c$ onto $s$ is the half-tape view of $s$ with $c$ pushed onto its front.

For the blank cell this holds because the half-tape is blank beyond its end.

articles.title: Pushing a cell onto a stack tape of non-blank symbols
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma_0$ be an alphabet with
blank symbol $b$ and $N = \Gamma_0 \setminus \{b\}$. Read a cell over $N$ as a symbol of
$\Gamma_0$: $b$ for the blank cell, $x$ for a cell holding $x$. For every cell $o$ and every stack
tape $s$ over $N$, the half-tape read from the stack tape obtained by pushing $o$ onto $s$ is the
half-tape read from $s$ with the symbol of $o$ pushed onto its front.

For the blank cell this holds because the half-tape is blank beyond its end.

articles.title: The half-tape view of stack tapes is injective
articles.statement:
If two stack tapes over $\Gamma$ have the
same half-tape view, then they are equal.

This holds because a stack tape does not end in a blank cell, so trailing blanks of a half-tape
do not come from cells.

articles.title: Distinct stack tapes of non-blank symbols read as distinct half-tapes
articles.statement:
For an alphabet
$\Gamma_0$ with blank symbol $b$, two stack tapes over the non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$ that read
as the same half-tape over $\Gamma_0$ are equal.

A stack tape does not end in a blank, so the trailing blanks of a half-tape do not come from
cells.

articles.title: Half-tape view of a word
articles.statement:
For every word $a_1 \cdots a_n$ over $\Gamma$, the half-tape
view of the stack tape whose cells are the non-blank cells $a_1, \dots, a_n$ is the half-tape
whose first $n$ cells are $a_1, \dots, a_n$ and whose later cells are blank.

articles.title: A word of non-blank symbols reads as itself
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $\Gamma_0$ with blank symbol
$b$ and a word $w$ of non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$, the half-tape read from the stack tape whose
cells hold the letters of $w$ in order is the half-tape of $w$, viewed as a word over $\Gamma_0$.

articles.title: Half-tape view of the empty stack tape
articles.statement:
The half-tape view of the empty stack tape over
$\Gamma$ is the half-tape all of whose cells are blank.

articles.title: The empty stack tape reads as the blank half-tape
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $\Gamma_0$ with blank
symbol $b$, the empty stack tape over the non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$ reads as the half-tape
of the empty list, all of whose symbols are $b$.

articles.title: Half-tape of a stack tape of non-blank symbols
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma_0$ be an alphabet with blank
symbol $b$ and $N = \Gamma_0 \setminus \{b\}$ its non-blank symbols. A stack tape $s$ over $N$, a
finite list of cells each blank or holding a symbol of $N$ and not ending in a blank cell, is read
as the TM0 half-tape over $\Gamma_0$ whose $i$-th symbol is that of the $i$-th cell of $s$: $b$
for a blank cell, $x$ for a cell holding $x$, and $b$ past the end of $s$.

articles.title: Cell view of a two-way tape
articles.statement:
A CSLib tape $t$ over an alphabet $\Gamma$ has a head cell
and two halves, each a finite list of cells not ending in a blank, where a cell is a symbol of
$\Gamma$ or the blank. Its cell view is the Mathlib tape over cells, with the blank as default
symbol, whose head is the head cell of $t$ and whose left and right halves are the halves of $t$,
blank past their ends. So the cell at position $i \in \mathbb{Z}$ of the view is the cell $i$
places to the right of the head of $t$ (to the left when $i < 0$).

articles.title: The tape view is injective
articles.statement:
If two two-sided tapes $t$ and $t'$ over $\Gamma$ (each a head
cell together with a left and a right stack tape) have the same tape view as a tape of cells,
then $t = t'$.

articles.title: Distinct tapes of non-blank symbols read as distinct TM0 tapes
articles.statement:
For an alphabet
$\Gamma_0$ with blank symbol $b$, two tapes over the non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$ that read,
cell by cell, as the same TM0 tape over $\Gamma_0$ are equal.

articles.title: The cell view of an input tape
articles.statement:
For every word $w = w_0 w_1 \cdots w_{n-1}$ over $\Gamma$,
the cell view of the input tape of $w$ is the Mathlib input tape of the list of non-blank cells
$w_0, \dots, w_{n-1}$: the head is on $w_0$, the letters $w_1, \dots, w_{n-1}$ lie to its right
in order, and every other cell is blank (for the empty word, every cell is blank).

articles.title: The Post–Turing reading of an input tape
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma_0$ be an alphabet whose default
symbol is the blank. For every word $l$ of non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$, the Post–Turing
reading of the two-way input tape of $l$ (the head on the first symbol of $l$, the rest of $l$ to
its right, every other cell blank) is the Post–Turing machine input tape of $l$ read as a word
over $\Gamma_0$, with the head on the first symbol of $l$ and the rest of $l$ to its right.

articles.title: The cell view commutes with head moves
articles.statement:
For every tape $t$ and each direction $d$ (left or
right), the cell view of the tape obtained from $t$ by moving the head one cell in direction $d$
equals the tape obtained from the cell view of $t$ by moving its head one cell in direction $d$.

articles.title: Head moves commute with the Post–Turing reading of a tape
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma_0$ be an alphabet
whose default symbol is the blank, and for a two-way tape $t$ whose cells are blank or hold
non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$, let $\tau(t)$ be the Post–Turing reading of $t$, a Post–Turing
machine tape over $\Gamma_0$. For every such $t$ and every direction $d$, left or right, $\tau$ of
$t$ with its head moved in direction $d$ is $\tau(t)$ with its head moved in direction $d$.

articles.title: The cell view commutes with optional head moves
articles.statement:
For every two-way tape $t$ over $\Gamma$
and every optional head move $d$, which is either no move or a move one cell in a direction, the
cell view of the tape obtained from $t$ by the optional move $d$ is the cell view of $t$ when $d$
is no move, and the cell view of $t$ with its head moved one cell in direction $d$ when $d$ is a
direction.

articles.title: Optional head moves commute with the Post–Turing reading of a tape
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma_0$ be an
alphabet whose default symbol is the blank, and for a two-way tape $t$ whose cells are blank or
hold non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$, let $\tau(t)$ be the Post–Turing reading of $t$, a
Post–Turing machine tape over $\Gamma_0$. For every such $t$ and every optional move $d$, which is
either no move or a direction, $\tau$ of $t$ after the optional move $d$ is $\tau(t)$ when $d$ is
no move, and $\tau(t)$ with its head moved in direction $d$ when $d$ is a direction.

articles.title: The cell view commutes with writing
articles.statement:
For every tape $t$ and every cell $a$ (a symbol or
the blank), the cell view of the tape obtained from $t$ by writing $a$ under the head equals the
tape obtained from the cell view of $t$ by writing $a$ under its head.

articles.title: Writing commutes with the Post–Turing reading of a tape
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma_0$ be an alphabet
whose default symbol is the blank, and for a two-way tape $t$ whose cells are blank or hold
non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$, let $\tau(t)$ be the Post–Turing reading of $t$, a Post–Turing
machine tape over $\Gamma_0$. For every such $t$ and every cell $o$, blank or holding a non-blank
symbol, $\tau$ of $t$ with $o$ written under the head is $\tau(t)$ with the symbol of $o$ written
under the head, where the symbol of $o$ is $x$ if $o$ holds $x$ and the blank of $\Gamma_0$ if $o$
is blank.

articles.title: Post–Turing reading of a tape over the non-blank symbols
articles.statement:
Let $\Gamma_0$ be an alphabet
whose default symbol is the blank. The Post–Turing reading of a two-way tape $t$ whose cells are
blank or hold non-blank symbols of $\Gamma_0$ is the Post–Turing machine tape over $\Gamma_0$
obtained cell by cell: take the view of $t$ as a tape of cells, each cell at its position relative
to the head and blank cells past the ends, and replace each cell by its symbol, a non-blank symbol
$x$ by $x$ itself and the blank cell by the blank of $\Gamma_0$.

articles.title: Forgetting the restriction on a configuration
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a set of states of a
single-tape Turing machine with tape alphabet $\Gamma$ and states $\Lambda$. A configuration with
state $q \in S$ and tape $T$ is sent to the configuration with state $q$, viewed as an element of
$\Lambda$, and the same tape $T$.

articles.title: The restricted machine evaluates like the original
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape Turing machine
with tape alphabet $\Gamma$ and states $\Lambda$, and let $S \subseteq \Lambda$ be a set of states
that supports $M$: it contains the default state and is closed under the transitions of $M$. If the
default state of the restriction of $M$ to $S$ is the default state of $M$, then for every input
list $l$ over $\Gamma$ the evaluation of the restricted machine on $l$ equals that of $M$: either
both fail to halt, or both halt with the same output.

articles.title: The original machine simulates the restricted one step for step
articles.statement:
Let $S$ be a set of states
supporting a single-tape Turing machine $M$, and relate a configuration of the restriction of $M$
to $S$ to the configuration of $M$ with the same state, viewed as a state of $M$, and the same
tape. Suppose the configuration $c$ of the restricted machine is related to the configuration $d$
of $M$. If the restricted machine steps from $c$ to $c'$, then $M$ reaches, in one or more steps
from $d$, the configuration related to $c'$. If the restricted machine has no step from $c$, then
$M$ has no step from $d$.

articles.title: Restriction of a single-tape machine to a supporting set of states
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape
Turing machine with tape alphabet $\Gamma$ and states $\Lambda$, and let $S \subseteq \Lambda$
support $M$: $S$ contains the default state and every transition of $M$ from a state in $S$ leads to
a state in $S$. The restriction of $M$ to $S$ is the machine with states $S$ that, in state
$q \in S$ reading $a$, does what $M$ does in state $q$ reading $a$: it halts if $M$ halts, and
otherwise performs the same action and moves to the same next state, which lies in $S$.

articles.title: Embedding the first machine's configurations into a composite
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be
single-tape Turing machines over the same alphabet, and let $M$ be their composite, whose states
are the disjoint union of those of $M_1$ and of $M_2$: $M$ starts in the start state of $M_1$ and
runs $M_1$, where $M_1$ would halt it enters the start state of $M_2$ instead, and it then runs
$M_2$ and halts where $M_2$ halts. A configuration of $M_1$ with tape $t$ is sent to the
configuration of $M$ with the same tape $t$ whose state is the copy of $q$ if $M_1$ is in state
$q$, and the start state of $M_2$ if $M_1$ has halted.

## Sources

articles.title: Embedding the second machine's configurations into a composite
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be
single-tape Turing machines over the same alphabet, and let $M$ be their composite, whose states
are the disjoint union of those of $M_1$ and of $M_2$: $M$ starts in the start state of $M_1$ and
runs $M_1$, where $M_1$ would halt it enters the start state of $M_2$ instead, and it then runs
$M_2$ and halts where $M_2$ halts. A configuration of $M_2$ with tape $t$ is sent to the
configuration of $M$ with the same tape $t$ whose state is the copy of $q$ if $M_2$ is in state
$q$, and which is halted if $M_2$ has halted.

## Sources

- public version of upstream CSLib's private `toCompCfg_right`.

articles.title: Timed outputs compose
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be single-tape Turing machines over the same
alphabet, and let $M$ be their composite, whose states are the disjoint union of those of $M_1$
and of $M_2$: $M$ starts in the start state of $M_1$ and runs $M_1$, where $M_1$ would halt it
enters the start state of $M_2$ instead, and it then runs $M_2$ and halts where $M_2$ halts. Say
that a machine outputs a word $w$ on a word $v$ within $t$ steps when, started in its start state
on a tape holding $v$, it reaches in at most $t$ steps the halted configuration whose tape holds
exactly $w$, with the head at the start of $w$. For all words $a$, $b$, $c$ and all natural
numbers $t_1$, $t_2$: if $M_1$ outputs $b$ on $a$ within $t_1$ steps and $M_2$ outputs $c$ on $b$
within $t_2$ steps, then $M$ outputs $c$ on $a$ within $t_1 + t_2$ steps.

articles.title: Outputs compose
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be single-tape Turing machines over the same
alphabet, and let $M$ be their composite, whose states are the disjoint union of those of $M_1$
and of $M_2$: $M$ starts in the start state of $M_1$ and runs $M_1$, where $M_1$ would halt it
enters the start state of $M_2$ instead, and it then runs $M_2$ and halts where $M_2$ halts. Say
that a machine outputs a word $w$ on a word $v$ when, started in its start state on a tape
holding $v$, it reaches the halted configuration whose tape holds exactly $w$, with the head at
the start of $w$. For all words $a$, $b$, $c$: if $M_1$ outputs $b$ on $a$ and $M_2$ outputs $c$
on $b$, then $M$ outputs $c$ on $a$.

articles.title: Runs of a composite from configurations of the second machine
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be
single-tape Turing machines over the same alphabet, and let $M$ be their composite, whose states
are the disjoint union of those of $M_1$ and of $M_2$: $M$ starts in the start state of $M_1$ and
runs $M_1$, where $M_1$ would halt it enters the start state of $M_2$ instead, and it then runs
$M_2$ and halts where $M_2$ halts. Let $\iota_2$ send a configuration of $M_2$ to the
configuration of $M$ with the same tape whose state is the copy of the state of $M_2$, halted if
$M_2$ has halted. If $c$ is a configuration of $M_2$ and $M$ moves from $\iota_2(c)$ to a
configuration $d$ in finitely many (possibly zero) steps, then there is a configuration $c'$ of
$M_2$ such that $M_2$ moves from $c$ to $c'$ in finitely many (possibly zero) steps and
$d = \iota_2(c')$.

articles.title: Halting of a composite
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be single-tape Turing machines over the same
alphabet, and let $M$ be their composite, whose states are the disjoint union of those of $M_1$
and of $M_2$: $M$ starts in the start state of $M_1$ and runs $M_1$, where $M_1$ would halt it
enters the start state of $M_2$ instead, and it then runs $M_2$ and halts where $M_2$ halts. Say
that a machine outputs a word $w$ on a word $v$ when, started in its start state on a tape
holding $v$, it reaches the halted configuration whose tape holds exactly $w$, with the head at
the start of $w$. For all words $a$ and $b$ such that $M_1$ outputs $b$ on $a$: $M$, started in
its start state on a tape holding $a$, halts if and only if $M_2$, started in its start state on
a tape holding $b$, halts.

articles.title: Step function of a composite on configurations of the second machine
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$
be single-tape Turing machines over the same alphabet, and let $M$ be their composite, whose
states are the disjoint union of those of $M_1$ and of $M_2$: $M$ starts in the start state of
$M_1$ and runs $M_1$, where $M_1$ would halt it enters the start state of $M_2$ instead, and it
then runs $M_2$ and halts where $M_2$ halts. Let $\iota_2$ send a configuration of $M_2$ to the
configuration of $M$ with the same tape whose state is the copy of the state of $M_2$, halted if
$M_2$ has halted. For every configuration $c$ of $M_2$: if $M_2$ moves from $c$ to $c'$ in one
step, then $M$ moves from $\iota_2(c)$ to $\iota_2(c')$ in one step, and if $c$ has no successor
in $M_2$, then $\iota_2(c)$ has no successor in $M$.

## Sources

articles.title: The composite simulates steps of the first machine
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be single-tape
Turing machines over the same alphabet, and let $M$ be their composite, whose states are the
disjoint union of those of $M_1$ and of $M_2$: $M$ starts in the start state of $M_1$ and runs
$M_1$, where $M_1$ would halt it enters the start state of $M_2$ instead, and it then runs $M_2$
and halts where $M_2$ halts. Let $\iota_1$ send a configuration of $M_1$ to the configuration of
$M$ with the same tape whose state is the copy of the state of $M_1$, or the start state of $M_2$
if $M_1$ has halted. If $M_1$ moves from a configuration $c$ to a configuration $c'$ in one step,
then $M$ moves from $\iota_1(c)$ to $\iota_1(c')$ in one step.

## Sources

- upstream CSLib's private `map_toCompCfg_left_step`, stated as a relation.

articles.title: The composite simulates steps of the second machine
articles.statement:
Let $M_1$ and $M_2$ be single-tape
Turing machines over the same alphabet, and let $M$ be their composite, whose states are the
disjoint union of those of $M_1$ and of $M_2$: $M$ starts in the start state of $M_1$ and runs
$M_1$, where $M_1$ would halt it enters the start state of $M_2$ instead, and it then runs $M_2$
and halts where $M_2$ halts. Let $\iota_2$ send a configuration of $M_2$ to the configuration of
$M$ with the same tape whose state is the copy of the state of $M_2$, halted if $M_2$ has halted.
If $M_2$ moves from a configuration $c$ to a configuration $c'$ in one step, then $M$ moves from
$\iota_2(c)$ to $\iota_2(c')$ in one step.

articles.title: The initial configuration of a bundled multi-stack machine
articles.statement:
For a bundled multi-stack Turing
machine and every list $l$ over the alphabet of its input stack, the initial configuration of the
bundled machine on $l$ equals the generic multi-stack initial configuration with $l$ on the input
stack, when the main label is taken as the default label.

articles.title: Every statement is supported by all labels
articles.statement:
If the label type $\Lambda$ is finite, then
every statement of a multi-stack Turing machine with labels $\Lambda$ is supported by the finite set
of all labels: every label it can jump to lies in this set.

articles.title: A multi-stack machine is supported by all its labels
articles.statement:
A multi-stack Turing machine with
finitely many labels is supported by the set of all its labels: this set contains the default label,
and every statement of the machine is supported by it.

articles.title: The emulation halts iff the multi-stack machine halts
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack Turing
machine with stacks indexed by $K$, let $k \in K$, and let $L$ be a list over the alphabet of stack
$k$. The single-tape emulation of $M$, started on the tape encoding of the stacks with $L$ on stack
$k$ and all other stacks empty, halts if and only if $M$, started with $L$ on stack $k$ and all
other stacks empty, halts.

articles.title: The emulation visits finitely many states
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a multi-stack Turing machine whose
internal state type is finite, and let $S$ be a finite set of labels that supports $M$. Then the
single-tape emulation of $M$ is supported by an explicit finite set of states built from $S$ through
the two translations: this set contains the initial state and is closed under the transitions of the
emulation.

articles.title: Two-step single-tape translation of a multi-stack machine
articles.statement:
For a multi-stack Turing
machine $M$ with stacks indexed by $K$ and stack alphabets $\Gamma_k$, this is the single-tape
machine obtained by translating $M$ first into a single-tape machine with a store and then into a
plain single-tape machine. Its tape alphabet consists of a bottom-of-stack flag together with one
optional symbol of $\Gamma_k$ for each stack $k$. Its states are pairs of an optional statement of
the intermediate machine and a value of the internal state of $M$.

articles.title: The tape update
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code, $k$ a configuration and $t$, $q'$, $s$ natural
numbers. Started at the label $\mathsf{act0}$, with any value of its internal variable, on the
stacks holding the code $c$, the clock $t$ and the configuration $k$, with $q'$ on the next-state
stack, $s$ on the action stack and all other stacks empty, the program of the clocked universal
machine reaches the label $\mathsf{fin}$, with some value of its internal variable, on the stacks
holding $c$, $t$ and the configuration obtained from $k$ by entering the state $q'$ and doing the
action coded by $s$, with the next-state, action and all other stacks empty. It does so in at
most as many steps as the step bound of the tape update for $k$, $q'$ and $s$.

articles.title: Step bound of the tape update
articles.statement:
For a configuration $k$ with state $q$, head cell $h$,
cells $\ell$ left of the head and cells $r$ right of the head (nearest first), a next state $q'$
and an action $s$, the step bound of the tape update is $q + q' + s + h + \ell_0 + r_0 + 8$, where
$\ell_0$ and $r_0$ are the first entries of $\ell$ and $r$, taken to be $0$ for an empty list.

articles.title: Configurations bounded by $M$
articles.statement:
A configuration $k$ is bounded by a natural number $M$
when its state, its head cell and every cell left and right of the head are at most $M$.

articles.title: The cell of a number
articles.statement:
The cell of a natural number $n$ is the list of bits consisting of
$n$ copies of the bit true (units) followed by one bit false (a marker).

articles.title: The cells of a list of numbers
articles.statement:
The cells of a list $(n_1, \ldots, n_m)$ of natural numbers
are the concatenation of the cells of $n_1, \ldots, n_m$ in this order, so that the cell of $n_1$
comes first (on top of a stack).

articles.title: Step bound of the clocked simulation
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ and a clock $T$, let $|C|$ be the
length of the code stack of $c$. The step bound of the clocked simulation on the clock $T$ is
