$T + 1$ times the cost of one round of the loop on configurations whose numbers are at most
$|C| + 2$, that is, $(T + 1)(14|C| + 19)$.

articles.title: The clocked universal machine on stacks
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code, $x$ a list of bits and $T$ a
natural number, and let $|C|$ be the length of the code stack of $c$. Start the program of the
clocked universal machine at the label $\mathsf{sc0}$, with any value of its internal variable,
on the stacks holding the code $c$, the clock $T$ and the initial configuration on $x$, all other
stacks empty. If the clocked evaluation of $c$ on $x$ for $T$ steps is defined, the machine
reaches the label $\mathsf{hlt}$ on the stacks holding $c$, some clock $t'$ and the configuration
of $c$ after $T$ steps on $x$; otherwise it reaches the label $\mathsf{tmo}$ on the stacks holding
$c$, the clock $0$ and some configuration. In both cases the internal variable ends with some
value, all other stacks are empty, and the run takes at most $(T + 1)(14|C| + 19)$ steps, the
step bound of the clocked machine on the clock $T$.

When the clocked evaluation is defined, its value is the output of the configuration of $c$ after
$T$ steps on $x$.

articles.title: The code stack
articles.statement:
The code stack of a code $c$ is the list of bits formed by the cells of the
numbers $q, a, q', s$ of every entry $(q, a, q', s)$ of $c$ (a table position $(q, a)$ holding the
transition $(q', s)$), with the entries ordered by $q$ and then by $a$, and the four numbers of an
entry in the order $q, a, q', s$.

articles.title: Decoding units
articles.statement:
The unit decoder sends the bit true (a unit) to the bit true, and sends
the bit false (a marker) to no bit, which ends a block.

articles.title: Input encoding of the clocked universal machine
articles.statement:
For a code $c$, a list of bits $x$ and a
clock $T$, the input of the clocked universal machine is the list of bits formed by the cell of
$T$, then the cells of the input word of $x$, then the cell of $0$ (a blank cell, the single bit
false), then the code stack of $c$ in reverse order.

articles.title: Output encoding of the clocked universal machine
articles.statement:
The output bits of an optional list of
numbers: no result (a timeout) is encoded as the single bit false, and a result $l$ is encoded as
the bit true followed by the cells of $l$, where a number $n$ is written as $n$ bits true followed
by one bit false.

articles.title: Entries of a code
articles.statement:
For a code $c$, the list of quadruples $(q, a, q', s)$, one for each
state $q$ and symbol $a$ inside the table of $c$ whose table entry is a transition $(q', s)$
(enter the state $q'$ and do the action coded by $s$); halting positions are skipped. The
quadruples are listed row by row, by increasing $q$, and within a row by increasing $a$.

articles.title: Cost of scanning past one entry
articles.statement:
The step budget for scanning past an entry
$(q, a, q', s)$ of the code stack is $5q + 5a + 2q' + 2s + 30$.

articles.title: Numbers of a list of entries
articles.statement:
For a list of quadruples of natural numbers, the list of
natural numbers obtained by replacing each quadruple $(q, a, q', s)$ by the four numbers
$q, a, q', s$ in this order, keeping the order of the quadruples.

articles.title: Scanning the entries finds the table entry
articles.statement:
For every code $c$ and all natural numbers
$q$ and $a$, looking up the key $(q, a)$ in the entries of $c$ gives the entry of the table of
$c$ at state $q$ and symbol $a$: the pair $(q', s)$ if that position holds the transition
$(q', s)$, and no result if it halts, including every position outside the table.

articles.title: Looking up a key in a list of entries
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $q$ and $a$ and a list of
quadruples $(q_i, a_i, q'_i, s_i)$ of natural numbers, the result is the pair $(q'_i, s_i)$ of
the first quadruple in the list with $q_i = q$ and $a_i = a$, and no result if no quadruple has
the key $(q, a)$. This is the order in which the machine scans the code stack.

articles.title: Stacks of the clocked universal machine
articles.statement:
The clocked universal machine has fifteen
stacks: the state $Q$, the next state $N$, the action $A$ and the head cell $H$ (these four hold
counters of units), the cells left ($L$) and right ($R$) of the head, the code $C$, the scan
buffer $B$, the scratch counters $T$, $U$, $V$, the clock $\mathrm{Ck}$, and the parsing stacks:
the encoded input $X$, the parse buffer $P$ and the output $O$.

articles.title: Labels of the clocked universal machine
articles.statement:
The labels of the program of the clocked
universal machine: the tape update (`act0`–`act3`, `wr0`, `wr1`, `mvL0`–`mvL3`, `mvR0`–`mvR3`)
and the clock tick `fin`; the scan, which starts at `sc0` and has labels for the state
(`rq0`–`rq2`; `cqA o` and `cqB o` for each comparison outcome `o`; `sq0 m` and `sq1 m` for each
bit `m`), for the head cell (`ra0`–`ra2`; `caA o`, `caB o`; `sa0 m`, `sa1 m`), for skipping the
rest of an entry (`sk3a`, `sk3b`, `sk2a`, `sk2b`, `sk1a`, `sk1b`) and for reading a match
(`rd0`–`rd7`); the restores `rs` and `nf`; the exits `hlt` and `tmo`; the parse of the encoded
input (`pc0`, `pc1`, `px0`–`px6`, `pk0`); and the output phase (`o1`–`o6`, `done`).

articles.title: The clocked loop
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code, let $M$ be at least the length of the code stack of
$c$, let $k$ be a configuration whose state and cells are all at most $M$, let $t$ be a natural
number and $v$ a bit, and let $k_t$ be the result of $t$ steps of $c$ from $k$, where a halted
configuration stays put. Start the program of the clocked universal machine at label `sc0` with
variable $v$ and the stacks of $c$, the clock $t$ and $k$ (next state and action $0$). If $k_t$
has halted, then within $(t + 1) \cdot L(c, M)$ steps, where $L(c, M)$ is the loop step time,
the program reaches label `hlt` with some variable and the stacks of $c$, some clock $t'$ and
$k_t$ (next state and action $0$). If instead $c$ steps $k_t$ to $k''$, then within the same
number of steps it reaches label `tmo` with some variable and the stacks of $c$, the clock $0$
and $k''$ (next state and action $0$).

articles.title: Step bound of the clocked loop
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ and a number $M$, the loop step time is
$10\ell + 4M + 11$, where $\ell$ is the length of the code stack of $c$. It serves as the cost
bound of one round of the loop (a simulated step and a clock tick) on configurations whose numbers
are at most $M$.

articles.title: Moving a marker onto the scan buffer
articles.statement:
For a label $\ell$, this instruction pops the top
symbol of the code stack $C$ and discards it (doing nothing if $C$ is empty), pushes a marker (the
bit false) onto the scan buffer $B$, and goes to $\ell$; the state bit is unchanged.

articles.title: The clocked universal function is polynomial-time computable
articles.statement:
There are a multi-stack
Turing machine with finitely many stacks, labels and internal states, whose input and output
alphabets are in bijection with the bits, and a polynomial $p$ with natural-number coefficients,
such that for every code $c$, list of bits $x$ and clock $T \in \mathbb{N}$ the following holds.
Let $n$ be the length of the input encoding of $(c, x, T)$. Started at its main label in its
initial internal state, with the input encoding of $(c, x, T)$ on its input stack and every other
stack empty, the machine halts within $p(n)$ steps, with its internal state again the initial
one, the output encoding of the result of the clocked evaluator on $c$, $x$ and $T$ on its output
stack, and every other stack empty; both encodings are translated letter by letter through the
inverses of the bijections.

In the proof, $p$ has degree $2$: the clocked universal machine itself takes at most
$18 (n + 1)^2$ steps, and running it as a component of the reduction host keeps the degree.

articles.title: Writing the output
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code, $t$ a natural number, $k$ a configuration and $v$ a
bit, and let $N$ be the length of the cells of the head symbol of $k$ followed by the symbols to
its right (a symbol $a$ takes $a + 1$ bits). Started at the label $\mathsf{hlt}$ with state bit $v$
and the stacks of the code $c$, the clock $t$ and the configuration $k$ with next state and action
$0$, the clocked universal program reaches the label $\mathsf{done}$ within $4N + 8$ steps, with
some state bit and stacks in which the output stack $O$ holds the encoding of the output of $k$:
the bit true followed by the cells of the output of $k$.

articles.title: Reading the input
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code, $x$ a list of bits and $T$ a natural number, and let
$p$ be the cost of reading the input of $c$, $x$ and $T$. Started at the label $\mathsf{pc0}$ with
state bit false, the input encoding of $c$, $x$ and $T$ on the stack $X$ and every other stack
empty, the clocked universal program reaches the label $\mathsf{sc0}$ in exactly $p$ steps, with
some state bit and the stacks of the code $c$, the clock $T$ and the initial configuration on $x$,
with next state and action $0$.

articles.title: Cost of reading the input
articles.statement:
For a code $c$, a list of bits $x$ and a natural number $T$, let
$w_1, \dots, w_n$ be the input word of $x$ (false as the symbol $1$, true as $2$), with $w_1$ read
as $0$ when $x$ is empty, let $S_j = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (w_i + j)$, and let $m$ be the length of the
code stack of $c$. The cost of reading the input is
$T + 2 + (S_3 + 2) + (S_1 + 1) + (w_1 + 2) + (m + 1)$.

articles.title: The clocked universal program
articles.statement:
The program of the clocked universal machine gives an
instruction for every label. Numbers sit on stacks as counters of units (the bit true), and a cell
is a counter followed by a marker (the bit false).

Tape update. $\mathsf{act0}$ empties $Q$ and $\mathsf{act1}$ moves the counter $N$ onto $Q$.
$\mathsf{act2}$ pops $A$ and goes to $\mathsf{mvL0}$ if $A$ was empty, else to $\mathsf{act3}$,
which pops $A$ and goes to $\mathsf{mvR0}$ if $A$ was empty, else to $\mathsf{wr0}$; so the action
$0$ moves left, $1$ moves right and $a + 2$ writes $a$. $\mathsf{wr0}$ empties $H$ and
$\mathsf{wr1}$ moves the counter $A$ onto $H$. A left move ($\mathsf{mvL0}$ to $\mathsf{mvL3}$)
pushes a marker on $R$, moves the units of $H$ onto $R$, moves the units on top of $L$ onto $H$
and pops one more symbol of $L$; a right move ($\mathsf{mvR0}$ to $\mathsf{mvR3}$) does the same
with $L$ and $R$ exchanged. Writes and moves end at $\mathsf{fin}$, which pops the clock $Ck$ and
goes to $\mathsf{tmo}$ if it was empty, else to $\mathsf{sc0}$.

Scan. $\mathsf{sc0}$ goes to $\mathsf{nf}$ if $C$ is empty, else to $\mathsf{rq0}$. Then
$\mathsf{rq0}$, $\mathsf{rq1}$ move the units on top of $C$ onto $T$ and pop the next symbol of
$C$; $\mathsf{rq2}$ compares $T$ with $Q$ unit by unit, parking the popped units on $U$ and $V$;
$\mathsf{cqA}$, $\mathsf{cqB}$ move $U$ back onto $T$ and $V$ back onto $Q$; $\mathsf{sq0}$,
$\mathsf{sq1}$ move $T$ onto $B$, push a marker on $B$, and go to $\mathsf{ra0}$ if the two
counters were equal, else to $\mathsf{sk3a}$. The labels $\mathsf{ra0}$ to $\mathsf{sa1}$ do the
same with $H$ in place of $Q$, and go to $\mathsf{rd0}$ on equality, else to $\mathsf{sk2a}$.
From $\mathsf{sk3a}$, $\mathsf{sk2a}$ or $\mathsf{sk1a}$ the program moves three, two or one
further cells of $C$ onto $B$ (the units, then the next symbol replaced by a marker) and returns
to $\mathsf{sc0}$. The labels $\mathsf{rd0}$ to $\mathsf{rd3}$ move the units on top of $C$ onto
both $N$ and $B$, pop the next symbol of $C$ and push a marker on $B$; $\mathsf{rd4}$ to
$\mathsf{rd7}$ do the same with $A$ in place of $N$ and go to $\mathsf{rs}$. Finally
$\mathsf{rs}$ and $\mathsf{nf}$ move all of $B$ back onto $C$, one symbol at a time, and go to
$\mathsf{act0}$ and $\mathsf{hlt}$ respectively.

Parse. $\mathsf{pc0}$, $\mathsf{pc1}$ move the units on top of $X$ onto $Ck$ and pop the next
symbol of $X$. Then, while the top of $X$ is a unit, $\mathsf{px0}$ to $\mathsf{px2}$ move the
units on top of $X$ onto $P$, pop the next symbol of $X$ and push a marker on $P$; otherwise
$\mathsf{px3}$ pops $X$, $\mathsf{px4}$ moves all of $P$ onto $R$, $\mathsf{px5}$, $\mathsf{px6}$
move the units on top of $R$ onto $H$ and pop the next symbol of $R$, and $\mathsf{pk0}$ moves all
of $X$ onto $C$ and goes to $\mathsf{sc0}$.

Exits. $\mathsf{tmo}$ pushes a marker on $O$ and goes to $\mathsf{done}$. $\mathsf{hlt}$ pushes a
marker on $R$, $\mathsf{o1}$ moves the units of $H$ onto $R$, $\mathsf{o2}$ moves all of $R$ onto
$P$, $\mathsf{o3}$ pops the markers on top of $P$, $\mathsf{o4}$ pushes one marker on $P$ unless
$P$ is empty, $\mathsf{o5}$ moves all of $P$ onto $O$, and $\mathsf{o6}$ pushes a unit on $O$ and
goes to $\mathsf{done}$, where the program halts.

articles.title: One simulated step, halting case
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code, $k$ a configuration at which $c$ halts
(one step of $c$ from $k$ gives nothing), $t$ a natural number, $v$ a bit, and $b$ the step bound
of $c$ at $k$. Started at the label $\mathsf{sc0}$ with state bit $v$ and the stacks of the code
$c$, the clock $t$ and the configuration $k$ with next state and action $0$, the clocked universal
program reaches the label $\mathsf{hlt}$ within $b$ steps, with some state bit and the same
stacks.

articles.title: One simulated step, running case
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code, $k$ and $k'$ configurations such that
one step of $c$ from $k$ gives $k'$, $t$ a natural number, $v$ a bit, and $b$ the step bound of
$c$ at $k$. Started at the label $\mathsf{sc0}$ with state bit $v$ and the stacks of the code $c$,
the clock $t$ and the configuration $k$ with next state and action $0$, the clocked universal
program reaches the label $\mathsf{fin}$ within $b$ steps, with some state bit and the stacks of
$c$, $t$ and $k'$ with next state and action $0$.

articles.title: Step bound of one simulated step
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ and a configuration $k$ with state $q$,
head cell $h$, nearest left cell $l$ and nearest right cell $r$ (each read as the blank $0$ when
there is no such cell), let $|C|$ be the length of the code stack of $c$. The step bound of $c$
at $k$ is $10|C| + q + h + l + r + 10$.

articles.title: The stacks of a simulated configuration
articles.statement:
For a code $c$, a natural number $t$ (the clock),
a configuration $k$ and natural numbers $q'$ and $s$, the stacks of $c$, $t$ and $k$ with next
state $q'$ and action $s$ hold, as counters of units (the bit true): the state of $k$ on $Q$, $q'$
on $N$, $s$ on $A$, the head symbol of $k$ on $H$ and $t$ on $Ck$. The stacks $L$ and $R$ hold the
cells of the symbols left and right of the head, nearest first, $C$ holds the code stack of $c$,
and every other stack is empty.

articles.title: Writing a timeout
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code, $t$ a natural number, $k$ a configuration and $v$ a
bit. Started at the label $\mathsf{tmo}$ with state bit $v$ and the stacks of the code $c$, the
clock $t$ and the configuration $k$ with next state and action $0$, the clocked universal program
reaches the label $\mathsf{done}$ in exactly one step, with the same state bit and the same stacks
except that the output stack $O$ holds the timeout encoding, the single bit false.

articles.title: The clocked universal machine as a host component
articles.statement:
The component machine whose stacks
are the fifteen stacks of the clocked universal machine, each holding bits, whose labels and
program are those of the clocked universal machine, and whose list of stacks is, in order: the
state $Q$, the next state $N$, the action $A$, the head cell $H$, the cells left ($L$) and right
($R$) of the head, the code $C$, the scan buffer $B$, the scratch counters $T$, $U$, $V$, the
clock $\mathit{Ck}$, the encoded input $X$, the parse buffer $P$ and the output $O$.

articles.title: Step bound polynomial of the clocked universal machine
articles.statement:
The polynomial
$18 (X + 1)^2$ with natural-number coefficients, used as the step bound of the clocked
universal machine as a host component.

articles.title: Correctness and running time of the clocked universal machine
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code, $x$ a
list of bits and $T$ a natural number. Start the clocked universal stack program at the label
$\mathrm{pc0}$ with internal bit $\mathrm{false}$, with every stack empty except $X$, which holds
the input encoding of $(c, x, T)$: the cell of $T$, the cells of the input symbols of $x$ (the
symbol $1$ for $\mathrm{false}$ and $2$ for $\mathrm{true}$), the bit $\mathrm{false}$, and the
code stack of $c$ reversed, where the cell of a number $n$ is $n$ bits $\mathrm{true}$ followed
by the bit $\mathrm{false}$. Then within at most $N(c, x, T)$ steps, where $N$ is the step bound
of the whole machine, the program reaches the label $\mathrm{done}$ (with some internal bit and
some stack contents) with the output encoding of the clocked evaluation of $c$ on $x$ with clock
$T$ on the stack $O$: the single bit $\mathrm{false}$ if the coded machine does not halt within
$T$ steps, and otherwise the bit $\mathrm{true}$ followed by the cells of its output, the tape
from the head rightwards without trailing blanks.

articles.title: The step bound of the clocked universal machine is quadratic
articles.statement:
For every code $c$, list
of bits $x$ and clock $T \in \mathbb{N}$, the step bound of the whole clocked universal machine
on $(c, x, T)$ is at most $18 (n + 1)^2$, where $n$ is the length of the input encoding of
$(c, x, T)$.

articles.title: Step bound of the clocked universal machine
articles.statement:
For a code $c$, a list of bits $x$ and a
natural number $T$, the step bound of the whole machine on $(c, x, T)$ is the sum of three terms:
the cost of reading the input on $(c, x, T)$, the step bound of the clocked simulation on the
clock $T$, and the output bound $4\,(|x| + T + 1)\,(|C| + 3) + 8$, where $|x|$ is the length of
$x$ and $|C|$ is the length of the code stack of $c$.

articles.title: Stack alphabet of the clocked universal machine
articles.statement:
Every stack $k$ of the clocked universal
machine holds bits: its alphabet is $\Gamma(k) = \mathrm{Bool}$.

articles.title: The code of a machine takes its coded actions
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a binary multi-tape machine
with $k$ work tapes and a finite set of states $Q$, and let $e : Q \to \mathbb{N}$ be injective.
For every state $q \in Q$, every symbol $a$ under the input head and every tuple $w$ of symbols
under the $k$ work heads (each a bit or blank), the coded action of the code of $M$ under $e$ at
state $e(q)$ and symbols $a$, $w$ is the coding, with successor states numbered by $e$, of the
action of $M$ in state $q$ on $a$ and $w$.

articles.title: Action of a code at a key
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ with $k$ work tapes, a state
$q \in \mathbb{N}$, a symbol $a$ under the input head and symbols $w = (w_i)_{i < k}$ under the
work heads (each symbol a bit or the blank), the action of $c$ at $(q, a, w)$ is the coded action
of the first table entry of $c$ whose key is $(q, a, w)$, or, if there is no such entry, the
halting action, which moves no head, writes and emits nothing, and has no next state.

articles.title: Applying a coded action
articles.statement:
Given an input word $x$, a coded action $a$ and an explicit
configuration $e$, applying $a$ to $e$ gives the configuration whose state is the next state of
$a$; whose input head position is that of $e$, say $p$, moved by the coded input move of $a$,
where a left move gives $p - 1$ (truncated at $0$), staying gives $p$, and a right move gives
$\min(p + 1, |x| + 1)$; whose work tape $i$ is work tape $i$ of $e$ after writing the optional
symbol of $a$ for tape $i$ under the head and then moving the head by the coded move of $a$ for
tape $i$; and whose output is the output of $e$ followed by the output bit of $a$, if any.

articles.title: Cell of a zipper tape
articles.statement:
For a work tape $t$ in zipper form and an integer $j$, the cell of
$t$ at $j$ is the symbol at offset $j$ from the head: for $j = n \ge 0$ it is entry $n$ (counting
from $0$) of the list of cells from the head rightwards, and for $j = -(n + 1)$ it is entry $n$ of
the list of cells left of the head, nearest first; in either case it is the blank when the list
has no entry $n$.

articles.title: Coded actions
articles.statement:
A coded action for a machine with $k$ work tapes consists of a coded
input-head move; for each of the $k$ work tapes, an optional symbol to write, the symbol being a
bit or the blank (so a blank can be written), together with a coded head move; an optional
output bit; and an optional next state in $\mathbb{N}$, where no next state means halting. A
head move is coded by a natural number: $0$ moves left, $1$ stays, and any other number moves
right.

articles.title: Keys of a code's table
articles.statement:
A key of a table entry for a machine with $k$ work tapes is a
triple $(q, a, w)$ of a state $q \in \mathbb{N}$, the symbol $a$ under the input head and the
symbols $w = (w_i)_{i < k}$ under the $k$ work heads, where each symbol is a bit or the blank.

articles.title: Codes for multi-tape machines
articles.statement:
A code for a machine with $k$ work tapes over the binary
alphabet, with states in $\mathbb{N}$, is a finite list of table entries, each a key (a state
together with the symbols under the input head and the $k$ work heads) paired with a coded
action. The table is looked up by key, the first matching entry wins, and a missing key halts
the machine.

articles.title: Computability over codes
articles.statement:
Let $g : \alpha \to \beta$ be a function, let inputs in $\alpha$
and outputs in $\beta$ be encoded by injective maps into binary words, and let
$t, s : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$. Say a machine computes $g$ within $t$ and $s$ when, started on the
encoding of any input $x$, it halts with the encoding of $g(x)$ as output, halts within $t(x)$
steps, and visits at most $s(x)$ work-tape cells. Then some binary multi-tape machine with
finitely many states computes $g$ within $t$ and $s$ if and only if, for some number $k$ of work
tapes, the machine of some code with $k$ work tapes computes $g$ within $t$ and $s$.

articles.title: Computation by a code is finite-state computation
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code with $k$ work tapes,
let $g : \alpha \to \beta$ be a function, let inputs in $\alpha$ and outputs in $\beta$ be encoded
by injective maps into binary words, and let $t, s : \alpha \to \mathbb{N}$. If the machine of $c$,
started on the encoding of any input $x$, halts with the encoding of $g(x)$ as output, halts
within $t(x)$ steps, and visits at most $s(x)$ work-tape cells, then some binary multi-tape
machine with finitely many states computes $g$ within the same bounds in the same sense.

articles.title: A code computes exactly what its clocked evaluator returns
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ with $k$ work
tapes and binary words $x$ and $o$, the machine of $c$ computes $o$ on input $x$, that is, it
eventually halts on $x$ with output $o$, if and only if there is a clock $T \in \mathbb{N}$ such
that the clocked evaluator of $c$ run on $x$ for $T$ steps returns $o$.

articles.title: Explicit configurations of the code evaluator
articles.statement:
An explicit configuration for a machine
with $k$ work tapes consists of an optional state in $\mathbb{N}$ (none when the machine has
halted); the input head position, a natural number shifted by one, so that position $0$ is the
cell left of the input; the $k$ work tapes, each a zipper (the cells left of the head, nearest
first, and the cells from the head rightwards, all further cells blank); and the output written
so far, a binary word.

articles.title: Decidability over codes
articles.statement:
Let $L$ be a set of binary words and let $t$ and $s$ map binary
words to natural numbers. Say a machine decides $L$ within $t$ and $s$ when, started on any
binary word $w$, it halts with the one-bit output $\mathrm{true}$ if $w \in L$ and
$\mathrm{false}$ otherwise, halts within $t(w)$ steps, and visits at most $s(w)$ work-tape cells.
Then some binary multi-tape machine with finitely many states decides $L$ within $t$ and $s$ if
and only if, for some number $k$ of work tapes, the machine of some code with $k$ work tapes
decides $L$ within $t$ and $s$.

articles.title: Deciding by a code is finite-state decidability
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code with $k$ work tapes,
let $L$ be a set of binary words, and let $t$ and $s$ map binary words to natural numbers. If
the machine of $c$ decides $L$, that is, started on any binary word $w$ it halts with the one-bit
output $\mathrm{true}$ if $w \in L$ and $\mathrm{false}$ otherwise, and if on every binary word
$w$ it halts within $t(w)$ steps and visits at most $s(w)$ work-tape cells, then some binary
multi-tape machine with finitely many states decides $L$ within the same bounds.

articles.title: Code round-trip
articles.statement:
For every code $c$ with $k$ work tapes, decoding the natural number
$\operatorname{encode}(c)$ returns $c$: $\operatorname{decode}(\operatorname{encode}(c))$ is
defined and equals $c$.

articles.title: Decoding a Turing machine head move
articles.statement: Decode a head move: `0` moves left, `1` stays, anything else moves right.

articles.title: Decoding numbers to codes
articles.statement:
The code coded by a natural number $n$, if any: decoding
under the standard primitive recursive coding of codes, which identifies a code with its table,
a list of pairs of a key and a coded action. The result is empty when $n$ codes no code.

articles.title: Coding an action
articles.statement:
Let $e : Q \to \mathbb{N}$ number the states $Q$ of a binary multi-tape
machine with $k$ work tapes. The coded action of an action $a$ of the machine under $e$ records as
its input-head move the code of the input-head move of $a$ (left $0$, stay $1$, right $2$); for
each work tape it records what $a$ writes there and the code of the head move of $a$ there; it
records the output bit of $a$, if any; and its next state is $e(q)$ when $a$ enters the state $q$,
and it halts when $a$ halts.

articles.title: Injectivity of the numeric coding of codes
articles.statement:
If two codes $c$ and $c'$ with the same
number of work tapes have the same numeric code, then $c = c'$.

articles.title: Coding head moves
articles.statement:
A head move is coded as a natural number: left is $0$, stay is $1$
and right is $2$. Decoding a move code recovers the move.

articles.title: Numeric coding of codes
articles.statement:
The natural number coding a code $c$: its encoding under the
standard primitive recursive coding of codes, which identifies a code with its table, a list of
pairs of a key and a coded action.

articles.title: Explicit configurations as tuples
articles.statement:
The bijection between explicit configurations and
tuples $(q, p, t, o)$ that sends a configuration to its optional state $q$ (empty when halted),
its shifted input head position $p \in \mathbb{N}$, its family $t$ of $k$ work tapes (each a
zipper) and its output $o$ so far, a list of bits.

articles.title: Coded actions as tuples
articles.statement:
The bijection between coded actions and tuples $(m, w, b, q)$
that sends an action to its coded input head move $m \in \mathbb{N}$, its work tape instructions
$w$ (for each of the $k$ work tapes, an optional symbol to write and a coded head move), its
optional output bit $b$ and its optional next state $q$.

articles.title: Multi-tape codes as tables
articles.statement:
The bijection between codes for machines with $k$ work tapes
and finite lists of table entries, each a pair of a key and a coded action, that sends a code to
its table.

articles.title: Evaluator agreement
articles.statement:
For every code $c$, binary input $x$, clock $T \in \mathbb{N}$
and binary word $o$, the clocked evaluator of $c$ on $x$ with clock $T$ returns $o$ if and
only if the machine of $c$, run for $T$ steps from its initial configuration on $x$, has
halted and its output is $o$.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the clocked evaluator for multi-tape codes
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ for machines
with $k$ work tapes, a binary input $x$, a binary word $o$ and clocks $T \le T'$ in $\mathbb{N}$,
if the clocked evaluator of $c$ on $x$ returns $o$ with clock $T$, then it also returns $o$ with
clock $T'$.

articles.title: Clocked evaluator
articles.statement:
The clocked evaluator runs a code $c$ on a binary input $x$ for $T$
steps: it applies the evaluator's step $T$ times to the initial explicit configuration. If the
resulting configuration is halted, it returns that configuration's output; otherwise it
returns no result.

articles.title: Every finite-state machine has a code
articles.statement:
A binary machine with finitely many states is
simulated, up to an injective state relabelling, by the machine of some code.

articles.title: Numbering a finite type from a chosen element
articles.statement:
For every finite type $Q$ and every
$q_0 \in Q$ there is an injective map $e : Q \to \mathbb{N}$ with $e(q_0) = 0$.

articles.title: A number as a bounded state
articles.statement:
For natural numbers $N$ and $q$, this is $q$ as an element
of $\{0, \dots, N - 1\}$ if $q < N$, and no value otherwise.

articles.title: Transition function of a code on bounded states
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code with $k$ work tapes
and let $N$ be its state bound. For a state $q < N$, a symbol $a$ under the input head and
symbols $w$ under the $k$ work heads (each a bit or blank), this is the action of $c$ at
$(q, a, w)$ with the same input-head move, work-tape writes and moves, and output, and with its
successor state read as a state below $N$; a successor state that is not below $N$ is replaced
by halting.

articles.title: Halting action
articles.statement:
The default action of a missing table entry: halt without moving any
head, writing any symbol or emitting an output bit.

articles.title: Initial configuration of the clocked evaluator
articles.statement:
The initial explicit configuration has
state $0$, the input head on the first input cell (position $1$, positions being shifted by one),
every work tape blank (both halves of its zipper empty), and empty output.

articles.title: Input symbol under the input head
articles.statement:
For an input $x$ and a shifted input head position
$p$, the input symbol is the blank if $p = 0$; otherwise it is the entry of $x$ at index $p - 1$
(counting from $0$) if $p - 1 < |x|$, and the blank if $p - 1 \ge |x|$.

articles.title: The code of a machine simulates it
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a machine over the binary alphabet with
$k$ work tapes, a finite set of states $Q$ and initial state $q_0$, and let $e : Q \to \mathbb{N}$
be injective with $e(q_0) = 0$. Then the machine of the code of $M$ with states numbered by $e$
simulates $M$ up to the relabelling $e$.

articles.title: A code's machine simulates its finite-state machine
articles.statement:
For every code $c$, the machine of
$c$ simulates the finite-state machine of $c$ up to the relabelling that sends each state
$q < N$, where $N$ is the state bound of $c$, to the natural number $q$.

articles.title: The evaluator returns within the clock exactly when the machine runs in time
articles.statement:
For a code
$c$, an input $x$ and a clock $T$, the clocked evaluator of $c$ on $x$ with clock $T$ returns an
output if and only if the machine of $c$ runs in time $T$ on $x$, that is, every computation path
of that machine on $x$ with at least $T$ steps ends in a halted configuration.

articles.title: DSPACE over codes
articles.statement:
For every $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every language $L$ of
binary words, $L \in \mathsf{DSPACE}(s)$ if and only if there are natural numbers $c_1, c_2, k$
and a code $c$ with $k$ work tapes such that the machine of $c$ decides $L$, on every input $w$
runs in space $c_1 s(|w|) + c_2$, and for some $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ on every input
$w$ runs in time $t(|w|)$.

articles.title: DTIME over codes
articles.statement:
For every $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every language $L$ of
binary words, $L \in \mathsf{DTIME}(t)$ if and only if there are natural numbers $c_1, c_2, k$
and a code $c$ with $k$ work tapes such that the machine of $c$ decides $L$, on every input $w$
runs in time $c_1 t(|w|) + c_2$, and for some $s : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ on every input
$w$ runs in space $s(|w|)$.

articles.title: Input head move of the clocked evaluator
articles.statement:
For an input of length $n$, a shifted input head
position $p$ and a coded move $m$, the new position is $p - 1$ (truncated at $0$) if $m = 0$, $p$
if $m = 1$, and $\min(p + 1, n + 1)$ otherwise, so a move right never passes position $n + 1$,
one cell beyond the input.

articles.title: Moving the head of a zipper tape
articles.statement:
For a coded move $m$ and a work tape given as a zipper
$(l, r)$: if $m = 0$ the head moves one cell left, removing the first cell of $l$ (the blank if $l$
is empty) and putting it in front of $r$; if $m = 1$ the tape is unchanged; otherwise the head
moves one cell right, removing the first cell of $r$ (the blank if $r$ is empty) and putting it in
front of $l$.

articles.title: Next states of a code lie in its state set
articles.statement:
For a code $c$, a state $q$, an input symbol
$a$ and work tape symbols $w$, if the action of $c$ at $(q, a, w)$ has a next state $q'$ (rather
than halting), then $q'$ belongs to the set of states of $c$.

articles.title: The code of a finite-state binary machine
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a machine over the binary alphabet
with $k$ work tapes and a finite set of states $Q$, and let $e : Q \to \mathbb{N}$. The code of
$M$ with states numbered by $e$ has one table entry for each state $q \in Q$, symbol $a$ under
the input head and symbols $w$ under the $k$ work heads (each a bit or blank): its key is
$(e(q), a, w)$ and its value is the coded action of $M$ in state $q$ reading $a$ and $w$, with
the successor state numbered by $e$. The entries are listed in an unspecified order.

When $e$ is injective and sends the initial state of $M$ to $0$, the machine of this code
simulates $M$ up to the relabelling $e$.

articles.title: The evaluator is primitive recursive
articles.statement: **The evaluator is primitive recursive** in the code, the input and the clock.

articles.title: Symbol under the head of a zipper tape
articles.statement:
The symbol read from a work tape given as a zipper
$(l, r)$ is the first cell of $r$, or the blank if $r$ is empty.

articles.title: The evaluator tracks the machine run
articles.statement:
For a code $c$, an input $x$ and every $t$, the
explicit configuration obtained from the initial one by $t$ steps of the evaluator for $c$ on $x$
represents the configuration that the machine of $c$ reaches after $t$ steps from its initial
configuration on $x$.

articles.title: Explicit configurations representing machine configurations
articles.statement:
An explicit configuration $e$
represents a configuration $C$ of CSLib's multi-tape model on input $x$ when they have the same
state, the same shifted input head position and the same output, and for every work tape $i$ and
every cell $z \in \mathbb{Z}$, the content of cell $z$ of tape $i$ in $C$ equals the cell of tape
$i$ of $e$ at offset $z - p_i$ from its head, where $p_i$ is the head position of tape $i$
in $C$.

articles.title: State bound of a code
Codes denote finite-state machines
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code for a machine with $k$ work tapes.
For every binary input $x$ and every number of steps $t$, if the machine of $c$, run for $t$
steps from its initial configuration on $x$, has not halted and is in state $q$, then $q$ lies
in the finite set of states of $c$.

articles.title: States of a multi-tape code
articles.statement:
The states of a code $c$ for machines with $k$ work tapes
form the finite set of natural numbers consisting of the initial state $0$ and the next state of
every table entry of $c$ that does not halt.

articles.title: The evaluator simulates the machine step for step
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code and $x$ a binary
input. If an explicit configuration $e$ represents a configuration $C$ of the machine of $c$ on
$x$, then the evaluator's step of $e$ for $c$ on $x$ represents the successor of $C$ under the
machine of $c$.

articles.title: Step of the machine of a code
articles.statement:
For a code $c$, a binary input $x$ and a configuration $C$
of the machine of $c$ on $x$, the step of the machine of $c$ sends $C$ to its successor under
the transition function of $c$: $C$ itself if it has halted, and otherwise the result of
applying to $C$ the action that the transition function of $c$ selects for the state of $C$ and
the symbols under its heads.

articles.title: Evaluator step
articles.statement:
One step of the evaluator for a code $c$ on a binary input $x$ leaves an
explicit configuration $e$ unchanged if $e$ has halted; if $e$ is in state $q$, it applies to
$e$ the coded action of $c$ at $q$, the input symbol at the input head position of $e$ and the
symbols under the heads of the work tapes of $e$.

articles.title: Work tapes as zippers
articles.statement:
A work tape is a pair of finite lists of cells, each cell a bit or
blank: the cells left of the head, nearest first, and the cells from the head rightwards; cells
beyond both lists are blank.

articles.title: Decoding the coding of an action
articles.statement:
Let $Q$ be a type, $e : Q \to \mathbb{N}$ a map and $a$
an action of a binary machine with $k$ work tapes and states in $Q$. The action that the coded
action of $a$, with its successor state numbered by $e$, stands for is $a$ with its successor
state relabelled by $e$.

articles.title: Decoding a coded action
articles.statement:
A coded action $a$ stands for the action of CSLib's multi-tape
model that moves the input head by the decoded input move of $a$, on each work tape writes the
optional symbol that $a$ gives for that tape and moves its head by the decoded move, emits the
optional output bit of $a$, and enters the next state of $a$ (halting when there is none).

articles.title: The finite-state machine of a code
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ with $k$ work tapes and state bound
$N$, this is the binary machine with $k$ work tapes and states $0, 1, \dots, N - 1$ that starts
in state $0$ and, in a state $q < N$ reading $a$ under the input head and $w$ under the work
heads, takes the action of $c$ at $(q, a, w)$, with a successor state not below $N$ replaced by
halting. Since every state the machine of $c$ can enter is below $N$, it is the machine of $c$
with its states restricted to those below $N$.

articles.title: The multi-tape machine of a code
articles.statement:
The machine of a code $c$ for $k$ work tapes is the
machine of CSLib's multi-tape model with $k$ work tapes, the binary alphabet and states in
$\mathbb{N}$ whose initial state is $0$ and whose transition function is the transition function
of $c$.

articles.title: Transition function of a code
articles.statement:
The transition function of a code $c$ sends a state $q$,
the symbol $a$ under the input head and the symbols $w$ under the work heads (each a bit or
blank) to the action of CSLib's multi-tape model that the coded action of $c$ at $(q, a, w)$
stands for. That coded action is the one of the first table entry of $c$ with key $(q, a, w)$,
or, if there is none, the one that halts without moving, writing or emitting.

articles.title: Writing on a zipper tape
articles.statement:
Writing an optional symbol on a work tape leaves the tape
unchanged when no symbol is given; given a symbol $s$ (a bit or blank), it replaces the cell
under the head by $s$ and keeps all other cells.

articles.title: Acting on a configuration
articles.statement:
Let $k$ be a configuration with left cells $L$ (nearest
first), head cell $h$ and right cells $R$ (nearest first), let $q'$ be a state and let $s$ be an
action code. Acting on $k$ with $q'$ and $s$ gives a configuration with state $q'$, as follows.
For $s = 0$ (move left), its head cell is the first entry of $L$, or the blank $0$ if $L$ is
empty, its left cells are $L$ without its first entry, and its right cells are $h$ followed by
$R$. For $s = 1$ (move right), its head cell is the first entry of $R$, or $0$ if $R$ is empty,
its right cells are $R$ without its first entry, and its left cells are $h$ followed by $L$. For
$s = a + 2$ (write $a$), its head cell is $a$ and its left and right cells are $L$ and $R$.

articles.title: Symbol of an input bit
articles.statement:
The tape symbol of a bit $b$ is $1$ if $b$ is false and $2$ if $b$
is true; the symbol $0$ is the blank.

articles.title: Clocked configuration of a code
articles.statement:
For a code $c$, a list of bits $x$ and $T \in \mathbb{N}$,
the configuration of $c$ on $x$ after $T$ steps is obtained from the initial configuration on $x$
by applying $T$ times the step of $c$, where a step leaves a halted configuration unchanged. It is
the configuration after $T$ steps, or the halting configuration if the machine halts earlier.

articles.title: Explicit configurations
articles.statement:
A configuration of the simulation consists of a state
$q \in \mathbb{N}$, the list of the cells left of the head (nearest first), the symbol in the cell
under the head, and the list of the cells right of the head (nearest first); states and symbols
are natural numbers.

articles.title: Codes for single-tape machines
articles.statement:
A code is a transition table: a finite list of rows, row
$q$ belonging to the state $q \in \mathbb{N}$, each a finite list of entries, entry $a$ of a row
belonging to the symbol $a \in \mathbb{N}$. The entry in row $q$ and column $a$ is either empty,
meaning that the machine halts, or a pair $(q', s)$ of natural numbers, meaning that the machine
enters the state $q'$ and does the action coded by $s$: $0$ moves left, $1$ moves right and
$b + 2$ writes $b$. A state or symbol outside the table halts the machine.

articles.title: Decoding an action
articles.statement:
A natural number codes a statement of a single-tape Turing machine
with symbols in $\mathbb{N}$: $0$ moves the head left, $1$ moves the head right, and $a + 2$ writes
the symbol $a$.

articles.title: Halting is halting within some number of steps
articles.statement:
For a single-tape Turing machine $M$ and
an input word $l$, the evaluation of $M$ on $l$ is defined (that is, $M$ halts on $l$) if and only
if there is $T \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $M$ halts on $l$ within $T$ steps.

articles.title: Unclocked halting
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ and a list of bits $x$, the machine decoded from $c$ halts
on the input word of $x$ if and only if there is a clock $T \in \mathbb{N}$ for which the clocked
evaluator of $c$ on $x$ with clock $T$ returns a result.

articles.title: Configurations as tuples
articles.statement:
Configurations correspond bijectively to tuples in
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathrm{List}(\mathbb{N}) \times \mathbb{N} \times \mathrm{List}(\mathbb{N})$:
a configuration corresponds to the tuple of its state, its cells left of the head, its cell under
the head and its cells right of the head.

articles.title: Single-tape codes as tables
articles.statement:
Codes for single-tape machines correspond bijectively to
transition tables, that is, to lists of rows, each a list of entries that are either empty or a
pair of natural numbers: a code corresponds to its table.

articles.title: Clocked results agree with the machine's semantics
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code, $x$ a list of
bits, $T$ a natural number and $l$ a list of natural numbers. If the clocked evaluator, running
$c$ on $x$ for at most $T$ steps, returns $l$, then the decoded machine of $c$, started on the
input word of $x$, halts, and the tape from its head rightwards in the halting configuration is
$l$ followed by blanks.

articles.title: Characterization of clocked results
articles.statement:
For a code $c$, a list of bits $x$, a clock
$T \in \mathbb{N}$ and a list $l$ of natural numbers, the clocked evaluator returns $l$ on $c$,
$x$ and $T$ if and only if the configuration of $c$ after $T$ clocked steps on $x$ has no
successor step and its output is $l$.

articles.title: Monotonicity of the single-tape clocked evaluator
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code for a single-tape
machine, $x$ a list of bits, $l$ a list of natural numbers and $T \le T'$ natural numbers. If the
clocked evaluator returns $l$ on $c$ and $x$ with clock $T$, then it also returns $l$ with clock
$T'$.

articles.title: The clocked evaluator
articles.statement:
Given a code $c$, a list of bits $x$ and a clock $T \in \mathbb{N}$,
run the simulation of $c$ on $x$ for at most $T$ steps. If it halts within $T$ steps, the result
is the output of the halting configuration: the tape from the head rightwards, with trailing
blanks dropped. Otherwise there is no result.

articles.title: Universality of codes
articles.statement:
**Universality of codes**, for machines that read bit inputs. Let $M$ be a single-tape
Turing machine with a finite alphabet $\Gamma$ and a finite set of states that contains the
initial state and is closed under the transitions of $M$, and let $\iota$ be an injective map
from the bits to $\Gamma$ whose values are not the blank. Then there are a code $c$ and an
injective map $f$ from $\Gamma$ to the natural numbers, sending the blank to $0$ and each
$\iota(b)$ to the symbol of the bit $b$, such that for every word $l$ over $\Gamma$, writing
$f(l)$ for the word obtained by applying $f$ to each letter: the decoded machine of $c$ halts on
$f(l)$ exactly when $M$ halts on $l$, and its result (the tape from the head rightwards when it
halts) is then the result of $M$ on $l$ with $f$ applied to each cell; and for every
$T \in \mathbb{N}$, the decoded machine of $c$ halts within $T$ steps on $f(l)$ if and only if
$M$ halts within $T$ steps on $l$.

(So the alphabet has at least three symbols; a machine over a smaller alphabet cannot read a bit
input.)

articles.title: Bounded halting of a decoded machine through its simulation
articles.statement:
For a code $c$, a list of
bits $x$ and $T \in \mathbb{N}$, the decoded machine of $c$ halts within $T$ steps on the input
word of $x$ if and only if the explicit simulation of $c$, started from the initial configuration
on $x$, reaches after some $j \le T$ steps a configuration that has no successor step.

articles.title: Bounded halting of a single-tape machine
articles.statement:
A single-tape Turing machine $M$ halts within
$T$ steps on a word $l$ when, started in its initial state with $l$ on the tape and the head on
the first letter of $l$ (on a blank if $l$ is empty), it reaches after some $j \le T$ steps a
configuration that has no successor.

articles.title: The explicit initial configuration is the machine's
articles.statement:
For a list of bits $x$, the initial
configuration of the simulation on $x$, read as a configuration of a single-tape machine, is the
initial configuration of a single-tape machine on the input word of $x$.

articles.title: Initial configuration of the code simulation
articles.statement:
The initial configuration of the
simulation on a list of bits $x$ has state $0$, an empty list of cells left of the head, the
head on the first symbol of the input word of $x$ (the blank $0$ if $x$ is empty), and the
remaining symbols of the input word, in order, right of the head.

articles.title: Input word of a list of bits
articles.statement:
The input word of a list of bits $x$ is the list of natural
numbers obtained from $x$ by replacing each bit by its symbol: $1$ for false and $2$ for true.

articles.title: Definedness of the clocked evaluator
articles.statement:
For a code $c$, a list of bits $x$ and a clock
$T \in \mathbb{N}$, the clocked evaluator of $c$ on $x$ with clock $T$ returns a value if and
only if the simulation of $c$ has no step from the configuration after $T$ clocked steps on $x$
(the configuration after $T$ steps, or the halting configuration if the machine halts
earlier).

articles.title: Clocked halting
articles.statement:
For a code $c$, a list of bits $x$ and a clock $T \in \mathbb{N}$,
the clocked evaluator of $c$ on $x$ with clock $T$ returns a value if and only if the machine
of $c$, started on the input word of $x$, halts within $T$ steps.

articles.title: Iterated steps of the decoded machine
articles.statement:
Let $c$ be a code, $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $k$
an explicit configuration. Run the machine of $c$ for $n$ steps from the Mathlib configuration
of $k$, and run the explicit simulation of $c$ for $n$ steps from $k$, where a run that reaches
a configuration without a successor before completing $n$ steps has no result. Then the first
run has a result exactly when the second does, and its result is the Mathlib configuration of
the result of the second.

articles.title: Table lookup of a code
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ and numbers $q$ and $a$, the lookup of $c$ at
state $q$ and symbol $a$ is the entry in row $q$, column $a$ of the table of $c$: either a pair
$(q', s)$ of a next state and an action code, or no entry (halt). It is no entry when the
table has no row $q$ or that row has no column $a$.

articles.title: The machine of a single-tape code
articles.statement:
The machine of a code $c$ is the single-tape Turing
machine with states and symbols in $\mathbb{N}$ that, in state $q$ reading symbol $a$, halts if
the table lookup of $c$ at state $q$ and symbol $a$ has no entry, and otherwise, if the entry is
$(q', s)$, enters state $q'$ and does the action coded by $s$: $0$ moves left, $1$ moves right
and $a' + 2$ writes $a'$.

articles.title: Halting within a bound is monotone in the bound
articles.statement:
For a single-tape Turing machine $M$,
a list $l$ of symbols and numbers $T \le T'$, if $M$ started on $l$ halts within $T$ steps,
then $M$ started on $l$ halts within $T'$ steps.

articles.title: Output of a configuration
articles.statement:
The output of a configuration $k$ is the list consisting of the
symbol under the head of $k$ followed by the cells right of the head (nearest first), with all
trailing blanks $0$ removed.

articles.title: The clocked evaluator is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
The clocked evaluator is primitive
recursive in the code, the input and the clock.

articles.title: The output of a configuration as a Mathlib half-tape
articles.statement:
For every explicit configuration
$k$, the half-tape of the Mathlib configuration of $k$ from the head rightwards (the cell under
the head followed by the cells to its right) is the output of $k$, read with blanks beyond its
end.

articles.title: States of a single-tape code
articles.statement:
The set of states of a code $c$ is the finite set of natural
numbers consisting of the initial state $0$ and every state $q'$ such that some entry of the
table of $c$ is a pair $(q', s)$.

articles.title: One step of a code, or stay when halted
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ and a configuration $k$ of the
simulation, the configuration after one step of $c$ from $k$ if that step is defined, and $k$
itself if $c$ halts at $k$.

articles.title: Explicit steps agree with the decoded machine
articles.statement:
For every code $c$ and every configuration
$k$ of the simulation, the decoded TM0 machine of $c$ halts at the TM0 configuration of $k$
exactly when the step of $c$ from $k$ is undefined, and otherwise its step from the TM0
configuration of $k$ is the TM0 configuration of the step of $c$ from $k$.

articles.title: One step of a code
articles.statement:
For a code $c$ and a configuration $k$ of the simulation, look up the
table entry of $c$ at the state of $k$ and the symbol under the head of $k$. If there is no entry,
the step is undefined (the machine halts); if the entry is $(q', s)$, the step is the
configuration obtained from $k$ by entering the state $q'$ and doing the action coded by $s$.

articles.title: Codes denote finite machines
articles.statement:
The decoded machine is supported by the finite set of
states of its code.

articles.title: TM0 configuration of a simulation configuration
articles.statement:
The TM0 configuration of a configuration
$k$ of the simulation has the state of $k$, the cell under the head of $k$ as its head cell, and
as the halves of its tape left and right of the head the cells of $k$ left and right of the head,
nearest first, followed by infinitely many blanks.

articles.title: The ambiguity grammar of a PCP instance
articles.statement:
Let $P = [(t_0, b_0), \dots, (t_{m-1}, b_{m-1})]$
be a list of dominoes over an alphabet $\alpha$, with top words $t_i$ and bottom words $b_i$. The
ambiguity grammar of $P$ is the encoded context-free grammar over the terminals
$\alpha \sqcup \mathbb{N}$ (letters and indices) with nonterminals $S = 0$, $A = 1$, $B = 2$, start
symbol $S$, and the productions $S \to A$ and $S \to B$ together with, for every $i < m$, the
productions $A \to t_i\, A\, i$, $A \to t_i\, i$, $B \to b_i\, B\, i$ and $B \to b_i\, i$, in which
the index $i$ is a terminal.

articles.title: The canonical rule sequence along an index sequence
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a list of dominoes over
$\alpha$, let $\sigma$ assign a word over $\alpha$ to each domino, let $A$ be a natural number,
and for $i \in \mathbb{N}$ write $w_i$ for $\sigma$ applied to the $i$-th domino of $P$ (the domino
with both words empty when $i$ is past the end of $P$). For a sequence $i_1, \dots, i_n$ of
natural numbers, this is the list of productions, with terminals $\alpha \sqcup \mathbb{N}$ and
nonterminals $\mathbb{N}$, consisting of $A \to w_{i_k}\, A\, i_k$ for $k = 1, \dots, n - 1$ in
order, followed by $A \to w_{i_n}\, i_n$, where the letters of $w_{i_k}$ and the index $i_k$ are
terminals and $A$ is a nonterminal; the empty sequence gives the empty list.

articles.title: Leftmost derivations in the ambiguity grammar
articles.statement:
Let
$P = [(t_0, b_0), \dots, (t_{m-1}, b_{m-1})]$ be a list of dominoes, and let $S$, $A$, $B$ be the
nonterminals of the ambiguity grammar of $P$. Every leftmost derivation of a word $w$ from $S$ in
that grammar has one of two forms, for some nonempty sequence $i_1, \dots, i_n$ of indices less
than $m$: either it is $S \to A$ followed by the canonical rule sequence from $A$ for the words
$t_i$ along $i_1, \dots, i_n$, and $w = t_{i_1} \cdots t_{i_n}\, i_n \cdots i_1$; or it is
$S \to B$ followed by the canonical rule sequence from $B$ for the words $b_i$ along
$i_1, \dots, i_n$, and $w = b_{i_1} \cdots b_{i_n}\, i_n \cdots i_1$.

articles.title: The productions of $A$ and $B$ in the ambiguity grammar
articles.statement:
Let
$P = [(t_0, b_0), \dots, (t_{m-1}, b_{m-1})]$ be a list of dominoes, and let $A$, $B$ be the
nonterminals of the ambiguity grammar of $P$ for its top and bottom words. Every production of
that grammar with left-hand side $A$ is $A \to t_i\, A\, i$ or $A \to t_i\, i$ for some $i < m$,
and every production with left-hand side $B$ is $B \to b_i\, B\, i$ or $B \to b_i\, i$ for some
$i < m$.

articles.title: Leftmost derivations from $A$ and $B$ follow an index sequence
articles.statement:
Let
$P = [(t_0, b_0), \dots, (t_{m-1}, b_{m-1})]$ be a list of dominoes, let $A$, $B$ be the
nonterminals of the ambiguity grammar of $P$ for its top and bottom words, and let $u$, $v$ be
words of terminals. Every leftmost derivation of a word $w$ from the sentential form $u\,A\,v$ is
the canonical rule sequence from $A$ for the words $t_i$ along some nonempty sequence
$i_1, \dots, i_n$ of indices less than $m$, and
$w = u\, t_{i_1} \cdots t_{i_n}\, i_n \cdots i_1\, v$. Likewise, every leftmost derivation of $w$
from $u\,B\,v$ is the canonical rule sequence from $B$ for the words $b_i$ along such a sequence,
and $w = u\, b_{i_1} \cdots b_{i_n}\, i_n \cdots i_1\, v$.

articles.title: The ambiguity grammar of $P$ is ambiguous exactly when $P$ has a solution
articles.statement:
For every list
$P$ of dominoes, the ambiguity grammar of $P$ is ambiguous, that is, some word has two different
leftmost derivations from its start symbol, if and only if $P$ has a PCP solution.

articles.title: The leftmost derivation along an index sequence
articles.statement:
Let
$P = [(t_0, b_0), \dots, (t_{m-1}, b_{m-1})]$ be a list of dominoes, and let $A$, $B$ be the
nonterminals of the ambiguity grammar of $P$ for its top and bottom words. For every nonempty
sequence $i_1, \dots, i_n$ of indices less than $m$ and all words of terminals $u$, $v$, the
canonical rule sequence from $A$ for the words $t_i$ along $i_1, \dots, i_n$ is a leftmost
derivation of $u\, t_{i_1} \cdots t_{i_n}\, i_n \cdots i_1\, v$ from $u\,A\,v$, and the canonical
rule sequence from $B$ for the words $b_i$ along $i_1, \dots, i_n$ is a leftmost derivation of
$u\, b_{i_1} \cdots b_{i_n}\, i_n \cdots i_1\, v$ from $u\,B\,v$.

articles.title: Leftmost derivations from the start symbol along an index sequence
articles.statement:
Let
$P = [(t_0, b_0), \dots, (t_{m-1}, b_{m-1})]$ be a list of dominoes, and let $S$, $A$, $B$ be the
nonterminals of the ambiguity grammar of $P$. For every nonempty sequence $i_1, \dots, i_n$ of
indices less than $m$, the production $S \to A$ followed by the canonical rule sequence from $A$
for the words $t_i$ along $i_1, \dots, i_n$ is a leftmost derivation of
$t_{i_1} \cdots t_{i_n}\, i_n \cdots i_1$ from $S$, and the production $S \to B$ followed by the
canonical rule sequence from $B$ for the words $b_i$ along $i_1, \dots, i_n$ is a leftmost
derivation of $b_{i_1} \cdots b_{i_n}\, i_n \cdots i_1$ from $S$.

articles.title: PCP many-one reduces to ambiguity of context-free grammars
articles.statement:
For every alphabet $\alpha$
with a primitive recursive encoding by natural numbers and decidable equality, the Post
correspondence problem over $\alpha$ many-one reduces to ambiguity of encoded context-free
grammars over the terminals $\alpha \sqcup \mathbb{N}$: there is a computable function sending
each list $P$ of dominoes over $\alpha$ to such a grammar, which is ambiguous if and only if $P$
has a PCP solution.

articles.title: The ambiguity grammar is primitive recursive
articles.statement:
For every alphabet $\alpha$ with a
primitive recursive encoding by natural numbers, the map sending a list $P$ of dominoes over
$\alpha$ to the ambiguity grammar of $P$ is primitive recursive, where encoded grammars are
encoded as pairs of a start nonterminal and a list of productions.

articles.title: The start production $S \to A$
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $\alpha$ and a natural number $A$, this is
the production with terminals $\alpha \sqcup \mathbb{N}$ and nonterminals $\mathbb{N}$ whose
left-hand side is the nonterminal $S = 0$ and whose right-hand side is the single nonterminal $A$.

In the ambiguity grammar of a PCP instance it is used with $A = 1$ and $A = 2$.

articles.title: Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem
articles.statement:
A set $S$ of natural numbers is recursively
enumerable if and only if it is Diophantine, that is, there is a polynomial $p$ with integer
coefficients such that $n \in S$ exactly when $p(n, t_1, \dots, t_k) = 0$ for some natural numbers
$t_1, \dots, t_k$.

## Sources

- M. Davis, H. Putnam, J. Robinson, The decision problem for exponential Diophantine equations, Ann. of Math. 74 (1961); Y. Matiyasevich, Enumerable sets are Diophantine, Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR 191 (1970) 279–282; textbook in Matiyasevich, Hilbert's Tenth Problem

articles.title: The empty set is Diophantine
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi : A \to R$ be a ring homomorphism of commutative
rings, with $R$ nontrivial. For every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the empty subset of $R^k$ is Diophantine
over $R$ with coefficients from $A$ through $\varphi$.

It is cut out by the constant polynomial $1$.

articles.title: Diophantine subsets of a ring
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi : A \to R$ be a ring homomorphism of commutative
rings. A subset $S \subseteq R$ is Diophantine over $R$ with coefficients from $A$ through $\varphi$
when the set $\{(s) : s \in S\} \subseteq R^1$ of one-coordinate points with coordinate in $S$ is a
Diophantine subset of $R^1$ over $R$ with coefficients from $A$ through $\varphi$.

articles.title: The whole space is Diophantine
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi : A \to R$ be a ring homomorphism of
commutative rings. For every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the whole space $R^k$ is Diophantine over $R$ with
coefficients from $A$ through $\varphi$.

It is cut out by the empty set of polynomials, with no auxiliary variables.

articles.title: Diophantine sets
articles.statement:
Let $\varphi : A \to R$ be a ring homomorphism of commutative rings and
let $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Polynomials with coefficients in $A$ are evaluated at points with
coordinates in $R$ by first mapping their coefficients into $R$ by $\varphi$. A subset
$S \subseteq R^k$ is Diophantine over $R$ with coefficients from $A$ through $\varphi$ when there
are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a finite set $P$ of polynomials with coefficients in $A$ in the
variables $x_1, \dots, x_k, y_1, \dots, y_n$ such that for every $x \in R^k$, $x \in S$ if and
only if there is $y \in R^n$ with $p(x, y) = 0$ for all $p \in P$.

articles.title: The fenced machine halts on some padding of a word iff the machine halts on it
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be
a single-tape machine over a finite inhabited alphabet and $w$ a word over that alphabet. The
fenced machine of $M$ halts on the fenced input of $w$ with $i$ padding cells on the left and $j$
on the right for some $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$ if and only if $M$ halts on $w$.

A halting run of $M$ of $n$ steps stays within $n$ cells of its start, so it runs unchanged inside
the walls of the fenced input of $w$ with $n + 1$ padding cells on each side; conversely, the
fenced machine halts only by simulating a halting run of $M$.

articles.title: Emptiness of a linear bounded automaton on computable input slices is undecidable
articles.statement:
There
exist a finite inhabited alphabet $\Gamma$ with a primitive recursive encoding, a linear bounded
automaton $F$ over the fenced alphabet of $\Gamma$, and a primitive recursive map $e$ from codes of
partial recursive functions to words over $\Gamma$, such that the set of codes $c$ for which $F$
halts on none of the fenced inputs of $e(c)$, with $i$ padding cells on the left and $j$ on the
right for any $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, is neither computable nor recursively enumerable.

This is the code-free form of Sipser, Theorem 5.10. Take for $F$ the fenced machine of a
single-tape recognizer $R$ of the set of codes that halt on input $0$, and for $e(c)$ the input of
$c$ to $R$: then $F$ halts on no fenced input of $e(c)$ iff $c$ does not halt on $0$. The word
$e(c)$ does not see the paddings $i$ and $j$, so $F$ itself runs the computation within the space
they give.

Sipser's $E_{\mathrm{LBA}}$ is a language of machine descriptions, the LBAs with empty language;
without a type of codes for machines, this is the form available. Each slice, the set of fenced
inputs of $e(c)$ over all paddings, is regular because of its shape: a wall, any number of left
padding cells, the word $e(c)$, any number of right padding cells and a wall. Informally: with codes of machines, the LBA that checks that its input lies in the slice of $c$
and then runs $F$ has empty language iff $F$ halts on no input of the slice, and
$E_{\mathrm{LBA}}$ is undecidable by the same reduction.

articles.title: Fenced input
articles.statement:
For a word $w$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, the fenced
input of $w$ with $i$ padding cells on the left and $j$ on the right is the word over the fenced
alphabet of $\Sigma$ made of a wall, $i$ left padding cells, the letters of $w$ as symbols, $j$
right padding cells and a wall, in this order.

articles.title: A transition lifted to the fenced machine
articles.statement:
A transition of a single-tape machine $M$, made
of an optional symbol to write, an optional move and an optional next state, becomes the
transition of the fenced machine of $M$ that writes the symbol, or a right padding cell where $M$
writes a blank, makes the same move, and goes to the running state of the next state $q$ of $M$,
or halts where $M$ halts.

articles.title: The running transition of the fenced machine
articles.statement:
In the running state of a state $q$ of a
single-tape machine $M$, the fenced machine of $M$ acts on the cell under its head as follows: on a
symbol $a$ it makes the lifted transition of $M$ in state $q$ on $a$; on a left or right padding
cell it makes the lifted transition of $M$ in state $q$ on a blank; on a wall or a blank cell it
leaves the cell unchanged, does not move, and enters the trap.

articles.title: States of the fenced machine
articles.statement:
For a set of states $Q$, the states of the fenced machine are
two start states, a running state for each state $q \in Q$ of the simulated machine, and a trap
state.

articles.title: Fenced alphabet
articles.statement:
For an alphabet $\Sigma$, the tape alphabet of the fenced machine consists
of a symbol for each letter of $\Sigma$, two kinds of padding cells (left and right), which the
simulated machine reads as blanks, and the wall, which marks the ends of the input.

articles.title: The fenced machine
articles.statement:
For a single-tape machine $M$ over a finite inhabited alphabet $\Sigma$,
the fenced machine of $M$ is the single-tape machine over the fenced alphabet of $\Sigma$ whose
states are the states of the fenced machine for the states of $M$, which starts in the first start
state and acts on the cell under its head as follows. In the first start state, on a wall it moves
right into the second start state, and on any other cell it leaves the cell unchanged, does not
move and enters the trap. In the second start state, on a left padding cell it moves right and
stays in that state, and on any other cell it makes the running transition of the initial state of
$M$. In the running state of a state $q$ of $M$ it makes the running transition of $q$. In the
trap it leaves the cell unchanged, does not move and stays in the trap.

So on the fenced input of a word $w$ it moves right off the left wall and over the left padding,
then runs $M$ from its initial state, and enters the trap when it reads a wall or a blank cell. On
a blank cell, in every state, it writes a blank and does not move.

articles.title: The fenced machine halts on no padding of a word iff the machine does not halt on it
articles.statement:
Let
$M$ be a single-tape machine over a finite inhabited alphabet and $w$ a word over that alphabet.
The fenced machine of $M$ halts on none of the fenced inputs of $w$, with $i$ padding cells on the
left and $j$ on the right for $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, if and only if $M$ does not halt on $w$.

articles.title: Cells of a fenced input
articles.statement:
Let $w$ be a word of length $\ell$ and $i, j, n \in \mathbb{N}$.
The cell at position $n$, counting from $0$, of the fenced input of $w$ with $i$ left and $j$
right padding cells is the wall if $n = 0$; a left padding cell if $1 \le n \le i$; the letter of
$w$ at position $n - i - 1$, also counting from $0$, as a symbol, if $i < n \le i + \ell$; a right
padding cell if $i + \ell < n \le i + \ell + j$; the wall if $n = i + \ell + j + 1$; and there is
no cell at a larger position $n$.

articles.title: The fenced machine is a linear bounded automaton
articles.statement:
For every single-tape Turing machine
$M$, the fenced machine of $M$ is a linear bounded automaton.

On a blank cell, in every state, the fenced machine writes a blank and does not move.

articles.title: Length of a fenced input
articles.statement:
For a word $w$ of length $n$ and natural numbers $i$ and $j$,
the fenced input of $w$ with $i$ padding cells on the left and $j$ on the right has length
$i + n + j + 2$: the word, the two paddings and the two walls.

articles.title: A fenced cell of a write is never a wall
articles.statement:
For every cell $o$ of the simulated machine, a
symbol or a blank, the fenced cell of $o$ is not a wall.

articles.title: Fenced cell of a write
articles.statement:
For a cell $o$ of the simulated machine, a symbol or a blank,
the fenced cell of $o$ is the cell the fenced machine writes for a write of $o$: $o$ itself if
$o$ is a symbol, and the padding cell $\mathrm{pad}$ if $o$ is a blank.

articles.title: Reading back a copied cell
articles.statement:
Let $o$ be a cell of the simulated machine, a symbol or a
blank, and copy it to the fenced machine, a symbol as itself and a blank as a blank. Then the
simulated cell of the copy is $o$.

articles.title: Reading back a fenced cell of a write
articles.statement:
For every cell $o$ of the simulated machine, a
symbol or a blank, the simulated cell of the fenced cell of $o$ is $o$.

articles.title: Simulated cell of a fenced cell
articles.statement:
The simulated cell of a cell of the fenced machine is
the cell of the simulated machine that it stands for: a symbol of the simulated machine stands
for itself, and every other cell (a padding cell, a wall or a blank) stands for a blank.

articles.title: The continuation production
articles.statement:
For a list $P$ of dominoes, a map $\sigma$ assigning a word
over $\alpha$ to each domino, a nonterminal $A \in \mathbb{N}$ and an index $i \in \mathbb{N}$,
this is the production $A \to w_i\, A\, i$ in encoded form, where $w_i$ is $\sigma$ applied to the
$i$-th domino of $P$ (the domino with both words empty when $i$ is past the end of $P$): its
right-hand side is the letters of $w_i$ as terminals, then the nonterminal $A$, then the index
terminal $i$.

articles.title: The construction of derivations
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a list of dominoes, $\sigma$ a map assigning a
word over $\alpha$ to each domino, and $G$ the context-free grammar of the side grammar of $P$ for
$\sigma$, with start nonterminal $S$ and terminals $\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N}$ (letters and
indices). For every nonempty sequence $i_1, \dots, i_n$ of indices, each less than the length of
$P$, and all words $u, v$ over $\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N}$, $G$ derives the terminal word
$u\, w_{i_1} \cdots w_{i_n}\, i_n \cdots i_1\, v$ from the sentential form $u\, S\, v$, where
$w_i$ is $\sigma$ applied to the $i$-th domino of $P$.

articles.title: The $i$-th domino of a list
articles.statement:
For a list $P$ of dominoes and $i \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the
$i$-th domino of $P$ (counting from $0$) when $i$ is less than the length of $P$, and the domino
whose top and bottom words are both empty otherwise.

articles.title: A terminal word derives only itself
articles.statement:
Let $g$ be a context-free grammar with terminal
alphabet $\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N}$ and let $u$ be a word over $\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N}$. If $g$
derives a sentential form $v$ from $u$, read as a string of terminals, then $v = u$.

articles.title: Unique splitting of letters followed by markers
articles.statement:
Let $A, C$ be words over $\alpha$ and
$B, D$ words over $\beta$, all viewed as words over the disjoint union $\alpha \oplus \beta$. If
$AB = CD$ as words over $\alpha \oplus \beta$, then $A = C$ and $B = D$.

articles.title: Splitting a sentential form at its single nonterminal
articles.statement:
Let $N$ be a type of nonterminals,
$u, v$ words over $\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N}$, $A, B \in N$, and $p, q$ strings of terminals in
$\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N}$ and nonterminals in $N$. If $u\, A\, v = p\, B\, q$, where $u$ and $v$
are read as strings of terminals, then $p = u$, $B = A$ and $q = v$.

articles.title: The analysis of derivations
articles.statement:
Let $P$ be a list of dominoes, $\sigma$ a map assigning a word
over $\alpha$ to each domino, and $G$ the context-free grammar of the side grammar of $P$ for
$\sigma$, with start nonterminal $S$ and terminals $\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N}$ (letters and
indices). Let $u, v, x$ be words over $\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N}$. If $G$ derives the terminal word
$x$ from the sentential form $u\, S\, v$, then there is a nonempty sequence $i_1, \dots, i_n$ of
indices, each less than the length of $P$, such that
$x = u\, w_{i_1} \cdots w_{i_n}\, i_n \cdots i_1\, v$, where $w_i$ is $\sigma$ applied to the
$i$-th domino of $P$.

Such a derivation applies $S \to w_i\, S\, i$ for each index but the last and then
$S \to w_i\, i$.

articles.title: The letter part of an index sequence
articles.statement:
For a list $P$ of dominoes, a map $\sigma$ assigning
a word over $\alpha$ to each domino, and a sequence $i_1, \dots, i_n$ of natural numbers, this is
the word $w_{i_1} w_{i_2} \cdots w_{i_n}$ over $\alpha$, where $w_i$ is $\sigma$ applied to the
$i$-th domino of $P$ (the domino with both words empty when $i$ is past the end of $P$).

articles.title: The encoded index terminal
articles.statement:
For $i \in \mathbb{N}$, this is the index $i$ as an encoded
terminal over the alphabet $\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N}$: the element $\mathrm{inr}(\mathrm{inr}\, i)$
of $\mathbb{N} \oplus (\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N})$, whose left summand $\mathbb{N}$ holds the
nonterminals and whose right summand holds the terminals.

articles.title: The encoded letter terminal
articles.statement:
For a letter $a \in \alpha$, this is $a$ as an encoded
terminal over the alphabet $\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N}$: the element $\mathrm{inr}(\mathrm{inl}\, a)$
of $\mathbb{N} \oplus (\alpha \oplus \mathbb{N})$, whose left summand $\mathbb{N}$ holds the
nonterminals and whose right summand holds the terminals.

articles.title: PCP many-one reduces to nonemptiness of the intersection of two context-free languages
articles.statement:
**PCP many-one reduces to nonemptiness of the intersection of two context-free
languages.** Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with a primitive recursive encoding and decidable
equality. The Post correspondence problem over $\alpha$ is many-one reducible to the problem of
deciding, for a pair $(G_1, G_2)$ of encoded context-free grammars whose terminals are the letters
of $\alpha$ together with the natural numbers, whether some word lies in both the language of
$G_1$ and the language of $G_2$: there is a computable map sending each list $P$ of dominoes over
$\alpha$ to such a pair, with $P$ having a PCP solution if and only if the two languages share a
word.

articles.title: The language of a side grammar
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with decidable equality,
let $P = (d_0, \dots, d_{k-1})$ be a list of dominoes over $\alpha$, let $\sigma$ assign a word
over $\alpha$ to each domino, and write $w_i = \sigma(d_i)$. A word $u$ over the letters of
$\alpha$ and the index terminals $0, 1, 2, \dots$ lies in the language of the side grammar of
$\sigma$ and $P$ if and only if there is a nonempty sequence of indices $i_1, \dots, i_n$, each
less than $k$, with $u = w_{i_1} \cdots w_{i_n} \, i_n \cdots i_1$.

articles.title: Encoded nonterminal symbol
articles.statement:
For a natural number $A$, the nonterminal $A$ as a symbol of
the right-hand side of an encoded production over the terminals $\alpha \sqcup \mathbb{N}$: the
left injection of $A$ into $\mathbb{N} \sqcup (\alpha \sqcup \mathbb{N})$.

articles.title: A PCP instance is solvable exactly when its top and bottom grammars share a word
articles.statement:
Let
$P$ be a list of dominoes over an alphabet $\alpha$ with decidable equality. Then $P$ has a PCP
solution if and only if some word lies both in the language of the side grammar of $P$ for the
top words and in the language of the side grammar of $P$ for the bottom words.

articles.title: The side grammar of a PCP instance
articles.statement:
Let $P = (d_0, \dots, d_{k-1})$ be a list of dominoes
over $\alpha$, let $\sigma$ assign a word over $\alpha$ to each domino, and write
$w_i = \sigma(d_i)$. The side grammar of $\sigma$ and $P$ is the encoded context-free grammar
whose terminals are the letters of $\alpha$ and the index terminals $0, 1, 2, \dots$, whose start
nonterminal is $S = 0$, and whose productions are $S \to w_i \, S \, i$ and $S \to w_i \, i$ for
each $i < k$. Taking for $\sigma$ the top word of a domino gives the top grammar of $P$, and the
bottom word the bottom grammar.

articles.title: The productions of a side grammar
articles.statement:
Let $P = (d_0, \dots, d_{k-1})$ be a list of dominoes
over $\alpha$, let $\sigma$ assign a word over $\alpha$ to each domino, write $w_i = \sigma(d_i)$,
and let $A$ be a nonterminal. The side productions are the list of encoded productions
$A \to w_i \, A \, i$ and $A \to w_i \, i$ for $i = 0, 1, \dots, k - 1$, where the letters of
$w_i$ are terminals and $i$ is an index terminal.

articles.title: The side word of an index sequence
articles.statement:
Let $P = (d_0, \dots, d_{k-1})$ be a list of dominoes
over $\alpha$, set $d_i = (\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ for $i \ge k$, let $\sigma$ assign a word
over $\alpha$ to each domino, and write $w_i = \sigma(d_i)$. The side word of a sequence
$i_1, \dots, i_n$ of natural numbers is the word $w_{i_1} \cdots w_{i_n} \, i_n \cdots i_1$ over
the letters of $\alpha$ and the index terminals $0, 1, 2, \dots$: the letters of
$w_{i_1}, \dots, w_{i_n}$ followed by the indices in reverse order.

articles.title: The terminating production of a side grammar
articles.statement:
Let $P = (d_0, \dots, d_{k-1})$ be a list
of dominoes over $\alpha$, set $d_i = (\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ for $i \ge k$, let $\sigma$
assign a word over $\alpha$ to each domino, and write $w_i = \sigma(d_i)$. For a nonterminal $A$
and a natural number $i$, this is the encoded production $A \to w_i \, i$, whose right-hand side
is the letters of $w_i$ as terminals followed by the index terminal $i$.

articles.title: Bottom word of a domino sequence
articles.statement:
For a sequence $s = d_1, \dots, d_k$ of dominoes, the
bottom word of $s$ is the concatenation $b_1 b_2 \cdots b_k$, where $b_i$ is the bottom word of
$d_i$.

articles.title: The eight kinds of rules of the machine-simulating rewriting system
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a
single-tape Turing machine with a finite tape alphabet $\Gamma$, a default (blank) symbol
$\beta \in \Gamma$ and finitely many states. The symbols are the tape symbols, the states, the end
markers $\vdash$ and $\dashv$, and the halting symbol $H$. Every rule $l \to r$ of the rewriting
system simulating $M$ has one of the following eight forms, where $q, q'$ are states and
$a, b, c$ are tape symbols. Either $M$ has no transition in state $q$ reading $a$, and $l = q\,a$,
$r = H$; or in state $q$ reading $a$ the machine $M$ goes to state $q'$ and writes $b$, and
$l = q\,a$, $r = q'\,b$; or in state $q$ reading $a$ it goes to $q'$ and moves the head right, and
either $l = q\,a \dashv$, $r = a\,q'\,\beta \dashv$ or $l = q\,a\,c$, $r = a\,q'\,c$; or in state
$q$ reading $a$ it goes to $q'$ and moves the head left, and either $l = \vdash q\,a$,
$r = \vdash q'\,\beta\,a$ or $l = c\,q\,a$, $r = q'\,c\,a$; or $l = c\,H$, $r = H$; or $l = H\,c$,
$r = H$.

articles.title: PCP over a one-letter alphabet is decidable
articles.statement:
Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with at most one
letter whose elements have a computable encoding. Then the Post correspondence problem over
$\alpha$ is a computable predicate: some computable function decides, for every finite list $P$
of dominoes over $\alpha$, whether $P$ has a PCP solution.

articles.title: The rewrites from words with one control symbol are confluent
articles.statement:
Let $M$ be a single-tape
Turing machine with finitely many states and tape symbols, and call the states and the halting
